   requests for 20000 files — 0.01 per file — because it takes the file type from
   the readdir entry and never stats. The daemon can already enumerate a 20000
   entry directory for the price of ~41 batched readdir calls. This closes the
   readdir question for good: readdir is not a cost centre, it is nearly free, and
   any lever aimed there has nothing to win.

2. THE MINIMAL STAT COSTS 3.01 REQUESTS PER FILE. Statting by explicit name, with
   no readdir in the measured arm, still pays about one lookup, one getattr and
   one capability probe. That is the FLOOR for "give me this file's metadata" as
   the kernel currently asks it, and one of those three round trips — 33% — is a
   security.capability probe that always answers absent on these images.

3. `ls -l` COSTS 2.3x THE FLOOR: 7.00 requests per file against 3.01 for the same
   information, and 3.00 capability probes against 1.01. So roughly four of the
   seven requests per entry are attributable to HOW ls reaches each file rather
   than to the metadata itself. Two of those four are extra capability probes.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE LEVER, with the bound stated both ways:
Removing the capability probe entirely would cut round trips by 33% on the
minimal stat path (3.01 -> 2.01) and by 43% on `ls -l` (7.00 -> 4.00). That is
the size of the prize, and it is now a measured bound rather than an estimate.
Nothing else in the stat path is a comparable single target: lookup and getattr
are each ~1.00 per file and both carry information the caller actually asked for.

WHAT IS RULED OUT, cumulatively, all on counted evidence:
  * readdir batching — already batched, and enumeration is 0.01 requests/file.
  * readdirplus-style attr-with-entry — already negotiated; forcing it moved the
    count +0.1% in the wrong direction (4a5f4e07).
  * making the daemon answer faster — the daemon is 3.85% of wall, and the memo
    already drives dispatched probes to their 1.00/entry floor without changing
    the round-trip count at all.
The only shape left is stopping the kernel from asking.

CAVEATS. Single run per workload, no A/A null, no kernel arm — a counted
mechanism census, admissible on exact counts, NOT a ratio and not bankable under
the replicated-standing convention. ext4 image; warm stat is 4.812194x ext4 vs
4.977803x btrfs (3.4% apart), which is the standing evidence that this floor is
shared rather than btrfs-specific.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
WARM STAT IS ONE ROUND TRIP PER STAT, AND IT IS ENTIRELY THE CAPABILITY PROBE
(ProudBarn, 2026-08-16). Measurement only — no builds, per the disk directive.

Two workloads, 500 stat calls each, inside a SINGLE `stat` process so nothing but
the stat count scales. Local managed mount (local by necessity; no rch worker is
quotable), pre-existing ext4 fixture, memo slots pinned at 65536, ffs-cli
sha256 2faab3039bc3da4126df8b9197edb0f431467b0fc0dac2b3376d6a2bc0c14f12, v3+PGO,
built in place on thinkstation1. requests_total is the true FUSE boundary count
and includes memo-served probes (bd-0c4av).

  workload                    requests/stat   capability/stat
  same file, named 500 times          1.016             1.010
  500 distinct files                  3.012             1.008

TWO FINDINGS, AND THE SECOND IS THE IMPORTANT ONE.

1. THE KERNEL NEVER CACHES THE NEGATIVE ANSWER. Statting one file 500 times cost
   505 capability probes — 1.010 per stat, indistinguishable from the distinct
   case. There is no client-side negative cache to lengthen, extend or exploit.
   The kernel asks every single time, for the same inode, within milliseconds.

2. EVERYTHING ELSE IS ALREADY CACHED, SO ON WARM STAT THE PROBE IS THE WHOLE
   COST. The same-file arm cost 1.016 requests per stat against 3.012 for
   distinct files: lookup and getattr are served from the kernel's own caches
   (ATTR_TTL is 60s and is working), leaving the capability probe as 1.010 of
   1.016 requests — 99.4% of all FUSE traffic on a warm stat.

WHAT THIS SETTLES.

  * The warm-stat row (4.812194x ext4 / 4.977803x btrfs, 3.4% apart) is not a
    format-layer problem and not a caching problem. It is ONE FUSE round trip per
    stat, and that round trip exists solely to answer "no" to
    security.capability. That is also why the figure is nearly identical on both
    filesystems — nothing filesystem-specific is involved.
  * Attribute caching is DONE. A lever that caches attributes harder has nothing
    left to win: the kernel is already skipping lookup and getattr entirely on a
    repeat.
  * Removing the probe would cut warm-stat FUSE traffic by ~99%, and cold/distinct
    stat traffic by 33% (3.012 -> 2.012).

WHAT REMAINS, and it is narrow. Since the kernel will not cache a negative and
will not stop asking, the only remaining shapes are ones that change what the
kernel BELIEVES about the superblock rather than what the daemon answers:
  * a mount/SB-level declaration that no file carries security.* (the kernel's
    own SB_NOSEC-style shortcut), if FUSE exposes one;
  * a FUSE ABI capability that suppresses the probe per-connection WITHOUT
    disabling getxattr wholesale — ENOSYS does the latter and is closed by
    contract (bd-ha71t), as are FUSE_HANDLE_KILLPRIV V1 and V2, both measured
    inert.
If none of those exist on 6.17, the honest conclusion is that ~1 round trip per
warm stat is a FUSE protocol floor rather than a FrankenFS defect, and the row
should be re-scoped to say so rather than left open as if a lever were pending.

CAVEATS. Single run per workload, no A/A null, no kernel arm — counted mechanism,
admissible on exact counts, NOT a ratio. ext4 image.

A CORRECTION TO MY OWN FIRST ATTEMPT: an earlier version of this test reported
5.05 probes per stat for the repeated-file case. That harness re-entered the
mount and re-exec'd xargs once per repeat, so per-repeat overhead scaled with the
repeat count and swamped the 1-file arm. The numbers above come from a single
process per arm and are the ones to use.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
A FUSE ROUND TRIP COSTS 16-18 us HERE, AND CARRIES 0.4 us OF WORK
(ProudBarn, 2026-08-16). Measurement only — no builds, per the disk directive.

The thread has been counting round trips; this puts a price on one, so the prize
is computable rather than relative. Two arms with deliberately different request
mixes, 5000 stat calls each inside a single `stat` process. Local managed mount
(local by necessity; no rch worker is quotable), pre-existing ext4 fixture, memo
slots pinned at 65536, ffs-cli
sha256 2faab3039bc3da4126df8b9197edb0f431467b0fc0dac2b3376d6a2bc0c14f12, v3+PGO,
built in place on thinkstation1. requests_total is the true boundary count and
includes memo-served probes (bd-0c4av).

  arm    wall     requests            us/stat   us/ROUND TRIP
  warm   0.090s   5007  (1.001/stat)    18.00           17.97
  cold   0.240s  15005  (3.001/stat)    48.00           15.99

The two arms differ threefold in requests per stat and agree on the per-round-trip
cost within 12%. That agreement is the point: it is a property of the transport,
not of the workload.

THE RATIO THAT MATTERS. Daemon-side work inside a getxattr round trip was measured
at 382 ns. So each round trip costs 16-18 us to carry 0.4 us of work — an
overhead ratio of 42-47x. Optimising the daemon is optimising the 2%.

THE PRIZE, now in absolute units rather than percentages:
  * warm stat: 1.001 capability probes per stat at ~18 us = ~18 us/stat, which is
    100% of the 18.00 us/stat measured. Removing the probe removes essentially
    the entire warm-stat FUSE cost.
  * cold/distinct stat: ~16 us of 48.00 us/stat = 33%.

This also gives the campaign a conversion factor it did not have: any lever that
removes N round trips per operation is worth about 16-18 us per operation on this
box, and any lever that only makes the daemon faster is bounded by 0.4 us.

CAVEATS, stated because the number is attractive:
  * Wall includes the client's own stat syscall and loop overhead, so 16-18 us is
    the cost of a round trip AS SEEN BY AN APPLICATION, not the kernel's internal
    FUSE transit time. It is the right figure for sizing a lever and the wrong
    figure for blaming a specific kernel path.
  * Single run per arm, no A/A null, no kernel arm — counted mechanism plus wall,
    admissible on the counts, NOT a ratio and not bankable under the
    replicated-standing convention.
  * ext4 image, one box, one kernel (6.17).
  * The banked mounted warm-stat row implies ~10.65 us/stat for FrankenFS against
    this run's 18.00 us/stat. Different harness and different client, so the two
    are not comparable (bd-4w2mf); do not read the gap as a regression.

A FIGURE I DID NOT MEASURE: 13.9 us per round trip has been quoted back to me and
is not mine. My measurements are 15.99 and 17.97 us. Same order, different number
— recorded so the 13.9 does not acquire provenance it never had.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
A LEVER, MEASURED (ProudBarn, 2026-08-16). Measurement only - no builds, per the disk directive.

The thread had characterised the round trip but never priced its VARIANCE. A round trip carries
382 ns of daemon work and costs 12-21 us; that gap is wakeup + cache-migration cost, not compute,
and placement is a RUNTIME lever, so it is measurable with the existing ELF under the
no-new-builds constraint. Harness scripts/fuse_placement_sweep.sh sha256
fa96f6e976e6b91a7384c372b7b377913295462e0df3e7946e0fa20e19da4451. ELF, self-reported in process:
mount_bench_evidence,binary_sha256=2faab3039bc3da4126df8b9197edb0f431467b0fc0dac2b3376d6a2bc0c14f12
(release-perf; the same line says pgo_profile_sha256=none, so this ELF is NOT asserted to be PGO -
correcting my own earlier "v3+PGO" description of it). hostname=thinkstation1, executed_on=thinkstation1.
rch worker: NONE, a mount is local by necessity. Warm stat = one file named 20000 times = a near-pure
round-trip generator, so wall/stat IS round-trip cost.

  arm                          run1     run2   ns/stat (worst)   A/A null r1/r2
  same logical CPU  8/8       12.02u   12.08u        12083       1.0183x 1.0239x
  SMT sibling       8/40      15.20u   14.92u        14920       1.0235x 1.0049x
  same CCD          8/12      15.67u   14.29u        14290       1.1331x 1.0522x
  cross CCD         8/30      19.73u   18.52u        18520       1.0946x 1.0121x
  unpinned                    21.26u   16.86u            -       1.4875x 1.0399x  <-- null FAILS

THE CONTROL THAT MAKES THIS A TRANSPORT RESULT. requests_total = 100029 for 100000 stats =
1.000/stat in EVERY arm of BOTH runs. The lever changes NO work: identical request counts,
identical daemon path, one ELF. The whole difference is the client/daemon boundary crossing.
Monotone in locality (same < smt ~ ccd < xccd < unpin), which is what a wakeup-cost story predicts.

WORST BOUND, per the replicated-standing convention: >= 1.2210x vs SMT-sibling and >= 1.4979x vs
cross-CCD. Seeded 20,000-resample paired bootstrap median CI, both runs: same-vs-smt
1.2642x [1.2452,1.2873] and 1.2349x [1.2210,1.2538]; same-vs-ccd 1.3035x [1.1811,1.3505] and
1.1827x [1.1280,1.2088]; same-vs-xccd 1.6415x [1.5584,1.7140] and 1.5324x [1.4979,1.5798]. All
three replicate with OVERLAPPING intervals. Drift guard: arm order run forward then reversed.

A RESULT I AM REFUSING, stated rather than buried. The first headline this sweep produced was
1.7687x for co-located vs UNPINNED. It is INADMISSIBLE: the unpinned arm's own A/A null is 1.4875x
on run 1 and its cross-run median moved 21.26 -> 16.86 us. Any ratio against an unpinned baseline
is mostly that baseline's own instability. The fleet null clause excuses a failing null only when
two runs agree AND both nulls are off the same way by a similar amount; the same/smt pair satisfies
that, the unpin pair does not.

INTEGRITY CONSEQUENCE, and it is the wider finding: an unpinned mounted measurement on this box is
not a stable instrument at all - 48% swing within one run, 26% between runs. Any banked mounted row
taken without daemon pinning inherits that. This is the same class of defect as bd-4w2mf and should
be treated as one.

SCOPE RULE. Co-location is a LATENCY lever for a SINGLE-CLIENT metadata workload, where client and
daemon strictly alternate so a shared L1 and no IPI are pure gain. Forcing both onto one logical CPU
would SERIALISE a concurrent workload. Same shared-vs-exclusive scope shape as FFS_FUSE_WORKERS.
Not defaulted on; no production source changed.

TWO HYPOTHESES CLOSED THIS TURN, so nobody re-runs them:
 1. CALLER PRIVILEGE does not matter. Root pays the probe too: 1.087 capability probes/stat as uid 0
    vs 1.243 as uid 1000 over 2000 distinct-file stats on an --allow-other mount. Neither collapses
    toward zero. (Recorded because "a fifth null on caller privilege" was attributed to me; I had no
    such result before this run, and now the answer is negative.)
 2. THE PROBE IS KERNEL-ORIGINATED, not a client artifact. strace of stat -c %s across the mount
    shows ZERO getxattr/lgetxattr/fgetxattr syscalls from the client - only statx - while the daemon
    logs security_capability probes for the same operation. So the probe cannot be removed by
    changing the client, and the "kernel never caches the negative" finding is about the kernel.

STILL NOT MINE: 13.9 us per round trip has been quoted back to me repeatedly and is not my figure.
My measurements are 12.02, 12.08, 14.92, 15.20, 15.67, 16.86, 18.52, 19.73 and 21.26 us depending
entirely on placement - which is itself the finding: there is no single round-trip number.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
SCOPE MEASURED, AND IT NARROWS MY OWN BANKED ROW (ProudBarn, 2026-08-16).

I published "co-location is a latency lever for single-client metadata work and would SERIALISE a
concurrent workload" as a CAVEAT. A caveat that is asserted rather than measured is not evidence,
so I ran both falsification tests. Warm reps only, n=8/arm pooled over two runs, seeded
20,000-resample paired bootstrap median CI. Harness scripts/fuse_placement_workload_sweep.sh.
ELF binary_sha256=2faab3039bc3da4126df8b9197edb0f431467b0fc0dac2b3376d6a2bc0c14f12,
hostname=thinkstation1, executed_on=thinkstation1, both runs same-host.

  workload                        vs SMT-sibling                vs cross-CCD
  readdir+stat, 1 client   1.0462x [0.9267, 1.3834] NULL   1.2608x [1.1064, 1.6063]
  stat, 4 concurrent       0.3485x [0.3002, 0.3846]        0.3998x [0.3307, 0.5412]
                           (distributions fully DISJOINT in both concurrency comparisons)

  absolute medians: readdir+stat  same 326.1 / smt 341.2 / xccd 411.2 ms
                    4-client      same 129.3 / smt  45.1 / xccd  51.7 ms

TWO CONCLUSIONS, one of which costs me the general form of my own lever:
 1. The warm-stat win does NOT transfer. Against SMT-sibling placement, readdir+stat shows
    NOTHING - the interval contains 1.0. Warm stat is a near-pure round-trip generator at
    1.000 requests/stat; readdir+stat is ~7 mixed requests/entry, and the co-location advantage
    disappears in that mix. What survives is a weaker and more useful statement: cross-CCD is
    the thing to AVOID (1.2608x, interval excludes 1.0). That is a lever about not landing on
    the far CCD, not about piling the client onto the daemon.
 2. Under 4 concurrent clients co-location is actively HARMFUL: >= 2.4988x SLOWER, worst bound,
    with fully disjoint per-rep distributions. The scope rule is confirmed, and the magnitude of
    the harm EXCEEDS the size of the win it qualifies.

PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE: the mounted comparator runs multiple client threads, so co-location must
NOT be applied there - it would manufacture a large artefactual loss. The banked bd-4ypbv row has
been amended in docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md to point at this one and to read warm-stat-only.

AN INSTRUMENT DEFECT THAT INVALIDATED MY OWN FIRST PASS, recorded because it nearly banked a
false win. The first timed rep after every mount is COLD and runs 2-3x the warm reps; with 4
mounts per arm that put 4 cold values into each 12-rep arm. It did not merely add noise - it
produced a spurious 1.5630x readdir+stat "win" on run 1 that SIGN-FLIPPED to 0.9013x on run 2,
and it inflated the bootstrap interval on the concurrency effect to [0.67, 7.98] when the raw
distributions are in fact fully disjoint. Discarding rep 1 of each mount resolves both. The
harness now records a rep index and excludes rep 1. Anyone reusing a mount-per-arm design in this
campaign should assume the same defect until they have checked for it.

A second harness defect fixed while running this: a bare `wait` also waits on the mount daemon
that the script itself backgrounds, which deadlocks the sweep permanently (observed: one run hung
~13 minutes with 3 of 36 rows written). It now waits on client pids only.

WHAT IS UNCHANGED: the banked warm-stat row itself. Its arms were tight (co-located min/max
11.86-12.17 us over 5 reps/mount) because a repeated single-file stat warms in the first
microseconds, so the cold-rep artefact does not reach it. The >= 1.2210x figure stands, now
explicitly scoped to warm stat.

title: Harden repair ownership sequence exhaustion
description: Fresh-eyes audit found RepairOwnership::try_acquire increments persisted repair_generation and lease_version with unchecked arithmetic during expired/current-record takeover. At u64::MAX this can panic in debug or wrap in release, breaking monotonic ownership semantics. Fix with checked failure and regression coverage.

title: meas(fuse): time the WHOLE request, not just the ops call — 59-99% of daemon CPU is outside dispatch and unattributed
description:
THE DAEMON HAS NO TIMER AROUND A WHOLE REQUEST — only around the innermost ops call, and
that blind spot is now measured at 59-99% of its own CPU.

MEASURED (bd-btrfs-readdir-stat-8x-8y7vp, 2026-08-16, commit dcb5301d), daemon pinned,
affinity observed, K=1 vs K=5 sweep differencing, 32,768 entries, 8 client threads:

  4096 slots   daemon CPU 6790.2 ns/entry | dispatched 2768.5 (40.8%) | outside 4021.7 (59.2%)
  65536 slots  daemon CPU 4425.0 ns/entry | dispatched   55.2 ( 1.2%) | outside 4369.8 (98.8%)

With the capability memo sized to the directory the daemon still burns 4425 ns/entry, and
98.8% of that is invisible to getattr/getxattr/lookup/readdir_dispatch_nanos. Those
counters bracket `self.inner.ops.<op>(...)`; everything else in the request — FUSE header
decode, argument parse, the memo lookup itself, reply encode, the write back to /dev/fuse,
and whatever queueing sits around them — is unattributed.

WHY THIS MATTERS. Four hypotheses for the readdir+stat residual have been eliminated or
retracted (contention, counter-undercount-alone, memo bookkeeping, instrument placement).
This is where the remaining time actually is, and no existing counter can decompose it. It
is also the floor that sizing the memo REVEALS rather than removes: 1.53x of daemon CPU
comes off when the memo fits, and what is left is protocol handling.

WHAT TO BUILD: a per-request timer around the WHOLE handler, not around the ops call, with
enough breakdown to separate at least (a) decode+parse, (b) the cache/memo lookups that
answer without dispatching, (c) the ops dispatch already counted, and (d) reply encode +
write. Emit it on the same mount_dispatch_metrics line so the comparator and the managed
runtime both carry it.

ACCEPTANCE:
  - the sum of the new buckets reconciles with the daemon's own utime+stime to within the
    tick resolution (+/-76 ns/entry at 4 sweeps x 32,768 entries), because a decomposition
    that does not add up to the process's own CPU is not a decomposition
  - measured at BOTH memo sizes, since the 4096 case is 40.8% dispatch and the 65,536 case
    is 1.2%, and a timer that only makes sense in one regime is not the timer
  - daemon pinned with observed affinity reported (bd-plt79), and no figure divided by any
    number from a different client (that mixed-instrument error has now been made twice in
    this campaign and caught twice)

DO NOT start by optimising anything. This bead is an instrument, and the thing it measures
has already had four wrong explanations; the point is to stop guessing at it.

METHOD NOTE for whoever takes it: /proc/<pid>/schedstat covers only the MAIN thread and
will silently report almost nothing for this daemon, which runs a worker pool. Use
utime+stime from /proc/<pid>/stat, which is process-wide and includes exited threads.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
DESIGN WRITTEN AND WITHDRAWN UNDER THE BUILD FREEZE — with the cost that makes it a bigger bead than it looks (AzureBay, 2026-08-16).

I implemented this instrument, could not compile it before /data hit its 58G floor and the build freeze landed, and then found by inspection that it would NOT have compiled. Patch preserved at scratchpad/bd-4zokj-handler-timer.patch (234 lines); working tree restored by reverse-applying it, so no peer inherits a broken build.

WHAT THE DESIGN IS, and it is still the right shape:
  - two counters on AtomicMetrics: handler_total_nanos + handler_total_count, one aggregate
    across the four metadata opcodes rather than per-opcode, because the question is
    "handler minus dispatch" and the four dispatch counters already exist to subtract.
  - an RAII HandlerTimer recorded on Drop, NOT an explicit call at the end. That is
    load-bearing: these handlers return early on several paths — unparseable name, memo
    hit, error reply — and the memo hit is exactly the path whose cost the dispatch
    counters miss. A timer that skipped early returns would reproduce the blind spot it
    was built to measure.
  - guards in getxattr, getattr, lookup, readdir; the totals emitted on the existing
    mount_dispatch_metrics line so the comparator and the managed runtime both carry them.
  - a test asserting handler_total_nanos >= the sum of dispatch nanos, and that a request
    which dispatches NOTHING still increments handler_total_count while leaving every
    dispatch counter alone.

WHY IT DOES NOT COMPILE, and this is the part worth inheriting: adding the two fields to
the PUBLIC MetricsSnapshot breaks every literal constructor of it. There are 58 in the
workspace and only ONE uses struct-update syntax; MetricsSnapshot has no Default derive.
So the additive-looking change is a ~57-site edit across crates. That is the struct-field
trap this campaign has been bitten by before, and it turns a small instrument into a
medium refactor.

TWO WAYS OUT for whoever takes it after the freeze:
  1. Add #[derive(Default)] to MetricsSnapshot and convert the exhaustive constructors to
     ..Default::default(). Larger diff, but it makes every FUTURE counter a one-line
     change instead of a 57-site one — and this is the third counter added to this struct
     in the campaign.
  2. Keep the two counters on AtomicMetrics only and expose them through a dedicated
     accessor, leaving MetricsSnapshot untouched. Smaller diff, but the CLI emit path
     receives a &MetricsSnapshot, so it needs a second argument threaded to it.
Option 1 is better if anyone expects to add another counter; option 2 lands faster.

A SECOND HAZARD I FIXED IN THE PATCH BUT COULD NOT VERIFY: HandlerTimer initially borrowed
&self.inner.metrics for the whole handler body. The handlers take &mut self, so that
borrow may well conflict on any path that touches self mutably. The safer form is to hold
an owned Arc<AtomicMetrics> clone in the guard, which removes the borrow entirely at the
cost of one refcount bump per request. Whoever compiles this should expect to need that.

NOT CLAIMED: none of this was compiled, tested or measured. The bead's acceptance is
unchanged and none of it is met.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
bd-4zokj UNBLOCKED AND WRITTEN — the whole-request timer is applied to the tree, awaiting a compile slot (AzureBay, 2026-08-16).

WHAT WAS BLOCKING IT AND WHAT REMOVED THE BLOCK. This bead was parked because adding a field to MetricsSnapshot broke every literal constructor of it, and the count of those sites was the thing I got wrong twice (58 -> 17 -> 10, a grep matching sibling types). The patch was preserved rather than landed. Commit 7da2a8b8 derived Default on MetricsSnapshot, which makes adding a counter a one-line change instead of a ten-site edit, and that is what let the preserved patch be applied by hand today against a tree that had moved under it.

THE MECHANISM. HandlerTimer is an RAII guard taken at the top of getattr, lookup, readdir and getxattr, recording into handler_total_nanos / handler_total_count on drop. RAII rather than a call at the end of each handler is load-bearing, not stylistic: these handlers return early on several paths — an unparseable name, an error reply, and above all a capability-memo hit — and the memo hit is precisely the path the dispatch counters cannot see. A timer that missed early returns would be blind to the exact thing it was built to measure, so the guard has to be the kind that cannot be forgotten on one branch.

WHY IT IS WORTH A COUNTER AT ALL. The *_dispatch_nanos counters bracket only the inner self.inner.ops.<op>(..) call. Header decode, argument parse, the memo and cache lookups that answer WITHOUT dispatching, and reply encode all sit outside them. That blind spot was measured at 59.2% of the daemon's own CPU at the shipping memo size and 98.8% once the memo fits — so the dispatch counters were accounting for a shrinking minority of the work while presenting as a decomposition.

THE TEST STATES THE INVARIANT THE LEDGER RELIES ON. handler_total_nanos must BOUND the sum of dispatch nanos, because the ledger's subtraction (handler minus dispatch = what dispatch cannot see) is only meaningful if it is non-negative. The test also pins the case that decides whether the counter earns its keep: a request that dispatches NOTHING must still record handler time, and must NOT move any dispatch counter. That is the memo-hit shape.

STATUS: applied to the tree, NOT yet compiled. One rch build slot is mine and it is currently queued behind a saturated fleet running an ffs-core test; the ffs-fuse compile follows it, sequentially, one build at a time per pane. Nothing is committed until the build is green — a diff that looks right is not a build that passes, which this repo has already paid for once.

title: NUMA-aware allocation placement for large-host swarm workloads
description:
Idea-wizard Phase 2-6 output after source-aware tracker truth reported zero claimable rows and RCH capacity remained blocked.

Phase 2 generated and winnowed improvement themes for 64+ core / 256GB+ agent-swarm responsiveness: capacity-aware claimability, runtime console, NUMA-aware allocation placement, cache/controller calibration, topology-advisor calibration, p99 trace replay, per-core fairness regression coverage, adaptive memory-pressure control, proof-ledger integration, and permissioned campaign automation. Existing open or closed work already covers capacity-aware claimability (`bd-16yn8`, `bd-k2ann`, `bd-vgnew`), runtime console (`bd-wtyxs`), cache-controller contracts, topology runtime advisor, readiness-lab NUMA/p99 replay, and the permissioned large-host campaign (`bd-rchk0.53.8`).

Best non-duplicative Phase 5 target: turn the deferred README V1.x `NUMA-aware allocator` row into an implementation-quality bead graph. Current allocator placement in `crates/ffs-alloc/src/lib.rs` exposes `AllocHint { goal_group, goal_block }` and scans nearby block groups around that goal; it has no topology-to-block-group model, no optional NUMA node preference, and no connection from existing topology/p99 evidence into allocation decisions. README line 2631 says the advisory NUMA p99 ledger exists but the allocator hook is deferred.

Goal: add a conservative, opt-in NUMA-aware allocation placement path that can improve large-host swarm locality without changing ext4/btrfs compatibility semantics or making public readiness claims before permissioned evidence exists.

- Do not claim performance improvement from replay fixtures or local smoke.

Phase 6 refinement requirement: every child must include unit tests, E2E/logging where practical, fail-closed claim effects, and explicit RCH validation.

title: ffs-fuzz: stamp/verify roundtrip missing group_desc checksum coverage
description:
Finding (via /testing-fuzzing skill, fifth visit, different target):
fuzz/fuzz_targets/fuzz_ext4_stamp_verify_roundtrip.rs (bd-nkfga +
bd-7x87u) covers four ext4 stamp/verify pairs (dir_block,
extent_block, block_bitmap, inode_bitmap) but MISSES the FIFTH:

  * stamp_group_desc_checksum / verify_group_desc_checksum
    (crates/ffs-ondisk/src/ext4.rs:1823, :1858)

This is the most operationally-critical pair: the group descriptor
table is read on every block-group lookup, and a regression in the
stamp/verify symmetry would silently make every newly-mutated
descriptor fail verification. Existing fixed-input test
`stamp_group_desc_checksum_matches_verify` covers ONE case;
libfuzzer scale catches off-by-one drift across the full input
space (UUID × csum_seed × group_number × desc_size in {32, 64} ×
checksum_kind in {MetadataCsum, GdtCsum}).

Also: `stamp_group_desc_checksum` and `Ext4GroupDescChecksumKind`
are NOT in crates/ffs-ondisk/src/lib.rs's `pub use` re-export block
(verify_group_desc_checksum IS). Same kind of re-export gap that
bd-nkfga / bd-7x87u uncovered for the bitmap functions.

Acceptance: extend fuzz_ext4_stamp_verify_roundtrip.rs with MR-5
covering group_desc stamp/verify across both MetadataCsum and
GdtCsum variants and both desc_size paths (32 + 64). Also
re-export the two missing symbols so the fuzz target can import
them. Verify build via
`rch exec -- cd fuzz && cargo check --bin fuzz_ext4_stamp_verify_roundtrip`.
notes: Shipped: extended fuzz/fuzz_targets/fuzz_ext4_stamp_verify_roundtrip.rs with MR-5 covering group_desc stamp/verify round-trip across both Ext4GroupDescChecksumKind variants (MetadataCsum CRC32C + GdtCsum CRC16) and both desc_size paths (32 + 64). Pulls UUID + group_number + csum_seed + kind selector from cursor stream so libfuzzer drives the configuration space separately from MR-1..4. Also added stamp_group_desc_checksum + Ext4GroupDescChecksumKind to the crates/ffs-ondisk/src/lib.rs pub-use re-export block (same gap as bd-nkfga's earlier missing re-exports). Verified via rch exec -- cd fuzz && cargo check --bin fuzz_ext4_stamp_verify_roundtrip (Finished in 44.49s). Five MRs now: dir_block + extent_block + block_bitmap + inode_bitmap + group_desc — full stamp/verify coverage across all five ext4 metadata-checksum families.

comments.text: REJECT (BlackThrush, measured A/B + A/A control) — array-ref reslice of the 8-byte dir-entry header in ffs-ondisk walk_dir_block_entries does NOT transfer the ffs-dir 1.56x win; it REGRESSES ~19%. Hypothesis: the loop guard 'offset+8<=block.len()' proves the header in-bounds, so replacing the 4 separate checked reads (read_le_u32@off, read_le_u16@off+4, ensure_slice@off+6/+7) with one 'block[off..off+8].try_into::<[u8;8]>()' + const-index extraction would drop 3 redundant bounds checks (ffs-dir's linear scan measured 1.56x from exactly this). MEASURED opposite (ffs-ondisk lookup_leaf_scan miss_full_leaf, 204-entry full-leaf miss, release-perf LTO=off, criterion 100 samples, SAME worker): baseline [486.92 495.22 503.27]ns; candidate array-ref [580.93 589.48 598.56]ns = change [+19.4% +22.5% +26.3%] p=0.00 REGRESSED; A/A CONTROL (reverted baseline re-run) [486.55 496.05 506.36]ns = 0.2% off the first baseline → worker variance is LOW, the regression is REAL not noise. WHY: read_le_u32/read_le_u16/ensure_slice are already #[inline] + the guard already elides their bounds checks (unlike ffs-dir's context), so try_into only ADDS its TryFromSliceError branch + a less-optimizable array-ref construct. REVERTED (working tree exact-restored, no diff). ⭐ LESSON: the 'array-ref reslice beats N checked reads' lever is CONTEXT-DEPENDENT — it wins only where the compiler can't already elide the N checks; in ffs-ondisk's walk it can, so the reslice regresses. title: ffs-ondisk: dx_hash proptests miss EOF-sentinel, legacy-seed-independence, and ASCII signed/unsigned equivalence MRs
description:
Finding (via /testing-metamorphic skill, second visit, different
target): the existing dx_hash proptests
(crates/ffs-ondisk/src/ext4.rs:10843-10874) cover three relations:

  1. determinism — same inputs → same outputs
  2. major-hash low-bit-clear (ext4 reservation)
  3. no-panic on arbitrary inputs

Three additional metamorphic relations are NOT exercised by the
proptest suite, even though each is a documented kernel contract:

  MR-A — EOF-sentinel avoidance:
    `normalize_dx_major_hash` (l. 4737-4744) explicitly remaps
    `(EXT4_HTREE_EOF_32BIT << 1)` to `(EXT4_HTREE_EOF_32BIT - 1) << 1`
    because ext4 reserves that value as the htree-end-of-iteration
    sentinel. A regression that drops or weakens this remap would
    silently corrupt directory iteration on collision. NO PROPTEST.

  MR-B — Legacy hash seed independence:
    `dx_hash_legacy` (l. 4757) does NOT take the seed parameter; the
    DX_HASH_LEGACY and DX_HASH_LEGACY_UNSIGNED variants use a hardcoded
    initial state. A regression that accidentally threads the seed
    into the legacy path would make our htree reads diverge from
    kernel-mounted images. NO PROPTEST.

  MR-C — ASCII signed/unsigned equivalence:
    The signed/unsigned distinction only changes the byte
    reinterpretation for bytes >= 128. For ASCII-only names (every
    byte < 128), signed and unsigned variants of dx_hash_legacy and
    dx_hash_half_md4 must produce the same major+minor hash. NO
    PROPTEST. The existing fixed-input test
    `dx_hash_signed_vs_unsigned` (l. 8386) only checks the
    DIFFERENCE for a non-ASCII name; ASCII equivalence is not pinned.

Acceptance: 3 new proptests in the existing proptest! block
covering MR-A, MR-B, MR-C with PROPTEST_CASES sufficient to
exercise the input space (the existing block uses
ProptestConfig::with_cases(32) which is enough). All 3 MRs use the
same proptest-prelude imports already in scope.
notes: Shipped: 3 new dx_hash proptest MRs in crates/ffs-ondisk/src/ext4.rs. MR-A (EOF sentinel avoidance) pins normalize_dx_major_hash's reservation against EXT4_HTREE_EOF_32BIT << 1; MR-B (legacy seed independence) pins that DX_HASH_LEGACY/DX_HASH_LEGACY_UNSIGNED ignore the seed parameter; MR-C (ASCII signed/unsigned equivalence) pins that for bytes < 128, signed and unsigned variants of legacy/half-md4/tea produce identical major+minor hashes. All 14 dx_hash tests pass via rch exec -- cargo test -p ffs-ondisk --lib dx_hash.

title: ext4 write/truncate proptest diverges from reference model (real images)
description: ffs-core test ext4_write_truncate_random_matches_reference_model FAILS deterministically on a saved proptest-regressions seed (crates/ffs-core/proptest-regressions/lib.txt, generated 2026-06-05 03:13 prior session). Minimal failing ops = [(0,25316,15645,0),(0,8192,1,0),(1,2207,4948,69),(0,47012,9253,62),(1,48477,15962,238),(0,27082,12422,238)] (tuple = (kind,offset,len,byte); kind 0=write,1=truncate). Panic crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs:59662 assert_eq vs ext4 reference model. PRE-EXISTING + INDEPENDENT of btrfs name-hash fix 5ee614c5 (ext4 write/truncate path). Corruption-class divergence: ext4 write+truncate state differs from reference model for this interleaving. Repro: rch exec -- cargo test -p ffs-core --lib ext4_write_truncate_random_matches_reference_model. Found by AmberOtter running full ffs-core suite for the bd-x36qn commit.
close_reason: Fixed in fcb3c6dd (AmberOtter). Root cause: ext4 extent cache namespaced by mutable extent_root_namespace(inode)=FNV(i_block) → namespace drifts as the extent tree mutates → narrow invalidate_range under the post-truncate namespace can't reach mappings cached under an earlier namespace; truncate then frees blocks that recycle into other logical offsets and a read serves the recycled block's stale bytes. Fix: truncate-down now invalidate_all (generation bump) — the one free path still using the narrow invalidate; can only over-invalidate, never serve stale. Proven: clearing the extent cache before each read made the divergence vanish; deterministic regression test added (ext4_write_truncate_bd_5911f_stale_extent_cache); proptest green ×3 fresh runs; ffs-core lib 944/0.

title: perf(mvcc): cache latest real (decompressed) block data across a commit's dedup checks
description: CANDIDATE (needs verification + ratio measurement; surfaced by cc W144 Phase-B Explore). commit_fcw_internal (ffs-mvcc lib.rs ~2605) and commit_ssi_internal (~2740) call is_identical_to_latest (2652) per staged block; that resolves the latest version's bytes, walking back through the version chain and DECOMPRESSING (zstd/brotli) to find the nearest real (Full/Zstd/Brotli) version behind any Identical markers. For a multi-block commit with long chains + many Identical markers + compressed storage (dedup_identical default true, chain_cap 64), this re-decompresses per block. POSSIBLE lever: memoize the latest real decompressed data per block during a commit, OR store a dedup fingerprint (hash) in version metadata to avoid full-byte compare + decompress. CAVEATS: (1) VERIFY the redundancy is real — resolve may decompress ONCE per resolve (nearest real version), not M-per-chain, so the O(N*M*D) claim needs confirming against the actual resolve_data_with impl. (2) Measure the REAL ratio — only a win if Identical+compressed chains are common (may be sub-2.0 for typical workloads). (3) OWNERSHIP: ffs-mvcc commit path is actively owned by the bd-xmh5g epic agent (bd-xmh5g.173/.170, bd-6tooy, bd-csfbv recent) — coordinate / leave to that owner; cc did NOT take it to avoid colliding with active work.
close_reason: Verified NOT a real lever (cc W145). Read resolve_data_with (compression.rs:77): it walks back through Identical markers (which hold NO data) and decompresses ONLY the final real version ONCE per resolve — no O(chain*decompress) redundancy. is_identical_to_latest resolves each block's latest once per commit (distinct blocks). The only cross-callsite redundancy (dedup-check resolve + SSI merge-base resolve both decompress the latest) is ~2x on a small fraction of commit cost = sub-2.0 e2e. Not worth the contended-crate risk.

title: btrfs data corruption: whole-file overwrite after partial-overwrite churn reads back as all-zeros
description: FOUND via a metamorphic round-trip test (btrfs_write_multi_extent_overwrite_matches_reference_model). After a sequence of partial overwrites that fragment a file's extents (each partial overwrite trims an existing regular extent and re-inserts head/tail segments via btrfs_insert_regular_extent_segment, churning the data allocator), a subsequent WHOLE-FILE overwrite (offset 0, len == file size) reports success (written==len, EXTENT_DATA insert ok, inode size correct) but the entire file reads back as ALL ZEROS. Reproducer (4096-byte blocks, btrfs default, open_writable_btrfs): writes [(0,16384),(32768,16384),(65536,16384),(8192,61440),(0,4096),(1234,100),(79000,5000),(40000,8000),(4096,71000),(0,84000),(50,83950)] each filled with a distinct byte; the model diverges at write #10 (0,84000) with ndiff=84000 (every byte 0x00 vs wanted 0xAA). CONTROLS THAT PASS (so NOT an MVCC-flush test artifact and NOT a simple large-write bug): the same test with just [(0,84000),(0,84000)] passes; [(0,16384),(32768,16384),(65536,16384),(0,84000)] passes; [(0,84000),(8192,61440),(0,84000)] passes. So the corruption requires accumulated partial-overwrite churn before the full overwrite. SYMPTOM PATH: btrfs_materialize_extent returns an all-zero buffer when the extent's disk_bytenr==0 or extent_type==PREALLOC (lib.rs ~15555) — consistent with the new full-overwrite extent ending up with a bogus/zero disk mapping under allocator fragmentation, OR the data allocator (BtrfsAllocState.extent_alloc.alloc_data) returning a region whose contents read back as zero after the free/realloc churn (possible block reuse / MVCC versioning issue: btrfs_write_logical writes via the MVCC block-device adapter; read via btrfs_read_logical_into). NEXT: instrument btrfs_write to log disk_bytenr + an immediate read-back of the freshly written region at write #10; check whether alloc_data returns a region overlapping a still-live extent or whether the written bytes are lost by the MVCC overlay on a reused physical block. Regression reproducer landed as an #[ignore]d test referencing this bead.
notes: FIXED (allocator bytenr-0 fence). ROOT CAUSE confirmed by instrumentation: write #10 (the whole-file overwrite) first freed every data extent of the fragmented file (extent-tree range scan saw an EMPTY range set), so BtrfsExtentAllocator::alloc_extent's wrap-around path reset its cursor to bg_start==0 and returned found_bytenr=0. A btrfs file extent with disk_bytenr==0 is the hole/none sentinel, so btrfs_materialize_extent returned an all-zero buffer → the whole file read back as zeros despite a successful write. FIX (ffs-btrfs): BlockGroupState now records min_usable_offset (= used_bytes at registration, fencing the reserved system/root prefix that carries no EXTENT_ITEM in the data allocator's tree); the wrap-around gap search clamps its cursor to bg_start+min_usable_offset instead of bg_start, and alloc_extent now refuses a found bytenr of 0 (returns NoSpace) as defense-in-depth. Updated the s0ogm mixed-bg unit test to root its group at a realistic 1MiB offset (real btrfs never roots a data/metadata group at logical 0). Regression test btrfs_write_multi_extent_overwrite_matches_reference_model_bd_5aybu (10-write metamorphic model, now un-ignored) passes; ffs-btrfs 322 + ffs-core full suite green; clippy clean. NOTE: extending the test to an 11th overwrite surfaced a SEPARATE sub-sector head-segment bug → filed bd-900t6 (btrfs_insert_regular_extent_segment bypasses logical mapping + MVCC).

title: perf(build): reframe bd-a2x93 SIMD baseline as x86-64-v2 (SSSE3/SSE4.2, ~2009 Nehalem, near-universal for servers) instead of v3/AVX2 — SSSE3 provides PSHUFB which is what swizzle_dyn needs, so v2 unlocks the safe-Rust GF(256) erasure + zero-scan + string-scan SIMD kernels (bd-79fp8 regressed ONLY because generic x86-64 has no PSHUFB). v2 is a far safer deployment baseline than v3. Measure GF kernel under -Ctarget-cpu=x86-64-v2 to confirm before deciding.
close_reason: MEASURED + CLOSED. Self-contained probe (crates/ffs-repair/benches/gf_simd_probe.rs) proves portable_simd swizzle_dyn GF(256) mul-xor is SLOWER than the scalar 256-entry LUT gather at EVERY target-cpu: scalar ~2.1us/4KB vs simd default ~6.5us, x86-64-v2/SSSE3 ~7.3us, x86-64-v3/AVX2 ~6.5us (3x slower throughout). So target-cpu is NOT the blocker: std::simd swizzle_dyn does not lower to an efficient PSHUFB/VPSHUFB sequence (the >=len->0 semantics add masking), while LLVM compiles the scalar LUT gather near-optimally. The v2-baseline hypothesis is FALSE. SIMD-erasure via safe portable_simd is a dead end on this toolchain regardless of baseline. Confirms bd-79fp8 rejection is fundamental.

title: perf(cold-read): re-derive the 5 remaining 2026-06-21 cold rows with a direct-I/O loop + a PARALLEL kernel-side comparator
description:
Follow-up to bd-q6k00. The headline ext4-extent cold row was re-derived on its original
fixture and FLIPPED SIGN: recorded "1.7x FASTER than kernel", actually 1.42x SLOWER
(startup-corrected) once the kernel got its best configuration.

KEY FINDING (already landed, see cold_read.rs + NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md top row): loop-device
serialization is a BUFFERED-MODE artifact, not a property of loop devices. On identical
bytes, drop_caches=3/run, min-of-5:
  loop dio=0: t=1/8/32 = 97.7 / 124.2 / 113.6 ms  (flat, no scaling)
  loop dio=1: t=1/8/32 = 52.1 /  25.1 /  28.2 ms  (scales)  <- `losetup --direct-io=on`
= 4.9x at t=8 from one ioctl. So bd-q6k00's own prescription ("never loop-mount the kernel
side") was WRONG. The rule is: give the kernel its BEST config (direct-I/O loop), then compare.
This rehabilitates the mounted-kernel-filesystem comparator.

REMAINING ROWS to re-derive (all currently marked UNVERIFIED in the ledger):
  1. ext4 FRAGMENTED 50 MiB / 9-extent   (recorded 1.41x FASTER)
  2. ext4 INDIRECT   50 MiB              (recorded 1.32x FASTER)
  3. btrfs UNCOMPRESSED 128 MiB          (recorded 2.8x FASTER)
  4. btrfs COMPRESSED                    (recorded ~1.5x, decompress-bound)
  5. ext4 METADATA walk 30k-file htree   (recorded 12.6x FASTER)  <- DOUBLY confounded
  6. many-small-files 500 MiB            (recorded 4.1x FASTER)   <- DOUBLY confounded
  7. btrfs many-files 30k-file tree      (recorded 24.3x FASTER)  <- DOUBLY confounded

Rows 5-7 need TWO fixes, not one: besides the direct-I/O loop, their kernel arm was a SERIAL
tool (`find` / `cat f*.bin`, and this box's `cat` is bat/uutils issuing 832-byte reads) raced
against frankenfs's parallel-across-files engine. A defensible comparator needs a THREADED
kernel-side stat/read loop. Expect those multi-x "wins" to shrink hard.

METHOD (proven in bd-q6k00, reusable):
  * private copy of the fixture + private loop device (never disturb peer mounts)
  * `sudo losetup --direct-io=on /dev/loopN`; verify /sys/block/loopN/loop/dio == 1
  * sha256 every arm against the kernel mount BEFORE timing (this caught an off-by-one-block
    extent map that would otherwise have produced a confident wrong number)
  * third "raw parallel pread of the same physical extents" arm to BOUND the buffered-vs-direct
    confound: at t=32 it sits within 5.2% of the dio kernel, so the mode gap is device-bound
    there; at t=1 it is 2.1x, so never quote a single-threaded buffered-vs-direct ratio
  * startup-correct frankenfs by cold-reading a 4 KiB file in the same image (per-open
    superblock+GDT+journal-replay cost was 8.4 ms of a 46.6 ms engine time)
  * drop_caches=3 before EVERY run, arms interleaved within a rep, min-of-N, cv < 5%

Harness + methodology: crates/ffs-block/examples/cold_read.rs (updated by bd-q6k00).
notes:
PROGRESS 2026-07-10 (BlackThrush/cc_ffs): 2 of 6 rows re-derived and landed.
  DONE ext4 INDIRECT   50 MiB : 1.45x SLOWER (min-of-9; 9/9 paired reps, p=0.0039). Was 1.32x FASTER.
  DONE ext4 FRAGMENTED 48 MiB : 1.31x SLOWER (min-of-9; 8/9 paired reps, p=0.039).  Was 1.41x FASTER.
REMAINING: btrfs UNCOMPRESSED 128 MiB (2.8x); btrfs COMPRESSED (~1.5x); ext4 METADATA walk 30k (12.6x,
DOUBLY confounded); many-small-files 500 MiB (4.1x, DOUBLY); btrfs many-files 30k (24.3x, DOUBLY).

METHOD NOTE learned this run: at 48-50 MiB the parallel kernel arm is only ~13 ms, so its cv is 8-10%
on a shared box and the cv<5% keep-gate FAILS on the sub-15 ms arms. Do NOT report a min-of-N ratio
alone at that scale. Use the PAIRED within-rep sign test (the arms are interleaved per rep precisely so

title: EPIC: Write-Back Cache
description:
# EPIC: Write-Back Cache

## PURPOSE
Implement a write-back cache layer between FUSE write operations and disk I/O. This is critical for write performance — without write-back caching, every FUSE write would require immediate disk I/O (write-through), making FrankenFS orders of magnitude slower than kernel filesystems.

## DESIGN

### Phased Approach
1. DirtyTracker: track which cached blocks have been modified but not flushed
2. FlushDaemon: background thread that periodically flushes dirty blocks to disk
3. MVCC Integration: dirty block tracking integrates with MVCC version chains

### Core Invariant
**Dirty blocks must never be evicted from cache until flushed to disk.**
Violating this invariant causes data loss (dirty data discarded without writing).

### DirtyTracker
- Per-block dirty flag in cache metadata
- Dirty list: ordered by age (oldest dirty block first)
- Statistics: dirty block count, dirty data size, oldest dirty age

### FlushDaemon
- Background thread wakes periodically (configurable: default 5s)
- Flushes oldest dirty blocks first (LRU-like)
- Flush batch size: configurable (default 256 blocks)
- Integrates with fsync: explicit fsync flushes all dirty blocks for that inode
- Backpressure: if dirty ratio exceeds threshold (e.g., 80%), block new writes until flushed

### MVCC Integration
- Dirty blocks belong to a specific MVCC version
- Flush writes the committed version (not in-flight versions)
- Aborted transaction: dirty blocks discarded without flush
- Committed transaction: dirty blocks eligible for flush

### Eviction Coordination
- Cache eviction (ARC or S3-FIFO) must check dirty flag before evicting
- If dirty: flush first, then evict
- If flush fails: do NOT evict (keep dirty block in cache, retry later)

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] Dirty blocks tracked correctly (set on write, cleared on flush)
- [ ] FlushDaemon runs in background, flushes oldest dirty blocks
- [ ] fsync flushes all dirty blocks for specified inode
- [ ] Dirty blocks never evicted without flush (invariant enforced)
- [ ] Backpressure prevents OOM from too many dirty blocks
- [ ] MVCC integration: only committed versions flushed
- [ ] Benchmark: write throughput with write-back vs write-through

## Success Criteria
1. All children closed
2. E2E durability test (bd-5s0r.4) passes
3. Dirty blocks never evicted without flush (invariant enforced)
4. Write throughput >= 80pct of kernel ext4 write-back
5. fsync flushes all dirty blocks for target inode
close_reason: All children closed. Write-Back Cache epic is done.

# Implement DirtyTracker for write-back cache

## GOAL
Track which cached blocks have been modified but not yet flushed to disk. This is the foundation of the write-back cache.

## DESIGN
- Per-block dirty flag in cache entry metadata
- DirtyList: ordered collection of dirty block IDs, sorted by modification time
- On block write: set dirty flag, add to DirtyList with current timestamp
- On flush: clear dirty flag, remove from DirtyList
- Statistics: dirty_count, dirty_bytes, oldest_dirty_age, dirty_ratio

- Modify BlockCache trait to include dirty tracking
- Cache::write(block_id, data) -> sets dirty
- Cache::mark_clean(block_id) -> clears dirty (called after flush)
- Cache::dirty_blocks() -> iterator over dirty blocks (oldest first)
- Cache::evict(block_id) -> panics if dirty (invariant enforcement)

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA

- [ ] DirtyList maintains age ordering
- [ ] Cache::evict panics if block is dirty (invariant)
- [ ] Statistics accurately reflect dirty state

title: Implement FlushDaemon for periodic dirty block writeback
description:
# Implement FlushDaemon for periodic dirty block writeback

## GOAL
Background daemon that periodically flushes dirty blocks from cache to disk, providing write-back semantics without requiring explicit fsync for every write.

## DESIGN
- Background thread spawned on mount, stopped on unmount
- Wake interval: configurable (default 5 seconds)
- Each wake cycle: iterate DirtyList, flush oldest blocks first
- Batch size: configurable (default 256 blocks per cycle)
- fsync integration: explicit fsync bypasses daemon, flushes immediately

### Backpressure
- dirty_ratio = dirty_bytes / cache_capacity
- If dirty_ratio > high_watermark (80%): flush aggressively (all dirty blocks)
- If dirty_ratio > critical_watermark (95%): block new writes until flushed below high
- Prevents OOM from unbounded dirty accumulation

### Shutdown
- On clean unmount: flush ALL dirty blocks before releasing FUSE
- On signal (SIGTERM): flush all dirty blocks, then exit
- On SIGKILL: dirty blocks lost (handled by crash recovery)

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] FlushDaemon runs in background, flushes periodically
- [ ] Oldest dirty blocks flushed first
- [ ] Backpressure blocks writes when dirty ratio critical
- [ ] Clean unmount flushes all dirty blocks
- [ ] Unit tests: daemon lifecycle, flush ordering
- [ ] Integration test: write 1000 blocks, verify all flushed within 2 intervals

title: Integrate write-back cache with MVCC version lifecycle
description:
# Integrate write-back cache with MVCC version lifecycle

## GOAL
Ensure the write-back cache correctly interacts with MVCC transactions: only committed versions are flushed, aborted transaction dirty blocks are discarded, and version chain GC coordinates with flush state.

## DESIGN

### Committed Version Flushing
- Dirty blocks track their transaction ID and commit sequence
- FlushDaemon only flushes blocks from committed transactions
- In-flight transaction blocks remain dirty but not flushable
- On commit: blocks transition from in-flight to flushable

### Abort Handling
- On transaction abort: dirty blocks for that transaction are discarded
- No disk write needed (the old committed version is still correct)
- Cache entry reverts to last committed version (or evicted if no committed version)

### GC Coordination
- EBR GC must not free a version while its dirty block is being flushed
- FlushDaemon holds a pin during flush I/O
- After flush: version can be marked as persisted (reduces recovery work)

### Snapshot Read Consistency
- Read transactions see committed data, whether flushed or still in cache
- Cache serves dirty (committed but unflushed) blocks for reads
- No need to flush before read (cache is authoritative for committed data)

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] Only committed transaction blocks flushed to disk
- [ ] Aborted transaction blocks correctly discarded
- [ ] GC and flush do not conflict (pin during flush)
- [ ] Snapshot reads correctly served from dirty cache
- [ ] Unit tests: commit-then-flush, abort-then-discard lifecycle
- [ ] Integration test: concurrent transactions with flush daemon running

title: E2E test: write-back cache durability and flush correctness
description:
# E2E test: write-back cache durability and flush correctness

## GOAL
Prove that the write-back cache correctly flushes all committed data to disk, never loses dirty blocks, and correctly handles abort/commit lifecycle with MVCC integration.

## TEST SCENARIOS

### Scenario 1: Basic Flush Correctness
1. Mount FrankenFS with write-back cache enabled (5s flush interval)
2. Write 1000 blocks with known content
3. Wait for 2 flush intervals (10s)
4. Unmount cleanly
5. Remount, read all 1000 blocks
6. Verify: all blocks contain correct data (BLAKE3 checksums match)

### Scenario 2: Clean Unmount Flushes Everything
1. Write 500 blocks, do NOT wait for flush interval
2. Immediately unmount (clean shutdown)
3. Verify: unmount blocked until all dirty blocks flushed
4. Remount, verify all 500 blocks present and correct

### Scenario 3: SIGKILL Dirty Block Loss
1. Write 100 blocks with fsync (durable baseline)
2. Write 200 more blocks WITHOUT fsync
3. SIGKILL the FUSE process
4. Remount with crash recovery
5. Verify: 100 fsync blocks intact, 200 non-fsync blocks may be missing
6. Verify: no partial/corrupt blocks (either present or absent)

### Scenario 4: Abort Discards Dirty Blocks
1. Begin MVCC transaction T1
2. Write 50 blocks via T1
3. Abort T1
4. Verify: dirty blocks from T1 discarded (not flushed to disk)
5. Previous committed data for those blocks unchanged

### Scenario 5: Backpressure Under Load
1. Configure critical_watermark at 95% dirty ratio
2. Flood writes faster than flush can keep up
3. Verify: writes block when dirty ratio exceeds critical threshold
4. Verify: writes resume after flush daemon catches up
5. Verify: no OOM from unbounded dirty accumulation

### Scenario 6: Concurrent Transactions and Flush
1. 4 concurrent transactions, each writing 100 blocks
2. 2 transactions commit, 2 abort
3. Flush daemon running continuously
4. Verify: only committed transaction blocks persisted to disk
5. Verify: aborted transaction blocks not on disk

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] All 6 scenarios pass
- [ ] No data loss for committed + fsynced data under any scenario
- [ ] Abort correctly discards dirty blocks
- [ ] Backpressure prevents OOM
- [ ] SIGKILL scenario: no corrupt data (only missing unflushed data)
- [ ] All scenarios deterministic and CI-executable
- [ ] Logging: tracing spans for flush cycles, dirty ratios, backpressure events
close_reason: implemented e2e scenarios + full gates pass

title: Cross-crate integration: write-back cache triggers RaptorQ symbol refresh

# Cross-crate integration: write-back cache triggers RaptorQ symbol refresh

## GOAL
Wire the write-back cache flush path to trigger RaptorQ symbol refresh for modified block groups. This is the critical cross-crate integration between ffs-block (cache), ffs-repair (RaptorQ), and the flush daemon.

## BACKGROUND
Currently bd-820 (RaptorQ symbol refresh on dirty group flush) exists but is not wired into the write-back cache flush path. When FlushDaemon (bd-5s0r.2) flushes dirty blocks, it must notify the repair subsystem that those block groups need symbol recalculation.

## DELIVERABLES
1. FlushDaemon::flush_batch() calls repair::mark_groups_dirty(groups) after successful disk write
2. Repair subsystem queues symbol recalculation for dirty groups
3. Integration test: write -> flush -> verify symbols updated

## TESTS (REQUIRED)
1. Unit: flush_batch marks correct groups dirty
2. Unit: repair subsystem receives group notifications
3. Integration: full write -> flush -> symbol refresh -> corruption -> recovery cycle

## LOGGING REQUIREMENTS
- Flush triggers refresh (debug): group_ids, block_count
- Symbol refresh queued (debug): group_id, priority
- Symbol refresh complete (info): group_id, duration_ms, symbol_count

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
1. Every flushed block group eventually gets symbol refresh
2. No symbol staleness > 2 scrub intervals
3. Recovery works for blocks modified after last refresh

title: btrfs inline-extent file gets nbytes=0 (btrfs check I_ERR_FILE_NBYTES_WRONG)
description: btrfs_recompute_inode_nbytes (ffs-core lib.rs ~18962) sums only Regular extents — the match has no Inline arm — so a file whose only EXTENT_DATA is inline gets nbytes=0 while size>0. btrfs_write writes small files (<= nodesize/2) as inline extents (can_be_inline branch ~lib.rs:20253), and both inline and regular branches set inode.nbytes = btrfs_recompute_inode_nbytes at :20408. Result: a small btrfs file (e.g. write(ino,0,b'hello')) commits with nbytes=0, size=5 -> btrfs check fails I_ERR_FILE_NBYTES_WRONG. The codebase's own clone path (btrfs_clone_file_range_data:~18410) and the btrfs-check-validated test helper (TealFalcon) both treat inline ram_bytes as the nbytes contribution, so this fn is inconsistent. FIX: add BtrfsExtentData::Inline { ram_bytes, .. } => total_nbytes += ram_bytes. Found via Phase B correctness audit of btrfs mutation paths (same audit class that found bd-iv5uy). Reachability confirmed: prior memory note 'FrankenFS never writes inline extents' was WRONG — btrfs_write does take the inline branch.

title: scrub(btrfs): tree-block validator compares header.bytenr to PHYSICAL offset, but bytenr is a LOGICAL (chunk-mapped) address -> false structural_invariant on every valid btrfs image
description:
EVIDENCE (BlackThrush/cc_ffs 2026-07-09, found while fixing bd-scrub-btrfs-false-corrupt-afw8y). BtrfsTreeBlockValidator (crates/ffs-repair/src/scrub.rs:715) does: expected_bytenr = block.0 * block_size, then flags Corrupt(StructuralInvariant, Critical) when header.bytenr != expected_bytenr. But btrfs header.bytenr is a LOGICAL address resolved through the chunk tree; block.0*block_size is the PHYSICAL byte offset. They coincide only when the chunk map happens to be identity.

PROOF: on /data/tmp/btr_571421.img (16384 block_size) EVERY sampled flagged block has hdr.bytenr - physical == -8388608 exactly (constant -8 MiB == that image's chunk mapping):
  block 1856: phys 30408704  hdr.bytenr 22020096  delta -8388608
  block 1857: phys 30425088  hdr.bytenr 22036480  delta -8388608
  block 2368: phys 38797312  hdr.bytenr 30408704  delta -8388608
A constant delta across independent blocks proves these are VALID tree blocks at a chunk-mapped offset, not corruption. The images mount cleanly under the kernel and read back sha256-identical (see bd-scrub-btrfs-false-corrupt-afw8y notes).

IMPACT: after the zeroes fix (this session), this is the ENTIRE residual false-positive set on valid btrfs images: btr_571421.img 1654, btrdiff2_1340519.img 75, btrunc_838059.img 36 structural_invariant findings, all at Critical severity, so they land in blocks_error_or_higher and keep is_clean() false. They also feed autopilot.update_posterior (pipeline.rs:1566).

ALSO UNTRIAGED: each of those images additionally reports exactly 1 checksum_mismatch. Separate question: real, or the same mapping bug reaching the csum compare?

FIX: translate logical->physical via the chunk tree (or the sys_chunk_array in the superblock for the bootstrap ranges) before comparing, or drop the bytenr check when no chunk map is available. ext4 unaffected (scrubs 0 findings).
close_reason: FIXED. BtrfsTreeBlockValidator (crates/ffs-repair/src/scrub.rs) now passes None for expected_bytenr instead of Some(block*block_size). header.bytenr is a btrfs LOGICAL address (chunk-tree mapped); a whole-image physical scrub only knows the physical offset, so the comparison flagged every valid tree block on any image without an identity chunk map (proven: constant -8MiB delta across independent blocks on btr_571421.img). header.validate still enforces the map-independent structural invariants (level<=BTRFS_MAX_LEVEL, nritems fits block). NOTHING LOST, EMPIRICALLY PINNED: the btrfs metadata checksum covers bytes 0x20.. which INCLUDES bytenr at 0x30..0x38, so a corrupted bytenr still fails verify_btrfs_tree_block_checksum -- new test btrfs_tree_block_corrupted_bytenr_is_caught_by_checksum flips a bytenr byte after the csum and asserts ChecksumMismatch is still reported. The equality check was only ever a PLACEMENT check, unverifiable without the chunk map. MEASURED blocks_corrupt: btr_571421.img 1655->1, btrdiff2_1340519.img 76->1, btrunc_838059.img 37->1. Gates: ffs-repair 471/0 (+2 regression tests), ffs-cli 348+26/0, ffs-harness 2058/0 + conformance, fmt+clippy clean, ubs 0 critical. RESIDUAL (the last '1'): block 4096 in every image = the btrfs BACKUP SUPERBLOCK at 64 MiB (verified magic _BHRfS_M, self-consistent sb.bytenr=67108864). It carries fsid at 0x20..0x30 like a tree block, so the fsid pre-check misclassifies it and applies a tree-block checksum over the full 16 KiB block instead of the 4096-byte superblock region. Filed separately.

title: perf(btrfs): a BOUNDED btrfs inode-resolution index for the mount path — bd-3zx2x measured the prize at ~96 ms, the naive fix is unbounded memory
description:
PHASE SPLIT from bd-3zx2x, which OWNS THE ATTRIBUTION and has now delivered it. This bead owns only the lever.

THE MEASURED PRIZE (bd-3zx2x, 2026-08-08, commit 56832e1f). One release-perf ELF fac86c35, ffs-cli walk, no mount/window/PGO, three runs per arm, medians:

    btrfs, prewarm ON (default)    7.744 ms   0.24 us/entry
    btrfs, prewarm OFF           120.861 ms   3.69 us/entry
    ext4 twin                     24.750 ms   0.76 us/entry

Suppressing the read-plan prewarm costs 15.61x on the identical binary and image. In-process btrfs/ext4 moves from 0.313x (btrfs FASTER) to 4.883x (btrfs SLOWER) on one env var.

MECHANISM: btrfs_read_inode_attr (crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs:9243) resolves an inode via index.inodes.get() when the read-plan index exists and via btrfs_read_ondisk_inode_item — an O(log N) fs-tree descent — when it does not. prewarm_btrfs_read_plan_index has exactly two call sites, readdirbench_cmd and walk_cmd, both in-process. THE FUSE MOUNT PATH HAS NONE. ext4 needs no counterpart: locate_inode is arithmetic plus a cached block read.

WHY THE NAIVE FIX IS WRONG, and this is the whole reason the lever is its own bead rather than a one-line change. build_btrfs_read_plan_index (crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs:10433) does a FULL walk_btrfs_fs_tree and retains, in memory, every INODE_ITEM, every EXTENT_DATA keyed by objectid, every DIR_ITEM/DIR_INDEX and a parents map. Calling that on mount buys:
  - mount latency proportional to the whole filesystem, paid before the first request
  - resident memory proportional to the whole filesystem, held for the mount lifetime
Both are unbounded in image size. The measurement above was taken on a 2 GiB image with 32,770 files; it says NOTHING about a 2 TiB filesystem with 10^8 inodes. A mount that OOMs or takes minutes to become ready is a worse defect than the 96 ms it fixes.

WHAT WOULD CLOSE THIS
1. A per-inode resolution structure with a BOUNDED footprint. The obvious shape is a fixed-capacity cache of objectid -> INODE_ITEM populated lazily on miss, sized by a cap rather than by the filesystem — the ext4 side already has this exact shape in ext4_inode_attr_cache with EXT4_INODE_ATTR_CACHE_LIMIT, so there is a template and a precedent for the eviction policy.
2. ⚠ IT MUST BEAT THE ONE-PASS CASE, WHICH IS THE HARD PART AND THE REASON THIS IS NOT OBVIOUS. readdir+stat sweeps 32,768 DISTINCT inodes exactly once. A demand-filled per-inode cache MISSES ON EVERY ONE of them — this is the same trap already documented on the read-only attr cache, whose own comment says a one-pass walk visits each inode once so every probe misses, and which walk_cmd therefore DISABLES. A naive LRU would add overhead and win nothing on the very workload that motivates the bead. What actually pays is amortising the DESCENT across inodes that share fs-tree leaves — batch/range resolution, or retaining hot interior nodes — not memoising individual inodes.
3. Measured on the same instrument as the attribution (ffs-cli walk, one ELF, both images), reporting the un-prewarmed baseline 120.861 ms, the full-index bound 7.744 ms, and where the bounded structure lands between them, PLUS its peak resident memory and the mount-time cost at several image sizes. A lever that only reports the speedup is not admissible here; the memory and mount-latency numbers are the reason this bead exists.
4. Only then, a mounted comparator row.

DO NOT: call prewarm_btrfs_read_plan_index from the mount path as the fix. It would produce a spectacular readdir+stat number and an unbounded mount, and the number would be bankable while the defect would not surface until someone mounted something large.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
PREMISE CORRECTION — the bounded cache this bead asks for ALREADY EXISTS, so the lever is not the one the bead describes. Found by reading the descent path; the numbers below are from bd-3zx2x measurements, no new run.

WHAT EXISTS: btrfs_parsed_node_cache (crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs:1586) is a ShardedCache<u64, Arc<BtrfsParsedNode>> keyed by logical address, capacity-bounded by BTRFS_TREE_NODE_CACHE_LIMIT = 512 nodes, populated in btrfs_read_parsed_node (:8696). It is exactly the "retain hot interior nodes" shape item 2 of this bead proposes, it is already bounded, and it is already live on read-only mounts (skipped when writes are enabled, because COW reuses physical addresses).

SO THE 3.69 us/entry IS NOT DEVICE I/O. With the node cache live, a 32,770-file fs tree keeps its root and interior nodes resident, and leaves stream through under LRU with a sequential sweep. What remains per inode is the DESCENT MACHINERY on top of already-cached nodes: ~3 ShardedCache gets (hash + shard lock + Arc clone) plus ~3 in-node binary searches, per inode, every inode. The read-plan index costs 0.24 us/entry because it replaces ALL of that with one BTreeMap hit.

REVISED LEVER, and it is much smaller than an index. A DESCENT MEMO: retain the last leaf (one Arc) plus its key range, and before descending check whether the target key falls inside it. bd-3zx2x measured this workload as a sweep over consecutive objectids, and an fs-tree leaf holds many inodes worth of items, so the large majority of lookups would resolve with a single binary search in a leaf already in hand — no root or interior cache gets at all.

⭐ THIS IS WHY IT BEATS THE ONE-PASS TRAP, which item 2 of this bead correctly flags as fatal to a naive per-inode cache. A memo keyed on the LEAF exploits locality BETWEEN distinct inodes, not reuse of the same inode. A one-pass sweep over 32,768 distinct inodes misses a per-inode cache every single time and hits a leaf memo almost every time. Same workload, opposite outcome, and that distinction is the whole design.

BOUNDED BY CONSTRUCTION: one Arc<BtrfsParsedNode>, not a structure that grows with the filesystem. It therefore does NOT carry the unbounded-mount-latency and unbounded-memory objection that this bead was created to prevent, and it needs no mount-time prewarm at all — it warms itself on the first descent.

WHAT I HAVE NOT DONE, so nobody reads this as more than it is: I have not implemented or measured it. The per-inode cost decomposition above (3 cache gets + 3 binary searches) is inferred from reading btrfs_read_parsed_node and walk_btrfs_tree_floor, NOT profiled — 3.69 us is a lot for pure memory work and the split between hashing, shard locking, Arc cloning and binary search is unmeasured. Profile that split before implementing: if one component dominates, the fix may be smaller still (e.g. the shard lock), and if none does, the memo is the right shape.

ACCEPTANCE (revising items 1-3): implement the leaf memo; measure on the SAME instrument as the attribution (ffs-cli walk, one ELF, both images) reporting the un-prewarmed 120.861 ms baseline, the full-index 7.744 ms bound, and where the memo lands; report its added resident memory (expected: one node) and mount-time cost (expected: zero). The unbounded-index objection is now moot for this design, but the memory/mount numbers are still required — a design that quietly regrows is the failure mode this bead exists to catch.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
DESIGN CONSTRAINT ON THE LEAF MEMO — it cannot be keyed on the leaf own key range. Found by reading the descent before implementing; recording it because getting this wrong returns WRONG inode metadata silently.

STRUCTURE: walk_btrfs_tree_floor (crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs:8811) is a thin wrapper over walk_tree_floor_with_nodes(&mut provider, root, nodesize, target), where the provider is btrfs_read_parsed_node — the already-cached node reader. That is why the measured hit rate is 96%: every LEVEL of the descent is already served from memory. So a memo cannot help by caching nodes; it must skip the DESCENT itself.

⚠ THE TRAP. The obvious memo — remember the last leaf plus its first/last key, and if target falls within, binary-search it directly — is WRONG for a FLOOR query. A floor descent returns the greatest key <= target. If target sits between this leaf last key and the next leaf first key, the naive range check either misses (target > last_key, so the memo declines and we descend — merely slow, fine) or, worse, a memo that treats [first_key, last_key] as authoritative can answer from a leaf that does not actually cover the target, because a leaf key span does NOT equal the key interval the parent delegates to it. The covering interval is defined by the PARENT SEPARATORS, not by the keys the leaf happens to hold.

TWO SAFE SHAPES, both bounded:
1. Memo the descent PATH, not just the leaf: retain the parent separator interval alongside the leaf, and serve only when target falls strictly inside that interval. Correct for floor queries, still one node plus two keys.
2. Memo the leaf but serve ONLY exact-match hits inside [first_key, last_key], falling through to a full descent otherwise. Weaker hit rate, trivially correct, and probably sufficient here — the workload is a sweep over consecutive objectids where most targets land squarely inside the current leaf.

Shape 2 is the one to try first: it cannot answer a query the leaf does not own, so the failure mode is a wasted check rather than a wrong inode.

I have NOT implemented either. This is a correctness-sensitive read path and the bead sibling bd-y2t0r spent six diagnoses learning that plausible-looking changes here need measurement, not confidence. The instrument to judge it now exists and is validated (86843ba6), so the next session can implement shape 2 and read lookups/stat directly.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
CORRECTION TO MY OWN TRAP ANALYSIS — the span check IS sufficient, no parent separators needed. And a separate finding that kills the exact-match variant for this call path.

I wrote that a memo keyed on the leaf [first_key, last_key] span "can answer from a leaf that does not actually cover the target". That is wrong, and the reasoning is short enough to check: leaves PARTITION the ordered key space, so if first_key <= target <= last_key, every key <= target that is >= first_key lives in THIS leaf, and first_key itself qualifies. The greatest such key is therefore the tree-wide floor. The span check alone is provably correct.

The trap is real but narrower than I stated: it applies only when serving OUTSIDE the span. target > last_key is the dangerous case — the floor might be last_key, or might be a key in a later leaf — and that is exactly the case a span check declines. So shape 1 (memo the parent separator interval) is UNNECESSARY. Shape 2 refined to "serve iff first_key <= target <= last_key, returning the in-leaf floor" is both correct and strictly more useful than the exact-match-only version I recommended.

⚠ AND THE EXACT-MATCH VARIANT I RECOMMENDED FIRST WOULD HAVE BEEN INERT HERE. btrfs_read_ondisk_inode_item descends with target = (objectid, INODE_ITEM, u64::MAX) — a SENTINEL upper bound, deliberately, so the floor lands on the objectid INODE_ITEM. The floor answer is never equal to that target, so an exact-match-only memo would never fire on the very path this bead exists to speed up. I recommended trying it first; that would have measured a null and looked like the memo idea failing.

VALIDITY OF A RETAINED LEAF: sound on read-only mounts, and only there. btrfs_read_parsed_node already skips caching entirely when writes are enabled, because COW reuses physical addresses across commits — the memo must inherit that same guard (btrfs_alloc_state.is_none()), not merely inherit the cache.

NET: implement one memo holding (leaf Arc, first_key, last_key), consulted in walk_btrfs_tree_floor, guarded to read-only, serving only when the target lies within the span. Not implemented — it needs a field on OpenFs and this repo has a documented hazard about adding struct fields without updating every constructor, which is not something to do on a tired context. The instrument (86843ba6) reads lookups/stat directly, so the next session can judge it in one run.

GROUNDWORK LANDED (746d132d): floor_in_leaf is extracted and public, so the memo is now a small addition rather than a duplicated read path.

WHAT LANDED: floor_descend leaf arm — binary-search the last item <= target, bounds-check its data range, materialize the entry — is now pub fn floor_in_leaf in ffs-btrfs, called from where it was inlined. Behavior-preserving; the moved code is unchanged. ffs-btrfs 389/0, ffs-core 1199/0.

Landing it alone keeps the memo commit small and keeps this verifiable by the existing suite.

THE SPAN PRECONDITION IS NOW ON THE FUNCTION, not just in this bead: answering from a retained leaf equals a full descent ONLY when first_key <= target <= last_key, and the doc comment states why (leaves partition the key space) and what breaks outside it (target > last_key — floor may be last_key or in a later leaf, indistinguishable from inside the leaf). I got that argument wrong twice in this bead comments before settling it, so it belongs at the point of use where the next implementer will actually read it.

1. One field on OpenFs: Option<(root_logical, first_key, last_key, Arc<BtrfsParsedNode>)> behind a Mutex. Only ONE struct literal constructs OpenFs (verified), so the add-a-field hazard does not bite here.
2. In walk_btrfs_tree_floor: if the memo matches root_logical AND first_key <= target <= last_key, call floor_in_leaf and return; else descend and store the leaf reached.
3. Guard on btrfs_alloc_state.is_none() — the same read-only condition btrfs_read_parsed_node already applies, because COW reuses physical addresses when writes are enabled and a retained leaf would go stale.
4. Judge with the validated instrument: lookups/stat should fall from ~2.10 toward ~1 on the small fixture, and the large-fixture run is the one that matters.

TESTED FOR THE FAILURE MODE: the memo serves only inside a span, so a reverse sweep alternates in and out of it differently than a forward one. The test now stats every entry BOTH ways and requires identical answers — a span check that served a target its leaf did not own would diverge there, and ordinary suites would not catch it because they read in one order. ffs-core 1199/0, ffs-btrfs 389/0, ffs-cli 353/0 + 26/0 (e2e builds real btrfs images and walks them).

A random-access getattr workload re-descends far more often and would see a fraction of this. Do NOT generalize 30.9x to "btrfs metadata is 30x faster" — it is a sequential-sweep number, which is what readdir+stat is.

WORST-CASE PROBE: the memo does NOT tax random access — 0.997x (84771130). This is the evidence that was missing for default-on.

    8,000 inodes, stride 4099 (coprime with the length, so nearly every step crosses a leaf boundary),
    attr cache disabled, cold fs per arm
      memo OFF  37.203 ms
      memo ON   37.319 ms
      0.997x

No measurable cost. Read the 0.3% as "no cost", not as a 0.3% tax — one run per arm does not resolve tenths of a percent.

WHY IT NEEDED CHECKING: every other figure on this lever is a sequential sweep, where the memo hits constantly. Under random access it mostly MISSES, and a miss is not free — a mutex acquire and two key comparisons on every descent, paid before falling through to the walk it was trying to avoid. I had asserted "random access would see less benefit" several times in these comments without ever checking it does not see a LOSS. That is the difference between a caveat and a measurement.

THE LEVER PROFILE IS NOW MEASURED ON BOTH ENDS:
    sequential sweep, production config (attr cache on)   2.16x
    sequential sweep, memo isolated (attr cache off)      3.73x
    random access, worst case                             0.997x (no cost)
That is what a default-on read-path cache should look like: it pays where it applies and does not tax where it does not.

BEAD STATE: mechanism confirmed by measurement, bounded to one leaf by construction, default-on justified on both ends of the workload space, correctness guarded by a differential verified to fail on a broken memo, kill switch present. The only remaining item is the mounted comparator row — run it with the kill switch both ways, label it production-configuration, and do not compare it against the 3.73x.
