comments.text:
CALLER AUDIT OF MY OWN CHANGE — three of four callers were unguarded (ef445f49).

The memo lives inside walk_btrfs_tree_floor, so EVERY caller gets it. I had verified one:

    btrfs_read_ondisk_inode_item   INODE_ITEM     covered
    btrfs_lookup_child             DIR_ITEM       NOT covered
    btrfs_read_file_into           EXTENT_DATA    NOT covered
    btrfs_fiemap_extent_items      extents        NOT covered

A memo defect on btrfs_read_file_into corrupts file CONTENT — a different order of severity from a wrong stat.

MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED: removing the span check and running the WHOLE ffs-core suite fails only my two bd-5vis3 tests. 1,199 others pass, including the btrfs file-read tests. So nothing outside those two guards this cache, and neither touched the read path. That is the same lesson as two turns ago — the suite is not sensitive to this class of defect, so the dedicated test has to be.

FIXED: the differential now also compares, memo on versus off, lookup results by name and the first 4 KiB of file CONTENT for a sampled 64 entries. Verified in both directions — on a broken memo the CONTENT assertion fires first; on the intact memo it passes.

⭐ AND THE FIXTURE WAS DECORATIVE UNTIL NOW: both builders wrote a single b"x" to every file, so an extent mix-up would have been invisible to any content comparison. They now write distinct bytes per file. A content differential over identical files proves nothing, and I would have shipped exactly that.

ffs-core 1201/0. Bead state otherwise unchanged: 2.16x production, 0.997x random-access worst case, bounded to one leaf, kill switch, mounted row still owed.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
THE KILL SWITCH WAS TEST-ONLY — fixed (d181a613). A claim I repeated in these comments and had not checked.

I wrote several times that the kill switch "stays for the mounted A/B and for removing the memo without a rebuild if it is ever implicated in a wrong-metadata report". The second half was FALSE as shipped. set_btrfs_floor_memo_disabled is a per-instance setter and EVERY call site is in the test module — no env var, no CLI flag, no mount option. In production there was no way to turn off a cache that sits on the metadata read path and is enabled by default. The switch existed for my A/Bs and for nobody else.

FFS_BTRFS_FLOOR_MEMO=0 now disables it at mount (accepts 0, false, off), mirroring FFS_BTRFS_PREWARM_READ_PLAN. The setter stays for in-process A/Bs.

WHY IT MATTERS HERE SPECIFICALLY: this memo is default-on, it changes results on FOUR read paths (inode item, dir item, extent data, fiemap), and if the span check is ever wrong the failure is wrong metadata or wrong file CONTENT — not a crash. The first thing an operator needs in that situation is to remove it from the picture and see whether the symptom follows. Shipping that capability only to the test suite defeats the point of having built it.

The parse test asserts the accepted spellings directly rather than through the environment, since env vars are process-global and a parallel suite would race on them.

ffs-core 1204/0. Bead state otherwise unchanged: 2.16x production, 0.997x random-access, bounded to one leaf, four callers guarded, mounted row still owed.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
THE COLD-READ TEST HELPER STOPPED BEING COLD — fixed (b61dc7b5).

btrfs_test_clear_node_cache exists so read-count tests can measure per-op descent structure against cold reads. It cleared only the parsed-node cache. The floor-leaf memo retains a leaf INDEPENDENTLY of that cache, so a following lookup inside the retained span is served without reading a node at all — after my change the helper stopped meaning what its name and its callers assume.

Nothing fails today; the existing callers still pass. The damage is LATENT and aimed at whoever writes the next read-count test against this helper: it would silently measure a warm path, report too few reads, and look like a win rather than a broken fixture. That is a worse outcome than a red test.

Fixed: the memo is cleared with the cache, with a comment at the site saying why.

⭐ THIS IS THE THIRD INSTANCE OF ONE CLASS ON THIS BEAD, and the class is worth naming for anyone adding a cache here: a default-on cache changes the MEANING of the things around it, and those things do not announce that they have changed. The three were (1) three of four callers of the memoized descent had no correctness guard, (2) the kill switch existed only for the test suite so no operator could disable it, and (3) the cold-read helper was no longer cold. None of the three was a defect in the memo itself — every negative control says the memo is correct — they were all defects in the surroundings the memo silently altered.

ffs-core 1204/0 default, 1255/0 with the feature.

comments.author: DarkMeadow
comments.text:
⚠ SCOPE WARNING BEFORE ANYONE SPENDS A SLICE HERE: a bounded btrfs inode-resolution index is
optimising 4% of the row it is meant to close. Measured today, in process, on the comparator's OWN
32,768-entry image. (DarkMeadow, 2026-08-14; full write-up on bd-3zx2x.)

The comparator preserves its arm images, so the decomposition ran on the exact btrfs image the
mounted row enumerates — not a seed tree — with one ELF (23e9706c…, x86-64-v3, PGO 6a22cfcf…), no
FUSE, no mount:

    readdir-bench steady state   0.0152 us/entry
    walk --no-stat               0.19   us/entry   6.13 ms   (incl. the one-time index build)
    walk (readdir + stat)        0.26   us/entry   8.60 ms
    => the stat half             0.075  us/entry

The mounted arms of the same shape: FrankenFS 6.470 us/entry (211.998 ms), kernel 0.845 us/entry
(27.702 ms). So the ENTIRE in-process job — including the one-time read-plan index build a mount
amortises to nothing — is 8.60 ms against 211.998 ms mounted. **The filesystem layer is 4.1% of the
mounted cost.** Our whole in-process job is also 3.2x faster than the kernel's whole mounted arm.

WHY THAT BEARS DIRECTLY ON THIS BEAD: this bead exists to make inode resolution cheaper. Inode
resolution is inside the 0.075 us/entry stat half, which is 1.2% of the mounted per-entry cost. Even
a PERFECT index — resolution reduced to zero — moves the mounted row from 6.470 to at best
6.395 us/entry, i.e. 7.73x to 7.64x. That is inside the 1.36% cross-window spread the btrfs
scorecard tells readers to quote for this row, so the improvement would not be distinguishable from
noise by the instrument that has to admit it.

WHERE THE COST ACTUALLY IS: 6.470 - 0.075 - 0.015 = ~6.38 us/entry of pure mount path, which is
bd-ha71t's per-path security.capability round trip (one uncached getxattr per path resolution,
name and size captured, 2003 probes per 2000 stats on BOTH filesystems). The mounted per-entry cost
also grows ~60% from 2,000 to 32,768 entries while the in-process cost is flat-to-better at twice
the entries — so the growth is in the mount path too, and this bead's surface does not have it to
give.

NOT A VETO — the ~96 ms figure this bead cites may still be real work worth removing for its own
sake, and bd-3zx2x's earlier stat measurement (btrfs 0.12 us/entry vs ext4 0.50) says btrfs
resolution is already ~4x CHEAPER than the ext4 twin's. What this rules out is spending the slice
here EXPECTING it to move the 7.7x row. If it is taken, take it as a small self-speedup with that
stated up front, not as the fix for the readdir+stat loss.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
ACCEPTANCE ITEM 3 PARTLY DELIVERED, and it found a regression (ProudBarn, 2026-08-16). The three measurement arms this bead asked for already existed as ignored tests and had never been run. Harness: cargo test -p ffs-core --release --lib bd_5vis3 -- --ignored. rch WORKER vmi1293453. One ELF, env-toggled via FFS_BTRFS_FLOOR_MEMO.

    LARGE sweep 20000 inodes:   211.129458ms -> 5.599509ms   = 37.705x, lookups 60000 -> 1395 (43.01x fewer)
    PRODUCTION, attr cache ON:   22.360080ms -> 7.752808ms   =  2.884x
    RANDOM ACCESS 8000 inodes:    7.907348ms -> 68.062258ms  =  0.116x  <-- the memo TAXES this 8.6x

The bead's item 2 warned the hard part was beating the one-pass case. It does — 37.7x on the sweep, 2.88x in production config — because the retained leaf amortises the DESCENT across inodes sharing a leaf, exactly the shape item 2 prescribed, rather than memoising individual inodes. But the adversarial case was never measured until now: random access pays 8.6x, and the memo is default-ON. Filed as bd-79li3.

ALSO FIXED while here (1e334993): the memo hit path held its mutex across floor_in_leaf. The inner if-let shadowed the MutexGuard, so the drop(memo) meant to release it dropped a reference — a no-op the compiler had been reporting as dropping_references in every ffs-core build. Gate: cargo test -p ffs-core --lib btrfs_floor on rch worker vmi1152480, 3 passed 0 failed, including the concurrent-sweep test.

STILL OPEN on item 3: peak resident memory and mount-time cost at several image sizes. The three arms report wall and lookup counts only, and the memory/mount numbers are, per this bead's own text, the reason it exists.

    executing ELF self-report bench_evidence,binary_sha256=

    20000 inodes, attr cache ON, cold fs per arm, 7 interleaved pairs

    A/B  median 3.031176x  bootstrap_median_ci95 [2.466613, 3.388613]
    A/A  median 0.862187x  bootstrap_median_ci95 [0.777040, 0.983771]

TWO RUNS NOW EXIST, ON DIFFERENT WORKERS:

    run 1  PRE-gate   vmi1153651  21 pairs  A/B 3.012337x [1.815917, 4.326150]
                                            A/A 1.140782x [0.798162, 1.293269]
    run 2  POST-gate  vmi1293453   7 pairs  A/B 3.031176x [2.466613, 3.388613]
                                            A/A 0.862187x [0.777040, 0.983771]

⛔ IT DOES NOT MEET THE REPLICATED-STANDING CONVENTION. Stating the failure precisely
rather than quoting the agreeable-looking medians:

  * Run 2's null FAILS: its CI95 [0.777040, 0.983771] does not contain 1.0.
  * The fleet rule excuses a failing null only when two runs agree with overlapping
    intervals AND both nulls are off in the SAME direction by a similar amount. The
    A/B intervals do overlap (run 2's is contained in run 1's). But run 1's null is
    +14.1% (1.140782) and run 2's is -13.8% (0.862187): same magnitude, OPPOSITE
    directions. That is precisely the case the rule does not excuse.
  * Opposite-signed nulls of that size are not a calibration offset that could be
    argued around; they are an instrument whose bias flips sign between runs. The
    cause is known and is mine: the A/A observations are not position-matched — they
    run 3rd and 4th in each round, the first straight after the memo-ON arm.
  * The two runs are also not clean replicates: 21 pairs vs 7, and pre-gate vs
    post-gate. Different configurations, so agreement between them is weaker evidence
    than it looks.

WHAT THE FAILING NULLS CAN STILL DECIDE, which is the useful half:

The A/B lower bound is 2.466613 (run 2) and 1.815917 (run 1). The worst null excursion
seen across BOTH runs spans [0.777040, 1.293269]. Even taking that worst edge, the
A/B's own worst lower bound sits 1.40x above it. A +-14% instrument bias cannot
manufacture a 3x effect. So the memo's production benefit is REAL AND GROSS; only its
VALUE is uncertifiable. Same shape as AzureBay's pre-gate 0.116x result: a wide or
biased null kills a small effect, not a large one.

QUOTABLE FORM, worst bound per the convention: >= 1.82x on the production config
(20000 inodes, attr cache ON, cold fs per arm), NOT 3.03x and NOT 3.01x, and flagged
NOT-STANDING until the nulls are fixed.

WHAT WOULD MAKE IT STANDING, in order:
  1. Position-match the A/A: run the null pair at the SAME schedule positions as the
     A/B pair rather than after it. That is the defect producing the +-14% swing.
  2. Re-run twice at the SAME pair count on two workers, post-gate both times.
  3. Then quote the worst lower bound of the two.
Until (1) lands, more runs will keep producing sign-unstable nulls and no amount of
replication will fix that.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
REPLICATED PRODUCTION RATIO — two runs, two workers, and an honest verdict on
whether it stands (ProudBarn, 2026-08-16, estimator b580eef3).

Harness in every row: cargo test -p ffs-core --release --lib bd_5vis3_prod -- --ignored
Config: 20000 inodes, attr cache ON, cold fs per arm, 7 rounds of a balanced
OFF,ON,ON,OFF square, seeded 20,000-resample paired bootstrap, one ELF per run
self-reporting its own SHA-256, each built in place on its executing worker.

  run  worker       A/B median   A/B ci95                 A/A median  A/A ci95                 null
   3   vmi1293453   3.152099x    [2.713078, 5.647945]     0.875932x   [0.718375, 0.981454]     FAILS
   4   vmi1227854   3.445466x    [2.859922, 4.255997]     0.957439x   [0.802895, 1.138524]     passes
  ELF run 3: 19fc3735b0380c22e5d5473819d1590b435e7f3b38c8b0c344883be9e6dc3549
  ELF run 4: f3665438f999a145c1fe199e0238714c84126d75990d0a64bfa427b97afcd18c

AGAINST THE CONVENTION, item by item:
  two runs                        YES
  different workers               YES — vmi1293453 and vmi1227854
  A/B intervals overlap           YES — [2.859922, 4.255997] lies inside run 3's
  ELF + build worker cited        YES, both, self-reported by the executing binary
  passing A/A nulls on both       NO — run 3's null excludes 1.0

So it does NOT fully meet the standing convention, and I am not going to file it
as though it does. The excusable-failing-null clause does not rescue it either:
that clause wants both nulls off the same way by a SIMILAR amount, and -12.4%
against -4.3% is a factor of three apart, even though both are on the same side
of 1.0.

WORST BOUND, per the convention: 2.713078x — the lowest lower edge either run
produced. Quote >= 2.71x, never 3.45x and never the 5.65x upper edge.

WHY THE FAILING NULL DOES NOT INVALIDATE THE A/B, which is the part worth
understanding rather than the number:
The null is biased DOWN because it compares an earlier arm to a later one and
each successive cold-fs arm is slower — monotonic drift within a round. The
balanced square gives `off` slots 1 and 4 and `on` slots 2 and 3, so the two
arms have IDENTICAL mean schedule position and that drift cancels in the A/B
while still showing up in the null. The null is reporting a real effect that
the A/B is constructed not to inherit. That is why run 3 can carry a failing
null and a usable A/B at the same time.
Corroboration rather than assertion: run 4, whose null passes, lands at
3.445466x — HIGHER than run 3's 3.152099x, not lower. If the drift were leaking
into the A/B, the drifting run would be the inflated one; it is the smaller one.

AND THE DRIFT IS A WORKER PROPERTY, not a test property: identical code, same
pair count, same fixture — null fails on vmi1293453 and passes on vmi1227854.
Same conclusion AzureBay reached about the SSH timeouts, which failed three
times on vmi1264463 and never on vmi1293453. Pin the worker before blaming the
test, in both directions.

A HYPOTHESIS OF MINE THAT THE DATA REFUTED, recorded so nobody re-runs it:
I predicted the +-14% sign-flipping null came from the A/A sitting at schedule
slots 3-4 while the A/B sat at 1-2, and that position-matching would fix it. It
did not — post-change the null is still ~-12% on vmi1293453. An A/A null is
early-vs-late by construction, so no re-pairing can escape monotonic drift. The
fix has to reduce the drift itself; every arm currently clones the whole image,
so per-arm allocation churn is the first place to look.

WHAT WOULD MAKE IT STAND: one more run on a THIRD worker with a passing null,
or a reduction in per-arm churn that makes vmi1293453's null pass. Either way
the quotable figure stays the worst lower bound across all admitted runs.

title: btrfs renameat2(RENAME_EXCHANGE) unimplemented -> EINVAL while ext4 supports it (feature/parity gap)
description: rename2 dispatcher (lib.rs ~26674) called ext4_rename2_exchange unconditionally for RENAME_EXCHANGE; that fn's staged path asserts FsFlavor::Ext4 and returns EINVAL for btrfs, so btrfs filesystems could not perform an atomic dual-entry swap that ext4 supports. EINVAL is the POSIX-correct errno for an unsupported flag, so this was a missing-feature/parity gap rather than a wrong-errno bug. FIX: implement btrfs_rename2_exchange (COW-tree path) and dispatch by flavor. Swap which inode each of the two existing entries references via remove+reinsert of both DIR_ITEM/DIR_INDEX pairs and both INODE_REFs; both names must exist (ENOENT otherwise); cross-parent directory moves get the descendant/loop guard (EINVAL); ctime bumped on both swapped inodes (new btrfs_touch_inode_ctime helper), mtime+ctime on both parents; nlink unchanged (btrfs dirs stay nlink==1, parent nlink fixed per bd-egyf6, parent linkage carried by INODE_REF so no '..' fixup unlike ext4). Validated: 4 in-memory model tests (same-parent swap incl content, missing-target ENOENT, cross-parent swap, dir-under-descendant EINVAL) + btrfs_rename2_exchange_passes_btrfs_check (real btrfs check accepts the swapped on-disk image).
close_reason: Implemented in c67b213e: btrfs_rename2_exchange + flavor dispatch in rename2. Atomic dual-entry swap (remove+reinsert both DIR_ITEM/DIR_INDEX + INODE_REF), ENOENT if either name missing, EINVAL on cross-parent dir loop, ctime on swapped inodes + mtime/ctime on parents, nlink fixed. Validated by 4 model tests + btrfs_rename2_exchange_passes_btrfs_check (real btrfs check accepts swapped image). 1060 ffs-core lib green + clippy -D warnings clean.

title: [perf] avoid repeated extent leaf reads for range mapping
description: Fresh rch Criterion profile on worker vmi1153651 for ffs-extent extent_resolve shows extent_sequential_100blocks_uncached at 440.57 us mean, while cached sequential is 7.8901 us. Profile-backed target: map_logical_to_physical(count > 1) repeatedly calls ffs_btree::search, rereading/reparsing the same depth-1 leaf for adjacent logical blocks. One lever: add a range-aware btree traversal and use it for multi-block extent mapping while preserving mapping order, hole segmentation, unwritten flags, and ext4 logical-boundary behavior.
close_reason: Shipped (commit pending): added range-aware btree traversal ffs_btree::walk_range (each overlapping subtree/leaf read at most once, preserving walk leaf order) and routed ffs_extent::map_logical_to_physical(count>1) through map_logical_range_by_walk (count==1 unchanged → single search). Preserves mapping order, hole segmentation, unwritten flags, u32 logical-boundary checks. Proof (machine-independent, included in the work): differential test map_depth1_range_matches_repeated_search_and_reads_leaf_once builds a 100-extent depth-1 tree, asserts walk output == old repeated-search output (isomorphism) AND that the range walk does exactly 1 leaf read vs the old path's many (instrumented MemBlockDevice read counter) — the direct fix for the profiled 440.57us extent_sequential_100blocks_uncached (repeated search rereads the same leaf per block). Isomorphism: ffs-btree 141/141, ffs-extent 140/140, ffs-core --lib 888/888, no warnings. (Implementation synced from PlumFern's worker; verified + landed.)

title: perf(core/ext4): bound ext4_lseek_hole extent collection to the query suffix (bd-yd3a0 sibling)
description: ext4_lseek_hole collects collect_extents_with_scope (WHOLE extent tree from block 0) per SEEK_HOLE call, while its sibling ext4_lseek_data already bounds to collect_extents_from_with_scope(from_block) (bd-yd3a0/W115). Sparse-file scans pay O(extents) per SEEK_HOLE on a fragmented file. Bound to the suffix from offset's block. Isomorphic: covered_until accumulates from 0 but every early return is gated on ext_logical_byte > offset, which no dropped (end<=offset) extent satisfies, so the hole position is identical. Same mechanism W115 benched at 3.92x (extent_collect_window.rs). Measurable on a real formatted ext4 image.
close_reason: Shipped cc8adc98: ext4_lseek_hole now bounds extent collection to collect_extents_from_with_scope(from_block) like its sibling ext4_lseek_data (bd-yd3a0), instead of collecting the whole tree from block 0. O(extents)->O(suffix) per SEEK_HOLE on a fragmented file. Isomorphic: covered_until accumulates from 0 but every early return is gated on ext_logical_byte > offset, which no dropped (end<=offset) extent satisfies; the covering leaf is always retained so covered_until is correct at/after offset. Verified empirically: new test writes a 400-extent multi-leaf sparse file on a real ext4 image and asserts SEEK_HOLE lands on every known hole position. 5 existing + 1 new lseek test green, clippy clean. Perf = the collect-window mechanism bd-yd3a0 benched at 3.92x (extent_collect_window.rs); lseek_hole now uses that path.

title: ffs-types: superblock offsets/sizes + BTRFS_MAGIC lack kernel-conformance pin
description:
Finding (via /testing-conformance-harnesses skill, NEW target): crates/ffs-types/src/lib.rs declares core ext4 + btrfs filesystem layout constants used by every superblock parser:

  EXT4_SUPERBLOCK_OFFSET    = 1024     (fs/ext4/ext4.h: 1024 bytes from start)
  EXT4_SUPERBLOCK_SIZE      = 1024     (sizeof(struct ext4_super_block) = 1024)
  EXT4_SECTOR_SIZE          = 512      (logical sector size)
  EXT4_SB_CHECKSUM_OFFSET   = 0x3FC    (offset of s_checksum within superblock)
  BTRFS_SUPER_INFO_OFFSET   = 64*1024  (fs/btrfs/disk-io.h)
  BTRFS_SUPER_INFO_SIZE     = 4096     (sizeof(struct btrfs_super_block))
  BTRFS_MAGIC               = 0x4D5F_5366_5248_425F  ("_BHRfS_M" LE)

Each constant determines where on disk the parser looks for the superblock and what magic it must find. A drift in any value would silently fail every mount of every image — but the constants currently have NO conformance pin (bd-jbilz pinned EXT4_SUPER_MAGIC + ext4 state flags but not these layout constants).

Critical: BTRFS_MAGIC is a u64 representation of the byte sequence "_BHRfS_M". A regression that swapped the byte order or changed any byte would silently fail to recognize every btrfs filesystem.

Acceptance: ext4_btrfs_layout_constants_match_kernel_header test in crates/ffs-types/src/lib.rs that pins all 7 values to canonical kernel macros from fs/ext4/ext4.h, fs/ext4/ext4.h checksum offset, fs/btrfs/ctree.h, and fs/btrfs/disk-io.h. Plus the BTRFS_MAGIC byte-decomposition asserting the on-disk byte sequence is "_BHRfS_M".
close_reason: done

title: hardlink to an append-only (and, on btrfs, immutable) file is wrongly allowed instead of EPERM
description: The kernel's vfs_link (fs/namei.c) rejects creating a hard link to an append-only OR immutable file with EPERM: 'A link to an append-only or immutable file cannot be created.' FrankenFS link paths under-enforce this: (1) ext4_link calls only ext4_reject_immutable (EXT4_IMMUTABLE_FL) and has NO EXT4_APPEND_FL check, so hardlinking an append-only file wrongly succeeds; (2) btrfs_link checks NEITHER immutable NOR append (BTRFS_INODE_IMMUTABLE=1<<6 / BTRFS_INODE_APPEND=1<<7), so hardlinking an immutable or append-only file wrongly succeeds. FIX: ext4_link rejects EXT4_APPEND_FL with EPERM (in addition to the existing immutable check); btrfs_link rejects link_target.flags & (BTRFS_INODE_IMMUTABLE|BTRFS_INODE_APPEND) with EPERM, placed before the nlink/EMLINK adjustment. Same audit-both-boundaries errno-parity class as bd-ilg79/bd-d9129/bd-a3fh8/bd-j12g7. Testable by injecting the flag on a file inode then attempting link -> expect EPERM (fails pre-fix: link succeeds).
close_reason: Fixed in 0b46ec62: ext4_link now rejects EXT4_APPEND_FL with EPERM (in addition to immutable); btrfs_link rejects BTRFS_INODE_IMMUTABLE|BTRFS_INODE_APPEND with EPERM before any mutation — matching the kernel's vfs_link. Tests: btrfs_link_to_immutable_or_append_is_eperm_bd_69ich + a link-to-append assertion added to immutable_and_append_attributes_enforced_on_metadata_ops_bd_hbld5 (whose comment had wrongly claimed append-only links were allowed). Full ffs-core 1082 green. NOTE follow-up: xattr_permission also rejects setxattr (MAY_WRITE) on append-only with EPERM — ext4/btrfs setxattr on append-only may be a separate gap (the bd-hbld5 comment also claimed xattr allowed on append); worth a check.

title: perf(btrfs): csum data writes from the in-memory buffer, not a device read-back (eliminate per-write read I/O + alloc)
description: btrfs_capture_data_extent_csums (per datasum data write, ffs-core ~18942) does btrfs_read_logical_into to READ BACK the just-written extent from the device + a vec![0; alloc_size] alloc, then csums it. For btrfs_emit_aligned_extent (the hot regular-write path) the caller ALREADY holds the exact sector-aligned bytes it just wrote (data, len==alloc_size, no padding), so the read-back returns byte-identical bytes — a redundant per-write read I/O + heap alloc + logical->physical map. Upstream csums the in-memory dirty page (no read-back); this is a vs-upstream gap. FIX: add Option<&[u8]> in-memory buffer param; emit_aligned passes Some(data) -> csum the buffer directly, skip read-back. Fall back to read-back for the materialize/re-insert callers (no buffer). Isomorphic: regular data round-trips so csum(data)==csum(read-back); btrfs-check csum tests (bd-x3fcu) + write-data-csum suites are the oracle. Removes one read + one alloc + one chunk-map per datasum write.
close_reason: btrfs_capture_data_extent_csums now takes Option<&[u8]>; emit-aligned (hot write path) csums the in-memory buffer directly, skipping the device read-back + vec![0;alloc_size] alloc + chunk-map (3aa8de1e). Materialize/re-insert callers pass None (keep read-back). Isomorphic: regular data round-trips, csum tree byte-identical; 321 ffs-core btrfs tests green (incl btrfs-check csum bd-x3fcu); clippy clean. Removes a per-write read I/O (vs-upstream gap; in-memory bench ~22.6ms vs ~30ms cross-worker, larger on disk-backed devices).

title: ffs-block: MemIoEngine lacks documented lock-order invariant (data → stats) and regression test
description:
Finding (via /deadlock-finder-and-fixer skill, NEW target): crates/ffs-block/src/io_engine.rs:247 has MemIoEngine = { data: Mutex<Vec<u8>>, stats: Mutex<IoEngineStats> }. submit_batch acquires data first (line 300), then stats inside the loop multiple times per op (line 301, 307, 319, 325, 337, 342). Stats is also acquired by stats() (line 355) and Debug fmt (line 293) WITHOUT holding data. The pattern is correct (data is the OUTER lock, stats is the INNER lock, never the reverse) but UNDOCUMENTED.

A future refactor that introduced a code path acquiring stats THEN data would create an AB-BA deadlock under contention. The Debug-fmt path takes only stats (safe); a refactor that added data-access to Debug-fmt would silently invert the order.

Pairs with bd-7zd94 (PersistentMvccStore lock-order), bd-bky2f (ShardedMvccStore), bd-pfv55 (FuseInodeLocks), bd-6owbg (FaultInjector + ThrottleInjector never-hold-both), bd-chmw4 (wal_writer atomic-rollback), bd-gqswx (commit_internal/rollback), bd-lebu5 (DurabilityNotifier invariants).

Acceptance: doc comment on MemIoEngine naming the data → stats lock-order invariant + the rule that any path holding both must acquire data FIRST. Plus a regression test that exercises high-contention concurrent submit_batch + stats() calls and asserts no deadlock + correct stats accumulation.
close_reason: done

(2) Regression test mem_io_engine_no_deadlock_under_concurrent_submit_and_stats with 4 writer threads (256 writes each) + 4 stats pollers running concurrently. Asserts no deadlock (joins return) and stats.writes == 1024 (4×256), proving the inner stats lock serialized correctly under the outer data lock. rch exit code 0.

title: perf(btrfs): the checksum-verify default was flipped ON 2026-08-15, invalidating the configuration-comparability of every banked mounted btrfs read row incl. the campaign's only WIN

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
FOUND 2026-08-15 by AzureBay while running the cold-cache row for
bd-btrfs-parallel-read-win-mechanism-iwzrx. This is a bank-integrity finding, not a perf number.

WHAT CHANGED, TODAY, IN TWO COMMITS:
  1c85fc23 00:15 correctness(btrfs): verify data checksums by default (bd-ntyuc)
           -> ffs-core OpenOptions::default() btrfs_verify_data_on_read: false -> TRUE (product default)
  e54146ee 00:28 perf(harness): parameterize btrfs checksum verification (bd-x78dw)
           -> ffs-mounted-kernel-bench Config default btrfs_verify_data_on_read: TRUE

WHY IT MATTERS: every banked mounted btrfs READ row was measured with verification OFF.
docs/MOUNTED_BTRFS_SCORECARD.md states it directly for the parallel-read row: 'this row's FUSE arms
did not [verify]' and 'the mount option ... is still off by default, so what this row measured is
unchanged'. As of 1c85fc23 that sentence is FALSE. The banked rows therefore describe a
configuration that no longer ships, and a NEW run of the same workload is not
configuration-comparable to them unless it passes --btrfs-verify-data-on-read false explicitly.

The affected rows include the campaign's ONLY honest_win: multi-file parallel read, banked
0.894290x and re-confirmed 0.893282x / 0.927352x FASTER than live kernel btrfs.

THE PROCESS PROBLEM, stated plainly: bd-btrfs-verify-default-decision-v81jt exists precisely to
decide this default, is P2 OPEN, and is explicitly BLOCKED on
bd-btrfs-parallel-read-win-mechanism-iwzrx producing the cost delta first. Its own text warned:
'flipping the default changes what every banked read row measured, including the campaign's only
WIN ... Doing that silently would be exactly the kind of configuration change that invalidates a
bank.' The default was flipped anyway, ~13 hours before this was noticed, while the deciding bead
sat blocked. bd-ntyuc's stated rationale was 'match kernel integrity contract ... retain explicit
opt-out only if later measured' -- i.e. ship first, measure later, which is the inverse of what
v81jt specified.

NOT ARGUING FOR A REVERT. Matching the kernel's integrity contract is very likely the right product
call, and correctness-by-default is defensible on its own terms. The defect is that it was done
without the measurement its own deciding bead was waiting on, and without re-scoping the rows it
invalidates.

WHAT THIS BEAD NEEDS:
  1. Correct the now-false 'still off by default' passage in docs/MOUNTED_BTRFS_SCORECARD.md.
  2. Re-scope every banked mounted btrfs read row as measured under verify=OFF, naming the flip
     commit -- re-scope, do not retract (same treatment as bd-4w2mf).
  3. Measure the cost: cold-cache and warm, verify on vs off, one ELF, same window. That number is
     what v81jt was blocked on and it is still not measured.

match the kernel integrity contract' followed by the pre-flip 'Opt-in to avoid a read-path
regression while the path matures'.

title: ext4 fast-commit recovery is verify-only: FC-only changes lost on mount after crash
description: FrankenFS's ext4 fast-commit replay (ffs_journal::replay_fast_commit) parses committed FC transactions into FcOperations, but apply_fast_commit_operations (ffs-core lib.rs ~3999) only VERIFIES each op against current metadata (verify_fast_commit_* read-only checks) — it never MUTATES the filesystem. Actual recovery is done solely by JBD2 full replay (maybe_replay_ext4_journal). So if an image crashed with changes that were fast-committed but not yet folded into a full JBD2 transaction, mounting it via FrankenFS recovers only to the last FULL JBD2 commit and SILENTLY LOSES the FC-only changes; real ext4 replays them. The code comment at lib.rs:2890 confirms the design ('filesystem state relies on JBD2 replay only'). Also: replay_fast_commit does not verify the ext4_fc_tail CRC32C (fc_crc) — harmless while verify-only, but required if/when ops are actually applied. SCOPE to close: implement FC-apply (mutate fs from FcOperation: AddRange/DelRange map extents, Create/Link/Unlink dir entries + nlink, InodeUpdate inode fields) AFTER tail-CRC verification, layered on top of JBD2 replay, transactional; reflink/snapshot-style corruption-sensitivity; validate against a kernel fast-commit image via btrfs... ext4 e2fsck. Multi-hour, dedicated session. Building blocks exist: FcOperation enum, the verify_fast_commit_* readers (mirror them for apply).
notes: InodeUpdate apply now e2fsck-validated for BOTH root (defaf7bb) + non-root regular-file (44d848f5) inodes — open_ext4_mke2fs now enable_writes so a test can create a file first. 988/988. ⚠️AddRange e2fsck E2E is FIXTURE-BLOCKED: the AddRange's physical block must be allocated in the block bitmap for e2fsck, and constructing a faithful 'crashed: block allocated+written but extent mapping lost' state (with correct bitmap/i_blocks) is too ext4-FC-semantics-dependent for a clean synthetic test. The AddRange single-leaf recovery is validated IN-MEMORY (fast_commit_external_single_leaf_recovery) + reuses the golden-tested ffs_btree::insert + has sound atomicity. ⚠️MVCC/RECOVERY INTERACTION (documented in the regular-file test): the apply writes DIRECT to dev (the from_device recovery path, no MVCC); on a writable test fs (enable_writes) reads go through the MVCC overlay and DON'T see the dev write — so e2fsck-on-device-snapshot is the authoritative check, not read-back. Real recovery runs pre-enable_writes (no MVCC) so this is a test artifact. ⭐bd-6nwjx STATUS: core 'verify-only' bug FIXED + e2fsck-validated for inline files + external single-leaf. REMAINING TAIL (real but lower-freq/harder data-loss): multi-leaf/depth-2 AddRange coordination + DelRange + Create/Link/Unlink dir-op applies (all still verify-only). RECOMMEND: pivot to fresh work; this tail is a P3-worthy dedicated follow-up.

title: ffs-block: FaultInjector + ThrottleInjector lack never-hold-both lock-ordering doc
description:
Finding (via /deadlock-finder-and-fixer skill, fourth visit,
different target): both `FaultInjector` and `ThrottleInjector`
(crates/ffs-block/src/lib.rs:4307, :4511) hold two `Mutex`es each
(`rules` + `log` for FaultInjector; `config` + `log` for
ThrottleInjector). Static audit confirms every callsite uses a
**never-hold-both** discipline:

  * `FaultInjector::check_fault` (l. 4367) acquires `rules`,
    explicitly drops it (`drop(rules)` on l. 4398), THEN acquires
    `log`. Never both held simultaneously.
  * `FaultInjector::reset` (l. 4360) acquires/releases `rules` and
    `log` sequentially.
  * `ThrottleInjector::apply_delay` (l. 4600) clones `config` from
    a brief `config.lock()` (released at end of expression), then
    later acquires `log.lock()` to push the record.
  * Both Debug impls acquire one Mutex per `.field()` call;
    successive `.field()` calls release their guards between calls.

There is NO function or doc currently holding both locks. But the
invariant is undocumented:

  1. **No struct-level doc comment** names the **never-hold-both**
     contract on either injector. A future contributor adding a
     "fail_and_log" combined function could nest `log.lock()` under
     `rules.lock()` and silently introduce a deadlock against any
     concurrent code path.
  2. **No regression test** exercises the lock acquisition paths
     under contention.

Same prevention pattern as bd-7zd94 (PersistentMvccStore),
bd-bky2f (ShardedMvccStore), bd-pfv55 (FuseInodeLocks). Difference:
those structs hold both locks (with a documented order); these
NEVER hold both — a stricter contract that's even easier to violate
silently.

Acceptance: doc blocks on both `FaultInjector` and `ThrottleInjector`
naming the **never-hold-both** invariant with rationale. Plus one
regression test per injector spawning concurrent fault/inject + log
+ reset workers with a watchdog timeout that catches any hang.
notes: Shipped: struct-level docs on FaultInjector + ThrottleInjector in crates/ffs-block/src/lib.rs naming the never-hold-both lock-ordering invariant (rules + log for FaultInjector; config + log for ThrottleInjector — neither lock is held while the other is acquired). Per-field doc on each Mutex annotates the constraint. Added two regression tests (fault_injector_concurrent_inject_and_reset_no_hang and throttle_injector_concurrent_apply_and_reset_no_hang) each spawning 4 concurrent workers (register/inject/log/reset) guarded by a 15s watchdog. Pairs with bd-7zd94 / bd-bky2f / bd-pfv55 (lock-order-fixed) — these are the stricter never-hold-both contract. Both tests pass in 0.05s via rch exec -- cargo test -p ffs-block --lib.

title: ffs-ondisk: ext4_casefold_{key,names_collide} lacks metamorphic relation tests
description:
Finding (via /testing-metamorphic skill, NEW target): ext4_casefold_key (crates/ffs-ondisk/src/ext4.rs:3331) and ext4_casefold_names_collide (l. 3336) implement the casefold collision contract used by lookup_in_dir_block_casefold for case-insensitive ext4 directories. The function has 4 hand-written unit tests but ZERO metamorphic-relation proptests. The contract should satisfy classic equivalence-relation laws plus idempotence and an ASCII case-substitution invariant — none of which are pinned.

Untested algebraic laws:
  * MR1 — Reflexivity: collide(x, x) MUST be true for ALL inputs (incl. invalid UTF-8, empty, long).
  * MR2 — Symmetry: collide(a, b) MUST equal collide(b, a).
  * MR3 — Idempotence of folding: key(key(name)) MUST equal key(name); folded output is stable under re-folding.
  * MR4 — Transitivity (via key equality): if key(a)==key(b) and key(b)==key(c), then key(a)==key(c) and collide(a,c) MUST be true.
  * MR5 — ASCII case-substitution invariance: for any ASCII bytestring, its uppercase variant MUST collide with itself.
  * MR6 — Diagnostics consistency: diagnostics(name).folded_key MUST equal key(name), and source_len MUST equal name.len().

Each MR catches a different class of regression: a determinism bug (e.g., a HashMap iteration leaking into the fold output) breaks MR1+MR3, a non-symmetric comparator breaks MR2, an unbalanced sharp-s expansion breaks MR3, an ASCII case bug breaks MR5, a divergence between diagnostics and the canonical key path breaks MR6.

Acceptance: 6 proptest cases co-located in the existing proptest! block at the end of crates/ffs-ondisk/src/ext4.rs that exercise these relations across UTF-8, invalid-UTF-8, and edge-case inputs.

title: EPIC: Killer Demo — Self-Healing Durability
description:
# EPIC: Killer Demo — Self-Healing Durability

## PURPOSE
Create a compelling, CI-executable demonstration of FrankenFS self-healing: flip random bits in blocks, show automatic repair using RaptorQ symbols, and output a human-readable repair ledger explaining exactly what was reconstructed. This is the "show, don't tell" proof of FrankenFS's core innovation.

## DEMO SCRIPT

### Setup (automated)
1. Create 128MB ext4 image with FrankenFS (RaptorQ enabled, 5% overhead)
2. Write 100 files with known content (photos, text, binaries)
3. Record BLAKE3 checksums for all files
4. Print: "Filesystem created: 100 files, all checksums verified"

### Corruption (visible to audience)
5. Print: "Injecting corruption: flipping random bits in 3% of blocks..."
6. Corrupt 3% of data blocks with random bit flips
7. Print block IDs and bit positions of corrupted blocks
8. Attempt to read files — show which files have corrupted bytes

### Repair (the magic moment)
9. Print: "Triggering self-healing scrub..."
10. Run scrub daemon (or explicit repair command)
11. Show real-time progress: "Scanning block group 1/32... corruption detected at block 1042... repairing with 4 symbols... OK"
12. Print: "Repair complete in 2.3 seconds"

### Verification (proof)
13. Read all 100 files, verify BLAKE3 checksums
14. Print: "All 100 files verified — zero data loss"
15. Print repair ledger: table of every repair action with timing, blocks, symbols used

### Output Format
```
=== FrankenFS Self-Healing Demo ===
Created: 100 files (128MB image, 5% RaptorQ overhead)
Corrupted: 47 blocks across 8 block groups (3% corruption rate)

Repair Results:
  Block Group  Corrupted  Repaired  Symbols Used  Time
  1            3          3         4             12ms
  4            8          8         12            34ms
  7            6          6         8             28ms
  ...
  Total        47         47        72            180ms

Verification: 100/100 files checksums match — ZERO DATA LOSS
Evidence ledger: 47 CorruptionDetected + 47 RepairSucceeded records
```

## REQUIREMENTS
- Must run without root (FUSE user mount)
- Must complete in < 30 seconds
- Must be deterministic (seeded corruption)
- Must be a single command: `cargo run --bin ffs-demo -- self-healing`
- Must work in CI (no GUI, no interactive input)

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] Demo runs successfully with single command
- [ ] All corrupted blocks repaired
- [ ] Repair ledger is human-readable and correct
- [ ] Demo completes in < 30 seconds
- [ ] Runs in CI without root
- [ ] Output suitable for README/blog post

## Success Criteria
1. All children closed
2. Demo runs with single command in < 30s
3. All corrupted blocks repaired (zero data loss)
4. Output suitable for README/blog post
5. CI-executable without root or FUSE
notes: DEPENDENCY NOTE: This demo is the capstone of the self-healing story. It depends on bd-15c.11 (5% corruption E2E test) which depends on the full scrub daemon pipeline. Do not attempt this until bd-15c.11 passes. The demo script should reuse the same test infrastructure but with human-readable output formatting. Consider adding a --verbose flag for technical audiences and a --summary flag for non-technical audiences.

title: perf(btrfs): binary-search the chunk map (map_logical_to_physical) — O(chunks)->O(log) per logical mapping
description: map_logical_to_physical (ffs-ondisk btrfs.rs ~567) LINEAR-scans the chunk list to find the chunk covering a logical address, on the HOTTEST path: every logical->physical mapping = every btrfs tree-node read + every data-block read. A large btrfs fs has hundreds-thousands of chunks (each data chunk <=1GB), so this is O(chunks) per read. Chunks cover DISJOINT logical ranges and the full list is sorted ascending by key.offset (walk_chunk_tree sorts it, ffs-btrfs ~6455), so the covering chunk is the last with key.offset<=logical -> partition_point O(log). Same pattern as bd-vzmis (ext4 extent resolution, 8.75x). Extract chunk_physical helper; LEN-GATE: binary for large (sorted) lists, keep linear for small bootstrap sys_chunk_array (correct regardless of order, cheap). Isomorphic: chunks non-overlapping so the binary candidate (pp-1) is the only possible cover. Bench: new ffs-ondisk benches/chunk_map.rs, N=1000 chunks, random lookups, linear vs map_logical_to_physical.
close_reason: Binary-searched map_logical_to_physical (6004515a): linear O(chunks) scan -> partition_point O(log) on the covering chunk; len-gated (>16 binary, small bootstrap linear); chunk_physical helper. Isomorphic (non-overlapping chunks -> binary candidate pp-1 is the only cover); 618 ffs-ondisk + 321 ffs-core btrfs tests green + chunk_map bench in-loop iso assert; clippy clean. A/B (chunk_map bench, 1024 lookups over 1000 chunks): linear 634us -> binary 62us = 10.2x. Hottest path (every logical->physical mapping = every tree-node + data-block read on large fs). Same lever as bd-vzmis.

title: btrfs commit fails 'node overflow: items' at scale: COW tree splits leaves by item COUNT not serialized byte size
description: FOUND via a new btrfs-check test creating 1000 empty files. btrfs_full_transaction_commit fails with Format("btrfs mutation: invalid config: node overflow: items") (ffs-btrfs/src/lib.rs:2238, leaf serialization into the fixed nodesize buffer). ROOT: InMemoryCowBtrfsTree (ffs-btrfs) splits leaves purely by item COUNT — insert_into_leaf at lib.rs:2692 splits only when items.len() > max_items, where max_items = (nodesize-101)/64 (set at lib.rs:4550) ASSUMES ~39 data bytes/item (25-byte descriptor + ~39 data = 64). Real items are larger (INODE_ITEM ~160B, DIR_ITEM name-dependent, inline EXTENT_DATA up to ~sectorsize). So a leaf can stay under max_items (count) yet exceed nodesize BYTES, and serialize_node overflows -> commit fails. IMPACT: FrankenFS btrfs cannot commit a filesystem with more than ~one-leaf's-worth of metadata (hundreds of small files, or fewer large-item files). All prior btrfs-check tests used few files (single leaf) so this was never hit. FIX (tractable, in ffs-btrfs, my lane): add a byte budget (nodesize - BTRFS_HEADER_SIZE 101) to InMemoryCowBtrfsTree and split a leaf when sum(BTRFS_ITEM_SIZE 25 + item.data.len()) > budget (in ADDITION to the max_items count cap, so the count-based unit tests with max_items=3 + tiny items + budget=usize::MAX stay unchanged); split at the byte-balanced index. Each item individually fits (inline capped < sectorsize by bd-jctlm), so a single byte-split always yields two fitting halves. Set the budget at each real-tree creation site from the actual nodesize; leave it usize::MAX for the count-only test trees. Regression: btrfs_many_files_multi_level_tree_passes_btrfs_check (1000 files -> commit -> btrfs check clean).
close_reason: Fixed in d84e1d26 (two coupled root causes). (1) InMemoryCowBtrfsTree split leaves by item COUNT only (max_items derived assuming ~39B/item) so leaves of larger items overflowed nodesize on serialize ('node overflow: items') -> added a per-leaf serialized-byte budget (nodesize-101) + byte-balanced split, defaulting usize::MAX so count-only test trees are unchanged; real trees set it from nodesize. (2) The node serializer wrote key_ptr[i].key = the CoW SEPARATOR (min of child[i+1]) + MAX_KEY for the last child, but btrfs requires key_ptr[i].key = min of child[i] -> every multi-leaf tree failed btrfs check 'Wrong key of child node/leaf'/'root dir not found' (latent: cause 1 blocked multi-leaf commits). Writeback now computes each child's subtree_min_key and passes child_min_keys to the serializer. Regression: btrfs_many_files_multi_level_tree_passes_btrfs_check (1000 files -> btrfs check clean). ffs-btrfs 335 + ffs-core 1036 green (incl. bd-iv5uy + random proptests), local btrfs-check suite clean, clippy clean. FrankenFS btrfs can now create+commit large multi-level filesystems that pass real btrfs check.

title: fix(ffs-ondisk): canonicalize btrfs superblock sys_chunk_array_size on serialize
description: BtrfsSuperblock::to_bytes currently writes the public sys_chunk_array_size field verbatim while independently truncating sys_chunk_array payload bytes to the BTRFS_SYS_CHUNK_ARRAY_MAX on-disk region. A caller with a stale length or oversized vector can therefore serialize bytes whose length field does not match the payload actually emitted, causing parse(to_bytes(sb)) to reject or return padded/truncated data under an internally inconsistent codec. Make to_bytes encode sys_chunk_array_size from the serialized payload length (min(vec.len(), max)) and add a proptest covering stale/oversized size fields so parse(to_bytes(sb)) returns the canonical serialized prefix and matching size. Pure ondisk correctness/parity hardening.
close_reason: Fixed BtrfsSuperblock::to_bytes to serialize sys_chunk_array_size from the payload length actually emitted (min(sys_chunk_array.len(), 2048)) instead of trusting a stale public field. Added btrfs_proptest_superblock_to_bytes_canonicalizes_sys_chunk_array_size covering stale and oversized size fields, asserting parse(to_bytes(sb)) re-parses with the canonical prefix and matching size. title: btrfs: truncate-down to an unaligned size and clone/reflink carve can still produce non-sector-aligned extents (bd-7mi0p write path done)
description: Follow-on to bd-7mi0p (write path fixed + validated by btrfs check in 9b99f16f via the sector-aligned RMW model). Two callers of btrfs_remove_overlapping_extent_data still pass UNALIGNED boundaries, so they can re-create non-sector-aligned extents that btrfs check would reject: (1) btrfs_setattr truncate-down calls btrfs_remove_overlapping_extent_data(cx, alloc, canonical, size, u64::MAX) with an unaligned  — the extent containing  is split at the unaligned boundary, re-inserting a left segment [extent_start, size) of unaligned length (num_bytes unaligned). Correct behavior: align the trim to round_up(size, sectorsize), drop only whole sectors fully past EOF, and zero the [size, aligned_size) tail of the EOF sector via RMW (so a later extend reads zeros, matching the in-memory model). (2) btrfs_clone_file_range_data carves partial reflinked extents with new_num_bytes = overlap_end - overlap_start (unaligned). No CI test currently commits a write+truncate or clone image to btrfs check, so this is uncaught; add such tests. NOTE: content correctness is unaffected today (reads cap by i_size; proptests are byte-exact and green) — this is on-disk extent-format parity only. The W60 deep re-scope on bd-7mi0p lists the full coupled set; items 1/2/3/5 for the write path are done, these are the remaining truncate/clone tails.
notes: TRUNCATE PART DONE + validated (a4a7239a): btrfs_setattr truncate-down now trims at the sector boundary above the EOF sector and rewrites that sector with head preserved + [size,aligned) tail zeroed (hole/all-zero head stays a hole). New shared helper btrfs_emit_aligned_extent (used by write RMW + truncate). Test btrfs_truncate_to_unaligned_size_passes_btrfs_check_bd_70gyh passes REAL btrfs check (BTRFS_CHECK_RAN ok=true) + btrfs_truncate_down_zeroes_eof_sector_tail. REMAINING: clone/reflink carve (btrfs_clone_file_range_data new_num_bytes = overlap_end-overlap_start can be unaligned; carved extent_offset/num_bytes must be sector-aligned). Note reflinks SHARE the disk extent, so the carve fix differs from write/truncate (adjust extent_offset + num_bytes on the shared extent, no new alloc). Verify reachability via FICLONERANGE before prioritizing.
close_reason: Both parts done. Truncate-down: a4a7239a (sector-align EOF rewrite). Clone/reflink: dd26c7da — clone_file_range enforces kernel remap_check_alignment (EINVAL unless src/dest offsets aligned and len aligned-or-reaches-src-EOF); the carve rounds the window up to the sector grid so shared dst extents stay aligned, with logical dest_end for i_size. Updated bd-iypb9 inline test to assert EINVAL (kernel parity) + whole-file inline reflink. Validated by REAL btrfs check (clone_file_range_unaligned_eof_tail_passes_btrfs_check_bd_70gyh, RAN ok=true) + truncate test. The bd-7mi0p sector-aligned extent model is now complete + btrfs-check-clean across write, truncate, AND clone. Full ffs-core 1079 green.

title: btrfs out-of-space surfaces as EINVAL instead of ENOSPC (errno parity)
description: btrfs_mutation_to_ffs (ffs-core lib.rs ~12395) routed BtrfsMutationError::NoSpace through the catch-all _ => FfsError::Format arm, and FfsError::Format maps to EINVAL (22) in to_errno. So a btrfs write/fallocate/clone/create that exhausts the filesystem returned EINVAL to userspace instead of ENOSPC (28) — real Linux btrfs returns ENOSPC, and programs key off it to handle disk-full. FfsError::NoSpace already exists and maps to ENOSPC (ext4 paths use it correctly); btrfs paths going through btrfs_mutation_to_ffs did not. Inconsistent even within btrfs (the tree-log fallback at ~19503 special-cases NoSpace). FIX: map BtrfsMutationError::NoSpace => FfsError::NoSpace. Regression: fill the 512KiB fsops image and assert the next btrfs write's to_errno()==ENOSPC. Surfaced while root-causing bd-lf4fa (flaky reflink proptest ENOSPC).

title: correctness(btrfs): reflink diverges from its reference model — 122 bytes wrong at offset 184198, reproducible on clean HEAD at PROPTEST_CASES=512
description:
`tests::btrfs_reflink_random_matches_reference_model` (crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs) finds a real
data divergence between the btrfs reflink implementation and its reference model. It is NOT
flaky-by-noise: it is a latent correctness bug that the default proptest case count usually
fails to reach.

REPRODUCED ON CLEAN HEAD, DETERMINISTICALLY ENOUGH TO ACT ON (PlumRiver, 2026-08-06):

  PROPTEST_CASES=512 cargo test -p ffs-core --lib -- btrfs_reflink_random_matches_reference_model

  clean HEAD (91a6cdac + peers):  FAILED
    "f0 content diverged step 20: 122 bytes differ (first at 184198)"
  with the bd-cjqhh btrfs commit fix applied: FAILED
    "f0 content diverged step 20: 122 bytes differ (first at 184198)"

Byte-for-byte the same divergence on both arms, so it is independent of bd-cjqhh. At the default
case count it passes: 15 consecutive runs, 0 failures. Each 512-case run takes ~250 s.

An earlier remote run also caught it at default cases with a different counterexample
("f2 content diverged step 13: 46357 bytes differ, first at 94208"), which is why this was
initially suspected as a bd-cjqhh regression. It is not — the base rate is simply low enough that
a single run is uninformative either way.

WHY THIS MATTERS: reflink is a data-integrity surface. A divergence from the reference model means
a reflinked file can read back bytes that differ from what the model says were written, which is
the same class of defect as bd-cjqhh (silent wrong data) rather than a performance or API issue.
122 bytes at a 184198 offset suggests a boundary case in extent splitting or the shared-extent
copy path rather than wholesale corruption.

WHAT TO DO
1. Reproduce with PROPTEST_CASES=512 (or higher) and let proptest shrink fully — raise
   PROPTEST_MAX_SHRINK_ITERS well above 192, since the remote run aborted shrinking at that limit
   and reported a minimal input that was still large.
2. Commit the shrunk counterexample to crates/ffs-core/proptest-regressions/lib.txt so it replays
   deterministically. That directory exists but is UNTRACKED (git ls-files returns nothing) and its
   only file dates from 2026-07-02 — so every counterexample proptest has ever found in this crate
   has been discarded. Tracking it is cheap and would have caught this months ago.
3. Fix, and keep the regression entry.

NOTE FOR ANYONE READING THE ffs-core SUITE: it currently has TWO pre-existing failures on clean
HEAD, neither caused by recent work — this one (at depth) and
`fast_commit_del_range_apply_punches_and_frees_passes_e2fsck` (at default cases). A memory note
claiming "2 fails pre-existing" was right about the count but I verified it rather than trusting
it, and the membership is not what a single run suggests.
close_reason: Fixed in 7fac4779: extent splits reference the same disk extent instead of copying, removing the allocation failure mode. Reflink proptest passes at PROPTEST_CASES=512; btrfs check accepts partial overwrites; refs 1->2 pinned for the two-remnant case; bd-cjqhh's mounted 64 MiB durability gate still passes. Remote: ffs-btrfs 381/0, ffs-core 1193 passed with only the pre-existing ext4 fast-commit failure.

comments.author: PlumRiver
comments.text:
PROGRESS (PlumRiver, 2026-08-06): now REPRODUCIBLE DETERMINISTICALLY, and two candidate
mechanisms ruled out by test. NOT FIXED.

LANDED in b11a31f4: `.gitignore` no longer ignores `proptest-regressions/`. That directory was
listed under "ephemeral files" and is the opposite — proptest replays saved seeds before novel
cases, so tracking it turns this from a ~never-at-default-cases failure into a 39-second
deterministic one:

  cargo test -p ffs-core --lib -- btrfs_reflink_random_matches_reference_model
  -> f2 content diverged step 13: 46357 bytes differ (first at 94208)

Note `cargo test -p ffs-core` now fails deterministically as a result. Intended: the suite was
already red on clean HEAD (fast_commit_del_range...), so this surfaces a hidden data-integrity
bug rather than breaking a green suite.

THE SHRUNK COUNTEREXAMPLE, DECODED. `PROPTEST_CASES=512 PROPTEST_MAX_SHRINK_ITERS=100000` shrank
to 21 ops (it could not go below that), failing at step 20 with "f0 content diverged: 122 bytes
differ (first at 184198)". Decoding the ops against the test's own arithmetic:

  step 18: clone f2[73728 .. +77824] -> f0 @106496   => shared region ends at EXACTLY 184320
  step 20: write f0 @153878 len 38635               => covers 153878..192513, i.e. the whole
                                                        tail of that shared region and past it
  divergence: 184198..184320 = the LAST 122 BYTES of the cloned region

So a write that fully covered a shared region's tail left the final 122 bytes reading as the old
shared contents. 184320 is block-aligned (45 x 4096); 184198 is not. The other observed
counterexample has the same shape from the other side: write f2 @97933 (mid-block) corrupts from
94208, the start of that same block, i.e. a partial-block boundary next to shared data.

TWO MECHANISMS RULED OUT BY TEST (both now committed as coverage in ffs-core, both PASS, so
neither is the bug):
- `btrfs_partial_write_over_shared_extent_preserves_head_bd_72tn8` — clone 8 blocks, then write
  mid-block into the shared region. Head preserved, source untouched. So plain COW
  read-modify-write over a shared extent is correct.
- `btrfs_write_over_tail_of_shared_region_leaves_no_stale_bytes_bd_72tn8` — reconstructs the
  counterexample's exact geometry (unaligned 163841-byte source, clone src@73728 len 77824 to
  dst@106496 ending at 184320, then write @153878 len 38635). PASSES. So the geometry alone is
  not sufficient; the bug needs more of the 21-op history — most likely a specific extent layout
  in f0 built by the earlier writes/clones/truncate, not the final clone+write pair.

WHERE I WOULD LOOK NEXT
`btrfs_remove_overlapping_extent_data` (crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs) is the overwrite-split path
and the strongest suspect, specifically its bounded scan window. It finds the lowest candidate
extent via `floor_key(range_start)` and scans `[floor, range_end]`, justified by a comment that
"file extents are non-overlapping, so any earlier extent ends before the floor starts". That
invariant is what a clone can plausibly break or blur — a cloned EXTENT_DATA carries an `offset`
into a shared extent and its own `num_bytes`, so `btrfs_extent_logical_len` and the key offset
are the only things establishing coverage. If any extent's key offset is below the floor while
its logical end reaches into the range, the scan misses it and its bytes survive the overwrite —
which is exactly the observed symptom (stale bytes at the END of a region, in a 122-byte tail).
Worth dumping f0's full EXTENT_DATA list immediately before step 20 and checking it for
overlap/ordering violations before reading more code.

NOT ATTEMPTED YET: replaying the 21 ops as a standalone test and bisecting by deleting ops. That
is the mechanical path to a truly minimal case and is what I would do next if the extent-dump
inspection does not immediately show the violation.

comments.author: PlumRiver
comments.text:
FIRST BUG FOUND AND FIXED (PlumRiver, 2026-08-06, 241093de). A SECOND, DISTINCT ONE REMAINS —
this bead stays open for it.

=== FIXED: write was not atomic on ENOSPC ===
`btrfs_write` removed the extents overlapping the write range and only then allocated the
replacement. `btrfs_emit_aligned_extent` rolls back its own partial work; nothing undid the
removal. So a write that ran out of space returned ENOSPC with the old data already destroyed,
i_size untouched, and the range reading back as zeros — silent loss on an error the caller is
entitled to treat as "nothing happened". Fixed by reserving the extent BEFORE the removal
(new `btrfs_emit_aligned_extent_at` takes the reservation; the old entry point still allocates
then delegates). Gate: `btrfs_write_that_hits_enospc_leaves_the_file_unchanged_bd_72tn8`, which
before the fix reported "destroyed 8192 bytes, first at 24576".

HOW IT WAS FOUND, because the method generalises: the read-back showed ZEROS where the model
held DATA. That meant the failing op was one the model deliberately SKIPPED (its ENOSPC branch),
not one that wrote wrong bytes — which inverted the obvious reading of "reflink copies the wrong
data" and pointed at write atomicity. A fiemap dump confirmed the extent at logical=180224 was
present before the failing write and gone after. The 21-op counterexample from the 512-case
shrink now passes.

=== STILL BROKEN: second counterexample, different mechanism ===
`btrfs_reflink_random_matches_reference_model` still fails on the OTHER saved seed
(cc afa994a8... in crates/ffs-core/proptest-regressions/lib.txt):

  f2 content diverged step 13: 46357 bytes differ (first at 94208)
  got  = [0, 0, 0, ...]      want = [251, 251, 251, ...]

Replaying its 14 ops with a fiemap dump:

  step 11: CLONE f1[4096..147456] -> f2@57344 len=143360   => f2 shared region 57344..200704
  step 13: write f2 @97933 len 7678                        => aligned range starts at 94208
  f2 fiemap AFTER: 24576(+32768) 81920(+12288) 147456(+8192, SHARED|LAST)
                   => a HOLE from 94208 to 147456, and f2's size is 140565

So the write at 97933 left NO extent covering its own range, and destroyed everything from the
aligned floor 94208 to 147456. 94208 = 81920+12288, i.e. exactly where the preceding extent ends.
The write's data is missing too, so this is not the ENOSPC path — the operation reported success
and still dropped the region.

STRONGEST HYPOTHESIS, UNVERIFIED: this is the SHARED-extent remnant re-insert inside
`btrfs_remove_overlapping_extent_data`. Removing a shared extent drops only this inode's
EXTENT_DATA_REF and re-inserts the non-overlapping left/right parts as freshly materialized
copies. That path has an explicit "skip all-zero data" optimisation. If the materialization of a
SHARED remnant reads back as zeros (rather than the shared extent's real bytes), the remnant is
silently skipped and becomes a hole — which is exactly the observed shape: a hole spanning from
the aligned floor to the start of the next surviving SHARED extent. Check
`btrfs_materialize_extent` on a shared (refs>1) extent whose `extent_offset` is non-zero before
reading further code.

REPRODUCE (deterministic, ~39 s, no proptest search needed):
  cargo test -p ffs-core --lib -- btrfs_reflink_random_matches_reference_model
The saved seeds are now tracked (b11a31f4), so this replays for everyone.

The diagnostic replay harness — the 14/21 ops hardcoded, with fiemap dumps and got/want context
at the divergence — is NOT committed (it is scaffolding, and the proptest already gates this). It
is reproducible in ~5 minutes by injecting the ops list next to `open_writable_btrfs` and calling
`btrfs_fiemap` at the failing step; that is how both dumps above were produced.

comments.author: PlumRiver
comments.text:
SECOND COUNTEREXAMPLE: MECHANISM FULLY IDENTIFIED, LOSS REDUCED 46357 -> 8192 BYTES, NOT CLOSED.
(PlumRiver, 2026-08-06, 9d64f4a1.) Bead stays open.

IT WAS NEVER A REFLINK COPY BUG. Both counterexamples are the same defect class as the first:
an operation that fails with ENOSPC has already destroyed data. The instrumented replay settles
it — step 13 prints:

  step 13 WRITE f2@97933 len=7678 val=57 -> Err("no space left on device")

and the model had correctly SKIPPED that op, so `want` held the pre-write (cloned) bytes and
`got` held zeros. The "reflink diverges from its reference model" framing in this bead's title
is wrong; reflink is only how the shared extents that get split are created.

THE ALLOCATING SPLIT. `btrfs_remove_overlapping_extent_data` deletes an overlapping extent,
frees its reference, then rebuilds the non-overlapping head/tail as fresh private copies.
Rebuilding allocates. Before/after fiemap of f2 around the failing write:

  BEFORE  24576(+32768)  81920(+20480 SHARED)  102400(+40960 SHARED)  147456(+8192 SHARED|LAST)
  AFTER   24576(+32768)  81920(+12288)                                147456(+8192 SHARED|LAST)

The first extent split cleanly (left remnant 81920..94208 rebuilt at a NEW physical address —
it allocated). The second extent was deleted and its right remnant 106496..143360 was never
rebuilt: `RIGHT REMNANT FAILED at 106496 len 36864: no space left on device`.

A BYTE-COUNTING PRE-FLIGHT DOES NOT WORK — I implemented it and it does not fire:

  PREFLIGHT remnant=49152 freed=61440 budget=135168   <- passes
  RIGHT REMNANT FAILED at 106496 len 36864: no space left on device

`total_free` is 73728 with a 36864-byte request. Each remnant needs a CONTIGUOUS run and the
free space is fragmented, so no sum-of-bytes check can predict the allocator. That approach was
removed rather than shipped.

LANDED INSTEAD (9d64f4a1): hold the original's disk reference until BOTH remnants are in place,
and on failure undo any remnant already inserted and re-insert the original item verbatim. Not
freeing during that window is what makes the prior state restorable.

REMAINING GAP, EXACTLY. The rollback is per-extent; the removal walks several. When a later
extent's remnant fails, earlier extents are already fully processed and their overlap regions
are legitimately gone — but the caller's write then fails, so those bytes are lost with nothing
written in their place. The counterexample now loses precisely the first extent's overlap,
[94208, 102400) = 8192 bytes.

TWO WAYS TO CLOSE IT:
(a) Roll back the WHOLE removal, not one extent at a time. Straightforward but grows an
    already-delicate undo path, and every added rollback step is itself a failure site.
(b) MAKE SPLITS NOT ALLOCATE. A split should emit two EXTENT_DATA items pointing at the SAME
    disk extent with adjusted extent_offset/num_bytes, which is what the kernel does. No copy,
    no allocation, no failure mode to recover from — and it also removes the pointless data
    copy that makes every overwrite-split more expensive than it should be. This is the right
    fix and is why I stopped rather than growing the rollback further.

Recommend (b). It is a real change to extent-split semantics and refcounting, so it wants a
fresh turn with room to test refcounts properly, not a tail-end patch.

REPRODUCE: cargo test -p ffs-core --lib -- btrfs_reflink_random_matches_reference_model  (~30 s,
seeds tracked as of b11a31f4). The diagnostic replay harness is scaffolding and is not committed;
the recipe is in the previous comment.

comments.author: PlumRiver
comments.text:
CLOSED by 7fac4779 (PlumRiver, 2026-08-06). Option (b) implemented: extent splits now emit two
EXTENT_DATA items that are VIEWS onto the same disk extent, inheriting the disk location, length,
ram_bytes and compression and narrowing only extent_offset/num_bytes. No read, no allocation.

THE TITLE OF THIS BEAD WAS WRONG AND IS WORTH CORRECTING FOR THE RECORD. Reflink did not
"diverge from its reference model". Both counterexamples were the same defect class as bd-cjqhh:
an operation that failed with ENOSPC had already destroyed data. The instrumented replay settled
it — the failing op printed `Err("no space left on device")` and the model had correctly SKIPPED
it, so `want` held the pre-write bytes and `got` held zeros. Reflink was only how the shared
extents being split came to exist.

THREE FIXES, IN ORDER, EACH MEASURED:
1. 241093de — write reserved its replacement extent BEFORE removing what it replaced. Fixed the
   first counterexample.
2. 9d64f4a1 — the removal holds the original's disk reference until both remnants are rebuilt,
   and rolls back on failure. Reduced the second counterexample's loss 46357 -> 8192 bytes. A
   byte-counting pre-flight was tried first and REMOVED: it does not fire, because each remnant
   needs a CONTIGUOUS run and the free space is fragmented (`remnant=49152 freed=61440
   budget=135168` passed, then a 36864-byte insert still failed).
3. 7fac4779 — splits stop allocating at all. Closes it.

REFCOUNT WORK, which is where the first attempt at (b) was wrong. Both halves resolve to the SAME
backref key (file_offset minus extent_offset is invariant across the split), so the count follows
the number of items: 1 surviving half inherits the reference, 2 halves add one, 0 halves drop it.
Emitting that second reference exposed a real gap in ffs-btrfs: `add_data_extent_ref` merged into
a matching KEYED EXTENT_DATA_REF but not into the INLINE one `insert_data_extent_item` writes, so
it appended a duplicate and btrfs check rejected it with "Extent back ref already exists ...
referencer count mismatch (root 5 owner 257 offset 0) wanted 1 have 2". btrfs wants one record
with count 2. Fixed in both directions — add merges into the inline ref, remove decrements an
inline count above 1 instead of draining it.

ONE TEST'S EXPECTATION CHANGED, AND NOT TO GO GREEN.
`btrfs_overwrite_drops_shared_extent_ref_bd_xkvcm` asserted refs 2 -> 1 after a PARTIAL overwrite.
That encoded the old copying behaviour (the head became a private extent, so this inode's
reference was dropped). Under a reference split the head remains a view of the shared extent and
inherits the reference, so 2 is correct. bd-xkvcm's real property — never FREE an extent another
holder references — is untouched, and the test now ALSO covers a TOTAL overwrite, where nothing
survives and the ref still drops 2 -> 1. Without that added case the assertion would no longer
exercise the drop path at all, which would have been a genuine weakening.

VERIFICATION
- btrfs_reflink_random_matches_reference_model passes, including PROPTEST_CASES=512.
- btrfs check (real btrfs-progs) accepts a partial overwrite — the arbiter that caught the
  duplicate-backref mistake and the reason the first attempt did not ship.
- New btrfs_middle_overwrite_leaves_two_views_of_one_extent_bd_72tn8 pins refs 1 -> 2 for the
  two-remnant case, because the btrfs-check test RETURNS SILENTLY when btrfs-progs is missing and
  would not have caught it on such a host.
- bd-cjqhh's mounted 64 MiB durability gate re-run after this change: fsync OK, every chunk
  byte-identical across unmount and remount. The P0 fix is intact.
- Remote (RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE, vmi1149989): ffs-btrfs 381/0; ffs-core 1193 passed, 1 failed —
  `fast_commit_del_range_apply_punches_and_frees_passes_e2fsck`, pre-existing on clean HEAD and
  ext4-only, tracked separately.
- clippy --no-deps -D warnings: ffs-core 122 sites vs 123 baseline, ffs-btrfs 20 = baseline.

SIDE EFFECT WORTH KNOWING: overwrite-splits no longer read and re-write the surrounding data, so
every partial overwrite of a large extent does strictly less I/O than before. I am deliberately
NOT quoting a speedup: the only before/after timing I have is a 512-case proptest run that went
250.68s -> 77.69s, and the slow side included proptest shrinking after its failure, so the
comparison is confounded. The copy is gone by construction; the magnitude is unmeasured.

comments.author: PlumRiver
comments.text:
RESIDUAL 8192-BYTE LOSS: CLOSED, and the closure rests on a structural change rather than a new
rollback. Verified by negative control, not by inference. (PlumRiver, 2026-08-06, 1e93977c.)

The residual came from the removal walking several extents: a per-extent rollback (9d64f4a1) could
not help when a LATER extent's remnant allocation failed, because earlier extents were already
fully processed and their overlap regions were gone. Splitting by reference (7fac4779) deleted the
failure site instead of recovering from it — remnants are now views onto the same disk extent, so
the removal allocates nothing and has nothing left to fail on. The only allocation in the whole
write path is the write's own extent, reserved before anything is destroyed (241093de).

WHAT GATES IT, confirmed by disabling the reference split and re-running:
  btrfs_middle_overwrite_leaves_two_views_of_one_extent_bd_72tn8  -> FAILS with the split
  disabled ("a None here means the EXTENT_ITEM was FREED"), because the old path freed the
  original and gave each half a fresh private extent. This is the real gate.

WHAT DOES NOT GATE IT, and is now labelled as such in its own doc comment:
  btrfs_failed_multi_extent_write_destroys_nothing_bd_72tn8 -> PASSES with the split disabled.
  I wrote it for the residual and it does not reproduce it: the write covers its extents
  completely, so they leave no remnants, so the old path had nothing to allocate. Reproducing the
  residual needs the write's own reservation to SUCCEED while a later extent's remnant allocation
  FAILS — a narrow space window I could not construct deterministically. It is kept as coverage
  and is explicitly not presented as a regression gate. Calling it one would have been a false
  claim about what is protected.

EMPIRICAL BACKSTOP: btrfs_reflink_random_matches_reference_model passes at PROPTEST_CASES=512,
the depth that originally found this, with the seeds now tracked so both counterexamples replay.

FULL CLASS STATUS — "an operation that fails with ENOSPC has already destroyed data":
  write reserves before removing                                241093de  CLOSED
  removal holds the original ref until remnants land, rolls back 9d64f4a1  CLOSED
  removal allocates at all                                      7fac4779  ELIMINATED
No known member of this class remains open in the btrfs write path.

ffs-core 1195 passed, 1 failed (fast_commit_del_range..., pre-existing, ext4-only). clippy
--no-deps -D warnings 122 sites = baseline; fmt clean. Verified in an isolated checkout of HEAD
because the shared worktree does not build: a peer's in-flight cache extraction leaves
crates/ffs-block/src/lib.rs:2257 unparseable.

comments.author: PlumRiver
comments.text:
=====================================================================
CLASS CLOSED: "an operation that fails with ENOSPC has already destroyed data"
=====================================================================
This is a CLASS CLOSURE, not three bugs that happened to get fixed. Recording the enumeration so
a future reader knows the search was exhaustive rather than opportunistic.

THE CLASS. In a copy-on-write filesystem, any path that destroys existing state before it has
secured the replacement can fail after the destruction and report a RECOVERABLE error. ENOSPC is
the archetype because callers are entitled to read it as "nothing happened". Every member of this
class is silent data loss wearing an error code that says otherwise.

THE ENUMERATION. Three sites in the btrfs write path could destroy before securing. All three are
now eliminated:

  1. THE WRITE ITSELF removed the extents it was replacing, then allocated.
     -> 241093de: reserve the replacement extent BEFORE the removal; free the reservation if the
        removal then fails. CLOSED.

  2. THE REMOVAL freed the original's disk reference, then rebuilt the non-overlapping head/tail
     as fresh private copies — which allocates.
     -> 9d64f4a1: hold the original's reference until both remnants are in place, and roll back
        (undo any inserted remnant, re-insert the original verbatim) on failure. CLOSED.

  3. THE REMOVAL ALLOCATED AT ALL. Rollback was per-extent and the removal walks several, so a
     later extent's failure still left earlier extents' overlap regions gone.
     -> 7fac4779: splits emit two EXTENT_DATA items that are VIEWS onto the same disk extent
        (narrowing extent_offset/num_bytes only). No read, no allocation. ELIMINATED — the
        failure site is deleted, not made recoverable.

WHY THE ENUMERATION IS BELIEVED COMPLETE. After (3) the only allocation remaining anywhere in the
write path is the write's own extent, and (1) reserves that before anything is destroyed. There
is no other site that mutates-then-allocates: the prealloc remnant path re-inserts reservations
without allocating, holes and inline extents are handled without a disk allocation, and the
truncate path's EOF-sector rewrite reads and re-emits within space it already holds. NO KNOWN
MEMBER OF THIS CLASS REMAINS OPEN IN THE BTRFS WRITE PATH.

THE BACKSTOP, so the claim is not purely structural: btrfs_reflink_random_matches_reference_model
passes at PROPTEST_CASES=512 — the depth that originally surfaced this — with BOTH counterexample
seeds now tracked in crates/ffs-core/proptest-regressions/ (b11a31f4), so each replays
deterministically for everyone instead of resurfacing as flakiness. That directory was gitignored
as "ephemeral"; every counterexample this repo ever found had been discarded.

WHAT GATES EACH FIX, verified by negative control rather than assumed:
  btrfs_write_that_hits_enospc_leaves_the_file_unchanged_bd_72tn8       gates (1)
  btrfs_middle_overwrite_leaves_two_views_of_one_extent_bd_72tn8        gates (3); FAILS with the
    reference split disabled, because the old path freed the original extent
  btrfs_failed_multi_extent_write_destroys_nothing_bd_72tn8             COVERAGE ONLY — passes
    with the fix disabled, labelled as such in its own doc comment, NOT a gate for (2)/(3)

HOW THIS CLASS WAS FOUND, because the method transfers. The symptom read as a reflink bug: a
reflinked file returning bytes that were never written to it. The inversion was in the VALUES —
`got` held zeros where the model held DATA, which meant the failing operation was one the model
had deliberately SKIPPED on its ENOSPC branch, not one that wrote wrong bytes. A fiemap dump then
showed the extent present before the failing write and gone after. Any "wrong data" report where
the observed value is ZERO and the expected value is REAL should be checked for a failed-and-
destructive operation before the read path is suspected.

SIBLING BUG, SAME REPO, SAME SHAPE: bd-cjqhh (P0) — the durable commit built leaves it could not
serialize, so fsync returned EINVAL and the unmount flush failed identically, meaning data above
~18 MiB per transaction was never persisted. Different mechanism, same lesson: the error the
caller saw did not describe what had already happened to their data.
