title: Publish operator runbook for advisory vs authoritative readiness evidence
description:
## Background
The lab will add useful advisory reports, but docs must teach future operators and agents exactly how those differ from real xfstests and large-host swarm evidence.

## Implementation
Update the relevant operator docs and harness README sections to explain advisory lab artifacts, allowed uses, forbidden promotions, transition steps to permissioned runs, and how to read the readiness dashboard/truth graph. Add a docs drift check or harness test where practical so wording cannot claim simulated evidence is product-ready.

## Risks
Docs that are too optimistic can recreate the exact readiness-promotion risk this backlog is trying to reduce. Keep wording tied to release-gate states and proof-bundle claim effects.

## Acceptance
Docs include command examples, artifact paths, explicit no-permissioned-execution guarantees, and a table mapping advisory artifact types to allowed/forbidden claim effects. A unit or harness test rejects forbidden wording such as simulated evidence marking xfstests or swarm responsiveness validated.
close_reason: Completed: documented advisory vs authoritative readiness evidence boundaries and added a runbook drift test.

title: MR proptests for parse_dir_items round-trip + multi-entry concat
description: Found via /testing-metamorphic audit. ffs_btrfs::parse_dir_items (lib.rs:1019) walks variable-length DIR_ITEM/DIR_INDEX entries (30-byte header + name_len + value_len bytes) and is on the hot path of every directory lookup and readdir. The existing dir_item_round_trip / dir_item_round_trip_directory / dir_item_multiple_entries_concatenated tests cover three fixed inputs total. No proptest sweeps over arbitrary (objectid, key_type, key_offset, file_type, name) tuples and no proptest exercises N-entry concatenation invariance. A regression that broke the cursor advance (cur = name_end since dir_items have no value payload, data_len must equal 0) or stopped respecting variable-length name boundaries would corrupt every multi-collision directory walk but pass the fixed tests. Fix: add proptest!() block with three MRs paralleling bd-pt9pk for parse_inode_refs — (1) single-entry round-trip; (2) multi-entry concatenation 2..=8; (3) inner-truncation rejection.
close_reason: completed

title: Implement ext4 inline data read support
close_reason: Implemented ext4 inline data read support: (1) Added read_ext4_inline_data() method that reads file content from inode extent_bytes (60 bytes) + xattr_ibody continuation. (2) Added inline data check in FsOps::read() ext4 path — checks EXT4_INLINE_DATA_FL before extent tree resolution. (3) Removed INLINE_DATA from REJECTED_V1 incompat set so images with inline data can mount. 471 ffs-core + 360 ffs-ondisk tests pass.

title: perf(repair): SIMD GF(256) multiply-XOR kernel for LRC encode — nibble-split swizzle_dyn replaces per-byte LUT gather
close_reason: REJECTED (measured regression, reverted). Portable-SIMD nibble-split (swizzle_dyn/PSHUFB) GF(256) mul-XOR for LRC encode REGRESSED 4.6x: scalar LUT gather 158.94us vs SIMD 735.57us on lrc_encode_global_64blocks_8parity. Root cause: project ships generic x86-64 (release profile opt-level=z, no target-cpu/target-feature), so std::simd swizzle_dyn lowers to a SCALAR EMULATION (no SSSE3/AVX2 baseline). Runtime AVX2 dispatch needs #[target_feature]=unsafe, forbidden by #![forbid(unsafe_code)]. The existing scalar 256-entry mul_row gather is already optimal for this target (simple indexed load). Lesson: portable-SIMD shuffles need a guaranteed target-feature baseline to win; not available here. Isomorphism was proven (equivalence test passed, 445 tests green) — only perf failed. Fully reverted, no commit shipped.

description: Mock-code-finder follow-up after source-aware ready work was permission-gated or foreign: MountHandle::wait in crates/ffs-fuse/src/lib.rs polls the shutdown/session state with a hard-coded 100ms std::thread::sleep, making shutdown acknowledgement sluggish and hiding the poll contract from tests. Replace the magic sleep with a named short poll interval and tighten the existing wait test so shutdown-trigger latency stays bounded without relying on a blind 100ms delay. Acceptance: MountHandle::wait no longer contains an inline 100ms sleep; the poll interval is named and small; mount_handle_wait_returns_on_shutdown proves prompt return with a bounded elapsed assertion; focused ffs-fuse tests plus fmt/check/clippy via rch pass; UBS on touched file is triaged.

title: perf(btrfs): the bd-5vis3 floor-leaf memo TAXES random-access metadata 8.6x — it is default-ON and the sign of the lever is workload-dependent

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
MEASURED 2026-08-16 (ProudBarn). Harness: cargo test -p ffs-core --release --lib bd_5vis3 -- --ignored --nocapture. rch WORKER: vmi1293453. One ELF, env-toggled A/B via FFS_BTRFS_FLOOR_MEMO (0/false/off disables), so this is an internal A/B and ISA/PGO cancel (bd-b9dug class C).

    arm                                        memo OFF         memo ON          ratio
    LARGE sweep, 20000 inodes              211.129458ms      5.599509ms      37.705x FASTER
      lookups                              60000 (3.00/stat) 1395 (0.07/stat)  43.01x fewer
    PRODUCTION config, attr cache ON, cold  22.360080ms      7.752808ms       2.884x FASTER
    RANDOM ACCESS, 8000 inodes               7.907348ms     68.062258ms       0.116x  <-- 8.6x SLOWER

THE FINDING: the lever's SIGN DEPENDS ON THE WORKLOAD, and it is enabled BY DEFAULT on
every read-only btrfs mount. A sequential sweep — which is what readdir+stat is, and what
motivated bd-5vis3 — gets 37.7x. A random-access stat workload pays 8.6x. That second
number is not a small tax; it is larger in magnitude than most wins in the bank.

WHY IT IS NOT JUST "a miss costs a span compare": a miss also REPLACES the memo (lock, Arc
clone, store) on every descent, so a random stream pays the update cost every single time
and never amortises it. The retained-leaf design assumes locality; random access is its
adversarial case, and it was measured only after the fact.

NOT A REVERT REQUEST. 37.7x on the sweep is real and the sweep is the motivating workload.
But a default-ON cache with an 8.6x adversarial regression needs either (a) a hit-rate-aware
disable — track hits/misses and stop REPLACING the memo once the recent hit rate collapses,
which costs nothing on a sweep and bounds the random case, or (b) an explicit statement that
btrfs random-access metadata is a known-regressed workload, banked as such.

MEASURED WITH the floor-memo lock-scope fix (1e334993) already applied, so the tax is NOT
lock contention — it is inherent to the update path. Before that commit the mutex was
additionally held across floor_in_leaf, which would make the concurrent random case worse.

NOTE: these three arms ALREADY EXISTED as ignored tests
(btrfs_floor_memo_ab_on_a_large_fixture_bd_5vis3_large, _random, _prod) and, as far as the
bead trail shows, had never been run — bd-5vis3 acceptance item 3 was still open. They build
their own btrfs fixture in process, so they need no external formatting tool and no quiet
window, and cost ~20s of test time once built. Run them.

STILL OPEN on bd-5vis3 proper: peak resident memory and mount-time cost at several image
sizes, which acceptance item 3 also requires and which these three arms do not report.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
GATE LANDED (AzureBay, 2026-08-16). The miss-streak gate this bead asked for as option (a) is in tree — it went in as part of b56aad87, which is not what its message says: ProudBarn staged crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs while my bd-79li3 edits were uncommitted in it, so their commit carries ~90 lines of mine. Nothing was lost, the merge is clean, and I have messaged them; recording it here so the next reader does not go looking for a bd-79li3 commit that does not exist.

WHAT THE GATE IS. OpenFs::btrfs_floor_memo_should_replace() (lib.rs:8928) counts consecutive misses. While the memo is being useful it replaces on every descent as before; once 32 consecutive misses land it backs off to refreshing one descent in 64.

  - A sweep never trips it. A sweep's misses arrive one per leaf crossing, each followed by a run of hits, and a hit resets the streak, so the 2.884x production path is untouched.
  - A miss-only stream does 131 replacements per 6400 descents instead of 6400 -- 48.9x less miss-path work, and the tax is bounded rather than linear in the access count.
  - It RE-ARMS. The 1-in-64 probe is load-bearing: without it a suppressed memo stays cold for the life of the mount, because a memo that is never replaced can never hit and so can never reset its own streak.

The saturating add matters too -- a wrapping counter on a long miss streak would fall back through 0 and read as "the memo just started working".

CORRECTNESS is a property of where the gate sits, not an argument about it. The gate only decides whether to RETAIN a leaf. Every hit is still gated on the key-span check that is bd-5vis3's whole correctness argument, and a stale retained leaf can only produce FEWER hits, never a wrong floor. The streak is reset on both edges of set_btrfs_floor_memo_disabled and alongside the existing memo invalidation, so an A/B whose disabled arm runs first cannot start its enabled arm already suppressed.

TEST: btrfs_floor_memo_miss_streak_gate_is_one_signed_bd_79li3 asserts the replacement SCHEDULE directly -- 10,000 hit-then-miss cycles with zero suppressions, the exact 131/6400 schedule on a miss-only stream, and re-arming after a reset. Deliberately not a timed arm: a wall-clock arm cannot separate "the gate suppressed replacements" from "the machine was quiet".

NOT YET VERIFIED, and this bead does not close until it is. cargo test -p ffs-core --lib btrfs_floor has been refused on five consecutive rch attempts (no admissible workers: insufficient_total_slots=4, active_project_exclusion). The gate compiles as part of b56aad87 but neither the new test nor the existing floor-memo suite has executed against it. Still owed after that: re-run bd_5vis3_prod post-gate to confirm the 2.884x production number did not move, and re-run the random arm to put a number on the tax after the gate rather than a predicted bound.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
MEASURED (AzureBay, 2026-08-16, commit 3bd2ecc5). The gate works. Harness: cargo test -p ffs-core --release --lib bd_5vis3_random -- --ignored. rch WORKER vmi1227854. 8000 inodes, 7 interleaved (off,on) pairs, A/A null on the identical schedule, seeded bootstrap over 20,000 resamples, one ELF self-reporting executing_elf_sha256 6d126781e652442666a73b832da86ef997d9b1b6383a6ca697afbabbbdb9f34d.

    A/B  memo OFF / memo ON   median 1.232888x   CI95 [0.711969, 1.553234]
    A/A  memo OFF twice       median 1.136846x   CI95 [0.902400, 3.308809]

READ IT CAREFULLY. The A/B sits INSIDE its own A/A null, so the post-gate ratio is NOT READABLE and 1.232888x is NOT a win. The null spans 0.90-3.31; the worker was loaded and 7 rounds cannot resolve anything against that. An earlier single pair on the same worker read 1.295x -- also noise. Nothing here is banked as a ratio.

What IS decidable is exactly what this bead asked. The pre-gate ratio was 0.116x, an order of magnitude BELOW the null's lower edge of 0.902. A wide null is what makes the comparison safe in this direction: an effect the instrument cannot see is smaller than its noise, and the pre-gate regression was far LARGER than its noise. Before the gate: measurably, grossly slower. After: indistinguishable from neutral. Neutral was the goal -- the gate was never meant to make random access faster, only to stop a locality-assuming cache from taxing a workload with no locality.

VERIFIED EARLIER (commit 31091fdd): btrfs_floor_memo_miss_streak_gate_is_one_signed_bd_79li3 passed its first execution on vmi1227854, 4 passed 0 failed 3 ignored, alongside the pre-existing floor-memo correctness suite -- zero suppressions across 10,000 hit-then-miss cycles, the exact 131-per-6400 schedule on a miss-only stream, and re-arming after a reset.

INSTRUMENT CHANGES: the random arm was a single off/on pair. It now carries interleaved pairs, an A/A null, a bootstrap median CI and an ELF self-report, and asserts DIRECTION (ab.high > null.low) rather than a magnitude -- pinning a number would turn an honest re-measurement on a slower worker into a spurious failure. FFS_BD_5VIS3_ROUNDS tunes the round count on both arms.

STILL OPEN before this bead closes: the PRODUCTION arm has not run post-gate. It could not complete -- [RCH-E104] SSH timeout at 1800s, three separate attempts on vmi1264463, and cutting 21 rounds to 7 did NOT help, which refutes "the rounds overrun the ceiling". Whatever dominates is upstream of the loop (the 20000-file fixture build, or the release compile). ProudBarn's earlier run DID complete on vmi1293453, so every failure is on one worker -- pin the worker before blaming the test. Until that arm runs, the claim that the gate is invisible to the sweep case rests on the schedule test, not on a wall-clock production number.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
POST-GATE PRODUCTION ARM RAN (ProudBarn, 2026-08-16) — the arm this bead was waiting on. Pinned to rch WORKER vmi1293453, harness cargo test -p ffs-core --release --lib bd_5vis3_prod -- --ignored, ELF 8c24ac2c1e1f3c9265cd0b67bc2477c53a1f5d800ec23ae1a7b4dd8d5b1bee94, 816s, no SSH timeout.

    A/B  median 3.031176x  ci95 [2.466613, 3.388613]
    A/A  median 0.862187x  ci95 [0.777040, 0.983771]

AzureBay's diagnosis was correct and is now confirmed: three failures on vmi1264463 versus success on vmi1293453 (twice) is a WORKER property, not a test property. 'Pin the worker before blaming the test' was the right call — cutting rounds 21 -> 7 did not help because the cost is upstream of the loop. Nothing about the test needs changing.

⛔ BUT THE GATE'S INVISIBILITY TO THE SWEEP IS STILL NOT ESTABLISHED BY A WALL-CLOCK NUMBER, and I want that stated rather than implied by a passing test. The post-gate production A/B (3.031176x) is statistically indistinguishable from the pre-gate one (3.012337x, run on vmi1153651) — which is the DESIRED result, since the gate is meant to be invisible on a sweep. But the two runs differ in pair count (7 vs 21) and both nulls FAIL, in OPPOSITE directions (+14.1% pre, -13.8% post). Per the fleet rule, a failing null is excusable only when both are off the same way by a similar amount; these are not, so 'the gate did not move the sweep' rests on the schedule test plus two uncertifiable numbers that happen to agree, not on a certified equivalence.

That is still a meaningful negative: an instrument biased +-14% cannot hide a change large enough to matter on a 3x effect. It bounds the gate's sweep impact as small; it does not prove it zero.

Full detail, including what would make it standing, is on bd-5vis3.

title: Canonical byte-layout snapshot for BtrfsExtentItem::to_bytes
description: BtrfsExtentItem::to_bytes encodes the 24-byte struct btrfs_extent_item per fs/btrfs/btrfs_tree.h: refs u64@0..8, generation u64@8..16, flags u64@16..24. EXTENT_ITEM is referenced by every extent allocation in btrfs (insert_extent_item, walk_chunk_tree, ffs_btrfs::flush_extent_tree). No canonical-bytes test exists — a regression that drifted refs↔generation or generation↔flags would silently corrupt every extent record. Add canonical_byte_layout test stamping each field with a UNIQUE non-zero magic, calling to_bytes, asserting the exact 24-byte [u8; 24] literal. title: SnapshotRegistry lock-ordering invariant doc + concurrent regression test
description: Found via /deadlock-finder-and-fixer audit. ffs_mvcc::SnapshotRegistry holds two parking_lot::RwLock — active: BTreeMap<CommitSeq, u64> and oldest_registered_at: Option<Instant>. The implementation maintains the lock ordering active → oldest_registered_at consistently: register() takes active.write() then briefly nests oldest_registered_at.read()/.write() (lines 3058-3065). release() takes active.write() then DROPS it before touching oldest_registered_at (lines 3088, 3127, 3129). check_stalls() reads oldest_registered_at and immediately drops the guard before calling watermark() which takes active.read(). This invariant is critical: any new method that acquired oldest_registered_at BEFORE active would deadlock against register() running concurrently. Currently NO struct-level doc and NO concurrent regression test. Fix: add struct-level lock-ordering invariant doc + concurrent regression test running 4 register threads + 2 release threads + 2 check_stalls threads under contention with a watchdog timeout.
close_reason: completed

title: perf: RANDOM read is the unmeasured axis; extent-cache shared-atomic hit counter is the likely bottleneck
description:
GAP-MAP (CrimsonFox cc/opus 2026-06-21, after verifying the full SEQUENTIAL read + metadata frontier dominates kernel materialize). The one classic FS benchmark axis NOT yet measured head-to-head is RANDOM read (fio-style: many small offset reads of one large file). SEQUENTIAL reads coalesce contiguous runs so they do few extent-cache lookups; RANDOM reads do one extent-cache lookup per access, so they would EXPOSE contention that sequential hides.

LIKELY BOTTLENECK (already located, not yet measured under random load): ffs-extent ExtentCache::lookup hot HIT path (crates/ffs-extent/src/lib.rs:1474) takes a SHARED .read() lock (good) but then bumps the per-shard SHARED  AtomicU64 on EVERY hit (line 1524 atomic_saturating_add(&inner.hits,1)) to derive the LRU clock for last_access. N parallel readers of ONE inode all route to ONE shard and ping-pong that single cache line — this is exactly the regression bd-xmh5g.382 measured (read-lock-atomic 0.81x vs write-lock in extent_cache_same_ns_8t) and it is LIVE in production. Sequential reads barely touch it (coalesced runs); random parallel reads would hammer it.

THE HARD CONSTRAINT (why .382 was rejected, must be solved): the LRU recency clock = hits+misses, an EXACT global monotonic counter, and the golden eviction-trace digest must stay byte-identical. Any sloppy/sampled counter changes the clock → changes eviction order → breaks the golden trace. A real fix needs either (a) an approximate-LRU (CLOCK/second-chance, per-entry referenced bit — no global counter, but new eviction semantics + new golden trace) or (b) a sloppy clock proven to preserve the exact victim selection, or (c) decouple the stats counter (sampled, for reporting only) from the LRU clock (exact, cheap source).

NEXT STEPS: (1) add a random-read harness (ffs-cli read --offset/--length or a randread subcommand, N parallel random 4KiB reads of one large file) and measure vs fio/a C pread loop (single + parallel) — first random-read head-to-head in the campaign; (2) if the extent cache shows up as the hotspot under random parallel load, pursue an approximate-LRU that re-bases the golden trace. ffs-extent is currently CLEAN/ownable. ffs-core read par_iter is occupied (cod-b).
close_reason: SUPERSEDED + RESOLVED (CrimsonFox). This gap-map bead (random read unmeasured; extent-cache hit-counter hypothesis) was superseded by bd-eflng once the rand-read harness (fa8108d8) measured the axis and perf root-caused the real cause (per-read snapshot register/release, NOT the extent-cache hit counter). bd-eflng is now FIXED+SHIPPED (9376f4d6, 88x->3.3x). The random-read axis is measured (warm/cold, ext4/btrfs) and the two big gaps (ext4 bd-eflng, btrfs bd-n5w92) are both shipped. Nothing left to track here.

title: [perf] cache read-only ext4 inode table blocks to remove remaining direct-read pread64
description: SCENARIO: post-bd-srh8m ffs-harness profile-read-path --fixture conformance/golden/ext4_8mb_reference.ext4 --duration-sec 2 --mode direct-read under strace -f -c. EVIDENCE: 37,953 iterations, checksum 16877, with 37,953 preadv and 37,963 pread64 calls. bd-srh8m removed the repeated group descriptor block read; the remaining scalar pread64 is the repeated inode-table block read in read_inode_raw_with_scope after read_group_desc_with_scope. ROOT CAUSE: read_inode_raw_with_scope reads the same ext4 inode table block every iteration via read_block_with_scope even in read-only direct-read with no staged write or MVCC-visible override. HYPOTHESIZED FIX: add a read-only, MVCC-aware ext4 inode-table block cache in OpenFs, keyed by BlockNumber and bypassed for writable opens, staged writes, and visible MVCC versions. title: btrfs_write regular extent uses raw write length for ram_bytes/num_bytes (not sector-aligned) -> btrfs check 'bad file extent'
description: FOUND while fixing bd-jctlm (the inline cap fix routed a 6000-byte file to the regular-extent path, exposing this). In btrfs_write's regular (non-inline) branch (lib.rs ~20794), the EXTENT_DATA was built with ram_bytes = num_bytes = write_len_u64 (the RAW write length), while disk_num_bytes = alloc_size (sector-aligned). btrfs requires an uncompressed regular extent to have ram_bytes == num_bytes == disk_num_bytes, ALL sector-aligned; the file's real unaligned length lives in the inode i_size and the last sector's tail is zero-padded. A non-sector-aligned num_bytes makes btrfs check report 'root R inode N errors 40, bad file extent' (I_ERR_BAD_FILE_EXTENT). PRE-EXISTING: affects ANY non-sector-aligned btrfs write (e.g. 6000, 10000 bytes) — never caught because prior btrfs-check tests only wrote sector-aligned sizes (4096, 16384). FIX: set ram_bytes = num_bytes = alloc_size (sector-aligned) in the regular branch. Validated by btrfs_write_sectorsize_boundary_extent_passes_btrfs_check_bd_jctlm (writes 4096, 6000, 100 bytes -> btrfs check clean) + the full ffs-core read/write model suite (reads cap by i_size, unaffected).
notes: PROGRESS (W61, amberfinch): coupled-set item (4) — btrfs_encoded_read i_size clamp — landed INDEPENDENTLY as bd-br44j (978b1279), since it was triggerable on its own via fallocate KEEP_SIZE. Remaining coupled set for the dedicated branch: (1) btrfs_write regular branch align offset/end + num_bytes=ram_bytes=disk_num_bytes + head/tail RMW; (2) btrfs_insert_regular_extent_segment align; (3) btrfs_recompute_inode_nbytes sum disk_num_bytes; (5) btrfs_remove_overlapping sector-split (mostly automatic once aligned). NEW HELPER still needed: lock-free read-current-file-bytes[a,b) (reuse btrfs_materialize_extent).
close_reason: Write path FIXED + validated in 9b99f16f: btrfs_write now uses a sector-aligned read-modify-write extent model (new btrfs_read_existing_range_into helper restores partial head/tail sectors; emits one aligned extent with ram_bytes==num_bytes==disk_num_bytes at an aligned key.offset; i_size carries sub-sector EOF). The pinned acceptance test btrfs_nonaligned_write_passes_btrfs_check_bd_7mi0p (6000-byte write) is un-ignored and passes REAL btrfs check (BTRFS_CHECK_RAN ok=true). Full ffs-core suite 1075 green incl partial_overwrite blocks==8 + byte-exact fallocate/truncate random model proptests. Remaining truncate-down/clone-carve alignment tails tracked in bd-70gyh (content-correct today; on-disk parity only).

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: Confirmed real but NOT a one-liner: setting ram_bytes=num_bytes=alloc_size (aligned) in btrfs_write's regular branch makes btrfs check pass BUT breaks 3 model tests (btrfs_write_partial_overwrite_regular_extent_preserves_surrounding_data, btrfs_write_fallocate_random_matches_reference_model, btrfs_write_truncate_random_matches_reference_model) — the read/overwrite/truncate paths treat num_bytes as the LOGICAL data length, not the aligned extent size. Proper fix: align num_bytes/ram_bytes to sectorsize at write AND make the read/overwrite/truncate/nbytes/fiemap paths use i_size (not num_bytes) for EOF/logical length. Coordinated refactor across all btrfs extent-consuming paths; verify against the random model proptests + a non-aligned btrfs-check test. Attempt reverted in e9828a0c; a documenting NOTE points here.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: DEEP DIAGNOSIS (2nd attempt). Re-applied num_bytes=ram_bytes=alloc_size and ran the failing tests with full output. The single failure mode is OVERLAPPING EXTENTS, not reads: btrfs_write_partial_overwrite asserts 'must not double-count logical bytes via overlapping extents' (left 15, right 8). Root: FrankenFS packs btrfs extents by UNALIGNED logical length so they tile tightly; rounding num_bytes up to a sector makes adjacent extents' ranges OVERLAP, which the overwrite/overlap/fallocate/truncate logic (and btrfs check) reject. GOOD NEWS: the MAIN read path (btrfs_read_file, lib.rs:7896) already caps by inode.size, so reads are i_size-safe and do NOT need changing; the encoded_read path (27799/27817) uses num_bytes directly and WOULD need an i_size clamp. SCOPE of the real fix = a sector-aligned extent model: btrfs_write must produce sector-aligned offsets+lengths via read-modify-write for sub-sector writes (read the partial head/tail sectors, merge, write the full aligned extent), and the overwrite/overlap/split/fallocate/truncate logic must operate on the aligned, non-overlapping sector grid. This is multi-session — NOT attemptable as a single-hour change without breaking the random model proptests (fallocate_random/truncate_random/partial_overwrite). Recommended increment-1: a tested btrfs_align_write_rmw helper that returns aligned extent params + merged sector data, unwired; then wire it + update overlap logic incrementally. An #[ignore]'d regression test btrfs_nonaligned_write_passes_btrfs_check_bd_7mi0p is committed (un-ignore when fixed).

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: DEFINITIVE SCOPE (3rd investigation) — this is a COUPLED, model-wide refactor; NO partial fix is proptest-safe. Evidence: (1) The unaligned-extent model is pervasive: btrfs_write (key=offset, num_bytes=logical), btrfs_remove_overlapping_extent_data (splits at logical boundaries → unaligned remnants), btrfs_clone_file_data reflink (carves sub-ranges via num_bytes/extent_offset, e.g. new_num_bytes=overlap_end-overlap_start, unaligned), truncate/fallocate. (2) nbytes is ALSO wrong: btrfs_recompute_inode_nbytes sums num_bytes(=logical); real btrfs i_blocks = sum(disk_num_bytes=aligned). For non-aligned files num_bytes<disk_num_bytes so btrfs check would flag BOTH 'bad file extent' (unaligned num_bytes) AND an nbytes mismatch. (3) The partial_overwrite test asserts blocks==8 (nbytes) and no overlap; the random proptests (fallocate/truncate_random) compare content+blocks vs a reference model. A 'gated simple-case' alignment (align only sector-aligned-offset+non-aligned-len+clear-tail writes) FAILS because a LATER random write into the aligned extent's [logical_end, aligned_end) padding overlaps it (same failure mode as the global align attempt), and the nbytes change ripples into the model comparison. REQUIRED FIX = enforce the invariant 'every EXTENT_DATA is sector-aligned (offset+num_bytes+extent_offset), extents tile the sector grid non-overlapping, logical EOF = i_size' across ALL mutators TOGETHER: (a) btrfs_write does read-modify-write to emit sector-aligned extents (read existing partial head/tail sectors from current extents — no re-lock needed: read from alloc.fs_tree + device via map_logical_to_physical — merge with new data, zero-pad, write full aligned extent); (b) btrfs_remove_overlapping_extent_data splits on SECTOR boundaries producing aligned remnants; (c) reflink-carve rounds to sectors; (d) truncate/fallocate keep extents aligned (i_size carries the unaligned EOF); (e) nbytes = sum(disk_num_bytes). Reads already cap by i_size (btrfs_read_file:7896) so the main read is unaffected; the encoded_read path (~27799) must switch from num_bytes to i_size-bounded length. VALIDATION: the existing content+blocks proptests (they emulate real btrfs accounting) + the ignored btrfs_nonaligned_write_passes_btrfs_check_bd_7mi0p + a NEW multi-write/overwrite btrfs-check test. This is a dedicated multi-session effort; landing pieces piecemeal breaks the proptests (they enforce the no-overlap + blocks invariants), so it must be developed on a branch and landed coordinated. DO NOT attempt a single-hour partial fix (3 sessions have now confirmed this).

title: Refine authoritative proof lanes with environment manifests and replayable host probes
description:
Supplemental refinement for bd-9vzzk. Authoritative mounted, xfstests, performance, and long-campaign lanes need a shared environment manifest so evidence can be replayed or rejected when host state drifts. A pass from an unknown worker, stale kernel/FUSE state, changed helper binary, or mismatched mount namespace should not upgrade public claims.

Scope: define an environment manifest consumed by authoritative lanes: lane id, environment kind, host/worker id, kernel, FUSE/fuser versions, mkfs/helper versions, cargo/toolchain, mount namespace, privilege model, filesystem tools, resource limits, git SHA, artifact schema version, probe timestamp, freshness TTL, and replay command.

Required proof before close:
1. Unit/schema tests reject environment manifests missing lane id, host/worker identity, kernel/FUSE details, helper versions where relevant, privilege model, resource limits, git SHA, timestamp, TTL, and replay command.
2. Unit tests cover stale manifest, host mismatch, worker mismatch, helper version mismatch, toolchain mismatch, privilege downgrade, missing /dev/fuse, changed mount namespace, resource-limit mismatch, and non-authoritative local run.
3. E2E/dry-run smoke emits manifests for local, host-skip, and fixture authoritative cases, then verifies readiness gates reject stale or mismatched manifests while preserving actionable remediation.
4. Logs include lane id, manifest version, host/worker id, probe commands, observed versions, freshness decision, mismatch diagnostics, remediation id, artifact paths, and reproduction command.
5. Proof bundles, release gates, and readiness reports must consume this manifest before treating mounted, xfstests, performance, or long-campaign evidence as authoritative.

title: [perf][no-gaps] word-at-a-time bitmap find-free scan (4.9x on full-block scan)
description:
NO-GAPS DIRECTIVE lever (first concrete win under bd-xmh5g). Buried-CS primitive: word-parallel bitmap scan.

GAP: ffs_alloc::bitmap_find_free_range scanned the free-block bitmap BYTE-at-a-time (one u8 per iteration, idx += 8) in its main loop. For a 4 KiB block-group bitmap (4096 bytes / 32768 bits) a late or absent free bit costs up to 4096 iterations — vs the kernel/e2fsprogs word-wise scan.

LEVER (one): add a u64 word-at-a-time fast path before the byte loop — read 8 bytes, `(!word).trailing_zeros()` gives the first free bit relative to idx (bit-identical to the byte loop), idx += 64. Falls through to the existing byte loop for the 8..63 tail and the bit loop for <8. 100% safe Rust (forbid(unsafe_code) intact); no SIMD intrinsics needed — trailing_zeros is a single instruction.

PROOF: same-binary same-worker criterion A/B (ffs-alloc bitmap_ops, find_free_full_scan group, all-0xFF 4K bitmap forcing a full scan): byte_at_a_time 1.3240 us [1.3042,1.3468] vs word_at_a_time 268.31 ns [265.02,271.97] = 4.94x faster, intervals non-overlapping. Isomorphism: ffs-alloc 197/197 tests pass (existing bitmap_find_free coverage proves bit-identical output) + a debug_assert in the bench that byte==word. Score ~4.9 >= 2.0.

Added a u64 word-at-a-time fast path to ffs_alloc::bitmap_find_free_range before the byte loop: reads 8 bytes/iter, (!word).trailing_zeros() = first free bit relative to idx, idx += 64; existing byte loop handles the 8..63 tail and the bit loop <8. 100% safe Rust. Proof: same-binary same-worker criterion A/B (bitmap_ops find_free_full_scan, all-0xFF 4K bitmap): byte_at_a_time 1.3240 us vs word_at_a_time 268.31 ns = 4.94x, non-overlapping. title: ffs-harness: ondisk_parse benches missing dx_hash latency floor across hash versions
description:
Finding (via /profiling-software-performance skill, sixth visit,
different target): `dx_hash` (crates/ffs-ondisk/src/ext4.rs:4720) is
the ext4 directory hash function called on every htree directory
lookup. It dispatches across 5 hash variants (LEGACY,
LEGACY_UNSIGNED, HALF_MD4, TEA, TEA_UNSIGNED) plus the half-md4
fallback for unknown versions. Each variant has different
performance characteristics — LEGACY is a simple multiply-add loop
(~10 cycles/byte); HALF_MD4 runs an MD4 round transform per 32-byte
chunk; TEA runs a Feistel round per chunk.

There is NO bench for any of these in the `ondisk` criterion gate.
A regression in any of them — accidentally swapping the LEGACY
multiplier, mis-aligning the MD4 chunk loop, or replacing TEA's
Feistel rounds with a slower abstraction — would silently slow
htree lookups without tripping any existing perf gate.

The proptest layer (bd-590tc) and fuzz coverage exist for
correctness; this bead adds the latency floor.

Acceptance: bench function in
crates/ffs-harness/benches/ondisk_parse.rs that exercises each
hash version on a representative directory-name workload (a fixed
set of 32 names of varying lengths). Registered in the existing
`ondisk` criterion_group!. Verified via
`rch exec -- cargo check -p ffs-harness --benches`.

title: PoR for cryptographic durability audit (Graveyard Entry 11.11)
description:
# PoR for cryptographic durability audit (Graveyard Entry 11.11)

## GOAL
Implement Proofs of Retrievability (PoR) for cryptographic verification that stored data is intact and retrievable, without reading the entire dataset.

## BACKGROUND
From Alien CS Graveyard 11.11: PoR (Juels-Kaliski 2007, Shacham-Waters 2008) allows a verifier to challenge a storage system with random queries. The storage system responds with proofs that specific blocks exist and are correct. If the proofs verify, the entire dataset is retrievable with high probability.

## DESIGN
- Challenge: verifier sends random block indices + random coefficients
- Response: storage computes linear combination of challenged blocks weighted by coefficients
- Verification: verifier checks response against precomputed authenticators
- Authenticators: computed once at file creation, stored alongside data

## APPLICABILITY
- Future feature: useful for cloud/remote storage verification
- Complementary to RaptorQ: PoR proves data exists, RaptorQ repairs it if it doesn't
- Useful for auditing: periodic PoR challenges prove filesystem integrity without full scan

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] PoR authenticator generation at file creation
- [ ] Challenge-response protocol implemented
- [ ] Verification: false positive rate < 2^-128
- [ ] Benchmark: challenge/response time for 1GB file
acceptance_criteria: PoR authenticator generation at file creation time. Challenge-response protocol implemented with configurable challenge count. Verification: false positive rate below 2^-128. Authenticators stored alongside data in reserved metadata area. Benchmark: challenge/response time for 1GB file. Benchmark: authenticator generation time per MB. Unit tests: generate authenticators, challenge, verify for small files. Unit tests: corrupted block causes verification failure. Unit tests: uncorrupted file passes all challenges. Property test: random challenge sets always verify on intact data.

title: btrfs send emits inodes in objectid order, can place a child before its parent dir
description: generate_send_stream (ffs-btrfs ~6496) iterates inodes in objectid (BTreeMap) order and emits each inode's create command (mkfile/mkdir/symlink/mknod) with its full path. btrfs receive applies these by PATH, so the parent directory must already exist. btrfs allocates objectids parent-before-child for simple trees, but a RENAME can move a file (low objectid) under a directory created later (higher objectid); plain objectid order then emits the child's mkfile BEFORE the parent's mkdir, and the receive fails ('No such file or directory'). Not silent data loss (receive errors), but a real send-fidelity gap for rename-reorganized trees. FIX: emit all DIRECTORIES first in topological order (parent dirs before child dirs, via the inode_parents depth), then all non-directory inodes — guaranteeing every create's parent path exists. No regression for normal trees (depth order == objectid order there).

description:

covers two stamp/verify round-trip pairs (dir_block, extent_block)

  * stamp_inode_bitmap_checksum / verify_inode_bitmap_checksum

Ext4GroupDesc field (block_bitmap_csum / inode_bitmap_csum) which

`bitmap_checksum_helpers_roundtrip` fixed-input test covers one

across the full input space.

additional MRs:

title: ffs-mvcc: PersistentMvccStore lock-ordering invariant is undocumented and untested
description:
Finding (via /deadlock-finder-and-fixer skill, Class 1: classic
mutex deadlock prevention): `PersistentMvccStore` (crates/ffs-mvcc/
src/persist.rs:176) holds three `parking_lot::RwLock`s — `store`,
`wal`, and `stats` — and the production code paths consistently
acquire them in the order **store → wal → stats**:

  * `commit_with_options` (l. 404→422→437): store(W) → wal(W) → stats(W)
  * `checkpoint`          (l. 526→565):    store(R) → stats(W)
  * `truncate_wal`        (l. 589→599→628): store(R) → wal(W) → stats(W)

Pairwise the order is consistent everywhere. But:

  1. **No struct-level doc comment names the invariant.** A future
     contributor could introduce a function like `repack_wal` that
     acquires `wal.write()` before `store.write()` and instantly
     create an AB-BA deadlock with `commit_with_options`, which
     holds `store.write()` while waiting on `wal.write()`. The
     existing inline comments on `checkpoint`/`truncate_wal` explain
     WHY they hold `store` first, but there's no central pin.

  2. **No regression test exercises the lock ordering under
     contention.** All existing tests run commit, checkpoint, and
     truncate_wal serially. A future deadlock would only manifest
     under concurrent load and would silently regress the gate.

This is a Class 1 prevention finding (no existing deadlock — the
audit confirmed the order is currently consistent), but the lack of
a documented + tested invariant makes the code fragile to refactor.

Acceptance: a doc comment on `PersistentMvccStore` names the canonical
order **store → wal → stats** with rationale, and one unit test in
the `tests` module spawns concurrent commit + truncate_wal threads
with a watchdog timeout that fails if any thread hangs (proving the
order holds under contention).
notes: Shipped: struct-level doc on PersistentMvccStore documenting the canonical lock order store → wal → stats with a per-field rank annotation (rank 0/1/2) and a table of production callers showing compliance. Added lock_ordering_under_concurrent_commit_and_truncate regression test that spawns 2 concurrent workers exercising commit (store.W→wal.W→stats.W) and checkpoint+truncate_wal (store.R→{wal.W,stats.W}) with a 15s watchdog that panics on hang. Verified via rch exec -- cargo test -p ffs-mvcc --lib lock_ordering_under_concurrent_commit_and_truncate (passes in 0.16s).

title: Implement RaptorQ symbol refresh on dirty group flush
description:
# Implement RaptorQ symbol refresh on dirty group flush

## GOAL
Ensure repair symbols are regenerated when block groups are modified, as mandated by spec §0.4: "A block write that never triggers repair symbol refresh for its group is a spec-conformance bug."

## BACKGROUND
Currently repair symbols are generated at image creation. When blocks are modified:
1. Group becomes "stale" (symbols no longer match data)
2. Must regenerate before corruption can be recovered
3. Two modes: lazy (on next scrub) or eager (on fsync)

## TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS

### 1. Dirty Group Tracking
```rust
pub struct DirtyGroupTracker {
    dirty: BitVec,  // One bit per group
}

impl DirtyGroupTracker {
    pub fn mark_dirty(&mut self, group: GroupNumber);
    pub fn is_dirty(&self, group: GroupNumber) -> bool;
    pub fn clear(&mut self, group: GroupNumber);
    pub fn dirty_groups(&self) -> impl Iterator<Item = GroupNumber>;
}
```

### 2. Refresh Triggers
- **Lazy**: Background scrub regenerates symbols for dirty groups
- **Eager (fsync)**: Regenerate immediately for committed groups
- **Configurable**: MountConfig.repair_refresh_policy

### 3. Refresh Flow
```rust
pub fn refresh_group_symbols(
    group: GroupNumber,
    device: &dyn BlockDevice,
    storage: &mut RepairGroupStorage,
    cx: &Cx,
) -> Result<()> {
    // 1. Read all blocks in group
    // 2. Regenerate RaptorQ symbols
    // 3. Write to repair storage slots
    // 4. Clear dirty flag
}
```

### 4. Budget Integration
- Refresh respects Cx budget
- Can be interrupted and resumed
- Progress tracked per-group

## TESTS
1. Unit: Dirty tracking set/clear
2. Integration: Write marks group dirty
3. Integration: Scrub refreshes dirty group
4. Integration: fsync refreshes if eager mode
5. E2E: Corruption after refresh -> recovery works

## LOGGING
- Mark dirty (trace): group number, cause
- Refresh start (debug): group, block count
- Refresh complete (info): group, duration, symbol count

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
1. Every modified group eventually refreshed
2. Lazy mode: refreshed within scrub interval
3. Eager mode: refreshed on fsync
4. Recovery works for refreshed groups
close_reason: Implemented dirty-group refresh APIs (mark/query/flush), aligned refresh logging, and added flush-path + tracker tests in ffs-repair pipeline; validated via rch cargo test/check/clippy and cargo fmt --check.

description: test tests::arc_cache_pressure_prefers_evicting_cold_clean_entries FAILS deterministically on main: 'cold block should be evicted first under pressure, left: 4 right: 5' (crates/ffs-block/src/lib.rs:7760/7792). Verified PRE-EXISTING + independent of any uncommitted work (reproduced with all my edits reverted). Most recent ffs-block commit is e72423b5 'perf(ffs-block): bypass one-pass S3-FIFO scans (bd-xmh5g.29)' which changed the S3-FIFO eviction/scan path — the eviction-order assertion this test checks. notes: FIXED (8d1ab5e0): root cause was a STALE TEST, not an eviction regression. arc_cache_pressure_prefers_evicting_cold_clean_entries warmed the cache with sequential reads 0,1,2,3 and assumed all four become resident T1 entries (pre-S3-FIFO ARC layout). Under the default s3fifo feature, the consecutive read-miss streak is detected as a one-pass scan and admitted ghost-only (e72423b5/bd-xmh5g.29), so blocks 2,3 never become resident — leaving only 0,1 resident, so High pressure (target 2) evicts nothing and block 1 stays (assertion left 4 right 5). e72423b5's proof filter 'test ... s3fifo' did not match this test, so the breakage reached main. VERIFIED the eviction logic itself is correct: next_pressure_victim selects non-dirty T1 victims oldest-first then T2 (cold-before-hot intact), and byte outputs/golden sha256 were unchanged by the bypass. Fix rewrites the test to warm 7 cold + 1 hot block with a stride of 2 (keeps the sequential-scan detector disarmed so all blocks are genuinely admitted), forces real eviction (8 residents, High target 4), and asserts the hot block survives while the oldest cold block misses — the invariant is still fully exercised (fails if hot evicted before cold). Passes under BOTH default (s3fifo) and --no-default-features (classic ARC); clippy/fmt clean. main is GREEN again.

title: ffs-ondisk: Ext4Inode::extra_nsec/extra_epoch bit-pack helpers lack metamorphic relation tests
description:
Finding (via /testing-metamorphic skill, NEW target): crates/ffs-ondisk/src/ext4.rs:2725 has Ext4Inode::extra_nsec(extra) = extra >> 2 and extra_epoch(extra) = extra & 0x3 — the bit-pack helpers that decode the on-disk *_extra timestamp field used by every inode timestamp read on ext4 v6+ filesystems. The unit test  covers 4 fixed inputs but ZERO metamorphic-relation proptests pin the algebraic contract.

The bit-pack contract is critical: extra is a u32 split into [nsec:30][epoch:2]. The kernel uses bits [1:0] as epoch extension (adds 2^32 seconds to timestamps) and bits [31:2] as nanoseconds (max valid ~10^9). A regression that swapped the masks would silently corrupt every timestamp on every ext4 v6+ image — a high-leverage class of bug invisible to substring-style tests.

Untested algebraic laws:
  * MR1 — Bit-pack inverse: for any u32 x, (extra_nsec(x) << 2) | extra_epoch(x) == x
  * MR2 — Epoch bound: extra_epoch(x) ≤ 3 for all u32 x
  * MR3 — Nsec bound: extra_nsec(x) ≤ 0x3FFF_FFFF for all u32 x
  * MR4 — Disjoint fields: extra_nsec(epoch_only) == 0 when epoch_only & ~0x3 == 0; extra_epoch(nsec_only) == 0 when nsec_only & 0x3 == 0
  * MR5 — Determinism: same input always gives same output

Pairs with bd-bevt2 (feature flags), bd-jbilz (magic numbers + state flags), bd-k81lq (reserved inodes) — those pin SCALAR conformance; this pins the BIT-PACK ALGEBRA.

Acceptance: 5 proptest cases in the existing proptest! block at the end of crates/ffs-ondisk/src/ext4.rs.
close_reason: done

title: rename onto an immutable/append-only target (and btrfs rename of an immutable/append source) is wrongly allowed instead of EPERM
description: The kernel's vfs_rename calls may_delete on the rename SOURCE and, when the destination exists, on the VICTIM being clobbered; may_delete returns EPERM if the inode is immutable or append-only (IS_IMMUTABLE||IS_APPEND). FrankenFS gaps: (1) ext4_rename checks the source via ext4_reject_immutable_or_append(child_inode) but reads+clobbers the existing target (existing_inode) with NO such check -> renaming onto an immutable/append-only file wrongly destroys it; (2) btrfs_rename checks NEITHER the source NOR the victim -> renaming an immutable/append-only file, or onto one, both wrongly succeed. FIX: ext4_rename rejects existing_inode immutable/append before removing it; btrfs_rename reads the source + target inodes and rejects immutable/append (BTRFS_INODE_IMMUTABLE|BTRFS_INODE_APPEND) — all EARLY, before any mutation (the same-inode-hardlink no-op short-circuits first, matching vfs_rename's source==target early return). Sibling of bd-69ich (link) / bd-kf7uw (xattr) — same vfs append+immutable enforcement class. Tests: inject the flag on source/target then rename -> EPERM with no partial mutation; both ports.
close_reason: Fixed in c183dd49: ext4_rename rejects an immutable/append-only victim before clobbering; btrfs_rename rejects immutable/append on BOTH source and victim, all before mutation (matching vfs_rename may_delete). Tests ext4_rename_onto_immutable_target_is_eperm_bd_85rav + btrfs_rename_immutable_source_or_target_is_eperm_bd_85rav. Full ffs-core 1085 green. Completes the vfs append/immutable enforcement audit alongside bd-69ich (link) + bd-kf7uw (xattr).

title: Epic: Non-permissioned swarm-scale readiness lab
description:
## Background
FrankenFS has strong proof-bundle, release-gate, permissioned-campaign, and readiness-dashboard machinery, but the remaining open leaves require destructive xfstests execution or a real 64-core/256GB-class host. Future agents still need useful, non-permissioned work that improves confidence before an operator grants those ACKs.

## Goal
Build a non-permissioned readiness lab that simulates large-host swarm pressure, xfstests campaign preconditions, RCH scheduling, evidence graph freshness, and permissioned-run handoff quality without mutating scratch devices or claiming authoritative product evidence.

## Non-goals
Do not execute real xfstests, do not run the authoritative large-host swarm campaign, do not change public readiness wording from simulated evidence, and do not bypass existing ACK boundaries.

## Acceptance
The child beads define self-contained implementation slices with unit tests, E2E scripts, detailed logs, artifact schemas, and explicit proof that simulated evidence remains advisory/detection-only until replaced by permissioned product evidence.
design:
## Idea-wizard Phase 2 top 5
1. Evidence truth graph over proof, release, operational, permissioned, and advisory artifacts.
2. Non-permissioned readiness-lab artifact contract with fail-closed advisory claim effects.
3. RCH-aware validation scheduler dry-run for swarm agents and isolated target dirs.
4. Large-host capability simulation and NUMA/p99 replay fixtures derived from existing swarm validators.
5. Permissioned-run rehearsal packets that make xfstests and swarm ACK boundaries safer without executing them.

## Phase 3 next 10 considered
Dashboard advisory integration, single E2E orchestrator, operator runbook drift checks, tracker/Agent-Mail health surfacing, artifact retention budgets, command recommender over evidence blockers, synthetic failure minimization, RCH worker-capability fixtures, proof-bundle advisory-lane rejection fuzzing, and release-gate wording guards. The first eight are operationalized in this epic; the others should be folded into implementation details unless a future agent finds a concrete uncovered gap.

## Dependency shape
Start with bd-lp0xy contracts. Then implement bd-4532j, bd-hejjl, bd-xyypn, bd-c7fqh, and bd-w6nuy. Dashboard integration bd-919xg waits on truth graph plus simulator/replay outputs. The E2E orchestrator bd-wt1rq waits on dashboard, scheduler, and xfstests rehearsal. Docs bd-76u5y waits on the orchestrator so runbook wording matches real artifacts.

## Overlap handling
This backlog explicitly extends closed beads bd-4v16z.9, bd-4v16z.10, bd-4v16z.6, bd-4v16z.3, and bd-4v16z.4. It must not duplicate their validators or promote simulated evidence into authoritative readiness.

title: Implement permissioned mounted crash replay lanes

Artifacts include lane id, host capability proof, image path/hash, mountpoint path, daemon pid/termination method where applicable, operation trace, crash point, expected survivors, observed survivors, repair ledger rows for the repair case, stdout/stderr paths, cleanup status, and reproduction command.

title: Refine writeback-cache gate with dirty-page ordering and fsync oracle
description:
Supplemental refinement for bd-rchk0.2.1.1. The negative-option audit proves unsafe mounts do not accidentally enable writeback_cache, but safe opt-in also needs a positive ordering oracle: dirty data, metadata updates, flush, fsync, fsyncdir, cancellation, unmount, crash/reopen, and repair-symbol refresh must produce evidence that the kernel cache boundary preserves the declared durability contract.

Scope: define a dirty-page and fsync/fsyncdir ordering oracle for writeback-cache opt-in. The oracle should treat flush as non-durable, fsync/fsyncdir as durability boundaries where supported, and metadata-after-data ordering as an invariant. It must explicitly cover cancellation and repair interaction rather than only happy-path write/readback.

Required proof before close:
1. Unit/policy tests cover dirty-page state transitions, flush non-durability, fsync data durability, fsyncdir metadata durability, metadata-after-data ordering, cancellation before writeback, unmount with dirty pages, stale epoch state, and repair-symbol refresh after accepted writeback.
2. Unit tests reject opt-in when any invariant I1-I6 lacks a test id, artifact field, release-gate consumer, or documented unsupported rationale.
3. E2E or mounted dry-run scenarios emit artifacts for default-off, accepted opt-in where supported, rejected opt-in, fsync boundary, fsyncdir boundary, cancellation, and crash/reopen or explicit host-skip.
4. Logs include mount option set, raw fuser option list, gate version, invariant ids, dirty-page state, flush/fsync/fsyncdir calls, epoch id, repair symbol generation, expected ordering, observed ordering, artifact paths, cleanup status, and reproduction command.
5. Release gates cannot mark writeback-cache stronger than experimental unless the positive ordering oracle and negative-option audit both pass on fresh authoritative evidence.
close_reason: Implemented dirty-page ordering oracle, CLI/report contract, 21-scenario dry-run suite, docs, and validation evidence for writeback-cache experimental gate.

title: Add btrfs write-path FUSE E2E tests mirroring ext4 coverage
description:
## What
Add btrfs write-path FUSE E2E tests that exercise create/write/mkdir/rename/unlink/truncate/
xattr/fallocate/symlink through the actual FUSE mount interface, mirroring the ext4 FUSE E2E
tests that already exist in fuse_e2e.rs.

## Why
ext4 has comprehensive FUSE E2E tests: fuse_create_and_read_file, fuse_write_overwrite_and_append,
fuse_mkdir_and_nested_create, fuse_unlink_removes_file, fuse_rename_file, fuse_hard_link,
fuse_symlink_create_and_follow, fuse_setattr_truncate — all exercising real kernel VFS through
FUSE mount.

btrfs write operations are tested only at the unit level (OpenFs methods in ffs-core) and in
the crash matrix. There are NO btrfs FUSE E2E write tests that go through the kernel.

## What Already Exists
- ext4 FUSE E2E write tests in crates/ffs-harness/tests/fuse_e2e.rs (lines 531-673)
- btrfs FUSE E2E read tests exist (mount + read files)
- Helper: with_rw_mount() for ext4 RW FUSE mounts
- btrfs mkfs.btrfs image creation in fuse_e2e.rs (line 1889-1910)
- btrfs unit write tests in ffs-core (create, mkdir, rename, fallocate, etc.)

## Implementation Plan
Add to crates/ffs-harness/tests/fuse_e2e.rs, using a with_btrfs_rw_mount() helper:

fn fuse_btrfs_create_and_read_file()
  - mkfs.btrfs → mount --rw → create file → read back → verify content → unmount

fn fuse_btrfs_write_and_read_back()
  - mount → create → write 4KB → read → verify → unmount

fn fuse_btrfs_mkdir_and_nested_create()

- Create 256MB sparse file
- mkfs.btrfs -f on it
- Mount via FrankenFS FUSE with --rw
- Run test closure
- Unmount
- Skip if mkfs.btrfs or /dev/fuse unavailable

- All tests skip cleanly when either is unavailable

title: Idempotence MR for ext4_casefold_key

title: ffs-core: ext4 fast-symlink boundary off-by-one (60-byte target stored inline without NUL)
description: ext4_symlink (lib.rs:12790) uses fast_storage = target_bytes.len() <= EXT4_FAST_SYMLINK_MAX (60), storing a 60-byte target inline in the 60-byte i_block. But the kernel stores target+NUL inline and decides fast iff len+1 <= 60 (i.e. len <= 59); a 60-byte target is a SLOW (block-mapped) symlink. FrankenFS zero-fills i_block then copies the target, so for len<=59 byte[len]=0 (NUL present, kernel-compatible) but for len==60 the 60 bytes are fully used with NO NUL terminator. The kernel follows fast symlinks as NUL-terminated C strings (link_path_walk has no i_size cap), so following a FrankenFS-created 60-byte fast symlink over-reads past i_block into adjacent inode fields -> wrong/oversized target resolution. e2fsck accepts it (strnlen capped at 60 == i_size) so it is not fsck-dirty, but it is a real on-traversal parity bug: the kernel never creates a 60-byte fast symlink. FIX: fast_storage = len < EXT4_FAST_SYMLINK_MAX (len <= 59), matching the kernel; 60-byte targets route to the slow path. Add a pure boundary-policy unit test (runs on rch; the E2E symlink helpers are mkfs/fixture-gated).
close_reason: Fixed: ext4_symlink fast/slow boundary now matches the kernel via ext4_symlink_target_is_fast(len)=len<60 (was len<=60). A 60-byte target had no room for the NUL in the 60-byte i_block, so a kernel following that fast symlink (as a NUL-terminated string) over-read past i_block; 60-byte targets now route to the slow path. Pure boundary unit test (fast 0/1/59, slow 60/61) runs on rch; 17 symlink tests pass.

title: btrfs: sub-sector head-segment re-insertion loses data on overwrite after heavy extent churn
description: Discovered while fixing bd-5aybu. With the allocator bytenr-0 fix in place, extending the metamorphic test (btrfs_write_multi_extent_overwrite_matches_reference_model_bd_5aybu) with an 11th write (50, 83950, 0xBB) — overwriting [50,84000) of an 84000-byte file — corrupts the preserved head [0,50): exactly the first 50 bytes read back wrong (50 of 84000 bytes differ, first at 0). The overwrite's btrfs_remove_overlapping_extent_data trims the existing [0,84000) extent and re-inserts the head segment [0,50) via btrfs_insert_regular_extent_segment, which should preserve the prior 0xAA bytes there. SUSPECT: btrfs_insert_regular_extent_segment (ffs-core lib.rs ~15605) writes the segment bytes via self.dev.write_all_at(ByteOffset(allocation.bytenr), data) — i.e. it treats the LOGICAL bytenr as a physical byte offset and bypasses both the logical->physical chunk mapping AND the MVCC overlay that the main write path (btrfs_write_logical) and the read path (btrfs_read_logical_into) use. A sub-sector (50-byte) head segment exposes this; an aligned multi-sector head ([0,8192) in write #4 of the same test) reads back correctly, so the bug is specific to small/sub-sector segments and/or the post-full-overwrite state. REPRO: re-add the 11th write to the bd-5aybu regression test. NEXT: make btrfs_insert_regular_extent_segment write through btrfs_write_logical (logical mapping + MVCC) like the main path, and add the 11th write to the regression test once fixed.
notes: FIXED (70bad369): btrfs_insert_regular_extent_segment wrote segment bytes via self.dev.write_all_at(ByteOffset(allocation.bytenr), ..) — treating the LOGICAL bytenr as a physical device offset, bypassing both the logical->physical chunk mapping and the MVCC overlay used by the main write path (btrfs_write_logical) and all reads (btrfs_read_logical_into). A re-inserted head/tail segment (e.g. the sub-sector head [0,50) left by overwriting [50,84000)) could read back zero/stale. Fix routes the segment write through btrfs_write_logical like the main path. PROOF: extended the bd-5aybu metamorphic regression test to an 11th write (50,83950) that leaves a sub-sector head to re-insert; full file matches the byte-exact model after every write. ffs-core suite green, clippy/fmt clean.

title: ext4 fast-commit tag values were all wrong vs kernel fast_commit.h
description: ffs_journal::FcTag used non-kernel discriminants (Link=1,Unlink=2,AddRange=3,DelRange=4,Creat=5,Inode=7,Pad=8,Tail=9,Head=0xA). Since fast-commit recovery parses kernel-written journals, every tag was misread (kernel HEAD=9 read as Tail; ADD_RANGE=1 read as a Link dentry; INODE=6 unknown->fallback) so FC recovery could never correctly process a real image. Also ext4_fc_head is 8 bytes so the payload.len()<16 HEAD check rejected valid heads (fixed to <8). Tests had encoded the same wrong values (self-consistent, didn't validate against kernel). FIXED: corrected enum+from_u16+HEAD-check, remapped all test literals to kernel values, added golden fc_tag_values_match_kernel_fast_commit_h pinning the dispatch. Distinct from bd-6nwjx (FC-apply unimplemented); this is the tag-dispatch layer beneath it.

title: read_block_vec is uncached: htree-descent re-preads read-only dx_root/dx_node every metadata op (26x redundancy)
description: strace of 500 deletes: 1092 pread64 but only 42 UNIQUE block offsets = ~26x re-read of the same read-only blocks (dx_root, dx_node, dir-inode block, bitmaps). read_block_vec (ffs-core lib.rs) allocs vec![0;block_size] + dev.read_exact_at directly, NO cache. Every htree descent (lookup/add/remove/create-existence) re-preads the dir's dx_root + dx_node, which are read-only across a metadata-op stream. LEVER: a small read cache (sharded, keyed by block number, Arc<[u8]>) in read_block_vec, invalidated on write_block (tx_dev + dev). COHERENT because the re-pread blocks are unwritten/read-only during the session (written blocks are served from the MVCC overlay, never via this pread path) — so cache hits return current data; invalidate-on-write is defensive. PAYOFF: ~18% of delete wall is preads (2.2/op x ~2us of 25us/op) -> ~2.1x->~1.7x delete, AND broad (every htree-descending op: delete/rmdir/lookup/create/mkdir + warm file reads re-reading extent/inode blocks). RISK: cache coherence (a missed write path -> stale read -> corruption); must cover ALL write_block sites; for RMW callers (remove_entry reads-then-mutates) return a CLONE (saves the pread syscall, not the alloc) OR add read_block_arc for read-only htree-descent callers (saves both). Measured redundancy is real; deferred as substantial + coherence-critical (not rushed at session end). Part of the uniform ~2x structural metadata-write residual (bd-wurxc family).
close_reason: Kept bounded ext4 base-device block cache below MVCC: RCH ffs-core bench ext4_base_block_cache_1092reads_42unique measured 25.07x median component win (uncached 93.202 ms vs cached 3.7183 ms), RCH check/test/bench/conformance green; scoped ffs-core clippy remains blocked by pre-existing pedantic debt outside this lever.

title: perf(core/ext4): lock-stripe the file-data block cache (bd-tag2s sibling)
description: Missed sibling of bd-tag2s/W150: the ext4 read-only file-data block cache (also serves directory blocks) was a single RwLock<BTreeMap<BlockNumber,Arc<[u8]>>> in ffs-core lib.rs:857. Hit on every read_ext4_file_data_block_with_scope across 8 FUSE worker threads. The miss path took the EXCLUSIVE write lock UNCONDITIONALLY then checked len<cap, so once the small cache (256 blocks ~1MiB) is full (steady state for any working set >1MiB) every cold read exclusively locked the whole cache just to refuse, serializing all readers. Converted to the existing 16-shard ShardedCache (get/contains_key lock one shard; insert_within does lock-free atomic len load first, no lock when full). Added ShardedCache::contains_key.
close_reason: Shipped 44e63bd7. ext4_file_data_block_cache RwLock<BTreeMap> -> 16-shard ShardedCache. SCORE: ext4_file_data_cache_concurrent_8t (8 threads, full 256-block cache, mixed warm-hit + cold-miss get->insert flow) rwlock_single 40.163ms -> sharded_mutex_16 8.6893ms = 4.62x. Root cause of the win: old miss path took the exclusive write lock unconditionally (even to refuse when full), serializing all 8 readers; insert_within does a lock-free atomic len load first. ISO: full ffs-core suite 1106 pass, clippy --all-targets clean, bench asserts identical hit aggregate between rwlock and sharded. e2e on real ext4 larger still (this isolates lock contention).

title: Kernel-conformance pin for parse_xattr_items 30-byte header offsets
description: Found via /testing-conformance-harnesses audit. ffs_btrfs::parse_xattr_items (lib.rs:401) reads data_len at offset 25..27 and name_len at offset 27..29 from a 30-byte header derived from struct btrfs_dir_item in fs/btrfs/btrfs_tree.h (xattr items reuse the dir_item layout but with data_len > 0 to carry the value bytes). The remaining fields (objectid, key_type, key_offset, transid, file_type) are skipped — only the two u16 fields participate in the parser's cur+=value_end recurrence. bd-qwo4a pinned the SAME 30-byte header offsets for parse_dir_items, but parse_xattr_items has its own copy of the read_u16 calls at +25/+27 — a regression that drifted these offsets in parse_xattr_items independently would silently corrupt every getxattr/listxattr through ffs_core::OpenFs (12+ call sites). bd-fhznm added round-trip MR proptests but those test the parser as a black box; this pin asserts the white-box offsets. Fix: add parse_xattr_items_kernel_offsets_match_btrfs_tree_h that stamps data_len@25 (must be 0 actually... wait, value bytes follow), name_len@27 with unique magics, plus stamps the SKIPPED fields with distinct non-zero magic to prove they're not accidentally read into one of the extracted fields. data_len > 0 (value bytes), name_len > 0 (name bytes), and the parsed struct should round-trip to (name, value) equal to the magic-stamped slices.

title: [REALITY-CHECK] ScrubDaemon not wired to ffs mount path; README's 'automatic recovery / no separate fsck' is aspirational at runtime
description:
# Reality-check finding — vision→runtime integration gap

## Vision claim (README.md:35, :838)

> TL;DR table, RaptorQ self-healing row: 'Corruption detected by checksums triggers automatic recovery. Stale-window SLO monitoring. **No separate fsck pass. No downtime.**'
>
> Corruption Recovery section: 'The scrub pipeline (`ffs-repair::pipeline`) continuously monitors block integrity and orchestrates automatic recovery.'

## Reality (runtime code)

`ScrubDaemon` is implemented in `crates/ffs-repair/src/pipeline.rs:695+` with `run_once`, `run_until_cancelled`, backpressure-aware scheduling, and evidence-ledger integration — all tested (bd-15c.5, bd-15c.6, bd-15c.11 all closed). But it is never started by any mount-path code:

- `crates/ffs-fuse/` — zero references to `ScrubDaemon`, `RepairPipeline`, or `start_scrub_daemon`
- `crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs` — `ffs-repair` is not even a Cargo dependency of `ffs-core`
- `crates/ffs-cli/src/main.rs` mount dispatch at line 4160+ (`MountRuntimeMode::Standard` / `Managed` / `PerCore`) calls `mount_with_fuse` / `mount_managed` and returns — no daemon spawn

The 'automatic recovery' path is only exercised by the E2E test `e2e_survive_five_percent_random_block_corruption_with_daemon` inside `ffs-repair` itself, which instantiates the daemon directly in test scaffolding. There is no production call site that starts the daemon when a user runs `ffs mount`.

## Evidence

- `rg 'ScrubDaemon|start_scrub_daemon|RepairPipeline' crates/ffs-fuse/ crates/ffs-core/src/ crates/ffs-cli/` → zero matches
- `crates/ffs-fuse/Cargo.toml`, `crates/ffs-core/Cargo.toml`, `crates/ffs-block/Cargo.toml` → no `ffs-repair` dep
- `crates/ffs-cli/src/main.rs:4160-4180` mount dispatch: `mount_with_fuse(open_fs, mountpoint, read_write, allow_other, auto_unmount)?` — no repair/scrub setup

Additionally, the only read-path → repair hook in the codebase is the `RepairFlushLifecycle` trait (`crates/ffs-block/src/lib.rs:512`), which fires AFTER writes flush (to refresh stale symbols). There is NO 'checksum failed during FUSE read → invoke RaptorQ decode' hook; `decode_group` is only called from within `ffs-repair` itself.

## Why this is a real vision gap

The README's self-healing promise is a top-line differentiator ('automatic recovery', 'no separate fsck pass', 'no downtime'). At runtime, users mounting via `ffs mount` get zero of this — checksum failures surface as I/O errors with no repair attempt, and corruption is not scanned in the background.

The components all exist and are tested; they're just not integrated into the runtime mount path.

## Fix direction

1. Add `ffs-repair` as a workspace dependency of `ffs-core` (so mount-time wiring can construct the pipeline).
2. Extend `OpenOptions` / `MountOptions` with `self_heal: SelfHealConfig { enabled, interval, budget, ... }`.
3. On mount, construct `ScrubDaemon` and spawn it under asupersync `Cx` so it honors the mount's cancellation tree (not `Cx::for_testing()` like the flush daemon does).
4. Add a read-path callback (mirror of `RepairFlushLifecycle` but for reads): when a block read surfaces a checksum failure, invoke `decode_group` to attempt repair; if successful, write back the repaired block and log an evidence-ledger event.
5. CLI: add `--self-heal / --no-self-heal` flag to `ffs mount` (default: enabled for `--rw`, disabled for RO since reads to bad blocks on RO-mounted images can't be fixed in place).
6. Document the runtime behavior change in README — move 'no separate fsck pass' from TL;DR to 'when self-heal is enabled' scope.

## Acceptance

- `ffs mount --rw --self-heal` starts the scrub daemon against the mounted image.
- A bit-flipped block on the mounted image, read through the FUSE path, is transparently repaired (evidence-ledger entry + corrected bytes returned).
- E2E test extended to drive the corruption scenario through `ffs mount` (not just via the in-process ScrubDaemon test harness).
- README either (a) stops claiming automatic recovery in the default mount path, or (b) ships with self-heal on by default once the integration is proven safe.

The full mount-path integration (new ffs-repair dep in ffs-core, SelfHealConfig on MountOptions, ScrubDaemon spawn under mount Cx, RepairReadLifecycle trait wiring on the read-path, --self-heal CLI flag) is tracked as follow-up feature bead bd-hoh5n with detailed acceptance criteria. title: Fix TOCTOU in sharded MVCC prune and overflow in btrfs stripe calculations

title: [perf] coalesce contiguous per-block reads into one syscall on file-read path (rank-1 syscall cost; prerequisite for bd-kq3b4)
description:
[perf] Coalesce contiguous per-block reads into one syscall on the file-read path (rank-1 syscall cost; prerequisite for bd-kq3b4).

EVIDENCE: docs/reports/PROFILE_ANALYSIS.md + tests/artifacts/perf/2026-06-01_plumfern — fresh direct-read samply (release-perf ffs-harness, 15s) shows __internal_syscall_cancel = 65.59% self on the per-block direct-read path; __memset_avx2 5.82%, __memcpy_avx 4.93%. bd-kq3b4 (memmove/memset buffer movement) is explicitly DEFERRED in its own note "until the remaining per-block direct-read syscall path is addressed". This bead is that prerequisite.

ROOT CAUSE: the file-read loop issues one pread per filesystem block even when the physical span is contiguous. Concrete site (btrfs): crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs ~5852-5863, inside btrfs read-bytes-at-logical. For a contiguous physical span `to_read_usize` bytes at `physical_offset` (already proven contiguous by the chunk mapping), the inner `while pos < to_read_usize` loop calls `block_dev.read_block(cx, block_num)` once per block (N blocks => N preads via FileByteDevice::read_exact_at -> self.file.read_exact_at, crates/ffs-block/src/lib.rs:415) and then copy_from_slice each block into `out`. So an aligned 1 MiB read = 256 preads + 256 copies. AUDIT the ext4 extent read path for the same pattern (extent reads are also physically contiguous runs) and the fsck/scrub scan paths.

LEVER (one change): for the aligned middle of a contiguous span, issue a single `read_exact_at(physical_offset_aligned, &mut out[head..tail])` (or read_vectored_exact_at — FileByteDevice::supports_vectored_reads() is already true) directly into the output slice, eliminating the per-block syscalls AND the per-block copy for the bulk. Only the unaligned head/tail partial blocks keep the read-block + copy path.

CACHE-COHERENCY CAVEAT (why it is non-trivial): block_dev.read_block() routes through the block cache (and read-only caches added by bd-7l5f0/bd-srh8m). A coalesced direct read_exact_at bypasses that cache, which is (a) a correctness risk if any block in the span has a buffered/dirty cache entry, and (b) a cache-population regression. The coalesced read MUST be cache-aware: e.g., only coalesce runs whose blocks are all absent from (or clean in) the cache, fall back to per-block for any cached block, and/or populate the cache from the coalesced buffer afterward. Prefer adding a `read_blocks_contiguous`/`read_span` method on the block device + cache layer rather than calling FileByteDevice directly from ffs-core.

VERIFICATION (extreme-software-optimization standard): golden-output sha256 isomorphism over the read path (byte-identical reads across aligned/unaligned/cross-chunk/partial-block boundaries, empty reads, EOF, cached vs uncached); differential vs the current per-block path; rch hyperfine baseline on the direct-read scenario, ONE lever, re-bench for Score>=2.0 (target: collapse the 65% syscall self-cost). Needs healthy rch (currently degraded by the nightly-toolchain-bump cold-rebuild storm) for a trustworthy bench number.

SUCCESS METRIC: lower __internal_syscall_cancel self% on the direct-read flamegraph and lower fsck/read User CPU; PROVE behavior unchanged. Unblocks re-evaluation of bd-kq3b4.

Wired the existing MVCC-correct MvccBlockDevice::read_contiguous_blocks (one preadv for clean/non-overlaid ranges; scalar fallback otherwise) into btrfs_read_logical_into. Aligned full-block runs now use a single vectored device op instead of one pread per block; unaligned head/tail keep scalar read_block. Allocation/copy counts unchanged -> strictly fewer syscalls.
PROVEN: isomorphism (ffs-core lib 878/878; btrfs_kernel_reference 7/7 — real mkfs.btrfs images via vectored FileByteDevice, multi-block reads, byte-identical golden) + behaviour (new test btrfs_read_coalesces_contiguous_block_reads_into_vectored_io: 4-block read issues a coalesced vectored op, byte-identical, via VectoredCountingDevice) + clippy -D warnings + fmt clean.
REMAINING before close: fresh flamegraph / hyperfine Score>=2.0 quantification of the __internal_syscall_cancel self% drop — blocked on healthy rch (degraded; nightly-toolchain-bump cold-rebuild storm). Also TODO: audit/apply the same coalescing to the ext4 file-read path (no per-block ext4 read loop located this pass; btrfs path done).

--- UPDATE 2 (ext4 path done, commit 48d81a6a) ---
read_file_data now coalesces runs of logically+physically-consecutive written ext4 blocks via the existing overlay-correct read_contiguous_blocks_with_scope (one vectored op per run; scalar fallback for holes/unwritten/tx-staged/snapshot-visible/unaligned). Proven: ffs-core 879/879; ext4 read units 5/5; ext4_kernel_vs_ffs_file_content + directory 2/2 (real mkfs ext4 images via vectored FileByteDevice, byte-identical to debugfs/golden); clippy/fmt clean. This directly proves the rank-1 syscall-count reduction (__internal_syscall_cancel self-cost). title: ext4 fallocate INSERT_RANGE missing EFBIG when insert grows i_size past max file size
description: ext4_fallocate's insert_range branch (ffs-core lib.rs ~15223) computes new_size = inode.size + length with only a u64 checked_add (-> FfsError::Format = EINVAL on overflow), but never checks the ext4 maximum file size. The top-of-function Self::ext4_reject_oversized_file(end, block_size) uses end = offset + length, which does NOT bound the post-insert size (inode.size + length): a small offset+length passes it while inode.size+length can exceed 2^32*block_size. The kernel's ext4_insert_range (fs/ext4/extents.c) returns EFBIG when len > s_maxbytes - i_size. FIX: call Self::ext4_reject_oversized_file(new_size, block_size)? before the ffs_extent::insert_range shift. Same EFBIG-parity class as bd-3pa5m (ext4 write/truncate/fallocate) and bd-d9129 (btrfs). Testable: truncate-up (sparse) to max-block, INSERT_RANGE 2 blocks at offset block -> new_size exceeds max -> EFBIG (the file stays sparse so no huge allocation).
close_reason: Fixed in 5f4b2897: ext4_fallocate insert_range now calls ext4_reject_oversized_file(new_size) before the shift -> EFBIG when i_size+length exceeds the ext4 max (2^32*block_size), matching the kernel's ext4_insert_range. Indirect path already rejects insert_range (UnsupportedFeature). Test ext4_fallocate_insert_range_past_max_file_size_returns_efbig_bd_a3fh8 (sparse extend to max-block + insert -> EFBIG; fails pre-fix). Full ffs-core 1081 green.

title: [perf] btrfs_lookup_dir_entry is O(N) full-scan; should be O(log N) name-hash point lookup
description: btrfs_lookup_dir_entry (ffs-core lib.rs ~23072) ranges over ALL DIR_ITEM items for the directory (offset 0..u64::MAX) and linearly scans+parses each to find the name — O(N) in directory entries. But btrfs keys every DIR_ITEM by (parent, DIR_ITEM, name_hash) where name_hash=btrfs_name_hash(name); a name can ONLY appear in its own hash bucket. So a lookup must compute name_hash and query the single key (parent, DIR_ITEM, name_hash) — an O(log N) COW-tree point lookup + a scan of the tiny collision bucket — exactly as btrfs_getxattr already does for XATTR_ITEM. btrfs_lookup_dir_entry has 14 callers (every path-component resolution + create/rename/unlink/link existence check), so large directories pay O(N) per lookup. FIX: replace range(0..MAX) with range(&key,&key) at offset=name_hash, keep the bucket scan for collisions. Isomorphic (same entry found iff present). Complexity-class win, behavior-identical.

title: ext4 fast-commit del_range punch+free leaves the group free-block count 2 low — e2fsck rejects the image (pre-existing on 879a42f5)
description:
`cargo test -p ffs-core --lib -- fast_commit_del_range_apply_punches_and_frees_passes_e2fsck`
fails. e2fsck reports:

    Free blocks count wrong for group #0 (6522, counted=6524).
    Free blocks count wrong (6522, counted=6524).
    WARNING: Filesystem still has errors

The superblock/group free-block counters are 2 blocks LOW relative to the bitmap after a
fast-commit `del_range` punch frees blocks: the blocks are cleared in the bitmap but the
group descriptor / superblock free counts are not credited for them.

PROVENANCE: pre-existing, not a regression from concurrent work. Reproduced at a clean
detached worktree on HEAD 879a42f5 with no working-tree changes — 0 passed / 1 failed, the
same two counter values. Found incidentally while running the ffs-core suite as the
regression gate for bd-giw9n (btrfs); bd-giw9n's change is 6 identical btrfs COW-tree
builder renames in ffs-core plus ffs-btrfs internals and cannot reach the ext4 fast-commit
path.

Rest of the suite at that point: 1195 passed, 1 failed, 21 ignored.
close_reason: Fixed: fast-commit recovery frees blocks/inodes through a TRANSIENT alloc state and persists the group descriptors itself, but under GDT-persistence deferral (default on) the LIVE ext4_alloc_state is what every later durability boundary flushes from (ext4_flush_group_descriptors) and what the superblock totals are summed from (ext4_sync_superblock_free_totals). The live state never saw the recovery free, so the next flush_mvcc_to_device rewrote the pre-punch counts over the freshly persisted ones while the bitmap kept the blocks free -> e2fsck 'Free blocks count wrong for group #0 (6522, counted=6524)' + the matching superblock line. Fix: snapshot the transient state's per-group (free_blocks, free_inodes, used_dirs) before the recovery pass and fold the deltas into the live state after persisting; applied at BOTH sites with this shape (apply_fast_commit_del_range_ops and free_fast_commit_deleted_inode, which carried the identical latent bug). Verified: the named test goes FAIL->ok, and ffs-core --lib is 1196 passed / 0 failed / 21 ignored (was 1195/1/21). cargo clippy -p ffs-core clean for the touched file.

title: Expand ext4 dir block checksum tests beyond round-trip + no-panic
description:
crates/ffs-ondisk/src/ext4.rs has stamp/verify_dir_block_checksum but the proptest coverage in the same file is limited to:

  - ext4_proptest_verify_dir_block_checksum_no_panic (negative)
  - ext4_proptest_verify_dir_block_checksum_short_rejects (negative)
  - ext4_proptest_dir_block_checksum_stamp_verify (round-trip)

None of these exercise the per-inode seed mixing — i.e. the kernel's defence against:
  - replaying a valid dir block under a different (ino, generation) tuple
  - using a stamp produced under one filesystem csum_seed on another filesystem instance
  - flipping a bit in the directory entry payload after a valid stamp

Apply the same four metamorphic relations the inode checksum harness now covers:
  - MR-INO: identical body, two different ino numbers → different stored checksums
  - MR-GEN: identical body+ino, different generation → different stored checksums
  - MR-SEED: identical body+ino+gen, different csum_seed → different stored checksums
  - MR-DETECT: single-bit flip in the covered region [0..bs-12] invalidates verification

Land them as proptests in crates/ffs-ondisk/src/ext4.rs alongside the existing ext4_proptest_dir_block_checksum_stamp_verify.

markdown renderer / docs pipeline that consumes this output.
