title: perf(repair): binary-search expected_current in build_writeback_blocks (O(M·N)->O(M·log N))
description: RecoverySession::build_writeback_blocks (ffs-repair recovery.rs:444) maps each decode.recovered block back to its scrub-time expected bytes via expected_current.iter().find(|(block,_)| *block==recovered.block) — an O(N) linear scan inside the loop over decode.recovered (M items), so O(M·N) ~ O(N²) when most blocks are recovered. expected_current is built by capture_expected_current_blocks from the NORMALIZED corrupt_indices (normalize_indices sort_unstable+dedup) with block=source_first_block+index, so it is STRICTLY ASCENDING and UNIQUE by BlockNumber (Copy+Ord). LEVER: replace .iter().find() with binary_search_by_key(&recovered.block,|(b,_)| *b) -> O(log N) per lookup, O(M·log N) total. Iso-correct: unique keys => binary_search hits the same element find would; Err arm preserves the existing 'missing scrub-time bytes' RepairFailed error. Hot path: erasure-coded block recovery after corruption/scrub-repair; N=corrupt block count can be large in a real recovery. Bench target: recovery_build_writeback_blocks (linear_find vs binary_search across N=64/512/4096, M=N) with assert_eq isomorphism guard. ffs-repair has criterion wired. cc filed from quiet-crate frontier (ffs-mvcc/ffs-core/ffs-extent contended).
close_reason: VERIFIED bench recovery_build_writeback_blocks: linear_find vs binary_search 5.43x(N=64)/15.99x(N=512)/58.10x(N=4096) — algorithmic O(M·N)->O(M·logN), scales with N. KEEP.

title: MR proptests for parse_root_ref round-trip + append/truncation rejection
description: Found via /testing-metamorphic audit. ffs_btrfs::parse_root_ref (lib.rs:688) is the parser used by every subvolume enumeration to extract (dirid, sequence, name) from a ROOT_REF leaf entry. Existing tests cover 3 fixed inputs (parse_root_ref_valid, parse_root_ref_too_short, parse_root_ref_adversarial_samples_exercise_boundaries) but no proptest sweeps over arbitrary (dirid, sequence, name) tuples. parse_root_ref has stricter length semantics than parse_inode_refs: it rejects both data.len() < name_end AND data.len() > name_end (exact match required). A regression that loosened either bound would silently accept truncated or append-padded payloads but pass the named tests. Fix: add proptest!() block with three MRs — (1) round-trip via a stamp helper for arbitrary (u64, u64, name 1..=64); (2) append-rejection sweeping arbitrary suffixes 1..32 bytes; (3) truncation-rejection sweeping arbitrary 1..len truncation offsets.

title: btrfs_fs_tree_root_bytenr full-walks the root tree per read op; range-descend the ROOT_ITEM
description:
Every read-only btrfs op resolves its subvolume's fs-tree root via btrfs_fs_tree_root_bytenr → walk_btrfs_root_tree, a FULL O(R) walk of the root tree, then .find()s the single ROOT_ITEM for subvol_id. On a multi-subvolume / snapshotted filesystem the root tree spans many leaves (ROOT_ITEM + ROOT_REF/BACKREF + DIR + UUID items per subvol), so this is O(R) node reads per read op — and it now dominates the per-op cost after bd-n040r made the fs-tree walk O(log N).

LEVER: range-descend sb.root for [(subvol_id,ROOT_ITEM,0),(subvol_id,ROOT_ITEM+1,0)) via the existing walk_tree_range primitive (bd-n040r), reading O(log R) nodes. The root tree is NOT subject to the fs-tree tree-log overlay, so no overlay handling needed. Isomorphic: .find() takes the first (objectid,ROOT_ITEM) in key order; range descent returns the same items in key order. PROOF: 2-level multi-leaf root-tree fixture + device-read count A/B, target Score>=2.0.
close_reason: done

title: perf(isa): the benchmarked release-perf binary is x86-64 BASELINE (SSE2) for ffs's own code — production build-perf.sh uses target-cpu=x86-64-v3+PGO. Benchmark binary != production binary.
description:
FINDING (BlackThrush/cc_ffs 2026-07-10). The ISA question for this repo, answered.

DOES ffs EMIT BASELINE OR AVX2? For its OWN code: BASELINE (SSE2). Only runtime-dispatched deps use AVX2.

EVIDENCE (binary sha256=03b7456d8cd6fa118bd214b2fdf8a03e56cac79e6768b7311613b039c8ae81eb, the binary
used for the ENTIRE cold-read campaign):
  * RUSTFLAGS unset; no target-cpu / target-feature in .cargo/config.toml, Cargo.toml, or
    rust-toolchain.toml. => a plain `cargo build --profile release-perf` compiles ffs's OWN code for
    the default x86-64 baseline (SSE2), NOT x86-64-v3.
  * ffs's own SWAR hot functions (names_eq, dx_hash, word-at-a-time) disassemble to scalar GPR ops --
    no ymm/zmm. The SWAR primitives are baseline-compatible by design (u64 GPR tricks), so they do not
    benefit from a higher target-cpu, but any AUTOVECTORIZABLE ffs loop (block scans, extent parse,
    copy-shaped loops) is emitted as SSE2 in this binary.
  * The 1401 AVX2 + 2018 AVX-512(zmm) mnemonics in the binary come from RUNTIME-DISPATCHED dep crates
    (crc32c, xxhash-rust, memchr, blake3), which ship multiple ISA variants and pick at runtime. The
    AVX-512 variants are dead on this host (/proc/cpuinfo: avx2 bmi2 sse4_2, NO avx512f). This is the
    correct, portable pattern for deps -- not a gap.

THE GAP: the PRODUCTION build is scripts/build-perf.sh, which sets `RUSTFLAGS=-C target-cpu=x86-64-v3`
(AVX2/BMI2/FMA) + fat LTO + PGO. Its own header records target-cpu=x86-64-v3 = ~8.5% fewer create
instructions, ~3% lookup (measured 2026-07-03, not re-measured here). rch's plain `cargo build
--profile release-perf` does NOT apply those RUSTFLAGS. So the benchmark binary != the production binary.

IMPACT:
  * A/B RATIOS are unaffected -- both arms use the same binary (bd-ddryj 1.21x, null 1.02x stand).
  * ABSOLUTE vs-kernel numbers are affected: the honest cold-read gap (1.41x as-shipped, 1.15x capped)
    is an UPPER BOUND for a SECOND reason (baseline codegen) on top of the 3.10 ms harness constant.
    The production v3+PGO binary is faster -> the real gap is tighter than 1.41x.
  * EVERY future workload-class benchmark (fsync, small-file storms, readdir+stat, xattr) must use the
    v3+PGO production binary (build-perf.sh output), or explicitly note it is a baseline build.

WHAT TO DO:
  1. Decide whether release-perf itself should carry target-cpu=x86-64-v3 (portability: requires a
     2015+ CPU; build-perf.sh already documents this trade). If perf benchmarks are meant to reflect
     production, the benchmark binary should match production ISA.
  2. Re-run the headline cold-read + create/lookup numbers on the build-perf.sh binary to get the
     production-ISA gap vs kernel, replacing the baseline-binary numbers.
  3. Consider auto-vectorization opportunities in ffs's own hot loops that only pay off at v3
     (needs the v3 binary to measure -- do not assume).
BLOCKED on the same build blocker (cannot produce a binary via rch). build-perf.sh runs locally and is
disk-heavy, so it needs an owner-granted build window under the disk constraint.
notes:
CORRECTED BUILD-WIDEN TARGET 2026-07-10 (BlackThrush/cc_ffs). The SWAR paths are NOT the beneficiaries.

A build-widen (target-cpu=x86-64-v3) only changes what the COMPILER AUTO-EMITS. It cannot rewrite
hand-written u64 SWAR (GPR XOR/mask/shift tricks) into vector code. So the SWAR hash paths named as
candidates -- extent_root_namespace (7.14x), names_eq, symlink NUL-trim, casefold -- do NOT benefit:
they are ISA-INDEPENDENT by construction and run identically on baseline and v3. Widening the build will
not touch them, and rewriting them as explicit AVX2 is a CODE change blocked by forbid(unsafe_code)
(std::arch SIMD intrinsics are unsafe).

WHERE THE MEASURED v3 UPLIFT ACTUALLY COMES FROM. build-perf.sh's own header records target-cpu=x86-64-v3
as ~8.5% fewer CREATE instructions and ~3% LOOKUP -- NOT read. Those paths' hot inner loops include the
allocator bitmap bit-scan (crates/ffs-alloc/src/succinct.rs: trailing_zeros at :426/:435, count_zeros) and
bit-manipulation that v3's BMI1/BMI2 (tzcnt/lzcnt, and potentially pdep/pext) accelerate over baseline
bsf/bsr. Corroborating: the baseline benchmark binary has pdep/pext/blsr = 0 (BMI2 has no baseline
fallback) and 922 bsr vs 34 lzcnt -- consistent with baseline codegen.

=> The build-widen beneficiary is the ALLOCATOR + metadata (create/lookup) path, which is cod_ffs's active
   alloc lane (recent: word-at-a-time bitmap set/clear up to 113x). NOT the SWAR hash paths, NOT the read
   path (v3 gave read ~0; the read gap is copy + userspace, per the cold-read closeout).

ACTIONABLE:
  1. Decide whether release-perf itself should set target-cpu=x86-64-v3 so benchmarks match the production
     binary (portability: 2015+ CPU required; build-perf.sh already documents the trade). This is a
     build-config decision, not a code lever.
  2. If pursued, the create/lookup uplift lands in cod's allocator lane -- coordinate, do not collide.
  3. The SWAR paths need no action from a build-widen.

title: Add randomized batch-vs-single allocation metamorphic coverage
description:
Discovery from testing-metamorphic while source-aware tracker hygiene reported zero local claimable rows and RCH capacity remained blocked.

`crates/ffs-alloc/src/lib.rs` now has `alloc_blocks_batch_persist` for amortized single-block allocation, with fixed tests for zero/single/multiple counts, free-space accounting, locality, no-space, spillover, and one clean-state `batch_vs_single_equivalence` check. The property surface is broader than those examples: batch allocation should be observationally equivalent to repeated `alloc_blocks_persist(count=1)` for the same starting geometry, group state, bitmap contents, request size, and goal hints. Search evidence found no randomized/proptest coverage for `alloc_blocks_batch_persist` equivalence across fragmented bitmaps, partially exhausted goal groups, cross-group spillover, and goal_block-vs-goal_group precedence.

Metamorphic relation: for any valid synthetic allocator state and bounded `n`, running batch allocation once or running `n` single allocations in sequence must produce the same allocation set/order where the algorithm promises determinism, the same per-group free-block deltas, the same bitmap bits for allocated/free blocks, and equivalent failure semantics with rollback/no persistent leak when space is insufficient.

Acceptance:
1. Add proptest coverage in `crates/ffs-alloc/src/lib.rs` or a crate-local test module that generates bounded fragmented block bitmaps, group free counters, request sizes, and `AllocHint` variants.
2. The test must compare `alloc_blocks_batch_persist` against repeated `alloc_blocks_persist(count=1)` from cloned devices/groups, asserting allocation order or an explicitly documented weaker equivalence if order differs by design.
3. Cover at least goal group with enough space, goal group spillover, goal_block in another group, reserved metadata holes, and insufficient-space rollback; after failure, bitmap/free counters must match the pre-call snapshot.
4. Preserve existing fixed examples and benchmark intent; do not weaken the batch allocator to pass tests by delegating multi-block requests back to the slow path.
5. Validate with `rch exec -- cargo test -p ffs-alloc batch -- --nocapture`, `rch exec -- cargo test -p ffs-alloc proptest -- --nocapture` or a focused test filter, `rch exec -- cargo check -p ffs-alloc --all-targets`, `rch exec -- cargo clippy -p ffs-alloc --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `rch exec -- cargo fmt -p ffs-alloc --check`, `jq empty .beads/issues.jsonl`, `git diff --check`, `br dep cycles --no-db --no-auto-import --json`, and source-aware hygiene. If RCH still has no admissible workers, keep this blocked on `bd-oowwx` and do not use local cargo as proof.
close_reason: Completed: added bounded metamorphic coverage comparing alloc_blocks_batch_persist against repeated alloc_blocks_persist single-block allocation from identical seeded bitmap/GDT states. The new randomized property covers fragmented bitmaps, goal group, goal block, and combined hint variants; deterministic regressions cover goal-group spillover, foreign goal_block precedence under goal_group, reserved metadata holes, and insufficient-space rollback to the pre-call bitmap/free-counter/GDT snapshot. Validated remotely on ts1 with cargo test -p ffs-alloc batch -- --nocapture, cargo check -p ffs-alloc --all-targets, and cargo clippy -p ffs-alloc --all-targets -- -D warnings; local cargo fmt -p ffs-alloc --check passed after RCH declined fmt as non-compilation; JSONL, diff check, and dependency cycles passed.

title: ext4 write path does not coalesce contiguous extents (fragments sequential writes; e2fsck i_blocks/free-count for >4-block files)
description: ROOT CAUSE behind bd-nd61w (whose 'sb free count' framing was a symptom). ext4_write (ffs-core lib.rs ~15340) fills a write block-by-block: for each logical block it calls ffs_extent::allocate_extent(logical, 1) and inserts a separate 1-block extent — even when the allocator returns a CONTIGUOUS run. PROVEN: fs.write(0, 5120) on a fresh file yields 5 single-block extents at contiguous phys 1666..1670 instead of one extent [0,5). CONSEQUENCE: a >4-block contiguous write exceeds the 4-entry inline extent root, forcing tree growth into a metadata leaf block; the write path does NOT count that metadata block in i_blocks -> e2fsck 'Inode i_blocks is X, should be X+...' AND the free-block total is off. (<=4-block writes stay inline and ARE e2fsck-clean — so data-block alloc DOES keep the sb/GD/bitmap consistent; only the no-coalescing-induced tree-growth metadata is mis-accounted.) ⚠️FAILED APPROACH (do not repeat): adding coalescing to ffs_btree::insert (merge new extent with a logically+physically-contiguous same-state predecessor) FIXES sequential writes (8 contiguous blocks -> 1 extent, e2fsck-clean) BUT CORRUPTS collapse_range/insert_range — they re-insert shifted extents via ffs_btree::insert and rely on it NOT coalescing; the curated + randomized fallocate proptests caught it ('content diverged ... 8192 bytes differ'). CORRECT APPROACH: scope coalescing to the data-write path only — either (a) ext4_write detects a contiguous run and allocates+inserts it as ONE extent, or (b) a coalesce flag/opt-in variant of ffs_btree::insert used ONLY by ext4_write (all other callers — collapse/insert/punch/FC-recovery — keep non-coalescing insert). VALIDATE: 8-block contiguous write -> 1 extent + e2fsck-clean; ffs-extent suite + ffs-core write/truncate/fallocate proptests stay green (they caught the bad global approach). RESIDUAL (separate, rarer): a genuinely-fragmented file (>4 NON-contiguous extents) still grows the tree and the metadata block is uncounted in i_blocks — fix the tree-growth allocator to bump i_blocks for metadata blocks.
close_reason: done

title: ffs-ondisk: Ext4{Compat,Incompat,RoCompat}Features lack kernel-conformance test for 40 feature bits
description:
Finding (via /testing-conformance-harnesses skill, eighth visit,
different target): the three ext4 feature-flag wrapper structs in
crates/ffs-ondisk/src/ext4.rs declare 40 feature-bit constants in
total:

  * `Ext4CompatFeatures` (l. 148-196): 10 flags (DIR_PREALLOC=0x1
    .. ORPHAN_FILE=0x1000)
  * `Ext4IncompatFeatures` (l. 210-...): 16 flags (COMPRESSION=0x1
    .. CASEFOLD=0x20000)
  * `Ext4RoCompatFeatures` (l. 327-...): 14 flags (SPARSE_SUPER=0x1
    .. ORPHAN_PRESENT=0x10000)

Each mirrors a kernel macro from `fs/ext4/ext4.h` (EXT4_FEATURE_*).
The flags control mount eligibility:
  * COMPAT bits: advisory; unknown bits are safe to ignore.
  * INCOMPAT bits: unknown bits MUST cause mount failure.
  * RO_COMPAT bits: unknown bits cause read-only mount.

There is **no kernel-conformance test** pinning the 40 values. A
regression that swapped, e.g., FILETYPE (0x2) and EXTENTS (0x40)
would silently mis-classify every ext4 image. A regression in BIT64
(0x80) would silently fail to recognize 64-bit field layout.

Pairs with bd-tyeic (27 EXT4_*_FL inode flags), bd-k81lq (reserved
inodes), bd-343v3 (file types), bd-khzn4 (btrfs tree objectids),
bd-f0q7n (btrfs item keys), bd-xhswi (btrfs csum types), bd-vnfhb
(POSIX S_IS predicates).

Acceptance: kernel-conformance unit test pinning all 40 feature
flag constants to their canonical kernel macro values, plus the
structural invariant that each flag is a single power-of-2 bit and
no two flags within the same set share a bit.
close_reason: done

title: parallel metadata writes negatively scale: residual malloc-arena + MVCC commit-lock contention (8.3x vs kernel at 8t)
description: After sharding the name-index (bd-par1, fixed the rayon-convoy layer, 16x->8.3x), parallel creates STILL negatively scale: frankenfs 8t=17193 vs kernel 143117 = 8.3x; frankenfs 1t=31866 vs 8t=17193 (NEGATIVE) while kernel scales 30927->143117 (4.6x). The real cost is PURELY PARALLEL — N threads' cheap in-order commits convoy on the ONE global CommitPublicationGate + active_snapshots lock. comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: 2026-07-02 BlackThrush (profiled the correctly-framed parallel workload): create-bench negative-scales 1t=122k -> 4t=71k -> 8t=69k creates/s. perf @8t: ShardedMvccStore::commit 3.47% self + parking_lot rwlock lock/unlock_exclusive_slow ~1.1% = top contention. PINPOINTED the serialization mechanism: CommitPublicationGate::publish (crates/ffs-mvcc/src/sharded.rs:72-97) enforces IN-ORDER publication — a commit with seq N Condvar-waits (wait_lock Mutex + ready Condvar) until ALL seqs < N have published (advance_ready_prefix over a BTreeSet). So N parallel committers convoy: the fast thread holding seq N blocks until slower earlier-seq threads publish. Plus notify_all on each prefix advance = O(waiters) thundering-herd wakeups. This is INHERENT to contiguous-prefix MVCC snapshot consistency (a snapshot at seq N must see a gap-free prefix), so it's loom-gated owner-lane, NOT a quick fix. Candidate directions (all loom-gated): per-shard/independent publication sequences so disjoint-shard commits don't order against each other; or targeted wakeup (per-seq signal) to kill the notify_all herd. Also tested read-only parallel WALK (safe) — does NOT scale warm (page-cache-resident + rayon coordination overhead), so no safe read-side contention lever there either.

comments.text: 2026-07-02 BlackThrush (broad parallel profile — FUNDAMENTAL CONSTRAINT): @8t the create cost is memmove 9.5% (MVCC version copy) + crc32c ~5.6% (metadata_csum, already HW crc_u64_parallel3) + ShardedMvccStore::commit 3.47% + add_entry_reject_existing 2.79% — ALL executed while holding ext4_create's alloc_mutex.write() (lib.rs:16858) for the whole op. So two serializers stack: (1) the single alloc_mutex serializes EVERY create (whole inode-alloc + dir-insert incl the CPU-heavy crc/memmove), and (2) the MVCC in-order CommitPublicationGate. ⚠️FUNDAMENTAL WALL for the bead's 'per-group inode-table/bitmap partitioning' idea: ext4 packs 32 group descriptors per block, so the group-descriptor update for ANY group lands in a SHARED block (block 1 for the first 32 groups) -> every create writes that shared block -> MVCC block-granularity first-committer-wins CONFLICT even for disjoint-group creates. So per-group alloc sharding alone canNOT make disjoint creates touch disjoint blocks — the shared GDT block is an on-disk-FORMAT constraint. A real fix needs GDT accounting decoupled from the per-op block write: e.g. defer/batch group-descriptor free-count updates to flush time (in-memory GroupStats already hold the counts; persist GDT once at sync, not per-create) so per-create writes touch only per-group inode-table+bitmap blocks (disjoint) + the MVCC gate. That deferral is the real owner-lane lever; loom + e2fsck(free-counts)-gated.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: 2026-07-02 BlackThrush CORRECTION to my previous comment: the 'shared GDT block is a fundamental per-create write' claim is WRONG. gdt_persistence_deferred() (ffs-alloc/src/lib.rs:1720) is DEFAULT-ON (bd-cc-gdt-defer-default, FFS_SKIP_GDT!=0): the per-op group-descriptor write is ALREADY SKIPPED (persist_group_desc_with_bitmap_overrides returns early at :1744) — GroupStats is the authoritative in-memory count, GDT flushed ONCE at the durability boundary. So a create does NOT write the shared GDT block per-op; it writes only per-group inode-table + inode-bitmap (+ the parent dir block). Therefore the shared-block MVCC-conflict wall I described does NOT apply to disjoint-group/disjoint-parent creates. The ACTUAL serializers under the measured negative scaling (1t=122k->8t=69k, all at default config with GDT already deferred): (1) ext4_create holds the WHOLE-STATE alloc_mutex.write() (lib.rs:16858) for the entire op incl the CPU-heavy crc32c (~5.6%) + MVCC version memmove (~9.5%), serializing ALL creates regardless of group; (2) for a same-parent create storm (create-bench into one dir) the parent DIR block + parent inode are shared -> MVCC conflict on them; (3) the in-order CommitPublicationGate. Real levers (owner-lane, loom-gated): shard the alloc_mutex per-group (now UNBLOCKED since GDT defer removed the shared-GDT write) so disjoint-group creates parallelize; for same-dir storms the shared dir-block is inherent. Net: the create write set is already minimal per-op; the gap is lock/gate serialization, not write count.

title: perf(fuse): negotiate FUSE_POSIX_ACL so the kernel CACHES acl lookups — 2 of the 4 getxattr per entry on the 7.728937x readdir+stat row
description:
AIMED AT THE CAMPAIGN'S WORST MEASURED vs-INCUMBENT RATIO: btrfs readdir+stat 7.728937x.

THE MECHANISM, already counted rather than guessed. That row pays ~7.00 FUSE requests per
entry, and getxattr is 4.00 of them - the single largest component, larger than the
lookup+getattr pair (2.00) that readdirplus exists to fold away. The bounded xattr census
names exactly what is probed: security.capability, security.selinux, system.posix_acl_access,
system.posix_acl_default.

WHY THIS IS THE REMAINING SHAPE. security.capability is CLOSED (bd-z0rb8, closed negative):
kernel-originated, caller-independent, and the entire 6.17 FUSE INIT flag space is write-side
killpriv semantics with no read-side suppression. But the two system.posix_acl_* probes were
never examined, and unlike the capability probe there IS an ABI flag for them:
FUSE_POSIX_ACL, bit 20 (uapi/linux/fuse.h:467, present in the vendored fuser at
ll/fuse_abi.rs:229 and re-exported through `consts`). We have never negotiated it - grep for
POSIX_ACL across crates/ returns only ext4 on-disk xattr index constants in a harness test.

Without the flag the kernel sets no SB_POSIXACL, keeps no ACL cache for our inodes, and
forwards every ACL query as a fresh round trip. With it the kernel resolves ACLs itself and
caches the answer, INCLUDING the negative answer - which is the common case, since the fixture
images carry no ACLs. That is the one thing a daemon-side memo can never do: bd-2pq73 cut
format-level getxattr work 40x with requests_total UNCHANGED, because a memo still costs a
boundary crossing. This removes the crossing.

SIZE OF THE PRIZE, stated as arithmetic rather than a promise: if both ACL probes go away,
readdir+stat drops from ~7.00 to ~5.00 requests per entry. At the measured per-round-trip cost
that is the largest single reduction available on this row. It does NOT follow that the ratio
improves by 7/5 - the round trip cost is placement-dependent (bd-4ypbv) and the kernel arm is
unaffected - so the claim to test is the REQUEST COUNT first, which is exact and cheap to
count, and only then the wall.

WHAT IS WRITTEN (ProudBarn, 2026-08-16), unGATED because /data was at 54G against the 59G
threshold all turn:
  - POSIX_ACL_CAPABILITY + posix_acl_capability_from_env(), split into a PURE
    posix_acl_capability_from_value(Option<&str>) so the parsing is testable without mutating
    process-global env (racy under the parallel harness, and unsafe from edition 2024).
  - negotiated in init() only when the knob is on, guarded by `if posix_acl != 0` so the
    default path cannot change negotiation at all.
  - test posix_acl_knob_is_opt_in_and_inert_when_unset_bd_<this bead>: unset and every
    unrecognised value negotiate NOTHING; only 1/true/on (case- and whitespace-insensitive)
    negotiate exactly FUSE_POSIX_ACL; the bit is 1<<20; and it does not overlap the
    readdirplus bits.
Syntax verified with `rustfmt --edition 2024 --check` (parses clean, zero diff). NOT
type-checked - that needs a build.

DEFAULT OFF, and for a CORRECTNESS reason rather than caution. This flag is a CLAIM: it tells
the kernel the filesystem supports POSIX ACLs, after which the kernel performs its own
ACL-based permission checks from its cache instead of deferring to us. If our getxattr does not
report ACLs faithfully, ACCESS DECISIONS CHANGE. That is a semantic change, not a speed change,
and it must not ride in as a default on the strength of a latency argument. Opt-in polarity is
deliberate: a typo fails CLOSED.

ACCEPTANCE, in order:
 1. GATE the code (cargo test -p ffs-fuse --lib).
 2. CORRECTNESS FIRST, before any timing: with the knob ON, verify permission behaviour is
    unchanged on an image with no ACLs, and verify getxattr(system.posix_acl_access) still
    returns ENODATA rather than a malformed blob. If the kernel is caching an answer we
    generate incorrectly, the lever is void regardless of its speed.
 3. COUNT, not wall: one ELF, knob OFF vs ON, same mount, measure requests per entry on
    readdir+stat. The prediction is 7.00 -> 5.00. If the count does not move, the kernel is
    not caching what this flag was expected to make it cache, and the lever is dead - record
    it and stop, do not chase the wall.
 4. Only if the count moves: wall, with the daemon PINNED (bd-plt79 - an unpinned mounted
    measurement is unstable to 1.4875x on its own A/A null), two runs, worst bound quoted,
    absolute medians alongside the ratio.

RISK TO STATE PLAINLY: if the images DO carry ACLs, the kernel enforcing them from its own
cache is a behaviour change that could differ from our enforcement. Step 2 exists to catch that
before any number is quoted.
close_reason: done

comments.text:
ACCEPTANCE STEP 3 HARNESS LANDED (ProudBarn, 2026-08-16): scripts/fuse_xattr_count_ab.sh. Ready to run the moment the knob is gated; needs no further authoring.

IT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT TIME ANYTHING. The prediction here is exact and countable (7.00 -> 5.00 requests/entry), and a count is decidable in ONE run where a wall ratio needs pinning, replication, nulls and a worst-bound quote. If the count does not move, the kernel is not caching what FUSE_POSIX_ACL was expected to make it cache and the lever is dead - the script says so in its own verdict and tells the operator to STOP rather than proceed to wall.

FOUR TRAPS BUILT IN, each one already paid for elsewhere in this campaign:
 - assert_knob() requires the 'FUSE_POSIX_ACL negotiated' line in the ON arm and its ABSENCE in the OFF arm, failing closed on either. Without it an arm that silently failed to enable the knob would 'pass' while comparing two controls - the all-failing-workload trap.
 - rep 1 after every mount is discarded as cold; that artefact produced a spurious 1.5630x readdir+stat 'win' that sign-flipped on replicate (bd-4ypbv scope row).
 - the daemon is pinned, because an UNPINNED mounted measurement is unstable to 1.4875x on its own A/A null (bd-plt79). The client sits on the SMT sibling, NOT co-located: co-location is warm-stat-only, measured NULL on readdir+stat and inverting under concurrency.
 - it emits the per-name xattr census alongside the total, so a moved count can be ATTRIBUTED rather than assumed. If the total drops but the posix_acl probes did not, something else changed and the result is not this lever's.
Missing binary or image exits 2 rather than reporting an empty comparison; both paths verified.

STILL BLOCKED ON THE GATE: the knob itself (503c3b16) is syntax-verified only. /data has been 54-59G against the 59G threshold, so no build has been possible. Order of work when disk allows: gate the knob, then acceptance step 2 (correctness - does getxattr still report ACLs faithfully with the kernel caching them), then this script, and only then wall.

comments.text:
PREMISE REFUTED BY MEASUREMENT — CLOSING VOID (ProudBarn, 2026-08-16). I filed this bead this morning on an inherited figure and did not verify it first. Verifying it before spending a build is the only reason the mistake was cheap.

MEASURED against this row's OWN workload (ls -lU, 20001 entries, ext4 fixture, memo 65536, ELF binary_sha256=2faab3039bc3da4126df8b9197edb0f431467b0fc0dac2b3376d6a2bc0c14f12, hostname=thinkstation1):

  DAEMON   getattr 20394 (1.020/entry)   getxattr 20002 (1.000/entry)
           lookup  19808 (0.990/entry)   readdir     82 (0.004/entry)
           requests_total 60295 = 3.014 requests/entry
           the four counters sum to 60286 of 60295 — 99.99% ACCOUNTED
  CLIENT   strace counted ZERO getxattr/lgetxattr/fgetxattr
           statx 20019, getdents64 73, listxattr 20001 (ALL 20001 errored)

THE BEAD SAID 4.00 getxattr/entry OF WHICH TWO ARE system.posix_acl_*. It is 1.000 getxattr/entry and none of them is an ACL probe. The client never asks for system.posix_acl_access by name — ls probes with listxattr first, gets nothing back, and never issues the getxattr. There is nothing for FUSE_POSIX_ACL to cache, so the lever is void. The budget reconciling to 99.99% is what makes this conclusive rather than suggestive: there is no room left for three unaccounted getxattr per entry.

A GOOD RESULT HIDING IN THE DATA: 20001 client listxattr syscalls produced NO daemon dispatches and no measurable share of requests_total. We answer the first ENOSYS and the kernel short-circuits every later one for the life of the connection — the per-connection ENOSYS semantic doing exactly its job at ~3 us of client-only cost. That path is already optimal and needs no lever.

WHAT THE WORST-RATIO ROW ACTUALLY PAYS, corrected: of 3.014 requests/entry, 1.000 is the security.capability probe (closed as a protocol floor, bd-z0rb8) and 2.01 is the lookup+getattr pair — exactly what readdirplus folds away, already measured and REJECTED at +0.1% (bd-4ypbv). This run independently CONFIRMS that readdirplus observation (0.99 lookup, 1.02 getattr per entry — the signature of plain readdir being chosen) while refuting the getxattr number recorded next to it.

SO THE ROW'S REQUEST BUDGET IS NOW FULLY ATTRIBUTED AND EVERY COMPONENT IS EITHER A CLOSED FLOOR OR AN ALREADY-REJECTED LEVER. The 7.00 requests/entry figure on bd-4ypbv must not be reused without re-measurement; whatever it counted, it is not what this workload issues.

THE CODE STAYS: the knob is default OFF and inert (add_capabilities is guarded by 'if posix_acl != 0'), and scripts/fuse_xattr_count_ab.sh remains a working count-first A/B harness reusable for any future xattr lever. Neither is reverted; neither should be measured.

GATE STATUS, unresolved and not mine to resolve: the knob is still syntax-verified only. The remote gate ran (cargo test -p ffs-fuse --lib posix_acl) and failed to COMPILE on another agent's in-flight uncommitted work — missing fields other_dispatch_count/other_dispatch_nanos in an AtomicMetrics initializer and handler_total_count/handler_total_nanos in a MetricsSnapshot initializer. rch transfers the working tree, so no ffs-fuse gate can pass for anyone until that file is consistent.

MY PROPOSED MECHANISM WAS ALSO WRONG, which is the part worth keeping. I explained the 4.00 figure as `ls -l` calling getxattr(system.posix_acl_access) per entry to decide whether to print the trailing '+'. ProudBarn's strace refutes that directly: the client makes ZERO getxattr/lgetxattr/fgetxattr calls. `ls` probes with listxattr FIRST, gets an error, and never asks for an ACL by name — 20001 listxattr calls, all returning errors, producing no daemon dispatches at all because we answer the first ENOSYS and the kernel short-circuits the rest for the life of the connection. So the four-name list in the bead describes an image's STORED xattrs, not this host's probe stream, and my "client behaviour" story was a plausible reconstruction that the counted evidence does not support.

WHAT I ADD, and it is small: an independent confirmation from a DIFFERENT filesystem and a DIFFERENT client. Their 1.000 getxattr/entry is ext4 under `ls -lU`; mine is btrfs, 32,768 entries, under the comparator's actual client (fs::read_dir + fs::symlink_metadata, ffs_mounted_kernel_bench.rs:3601 and :3624 — an lstat, which requests no xattr at all). Two filesystems and two clients agreeing at 1.000 is worth one line, not a ledger row.

ALSO CHECKED AND CONSISTENT: SELinux is not enabled on this host — no /sys/fs/selinux, and /sys/kernel/security/lsm reads lockdown,capability,landlock,yama,apparmor,ima,evm. A per-entry security.selinux probe cannot originate from the SELinux LSM here, which independently supports reading the four-name list as stored-xattr provenance rather than probe traffic.

PROCESS NOTE, since this is the second time in two turns the same thing bit me: I reconstructed a route list from bead TEXT and then went looking for evidence, instead of reading the ledger first. The ledger already contained both the answer (row 51) and the refutation of my explanation. Checking the ledger before writing costs one grep; checking it after costs a withdrawn row.

title: [parity] ext4 xattr parser rejects entire block when any attribute is EA-inode-backed
description: parse_xattr_entries (crates/ffs-ondisk/src/ext4.rs) reads e_value_offs and e_value_size from each 16-byte ext4_xattr_entry but never reads e_value_inum (offset+4). On the EA_INODE feature, a large attribute value is stored in a separate EA inode and the entry carries e_value_inum != 0 with e_value_offs == 0. The value-resolution step then treats e_value_offs (0) as an in-block offset, hits the 'value overlaps xattr header or entry table' guard (0 < min_value_offset), and returns Err for the WHOLE block — so getxattr/listxattr on such an inode fail for EVERY attribute, including small in-block siblings that are perfectly readable. Real ext4 with EA_INODE + any large value makes the inode's whole xattr set unreadable by FrankenFS. FIX: read e_value_inum; for entries with value_inum != 0, surface the attribute with its name and an empty value (so listxattr is complete and in-block siblings stay readable) rather than misreading e_value_offs. REMAINING (separate follow-on): resolving the EA-inode payload bytes themselves (read the EA inode's data as the value) needs the value-base caller to pass device access into the parser or a parallel parse path; getxattr of the large value returns empty until then.
close_reason: Fixed: parse_xattr_entries now reads e_value_inum and surfaces EA-inode-backed attributes with their name + empty value instead of returning Err for the whole block. listxattr is now complete and in-block sibling attributes stay readable on EA_INODE inodes (previously every attribute was unreadable). Test parse_xattr_entries_lists_ea_inode_backed_value_without_rejecting_block_bd_bj00n. ffs-ondisk 601/601, ffs-core xattr 35/35, clippy/fmt clean. FOLLOW-ON (separate, lower priority): resolving the EA-inode payload bytes themselves (read the EA inode's data as the value) so getxattr of the large value returns content rather than empty — needs device access threaded into the parser or a parallel parse path.

title: ffs-mvcc: ShardedMvccStore lock-ordering invariant is undocumented and untested
description:
Finding (via /deadlock-finder-and-fixer skill, second visit, different
target): `ShardedMvccStore` (crates/ffs-mvcc/src/sharded.rs:115)
holds five `parking_lot::RwLock`s — `shards: Vec<RwLock<MvccShard>>`,
`active_snapshots`, `conflict_policy`, `contention_metrics`, plus
`publication_gate.wait_lock: Mutex<()>` for the publication ordering.
Static audit confirms the canonical implicit lock order:

  active_snapshots (rank 0) → shards (rank 1) → contention_metrics (rank 2)

Production callers comply:

  * `commit` / `commit_ssi`: shards.W (via lock_shards) → preflight_fcw_locked → contention_metrics.W (briefly) → drop shards. No active_snapshots touch.
  * `prune_safe`: active_snapshots.W → prune_versions_older_than → shards.W per shard. No contention_metrics touch.
  * `register_snapshot` / `release_snapshot` / `watermark` / `active_snapshot_count`: active_snapshots only (leaf).
  * `set_conflict_policy` / `effective_policy`: conflict_policy only (leaf).

The order is consistent — no AB-BA in production. But:

  1. **No struct-level doc comment names the invariant.** A future
     contributor adding e.g. a `gc_with_metrics` function that took
     `contention_metrics.write()` BEFORE `active_snapshots.write()`
     would silently introduce a deadlock against `prune_safe`, which
     holds `active_snapshots.write()` while waiting on shard locks
     (which `commit` holds while waiting on `contention_metrics.write()`).

  2. **No regression test exercises the lock ordering under
     contention.** The existing tests in this crate run commit,
     prune, and snapshot ops sequentially. A future deadlock would
     only manifest under concurrent load and would silently regress
     the gate.

Pairs with bd-7zd94 (PersistentMvccStore lock-ordering doc + test);
this one covers the sharded store's larger lock graph.

Acceptance: a doc comment on `ShardedMvccStore` names the canonical
order with rationale, per-field rank annotations, and a table of
production callers showing compliance. One unit test in the `tests`
module spawns concurrent commit + prune_safe + register/release
threads with a watchdog timeout that fails on hang.
notes: Shipped: struct-level doc on ShardedMvccStore documenting the canonical lock order active_snapshots → shards → contention_metrics with per-field rank annotations (rank 0/1/2 + leaf for conflict_policy) and a table of production callers showing compliance. Added lock_ordering_under_concurrent_commit_prune_and_register regression test with 3 concurrent workers (64 commits, 32 prune_safe calls, 64 register/release_snapshot pairs) guarded by a 15s watchdog that panics with bd-bky2f tag on hang. Verified via rch exec -- cargo test -p ffs-mvcc --lib lock_ordering_under_concurrent_commit_prune_and_register (passes in 0.05s).

title: perf(repair): parallelize RaptorQ encode_group repair-symbol GF combine across cores (rayon)
description: ffs-repair codec.rs encode_group computes each of the R repair symbols SERIALLY: for each esi, repair_symbol_into(coefficients) then a GF256 linear combine of the K source symbols into a fresh data block (gf256_addmul_slice), O(R*K*block_size) serial CPU. Each repair symbol is INDEPENDENT (own coefficients+data buffers; coefficient_encoder is an Arc so repair_symbol_into is &self; source_symbols read-only). Parallelize across repair symbols with rayon into_par_iter (mirrors the already-parallel lrc.rs:352 global-parity loop) -> ~min(R,Ncores)x on the encode. R goes up to k (source count) so commonly >= cores. Isomorphic: order-preserving collect; same EmittedSymbols; the serial overflow-break becomes a precomputed valid_count = min(repair_count, u32::MAX-start_esi+1) (esi monotonic so the valid set is the same prefix). MEASURABLE on pure CPU (encode_group serial vs parallel, no filesystem image needed). The directive's parallelization primitive; rayon already a workspace dep.
close_reason: Shipped 24183301: RaptorQ encode_group repair-symbol GF combine parallelized across cores via rayon into_par_iter (each repair symbol independent; coefficient encoder shared read-only via Arc). Mirrors the already-parallel LRC loop. Isomorphic (precomputed valid_count for the overflow-break; ordered collect; bench asserts parallel==serial; 30 codec tests green). A/B (K=64,R=16,4KiB): serial 6.24ms -> parallel 2.60ms = 2.40x (memory-bandwidth-bound). clippy clean. The directive's parallelization primitive.

title: btrfs snapshot of a subvolume with file data extents (shared-extent refcount accounting)
description: create_snapshot (bd-tm48j) currently snapshots only a FILE-LESS source subvolume: it copies the source fs-tree metadata into a fresh tree committed as its OWN blocks, so it shares NO on-disk blocks. A source WITH data extents would have its EXTENT_DATA items copied into the snapshot tree, making those data extents referenced by BOTH trees while their EXTENT_ITEM refcount stays 1 -> btrfs check extent-ref failure. btrfs_create_snapshot returns UnsupportedFeature for that case. To support it: for each copied EXTENT_DATA's (disk_bytenr, disk_num_bytes), increment the data extent's EXTENT_ITEM refs + add an EXTENT_DATA_REF for the snapshot root (the bd-xkvcm/bd-ngt1y refcount machinery: add_data_extent_ref). The truly space-efficient approach is COW-sharing the source's tree ROOT block (refs++ on the shared metadata block, lazy COW on modify) rather than a full metadata copy — a larger change. Validate via btrfs check on a snapshot of a subvol containing a file.
close_reason: done

comments.text: FIXED (above commit): create_snapshot now shares data extents. After copying the source fs-tree, for each Regular EXTENT_DATA with disk_bytenr!=0 it calls add_data_extent_ref(disk_bytenr, disk_num_bytes, snapshot_id, inode, key.offset-extent_offset) — bumps the EXTENT_ITEM refs + adds a snapshot-root-keyed EXTENT_DATA_REF (distinct from the source's). VALIDATED: btrfs_snapshot_with_file_data_passes_btrfs_check_bd_bndbz — 16KiB file -> snapshot -> commit -> btrfs check 'no error found' ALL 8 PHASES incl [3/8] checking extents (refcounts) + 'file data blocks allocated 32768 referenced 32768' (no leak). 1018 ffs-core green. Snapshots now work for real (non-empty) subvolumes. NOTE: metadata is still a full copy (own blocks), NOT COW-shared — that's a pure space optimization, not a correctness gap. Closing.

title: ext4 indirect-mapped (legacy) file reads are scalar per-block; coalesce into vectored reads
description:
read_ext4_indirect reads each data block of an indirect-mapped (non-extent, legacy ext2/3-style) file with a separate scalar device op (read_block_with_scope per logical block in the assembly loop). The extent read path already coalesces contiguous physical blocks into vectored reads (bd-a384r), and read_dir now does too (bd-q2tq5), but the indirect file read path does not — so a sequential read of any indirect-mapped file (present in older/converted images) is N scalar device ops.

LEVER (batched I/O): in read_ext4_indirect, for full-block-aligned spans build contiguous-physical runs of present blocks (resolve_indirect_block giving consecutive physical) and read each run via read_contiguous_blocks_with_scope (one vectored op); holes break runs (already zero-filled); partial head/tail blocks stay scalar. Mirrors btrfs_read_logical_into's vectoring. Isomorphic (same bytes; holes still zero-filled).

PROOF: indirect-file fixture with a contiguous multi-block data region + VectoredCountingDevice: sequential read does 1 vectored op vs N scalar, Score = N.

title: btrfs BTRFS_IOC_ENCODED_READ ignores i_size -> returns data/length past EOF for an extent beyond i_size (fallocate KEEP_SIZE prealloc)
description: btrfs_encoded_read (ffs-core lib.rs ~28288) never reads the inode's i_size: it locates the extent at file_offset and returns unencoded_len=num_bytes with up to disk_num_bytes of data, regardless of EOF. The kernel's encoded read returns 0 at/past i_size and never reports unencoded bytes beyond it. An extent can legitimately extend past i_size today via fallocate(FALLOC_FL_KEEP_SIZE) (a prealloc extent on a shorter/empty file), so an encoded read at an offset >= i_size returns prealloc bytes the kernel would not. This also becomes routine once extents are sector-aligned (bd-7mi0p item 4). FIX: read i_size via btrfs_read_inode_attr (works on writable + read-only paths); if file_offset >= i_size return the bare 32-byte metadata header with len=unencoded_len=0 (EOF); cap reported unencoded_len to file_size-extent_start. Standalone, deterministically testable via fallocate KEEP_SIZE + encoded_read at EOF. Carved out of bd-7mi0p's coupled set as an independently-correct fix.
close_reason: Fixed in 978b1279: btrfs_encoded_read now reads i_size via btrfs_read_inode_attr, returns the bare metadata header (len=0) at/past EOF, and caps unencoded_len to file_size-extent_start. Test btrfs_encoded_read_respects_i_size_past_eof_bd_br44j; full ffs-core suite green.

title: ext4 writable-path directory data blocks fail metadata_csum tail after namespace churn (e2fsck 'directory passes checks but fails checksum')
description: Surfaced by enabling a real e2fsck pass at the end of ext4_namespace_churn_matches_reference_model_and_e2fsck (ffs-core lib.rs) on a metadata_csum image (the open_writable_ext4 format helper uses the ext4 formatter default features incl. metadata_csum). After mkdir pa + mkdir pb + a single create in root, e2fsck pass 2 reports: 'Directory inode 13, block #0: directory passes checks but fails checksum' (and inode 14) — i.e. the EXT4_FT_DIR_CSUM tail on the directory data block is wrong on the writable path for these directories. Minimal failing proptest input: ops=[(0,0,0,0,0)] (one create) with the two setup mkdirs (pa=inode13, pb=inode14). NOT a used_dirs/accounting issue (pass 5 group summary is clean) and NOT reproduced on no-metadata_csum images. bd-0ta4z (metadata_csum, single subdir) passes, so it is specific to some directory state under churn (multiple sibling subdirs and/or a subsequently-modified parent). FIX AREA: stamp_ext4_dir_block / ext4 dir-block metadata_csum tail on the writable path (likely the csum seed / inode-generation inputs, or a missing re-stamp after a dir-block mutation). Once fixed, re-enable the deferred churn e2fsck pass (NOTE in that test) to also cover ../link-count invariants.
close_reason: Fixed in 72628d62: the mkdir path wrote a freshly init_dir_block'd directory data block WITHOUT stamping its metadata_csum tail; only add_entry paths restamp, so an EMPTY directory reached disk with a zero CRC32C and e2fsck pass 2 reported 'directory passes checks but fails checksum'. (single-subdir bd-0ta4z passed because its subdir gets a file, which restamps.) Fix stamps the new dir block keyed on the new dir's inode#+generation before write_block. Regression test ext4_empty_dir_block_csum_stamped_passes_e2fsck_bd_bribi (two empty subdirs + one create, real e2fsck clean); proven to fail without the stamp.

title: jbd2 csum-v2 descriptor-tag size wrong (10/14 vs kernel 8/12): mis-maps multi-tag transactions on recovery
description: ffs-journal lib.rs:45-46 JBD2_TAG_SIZE_CSUM_V2_32=10 / _64=14 are wrong. The kernel on-disk journal_block_tag_t is { __be32 t_blocknr; __be16 t_checksum; __be16 t_flags; __be32 t_blocknr_high } = 8 bytes (32-bit) / 12 (64-bit). The t_checksum is INSIDE the struct in both v1 and v2 — csum-v2 does NOT append 2 bytes. The code is internally inconsistent: read_descriptor_tag_flags_and_checksum reads checksum@4 + flags@6 (within 8 bytes) and the parser reads blocknr_high@8 (ending at 12), yet sizes the tag at 10/14 (2 phantom bytes). CONSEQUENCE: recovering a REAL kernel-written csum-v2 ext4 journal (older e2fsprogs with metadata_csum sets JBD2_FEATURE_INCOMPAT_CSUM_V2=0x8; recovery selects CsumV2 from the on-disk sb) where a descriptor has >=2 tags reads every tag after the first at a +2 wrong stride -> journaled blocks mapped to WRONG physical destinations / LAST flag misread = SILENT CORRUPTION on replay. Single-tag descriptors happen to work. FrankenFS's own writer only emits Legacy/CsumV3 so self-round-trip never caught it; the pinning test jbd2_csum_v2_descriptor_tag_geometry_matches_kernel_tag_bytes tautologically asserts the wrong 10/14. Found via Phase B journal-recovery audit. FIX: CSUM_V2 sizes = 8/12 (same as legacy).

title: Kernel-conformance pin for Ext4Extent leaf entry 12-byte offsets
description: Found via /porting-to-rust audit. ffs_ondisk::ext4::parse_extent_leaf (lib.rs:2946) reads 12-byte struct ext4_extent entries per fs/ext4/ext4_extents.h: ee_block u32@0..4 (logical_block), ee_len u16@4..6 (raw_len), ee_start_hi u16@6..8 (physical high 16), ee_start_lo u32@8..12 (physical low 32). Combined as physical_start = (start_hi << 32) | start_lo. The Ext4ExtentHeader is checked via EXT4_EXTENT_MAGIC (bd-jbilz pins the magic), and bd-9rxhw earlier work covers some extent-tree behavior, but no test pins each FIELD OFFSET within an extent entry with unique-magic stamping. A regression that drifted ee_start_hi to offset 4..6 (where ee_len lives) would still pass the existing parse_extent_tree round-trip if the writer were similarly broken, and would silently corrupt every physical-block address in extent trees. Fix: add ext4_extent_leaf_kernel_offsets_match_extents_h that builds a synthetic 1-entry extent tree (12-byte header + 12-byte entry = 24 bytes), stamps each field with unique magic, parses, and asserts every parsed field round-trips. Pattern matches bd-tpgp7 (Ext4MmpBlock kernel offsets), bd-qwo4a (parse_dir_items kernel offsets), bd-kelr0 (parse_inode_refs kernel offsets). parse_extent_leaf is on every ext4 file read / mmap path. Bead size: <50 min.
close_reason: completed

title: the contention gate samples placement CPUs ONCE before the run — add during-run external-load sampling, because a peer's load flipped a published verdict
description:
The mounted comparator's contention gate samples the PLACEMENT CPUs ONCE, BEFORE the run. That is not sufficient to certify a measurement window, and on 2026-08-08 it let a peer's load flip a published verdict.

WHAT HAPPENED (bd-ws9dg, closed). Two admitted runs of btrfs parallel-read, same ELF, same fixture, minutes apart, returned OPPOSITE verdicts — 1.019622x HONEST_NEUTRAL and 0.961107x HONEST_WIN, non-overlapping intervals, 6.09% spread. Re-run in a verified-quiet window the same day, the row is a stable win 2/2: 0.893282x and 0.927352x, spread 3.81%, landing 0.11% from the banked value.

THE GATE WAS NOT WRONG, WHICH IS THE POINT. `core_contention_preflight` printed verdict=clear and was CORRECT by its own definition: the peer's pytest (254% CPU) never touched the placement CPUs — max busy 0.020, mean 0.006 across CPUs 0-7/32-39. The arms genuinely had idle cores. The load sat on CPUs 16, 19, 48, 51, 54 elsewhere on the same socket, and memory bandwidth, LLC capacity and boost budget are SOCKET-WIDE, not per-core. A per-core, pre-run sample cannot see any of that.

bd-4sull already argued that a clear preflight is not evidence of comparability, from cross-WINDOW drift. This is the sharper form: it flips a verdict INSIDE ONE SESSION, on runs minutes apart.

PROPOSED FIX, and it is cheap. Sample host-wide EXTERNAL CPU (everything that is not the bench and its daemons) periodically DURING the run, and record the series in the report. Then either:
  (a) FAIL the row when external CPU exceeds a threshold for more than N consecutive samples, symmetric with how the pre-run gate already fails closed; or
  (b) at minimum, record max/median/p90 external CPU in the report so a reader can disqualify a row after the fact, and print a loud warning above a threshold.

(a) is preferable — it is the same fail-closed discipline the rest of the harness uses, and it would have refused both contended runs automatically. bd-ws9dg would never have been filed and the scorecard would never have carried a wrong verdict for an hour.

REFERENCE IMPLEMENTATION already in-tree: `scripts/sample_external_load.sh`, used to verify the quiet window for bd-ws9dg. It is six lines of shell — it excludes the bench processes by name and sums the rest, sampling every 3 s. Measured baseline on this host with no peers: median 113.5% of a 6400% box (~1.8% utilisation). Under the peer's pytest it would have read several hundred percent. The signal is unambiguous and needs no tuning.

IMPLEMENTATION NOTES
- Total CPU% is useless for this — the bench itself is the dominant consumer. It MUST exclude the harness, the FUSE daemons, and their children, which is why the reference script filters by name.
- Load average is a poor substitute: it lags by design and would not have flagged a short pytest burst.
- The sampler must run for the whole measured region, not just the arms, since fixture construction and cloning also compete.
- The threshold should be expressed as a fraction of total capacity, not an absolute percent, so it transfers across hosts.

ACCEPTANCE
- the report carries an external-load series (or its summary statistics) for every run;
- a run whose external load exceeds the threshold is refused, or at minimum flagged loudly enough that no reader could bank it unknowingly;
- the existing pre-run placement-CPU gate is retained unchanged — it catches a different failure and both are needed;
- a test pins that a synthetic external load trips the new check.
close_reason: Implemented and verified end-to-end in BOTH directions on live comparator runs (e4aa9439 + this commit). A sampler thread covers the whole measured region; external load is defined per-CPU as anything outside the placement set above 25% busy, needing no process-name matching. Thresholds calibrated on the two real windows from the harness's own reports (contended 5 CPUs above 0.2, quiet 0, worst 0.170). POSITIVE: quiet box -> samples=37, max_external_busy_cpus=2, over_limit=0, verdict=clear, block written to the report, and the A/A gate still speaks first. NEGATIVE: 4 off-placement CPUs pinned at 100% -> samples=23, max=5, over_limit=23, verdict=CONTENDED, run REFUSED with an actionable message. Decisively, that same refused run's report shows the PRE-RUN gate seeing placement CPUs at max 0.011 busy - it would have declared the window clear - which is exactly the failure that produced a wrong published verdict in bd-ws9dg, reproduced deliberately and now caught. 53 tests pass. Scope limits recorded on the bead: it catches per-CPU-visible contention only, does not retroactively annotate older rows, and the limit of 2 is a judgement call biased toward not refusing legitimate runs.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
IMPLEMENTED (2026-08-08). The harness now samples EXTERNAL load for the whole measured region and fails closed on contention.

WHAT LANDED (crates/ffs-harness/src/bin/ffs_mounted_kernel_bench.rs)
- A sampler thread runs for the entire measured region — every filesystem, fixture construction and cloning included, not just the timed arms — reusing the existing `sample_cpu_busy()`.
- "External load" is defined WITHOUT process-name filtering, which is the improvement over the shell reference implementation: it is any CPU **outside** the placement set (driver CPUs + driver guards + FUSE CPUs + FUSE guards) carrying more than `EXTERNAL_BUSY_CPU_FRACTION` busy. Per-CPU data makes the process filter unnecessary and removes a whole class of "did we match the right process name" bug.
- `external_load_during_run,...` is printed and an `external_load_during_run` block is written into the report ALWAYS — clean or not — so a later reader can disqualify a banked row without re-running it. That is the half of the bead's proposal (b) that matters most: the evidence exists even when the gate passes.
- The run then FAILS CLOSED if any sample exceeded the limit, ordered AFTER the A/A null gate so a row that fails its nulls still says so first. The report is written before the check, so a refused run stays diagnosable from its own external-load block.

THRESHOLDS CALIBRATED ON THE TWO REAL WINDOWS, not invented. Both figure sets are the harness's own `pre_measurement_cpu_busy`, read back from the reports of 2026-08-08:

    contended window   5 off-placement CPUs above 0.2 busy, one at 1.000, off-placement mean 0.081
    quiet window       0 off-placement CPUs above 0.2 busy, worst 0.170, off-placement mean 0.028

`EXTERNAL_BUSY_CPU_FRACTION = 0.25` sits above the quiet window's worst CPU and far below the contended window's, so the two separate cleanly with margin on both sides. `MAX_EXTERNAL_BUSY_CPUS = 2` is deliberately permissive — one background daemon does not invalidate a measurement, and the case that flipped a verdict showed five.

TESTS (53 passed / 0 failed, up from 51)
- `external_load_policy_separates_the_two_real_windows_bd_bt2dy` replays both real windows' CPU maps and asserts 5 vs 0. It also asserts that a FULLY SATURATED placement set counts as zero external load — that is the bench doing its job, and counting it would refuse every run. That third case is the one a naive implementation gets wrong.
- `external_load_witness_fails_closed_on_any_over_limit_sample_bd_bt2dy` pins that a single contended sample in an otherwise clean run refuses it (a burst is exactly what bd-ws9dg hit), that a clean run passes, and that exactly-at-the-limit is permitted rather than refused.

WHY PER-CPU RATHER THAN TOTAL CPU%: total is useless here because the bench is the dominant consumer — the shell sampler I used to verify the quiet window had to filter by process name to see anything, and it read 425-676% total while the box was idle apart from the bench. Excluding the placement set by CPU index is exact and needs no name matching.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO, so nobody assumes more than is there:
- It does not detect contention that is invisible in per-CPU busy — a co-tenant saturating memory bandwidth from few cores, or thermal throttling from another socket. It catches the case that actually bit us and is a floor, not a proof of quiescence.
- It does not retroactively annotate the rows already banked. Those that predate this carry no external-load block, and their absence is itself informative.
- The pre-run placement-CPU gate is unchanged and still needed: it catches a different failure (load ON the arms' cores at start) and both are required.

VERIFICATION STATUS: unit tests pass; end-to-end confirmation on a real run is in progress — a policy that only passes unit tests has not been shown to work.

    DURING-RUN gate view:                      5 off-placement CPUs busy, 23/23 samples over

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
POLICY CORRECTED (2026-08-08, same day). The gate I closed this bead on was TOO STRICT and was measured wrong within the hour. Reopening the record rather than quietly patching it.

WHAT WENT WRONG. The first version refused a run on a SINGLE contended sample. I wrote a unit test asserting exactly that, with the rationale "a burst is exactly what bd-ws9dg hit". That rationale was wrong: bd-ws9dg's contention was SUSTAINED — a peer's pytest running for minutes — not a burst.

MEASURED, on live runs, immediately after it shipped:

    synthetic sustained load (the negative test)   23/23 = 100.0%   REFUSED, correctly
    warm-stat run 1, quiet box                      2/71 =   2.8%   REFUSED, WRONGLY
    warm-stat run 2, quiet box                      1/70 =   1.4%   REFUSED, WRONGLY

Two consecutive legitimate runs on an idle machine — load average ~1-2, no co-tenant — were thrown away on scattered single samples of ordinary background churn. Both had already passed every other gate: A/A nulls clear on both filesystems, parity pass, verdicts HONEST_LOSS.

An asymmetry I did not anticipate made it worse: `placement_cpus_excluded` is 16 for an 8-thread workload but only **4** for a 1-thread one like warm-stat. So warm-stat watches 60 CPUs where parallel-read watches 48, and is correspondingly likelier to catch unrelated background activity. The gate was systematically stricter for exactly the cheap, high-iteration workloads one most wants to re-run.

THE CORRECTION. Refuse only SUSTAINED contention, on either of two signals:
  - `MAX_CONTENDED_SAMPLE_FRACTION = 0.10` — more than 10% of samples contended; and
  - `MAX_CONSECUTIVE_CONTENDED_SAMPLES = 3` — three back-to-back contended samples, which catches a dense burst inside a long run that the fraction alone would miss.
The witness now tracks `max_consecutive_over_limit` alongside the count, and both figures are reported and written to every report.

WHY THIS IS A CORRECTION AND NOT A CONVENIENCE. I am aware I am relaxing a threshold immediately after it blocked work I wanted, which is the classic way a gate gets quietly gutted, so the argument has to stand on its own:
  1. The measured separation is >3x in either direction — transient blips at or below 2.8%, genuine contention at 100%. 10% is not a fitted number; anything from ~4% to ~50% would separate these datasets.
  2. The estimator justifies the distinction independently of any threshold. A median-of-32-pairs four-round crossover is DESIGNED to absorb a perturbation touching a couple of pairs; that is what the median is for. Sustained load biases every pair and the median cannot help. Transient and sustained differ in KIND.
  3. The strictness is not free. A gate that refuses legitimate runs on an ordinary shared box gets bypassed by whoever needs a measurement, and a bypassed gate protects nothing. The failure mode of over-strictness here is the gate being disabled, which is strictly worse than the 3% blip it was rejecting.
  4. The consecutive-sample rule ADDS strictness where the fraction is blind, so this is not a uniform loosening.

TESTS (54 passed, was 53). `external_load_tolerates_transient_blips_but_not_sustained_load_bd_bt2dy` replays all three real datasets by their actual contended/total counts and asserts 2/71 and 1/70 now PASS while 23/23 still REFUSES, plus both sides of the 10% boundary and the three-consecutive burst case. The earlier single-sample test is renamed and its assertion inverted to sustained contention, so the wrong rationale is not left sitting in the suite.

STILL TRUE from the original close: the gate catches per-CPU-visible contention only; it does not retroactively annotate older rows; the `2` busy-CPU limit remains a judgement call. What has changed is only WHEN a contended sample refuses a run.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
CORRECTED GATE VERIFIED TO DISCRIMINATE — including by refusing me a third time, correctly.

    negative test (synthetic sustained)   23/23 = 100.0%   REFUSED  (correct)
    warm-stat run A                        8/67 =  11.9%   REFUSED  (correct — over the 10% limit,
                                                            max_consecutive=2, so the FRACTION rule fired)
    warm-stat run 1                        2/71 =   2.8%   would now PASS (unit-tested)
    warm-stat run 2                        1/70 =   1.4%   would now PASS (unit-tested)

So the policy separates cleanly across four real datasets spanning 1.4% to 100%, and the two rules do different work: run A tripped the fraction rule with `max_consecutive_over_limit=2`, under the consecutive limit of 3, which is exactly the case the fraction rule exists for.

I did NOT relax the threshold again to make run A pass. The box was genuinely busier (load ~4.1 versus ~0.4 in the earlier quiet window, my own rebuilds plus peers), so refusing was right.

⭐ AN OBSERVATION THAT ARGUES AGAINST ONE GLOBAL THRESHOLD, recorded rather than acted on. Across the three warm-stat attempts the ratios barely moved despite contention varying 8x:

    run              contended    ext4        btrfs
    r1                    2.8%    4.878463    4.812203
    r2                    1.4%    4.880928    4.789771
    rA                   11.9%    4.859600    4.812585
    spread across all three:      0.44%       0.48%

Warm stat is ~1-thread, ~4.5 ms kernel / ~22 ms FUSE per batch, and its ratio is dominated by per-request FUSE round-trip cost. It looks robust to socket-level contention at this magnitude. Parallel read, by contrast, FLIPPED VERDICT under comparable load (bd-ws9dg).

CONCLUSION, and the reason not to touch the threshold: contention sensitivity is WORKLOAD-DEPENDENT, so any single global limit is necessarily conservative for robust workloads and possibly still permissive for sensitive ones. The correct response is not to loosen the global limit for warm stat's benefit — it is to accept that a robust workload will occasionally be refused on a busy box, because the same limit is what protects the sensitive ones. A per-workload sensitivity calibration would be the principled alternative, and it is not something to invent from three data points.

NOT DELIVERED THIS TURN: bd-4sull item 1 for warm stat. Three attempts, all refused, none bankable. The numbers above are recorded ONLY as evidence about the gate's behaviour and the workload's robustness — they are from refused runs and must not be quoted as rows or used to supersede the banked ext4 4.812194x / btrfs 4.977803x. Re-run when the box is genuinely idle.

title: perf(btrfs): fsync/journal commit 1.98x slower than kernel btrfs
description:
Newly banked LOSE in docs/MOUNTED_BTRFS_SCORECARD.md (cb9fb128): 1.976308x [1.969150, 1.977948] slower against a twice-null margin of 1.021437x; kernel A/A 0.999326, FUSE A/A 1.000634, both CIs containing 1.0; pairs 32, threads 1 -> 1 observed with pinning attested; parity pass and post_unmount_validation clean. Kernel takes 101.5 ms per batch where FrankenFS takes 200.5 ms.

This workload could not execute at all until 2026-08-04 (bd-ftev0 EIO, then bd-btrfs-orphaned-csum-items-bmksa), so it has never been optimized — nobody has ever profiled it. That makes it the least-explored loss in either bank.

Shape: 8 x 4 KiB positioned writes to one file, fsync after each, single-threaded. So it is a pure durability path — no concurrency, no parallelism, no readdir. Each operation is write -> commit -> fsync, and on btrfs that means a full transaction commit per fsync unless the ephemeral tree-log path is taken (--btrfs-rw-ephemeral-ok, which trades durability and is NOT what the row measured). The obvious question to answer first is where the 100 ms of extra wall time goes: transaction commit work, the csum tree rewrite, the free-space tree rewrite, or FUSE round trips. Profile before proposing a lever.

Contract: kernel incumbent live in the SAME invocation, both A/A nulls, ACTUAL observed thread count, executing-ELF SHA-256 self-reported from inside the process, median-CI decision against the twice-null margin. One lever at a time; a rejection gets one negative-evidence row with a retry predicate.

The candidate and PGO profile used for the banked row are reusable: PGO_DIR=/data/tmp/ffs-pgo-ftev0 with SKIP_TRAIN=1 rebuilds in one ~6 min stage instead of three.

title: btrfs: read-side csum verification exists but no mount can enable it (ffs-core-only flag, default off)
description:
Found while auditing why FrankenFS beats kernel btrfs on warm parallel reads (docs/MOUNTED_BTRFS_SCORECARD.md). Every crc32c / csum path in ffs-btrfs builds EXTENT_CSUM items on the WRITE side (bd-x3fcu made the written image btrfs-check-clean end to end). There is no verify equivalent anywhere in the btrfs read path or the FUSE layer.

Two consequences, and the second is the serious one:

1. Benchmarking: a read comparison against kernel btrfs is not like-for-like if the incumbent verifies and we do not. That is tracked as bd-btrfs-parallel-read-win-mechanism-iwzrx.

2. CORRECTNESS: per-block data checksums are btrfs's headline durability feature. A btrfs filesystem whose reader never checks them silently returns corrupted data where the kernel would return EIO — exactly the failure mode the format exists to prevent. FrankenFS also advertises self-healing durability via repair symbols, and a repair layer that is never told a block is bad cannot heal it.

Scope to establish first, before designing the fix: which inodes carry datasum at all (NODATASUM inodes legitimately have none), what the kernel does on mismatch (EIO plus a rate-limited error, not a panic), and where verification belongs so it does not sit on the warm-cache hot path the parallel-read row measures.

Acceptance: a negative test that plants a wrong csum for a live extent and asserts the read fails rather than returning the corrupted bytes. A naive implementation that verifies nothing passes every positive test, so the negative case is the test that matters. Then re-measure the parallel-read row with verification on, and publish the delta honestly — if the win shrinks or reverses, that is the real number.
close_reason: Landed in 598d4d4b with the probe passing: build_mount_open_options_threads_btrfs_read_verification_both_ways (1 passed, 351 filtered) asserts --btrfs-verify-data-on-read reaches OpenOptions when set, stays off when not, and that the library default is unchanged. The gap this bead names — verification exists in ffs-core but no mount could enable it — is closed: a mount can now verify. The separate question of whether it SHOULD by default is bd-btrfs-verify-default-decision-v81jt, blocked on the measured cost, because flipping it silently would change what every banked read row measured. Also corrected the scorecard claim that no verify path existed.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
PREMISE CORRECTED. I filed this saying FrankenFS never verifies data checksums on read and
that no verify path exists. That is wrong, and the correction narrows the bead rather than
closing it.

What actually exists: 57d37c73 "feat(ffs-core): verify btrfs data checksums on read,
opt-in (bd-tkv2n)", landed 2026-06-04 and an ancestor of HEAD, with a later perf pass in
e0aa5a1b. crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs:10836 verifies every regular extent overlapping the
read range against the csum tree for a datasum inode and returns Corruption -> EIO before
returning any data, matching the kernel. It skips NODATASUM inodes. It carries its own
negative test, btrfs_verify_data_on_read_detects_corruption_bd_tkv2n (:51872), which plants
corruption and asserts the read fails.

Why the audit in docs/MOUNTED_BTRFS_SCORECARD.md missed it: the verify path lives in
ffs-core, and the audit grepped ffs-btrfs, where indeed every crc32c/csum path is
write-side only. The doc claim "there is no verify equivalent in the btrfs read path or the
FUSE layer" is false for ffs-core and needs fixing.

THE REAL GAP, which survives the correction and is sharper:

  crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs:518   btrfs_verify_data_on_read: false
  and the flag appears NOWHERE outside ffs-core — not in ffs-cli, not in ffs-fuse, not in
  the harness.

So no MOUNTED configuration can turn verification on. Every FUSE mount — every benchmark
arm and every real user mount — reads btrfs data without checking checksums, and there is
no way to opt in. A library capability nothing can reach is, from the mount's point of
view, the same as not having it, which is why the scorecard's conclusion was right about
mounts even though its reasoning about the source was wrong.

Two consequences, unchanged in substance:

1. Correctness: a mounted FrankenFS btrfs returns corrupted data where the kernel returns
   EIO, and the self-healing repair layer is never told there is anything to heal.
2. Benchmarking: the parallel-read row was measured against an incumbent that always
   verifies, by an arm that cannot. That caveat now has an exact statement instead of a
   suspicion.

DELIVERABLE for this bead, narrowed: expose the option through the mount path (ffs-cli ->
OpenOptions) with a test that a mount built with it actually verifies, and document that
mounts do not verify by default.

DEFAULT DELIBERATELY NOT FLIPPED HERE. Kernel btrfs always verifies, so parity argues for
on-by-default, but flipping it silently changes what every banked row measured — including
the campaign's only win. The default is a measured decision and belongs to
bd-btrfs-parallel-read-win-mechanism-iwzrx, which should run the row with verification on
and off and publish the delta. That is now a cheap experiment rather than a feature.
