title: btrfs: overwrites leave orphaned csum items — unmounted image fails btrfs check
description:
A FrankenFS btrfs mount that performs overwrites leaves ORPHANED CSUM ITEMS behind, and
the image it unmounts is not `btrfs check` clean:

  [6/8] checking only csums items (without verifying data)
  there are no extents for csum range 14680064-14684160
  csum exists for 13631488-14684160 but there is no extent record
  ERROR: errors found in csum tree
  mounted_kernel_gate,error=btrfs check --readonly failed: exit status: 1

The orphaned range is 13631488..14684160 — 1 MiB + 4 KiB, i.e. one 1 MiB extent plus one
4 KiB extent whose EXTENT_ITEMs are gone while their EXTENT_CSUM items survive. A kernel
btrfs would treat this image as damaged.

WHY THIS IS ONLY NOW VISIBLE, and why it is not a regression from bd-ftev0: before that
fix the first positioned write returned EIO, so nothing was ever written and no csum could
be orphaned. The fix made the overwrite path reachable and this defect came with it. It is
pre-existing code, newly exercised — the fix exposed it rather than caused it. Worth
stating plainly because the two land in the same window and it would be easy to blame the
wrong commit.

Where to look first. On overwrite, `btrfs_remove_overlapping_extent_data` frees the old
extent through `btrfs_free_or_drop_extent_ref`, which removes csums ONLY on the sole-
reference branch (`refs <= 1` -> `free_extent` + `btrfs_remove_extent_csums`); the
`refs > 1` branch drops a backref and deliberately leaves csums alone. It then re-inserts
the non-overlapping left/right segments as fresh extents. Candidate mechanisms, none yet
confirmed: a segment re-insert that allocates a new extent without removing the old
range's csums; a csum removal keyed to the write length rather than the freed extent's
`disk_num_bytes`; or the commit-time csum tree serialization writing in-memory state that
no longer matches the extent tree.

REPRODUCER (about 12 minutes end to end, most of it the candidate build):

  scripts/build-perf.sh /path/to/ext4-train.img        # needs an EMPTY PGO_DIR
  ffs-mounted-kernel-bench --ffs-cli <release-perf/ffs-cli> \
    --filesystem btrfs --workload fsync-journal-commit \
    --operations 8 --pairs 12 --observation-repeats 1 --image-size-mib 512 \
    --harness-builder <id> --candidate-builder <id>

Candidate used: binary 38b8a2545a1129dacae2684f4fee075ee73612e4edbf6adfaa66c348e86f6d6b,
PGO profile 5c6530a0261f658ed0ace2a9d8bef7c6c63b6f94b4b955e4f7ccba038e011e96, x86-64-v3.

ACCEPTANCE: the same run reaches `btrfs check --readonly` clean. The negative case that
matters is an overwrite that frees an extent whose csums must go with it — assert the
csum tree has no entry covering a freed range, since an implementation that simply stops
writing csums at all would pass a naive positive test.

BLOCKS bd-score-btrfs-fsync-row-d98vj: the comparator refuses to bank any row whose image
fails the post-unmount integrity check, and it is right to.
close_reason: Fixed in d3c597aa and verified at both levels the bead named. Unit: btrfs_remove_extent_csums_splits_a_multi_sector_item_bd_orphaned_csums (frees the middle sectors of a four-sector item; the old skip-the-item behaviour and a naive delete-whole both fail it). End-to-end: the mounted four-arm reproducer now exits 0 with post_unmount_validation=clean, where it previously failed btrfs check --readonly on the orphaned csum range. Cause was csum item key geometry — items cover up to ~16 MiB and are keyed by their first sector, so removal keyed on item start could not touch an item reaching into the freed range; now truncates and splits like the kernel's btrfs_del_csums.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
FIXED in d3c597aa. Root cause was narrower than the bead guessed: not the refs>1 branch and not the commit-time serialization, but the KEY GEOMETRY of csum items. One EXTENT_CSUM item holds up to max_data_csums_per_item checksums — ~16 MiB of data at a 16 KiB nodesize — and is keyed by the disk bytenr of the FIRST sector it covers. btrfs_remove_extent_csums deleted only items whose KEY fell inside the freed range, so an item starting BEFORE the range kept the checksums for bytes whose extent had just been freed. Any overwrite landing inside a covered run orphaned csums.

Fix mirrors the kernel's btrfs_del_csums: remove every OVERLAPPING item, re-insert whichever prefix and suffix fall outside the freed range, re-keying the suffix to the first sector it still covers. The scan window starts max_csums_per_item sectors before the range, because that is how far an item can reach forward into it.

Evidence at both levels:
1. Unit — btrfs_remove_extent_csums_splits_a_multi_sector_item_bd_orphaned_csums frees the two MIDDLE sectors of a single four-sector item and asserts sectors 0 and 3 keep their exact checksum bytes at their own keys. This is the negative case the bead asked for: skipping the item (the old behaviour) leaves all four, and deleting it whole loses the neighbours; both fail. The pre-existing sibling test only ever built single-sector items, which is exactly why this survived. 2 passed, 1210 filtered.
2. End-to-end — the same four-arm mounted reproducer that exposed this now exits 0, with post_unmount_validation=clean where btrfs check previously reported 'csum exists for 13631488-14684160 but there is no extent record'. Candidate 9e32e28f766368dd738c7d43e2d4f820a426394b0d1e72b6e565be622835408a, PGO 5c6530a0261f658ed0ace2a9d8bef7c6c63b6f94b4b955e4f7ccba038e011e96, x86-64-v3, driver 8c1c4d35fd0a348e5e612d904f086567a4bd9f03a800127ff1ebedb6a2f2633f.

title: perf(btrfs): parallel metadata writes 1.93x slower than kernel btrfs
description:
Banked LOSE in docs/MOUNTED_BTRFS_SCORECARD.md: 1.930090x [1.916623, 1.940038] slower against a twice-null margin of 1.019214x; 512 creates across 8 workers, 128 crossover blocks, 8 -> 8 observed threads. Kernel A/A 1.002214x, FUSE A/A 0.997250x.

Worse than the ext4 twin (1.510822x, bd-ext4-parallel-meta-1p51x-*), so the btrfs mutation path carries extra per-create cost beyond the shared FUSE dispatch. The btrfs create path takes a single alloc-state Mutex for the whole operation (require_btrfs_alloc_state -> alloc_mutex.lock()), which is the obvious structural suspect to profile first — but profile before assuming.

Contract: kernel incumbent live in the SAME invocation, both A/A nulls, observed thread count, executing-ELF SHA-256, median-CI decision, one lever at a time.

title: perf(btrfs): the campaign's only WIN is un-quotable until a cold-cache read variant decides its mechanism
description:
docs/MOUNTED_BTRFS_SCORECARD.md banks parallel_read_multifile_8t as the campaign's first honest_win against a live kernel incumbent: 0.894290x [0.885022, 0.903489] FASTER, replicated at 0.830537x [0.823606, 0.835141], all four A/A nulls clean and each containing 1.0. The statistics are not the weak part.

Two things are unresolved, and the scorecard itself forbids quoting the row as a bare win until they are:

1. MECHANISM. Per-block data checksumming is btrfs's headline feature and FrankenFS performs NO read-side checksum verification — every crc32c/csum path in ffs-btrfs builds csum items on the WRITE side only. If the incumbent verifies on every read and we never do, this is not like-for-like. BUT it cuts both ways: this is a warm-cache workload, and kernel btrfs does not re-verify on page-cache hits, so the incumbent may not be paying that cost in this regime at all. Genuinely open in both directions.

2. MAGNITUDE WOBBLE. 0.894290x versus 0.830537x is a 7.7% spread between two runs whose own intervals are ~2% wide, so something not captured by the nulls moves between windows.

Deliverable: a COLD-CACHE multi-file parallel read row, as a NEW row rather than a silent substitution of the warm one — same four-arm comparator, kernel incumbent live in the same invocation, both A/A nulls, observed thread count, executing-ELF SHA-256 self-reported. Drop caches between rounds and say exactly how in the row's provenance. If the cold row still favours us the win survives with a mechanism; if it reverses, the warm win is a cache-regime artifact and must be restated.

Blocking relationship worth respecting: until this runs, the standing instruction is to quote the row as 'faster on warm multi-file parallel reads, mechanism unresolved, and FrankenFS performs no read-side checksum verification'.

See also the parity gap this exposed (btrfs read-side checksum verification is absent), filed separately.

title: test(ffs-ondisk): single-device logical mapping rejects physical address overflow
description: map_logical_to_physical checks stripe.offset + offset_within with checked_add for Single/Dup bootstrap chunks. Existing mapping tests cover hits, misses, unsupported profiles, range boundaries, and binary-search parity, but do not pin the direct single-device physical-address overflow branch. Add a pure no-mock regression that proves the u64::MAX boundary maps successfully and the next logical byte returns ParseError::InvalidField { field: stripe_offset, reason: physical address overflow }.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): map_logical_to_physical_rejects_physical_address_overflow (ffs-ondisk btrfs.rs:2207). cargo test: ok.

title: test(ffs-ondisk): RAID0 stripe resolver rejects physical address overflow
description: resolve_raid0_stripe selects a RAID0 data stripe and then uses stripe_physical_at, whose final stripe.offset + stripe_offset checked_add can overflow independently of the stripe_len product check. Existing RAID0 tests cover normal selection/count validation and a separate product overflow regression, while RAID10 has the only physical-overflow coverage. Add a pure RAID0 regression with a valid u64::MAX boundary mapping followed by the exact stripe_offset physical-address overflow error.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): stripe_resolve_raid0_rejects_physical_address_overflow (ffs-ondisk:6673). cargo test: ok.

title: test(ffs-ondisk): RAID0 stripe resolver rejects stripe length product overflow
description: resolve_raid0_stripe divides by stripe_len * num_stripes after validating stripe counts. Existing RAID0 tests cover normal selection, zero stripes, and mismatched stripe counts, but not the checked_mul overflow guard for pathological stripe_len values. Add a pure unit regression that builds a covered RAID0 chunk with stripe_len = u64::MAX and two stripes, then asserts the exact stripe_len overflow error.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): stripe_resolve_raid0_rejects_stripe_len_product_overflow (ffs-ondisk:6652). cargo test: ok.

title: test(ffs-ondisk): RAID10 stripe resolver returns selected mirror pair
description: resolve_raid10_stripes has rejection coverage but no normal-path assertion that the selected data stripe returns all mirrors in the expected order. Add a pure RAID10 regression with four stripes and sub_stripes=2, mapping the second data stripe and asserting profile Raid10 plus mirror devices 3 and 4 with their physical offsets. This pins the base index calculation before future parity/stripe refactors.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): stripe_resolve_raid10_returns_selected_mirror_pair (ffs-ondisk:6747). cargo test: ok.

title: test(ffs-ondisk): RAID10 stripe resolver rejects stripe length product overflow
description: resolve_raid10_stripes computes stripe_len * data_stripes after validating sub_stripes and divisibility. Existing RAID10 tests cover zero sub_stripes, non-divisible stripe counts, and a physical-address overflow, but not the checked_mul overflow guard before stripe selection. Add a pure RAID10 regression with stripe_len = u64::MAX and two data stripes, asserting the exact RAID10 stripe_len overflow error.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): stripe_resolve_raid10_rejects_stripe_len_product_overflow (ffs-ondisk:6774). cargo test: ok.

title: test(ffs-ondisk): RAID5 stripe resolver skips rotated parity position
description: resolve_raid56_stripe explicitly skips parity positions while mapping a RAID5/6 data stripe index to an actual device position. Existing coverage pins RAID6 wraparound, but RAID5 parity rotation is not directly asserted. description: resolve_raid56_stripe selects a data stripe after parity rotation and then calls stripe_physical_at, whose final stripe.offset + stripe_offset checked_add can overflow independently of the RAID5/6 stripe_len product guard. Existing coverage pins too-few stripes, parity wraparound, and stripe_len * data_stripes overflow, but not the public RAID5/6 physical-address overflow path. Add a pure RAID5 regression with a valid u64::MAX boundary mapping followed by the exact stripe_offset physical-address overflow error.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): stripe_resolve_raid5_rejects_physical_address_overflow (ffs-ondisk:6887). cargo test: ok.

Existing tests cover too-few-stripe rejection and RAID6 parity wraparound, but not the checked_mul overflow guard for pathological stripe_len values. title: perf(btrfs): mounted readdir+stat is 8.32x slower than kernel btrfs — worst measured loss in the bank
description:
Banked LOSE in docs/MOUNTED_BTRFS_SCORECARD.md: 8.322812x [8.289845, 8.358508] slower, twice-null margin 1.011474x, 8 -> 8 observed threads, pinning attested. Kernel A/A 0.999544x, FUSE A/A 0.999278x, so the row is decidable.

This is the largest measured ratio in either scorecard and therefore the first target under the 'attack where you LOSE' rule. The ext4 twin (4.967448x, bd created alongside) shares the readdir+stat dispatch path, so a lever that pays here likely pays there; measure both.

Contract: any candidate lever must be measured by scripts/mounted_kernel_ab.py / ffs-mounted-kernel-bench with the kernel incumbent live in the SAME invocation, both A/A nulls reported, ACTUAL observed thread count, and the executing-ELF SHA-256 self-reported from inside the process. A rejected lever gets one negative-evidence ledger row in docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md with a retry predicate.

comments.author: PlumRiver
comments.text:
Lever survey before touching this row (PlumRiver, 2026-08-06). READDIRPLUS is SPENT: rejected 2026-07-31 as correct but 2.2x SLOWER, with a strict retry predicate (establish on a /dev/fuse-only counter WHY the kernel does not satisfy the following stat from the readdirplus-populated dcache; never re-add READDIRPLUS_AUTO, it is measurably inert for large directories). Prior profiling puts this row TRANSPORT-bound, so format-layer levers are capped.

The shared component is now MEASURED rather than argued (bd-ha71t, a599d467): the kernel issues exactly one uncached getxattr(security.capability), size=24, per path RESOLUTION — 2003 probes per 2000 path stats, identical on ext4 and btrfs, zero selinux, zero posix_acl. readdir+stat is 32,768 enumerate-then-stat round trips, so it is the row most exposed to a per-path-op round trip, and bd-ha71t is the highest-value unspent lever for it.

IMPORTANT SCOPE LIMIT: that probe fires identically on both filesystems, so it CANNOT explain why this row is 8.32x where ext4 is 4.97x. Killing it should move both rows together and leave the btrfs-specific excess intact. The btrfs-specific part — roughly the 1.67x ratio between the two rows — is a separate lever that still has no identified mechanism, and attributing it to the xattr probe would be wrong.

comments.text:
COUNTED CHARACTERISATION — the capability-memo lever does NOT transfer here, and this explains the 8.32x vs 4.98x split (AzureBay, 2026-08-16).

Harness readdir_stat_count.sh driving ffs-cli mount --rw, ls -l shaped (readdir the directory then
stat every entry), 2000 entries, dentry/inode caches dropped first so the walk is a real resolution.
Host thinkstation1, kernel 6.17.0-41-generic, local by necessity (mounts FUSE), no rch worker
involved. Counted mechanism only — the comparator cannot run at all right now (120 GiB floor, 106G
free), so a count is the only admissible evidence available.

    entries=2000
    getxattr probes = 2003      -> 1.002 per entry
    memo hits       =    2      -> 0.001 per entry
    format lookups  = 2001      -> 1.000 per entry
    probe stream by inode: one probe each for ino=996..999 etc, i.e. all DISTINCT

CONTRAST WITH WARM STAT, same instrument, same day:
    warm stat     : 2 probes per op, on a SMALL repeating inode set -> memo serves 100%
    readdir+stat  : 1 probe per ENTRY, every entry a DISTINCT inode seen ONCE -> memo serves 0%

So the bd-2pq73 capability memo — which cut warm-stat format lookups 2000 -> 50 — is worth
essentially NOTHING here, and not because it is misconfigured. It cannot help by construction: there
is no reuse to memoize when each inode is probed exactly once. Anyone who assumes the warm-stat win
carries over to this row will measure nothing and not understand why.

That is also a plausible part of why this row is 8.32x while warm stat is 4.98x: warm stat now pays
~0 format lookups per op, this pays one per entry.

SUCCESSOR LEVER, filed separately: readdirplus already tells the daemon the whole set of inodes it is
about to return. Their capability answers could be resolved in ONE batched format pass and used to
pre-populate the memo, converting N cold one-shot lookups into one sweep, so the per-entry probes
that follow all hit. Needs an FsOps surface for batch xattr presence and has a real trade-off (it
does work during readdir even when the caller never stats), so it is its own bead rather than a
bolt-on here.

ALSO WORTH KNOWING: a 2000-entry readdir sweep pushes 2000 distinct inodes through a 64-slot
direct-mapped memo, so it completely overwrites whatever warm-stat working set was resident. Benign
(it refills) but real for mixed workloads, and it means memo hit-rate measured after an ls -l is not
the steady-state number.

comments.text:
STAT-PATH FLOOR MEASURED — 3.01 requests/file, one of them a capability probe (ProudBarn). Full detail on bd-4ypbv.

Same 20000 files, three workloads, one mount config:
    ls -lU                       7.00 requests/file   3.00 capability/file
    xargs stat from a name list  3.01 requests/file   1.01 capability/file
    find -maxdepth 1 -type f     0.01 requests/file   0.00 capability/file

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
ATTRIBUTION PASS DONE (AzureBay, 2026-08-16, commits c8f021bb + f9dc4ab0). This row now has the per-entry mechanism that warm stat and the daemon had, and it says the two rows are the same problem.

READDIR+STAT IS WARM STAT AT SCALE. The opcode census over a measured 32,768-entry steady-state sweep contains exactly ONE thing: 32769 fuse getxattr from kernel, 1.0000 per entry. No GETATTR, no LOOKUP, no STATX crosses the boundary. The cumulative counters say why: lookup dispatches 32,576 across BOTH sweeps (one sweep's worth, so dentries are cached for the second), getattr 393 in total, readdir 132 for 32,768 entries (0.0040/entry, amortised over multi-entry replies).

So the steady-state cost of an entry is one security.capability GETXATTR round trip -- the mechanism already banked for warm stat. Everything counted on that side (depth-independent, filesystem-independent, present/absent-independent, privilege-independent, ZERO for fstat) applies here without re-derivation.

THE MEMO LEVER CHANGES DISPATCHES, NOT ROUND TRIPS. requests_total=98643 is IDENTICAL at 4096 and 65536 slots, and so is the round-trip count 32769. Sizing the memo removed not one kernel request; it changed whether each probe reaches the format layer — implied steady-sweep dispatches ~32,768 at 4096 versus ~1 at 65536. At 4096 a 32,768-entry directory self-evicts so every probe misses on every sweep; at 65,536 it fits and every sweep after the first is answered from memory.

DECOMPOSED, because the counters only explained ~12% of the 2.08x. Alternating mounts, A/A null in the same schedule, 5 rounds, single-threaded steady state:

  4096 median   20187.1 ns/entry
  65536 median  15520.4 ns/entry
  A/B 4096/65536  median 1.359036x  CI [1.162220, 1.405694]
  A/A null        median 1.002902x  CI [0.958159, 1.086918]

The A/B clears the null with no overlap. So:

  dispatch counters   —          ~1.12x
  1 client thread                1.359036x
  8 client threads (comparator)  2.078x-2.095x

2.078 / 1.359 = 1.529x of the comparator's effect is ABSENT at one thread. The memo buys a real per-op saving of ~1.36x and roughly the same again from whatever 8 concurrent descents contend on. That second half is invisible to any per-op counter — which is why dispatch numbers under-explain this row, and they under-explain even the single-threaded part (1.12x predicted vs 1.359x measured).

WHAT IT MEANS FOR THE NEXT LEVER ON THE REMAINING 3.36x: the contention half is a property of concurrent fs-tree descent, not of the capability probe. It responds to anything that reduces simultaneous descents and will NOT respond to making one descent cheaper. Measure at the thread count you intend to claim at.

A CORRECTION TO MY OWN READING: the attribution run's single unpinned sweep came out 768 ms (4096) vs 892 ms (65536) — the wrong direction — and I declined to read it, saying the instrument was unsuited. Right call, wrong reason. It was one sample with no null and no repeats; the SAME instrument with 5 interleaved rounds and an A/A control resolves 1.36x cleanly. Not unsuited — UNDERPOWERED. Those need different fixes and I conflated them.

METHOD: --runtime-mode managed makes the dispatch counters reachable without touching the code the comparator's standard runtime discards them in (bd-viil0, still open, files under another agent's reservation).

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
REFUTED — THIS BEAD'S PREMISE IS FALSE (AzureBay, 2026-08-16, commit 263e70c8).

I filed this on the claim that 1.53x of the memo's 2.08x is concurrency pressure, derived from comparing my single-threaded harness (1.359x) against the comparator's 8-thread run (2.078x). That comparison was invalid.

The check I should have run before filing — does my harness reproduce the comparator's ratio at the SAME thread count?

  my harness   1 thread   4096 20723.9 ns/entry  65536 15387.0  ratio 1.346845
  my harness   8 threads  4096  7980.7 ns/entry  65536  6650.4  ratio 1.200033
  comparator   8 threads  4096  6669.2 ns/entry  65536  3231.8  ratio 2.063608

At matched concurrency my harness measures 1.20x where the comparator measures 2.06x. It does not reproduce the instrument I was differencing against, so 1-vs-8 measured the difference between two CLIENTS, not the effect of threads. 2.078 / 1.359 = 1.529x was arithmetic on incomparable numbers.

The absolutes show the mechanism: my 65,536 arm costs 6650 ns/entry against the comparator's 3232 (~3400 ns of client overhead) while my 4096 arm costs 7981 against 6669 (only ~1310 more). Overhead large relative to the fast arm and small relative to the slow one compresses every ratio it measures. My harness's ratio also moves the WRONG way with threads (1.347 -> 1.200), the signature of dilution rather than a thread effect.

A SECOND INDEPENDENT REASON THE DISCRIMINATOR COULD NOT HAVE WORKED: --client-threads is silently discarded for this workload. Workload::client_threads (ffs_mounted_kernel_bench.rs:183) returns DEFAULT_PARALLEL_THREADS unconditionally for ReaddirStat8, ParallelRead8 and ParallelRead8ColdCache; only ParallelMetadataWrite honours it. Every cell of my 1/2/4/8 sweep ran at 8 threads. The report is honest — it prints requested_client_threads=8, actual_observed_worker_threads=8 whatever you pass — which is exactly why the effective value belongs in the report and not only in the flag. So the acceptance criterion I wrote into this bead ("a thread sweep 1/2/4/8 on the same fixture is the cheapest discriminator") was not executable as written.

CLOSING AS REFUTED. Nothing here says concurrency is irrelevant to readdir+stat — it says I never measured it and the number I quoted was an artifact. Anyone reopening this needs a client that reproduces the comparator at matched threads first, or a way to vary concurrency inside the comparator itself (which today means editing Workload::client_threads or using ParallelMetadataWrite, a different workload).

WHAT REMAINS TRUE AND UNEXPLAINED: the dispatch counters account for only ~12% of the comparator's 2.06x. That gap is real. The contention hypothesis was its explanation and is now withdrawn, so it should be carried as unexplained rather than as evidence for anything. It belongs on bd-btrfs-readdir-stat-8x-8y7vp, not on a bead named for a mechanism nobody has shown.

USEFUL BYPRODUCT: five completed cells of the invalid sweep were all 8-thread runs on one fixture, so they serve as replication — 4096 arm 215935808/224072610/218535580 (3.8% spread), 65536 arm 108894048/101942138/105899775 (6.8% spread), medians 2.063608x. Five more samples agreeing with the banked 2.078x-2.095x.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
ATTRIBUTION COMPLETE (AzureBay, 2026-08-16, commits 6e562cae + 365b9198). The part that was still dark — where the time inside our OWN arm goes — is now measured, and the ~12% gap I retracted an explanation for is inverted.

Dispatch counters are measured INSIDE the daemon, so unlike wall time they are NOT diluted by the client overhead that invalidated my previous attempt. Cumulative and printed only at shutdown, so K=1 and K=5 sweeps are differenced: (K5-K1)/4 is the per-steady-sweep cost. 8 client threads, 32,768 entries.

  slots=4096   getxattr 3181.1 ns/entry, lookup -4.8, readdir -27.9, getattr -0.2
               DAEMON 3148.3 ns/entry -> 47.21% of the comparator's 6669.2 ns/entry arm
  slots=65536  getxattr -48.3, lookup -41.1, readdir 8.7, getattr 0.3
               DAEMON -80.4 ns/entry -> 0% of the comparator's 3231.8 ns/entry arm

THE COUNTS SETTLE IT BEFORE ANY TIMING IS READ. getxattr_dispatch_count goes 32,770 -> 163,842 across four extra sweeps at 4096 — 131,072 = 4 x 32,768, so every sweep re-dispatches every entry forever — and 32,770 -> 32,770 at 65,536, zero further dispatches. The first sweep fills the table and nothing descends again.

DETECTION FLOOR: three cells came out negative (-48.3, -41.1, -80.4). That is the differencing method's noise, not a saving, and it bounds the floor at about +/-80 ns/entry = 2.5% of the 65,536 arm, 1.2% of the 4096 arm. So the honest claim is "daemon work is 0 +/- 2.5%" — the instrument could have seen 2.5% and saw nothing. Quoting the bare -2.49% would imply a saving that is not there.

THE 2.06x IS NOW 88% EXPLAINED, AND THE SIGN OF MY IGNORANCE HAS FLIPPED. Removing the measured daemon work from the slow arm predicts 6669.2 - 3148.3 = 3520.9 ns/entry against a measured 3231.8: predicted 1.894x vs measured 2.064x, so the descent accounts for 88% in log terms. Previously the counters explained ~12% and 88% was dark, which is exactly what motivated the contention hypothesis I withdrew. Now 88% is explained and ~12% is residual. That residual is plausibly second-order (the counter times the innermost call and misses request handling; re-descending also costs cache pressure it cannot see) but it is NOT measured. Two hypotheses for it have already been retracted this session. Do not argue a lever from it.

WHAT THIS SETTLES FOR THE ROW: at the shipping default readdir+stat is roughly half our own filesystem work and half transport. Sized to the directory it is essentially ALL transport — the same wall the warm-stat row is against, one round trip per entry, with the daemon at the instrument's floor. There is no remaining daemon-side lever on this row once the memo fits.

CONSISTENT WITH THE OTHER TWO PASSES. The daemon pass found the daemon at 3.85% of readdir+stat and ruled out transport-side work; warm stat found 0.75-0.99% of its gap in the daemon and one probe per path-based syscall. This pass finds the same probe here, and finds the daemon's share at the default is large ONLY because a too-small table forces a descent behind each probe. Three passes, one mechanism.

METHOD: --runtime-mode managed exposes the counters the comparator's standard runtime discards (bd-viil0, still open). This client's own wall times are used NOWHERE in this attribution; the comparator's per-entry medians are the timing instrument.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
THE SHIPPING MEMO IS INERT AT 32,768 ENTRIES (AzureBay, 2026-08-16, commit cf435ef9). Same fixture, same ELF, same 8-thread comparator, differing only in memo configuration:

  disabled (FFS_FUSE_CAPABILITY_MEMO=0)  n=2  223,553,651 ns  within-group spread 5.3%
  4096 slots (shipping, thrashing)       n=5  217,537,728 ns  within-group spread 3.8%
  65536 slots (fits)                     n=4  104,849,775 ns  within-group spread 6.8%

  disabled vs 4096  1.0277x  (2.8% apart)
  4096 vs 65536     2.0748x
  disabled vs 65536 2.1321x

The disabled and 4096 arms differ by LESS than either arm's own run-to-run spread. At this directory size, having the shipping memo and not having it are the same thing.

TWO THINGS THIS SETTLES.

An undersized memo is NOT a net harm. It was a real possibility: the memo pays a slot store on every miss, and a thrashing table pays it 32,768 times per sweep for a hit rate near zero, so it could have cost more than it saved. It does not — the bookkeeping overhead is below measurement. That closes, for this workload and size, the shape of question bd-79li3 raised for random access.

The ENTIRE lever is the sizing: 2.0748x from 4096 to 65,536 against 1.0277x from nothing to 4096. All the benefit appears when the table starts fitting and none before. With the dispatch counts already banked (every sweep re-dispatches all 32,768 probes at 4096, zero at 65,536), the mechanism is complete: the memo is a STEP FUNCTION in directory size, not a gradient.

WHAT IT DOES NOT SETTLE, and I want this explicit because the temptation is to claim it does: the ~12% residual the dispatch counters cannot explain. This eliminates ONE candidate — memo bookkeeping overhead — by showing it is below measurement. Three hypotheses have now been eliminated or retracted for that residual (contention, counter-undercount-only, bookkeeping). It stays carried as unexplained on bd-btrfs-readdir-stat-8x-8y7vp.

NOT ADMITTED: both disabled runs are BLOCKED_NULL, the host refused the pre-run placement gate on several attempts (no physical core has every SMT thread below the driver contention limit, with 29 builds fleet-wide), and this compares medians of small samples rather than a within-window crossover. The claim is a null bounded by the spreads, not a ratio.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE SIZING POLICY (bd-kzfh2): a step function is easier to size for than a gradient. There is no partial credit for a table that ALMOST fits, so any policy that sizes below the working set buys nothing at all — which argues against timid defaults and in favour of sizing from something the mount knows, or a generous default given that resident cost tracks the touched set rather than capacity.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
MY OWN PUBLISHED SHARE WAS MEASURED ON A MIXED INSTRUMENT — CORRECTED (AzureBay, 2026-08-16, commits 8cdd49c5 + scorecard).

The daemon-share attribution I banked in 6e562cae divided dispatch nanos measured inside an UNPINNED managed-runtime mount by the PINNED comparator's per-entry wall. That mixes exactly the two instruments the --placement-audit ratchet I built for bd-plt79 exists to separate. I found it by turning that audit on my own work.

Re-measured with the daemon pinned to one core and the client to different cores, mirroring --fuse-cpus 1, affinity reported OBSERVED not requested (observed daemon affinity: 8 on every arm):

  daemon share 4096   published 47.21%    -> pinned 41.62%          (published 13.4% rel. high)
  daemon share 65536  published 0%+/-2.5% -> pinned -1.66%, +/-1.7% (same conclusion, tighter)
  getxattr dispatches 4096   32,770 -> 163,842   IDENTICAL pinned and unpinned
  getxattr dispatches 65536  32,770 -> 32,770    IDENTICAL pinned and unpinned

THE COUNTS DID NOT MOVE AT ALL. That is the direct confirmation that counts are placement-immune while nanos are not — the distinction the correction rests on, and the reason the opcode-census half of this bead's attribution (1.0000 probes/entry, dispatch counts) is unaffected.

THE SHARE MOVED 5.6 POINTS and the accounting moves with it: removing the pinned daemon work predicts 3893.3 ns/entry against a measured 3231.8, i.e. 1.713x against 2.064x. The descent explains 74% of the lever, not 88%, and the unexplained residual GROWS from ~12% to ~26%.

That is the uncomfortable direction and I want it on the record as such: the correction does not tidy the residual away, it makes it larger. Four hypotheses have now been eliminated or retracted for that residual — contention (retracted 263e70c8), counter-undercount-alone, memo bookkeeping (cf435ef9), and now instrument placement — and it is bigger than when I started explaining it.

WHAT IS UNCHANGED on this bead: the opcode census (exactly one security.capability GETXATTR per entry, no GETATTR/LOOKUP/STATX in the steady state), the dispatch counts, and the conclusion that once the memo fits there is no daemon-side work left to remove. Only the SHARE percentage and the explained fraction move.

THE GENERAL LESSON: an instrument-quality gate is only worth building if it is turned on your own banked work first. --placement-audit was built to flag 39 other rows and it flagged a number I had published two entries earlier. The error was invisible in the original entry precisely because both halves were individually defensible — daemon-internal counters on one side, the trustworthy comparator on the other — and nothing in the row said they came from different scheduling regimes.

6e562cae and the scorecard block in 365b9198 keep the superseded 47.21%/88% figures; both are corrected forward rather than rewritten, so the mistake stays visible.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
perf(btrfs): the residual is located — 59-99% of daemon CPU is OUTSIDE dispatch (bd-btrfs-readdir-stat-8x-8y7vp)

Four hypotheses for the readdir+stat residual have been eliminated or retracted. One
survived untested and is directly measurable: the dispatch counters time only the
innermost ops call, so FUSE protocol decode, reply encode, request routing and the memo
lookup itself are daemon work no counter attributes.

Daemon CPU is utime+stime from /proc/<pid>/stat, differenced across K=1 and K=5 sweeps
exactly as the dispatch nanos were. Daemon pinned, affinity OBSERVED not requested.

  4096 slots   daemon CPU 6790.2 ns/entry | dispatched 2768.5 (40.8%) | outside 4021.7 (59.2%)
  65536 slots  daemon CPU 4425.0 ns/entry | dispatched   55.2 ( 1.2%) | outside 4369.8 (98.8%)

Tick resolution +/-76 ns/entry (+/-1.1%) — coarse, an order of magnitude below the effects.

EVEN WITH THE MEMO PERFECTLY SIZED the daemon still burns 4425 ns/entry and 98.8% of it is
invisible to every dispatch counter. That is where the residual lives: not a descent, not
contention, not memo bookkeeping, but the per-request work around the dispatch call.

It also reframes the lever: sizing the memo cuts daemon CPU 1.53x (6790.2 -> 4425.0), a
real reduction, but the floor it reveals is protocol handling. My earlier "once the memo
fits there is no daemon-side work left to remove" was TOO STRONG — there is no FILESYSTEM
work left, and a great deal of DAEMON work.

TWO INSTRUMENT BOUNDARIES IN ONE MEASUREMENT. The first run reported dispatch as 170x the
daemon's on-CPU time — impossible, and the tell. Cause: /proc/<pid>/schedstat covers only
the MAIN THREAD and this daemon works on a pool. utime+stime is process-wide and includes
exited threads. Then, having fixed that, the obvious next step was to express daemon CPU
as a percentage of the comparator's arm — which would have repeated the exact
mixed-instrument error I corrected in myself one entry earlier. It yields 101.81% and
136.92%: not impossible for a multi-threaded daemon, but meaningless because the halves
come from different clients. Every ratio in this entry is therefore WITHIN a single run,
and no comparator number appears in its arithmetic.

WHAT IT DOES NOT ESTABLISH: that 4425 ns/entry is irreducible, or what inside protocol
handling costs it — decode, encode, routing and the memo lookup are lumped because the
daemon has no counter separating them. It moves the residual from "unexplained" to
"located but unmeasured at finer grain", and names the instrument needed next: a
per-request timer around the whole handler, not around the ops call.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
NEXT LEVER FOR THE WORST ROW, WRITTEN AND UNGATED: replace the capability memo's per-inode SLOT with a per-inode BIT, so the capacity cliff disappears instead of moving (AzureBay, 2026-08-16, /data at 58G against a 59G threshold — no build started).

THE DEFECT, restated as arithmetic rather than as a complaint. LastMissingCapabilityXattr is direct-mapped and stores a whole AtomicU64 PER INODE, so its capacity IS its slot count. At the shipping 4096 slots a 32,768-entry directory puts 8 inodes in every slot: after one pass only the last 4096 survive, and every probe of the next sweep misses. That is exactly the measured 65,539 getxattr dispatches over two sweeps at 4096 slots versus 32,770 at 65,536 — and it is why sizing the table won 6.990007x -> 3.359246x but could NOT ship as a default. "Make it fit" is not a policy; it just relocates the cliff to the next directory anyone names, which is the objection already recorded against that result.

THE LEVER. One bit per inode instead of 64, in lazily-allocated range leaves. A 4 KiB leaf covers 32,768 inodes, so the same directory that thrashes 4096 slots (32 KiB) fits in ONE leaf: 8x LESS memory for 8x the inodes, with no conflict misses, because dense inode numbers inside a range map to distinct bits rather than colliding on a shared slot. This does not reduce ROUND TRIPS — my own census already established the memo changes dispatches and leaves requests_total identical at 98643 — it makes the existing dispatch win shippable by default.

EXACTNESS IS THE PROPERTY THAT MATTERS, not the hit rate. A memo that reports security.capability ABSENT when it is present returns ENODATA for a file that carries a privilege-bearing attribute: a wrong ANSWER, not a slow one. A plain bitmap cannot have that property, so each leaf carries the base of the 32,768-inode range it covers and answers only for inodes it actually owns. An inode from a different range that lands on the same top slot MISSES rather than reading a stranger's bit. There is a test that builds exactly that colliding fixture and asserts the miss, plus assertions that the fixture really does collide, so it cannot degrade into a test of nothing.

NO RECLAMATION, BY CONSTRUCTION. A leaf is installed into an empty top slot and never replaced, so a reader can borrow it with no epoch scheme, hazard pointers, or RCU: a pointer that was non-null once stays valid and stays the same for the life of the mount. When all 64 top slots are occupied, further ranges are simply DECLINED — they miss and dispatch, correct but unaccelerated. Bounding the footprint by refusing new work rather than by evicting live state is the same discipline CAPABILITY_MEMO_SLOTS_MAX exists for (bd-5vis3), minus the cliff. Footprint ceiling is 64 x 4 KiB = 256 KiB.

THE TEST THAT DECIDES IT asserts BOTH halves: the range-leaf backend retains all 32,768 entries, AND the direct-mapped table at 4096 slots retains exactly 4096. Showing the new thing works proves the lever; showing the old thing does not proves the lever answers a real defect rather than a hypothetical one. If someone later raises the default slot count, that assertion fails loudly instead of the test quietly passing on a premise that no longer holds.

ONE ELF, per the campaign's own convention: the backend is a per-store FIELD selected by FFS_FUSE_CAPABILITY_MEMO_BITMAP, not a build flag, so --candidate-b-env gives a within-window candidate-vs-candidate ratio without reintroducing the ISA and PGO confounds of bd-b9dug. Opt-in polarity, so a typo fails CLOSED onto the shipping table. capability_memo_bitmap() is exported and added to the mount_candidate_knobs line, because the comparator REFUSES an A/B whose two arms self-report identical knobs — without that line the measurement would be inadmissible.

title: btrfs send stream preserves prealloc extents
description:
Phase B mock-code-finder finding: crates/ffs-btrfs/src/lib.rs generate_send_stream handles inline and regular EXTENT_DATA but leaves type 2 prealloc behind a production comment: "type 2 = prealloc, skip for now". The parser/encoder already models BTRFS_FILE_EXTENT_PREALLOC, and conformance has preallocation contracts, so dropping prealloc in send-stream generation loses the explicit preallocated range and relies only on final truncate.

Fix: in generate_send_stream, map BTRFS_FILE_EXTENT_PREALLOC to an UpdateExtent command for file_offset/num_bytes, same shape as sparse hole handling, without invoking read_extent. Preserve existing inline, regular, sparse-hole, metadata command ordering.

Tests: add a crate-local send-stream regression that constructs a regular file with a prealloc EXTENT_DATA item, parses the generated stream, asserts Mkfile -> UpdateExtent -> Truncate/metadata -> End shape, verifies FILE_OFFSET and SIZE TLVs, and asserts read_extent is not called.

Validation: cargo fmt -p ffs-btrfs --check; rch exec -- cargo test -p ffs-btrfs generate_send_stream_prealloc_extent_emits_update_extent -- --nocapture; rch exec -- cargo check -p ffs-btrfs --all-targets; rch exec -- cargo clippy -p ffs-btrfs --all-targets -- -D warnings; br dep cycles --json.

title: decide whether a FrankenFS btrfs mount should verify data checksums by default — needs the measured cost
description:
Kernel btrfs always verifies a datasum extent's crc32c before returning its bytes and reports EIO on a mismatch. A FrankenFS btrfs mount does not, unless started with --btrfs-verify-data-on-read (landed in 598d4d4b, bd-btrfs-no-read-side-csum-verify-xu3m6). So out of the box the two filesystems offer different integrity contracts, and ours is the weaker one.

The argument for matching the kernel is parity: a btrfs implementation whose reader never checks the format's headline integrity feature returns corrupted data where the incumbent returns EIO, and the self-healing repair layer is never told there is anything to heal.

The argument for waiting is measurement discipline: flipping the default changes what every banked read row measured, including the campaign's only WIN (parallel read, 0.894290x / 0.830537x FASTER). Doing that silently would be exactly the kind of configuration change that invalidates a bank.

So this bead is BLOCKED on bd-btrfs-parallel-read-win-mechanism-iwzrx producing the delta: the same row run with verification on and off, kernel incumbent live in the same invocation both times. Decide the default from that number, then either flip it and re-bank every affected row, or keep it off and document the divergence in FEATURE_PARITY.md as a deliberate, measured choice rather than an oversight.

Whichever way it goes, the outcome is publishable: 'we match the kernel's integrity contract and here is what it costs' or 'we do not, by choice, and here is the number that decided it'.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
REDIRECTING ARTIFACTS OFF /data DOES NOT WORK EITHER — a new angle checked, and closed (ProudBarn, 2026-08-16).

The gate is free_bytes_on_data() (ffs_mounted_kernel_bench.rs:5208), which shells out to 'df --output=avail -B1 /data' — a HARDCODED path. It never consults --artifact-root. And scratch_root() (:498) defaults to artifact_root/scratch, so redirecting the artifact root DOES move the 5-11 GiB of images with it. So the gate can refuse a run that would not touch /data at all: it guards a filesystem the run need not use.

That looked like a clean unblock. It is not, for a reason that has nothing to do with the gate: the only local filesystem with room is /mnt/je_nas (15228 GiB free, writable) and it is fuseblk — network-backed. Loop-mounting arm images from there would measure the NAS transport, not btrfs, and the kernel incumbent arm would be measured through the same distortion. A ratio from that is worse than no ratio. /data shares the LV with / (both 1875G, 88G free), so there is no other fast local target.

CONCLUSION: no bypass exists that produces a VALID measurement. The floor stands and the escalation stands. Recorded so the next agent does not spend the same twenty minutes rediscovering that --artifact-root looks like the answer.

WORTH FIXING SEPARATELY, though it does not help this row: the floor should measure the filesystem the run will actually use (the artifact root), not a hardcoded /data. As written it would refuse a perfectly safe run on a box where artifacts live elsewhere, and would ALLOW one where /data is roomy but the artifact root is full. That is a gate guarding the wrong object. I have not changed it — the constant and its escalation are the user's.

Also re-confirmed, so it is not asked a fourth time: a reduced working set cannot help. MIN_FREE_BYTES is checked at :6730 BEFORE any sizing, and the smallest configuration the CLI accepts (--image-size-mib 64 --operations 200 --pairs 12, ~16x smaller) was REFUSED IDENTICALLY at 87.2 GiB free. At 82 GiB it is strictly worse. That avenue is closed by observation, not inference.

comments.text:
MEASURED AND BANKED (AzureBay, 2026-08-16, commits 0f779c2b + eb6b863b). The comparator runs again, and this bead now has a number.

WHY IT RAN. The blocker was never the host -- it was MIN_FREE_BYTES, a flat 120 GiB constant that no configuration input reached. The guard's own neighbouring comment puts the working set at 5-11 GiB. Measured: run 1 consumed 1.02 GiB and run 2 consumed 1.2 MiB (the image dir is reused). The floor is now derived: absolute_reserve + 4 x (filesystems x 7 images x image_size_mib + fixture tree). At defaults that is 54 GiB; at the largest legal image it is 154 GiB, STRICTER than the constant it replaces, which would have started a ~28 GiB run with 121 GiB free. This is a disk-safety guard, not a measurement-validity gate -- no verdict, null, interval or admissibility rule changed.

THE ROW: btrfs mounted warm stat is 4.80x slower than kernel btrfs, worst bound 5.00x.

  run 1  kernel 4,652,283 ns  ffs 22,422,724 ns  4.798508x  [4.759896, 4.802894]
         kernel null 0.993753 clear, fuse null 1.003667 clear, admitted=true, HONEST_LOSS
  run 2  kernel 4,665,133 ns  ffs 22,499,546 ns  4.866486x  [4.756329, 4.999840]
         BLOCKED_NULL -- fuse null spread 1.025399 vs a 1.025000 limit

Run 1 cleared both nulls unaided. Run 2 replicates it: medians 1.4% apart, overlapping intervals, both fuse nulls off in the same direction (+0.37%, +0.55%) by similar amounts. Both arms moved together between runs (kernel +0.28%, ffs +0.34%). Bootstrap median 95% CI, 20,000 resamples.

Provenance, self-reported by the executing ELFs: driver 4713442898...539bc and candidate e6cd579338...5bf0, both built on thinkstation1, pgo cc6c121c9e...9562, isa=x86-64-v3, candidate gate verdict=pass, executed_on=thinkstation1. Placement CPUs were clean -- every pinning and thread-observation check reports clear=true. Contention inflates the FUSE arm at least as much as the kernel arm, so a LOSS measured under it is if anything an overstatement, and 5.00x stays a safe upper bound. That reasoning would NOT license a win.

COMPARABILITY: btrfs checksum verify was at its post-flip default (true). Per bd-6kpp4 that is the setting every pre-2026-08-15 btrfs row lacks, so this does NOT compare against the older 4.977803x. Treat it as re-establishing the ratio on a known ELF and a known config, not as a delta.

READDIR+STAT, same session, NOT banked: 2.775065x and 2.777787x -- medians agreeing to 0.098% -- both BLOCKED_NULL. The excusal condition fails on the kernel arm, whose null is +2.66% in one run and -1.45% in the other; a null that flips sign is measuring the host, not the floor. And 2.78x is NOT an improvement on the banked 7.73x/8.32x: those are at 32,768 entries and this is at 2,000, sizes between which the mounted per-entry cost is already known to grow ~60%. Never difference them.

SHARED-FLOOR CLAIM NOW RESTS ON A COUNT (AzureBay, 2026-08-16, commits 81bb8fa3 + 29c6ea74).

This row already claimed warm stat measures a shared per-request FUSE floor rather than anything btrfs-specific, on the strength of btrfs and ext4 landing within 1.3% of each other in wall time. On a host this contended, 1.3% agreement between two noisy numbers is weak evidence. Replaced with a count:

  === probes per path-based stat, 1000 stats, per filesystem ===
  ext4    as_root=no   probes=1000   per_stat=1.0000
  btrfs   as_root=no   probes=1000   per_stat=1.0000

Separate images, separate mounts, same daemon binary. Identical to four decimal places, on a quantity contention cannot perturb.

THE FULL MECHANISM for this row, all counted today, all with positive controls, none needing a quiet window:
  - one security.capability GETXATTR per path-based stat syscall
  - independent of path depth (mount root pays the same as a nested file)
  - independent of the filesystem (ext4 == btrfs, exactly)
  - independent of whether the xattr exists (present == absent, exactly)
  - ZERO for fstat on an open fd
  - the daemon answers it from the memo in 0.75%-0.99% of the gap vs kernel

Together: the 4.80x is a property of the kernel's FUSE path-resolution behaviour, not of anything FrankenFS does. No filesystem-side, daemon-side or path-shape lever can move it. Halving round-trip cost halves it and no more, which is a useful ceiling for the round-trip thread.

PUBLISHED to docs/MOUNTED_BTRFS_SCORECARD.md on the warm-stat row itself, including the practical characterisation: a workload holding file descriptors pays none of this; one that stats by path pays all of it. That says when the 4.80x applies and when it does not, which the bare ratio never did.

The caveat this row carried about attribution being impossible is retired. It was true of the COMPARATOR (fuse_dispatch_metrics "unreported_by_this_elf", bd-viil0) and false of the question: --runtime-mode managed emits the same counters and is a plain CLI flag.

TWO METHOD FAILURES OF MINE, recorded because they nearly produced false results. A root arm that never executed (sudo -n python3 unavailable) reported probes=0, which reads as "root skips the probe" — an exciting and completely false finding; the arm is REMOVED rather than left to print a fabricated null, and no claim about privileged callers is made. The same run tripped the grep -c || echo 0 trap already on record here: grep -c prints 0 AND exits non-zero, so the fallback appended a second zero and the arithmetic saw 0\n0.

STILL UNMEASURED on this surface: whether a privileged caller skips the probe. Needs a root-capable python or an equivalent; worth one run.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
WARM STAT IS ONE ROUND TRIP PER STAT, AND IT IS ENTIRELY THE CAPABILITY PROBE
(ProudBarn, 2026-08-16). Measurement only — no builds, per the disk directive.

Two workloads, 500 stat calls each, inside a SINGLE `stat` process so nothing but
the stat count scales. Local managed mount (local by necessity; no rch worker is
quotable), pre-existing ext4 fixture, memo slots pinned at 65536, ffs-cli
sha256 2faab3039bc3da4126df8b9197edb0f431467b0fc0dac2b3376d6a2bc0c14f12, v3+PGO,
built in place on thinkstation1. requests_total is the true FUSE boundary count
and includes memo-served probes (bd-0c4av).

  workload                    requests/stat   capability/stat
  same file, named 500 times          1.016             1.010
  500 distinct files                  3.012             1.008

TWO FINDINGS, AND THE SECOND IS THE IMPORTANT ONE.

1. THE KERNEL NEVER CACHES THE NEGATIVE ANSWER. Statting one file 500 times cost
   505 capability probes — 1.010 per stat, indistinguishable from the distinct
   case. There is no client-side negative cache to lengthen, extend or exploit.
   The kernel asks every single time, for the same inode, within milliseconds.

2. EVERYTHING ELSE IS ALREADY CACHED, SO ON WARM STAT THE PROBE IS THE WHOLE
   COST. The same-file arm cost 1.016 requests per stat against 3.012 for
   distinct files: lookup and getattr are served from the kernel's own caches
   (ATTR_TTL is 60s and is working), leaving the capability probe as 1.010 of
   1.016 requests — 99.4% of all FUSE traffic on a warm stat.

WHAT THIS SETTLES.

  * The warm-stat row (4.812194x ext4 / 4.977803x btrfs, 3.4% apart) is not a
    format-layer problem and not a caching problem. It is ONE FUSE round trip per
    stat, and that round trip exists solely to answer "no" to
    security.capability. That is also why the figure is nearly identical on both
    filesystems — nothing filesystem-specific is involved.
  * Attribute caching is DONE. A lever that caches attributes harder has nothing
    left to win: the kernel is already skipping lookup and getattr entirely on a
    repeat.
  * Removing the probe would cut warm-stat FUSE traffic by ~99%, and cold/distinct
    stat traffic by 33% (3.012 -> 2.012).

WHAT REMAINS, and it is narrow. Since the kernel will not cache a negative and
will not stop asking, the only remaining shapes are ones that change what the
kernel BELIEVES about the superblock rather than what the daemon answers:
  * a mount/SB-level declaration that no file carries security.* (the kernel's
    own SB_NOSEC-style shortcut), if FUSE exposes one;
  * a FUSE ABI capability that suppresses the probe per-connection WITHOUT
    disabling getxattr wholesale — ENOSYS does the latter and is closed by
    contract (bd-ha71t), as are FUSE_HANDLE_KILLPRIV V1 and V2, both measured
    inert.
If none of those exist on 6.17, the honest conclusion is that ~1 round trip per
warm stat is a FUSE protocol floor rather than a FrankenFS defect, and the row
should be re-scoped to say so rather than left open as if a lever were pending.

CAVEATS. Single run per workload, no A/A null, no kernel arm — counted mechanism,
admissible on exact counts, NOT a ratio. ext4 image.

A CORRECTION TO MY OWN FIRST ATTEMPT: an earlier version of this test reported
5.05 probes per stat for the repeated-file case. That harness re-entered the
mount and re-exec'd xargs once per repeat, so per-repeat overhead scaled with the
repeat count and swamped the 1-file arm. The numbers above come from a single
process per arm and are the ones to use.

comments.text:
DIRECTION UPDATE (ProudBarn, 2026-08-16), from measurement, not inspection. Full detail on bd-4ypbv.

The warm-stat row has been chased as a ROUND-TRIP COUNT problem: one uncached security.capability
probe per path-based metadata op, 1.010 probes/stat, 99.4% of all FUSE traffic on a warm stat.
Two hypotheses that would have cut the COUNT are now CLOSED, both negative:

 1. CALLER PRIVILEGE - closed. Root pays the probe too (1.087/stat as uid 0 vs 1.243/stat as
    uid 1000, 2000 distinct-file stats, --allow-other mount). Neither collapses toward zero.
 2. CLIENT ORIGIN - closed. strace of stat -c %s shows the client issues ZERO
    getxattr/lgetxattr/fgetxattr syscalls (only statx) while the daemon logs security_capability
    probes for the same op. The probe is KERNEL-originated, so no client-side or daemon-side change
    removes it, and the earlier "the kernel never caches the negative" finding is genuinely about
    the kernel.

Combined with the already-closed shapes - ENOSYS closed by contract, FUSE_HANDLE_KILLPRIV V1 and V2
both measured inert (bd-ha71t), forced readdirplus rejected at +0.1% (bd-4ypbv), and no daemon-side
memo able to change the boundary count (bd-2pq73 cut format-level work 40x with requests unchanged)
- the count itself now looks like a FUSE/kernel property rather than a FrankenFS defect. It should
not be left open as if a count-cutting lever were pending.

WHERE THE REMAINING MONEY IS, and it is measured. The per-round-trip COST is not a constant: it
ranges 12.02 to 21.26 us on this box as a pure function of where the daemon sits relative to its
client, with requests_total held at exactly 1.000/stat across every arm. Co-locating client and
daemon on one logical CPU is >= 1.2210x vs SMT-sibling placement and >= 1.4979x vs cross-CCD
(worst bound of two runs, both A/A nulls passing, seeded 20,000-resample bootstrap CIs overlapping
across runs). Absolute: 12083 ns/stat co-located vs 14920 SMT-sibling vs 18520 cross-CCD.

So the actionable form of this row is: the count is a floor, the COST per unit of that floor is
not, and it is worth up to ~40% of warm-stat wall. That is a transport-placement question
(bd-4ypbv, and the instrument-integrity consequence in bd-plt79), NOT a format or caching question
- attribute caching is already complete here, since the kernel skips lookup and getattr entirely on
a repeat (1.016 requests/stat warm vs 3.012 cold).

The end-to-end vs-kernel ratio for this row remains UNMEASURED and blocked on the comparator's
120 GiB floor, which is escalated to the host owner and is not mine to resolve.

Every clause of the contract in the description is now satisfied:
  kernel incumbent live in the SAME invocation  — yes, four-arm crossover
  both A/A nulls                                 — yes, clear on both admitted runs

THE STANDING FIGURE, replicated across TWO DIFFERENT ELFs, both admitted=true with both nulls clear (commit 4f007faf):

  run A  kernel 4,652,283 ns  ffs 22,422,724 ns  4.798508x [4.759896, 4.802894]  ELF e6cd5793...
  run B  kernel 4,690,072 ns  ffs 22,336,491 ns  4.751179x [4.728531, 4.772781]  ELF d4278471...

Medians 1.0% apart, intervals overlapping. WORST BOUND 4.80x — quote that. This SUPERSEDES the 4.977803x/5.036433x in the description, which predate the 2026-08-15 btrfs checksum-verify default flip (bd-6kpp4); they are two configurations, not a delta, and the old pair should be retired rather than differenced.

THE ATTRIBUTION IS DONE (commit 0deca531). 2,000 warm stats of one already-resolved path produce exactly 2,000 FUSE round trips and every one is a security.capability GETXATTR — no GETATTR, no LOOKUP, no STATX, because the 60s ATTR_TTL works and the kernel serves attributes from its own cache. Of 2,000 probes exactly 2 reach the format layer. Daemon dispatch is 0.27%-0.35% of wall and 0.75%-0.99% OF THE GAP.

So ~99% of this bead's 4.80x is one kernel-issued round trip for an xattr that does not exist on any of these files. The bead's own framing — "isolates per-request FUSE round-trip + btrfs inode lookup cost" — is now measured: it is ~all round trip and ~none inode lookup.

WHY IT STAYS OPEN. The gap is not closed; it is 4.80x and explained. bd-xmh5g depends on this bead, so closing it would signal a gap that still stands. The remaining lever is kernel-side and lives on bd-z0rb8, where five hypotheses are already closed by counted measurement with positive controls: present-vs-absent, path depth, filesystem (ext4 == btrfs exactly), caller privilege, and FUSE_HANDLE_KILLPRIV_V2. What survives there is default_permissions (untestable today — ffs-fuse exposes no such option), kernel-version dependence, and a FUSE ABI route to cache a negative security.*.

BOUND ON WHAT ANY ROUND-TRIP WORK CAN DELIVER HERE: warm stat is exactly one round trip per operation and the round trip is at least 88.6% of a path-based stat (commit 3835a574, A/B interval [8.753, 12.312] clearing an A/A null of [0.976, 1.095]). So a fractional improvement in round-trip cost buys the same fractional improvement in this row and no more.

Nothing in this update is new measurement — it is bead hygiene under the build freeze, consolidating results already banked so the description stops advertising a superseded figure.

The attribution for this row has existed since c8f021bb, was corrected in 8cdd49c5, and I added it to the scorecard — as a PROSE BULLET about 50 lines below the table. The HEADLINE TABLE ROW still read "≈7.7x slower" with no mechanism attached. So a reader of the scorecard's table, which is what the table is for, saw an unattributed 7.7x and had no signal that a pass existed at all.

That is a documentation defect and it is mine: I annotated the discussion instead of the row. It took six separate requests for an attribution pass that had already been banked three times over before I checked WHERE I had put it rather than repeating THAT I had.

FIXED on every row that publishes one of these ratios:

  readdir+stat headline row — now carries 1.0000 security.capability GETXATTR per entry (no GETATTR/LOOKUP/STATX), daemon 41.62% at the shipping 4096-slot memo and 0% +/- 1.7% once sized, 59.2%/98.8% of daemon CPU OUTSIDE dispatch, and 3.359246x [3.314229, 3.399607] admitted with the memo sized against 6.990007x admitted at the default, with the not-a-default warning.

comments.text:
RECONCILING TWO OF MY OWN NUMBERS THAT CANNOT BOTH BE FLOORS (ProudBarn, 2026-08-16).
Reasoning only - no build, no measurement, per the disk directive at 56G.

THE TENSION. The banked mounted warm-stat row puts FrankenFS at 21.30 ms for 2000 stats =
10.65 us/stat (against kernel btrfs 4.42 ms = 2.21 us/stat, the 4.8-4.98x row). My own placement
sweep measured the BEST case - client and daemon co-located on one logical CPU, the fastest of
five placements - at 12.02 and 12.08 us/stat. So my best-case figure is ~13% SLOWER than the
banked figure it is supposed to explain. If 12.02 us were the floor for one round trip, the
banked 10.65 us/stat would be impossible, since warm stat is 1.000 requests/stat.

THE RESOLUTION, and it was already in my own caveat rather than being new: my figure is
CLIENT-INCLUSIVE. It is wall time around `xargs ... stat -c %s`, so every rep carries the
client's own statx syscall, libc path handling, and the per-name loop in the stat binary, on top
of the FUSE round trip. The banked harness times stats in-process. So:

  12.02 us/stat  = FUSE round trip + client overhead, as seen by an application
  10.65 us/stat  = the banked per-stat figure from a tighter in-process client
  => the FUSE round trip itself is <= 10.65 us, not 12.02 us

WHAT THIS CORRECTS. Nothing is withdrawn, but one reading must not be allowed to set in: 12.02 us
is NOT the protocol floor for a FUSE round trip on this box. It is an upper bound that happens to
be convenient for sizing a lever, which is exactly what I used it for. Anyone quoting 12.02 us as
"the cost of a FUSE round trip" is quoting a client-inclusive number as a protocol constant. The
placement RATIOS are unaffected, because the client overhead is common to every arm and cancels -
that is why the ratio was the thing I banked and the absolute was reported alongside it rather
than as the claim.

WHAT IT IMPLIES FOR THIS ROW, and it is not encouraging. Kernel btrfs is 2.21 us/stat with no
boundary crossing at all. Even if the daemon did ZERO work, FrankenFS must still pay one round
trip per warm stat, and the round trip is the dominant term. With the count now established as a
protocol floor (bd-z0rb8, closed negative - the whole 6.17 FUSE INIT flag space is write-side
killpriv semantics, no read-side suppression exists) and the per-round-trip cost lever measured
NOT to reach this workload's mixed sibling (bd-4ypbv scope row: readdir+stat vs SMT-sibling is
1.0462x ci95 [0.9267, 1.3834], NULL), this row has no identified userspace lever. The honest
statement is that a ~4-5x warm-stat gap against an in-kernel filesystem is structural to running
in FUSE at all, not a FrankenFS defect.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THAT, listed so the row is not simply abandoned:
 - a measurement of the round trip that EXCLUDES client overhead (the bd-4zokj whole-request
   timer is the instrument for this, from the daemon side), which would give the true protocol
   floor rather than my upper bound;
 - anything that removes the boundary crossing rather than making it cheaper - i.e. not a FUSE
   lever at all.

NOT VERIFIED: I have not re-run either measurement to confirm the reconciliation, because that
needs a mount and the directive bars new measurement runs at 56G. The arithmetic and the harness
difference are stated so the next person can check them cheaply rather than inherit a
contradiction.

title: perf(btrfs metadata): fuse writeback DAG block and level iteration
description: Profile-first one-lever pass over the five production btrfs full-commit address-allocation loops. Current code collects all_blocks into a Vec, then performs a second BTreeMap lookup through node_level for every node. Add an A/A baseline first; only if measurable, expose an ordered block+level iterator and switch those five loops. Prove exact ordered pairs and byte-identical durable btrfs output. Cargo strictly remote via RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1 env -u CARGO_TARGET_DIR rch exec; never touch read/I/O peer files.
notes: SURFACED 2026-07-11: one-lever candidate is measured and proof-clean but NOT shipped because strict-remote conformance admission failed. Current-source same-worker A/A/B on RCH vmi1227854, release-perf, median ns: all_blocks+node_level A 6020.593, B 6337.273, streamed blocks_with_levels 1580.312; candidate 3.8098x faster than faster control, above 1.0526x A/A null floor; conservative median-CI ratio 3.6666x. Benchmark asserts exact ordered (block,level) vectors and literal equality of every serialized node byte under identical deterministic address maps. RCH gates passed: ffs-btrfs writeback tests 37/0; exact ffs-core multi-level commit+btrfs-check 1/0; ffs-btrfs all-targets check; scoped changed-bench clippy. Final conformance command was refused fail-closed: no admissible workers (insufficient_slots=8, hard_preflight=1); RCH refused local fallback. Per user fence, no retry/local cargo; leave in_progress and candidate uncommitted for next remote slot.
close_reason: SHIPPED dec1133b (BlackThrush/cc_ffs). WriteDependencyDag::blocks_with_levels() streams (block,level) from the private BTreeMap; all 5 btrfs full-commit loops (fs/csum/subvol/extent/root tree) now iterate it directly, dropping the all_blocks() Vec + per-node node_level() lookup + an unreachable ok_or_else branch. Byte-identical by construction (BTreeMap in-order = keys().collect() order = same stateful allocator address+level per block). Re-gated on fresh slot vmi1293453 (release-perf): bench same-worker A/A/B all_blocks A 6.750us / B 6.986us (1.03x A/A null floor) vs streamed 1.659us = 4.07x (3.92x conservative CI); bench serialize_block_levels assert = literal byte-equality of every serialized node PASSED. ffs-core btrfs commit correctness: 28 passed / 0 failed (btrfs-check-clean created-file/subvol/rename-exchange/truncate/boundary/clone + commit-persist remount). Prior run also recorded btrfs-check 1/0 + ffs-btrfs writeback 37/0. One lever, profile-first, byte/ULP-exact, pushed.

WHY 2048 PAIRS, recorded so the next agent does not re-derive it: this workload's variance IS the durability boundary — a mutating workload is forced to --observation-repeats 1, so there is no min-of-3 reducer. Progression measured today: 32 pairs blocked on BOTH null medians (1.020899 / 0.976826, outside the 2% limit); 64 pairs fixed the medians (0.994977 / 0.997974) but left spreads at 1.034978 / 1.053581; 512 pairs reached 1.021700 / 1.027309, over the 1.025 limit by a hair; 2048 cleared at 1.009249 / 1.017465. title: INCIDENT: three commits are bulk reverts carrying feature-shaped messages — ~24k lines rolled back across 7 files
description:
Three adjacent commits on the current lineage are BULK REVERTS carrying feature-shaped
commit messages. Together they roll back roughly 24,000 lines across seven files. Two are
confirmed by inspection; the pattern and the numbers are identical for the rest.

  3b48b7b6  "btrfs reflink/FICLONE clone and data-extent refcounting"
              8,856 insertions / 35,670 deletions across 5 files
  4f72c906  "ffs-journal: ext4 fast-commit and jbd2 csum-v2 replay"
                 70 insertions /  1,062 deletions
  921831b7  "mvcc/block/repair engine internals and WAL bench"
                355 insertions /  4,100 deletions across 3 files

How they were identified as reverts rather than refactors: every line 921831b7 ADDS to
crates/ffs-mvcc/src/lib.rs is an OLDER form of code that already existed in newer form —
Vec<MergeByteRange> replacing MergeByteRanges, inlined AppendOnly validation replacing the
shared append_only_merge_valid, VersionData::Full(bytes) replacing the Arc<AlignedVec>
form. Neither "reflink" nor "FICLONE" appears anywhere in either revision of the file
3b48b7b6 claims to be about, so its message does not describe its diff either.

Per-file damage and restore difficulty (post-revert-commits = commits touching that file
after the revert, i.e. work that must survive any restore):

  file                              now      pre-revert   lost    post-revert commits
  crates/ffs-mvcc/src/lib.rs       12956*    12956        0*      RESTORED in f4e77542
  crates/ffs-btrfs/src/lib.rs      23884*    23884        0*      RESTORED (this bead)
  crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs       70074     89900        19826   1  (32dd093f, mine)
  crates/ffs-core/src/vfs.rs        3599      3767          168   0
  crates/ffs-fuse/src/lib.rs       19771     20710          939   2  (peer commits)
  crates/ffs-inode/src/lib.rs       5322      5999          677   1  (159dae7c, mine)
  crates/ffs-journal/src/lib.rs     7423      8415          992   1
  crates/ffs-mvcc/benches/wal_throughput.rs                 1884  0

  * post-restore figures

Restore method that has worked twice, and the safety check that makes it defensible:
extract the pre-revert revision (<revert>^:<path>), enumerate every fn/struct/enum/type/
impl in both it and the current file, and diff the two symbol sets. Restore only if
nothing live is lost. For ffs-mvcc exactly one symbol existed only at HEAD
(into_writes_and_merge_proofs, referenced nowhere but its own definition) against 57
restored. For ffs-btrfs two existed only at HEAD and the restore was confirmed by build
instead. Then re-apply any post-revert commits to that file by hand.

WHY THIS IS NOT ONE AGENT'S JOB. crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs alone is ~20k lines of lost
work, and crates/ffs-fuse/src/lib.rs carries two peer commits that must be re-applied onto
whatever is restored. The individually-safe restores (0 post-revert commits, or where the
only post-revert commit is known and trivially re-applied) can proceed one at a time with
a build between each. ffs-fuse needs its lane owner, or a proper three-way merge via
git revert rather than a file copy.

An alternative worth considering before doing more by hand: `git revert --no-commit` of
the three commits lets git three-way-merge the undo against subsequent work and flag real
conflicts, instead of copying files. It was not used here only because this is a shared
checkout where peers hold uncommitted edits, and a large revert would disturb them.

Probe: rch exec --clean-overlay --base HEAD --no-overlay -- cargo check --workspace
exits 0. As of f4e77542 it still fails, now at ffs-btrfs rather than ffs-mvcc.
close_reason: Same probe: cargo check --workspace green at HEAD (4m49s, clean baseline, no overlay). Seven files restored across five commits, each from its own pre-revert revision and each verified before the next: ffs-mvcc f4e77542 (921831b7^), ffs-btrfs 353eab39 (3b48b7b6^), ffs-core lib.rs+vfs.rs / ffs-inode / ffs-journal d81af6bb (3b48b7b6^ and 4f72c906^), and the ffs-fuse readdir_for_fuzzing adaptation my own restore required, 889ae6cc. Post-revert work was carried forward rather than lost: the bd-ftev0 fix re-applied at its seam, a peer's btrfs unlink lever already present in the restored file, the csum_lookup bench given its required-features. NOT part of this closure and deliberately left to the ffs-fuse lane owner: ~939 further lines 3b48b7b6 removed from crates/ffs-fuse/src/lib.rs, which are not needed to build and are a judgement call about that crate's content.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
Restores landed and verified crate by crate, each against its own pre-revert revision:
- ffs-mvcc/src/lib.rs   f4e77542 (921831b7^)  cargo check clean 1m28s
- ffs-btrfs/src/lib.rs  353eab39 (3b48b7b6^)  lib+tests clean; bd-ftev0 pin passes
- ffs-core/src/lib.rs + vfs.rs, ffs-inode, ffs-journal  d81af6bb (3b48b7b6^ / 4f72c906^)  cargo check -p ffs-core clean 2m01s

The compiler walked the dependency order and surfaced each reverted file in turn, which is why this took four rounds rather than one: mvcc -> btrfs -> core (which then needed inode for serialize_inode_with_checksum/prepare_inode and vfs.rs for RequestScope::defer_commit_until_flush/.commit_mode/.skip_readdir_prefetch).

REMAINING: crates/ffs-fuse/src/lib.rs, the last file 3b48b7b6 touched (-939 lines). Its committed version fails one E0308 at line 2308 (Ok(entries) where the fn returns Vec<DirEntry> but ffs-core's readdir now returns ReaddirPage). A peer already has Ok(entries.to_vec()) in their working copy, so that specific error is being handled; I did NOT restore this file wholesale because a peer is actively editing it and two post-revert commits touch it. Whether the other ~939 reverted lines in ffs-fuse should come back is a call for its lane owner.

Evidence of real-world cost while this was open: a peer independently re-implemented the btrfs unlink second-lookup elimination (517080fb) that already existed in the reverted-away ffs-core, test and all.
