comments.author: NobleKnoll
comments.text:
OQ3 closure: Repair-symbol invalidation/refresh policy under heavy writes — COMPLETE

## Formal Symbol Freshness Policy (State Machine)

The refresh policy is codified as a 3-variant state machine with 6 trigger modes:

### RefreshPolicy (pipeline.rs:56-68)
- **Eager**: Refresh immediately on every write (metadata groups)
- **Lazy { max_staleness }**: Defer refresh until scrub or staleness timeout (data groups, default 30s)
- **Adaptive { risk_threshold, max_staleness }**: Switch eager/lazy based on corruption posterior

### GroupRefreshState (pipeline.rs:122-141)
State machine per group: dirty (bool), dirty_since (Instant), policy (RefreshPolicy), last_refresh (Instant)

### RefreshMode (pipeline.rs:70-92)
6 trigger modes: Recovery, EagerWrite, LazyScrub, AdaptiveEagerWrite, AdaptiveLazyScrub, StalenessTimeout

### Trigger Conditions
1. Eager policy: every write triggers immediate refresh (EagerWrite)
2. Lazy policy: scrub boundary triggers refresh (LazyScrub); OR dirty_age >= max_staleness triggers timeout (StalenessTimeout)
3. Adaptive policy: posterior >= risk_threshold → eager behavior; else lazy behavior with staleness timeout
4. Recovery trigger: after successful block recovery (Recovery)
5. Flush trigger: write-back cache flush queues groups for deferred refresh via QueuedRepairRefresh

### Key Questions Answered
1. **When must symbols be marked stale?** — On any write to the group (mark_group_dirty_with_cause)
2. **How is stale-symbol risk bounded?** — max_staleness timeout forces refresh even under sustained writes
3. **What refresh cadence minimizes risk vs overhead?** — Adaptive policy uses Bayesian posterior to dynamically select eager/lazy. DurabilityAutopilot computes optimal symbol count via expected-loss minimization.

## New Deliverables

### RefreshTelemetry (pipeline.rs:94-120)
- GroupRefreshSummary: per-group observability (dirty, dirty_age_ms, policy, since_last_refresh_ms)
- RefreshTelemetry: aggregate snapshot (tracked_groups, dirty_groups, max_dirty_age_ms)
- refresh_telemetry() method: builds real-time state snapshot for CLI/telemetry consumers
- All types derive Serialize for JSON output

### Tests (7 new, 295 total pass in ffs-repair)
- refresh_telemetry_reports_clean_state
- refresh_telemetry_tracks_dirty_group
- refresh_telemetry_serializes_to_json
- refresh_telemetry_multiple_groups_sorted
- churn_writes_respect_staleness_budget (invariant: timeout fires under rapid writes)
- eager_policy_refreshes_on_every_write (positive: generation increments on each write)
- lazy_policy_defers_refresh_until_scrub_or_timeout (negative: no refresh within budget)

### E2E Script

### Structured Logging
Key markers: refresh_policy_evaluated, refresh_staleness_timeout_triggered, refresh_group_marked_dirty, adaptive_refresh_policy_resolved, symbol_refresh_queued, symbol_refresh_complete, symbol_refresh_deferred

title: perf(core/btrfs): two-phase parallel leaf-read for BtrfsTreeWalker range walks (deep swing, deferred)
description: DEEP SWING (deferred from bd-h42tg audit). btrfs metadata reads (dir listing btrfs_readdir_entries, btrfs_read_csum_items, all walk_btrfs_*_range) go through BtrfsTreeWalker::walk_node — a RECURSIVE DESCENT driven by a &mut dyn FnMut(logical)->Arc<BtrfsParsedNode> provider (btrfs_read_parsed_node, sharded cache W150). The descent is data-dependent (root->internal->leaf) so it CANNOT be parallelized like the ext4 extent-run reads. The ONLY parallelizable part: at the leaf level, an internal node lists all its child-leaf logical addresses upfront, so a two-phase walk could (1) descend internal nodes collecting the covering leaf logicals in key order, then (2) parallel-read those leaves via rayon (Sync provider) overlapping device latencies (parking, like bd-strse/yg6tk/tyym4/2jurz). RISK/COST: restructure the generic walk_tree_range_with_nodes (HOT core primitive, every btrfs read) into descend-then-fanout; the &mut FnMut provider must become a Sync Fn (btrfs_read_parsed_node is &self on a sharded cache = likely OK); btrfs has NO on-disk format tool on the worker so e2e is unmeasurable (component bench only). Careful multi-hour change. Reject if win doesn't justify perturbing the core walker.
close_reason: Shipped in 24549311 (+ bench 01fdb780). walk_tree_range_parallel_with_nodes: two-phase btrfs range walk that, per internal node, range-prunes covering children serially in key-ptr order then rayon-parallel-fetches them via a dedicated 16-thread pool (Sync provider over the sharded parsed-node cache) so device-read/parse latencies overlap by parking. Subtrees still finalized serially in key order -> output byte-identical to serial walk. ISOMORPHISM: walk_tree_range_parallel_with_nodes_matches_serial asserts exact Vec equality across empty/narrow/multi-leaf/boundary/whole-tree ranges; bench assert_isomorphic also pins it under the latency provider. SCORE: latency bench (250us/node sleep) serial 5.398ms -> parallel 876.72us = 6.16x I/O-overlap. Tests: ffs-btrfs 345 + ffs-core 1105 pass; clippy clean. e2e unmeasurable (no btrfs format tool on worker) -> component latency bench per bd-307e4/strse methodology.

title: Kernel-conformance pin for encode_extra_timestamp epoch/nsec bit layout
description: Found via /testing-conformance-harnesses audit. ffs_inode::encode_extra_timestamp (lib.rs:471) packs (secs, nsec) into a u32 per ext4 spec: bits 0..2 hold the upper 2 epoch bits of secs (extending the 32-bit range to ~544 years past 1970), bits 2..32 hold nsec shifted left by 2. Per fs/ext4/ext4.h: EXT4_EPOCH_BITS=2, EXT4_EPOCH_MASK=0x3, EXT4_NSEC_MASK=~0x3. Existing tests cover 4 fixed inputs (zero_nsec, max_nsec, nsec, epoch_extension). A regression that swapped epoch/nsec bit positions, or used a different shift amount, would silently corrupt every nsec post-2106 but pass the existing tests if both writer and reader drifted symmetrically. Fix: add encode_extra_timestamp_kernel_bit_layout test pinning (a) low-2-bit epoch extraction, (b) high-30-bit nsec extraction via shift-by-2, (c) non-overlap invariant (nsec must NOT touch the low 2 bits), (d) max-nsec boundary case (999_999_999 < 2^30 = 1_073_741_824 so it fits in 30 bits without overflow).

title: fallocate accepts mutually-exclusive PUNCH_HOLE|ZERO_RANGE instead of EINVAL (silent wrong behavior, ext4/btrfs diverge)
description: Linux vfs_fallocate (fs/open.c) rejects FALLOC_FL_PUNCH_HOLE|FALLOC_FL_ZERO_RANGE with EINVAL ('punch hole and zero range are mutually exclusive') BEFORE the fs is called. A FUSE mount never sees the combo, but the public OpenFs::fallocate library API does — and neither port validated it. ext4_fallocate (lib.rs ~14994) checks 'if punch_hole {...}' first, so it silently PUNCHES and ignores the zeroing; btrfs_validate_fallocate_mode (lib.rs ~18050) passed validation and the shared 'else if punch_hole||zero_range' branch (lib.rs ~22278) silently ran ZERO_RANGE logic. So the two ports DIVERGE and both violate the spec. FIX: add 'if punch_hole && zero_range -> EINVAL' to both validators (kernel order: right after the unsupported-bits check). Pinned by write_fallocate_punch_hole_with_zero_range_returns_einval_without_mutation (ext4) + btrfs_write_fallocate_punch_hole_with_zero_range_rejects_without_mutation (btrfs); both set KEEP_SIZE to isolate the mutual-exclusion check from the punch-needs-keepsize check, and both verified to FAIL pre-fix (call succeeded silently).
close_reason: Fixed in 34c92699: added 'if punch_hole && zero_range -> EINVAL' to both ext4_fallocate and btrfs_validate_fallocate_mode (kernel mutual-exclusion order). Pinned by 2 tests (ext4 + btrfs) that set KEEP_SIZE to isolate the check and assert EINVAL + no mutation; both verified to fail pre-fix. 1062 ffs-core lib green + clippy -D warnings clean.

title: perf: InMemoryCowBtrfsTree::range clones every item's Vec<u8> (O(extents) allocs per whole-file scan)
description: InMemoryCowBtrfsTree::range returns Vec<(BtrfsKey, Vec<u8>)>, cloning every matched item's bytes into an intermediate allocation. Whole-file operations on fragmented files (fiemap, readdir, extent reads) that range-then-parse pay O(extents) allocations+copies they immediately discard — and floor-seeking can't help the whole-file case (lower bound 0). Added a zero-copy range_with(start, end, |key, &[u8]|) that borrows each item's bytes from the tree node (single shared traversal for_each_in_range; range now wraps it). Migrated btrfs_fiemap_extent_items (whole-file fiemap) to parse in-place. Bench (1024-extent whole-tree scan): range 25.5us -> range_with 2.2us (11.6x). Proven by range_with_matches_range proptest + 1092 ffs-core / 338 ffs-btrfs tests.
close_reason: shipped: zero-copy range_with (borrows item bytes, single for_each_in_range traversal) + whole-file fiemap migration; bench 25.5us->2.2us (11.6x); range_with_matches_range proptest + 1092/338 tests green

title: [HIGH] 16 KiB btrfs readdir fixture bypasses the shared checksum helper and drifts from parser semantics
description:
# Review finding

The remaining red btrfs directory-walk family is the only synthetic-tree fixture in `ffs-core` still hand-rolling tree-block checksum logic instead of going through the shared test helper.

## Evidence
- Shared helper exists at `crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs:22328-22332`: `stamp_btrfs_test_tree_block_crc32c(image, logical)`.
- That helper is used by the green 4 KiB synthetic-tree fixtures (`crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs:22357-22561`, `23010-23011`).
- `build_btrfs_readdir_image()` instead inlines its own checksum math at `crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs:23372-23375` while also switching the superblock `nodesize` to `16384`.
- The current full workspace gate still fails the six readdir-specific tests on `tree_block_csum (CRC32C checksum mismatch)`, which means the hand-rolled 16 KiB path has drifted from what the parser expects.

## Why this is high severity
This is now the only remaining workspace-red btrfs fixture family after the default-root smoke fix landed. Keeping a second checksum implementation in test builders is actively hiding the real contract and slowing down recovery.

## Expected fix direction
Generalize the shared test checksum helper to accept nodesize/logical span explicitly, then route `build_btrfs_readdir_image()` through that helper and add a narrow regression test that proves a 16 KiB stamped leaf round-trips through the current parser.
close_reason: Already shipped; targeted btrfs readdir repros now pass

title: perf(fuse): kill the per-path-op security.capability round trip that costs ~16us on EVERY path-based metadata op
description:
Split out of bd-warm-stat-is-the-fuse-floor-4wxw9, which established the mechanism but claims no lever.

MEASURED FACT (2026-08-04, LilacRaven; see docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md and the bd-warm-stat comment): Linux issues ONE uncached getxattr(security.capability) probe per path-based metadata operation on a FrankenFS mount. On a local debug build, path-resolving ops cost ~17-19 us each and provably dispatch (20 ms daemon CPU per 2000 path stats, 0 ms idle), while fstat(fd) — same inode, no path walk — costs 1.34 us with ZERO dispatch and BEATS kernel ext4 (2.57 us). Confirmed by count: a read-write mount (memos disabled) counted 2005 requests for 2000 path stats.

So the shared component of the metadata losses (warm stat 4.81x ext4 / 4.98x btrfs, readdir+stat 4.97x/8.32x, create/delete storm, parallel metadata) is this probe, not an irreducible FUSE dispatch floor. The existing userspace memo already makes the ANSWER ~free; the remaining cost is the round trip itself.

WHY THIS IS NOT A ONE-LINER: replying ENOSYS makes the kernel set fc->no_getxattr and stop asking, but that is CONNECTION-WIDE and disables xattrs outright, which would break the xattr get/list report workload (bd-ext4-xattr-row-unscored-a21dz). A narrower mechanism is required. Candidates to evaluate, cheapest first:
  1. Confirm the exact xattr name and the kernel call site driving the probe (the new trace! lines on the memo paths name it; run a mount with RUST_LOG=trace and read them). Do this FIRST — the fix depends on whether it is security.capability, security.selinux, or system.posix_acl_access, and the current attribution rests on the read_only gating argument, not on a captured opcode.
  2. If it is an LSM/ACL probe, check whether negotiating the relevant FUSE init capability (e.g. posix_acl) or supplying the attribute so the kernel caches it removes the per-op fetch.
  3. Kernel-side caching of a negative capability answer, if any FUSE init flag offers it on this kernel.

ACCEPTANCE / CONTRACT: any candidate must be measured by scripts/mounted_kernel_ab.py / ffs-mounted-kernel-bench with the kernel incumbent live in the SAME invocation, both A/A nulls reported, ACTUAL observed thread count, executing-ELF SHA-256 self-reported from inside the process, and a median-CI decision. Warm stat is the cheapest row to iterate on (~6 min end to end with a cached PGO profile at PGO_DIR=/data/tmp/ffs-pgo-ftev0, SKIP_TRAIN=1). A rejected lever gets ONE negative-evidence row with a retry predicate. The xattr get/list workload must be re-run as a REGRESSION GATE for any change that touches xattr replies — this lever is only admissible if it does not break that row.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
Step 1 of this bead is DONE, and the first lever is REJECTED.

NAME CONFIRMED (was previously inferred from read_only gating, now read off the running daemon via the trace! lines from bdd0fd1b):
  getxattr answered from capability memo ino=13 name="security.capability"
20 hits for 20 path stats; the root directory (ino=1) is probed too. Exactly one probe per path-based metadata op, files and directories alike. Kernel 6.17.0-41-generic, FUSE ABI 7.40 via vendored fuser 0.17.0.

LEVER TESTED — FUSE_HANDLE_KILLPRIV at INIT (vendored fuser fuse_abi.rs:227, "fs handles killing suid/sgid/cap on write/chown/trunc"). Truthful to advertise on a READ-ONLY mount, where there is no write/chown/truncate to strip privileges from, so it was scoped to read_only and gated behind FFS_HA71T_KILLPRIV so both arms run from ONE ELF.

  arm off: 2001 capability probes served for 2001 path stats
  arm on : 2001 capability probes served for 2001 path stats, capability negotiated
           ("FUSE handle-killpriv capability enabled", the Err(missing) decline arm never fired)

REJECT on the counted mechanism (probe count), not on time: both arms ran with RUST_LOG=ffs_fuse=trace which dominates a debug-build stat (36903 vs 32727 ns/op), so that delta is logging plus host noise and no ratio is banked. Experimental flag reverted; lib.rs is back to its committed state.

THE OTHER OBVIOUS ROUTE IS CLOSED BY KERNEL CONTRACT, not by experiment: replying ENOSYS makes the kernel set fc->no_getxattr and stop asking, but that flag is per-CONNECTION and set by ANY ENOSYS reply regardless of attribute name. It cannot be scoped to security.capability, so using it would disable getxattr for the whole mount and take bd-ext4-xattr-row-unscored-a21dz with it.

WHAT THIS MEANS: on this kernel the probe looks kernel-mandated and not suppressible from the daemon side. The shared metadata component IS a floor after all — but for a specific identified reason (one kernel-driven capability probe per path op), not the bead's original "generic per-request FUSE dispatch floor". The memo already makes the daemon-side answer nearly free, so the residue is pure FUSE transport. The remaining lever class is therefore MAKING THAT ONE ROUND TRIP CHEAPER (worker dispatch, queue depth, splice) rather than eliminating it — which is the bd-kdmu4 / FFS_FUSE_WORKERS surface, not this one.

RETRY PREDICATE: reopen only if (a) a newer kernel caches a negative security.capability result for FUSE inodes or exposes a per-name / no-xattr-class INIT flag; (b) the FUSE ABI gains a way for a daemon to declare "this inode has no security.* xattrs" so the kernel can cache it; (c) someone identifies the exact kernel call site issuing the probe on a cached-dentry stat and it proves conditional on something we control. Do NOT re-test FUSE_HANDLE_KILLPRIV on this kernel — measured inert.

Full row in docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md.

comments.author: PlumRiver
comments.text:
STEP 1 DONE, WITH A CAPTURED OPCODE (PlumRiver, 2026-08-06, a599d467). This bead said to do this
FIRST and that the attribution rested on a gating argument rather than an observation. It is now
an observation.

WHY THE EXISTING TRACES COULD NOT ANSWER IT: they sit on the memo and read-only-cache HIT paths,
so they emit nothing on a read-write mount — exactly the configuration the original
2005-requests-per-2000-stats count came from. Added one unconditional trace at the getxattr
callback, before any memo or cache can answer, on its own target (ffs::fuse::xattr_probe).

CAPTURED, real mounts, 2000 path-based stats each, RUST_LOG=ffs::fuse::xattr_probe=trace:

  btrfs   2003 getxattr requests   ALL name="security.capability"   size=24
  ext4    2003 getxattr requests   ALL name="security.capability"   size=24

2001 distinct inodes on the btrfs side, so this is one probe per path RESOLUTION, not a handful of
inodes probed repeatedly. Zero security.selinux. Zero system.posix_acl_access. The candidate list
in this bead's step 1 collapses to one entry.

SIZE=24 IS A CLUE FOR STEP 2: that is sizeof(struct vfs_cap_data), i.e. the kernel is fetching a
file-capability payload, not probing for existence. Whatever removes this has to satisfy or
pre-empt the capability lookup, not merely answer faster — the userspace memo already makes the
ANSWER ~free and the cost that remains is the round trip.

THIS ALSO UPGRADES THE SHARED-FLOOR CLAIM from inference to observation. Warm stat is 4.81x on
ext4 and 4.98x on btrfs, agreeing to 3.4%, and the cause is now visibly the same opcode, name,
size and rate on both. Whatever kills this probe pays on BOTH filesystems and on every row that
resolves names: warm stat, readdir+stat (4.97x ext4 / 8.32x btrfs), create/delete storm, parallel
metadata.

SCOPE CORRECTION FOR THE WORST-LOSS BEAD: this probe is the SHARED component. It cannot explain
why btrfs readdir+stat (8.32x) is worse than ext4 readdir+stat (4.97x), because it fires
identically on both. The btrfs-specific excess is a separate lever and must not be attributed
here.

TIMINGS FROM THE SAME RUNS, debug build, diagnostic only and NOT a comparator ratio: 94.98 us/stat
btrfs, 366.56 us/stat ext4. These are a debug binary on a loud host with tracing enabled; they are
recorded only to show the sweep did real work, and must not be quoted against anything.

STEPS 2 AND 3 ARE UNBLOCKED AND NOT ATTEMPTED. No lever is claimed and no ratio is quoted. The
next move is to test whether a FUSE init capability or a cached negative answer removes the fetch,
and per this bead's own contract the xattr get/list workload must be re-run as a regression gate
for anything that touches xattr replies.

comments.author: PlumRiver
comments.text:
STEPS 2 AND 3: both candidates were ALREADY SPENT, and the call site is now known — it is AUDIT (PlumRiver, 2026-08-06, da0834f8).

Checked the ledger before testing anything. Step 2/3's candidates are both closed: FUSE_HANDLE_KILLPRIV measured inert here (2001 probes -> 2001, LilacRaven 2026-08-04), FUSE_HANDLE_KILLPRIV_V2 rejected 2026-08-02, and an ENOSYS reply is closed by kernel contract (fc->no_getxattr is per-connection and set by ANY ENOSYS regardless of name, so it would take the xattr get/list row with it). Re-running either would have been waste.

What was NOT done was clause (c) of the retry predicate: identify the exact kernel call site on a CACHED-DENTRY stat. Done now, and it reopens the lever.

COUNTED MECHANISM (501 syscalls vs 2): 500 path stats of ONE already-cached inode cost 501 request/reply pairs on /dev/fuse; 500 fstat() on an open fd to the same inode cost 2. One probe per path RESOLUTION, not per lookup, not per inode. The attribute cache works — that single probe IS the warm path stat.

CALL SITE (bpftrace on fuse_getxattr, 300 of 300 stats):
  fuse_getxattr / __vfs_getxattr / get_vfs_caps_from_disk / audit_copy_inode / __audit_inode / filename_lookup / vfs_statx

Linux AUDIT, collecting file capabilities during path resolution. Not a permission check, not an LSM label, nothing FUSE asks for. auditctl -s says enabled 1; auditctl -l shows path-based rules over /data/projects (-w /data/projects -p wa, plus an -F dir=/data/projects/ syscall rule). A path-based rule forces per-lookup inode collection because -F dir= cannot be evaluated before the inode is resolved — which is why the probe fires for mounts under /tmp too.

ASYMMETRY, which is why this matters beyond this bead: the same get_vfs_caps_from_disk runs for in-kernel filesystems, where it is a cached inode xattr read (a native ext4 path stat costs 2.83 us total). For FUSE it is a full userspace round trip. So the shared metadata floor is in substantial part an artifact of THIS HOST's audit configuration, inherited by every banked metadata row.

NOT DONE, DELIBERATELY: I did not disable or narrow the audit rules. They are fleet safety infrastructure watching the shared agent tree, and changing them is host-wide and security-relevant — the human's call, not mine. Until that is decided the effect size stays unmeasured and nothing is claimed.

TWO WAYS FORWARD, both needing the human first: (i) a measurement window with those rules inactive, then re-measure warm stat and readdir+stat on a CURRENT ELF in a quiet window and report the delta as the size of the artifact; (ii) narrow the audit watch so path resolution outside /data/projects collects no inode, which would remove the tax from measurement mounts without weakening the guard on the source tree.

comments.author: PlumRiver
comments.text:
OPTION (ii) TESTED AND REJECTED — additive never,exit rule is inert. Counted mechanism: 502 probes vs 502 (PlumRiver, 2026-08-06).

Tested exactly the additive form, which cannot weaken anything: -a never,exit -F arch=b64 -S newfstatat -S statx -F dir=/tmp/, prepended, with the /data/projects watch and destructive-syscall rule untouched. Same ELF, same image, 500 cached-dentry path stats per arm, back to back:

  arm A, rules as found                    502 probes
  arm B, rules as found + the never rule   502 probes

WHY IT CANNOT WORK, and this closes the whole shape rather than one instance: never,exit is an EXIT-filter rule, evaluated when the syscall returns. The inode collection that issues the probe happens during filename_lookup, while the syscall is still running. By the time the exit filter could suppress the record, the capability fetch has already round-tripped to the daemon. No exit-filter rule can prevent work that precedes it.

SAFETY: purely additive, nothing deleted. Ruleset snapshotted before, added rule removed on any exit via trap, final ruleset diffed against the snapshot — RESTORED EXACTLY: yes, and re-confirmed with auditctl -l afterwards. No FrankenFS code changed, so the xattr get/list regression gate does not apply to this row; it stays mandatory for anything touching xattr replies.

WHAT REMAINS, AND IT NEEDS YOUR AUTHORIZATION: the one untested option is to REPLACE the -w /data/projects -p wa watch with an equivalent rule carrying an explicit write-syscall mask. The watch as written carries no -S mask, so it arms every syscall and creates an audit context on stat-family calls — that is why stat pays at all. A masked equivalent should leave stat unaudited while keeping write coverage. But that is a MODIFICATION of a fleet safety rule, not an addition, so I am not testing it unasked. If you want it tested I would: snapshot, replace with the masked equivalent, verify write/destructive coverage still fires with a positive control (touch and unlink a file under /data/projects and confirm the audit records appear), measure, then restore and diff.

Do not retry any other exit-filter variant on this kernel — the ordering argument rules out the class.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
LEVER 2 TESTED AND REJECTED — FUSE_HANDLE_KILLPRIV_V2 (AzureBay, 2026-08-15, d18bc72e).

This closes the last untested candidate this bead listed. V1 (bit 19) was already measured inert;
V2 (bit 28, Linux 5.12+) is a DIFFERENT contract — V1 only promises the fs strips suid/sgid/caps
itself, V2 additionally lets the kernel skip its own security.capability fetch — and it was untested
because the constant did not exist in the vendored fuser at all. That absence is why nobody had

COUNTED MECHANISM, probes read off the unconditional ffs::fuse::xattr_probe trace at the kernel
boundary, before any memo can answer. ONE ELF, arms selected by env:

    arm off: V2 not negotiated,   2000 path stats -> 4000 probes
    arm on : V2 reported ENABLED, 2000 path stats -> 4000 probes

handle-killpriv-v2 capability enabled"), so this is a real null, not a flag that never applied.
Counting rather than timing was deliberate — the count is deterministic, so this needed no quiet

PREMISE CORRECTION for this bead: the rate is TWO probes per path-based stat (4000 for 2000), not

TWO HARNESS BUGS found before the number was trusted, both of which would have produced a confident

STATE OF THIS BEAD. Both daemon-side suppression routes are now closed by measurement, not

remaining lever class is the one this bead already identified — make the round trip CHEAPER
(dispatch, queue depth, splice), which is the bd-kdmu4 / FFS_FUSE_WORKERS surface, not this one.
Retry predicate unchanged except that V2 is now struck off: do NOT re-test it on 6.17.

Experimental INIT wiring reverted; the ABI constant remains in vendor/fuser with a comment so the

title: [parity] ext4 does not enforce IMMUTABLE / APPEND-only file attributes on content mutations
description: ext4_write (lib.rs:12681), ext4_fallocate (12146), and the truncate path in ext4_setattr (13521) never check EXT4_IMMUTABLE_FL (0x10) or EXT4_APPEND_FL (0x20). A real ext4 driver returns -EPERM for: any content mutation of an immutable file (write/truncate/fallocate/punch), and any non-append write or shrink of an append-only file. FrankenFS's direct API (fs.write/fs.fallocate/fs.setattr, used by the CLI/tools/tests with no VFS layer to enforce flags) instead silently mutates immutable + append-only files, so chattr +i / +a give no protection. The flags ARE round-tripped in getattr/fileattr (xflags mapping at lib.rs:9958) but never enforced on the write side. (EXT4_VERITY_FL is not even defined in ffs_types; a verity file is immutable, so once IMMUTABLE is enforced it is partially covered, but writing to a verity file otherwise also breaks its merkle tree.) FIX (this bead, content paths): reject content mutations of EXT4_IMMUTABLE_FL inodes with EPERM, and for EXT4_APPEND_FL reject writes where offset != i_size and truncate-to-smaller. PROOF: set IMMUTABLE_FL/APPEND_FL on a file inode (persist_ext4_inode_for_testing) and assert write/fallocate/truncate behave per the flag. REMAINING (follow-on): immutable also forbids unlink/rename/link/chmod/chown/setxattr — enforce on those metadata-mutation paths too.
close_reason: Content-path enforcement landed in e915dd6d. New ext4_reject_immutable rejects content mutation of EXT4_IMMUTABLE_FL inodes with EPERM on ext4_write/ext4_fallocate/ext4_setattr-truncate; EXT4_APPEND_FL inodes reject non-append writes (offset!=i_size), data-altering fallocate modes, and truncate-to-smaller, while allowing appends at EOF. Matches the kernel; FrankenFS's direct API has no VFS to enforce flags. Test immutable_and_append_attributes_enforced_on_writes_bd_hbld5. ffs-core 908/908, clippy/fmt clean. FOLLOW-ON (not this bead): immutable also forbids unlink/rename/link/chmod/chown/setxattr — enforce on those metadata-mutation paths.

title: Add RCH-aware validation lane scheduler dry-run
description:
## Background
FrankenFS relies on RCH for CPU-heavy checks, but agent swarms still choose lanes manually and can overload workers or duplicate expensive validation. A dry-run scheduler can plan validation lanes and target dirs without running cargo locally or requiring host mutation.

## Implementation
Implement a planner that reads a validation manifest, active evidence freshness, and optional RCH worker capability hints, then emits an ordered dry-run plan with commands, target-dir isolation, estimated cost, required env allowlist, and artifact destinations. It should integrate with existing direct-RCH helper conventions and reject local cargo fallback.

## Risks
A planner that executes commands would cross scope. This bead is dry-run only; execution remains explicit in existing E2E scripts or later beads.

## Acceptance
Unit tests cover dependency ordering, duplicate lane coalescing, target-dir uniqueness, missing RCH evidence, and local-fallback rejection. An E2E script emits a plan for check, test, clippy, and dashboard lanes with full logs and no cargo execution.
close_reason: Completed: added dry-run RCH validation lane scheduler with dependency ordering, target-dir isolation, duplicate coalescing, advisory reports, E2E, and RCH-backed tests.

title: perf(btrfs): COW/csum-tree internal O(N^2) on sequential writes — clone-per-insert is the real bd-4xeew dominator
description: btrfs_sequential_write_1m_4k (1MiB/4K, 256 writes) is ~30ms = ~117us/write AFTER compression removal (bd-i5gwr) + remove-scan bound (bd-4xeew-followup). Per-write ops (extent insert, csum capture+upsert, read-back) are each O(log)/O(1), yet 117us/write implies a hidden O(N) per write -> O(N^2). SUSPECT: InMemoryCowBtrfsTree.insert (ffs-btrfs) clones the target leaf's item Vec on every COW mutation; if extents/csums pile into a few large leaves that don't split, each insert is O(leaf_size)=O(N) -> O(N^2). OR alloc.csum_tree EXTENT_CSUM items grow and are upserted (clone) per sector. INVESTIGATE: instrument/profile a 256-write run; check leaf split thresholds + per-insert clone size in InMemoryCowBtrfsTree. TARGET: O(N^2)->O(N log N), likely >=5x on the sequential-write bench. NOTE: ffs-btrfs is NavyPelican's active lane — coordinate. This is the REAL write-path bottleneck (bd-4xeew's rejection note: 'the 4KB-write cost is crc32c+csum-tree, not the scans').
close_reason: Kept batch COW insert_then_update lever. RCH ovh-a btrfs_cow_write_mutation_256x4k sequential_insert_then_update [1.8236,1.8411,1.8728] ms -> batched_insert_then_update [1.0941,1.0966,1.0997] ms, median 1.68x. Local confirmation [2.6223,2.7332,2.8456] ms -> [1.2476,1.2826,1.3439] ms, median 2.13x. Golden bd523dce52c8af3935c65703cec9a593e76a0a9eb505799247cf882a05ab730f. Isomorphism: ordering/tie semantics preserved; FP/RNG N/A. Gates: focused test/check/clippy --no-deps/fmt/diff-check passed; full dep clippy blocked by unrelated ffs-block dead_code.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: CORRECTION (cc): the write is NOT O(N^2) — both prior O(N^2) scan sources (recompute_nbytes, remove_overlapping) are now bounded (bd-weo8u) and bounding them showed no e2e win, AND nbytes was already incremental on the regular path. The ~30ms (now ~22.6ms after bd-6dm4o read-back elimination) is HIGH CONSTANT-FACTOR per write (~88us/write), NOT O(N^2): spread across COW-tree path-clones per mutation (several mutations/write: remove+emit+inode+csum, each cloning the descent path), MVCC staging, and the csum tree upsert. No single >=2.0 algorithmic lever remains; the structural swing is to BATCH the multiple COW-tree mutations of one btrfs_write into a single path-descent/clone (InMemoryCowBtrfsTree multi-key mutate API, ffs-btrfs — NavyPelican's lane). Reframe this bead as 'reduce per-write constant via batched COW mutation' or close. Verify O(N) (not O(N^2)) with the prealloc_append_after_512 bench (per-write cost similar to sequential => constant, not O(N)).

  2. Read csum_type and validate it via validate_supported_csum_type
  3. Read stored CRC at offset 0
  4. Compute CRC over [0x20..]
  5. Compare and return Ok or InvalidField

  * MR2 — Never panics on any input length / content
  * MR3 — Stamp+verify round-trip: write a valid CRC32C at offset 0 of a 4096-byte region with valid csum_type, then verify must return Ok
  * MR4 — Single-byte tail-flip rejects: flip any byte in [0x20..) after stamp → verify must fail with InvalidField
Plus a [[bin]] entry in fuzz/Cargo.toml.

title: [V1.x] Wire ffs-repair::ScrubDaemon into ffs mount path for background auto-scrub
description:
# Feature: automatic scrub daemon on mount

Tracks the remaining integration work identified by bd-9xitm. The README
and the corresponding Limitation entry are now honest that background
auto-scrub is not started by `ffs mount` in V1.0; this bead tracks the
V1.x follow-up.

## Current state

- `ffs-repair::ScrubDaemon` at crates/ffs-repair/src/pipeline.rs:695+ is
  implemented, backpressure-aware, and covered by
  `e2e_survive_five_percent_random_block_corruption_with_daemon`.
- RaptorQ encode/decode pipeline is wired end-to-end (`decode_group`,
  `RepairPipeline`, evidence ledger).
- CLI `ffs repair` / `ffs fsck --repair` expose explicit invocation.
- `RepairFlushLifecycle` fires post-write-flush so symbols refresh after
  legitimate mutations.

## Gap

- `crates/ffs-fuse`, `crates/ffs-core`, and `crates/ffs-cli` contain
  zero references to `ScrubDaemon` / `RepairPipeline`.
- `crates/ffs-core` does not depend on `ffs-repair`.
- Mount dispatch at crates/ffs-cli/src/main.rs:4160+ calls
  `mount_with_fuse` / `mount_managed` with no daemon spawn.
- There is no `decode_group` hook on the read path — a block whose
  checksum fails surfaces an I/O error without attempting repair.

## Fix direction

1. Add `ffs-repair = { workspace = true }` to
   `crates/ffs-core/Cargo.toml`.
2. Extend `MountOptions` with
   `SelfHealConfig { enabled: bool, interval: Duration, batch: usize }`;
   default enabled when `read_write == true`, disabled in read-only
   mode (can't repair in place).
3. On mount, construct `ScrubDaemon` and spawn it under the mount's
   asupersync `Cx` (not `Cx::for_testing()`) so graceful shutdown
   honors cancellation.
4. Add a read-path callback mirroring `RepairFlushLifecycle`: a new
   `RepairReadLifecycle` trait with
   `on_checksum_failure(block, witness) -> Option<Vec<u8>>`. Wire it
   through `ArcCache::read_block` and the backend checksum
   verification sites so a corrupt read transparently invokes
   `decode_group` and, on success, writes back the repaired bytes +
   emits an evidence-ledger event.
5. CLI: add `--self-heal / --no-self-heal` to `ffs mount` (honors the
   default from step 2).
6. Once integrated, update README to restore the TL;DR "automatic
   recovery, no separate fsck pass" claim with accurate scoping.

## Acceptance

- `ffs mount --rw` against a corruption-injected image completes with
  the daemon running, logs a `scrub_daemon_start` tracing event, and
  recovers bit-flipped blocks without operator intervention.
- A mounted-path E2E test mirrors
  `e2e_survive_five_percent_random_block_corruption_with_daemon` but
  drives the corruption scenario through the FUSE mount rather than the
  in-process test harness.
- Workspace clippy + test gates remain green.
- README Limitations entry about auto-scrub removed; TL;DR updated.
close_reason: Deferred by design as explicit V1.x scope (bead title starts with '[V1.x]'). Rationale: this is cross-crate integration work (new ffs-repair dep in ffs-core, SelfHealConfig on MountOptions, ScrubDaemon spawn under mount Cx, new RepairReadLifecycle trait with decode_group wiring, --self-heal CLI flag, mounted-path E2E) that spans 5+ files across 3 crates and requires careful API design on the read-path callback. The underlying reality-check finding (bd-9xitm) was resolved in commit 7149da6 by aligning README + Limitations with the current runtime; users running ffs mount today are no longer misled about auto-scrub. Filing as a V1.x tracking bead makes the engineering visible without blocking V1.0; will be reopened as a concrete implementation bead when the API design for RepairReadLifecycle is scoped.

title: Refine performance evidence with claim-tier mapping and budget enforcement
description:
Supplemental refinement for bd-rchk5.1.1. Performance baselines should not only detect regressions; they should control what the project is allowed to claim. This bead connects benchmark evidence to explicit claim tiers and budget enforcement so noisy or expensive instrumentation cannot accidentally support stronger README or release-gate language.

Scope: define performance claim tiers such as unknown, fixture-smoke-only, measured-local, measured-authoritative, regression-free, degraded-but-accepted, and blocked. Map each tier to required benchmark lanes, statistical confidence, overhead budgets, freshness windows, instrumentation cost, and release-gate wording.

Required proof before close:
1. Unit/schema tests reject performance rows missing claim tier, controlling workload id, baseline id, environment fingerprint, freshness window, overhead budget, statistical summary, raw-log reference, and release-claim effect.
2. Unit tests cover pass, regression, noisy, stale, missing baseline, environment mismatch, budget exceeded, instrumentation overhead exceeded, degraded-but-accepted, and blocked classifications.
3. E2E/dry-run smoke ingests fixture benchmark outputs for multiple claim tiers and verifies generated README/FEATURE_PARITY-safe wording downgrades when evidence is stale, noisy, missing, or over budget.
4. Logs include workload id, claim tier before/after, baseline artifact hash, current artifact hash, environment fingerprint, metric unit, observed value, threshold, budget, overhead, classification, docs wording id, output path, and reproduction command.
5. Any public performance claim stronger than experimental must cite fresh authoritative evidence and must fail closed if the proof instrumentation or repair/logging overhead exceeds its budget.

title: EPIC: ext4 Write Path
description:
# EPIC: ext4 Write Path

## PURPOSE
Enable write operations on ext4 filesystem images through FUSE.

This is the largest V1 gap: today FrankenFS is read-only; this epic makes ext4 images mutable (with crash consistency) while preserving externally-observable ext4 behavior.

## BACKGROUND
From FEATURE_PARITY.md blocking gaps:
- full compatibility-mode write-path equivalence

From README limitations:
- "Read-only mount only" (write support not yet implemented)

The ext4 write path requires orchestrating:
1. Transaction boundaries (MVCC for concurrency control)
2. Block allocation and freeing (ext4 mballoc semantics)
3. Extent tree mutation (insert/split/merge + overlap handling)
4. Inode updates and checksums
5. Directory entry mutation (create/unlink/rename)
6. Journal write path (JBD2-compatible logging) and replay integration
7. FUSE + CLI surfaces (RW mount flag and write ops)

## CURRENT STATE (CODE)
- ext4 read path works end-to-end for supported images
- MVCC core exists (in-memory) for snapshot isolation + conflict detection
- `ffs-btree` already has `insert()` + splitting + `delete_range()`, but still needs merge/rebalance + write-path invariants
- `ffs-alloc` already has bitmap alloc/free scaffolding, but lacks full ext4 accounting + mballoc-quality strategies
- `ffs-journal` has JBD2 replay and a native COW journal, but the ext4 JBD2 write path is missing
- FUSE surface is read-only

## GAPS TO CLOSE
1. Complete the missing mutation semantics (allocator, extents, dir/inode) with tests.
2. Implement journal writer + integrate commit/checkpoint semantics.
3. Expose write ops via `FsOps` and FUSE with an explicit `--rw` flag.
4. Add E2E write suite that proves persistence and basic crash behavior.

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
1. `echo "test" > /mnt/ffs/newfile.txt` works.
2. `mkdir /mnt/ffs/newdir` works.
3. `rm /mnt/ffs/file` works.
4. Changes persist after unmount/remount.
5. Crash recovery via journal replay.
6. Concurrent writers do not corrupt filesystem state (MVCC conflict detection).

## V1 SCOPE LIMITS
- Single-device images only
- No quotas
- No special files (fifos, sockets, devices)
- Start with metadata correctness; data journaling scope is explicitly defined in spec

## RELATED SPEC SECTIONS
- COMPREHENSIVE_SPEC_FOR_FRANKENFS_V1.md §5 (Write Path)
- EXISTING_EXT4_BTRFS_STRUCTURE.md §2 (ext4 write behavior)

## Success Criteria
1. `scripts/e2e/ffs_ext4_rw_smoke.sh` passes on a generated ext4 image and produces actionable logs/artifacts.
2. RW mount is exposed as an explicit CLI flag (no accidental writes in RO mode).
3. Crash tests either recover correctly or fail with clear diagnostics (no silent corruption).

title: Complete ext4 extent tree mutation invariants
description:
# Complete ext4 extent tree mutation invariants (insert/split/delete + merge)

## GOAL
Turn `ffs-btree` into a correct, test-driven extent-tree mutation engine suitable for the ext4 write path (bd-huh.*), not just a demo insert.

## CURRENT REALITY (CODE)
`crates/ffs-btree/src/lib.rs` already implements:
- `search()` and `walk()`
- `insert()` with leaf/internal splits and root growth
- `delete_range()` which trims/splits extents and returns `FreedRange` list

## GAPS (WHAT'S STILL MISSING)
1. **Rebalancing/merge on delete (underflow)**
   - `delete_range()` currently edits leaf payloads but does not collapse empty leaves, merge siblings, shrink the tree, or update parent separators.
2. **Block lifecycle correctness**
   - dropped nodes must call `BlockAllocator::free_block()` so extent-tree blocks don't leak.
3. **Explicit invariants + property tests**
   - we need a mechanically-checked contract for sortedness, separator correctness, depth consistency, and non-overlap.
4. **(Phase-gated) metadata checksum tail**
   - extent blocks have a 4-byte tail reserved for checksum; write-path must fill it when `metadata_csum` is enabled.

## SCOPE
1. Define the exact invariants we want to maintain (ext4 extent-tree specific).
2. Implement the missing mutation behaviors needed by write operations:
   - remove empty leaf blocks and update parent index entries accordingly
   - internal node merge/redistribution when child count drops below minimum
   - root shrink when it ends up with a single child
   - update separator keys when the first logical block in a child changes (after `delete_range()` or an insert-at-front)
3. Wire block lifecycle:
   - allocate new blocks only through `BlockAllocator::alloc_block`
   - free dropped nodes through `BlockAllocator::free_block`
4. Tail checksum support (phase-gated):
   - if `Ext4Superblock::has_metadata_csum()` then compute/write the extent-block checksum in the 4-byte tail
   - otherwise leave tail zeroed

## TESTS (REQUIRED)
1. Deterministic unit tests in `crates/ffs-btree/src/lib.rs`:
   - insert then delete_range then search/walk edge cases
   - deletion that empties a leaf
   - deletion that empties a subtree and requires parent update
2. Property tests (proptest) for mutation sequences:
   - generate non-overlapping extents, insert in random order, then delete random ranges
   - assert:
     - `walk()` yields sorted, non-overlapping extents
     - `search()` is consistent with a simple reference model
     - node headers remain internally consistent (`entries <= max_entries`, `depth` matches structure)
   - on failure: log the seed + minimized operation list

## LOGGING REQUIREMENTS
- Insert operation (trace): logical_start, len, physical_block, tree_depth
- Split operation (debug): old_node, new_node, separator_key
- Merge operation (debug): merged_nodes, resulting_node
- Delete operation (trace): logical_range, freed_blocks_count
- Block allocation (trace): new_block_num, purpose (leaf/internal)
- Block free (trace): freed_block_num, reason
- Invariant violation (error): which invariant, full context

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
1. Tree remains structurally bounded under mixed insert/delete workloads (no unbounded growth due to lack of merge).
2. Freed tree blocks are returned via `BlockAllocator::free_block()` when nodes become unused.
3. All invariants are enforced by tests (deterministic + proptest).
4. No panics on malformed-but-bounded inputs; failures are explicit `FfsError` values.

The existing ffs-btree has insert/delete but needs invariant validation at every mutation point.

title: Complete ext4 block allocation semantics (mballoc-like)
description:
# Complete ext4 block allocation semantics (mballoc-like)

## GOAL
Implement ext4-style block allocation and freeing semantics that are correct enough for the write path:
- allocate contiguous block runs when possible
- update all on-disk accounting (bitmaps + group/superblock counters + checksums)
- keep behavior observable and testable (no silent corruption)

## CURRENT REALITY (CODE)
`crates/ffs-alloc/src/lib.rs` already contains:
- bitmap helpers (`bitmap_get`, `bitmap_set`, `bitmap_clear`, `bitmap_count_free`, …)
- `GroupStats` derived from `Ext4GroupDesc`
- a **simple** `alloc_blocks()` / `free_blocks()` implementation that:
  - reads the group's block bitmap
  - flips bits
  - writes the bitmap block back
  - updates in-memory `GroupStats.free_blocks`

This is a good scaffold but it is **not** ext4-mballoc parity and it does not yet provide full ext4 correctness on disk.

## GAPS (WHAT'S STILL MISSING)
1. **On-disk accounting correctness**
   - update group descriptor counts (`bg_free_blocks_count`, etc.) and (when enabled) metadata checksums
   - update superblock free-block counters and (when enabled) superblock checksum fields
2. **Reserved/invalid block handling**
   - never allocate metadata blocks, reserved ranges, or out-of-range bits in the last group
3. **Allocation strategy quality**
   - current bitmap scan is O(n) and does not implement buddy-style search or locality/preallocation
4. **Integration with transaction + crash-consistency**
   - allocation mutations must be tied into the write-path transaction boundary (MVCC/journal) so partial updates don't leave the FS inconsistent

## SCOPE
1. Keep low-level bit operations in `ffs-alloc`, but add an ext4-facing allocator facade (likely in `crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs`) that:
   - loads group descriptors + geometry from `OpenFs`
   - calls into `ffs_alloc::*` to pick and mark blocks
   - persists *all* required ext4 metadata updates (bitmap + group desc + superblock)
2. Implement a better allocation strategy in phases:
   - Phase A (required): correctness-first contiguous search with explicit exclusions + correct accounting
   - Phase B (recommended): buddy-style free-extent search for faster contiguous allocation
   - Phase C (optional): per-inode / locality preallocation
3. Ensure all mutations are `&Cx`-aware and return explicit errors.

## TESTS (REQUIRED)
1. Pure unit tests (no external tools):
   - allocate/free on an in-memory block device and assert bitmap bits flip as expected
   - edge cases: last group partial bitmap, wraparound search, bounds
2. Harness integration tests (skip if kernel tools missing):
   - generate an ext4 image with `mkfs.ext4`
   - run a small number of allocations + frees via FrankenFS code paths
   - compare kernel tool output (`dumpe2fs -h` / `tune2fs -l`) before/after:
     - free block counts
     - group descriptor counters
   - log all parameters and any mismatches in a field-level diff

## LOGGING REQUIREMENTS
- Allocation request (debug): requested_count, goal_block, group_hint
- Allocation result (info): allocated_start, allocated_count, group, duration_us
- Free request (debug): block_start, block_count
- Free result (info): freed_count, group
- Bitmap update (trace): group, bitmap_block, bits_changed
- Group descriptor update (trace): group, old_free, new_free
- Superblock update (trace): old_total_free, new_total_free
- Allocation failure (warn): reason (no_space, fragmented, reserved_range)
- Accounting mismatch (error): expected vs actual, full context

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
1. Allocated blocks are never outside the valid data-block range.
2. Bitmaps, group descriptors, and superblock counters remain self-consistent after allocations/frees.
3. Tests catch obvious corruption (no "it seems fine").
4. This bead remains strictly about the allocator; higher-level inode/extent updates happen in other bd-huh beads.

title: Implement ext4 JBD2 journal write path
description:
# Implement ext4 JBD2 journal write path

## GOAL
Add the **write-side** of ext4’s internal journal (JBD2) so the ext4 write path can be crash-consistent and mount-compatible.

## CURRENT REALITY (CODE)
`crates/ffs-journal/src/lib.rs` already provides:
- `replay_jbd2()` (descriptor/commit/revoke replay)
- a native append-only `NativeCowJournal` (FrankenFS-internal)

What’s missing for compatibility-mode ext4 writes is the JBD2 **writer**:
- begin transaction
- write descriptor blocks + data blocks into the journal region
- write commit block
- checkpoint to home locations and advance tail
- maintain/update the journal superblock fields as needed

## SCOPE (PHASED)
1. **Phase A (required): JBD2 write format + self-replayability**
   - Implement a minimal JBD2 writer that produces journal blocks that `replay_jbd2()` can successfully replay.
   - Support descriptor + data blocks + commit blocks.
   - Revoke support can be phase-gated, but must be explicitly documented.
2. **Phase B (required): ext4 integration boundary**
   - Define a stable interface from the ext4 write-path commit code into the journal writer.
   - Ensure journal writes are tied to the transaction boundary (MVCC commit) so we never “half-commit”.
3. **Phase C (recommended): checkpoint + space management**
   - implement tail advancement and checkpointing policy so the journal region does not fill permanently.

## FILES (LIKELY)
- `crates/ffs-journal/src/lib.rs` (add JBD2 writer types next to replay)
- `crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs` (wire write-path commits to journal writer)

## TESTS (REQUIRED)
1. Unit tests for JBD2 record layout:
   - produce a synthetic transaction that “writes block X with payload P”
   - assert descriptor tag encoding is correct (target block numbers, LAST flag)
2. Integration test (in-memory block device):
   - write a journal transaction into a mock journal region
   - run `replay_jbd2()` against that region
   - assert the home block now contains payload P
3. Crash-tolerance tests (bounded):
   - simulate partial journal writes (truncate last block / omit commit)
   - ensure replay ignores incomplete txns and does not panic

## LOGGING REQUIREMENTS
- On commit: log (at trace) the txn sequence, number of tagged blocks, and journal head/tail movement.
- On replay mismatch in tests: print a structured diff (sequence, tag list, expected targets).

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
1. A transaction written by the new writer is replayed correctly by `replay_jbd2()`.
2. Incomplete transactions do not apply.
3. All new behavior is covered by tests with actionable failure output.
close_reason: done

title: Implement FUSE write operation surface (FsOps + fuser)
description:
# Implement FUSE write operation surface (FsOps + fuser)

## GOAL
Expose ext4 write-path functionality through the user-facing FUSE mount:
- `write`
- `create`
- `mkdir` / `rmdir`
- `unlink`
- `rename`
- `setattr` / `truncate`

This bead is the “plumbing” layer: it does not invent write semantics; it wires the already-implemented write-path primitives into the mount surface.

## CURRENT REALITY (CODE)
- `FsOps` lives in `crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs` and is explicitly **read-only** today.
- `crates/ffs-fuse/src/lib.rs` only overrides read operations (getattr/lookup/readdir/read/readlink/xattr) and delegates to `FsOps`.
- CLI mount (`crates/ffs-cli/src/main.rs`) mounts ext4 read-only.

## SCOPE (PHASED, DO NOT OVERSCOPE)
### Phase A (required): minimal RW surface to satisfy bd-huh.5
1. Extend `FsOps` (in `crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs`) with the minimal write operations needed for the RW smoke test:
   - `write`
   - `create`
   - `mkdir`
   - `unlink`
   - `rmdir`
   - `rename`
   - `setattr` / `truncate` (only what’s required for correctness)
2. Implement those methods for ext4 (in `crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs`):
   - begin a transaction (MVCC)
   - mutate metadata (allocator + extent tree + inode + dir)
   - journal the changes (bd-huh.3)
   - commit/rollback with explicit error mapping
3. Wire `crates/ffs-fuse/src/lib.rs` fuser callbacks to call the new `FsOps` methods.
4. Enforce mount mode:
   - default remains read-only
   - add an explicit CLI flag for RW mount (e.g. `ffs mount --rw ...`)
   - if mounted RO, write operations must fail with `EROFS`.

### Phase B (follow-ups, only if Phase A is stable)
- symlink/hardlink
- xattr mutation
- fsync/flush semantics

## TESTS (REQUIRED)
1. FsOps-layer integration tests (no FUSE) in `crates/ffs-harness/tests/`:
   - create/write/read roundtrip
   - unlink removes the name and decrements link count correctly
   - rename moves entry atomically (best-effort within V1)
   - truncate reduces/extends size with correct extent updates
2. E2E:
   - bd-huh.5 must pass and provide actionable logs.

## LOGGING REQUIREMENTS
- Every write op must log (trace) the op name, inode(s), offsets/lengths, and the commit/journal sequence identifiers.
- On error, logs must include enough context to reproduce (which inode, which block group, etc.).

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
1. FUSE RW operations are implemented end-to-end for ext4 and fail with correct errnos on unsupported operations.
2. RO mount never mutates the image.
3. bd-huh.5 smoke script passes (Phase A scope).
4. All new behavior is covered by tests with clear failure output.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text: REVIEW FIX: Removed blocks dependency on bd-cebm (fsync/flush). Basic write operations (create/write/mkdir/unlink) are independent of fsync—this bead's own description lists fsync as Phase B. Removing this dep shortens the critical path by 3 hops (cebm→20p→22w.6→22w.5) and enables earlier write path work. fsync is still gated for E2E (bd-3en1 depends on bd-cebm).

title: Add E2E test suite for ext4 write path (FUSE RW + crash checks)
description:
# Add E2E test suite for ext4 write path (FUSE RW + crash checks)

## GOAL
Add an end-to-end script that mounts an ext4 image read-write via FrankenFS and validates correct behavior for core write operations.

This is a user-facing guarantee: if we claim we can write, we must have an E2E script that proves it.

## DELIVERABLES
1. `scripts/e2e/ffs_ext4_rw_smoke.sh`
2. Uses `scripts/e2e/lib.sh` conventions (logging/cleanup).
3. Document prerequisites for RW mount (FUSE permissions, and any tool requirements for generating the test image).

## FIXTURE INPUT (NO CHECKED-IN IMAGES REQUIRED)
The script should generate a fresh ext4 image in a temp dir using kernel tools:
- `mkfs.ext4` + `debugfs` (preferred, rootless)
- Use a larger size than the RO smoke (e.g., 64MiB) to ensure there is space for multiple operations.

If required tools are missing, the script must SKIP with a clear message and exit 0.

## SCRIPT DESIGN
- Never mutate any checked-in artifact in-place.
- Always operate on a temp workdir:
  - create `<tmp>/base.ext4`
  - copy to `<tmp>/work.ext4` before mounting RW
- Mount `<tmp>/work.ext4` to `<tmp>/mnt` with an explicit RW flag (to be implemented as part of bd-huh): `ffs mount --rw`.
- Run a bounded set of operations and verify results.
- Unmount.
- Re-mount the same `<tmp>/work.ext4` read-only and re-verify persistence.

## REQUIRED OPERATIONS
1. Create/write/overwrite:
   - `echo hello > <mnt>/newfile.txt`
   - `cat <mnt>/newfile.txt` == `hello`
   - overwrite with different content, verify
2. mkdir/rmdir:
   - `mkdir <mnt>/newdir`
   - `rmdir <mnt>/newdir` (after empty)
3. rename:
   - `mv <mnt>/newfile.txt <mnt>/renamed.txt`
4. unlink:
   - `rm <mnt>/renamed.txt`
5. metadata (phase-gated):
   - `chmod 600 <mnt>/somefile` (only if permissions are supported)
   - `stat` checks: size, mode, mtime monotonicity

## CRASH / RECOVERY MINI-HARNESS (PHASED)
We want to validate journal replay correctness.

### Phase A (required): clean shutdown persistence
- After unmount/remount, all writes persist.

### Phase B (best-effort): simulated crash during write
- Run `ffs mount --rw` in background.
- Perform writes.
- Kill the mount process abruptly.
- Re-open the image with `ffs inspect` and/or remount and verify either:
  - journal replay restores the committed state, or
  - mount fails with a clear diagnostic if recovery isn’t implemented yet.

The script must produce logs sufficient to debug recovery.

## LOGGING REQUIREMENTS
- `RUST_LOG=trace RUST_BACKTRACE=1`.
- Log file must include:
  - before/after directory trees (bounded depth)
  - per-operation assertions
  - mount/unmount commands and their outputs

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
1. Script does not require root (except optional image creation if debugfs path is insufficient).
2. It exits 0 on success and non-zero on failure.
3. It never leaves a mounted FUSE filesystem behind.
4. It prints a concise PASS/FAIL summary and points to the detailed logs.

## NOTES
- RW mount flag and correctness are implemented elsewhere in bd-huh; this bead is strictly test infrastructure.

title: Add comprehensive unit tests for ext4 write path invariants
description:
# Add comprehensive unit tests for ext4 write path invariants

## GOAL
Verify all invariants of the ext4 write path: extent tree mutation, block allocation, journal commit, inode updates.

## DELIVERABLES
1. Extent tree mutation tests:
   - Insert extent, split node, verify tree invariants
   - Delete extent, merge nodes, verify tree invariants
   - Truncate: remove extents beyond size
2. Block allocation tests:
   - Allocate in preferred group, verify bitmap updated
   - Allocate when preferred group full, verify fallback
   - Free blocks, verify bitmap cleared
   - Contiguous allocation preference
3. Journal commit tests:
   - Transaction bracket: begin → operations → commit
   - Rollback: begin → operations → abort → verify no changes
   - Crash simulation: commit interrupted, verify recovery
4. Inode update tests:
   - Size update after write
   - Timestamp update (mtime, ctime)
   - Link count update after link/unlink
   - Checksum recalculation

## TESTS (≥25 individual test cases)

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
1. ≥25 unit tests for ext4 write path
2. All tree/allocation invariants verified
3. Crash recovery tested
close_reason: Verified ext4 write-path invariant tests across extent/alloc/journal/inode/core suites via rch; acceptance met

title: meas(fuse): add dispatch counters for the MUTATION opcodes — three of five remaining mounted losses perform none of the four opcodes the daemon counts
description:
THREE OF THE FIVE REMAINING MOUNTED LOSE ROWS ARE MUTATING WORKLOADS, AND THE DAEMON HAS
NO DISPATCH COUNTER FOR A SINGLE OPCODE ANY OF THEM PERFORMS.

`RequestOp` covers exactly four opcodes: Getattr, Getxattr, Lookup, Readdir. All four are
read-metadata. The mounted scorecard's remaining losses are:

  small-file create/delete storm   2.358280x   create, fsyncdir, delete, fsyncdir
  fsync/journal commit             1.976308x   write, fsync
  parallel metadata writes         1.930090x   create, fsync
  (warm stat and readdir+stat are attributed; parallel read is a WIN)

MEASURED CONSEQUENCE (bd-btrfs-create-delete-storm, 2026-08-16, commit banked in the
negative-evidence ledger): a create/delete storm run reports counted dispatch of 1530.6
ns/op against a 170134.4 ns/op arm — 0.90%. That figure is a strict LOWER BOUND and not
an attribution, because the 99.1% it leaves is not transport, it is unmeasured, and it
必 contains the creates, unlinks and two directory fsyncs per operation where a mutating
workload's cost must be.

The counters DO resolve the incidental metadata traffic exactly: getattr:getxattr:lookup =
2.00:1.00:1.00 per operation, cross-checked against the schedule (80026/2 = 40013 ops
against (12 pairs + 8 warmup) x 2000 = 40000). So every create/delete operation drags two
getattrs, a lookup and a capability probe behind it. Useful, but incidental rather than
the work.

WHAT TO ADD: dispatch counters on the mutation path — create, unlink, mkdir, rmdir,
fsync, fsyncdir, setattr, write — in the same shape as the existing four, emitted on the
same mount_dispatch_metrics line so the comparator report carries them (bd-viil0 made that
line reach the report; this widens what it says).

ACCEPTANCE:
  - a create/delete storm run reports non-zero create/unlink/fsyncdir dispatch counts, and
    their sum plus the existing four is compared against the arm rather than the existing
    four alone
  - the counts cross-check against the schedule the way the read counters did: 2000
    operations per observation must produce 2000 creates and 2000 unlinks per observation,
    and if they do not, the discrepancy is the finding
  - measured on the comparator, not a managed-runtime side harness

SEQUENCING, because these interact. bd-4zokj separately measured that 59.2%-98.8% of the
daemon's own CPU is OUTSIDE dispatch even for opcodes that ARE counted. So a mutating row
needs BOTH the missing opcodes and the whole-request timer before its arm can be
decomposed; adding these counters alone will produce a larger lower bound, not an
attribution. Worth doing anyway — a larger lower bound on a 2.36x row is worth having, and
it is the cheaper half.

COST NOTE: this adds counters to AtomicMetrics and MetricsSnapshot, so it collides with
bd-k3g3g — MetricsSnapshot has no Default derive and 58 literal constructors, of which one
uses struct-update syntax. Adding eight counters without bd-k3g3g first is an eight-field
edit across ~57 sites. Do bd-k3g3g first.

comments.text:
perf(btrfs): create/delete storm cannot be attributed — the daemon counts none of the opcodes it performs (bd-i353e)

With readdir+stat and warm stat attributed, the worst remaining unattributed mounted row
is the small-file create/delete storm at 2.358280x. It is a MUTATING workload, so none of
the capability-probe findings carry over and it needed its own pass. The pass produced a
refusal rather than a share, and the refusal is the result.

Measured on the comparator itself — no managed-runtime workaround, because bd-viil0 is
fixed and the report now carries the counters:

  fuse_over_kernel_median=2.304140 [2.184918, 2.344368]  (consistent with the banked 2.358280x)
  kernel 152,829,492 ns   ffs 340,268,822 ns
  fuse_a getattr 80026  getxattr 40044  lookup 40001  readdir 12
  fuse_b identical counts

WHAT THE COUNTERS DO RESOLVE, exactly: getattr:getxattr:lookup = 2.00:1.00:1.00 per
operation. The counts also cross-check the schedule — 80026/2 = 40013 operations against
(12 pairs + 8 warmup) x 2000 = 40000 expected — so the derivation is confirmed by a number
nobody chose. Counted dispatch is 1530.6 ns/op against a 170134.4 ns/op arm, i.e. 0.90%.

WHY 0.90% IS NOT AN ATTRIBUTION. The daemon has dispatch counters for getattr, getxattr,
lookup and readdir. This workload performs create, fsyncdir, delete, fsyncdir. Not one
opcode it exists to measure is counted. So 0.90% is a strict LOWER BOUND, and the 99.1%
it leaves is not "transport" the way it was for warm stat — it is unmeasured, and it
certainly contains the creates, unlinks and two directory fsyncs per operation where a
mutating workload's cost must be. Publishing 0.90% as this row's daemon share would be
the same class of error as dividing an unpinned daemon by a pinned arm: arithmetically
valid, answering a different question than the one asked.

The 2:1:1 traffic is still worth having — every create/delete operation drags two
getattrs, a lookup and a capability probe behind it, which is the same per-path-op probe
already banked for the read rows turning up on the write path. But that is the incidental
traffic, not the work.

THE INSTRUMENT GAP, filed as bd-i353e: three of the five remaining mounted LOSE rows are
mutating (create/delete storm 2.36x, fsync/journal commit 1.98x, parallel metadata writes
1.93x), so this is not a one-row gap. It also compounds with bd-4zokj, which measured
59.2%-98.8% of daemon CPU sitting outside dispatch even for counted opcodes: a mutating
row needs both the missing opcodes and the whole-request timer before its arm can be
decomposed.

NOT CLAIMED: the run is BLOCKED_NULL (load average 20.6; the placement gate refused two
earlier attempts outright) and no ratio is banked — the banked 2.358280x stands. Nothing
here says the daemon is or is not the cost on this row; it says the instrument cannot
answer, and names what it would take.

No build was started: df -h /data was 63G and the existing ELF (672ccf09...) already
carried the bd-viil0 fix.

comments.text:
## 2026-08-16 — AUDIT CORRECTED (no perf claim): adding a counter to `MetricsSnapshot` is a 17-site edit, not the ~57 I published, and the bead dependency that figure justified is withdrawn (bd-k3g3g, bd-i353e, bd-4zokj, AzureBay)

When the build freeze stopped me landing `bd-4zokj`'s whole-request timer, I reported by
inspection that adding two fields to `MetricsSnapshot` "fails to compile in ~57 places",
counted `58` literal constructors, and used that figure to file `bd-k3g3g` and to sequence
`bd-i353e` behind it. **The count was wrong and the sequencing it justified was wrong with
it.**

My grep was `MetricsSnapshot {`, which matches every sibling type ending in the same word.
Resolving them:

    CoreMetricsSnapshot            10   crates/ffs-fuse/src/per_core.rs
    RepairRuntimeMetricsSnapshot    6   crates/ffs-repair/src/pipeline.rs
    RepairMetricsSnapshot           3   crates/ffs-repair/src/pipeline.rs
    CacheRuntimeMetricsSnapshot     4+2 crates/ffs-block/{lib,cache}.rs
    ... plus ffs-mvcc and ffs-block bench types

The actual `ffs_fuse::MetricsSnapshot` constructors are **17**, in **three** files:

    crates/ffs-fuse/src/lib.rs        10
    crates/ffs-cli/src/main.rs         4
    crates/ffs-harness/src/metrics.rs  3

### What the error cost, and what it changes

`bd-k3g3g` was filed as a standalone refactor worth doing for its own sake, and
`bd-i353e` (mutation-opcode counters, the instrument three mounted LOSE rows are blocked
on) was explicitly sequenced BEHIND it on the grounds that "adding eight counters without
bd-k3g3g first is an eight-field edit across ~57 sites". At 17 sites in three files that
argument does not hold: the mutation counters can be added directly, and `bd-k3g3g`
becomes a small tidiness change rather than a prerequisite.

**So the dependency I published was an artifact of a bad grep, and it was pointing the
next agent at a refactor instead of at the instrument.** Both beads are corrected.

### The general failure, which is the reusable part

A count produced by a pattern that can match more than the thing being counted is not a
measurement, and I treated it as one — in a campaign whose whole discipline is that
counts are trustworthy precisely because they are exact. The tell was available and I
skipped it: `58` literal constructors of a struct with `13` fields, spread across
`ffs-repair` and `ffs-block` and `ffs-mvcc`, none of which have any business constructing
a FUSE metrics snapshot. **A count that implies an implausible topology should be
re-derived before it is published**, and the re-derivation here was one narrower grep.

This is the second cost-shaped claim of mine to be refuted by a stricter re-measurement
today; the first was the daemon share that mixed a pinned arm with an unpinned daemon.
Both had the same shape: an individually reasonable step, published without the check
that would have caught it.

Counted mechanism: **58 constructors counted vs 17 constructors actual**, the difference
being sibling types the pattern could not exclude. No build was involved in either the
error or its correction, and `df -h /data` was 63G throughout. Nothing deleted.

LANDED (AzureBay, 2026-08-16, commit 3145d182). Mutating dispatches are counted.

THE CAUSE WAS ONE LINE. record_dispatch_duration matched Getattr/Getxattr/Lookup/Readdir and sent everything else to `_ => {}`. The mutating RequestOp variants already existed and already flowed through with_request_scope — they were discarded at the counter, not missing from the daemon. So this bead was much smaller than it looked; what made it look large was my own bad cost estimate.

NOW AGGREGATED into mutation_dispatch_count/nanos across create, mkdir, unlink, rmdir, rename, link, symlink, fallocate, setattr, setxattr, removexattr, write, fsync, fsyncdir and repair-writeback, emitted on the mount_dispatch_metrics line so the comparator report carries them.

ONE AGGREGATE RATHER THAN A PAIR PER OPCODE, with the reason on the match arm: these rows ask "how much of the arm is our mutation work", and a 15-variant breakdown is 30 fields to answer it. Splitting it later is a follow-up with a reason rather than a guess.

MY COST ESTIMATE WAS WRONG THREE TIMES, each refinement a narrower grep:
  58 sites — `MetricsSnapshot {`, which also matches CoreMetricsSnapshot, RepairRuntimeMetricsSnapshot, CacheRuntimeMetricsSnapshot and more
  17 sites — sibling types excluded, but still counting `-> MetricsSnapshot {` return types and ffs-harness's OWN unrelated MetricsSnapshot type
  10 sites — true literal constructions, of which 3 are the definition and the snapshot() body
The real edit was 5 test constructors plus the emit line. The 58 figure is what sequenced this bead behind bd-k3g3g; that dependency is withdrawn and bd-k3g3g is now optional tidiness, not a prerequisite.

DELIBERATELY NOT DONE: the hand-written Debug impl is not extended. A Debug-output string assertion at lib.rs:15699 pins its exact text, and leaving the impl alone keeps that test valid and keeps this change to the counters. If someone wants the new fields in Debug output, that test moves with it.

GATE: cargo check -p ffs-fuse -p ffs-cli --all-targets on rch, clean in 2m07s (the unused-`cx` warning at lib.rs:5262 is pre-existing). df -h /data checked at 62G before starting, above the 60G threshold; ONE build from this pane, second of the project's two slots.

NOT CLAIMED: no measurement yet. The counters compile and are wired to the report. Whether the create/delete storm's mutation share is large is the next run's question — and per bd-4zokj it will STILL be a lower bound until the whole-request timer exists, because 59.2%-98.8% of daemon CPU sits outside dispatch even for opcodes that are counted. Adding these counters buys a larger lower bound, not an attribution; that was true when this bead was filed and is still true now.

FIRST ROUND-TRIP CENSUS OF A MUTATING ROW (AzureBay, 2026-08-16, commit 49d32280).

The mutation dispatch counters landed this turn but the candidate ELF predates them and both project build slots were taken, so this used what the current ELF already reports: requests_total, which has always counted EVERY request at the FUSE boundary including the creates and unlinks the old dispatch counters dropped.

Daemon pinned, client pinned to a disjoint set, K=1 vs K=5 differencing:

  requests_total     11.003 round trips per create+delete op
  metadata_requests   3.001 per op (27.3%)

Both divide cleanly (88024/4/2000 and 24008/4/2000), so these are exact per-op costs.

THE COMPARISON:
  warm stat      1.000 round trips/op — one security.capability GETXATTR, nothing else
  readdir+stat   1.000 per entry — same probe
  create+delete  11.003

The read rows cost one crossing per operation and are ~99% transport; this path costs eleven. That is the concrete justification for having refused to transfer the probe finding here: it is a different shape of problem, not a scaled one.

3.001 of the eleven are metadata requests, consistent with the earlier dispatch census (2 getattr + 1 lookup + 1 getxattr of incidental read traffic per op). The other ~8 are the mutating work plus the opens, flushes and releases around it — and that composition is exactly what this turn's counters resolve, needing one rebuild and a free slot.

A WORKLOAD MISMATCH WORTH KNOWING BEFORE ANYONE REPRODUCES THIS. The comparator's create/delete storm carries the durability contract create_fsyncdir_delete_fsyncdir (ffs_mounted_kernel_bench.rs:212) — a directory fsync PER OPERATION. My harness fsyncs once per SWEEP of 2,000 operations. So 11.003 OMITS two fsyncdirs per op and is a strict LOWER BOUND on the comparator's workload; the 2.358280x row must not be decomposed with it. The path-to-path ratio (11 vs 1) is unaffected by that difference, which is why the row is banked at all.

NEXT, in order: rebuild the candidate when a slot frees, re-run this census plus the mutation dispatch counters together, and match the harness's per-op fsyncdir so the numbers apply to the banked row rather than to a cheaper cousin of it. Per bd-4zokj the result will still be a lower bound on daemon share until the whole-request timer exists.

BUDGET: no build started. df -h /data was 61G, above the 60G threshold, but the project already had TWO builds in flight which is the cap, so this turn used measurement only.

## 2026-08-16 — REFUTED by reading, before it cost a measurement: the mutation counters will NOT attribute the create/delete row's uncounted crossings — Open, Flush and Release are still invisible (bd-i353e, AzureBay)

I banked, twice, that the mutation dispatch counters landed in `3145d182` "will attribute
the `8.999`" uncounted crossings per create+delete operation. **That is wrong**, and a
build-free read of the enum against the match arms shows it without spending a
measurement.

`RequestOp` has **30** variants. After this turn's change:

    counted (read-metadata) :  4   Getattr, Getxattr, Lookup, Readdir
    counted (mutation, new) : 15   Create, Mkdir, Unlink, Rmdir, Rename, Link, Symlink,
                                   Fallocate, Setattr, Setxattr, Removexattr, Write,
                                   Fsync, Fsyncdir, RepairWriteback
    STILL uncounted         : 11   Statfs, Listxattr, Flush, Open, Release, Opendir,
                                   Read, Readlink, Lseek, IoctlRead, IoctlWrite

**Of the still-uncounted eleven, a create+delete operation issues Open, Flush, Release,
Opendir and Statfs.** The workload is `open(O_CREAT)` + `close` + `fsync(dirfd)` +
`unlink` + `fsync(dirfd)`, and `close` alone produces FLUSH and RELEASE. So the new
counters capture the create, the unlink and the two fsyncdirs — roughly four of the nine
uncounted crossings — and leave the open/flush/release family exactly as invisible as
before.

### The classification error, which is the reusable part

I split the opcode space into "read-metadata" and "mutating" and assumed those two
partitioned it. They do not: **FUSE's session lifecycle opcodes are neither.** `Open`,
`Flush` and `Release` do no filesystem mutation and return no metadata, so a taxonomy
built from those two categories drops them silently — which is precisely how the original
`_ => {}` arm came to exist, reproduced one level up.

The tell was available in my own data and I walked past it: the census showed `3.001`
metadata requests and, after this change, at most ~4 mutating crossings, against `13.002`
total. Four plus three is seven, not thirteen. **The arithmetic never closed, and I did not
check it before predicting the counters would.**

### What this changes

`bd-i353e`'s acceptance is not met by the counters as landed. Attributing the create/delete
row needs Open/Flush/Release counted as well — a third category, or an honest catch-all
that counts whatever the two named categories miss so the total is forced to reconcile
with `requests_total`.

**A reconciliation check belongs in that bead's acceptance**: the sum of all dispatch
counters must equal `requests_total` minus memo-served replies, and if it does not, the
difference names the opcodes still falling through. That check would have caught this at
the point of writing rather than after two ledger rows predicted otherwise.

No measurement was spent to establish any of this, no build was started, and `df -h /data`
is `56G` — below the floor, which is why this turn is read-only. Counted mechanism: **30
variants vs 19 counted**, leaving 11 uncounted, five of which this workload issues.

WORK WRITTEN, UNGATED, STASHED (ProudBarn, 2026-08-16). stash@{0}: 'bd-i353e READY-TO-GATE ... other_dispatch catch-all + reconciliation test'. Recover with: git stash pop stash@{0} (verify the ref first, stash indices shift).

WHAT IT DOES, addressing the reopen reason directly (Open/Flush/Release still uncounted):
 - AtomicMetrics gains other_dispatch_count / other_dispatch_nanos.
 - The bare `_ => {}` arm in record_dispatch_duration is REPLACED by a counting arm, so nothing is dropped. I did not enumerate Open/Flush/Release individually: the bead asked for 'a third category, or an honest catch-all that counts whatever the two named categories miss so the total is forced to reconcile'. A catch-all is the version that cannot go stale — a new RequestOp added later lands in it automatically, whereas an explicit list silently regrows the same hole. Anything accumulating there is a candidate for promotion with a reason.
 - MetricsSnapshot gains the two fields; snapshot() wires them; the ffs-cli mount_dispatch_metrics line emits them so the reconciliation is visible in reports rather than only in tests.
 - NEW TEST every_dispatch_lands_in_exactly_one_category_bd_i353e: records 11 dispatches across named, mutation and previously-dropped opcodes (Open/Flush/Release/Read) and asserts the six categories SUM to the dispatch count, and that the nanos decomposition reconciles on the same terms. That is the reconciliation check the reopen asked to add to acceptance.

WHY IT IS NOT COMMITTED: I could not gate it. The disk gate refused at 54G against the 59G threshold (a peer build took the headroom mid-turn). This bead's own text says 'DO THIS UNDER A BUILD, not during the freeze', and committing unverified code to a SHARED worktree risks breaking every peer's build — the repo has been made unbuildable that way before. So it is stashed rather than pushed or discarded.

TO LAND IT: df -h /data; at >= 59G, git stash pop, then cargo test -p ffs-fuse --lib remotely. Expect 587 passing.

TWO TRAPS ALREADY PAID FOR, so the next person does not pay them again:
 1. MountHandle derives Debug and its golden mount_handle_debug_format spells out every MetricsSnapshot field, so a new counter must be added there too. I have already done this in the stash. A Debug golden is a THIRD place a field must be updated, and neither the Default derive (bd-k3g3g) nor struct-update syntax protects it.
 2. AtomicMetrics's Debug is HAND-WRITTEN (lib.rs ~1206) and deliberately omits mutation_dispatch_*. I matched that treatment and did NOT add other_dispatch_* to it, so ATOMIC_METRICS_DEBUG_GOLDEN stays valid. If someone later adds these to that impl, that golden must change in the same commit.

ONE CORRECTION TO A CLAIM ON THIS BEAD: the reopen says the counters 'do not meet acceptance' because of uncounted opcodes, which is right. But note the acceptance arithmetic cited (4+3=7 vs 13.002 crossings) compares DISPATCH counts against BOUNDARY crossings, and those are different quantities — memo-served replies cross the boundary without dispatching (bd-0c4av). The catch-all closes the dispatch-side gap; it will NOT by itself make dispatches equal requests_total, and the residual is the memo-served set. The test therefore reconciles categories against dispatches, not against requests_total, which is the only form of the check that can actually hold.
