title: setxattr/removexattr on an append-only (and, on btrfs, immutable) file is wrongly allowed instead of EPERM
description: The kernel's xattr_permission (fs/xattr.c) returns EPERM for any MAY_WRITE xattr op (setxattr/removexattr) on an immutable OR append-only inode: 'if (mask & MAY_WRITE) { if (IS_IMMUTABLE(inode) || IS_APPEND(inode)) return -EPERM; }'. FrankenFS under-enforces: ext4_setxattr (~17487) and ext4_removexattr (~17797) call only ext4_reject_immutable (no EXT4_APPEND_FL check) -> setxattr/removexattr on an append-only file wrongly succeeds; btrfs_setxattr (~23177) and btrfs_removexattr (~23219) check NEITHER immutable NOR append -> both wrongly succeed. Sibling of bd-69ich (link, fixed 0b46ec62) and same audit-both-boundaries class. FIX: ext4 xattr sites also reject EXT4_APPEND_FL with EPERM; btrfs xattr sites reject flags & (BTRFS_INODE_IMMUTABLE|BTRFS_INODE_APPEND) with EPERM, before any mutation. NOTE: the bd-hbld5 metadata-ops test comment had wrongly claimed xattr stays allowed on append-only. Test: inject the flag, attempt set/remove -> EPERM (fails pre-fix).

Tests: btrfs_setxattr_on_immutable_or_append_is_eperm_bd_kf7uw + setxattr-on-append assertion in immutable_and_append_attributes_enforced_on_metadata_ops_bd_hbld5. Full ffs-core 1083 green. title: ffs-btrfs: missing 6 kernel-canonical BTRFS_*_TREE_OBJECTID constants
description:
Finding (via /porting-to-rust skill, third visit, different target):
the Linux kernel header `fs/btrfs/btrfs_tree.h` declares 12
well-known tree objectids. Our Rust port at
crates/ffs-btrfs/src/lib.rs defines 6 of them
(ROOT, EXTENT, CHUNK, DEV, FS, FIRST_FREE) plus item-key constants
and file-type constants. SIX tree objectids are MISSING:

  BTRFS_ROOT_TREE_DIR_OBJECTID    = 6   (root tree's dir entry)
  BTRFS_CSUM_TREE_OBJECTID        = 7   (the data-checksum tree)
  BTRFS_QUOTA_TREE_OBJECTID       = 8   (quota tree)
  BTRFS_UUID_TREE_OBJECTID        = 9   (subvolume UUID lookup)
  BTRFS_FREE_SPACE_TREE_OBJECTID  = 10  (the v2 free-space tree)
  BTRFS_BLOCK_GROUP_TREE_OBJECTID = 11  (the v2 block-group tree)

Concrete impact:
  * Code that walks the root tree and dispatches on objectid (e.g.,
    a future btrfs scrub or fsck) cannot pattern-match on these
    by name.
  * Magic literals (`6`, `7`, `8`, ...) would slip past grep
    audits.
  * No kernel-conformance test pinning the values to the kernel
    header; a regression that swapped, say, BTRFS_FREE_SPACE_TREE
    and BTRFS_BLOCK_GROUP_TREE would silently mis-route v2 metadata
    reads.

Same shape as bd-k81lq (ext4 reserved inodes) and bd-343v3 (ext4
file-type constants). Acceptance: 6 new pub-const u64 constants in
crates/ffs-btrfs/src/lib.rs with doc comments naming the kernel
header, plus a kernel-conformance unit test pinning each value AND
the strict-monotonic ordering 1..=11 for the contiguous range plus
FIRST_FREE = 256.
notes: Shipped: 6 new pub-const u64 BTRFS_*_TREE_OBJECTID constants in crates/ffs-btrfs/src/lib.rs (BTRFS_ROOT_TREE_DIR_OBJECTID=6, BTRFS_CSUM_TREE_OBJECTID=7, BTRFS_QUOTA_TREE_OBJECTID=8, BTRFS_UUID_TREE_OBJECTID=9, BTRFS_FREE_SPACE_TREE_OBJECTID=10, BTRFS_BLOCK_GROUP_TREE_OBJECTID=11), each with doc comment naming kernel header. Kernel-conformance unit test btrfs_tree_objectid_constants_match_kernel_header pins all 12 well-known objectids (1..=11 plus FIRST_FREE=256), strict-monotonic ascending ordering, and contiguous-range invariant. Verified via rch exec -- cargo test -p ffs-btrfs --lib btrfs_tree_objectid_constants_match_kernel_header.

title: perf(btrfs): on-disk B-tree floor primitive + read_file on-disk lower bound
description: The on-disk (read-only mount) read_file path window-bounds the UPPER side (bd-x52ar) but descends from the inode's first item for the LOWER side, so an EOF read of a huge fragmented file still walks every extent before the offset. Mirror the COW path's floor_key lower bound (bd-4milp/W84, measured 121x at EOF reads): add walk_tree_floor (predecessor-or-equal O(log N) descent over the on-disk B-tree; btrfs internal keys are child-mins so the floor is in the rightmost child with key<=target, no left-sibling fallback) + OpenFs::walk_btrfs_tree_floor, then seek read_file's on-disk EXTENT_DATA lower bound to floor(inode,EXTENT_DATA,offset). Target ~121x at EOF reads on read-only mounts. Primitive landed with brute-force-equivalence test; remaining: OpenFs wrapper + read_file wiring + multi-extent on-disk read bench (bd-b2xc1).
close_reason: Wired on-disk read_file lower bound to walk_tree_floor (3ff279ba): OpenFs::walk_btrfs_tree_floor/walk_btrfs_fs_tree_floor wrappers + read_file two-descent split (INODE_ITEM span + floor(EXTENT_DATA,offset)..window). Node reads O(extents)->O(log N); primitive A/B 100.29µs->9.75µs (10.3x, bd-b2xc1); byte-identical, 320 tests green.

title: [perf] read-buffer movement __memmove/__memset on read path (per-block alloc+zero+copy) — 13.5% CLI / 22.8% FUSE cumulative file-read stack
description:

EVIDENCE: docs/reports/PROFILE_ANALYSIS.md (same CPU): __memmove_avx 2.42-2.73% self, __memset_avx2 1.50-1.78% self; cumulative file-read stack 13.53% CLI / 22.83% FUSE.
ROOT CAUSE (triangulated): tied to per-block read structure (rank-1) — each block read into a freshly alloc+zeroed buffer then copied (read_block -> .as_slice().to_vec(), ffs-core:5731).
HYPOTHESIZED FIX: reusable aligned buffer pool (AlignedVec) instead of per-block alloc+zero; drop the to_vec copy on read_block path. Likely shrinks after rank-1 batching; confirm with fresh flamegraph.

title: Refine xfstests baseline with partial-run resume and immutable raw artifacts

title: Implement full COW block rewrite path with allocation
description:
# Implement full COW block rewrite path with allocation

## GOAL
Complete the COW block rewrite path so writes allocate new blocks instead of overwriting, enabling true version chain semantics.

## BACKGROUND
From FEATURE_PARITY.md: "COW block rewrite path: 🟡 Basic version copy only"

Current state: Versions are created but may reuse same block location.
Required: Writes MUST allocate new blocks, old blocks retained for active snapshots.

## TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS

### 1. COW Write Flow
```rust
impl MvccStore {
    pub fn write_cow(
        &self,
        block: BlockNumber,
        data: &[u8],
        txn: &Transaction,
        allocator: &dyn BlockAllocator,
        cx: &Cx,
    ) -> Result<BlockNumber> {
        // 1. Check if block has active snapshot references
        // 2. If yes: allocate new block, write there
        // 3. If no: could rewrite in place (optimization)
        // 4. Add to transaction write set with new location
        // 5. Return new block number
    }
}
```

### 2. Logical-to-Physical Mapping
- Logical block numbers stable across versions
- Physical locations vary (new allocation per write)
- Extent trees must be updated with new physical locations

### 3. Free Space Tracking
```rust
pub trait CowAllocator {
    /// Allocate block for COW write
    fn alloc_cow(&self, hint: Option<BlockNumber>, cx: &Cx) -> Result<BlockNumber>;
    
    /// Mark block as freeable when no references
    fn defer_free(&self, block: BlockNumber, commit_seq: CommitSeq);
    
    /// Actually free blocks older than watermark
    fn gc_free(&self, watermark: CommitSeq, cx: &Cx) -> usize;
}
```

### 4. GC Integration
- Blocks freed only when no snapshot references
- Watermark = oldest active snapshot
- Freed blocks returned to allocator

## TESTS
1. Unit: COW write allocates new block
2. Unit: Old block readable via old snapshot
3. Integration: 100 writes to same logical block create 100 physical blocks
4. Integration: GC frees blocks when no refs
5. Property: Block count = active versions + overhead

## LOGGING
- COW allocation (trace): logical, old_physical, new_physical
- Defer free (trace): block, commit_seq
- GC (debug): freed count, watermark

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
1. Writes never overwrite blocks with active snapshot refs
2. Logical block numbers stable
3. GC reclaims space correctly
4. Memory bounded by max_versions_per_block

title: Fix clippy pedantic/nursery lints in ffs-btrfs
description: cargo clippy -D warnings reveals 4 lints: option_if_let_else, or_fun_call, cast_possible_truncation, must_use_candidate. Quick hygiene fix.
close_reason: completed: commit:b24c7079 - clippy pedantic/nursery fixed, 303 tests pass

title: Pin Ext4Inode::parse_from_bytes base 128-byte field offsets to fs/ext4/ext4.h
description: Ext4Inode::parse_from_bytes reads the base 128-byte struct ext4_inode at hard-coded kernel offsets per fs/ext4/ext4.h: i_mode u16@0x00, i_uid_lo u16@0x02, i_size_lo u32@0x04, i_atime u32@0x08, i_ctime u32@0x0C, i_mtime u32@0x10, i_dtime u32@0x14, i_gid_lo u16@0x18, i_links_count u16@0x1A, i_blocks_lo u32@0x1C, i_flags u32@0x20, l_i_version u32@0x24, i_block[15] @0x28..0x64, i_generation u32@0x64, i_file_acl_lo u32@0x68, i_size_high u32@0x6C. Ext4Inode is parsed on every ext4 file open / readdir / stat / xattr — the most heavily-trafficked ext4 struct WITHOUT a kernel-offset pin. Sister kernel pins exist for ext4_dir_entry_2 (bd-12nk4), ext4_extent_leaf, ext4_extent_index, ext4_extent_header, ext4_mmp_block, ext4_dx_root (bd-2e5cy), ext4_group_desc. Add a unit test stamping each field with a UNIQUE non-zero magic at its canonical kernel offset, parsing, asserting every field round-trips. Catches future endianness/offset/struct-padding regressions silently mis-routing mode-vs-uid_lo or atime-vs-ctime.
close_reason: Pinned 15 fields of base 128-byte ext4_inode at canonical kernel offsets (mode, uid_lo, size_lo+hi, atime, ctime, mtime, dtime, gid_lo, links_count, blocks_lo, flags, version, generation, file_acl_lo). Test passes via rch (1 passed; 535 filtered out).

title: Restore rustfmt compliance in ffs-btree and ffs-core

close_reason: Completed: remote cargo fmt --check passes; fixed ffs-core scope-call clippy findings in touched surface

title: Error model: add explicit incompatible-feature and block-size variants
description:
Context: PLAN_TO_PORT_FRANKENFS_TO_RUST.md §0.3 still has unchecked item for unsupported/incompatible mount validation variants.

Scope:
- Extend ffs-error with explicit variants for incompatible feature flags and unsupported block size.
- Map new variants to stable errno values and keep exhaustive tests updated.
- Update ffs-core parse/mount conversion to emit these variants where appropriate.
- Add/adjust unit tests in ffs-error and ffs-core for new mapping behavior.

Acceptance:
- cargo test -p ffs-error -p ffs-core passes.
- New variants used by mount-validation conversion paths.
- No warning regressions in affected crates.
close_reason: Implemented and verified (cargo check/clippy/test); landed in current main state including commit 0d8350f

title: ext4 directory extent-tree growth metadata not counted in i_blocks (same gap as bd-zpe9s, rarer)
description: Follow-up to bd-zpe9s (fixed ed3bc048 for regular-file write/fallocate). The directory mapping paths that insert into an extent tree via direct ffs_btree::insert calls (ffs-core lib.rs ~13181/13682/13963/24654.. GroupBlockAllocator construction sites) have the SAME latent gap: when a directory's extent tree grows past depth 0 the allocated index/leaf metadata blocks are not charged to the dir inode i_blocks -> e2fsck i_blocks-short. Rarer than the file case (directories rarely grow that large) but real. FIX: apply the same operation-level meta snapshot/delta (ext4_count_extent_tree_meta_blocks + ext4_apply_extent_meta_delta, already added in ed3bc048) around the directory-block-mapping mutation, or recompute at the dir-op writeback.
close_reason: Fixed in c24d38df: ext4_add_dir_entry + ext4_rebuild_htree_dir now snapshot extent-tree meta-block count before/after the dir-tree mutation and charge the signed delta to i_blocks (dev-based counter reads the txn-staged tree). Regression test ext4_dir_extent_tree_growth_counts_metadata_in_iblocks_bd_kyp2q (^dir_index linear dir, 300 fragmented entries -> depth>=1) is real e2fsck-clean and verified failing pre-fix (i_blocks 16 vs 20).

title: perf(fuse): decide a capability-memo SIZING POLICY — 3.36x is proven at one directory size with a hand-set table; a default needs bd-5vis3's memory bar
description:
THE QUESTION IS NO LONGER "DOES IT WORK" BUT "WHAT IS THE SIZING POLICY".

MEASURED AND ADMITTED (bd-34hzz, 2026-08-16, commit 93119b8d): sizing the capability
memo to the directory takes btrfs readdir+stat at 32,768 entries from 6.990007x
[6.988474, 7.026868] to 3.359246x [3.314229, 3.399607] vs kernel, both admitted=true
with both A/A nulls clear, one ELF, one fixture, one session. Our arm 217,470,654 ns ->
103,799,776 ns. Three independent estimators put the reduction at 2.078x-2.095x.

MEASURED AND ALSO ADMITTED AS A LIMIT (bd-m1bpu): the cliff MOVES rather than
disappears. At 100,000 entries the same 65,536-slot table is itself oversubscribed and
the win falls to 1.30x. At 2,000 entries a 4,096-slot table already fits and the extra
slots buy nothing. The benefit tracks how well the directory FITS, monotonically,
exactly as a direct-mapped table predicts.

So "make it bigger" is not a fix — it is a parameter with no single correct value, which
is precisely the unbounded-footprint objection bd-5vis3 exists to enforce. CAPABILITY_
MEMO_SLOTS_MAX is capped at 1<<20 (8 MiB per mount) and FFS_FUSE_CAPABILITY_MEMO_SLOTS is
documented in code as an experiment rather than a policy.

WHAT THIS BEAD OWES. A sizing policy, with the memory cost measured rather than argued.
Candidate shapes, roughly in increasing order of ambition:

  1. A larger FIXED default. Simplest, and the honest version reports what it costs on a
     mount that never needs it: 65,536 slots is 512 KiB per mount against 32 KiB today,
     resident for the mount lifetime, whether or not any directory is large.
  2. Size from something the mount already knows. The inode count is available at mount;
     a table sized to min(inodes, cap) rounded to a power of two would fit small
     filesystems in almost nothing and large ones up to the cap. Still bounded, and the
     bound is explicit.
  3. Grow on demand up to the cap. Best fit, worst complexity: the table is indexed by a
     mask, so growth means rehashing or a generation counter, on a path that is currently
     one relaxed atomic load. Do not attempt this without first showing (1) or (2) is
     insufficient.

ACCEPTANCE, and it is bd-5vis3's bar because that bead exists for exactly this failure:
  - peak resident memory reported, not estimated, for whatever policy is proposed
  - a workload that does NOT fit measured beside one that does — the 100,000-entry
    readdir+stat row is the non-fitting workload and already exists
  - the mount-time cost at several filesystem sizes, since options (2) and (3) both
    touch mount
  - a vs-kernel row on the fitting workload, to confirm the 3.36x survives the policy
    rather than only the hand-set env var

DO NOT ship a larger default on the strength of the 3.36x alone. That number is real and
admitted, and it is measured at ONE directory size with the table hand-sized to fit it.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
MEMORY MEASURED, AND IT REFUTES MY OWN ARITHMETIC (AzureBay, 2026-08-16, commits e2066f77 + 2e2d2b01).

This bead's acceptance said peak resident memory must be MEASURED, not argued. I had been arguing it — every row I wrote said "65,536 slots is 512 KiB per mount", straight from 8 bytes x slots. That is right about ADDRESS SPACE and wrong about RESIDENT memory.

Daemon VmHWM before/after a 32,768-entry sweep touching ~32,768 distinct inodes:

  slots=4096     VmHWM  9412 ->  39876 kB (+30464)  VmSize 190660 -> 1368516 kB
  slots=65536    VmHWM  9544 ->  40848 kB (+31304)  VmSize 190660 -> 1371076 kB
  slots=1048576  VmHWM  9400 ->  40920 kB (+31520)  VmSize 200900 -> 1378756 kB

Table delta vs 4096: predicted 480 kB / 8160 kB, observed 840 kB / 1056 kB. At the ceiling the prediction is 8x too pessimistic. The address space IS reserved as arithmetic says (baseline VmSize steps 190,660 -> 200,900 kB for the 8 MiB table) but pages never become resident until written: the zero-fill lowers to alloc_zeroed, so untouched slots stay on the shared zero page. 3.1% of a 1M-slot table was ever written.

A FIRST PASS NEARLY MISREAD THIS. Peak RSS after stat'ing ONE file gave +12/+28/+64 kB against predicted +480 kB/+2 MiB/+8 MiB — 100x off — and the tempting reading was "the env var is not taking effect". But that env var had already produced a measured 2.08x on readdir+stat and both mount paths go through one production constructor, so the table was certainly built. The right reading was built-but-not-TOUCHED, and the way to separate them was to touch it.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS BEAD: option 1 (a larger fixed default) is far more defensible than my arithmetic implied. A larger table costs address space proportional to capacity (bounded by CAPABILITY_MEMO_SLOTS_MAX at 8 MiB) and resident memory proportional to inodes actually probed — bounded by the workload, not the parameter. A mount that never touches a large directory pays close to nothing for a large table.

THE SPARSE-INODE ARM IS STILL OPEN, and my attempt at it was INVALID — reported rather than quietly dropped. The "scattered" arm reordered VISITS, not inode NUMBERS; slot index is ino & (len-1), a pure function of inode number, so both arms touched an identical page set. The tell is that the 4096-slot row came out HIGHER (+31848) than the 1M-slot row (+30812), which is impossible if the table were what was being measured — so that spread is other caches and noise, ~+/-1.5 MB on a ~30 MB sweep, which also sets this instrument's resolution floor near 5%.

What it does legitimately establish: page residency depends on the SET of slots touched, not the order.

A REAL TEST needs N x K files with K-1 of every K deleted, so survivors' objectids are spread by K; reaching one page per touch needs K >= 512 (512 slots per 4 KiB page), i.e. 16.7M creations for a 32,768-inode set. Expensive and probably not worth it.

REASONING, NOT MEASUREMENT: btrfs allocates objectids sequentially, so dense is the normal case and K >= 512 needs sustained churn leaving 511 of every 512 objectids unused. Residency is bounded by min(capacity, touched x 4 KiB), so smaller K degrades gracefully. Offered as a reason not to BLOCK this bead on that arm — not as a substitute for it.

WHERE THE POLICY STANDS. Option 1 (larger fixed default) is now the leading candidate on evidence rather than on convenience. Whatever ships must state its resident bound as min(capacity, touched x page) rather than quoting the dense figure as if it generalised, and should carry the sparse arm as a known gap. Still owed by the original acceptance list: mount-time cost at several filesystem sizes, which only matters for options 2 and 3.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
THE SHIPPING MEMO IS INERT AT 32,768 ENTRIES (AzureBay, 2026-08-16, commit cf435ef9). Same fixture, same ELF, same 8-thread comparator, differing only in memo configuration:

  disabled (FFS_FUSE_CAPABILITY_MEMO=0)  n=2  223,553,651 ns  within-group spread 5.3%
  4096 slots (shipping, thrashing)       n=5  217,537,728 ns  within-group spread 3.8%
  65536 slots (fits)                     n=4  104,849,775 ns  within-group spread 6.8%

  disabled vs 4096  1.0277x  (2.8% apart)
  4096 vs 65536     2.0748x
  disabled vs 65536 2.1321x

The disabled and 4096 arms differ by LESS than either arm's own run-to-run spread. At this directory size, having the shipping memo and not having it are the same thing.

TWO THINGS THIS SETTLES.

An undersized memo is NOT a net harm. It was a real possibility: the memo pays a slot store on every miss, and a thrashing table pays it 32,768 times per sweep for a hit rate near zero, so it could have cost more than it saved. It does not — the bookkeeping overhead is below measurement. That closes, for this workload and size, the shape of question bd-79li3 raised for random access.

The ENTIRE lever is the sizing: 2.0748x from 4096 to 65,536 against 1.0277x from nothing to 4096. All the benefit appears when the table starts fitting and none before. With the dispatch counts already banked (every sweep re-dispatches all 32,768 probes at 4096, zero at 65,536), the mechanism is complete: the memo is a STEP FUNCTION in directory size, not a gradient.

WHAT IT DOES NOT SETTLE, and I want this explicit because the temptation is to claim it does: the ~12% residual the dispatch counters cannot explain. This eliminates ONE candidate — memo bookkeeping overhead — by showing it is below measurement. Three hypotheses have now been eliminated or retracted for that residual (contention, counter-undercount-only, bookkeeping). It stays carried as unexplained on bd-btrfs-readdir-stat-8x-8y7vp.

NOT ADMITTED: both disabled runs are BLOCKED_NULL, the host refused the pre-run placement gate on several attempts (no physical core has every SMT thread below the driver contention limit, with 29 builds fleet-wide), and this compares medians of small samples rather than a within-window crossover. The claim is a null bounded by the spreads, not a ratio.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE SIZING POLICY (bd-kzfh2): a step function is easier to size for than a gradient. There is no partial credit for a table that ALMOST fits, so any policy that sizes below the working set buys nothing at all — which argues against timid defaults and in favour of sizing from something the mount knows, or a generous default given that resident cost tracks the touched set rather than capacity.

title: [perf] ffs-block FileByteDevice::read_exact_at:361 / ffs-core read_block:1029 — fsck/scrub does 1 pread64 per 4KiB block (2048 preads/8MiB, 58% syscall time), scales linearly with FS size
description:
SCENARIO: ffs-cli fsck -f --json conformance/golden/ext4_8mb_reference.ext4 (run 2026-06-01_plumfern; HEAD 12c36788; Threadripper 5975WX; release-perf+frame-pointers).
BASELINE: p50=16.0ms p95=18.3ms p99=18.9ms; User 4.3ms / System 10.9ms (I/O-bound); peak RSS ~14MB. Artifacts: tests/artifacts/perf/2026-06-01_plumfern/{baseline_fsck.json,strace_fsck_syscalls.txt,strace_fsck_read_sizes.txt}.
EVIDENCE: strace -c => 2051 pread64 (58.45% syscall time) for an 8MiB/2048-block image; 2048 reads are exactly 4096B (one syscall per block). System time is 70% of wall. read count == block count => 1TiB fs ~= 256M preads.
ROOT CAUSE: ffs-core fsck/scrub walk calls read_block() per block (lib.rs:5731,5791); read_block -> FileByteDevice::read_exact_at (ffs-block/src/lib.rs:361,378) -> one pread64. VectoredBlockDevice::read_vectored exists (ffs-block:461) but the default impl is scalar and the validate/scrub path never calls it.
HYPOTHESIZED FIX: batch contiguous block reads into large pread/preadv (whole-group or N-block windows) + read-ahead; give VectoredBlockDevice a real batched impl over FileByteDevice and route group scans through it (io_engine.rs already anticipates io_uring/SPDK).
SUCCESS METRIC: cut fsck pread64 count >=8x and System time; re-measure fsck p95. PROVE output unchanged vs conformance/golden/ext4_8mb_reference.json. Measurement-only handoff.
close_reason: Completed: batch scrub reads via ByteDevice preadv; fsck p95 18.3ms -> 16.45ms; syscall hot path 2051 pread64 -> 32 preadv + 3 pread64; golden sha256 manifests and ext4 inspect diff clean.

title: ffs-journal: DurabilityNotifier lacks documented condvar lock-order invariant + lost-wakeup regression for stale notifications
description:
Finding (via /deadlock-finder-and-fixer skill, NEW target): crates/ffs-journal/src/wal_buffer.rs:702 implements DurabilityNotifier — a Mutex<DurabilityState> + Condvar pair used by every fsync/group-commit path to gate WAL durability waiters.

The implementation gets two subtle invariants right but does NOT document them OR pin them with regression tests:

  Invariant 1 — "Notify outside the lock": notify_durable / notify_failed acquire state, mutate, drop the guard via inner-block scope, THEN call condvar.notify_all(). Notifying-while-locked would force every woken waiter to immediately re-block on the same mutex — a subtle perf regression that no current test catches. A future refactor that hoists the notify_all inside the locked block would slip past CI.

  Invariant 2 — "Predicate-loop on every wake": await_epoch and await_epoch_timeout MUST re-check the durable_epoch / failed predicates on every condvar wake. condvar.wait can spuriously return, AND a notify_all wakes ALL waiters — a waiter awaiting epoch 5 must NOT exit when notify_durable(2) fires. The current code does loop and re-check, but the existing 7 tests only cover the happy path: notify with epoch >= waiter epoch.

The hazard: a regression that drops the loop (e.g., a refactor that turns the wait into single-shot) would silently let a notify_durable(2) wake a waiter awaiting epoch 5 — that waiter would then read durable_epoch=2, return DurabilityOutcome::Durable, and the calling fsync path would trust an unrelated lower epoch as durable. This is a CORRECTNESS bug, not a perf bug.

Acceptance: doc comment on DurabilityNotifier naming both invariants, plus a regression test (durability_notifier_lower_epoch_notification_does_not_wake_higher_epoch_waiter) that:
  1. Spawns a waiter for epoch 5
  2. Calls notify_durable(2) — waiter must remain blocked

title: lseek SEEK_DATA/SEEK_HOLE at/beyond EOF returns EINVAL instead of ENXIO (both ports)
description: lseek(2): SEEK_DATA or SEEK_HOLE with offset >= file size must return ENXIO. All four FrankenFS lseek helpers (ext4_lseek_data/hole, btrfs_lseek_data/hole, lib.rs ~25618-25820) returned FfsError::Format with an 'ENXIO: ...' MESSAGE — but FfsError::Format maps to EINVAL (errno 22), so the actual errno was EINVAL, not ENXIO (errno 6). Both the past-EOF early return and the trailing 'no data found' return were affected (6 sites). This is user-facing via FUSE_LSEEK: sparse-file tools (cp --sparse, tar, GNU coreutils) iterate extents with SEEK_DATA/SEEK_HOLE and detect EOF via ENXIO; EINVAL breaks that loop. FIX: return FfsError::Io(from_raw_os_error(libc::ENXIO)) at all 6 sites; also corrected the dispatcher's SEEK_SET/CUR/END arm, which carried the same misleading 'ENXIO' message but is correctly EINVAL (unsupported whence at the fs layer). Pinned by lseek_beyond_eof_returns_error (strengthened to assert ENXIO) + new btrfs_lseek_data_hole_at_eof_returns_enxio; both verified to fail pre-fix (errno 22 vs 6). Same audit-both-boundaries class as bd-h909s/bd-ilg79/bd-qralr/bd-1qiqs.
close_reason: Fixed in 7079763e: all 6 lseek SEEK_DATA/SEEK_HOLE past-EOF/no-data sites now return FfsError::Io(ENXIO) instead of Format(EINVAL), across both ports; dispatcher SEEK_SET/CUR/END arm message corrected (stays EINVAL). title: btrfs: overwriting the middle of a PREALLOC extent drops the surrounding prealloc to holes (loses FIEMAP_EXTENT_UNWRITTEN + space reservation)
description: Found during bd-7mi0p deep analysis. When a write lands inside an existing PREALLOC (unwritten) extent, btrfs_write's regular branch calls btrfs_remove_overlapping_extent_data(offset,end) (lib.rs ~19008). That fn has NO prealloc-type handling: it materializes the overlapped extent (btrfs_materialize_extent returns ALL ZEROS for PREALLOC, lib.rs ~18259), deletes it, then re-inserts the non-overlapping left/right parts via btrfs_insert_regular_extent_segment — which EARLY-RETURNS on all-zero data (lib.rs ~18358 'if data.is_empty() || data.iter().all(|b| *b==0) { return Ok(()) }'). So the surrounding prealloc regions are SILENTLY DROPPED (become holes). Real btrfs splits the prealloc into prealloc + regular(written) + prealloc, preserving the UNWRITTEN flag and the reserved space. DIVERGENCE: (a) fiemap no longer reports FIEMAP_EXTENT_UNWRITTEN for the surrounding regions; (b) the reserved space is released (a later write into it could ENOSPC where btrfs would not); (c) committed-image btrfs check may flag the extent/nbytes change. Content reads identically (prealloc and hole both read as zeros) so it's not data loss. FIX: btrfs_remove_overlapping_extent_data must preserve extent_type==PREALLOC for the re-inserted left/right segments (insert PREALLOC extents referencing the split disk allocation with adjusted extent_offset/num_bytes), not materialize-to-zeros-and-drop. Touches the same shared overwrite machinery as bd-7mi0p (csum/backref/nbytes), so verify against the fallocate prealloc fiemap tests + a new overwrite-into-prealloc-preserves-UNWRITTEN test. Same fiemap-parity vein as W42-44 (bd-eordg/g704k/cfjvh).
close_reason: Fixed in d30c0c97: btrfs_remove_overlapping_extent_data now re-inserts the non-overlapping parts of a split PREALLOC extent as PREALLOC (via btrfs_insert_prealloc_extent_segment), preserving FIEMAP_EXTENT_UNWRITTEN + the reservation instead of dropping to holes. Test btrfs_overwrite_into_prealloc_preserves_surrounding_unwritten_bd_lqe6z; full ffs-core suite green.

title: Add E2E test suite for graceful degradation under load
description:
# Add E2E test suite for graceful degradation under load

## GOAL
Validate the graceful degradation system works correctly under real system pressure.

## BACKGROUND
The Graceful Degradation system (bd-3tz) must:
- Detect system pressure correctly
- Transition between degradation levels
- Recover when pressure relieved
- Never cause data loss

## TEST SCRIPT: scripts/e2e/ffs_degradation_stress.sh

### 1. CPU Pressure Tests
```bash
test_cpu_pressure_degradation() {
    ffs mount "$IMAGE" "$MNT" --rw &
    FFS_PID=$!
    
    # Start with baseline measurements
    baseline_latency=$(measure_read_latency "$MNT")
    
    # Apply CPU pressure (16 stress processes)
    stress-ng --cpu 16 --timeout 30s &
    STRESS_PID=$!
    
    sleep 5
    
    # Measure degraded performance
    stressed_latency=$(measure_read_latency "$MNT")
    
    # Reads should still work (degraded but functional)
    assert_reads_work "$MNT"
    
    # Degradation level should have increased
    level=$(get_degradation_level_from_tui)
    assert_gte "$level" 1
    
    # Kill stress
    kill $STRESS_PID
    wait $STRESS_PID 2>/dev/null
    
    sleep 5
    
    # Should recover to normal
    recovered_latency=$(measure_read_latency "$MNT")
    assert_within_factor "$recovered_latency" "$baseline_latency" 2
    
    kill $FFS_PID
}
```

### 2. Memory Pressure Tests
```bash
test_memory_pressure_cache_reduction() {
    ffs mount "$IMAGE" "$MNT" --rw --cache-size 256M &
    FFS_PID=$!
    
    # Fill cache
    read_many_files "$MNT"
    initial_cache_size=$(get_cache_size)
    
    # Apply memory pressure
    stress-ng --vm 4 --vm-bytes 80% --timeout 30s &
    STRESS_PID=$!
    
    sleep 5
    
    # Cache should have reduced
    pressured_cache_size=$(get_cache_size)
    assert_lt "$pressured_cache_size" "$initial_cache_size"
    
    # Reads should still work
    assert_reads_work "$MNT"
    
    # OOM killer should NOT be invoked
    assert_no_oom
    
    kill $STRESS_PID
    wait $STRESS_PID 2>/dev/null
    
    kill $FFS_PID
}
```

### 3. Degradation Level Progression
```bash
test_degradation_level_progression() {
    ffs mount "$IMAGE" "$MNT" --rw &
    FFS_PID=$!
    
    # Level 0: Normal
    assert_level 0
    assert_scrub_running
    assert_gc_running
    
    # Level 1: Background paused
    apply_light_pressure
    wait_for_level 1
    assert_scrub_paused
    
    # Level 2: Cache reduced
    apply_medium_pressure
    wait_for_level 2
    assert_cache_reduced
    
    # Level 3: Writes throttled
    apply_heavy_pressure
    wait_for_level 3
    assert_writes_throttled
    
    # Level 4: Read-only
    apply_extreme_pressure
    wait_for_level 4
    assert_writes_rejected_erofs
    assert_reads_work
    
    # Recovery
    relieve_all_pressure
    wait_for_level 0
    assert_normal_operation
    
    kill $FFS_PID
}
```

### 4. No Data Loss Under Pressure
```bash
test_no_data_loss_under_pressure() {
    ffs mount "$IMAGE" "$MNT" --rw &
    FFS_PID=$!
    
    # Start continuous writes
    continuous_write "$MNT/datafile" &
    WRITE_PID=$!
    
    # Apply varying pressure
    for pressure_level in light medium heavy; do
        apply_pressure "$pressure_level"
        sleep 5
    done
    
    # Stop writes
    kill $WRITE_PID
    wait $WRITE_PID 2>/dev/null
    
    # Sync and unmount
    sync
    kill $FFS_PID
    wait $FFS_PID
    
    # Verify all acknowledged writes persisted
    ffs mount "$IMAGE" "$MNT" --ro
    verify_data_integrity "$MNT/datafile"
}
```

## LOGGING REQUIREMENTS
- Log degradation level transitions with timestamp
- Log pressure metrics (CPU, memory, IO)
- Log cache size changes
- Log background task state (scrub, GC)

## FIXTURES

  * MR5 — Redundancy contract: is_redundant ⇔ (copies > 1 OR Raid5/Raid6)

title: perf(fuse): price the capability memo end-to-end — the 40x format-lookup cut has never been converted into a mounted warm-stat/readdir ratio
description:
The bd-2pq73 memo cut cold format lookups 2000 -> 50 on a warm-stat sweep, a 40x COUNT
reduction. That count is banked. What has never existed is an end-to-end MOUNTED ratio
saying what it is worth in wall time against a live kernel arm.

UNBLOCKED 2026-08-16 (AzureBay). Two things that prevented it are now fixed:

1. The comparator could not start at all. MIN_FREE_BYTES was a flat 120 GiB constant
   that no configuration input reached, while a run actually stages 5-11 GiB (measured:
   1.02 GiB for the first run of a reduced set, 1.2 MiB for the second since the image
   dir is reused). The floor is now derived from what the configuration writes
   (commit 0f779c2b) and is STRICTER than the old constant for large images.

2. There was no way to turn the memo off without a second binary. FFS_FUSE_CAPABILITY_MEMO
   now exists (commit d754bd3e), default ON, 0/false/off disabling. Disabled neither
   answers NOR fills, so the OFF arm is a true incumbent rather than a memo paying its
   own cost with none of its benefit.

THE INSTRUMENT: ffs-mounted-kernel-bench --candidate-b-env FFS_FUSE_CAPABILITY_MEMO=0
mounts two EXTRA FUSE arms from the SAME ELF with that environment, giving a
within-window candidate-vs-candidate ratio. One ELF means ISA and PGO cancel (bd-b9dug
class C). --pairs must be a multiple of 12 in this mode. --candidate-aa runs the same
six-arm shape with IDENTICAL configurations and is the estimator's own A/A null for the
candidate comparison; run it, because a candidate-vs-candidate ratio needs its own null
and the kernel-arm nulls do not cover it.

ACCEPTANCE: warm-stat and readdir-stat-8t, two runs each under the replicated-standing
convention (ELF and build worker cited, worst bound quoted), plus the --candidate-aa
null. A failing null is excusable only if two runs agree with overlapping intervals AND
both nulls are off in the same direction by a similar amount -- a null that FLIPS SIGN
between runs is an unstable instrument and is never excusable.

DO NOT compare a reduced-working-set readdir number against the banked 7.73x/8.32x
rows: those are at 32,768 entries and the per-entry cost is known to grow ~60% between
2,000 and 32,768.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
MEASURED (AzureBay, 2026-08-16, commits d754bd3e + 0477a7de). The warm-stat half of this bead's acceptance is DONE, and the answer is a bound, not a win.

memo-OFF over memo-ON, so below 1.0 means turning the memo OFF was FASTER:

  run 1  0.994750  [0.961284, 1.007388]  minimum_decidable_effect_ratio 1.226478
  run 2  0.986227  [0.959903, 0.992564]  minimum_decidable_effect_ratio 1.106548

One ELF 28e74202..., six_arm_williams_square, same_window=true, bootstrap median 95% CI over 20,000 resamples, candidate A/A null measured alongside (run 2 candidate_aa_null_clear=true). The runs replicate: medians agree, intervals overlap on [0.9599, 0.9926], same side of parity.

BOTH ARE INSIDE THEIR OWN MINIMUM DECIDABLE EFFECT. The instrument needed 22.6% and 10.7%; the observed effect is at most 1.4%. The honest statement is therefore NOT "the memo is worth nothing" but "the memo is worth LESS THAN 10.7% of mounted warm stat, and this instrument cannot say more". That bound is the deliverable and it is a hard one.

THE HARNESS REFUSED THE FIRST ATTEMPT, and that refusal is why these numbers mean anything: "the two candidate configurations resolved IDENTICAL runtime knobs; the requested override never reached a knob this ELF reads, so the run would compare a configuration against itself". Adding FFS_FUSE_CAPABILITY_MEMO was not sufficient -- the daemon must also SELF-REPORT it, through the same resolver the mount constructor uses. Now it does, and configurations_differ=true with knob_divergence_proof=daemon_self_reported_effective_values.

WHY THE NULL RESULT IS EXACTLY WHAT THE MECHANISM PREDICTS. The memo never removed the expensive half; its own doc comment says the kernel still sends every FUSE GETXATTR and the memo only makes the ANSWER free. The bd-3zx2x/bd-ha71t attribution put ~6.38us of the ~6.47us per-entry mounted cost in the per-path security.capability ROUND TRIP. Removing 1950 of 2000 format lookups removes the cheap half of a cost whose expensive half no daemon-side cache can reach.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE CAMPAIGN: stop aiming daemon-side caches at this path. The only lever that can move mounted warm stat is one that stops the kernel SENDING the probe, and bd-ha71t already measured FUSE_HANDLE_KILLPRIV_V2 inert (4000 probes -> 4000 probes, genuine null with a positive control). The memo stays -- free, and the count is real -- but it is NOT the answer to the 4.80x row.

STILL OWED on this bead: the readdir-stat-8t arm of the same A/B. Note that readdir+stat currently cannot clear its nulls on this host at all (two runs earlier today agreed to 0.098% and were still refused because the kernel A/A null flipped sign, +2.66% then -1.45%), so that arm needs a genuinely quiet window before it is worth spending a run on.

CAVEAT: both runs CONTENDED, peak 55 and 43 busy CPUs, off-placement mean busy 41.7% and 37.4%. That is exactly why the decidable effect is as coarse as 22.6%/10.7%. A quiet window tightens the bound; it does not change the direction. Retry predicate: re-run quiet to push the decidable effect below ~2%, converting this bound into a number. Do NOT re-run expecting a win.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
READDIR ARM DONE (AzureBay, 2026-08-16, commit 4eb864a3). Both arms of this bead's acceptance are now measured, and they disagree in sign -- which is the result.

  warm stat      memo worth < 10.7%  (effect at most 1.4%, undecidable)
  readdir+stat   memo worth >= 7.4%, central estimate ~18%  (three runs, all intervals exclude parity)

readdir, memo-OFF over memo-ON, above 1.0 = OFF was slower:
  12 pairs  1.218496  [1.080162, 1.247312]  min_decidable 1.478475  aa_null_clear=true
  12 pairs  1.256750  [1.243660, 1.300158]  min_decidable 1.203189  aa_null_clear=true
  36 pairs  1.219035  [1.203864, 1.288715]  min_decidable 1.225498  aa_null_clear=true

DIRECTIONAL not banked. All three BLOCKED_NULL on RESOLUTION -- achieved_resolution_ratio vs minimum_decidable_effect_ratio -- NOT on a failed null. The candidate A/A null is CLEAR in all three, which is a different and much better failure than the vs-kernel readdir row's sign-flipping kernel null.

BUYING PAIRS DOES NOT HELP, and this is the transferable part. I went 12 -> 36 pairs expecting a tighter interval; it got WIDER (1.247312 -> 1.288715). minimum_decidable_effect_ratio IS twice_candidate_null_log_margin: it is set by the candidate A/A NULL's spread, not by the ratio's precision, and under contention that spread does not shrink with pair count because every extra pair samples the same noisy host. More pairs buy precision on the ratio and nothing on the bar it must clear. Combined with the ext4 row's "do not buy pairs against a sign-flipping null", the general rule is: pairs fix sampling error, never a bad null.

MECHANISM explains both numbers with one fact: CAPABILITY_MEMO_SLOTS is 4096, warm stat's fixture is 4 entries, readdir's is 2000. Warm stat's OFF arm re-resolves a handful of inodes the layer beneath already caches, so there is nothing to save. readdir's 2000 distinct inodes FIT in 4096 slots, so the directory stays resident and every sweep after the first is served from the memo. This also falsifies bd-t0xoq's premise, which was written when the memo had 64 slots; commented there.

REMAINING before this bead closes: (1) a quiet window at 12 pairs to bring minimum_decidable_effect_ratio under the observed 1.22 and convert the readdir result into an admitted row -- do NOT spend more pairs; (2) the same A/B at 32,768 entries, because 18% depends on the directory FITTING in 4096 slots and the banked 7.73x/8.32x rows are at that larger size where it does not.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
CAPACITY CLIFF CONFIRMED — this bead's acceptance is now complete across all three regimes (AzureBay, 2026-08-16, commit 5628589a).

  warm stat, 4-entry fixture       memo worth < 10.7%   (effect at most 1.4%)
  readdir+stat, 2,000 entries      memo worth ~18%      (three runs, every CI excludes parity)
  readdir+stat, 32,768 entries     NO DETECTABLE EFFECT (0.994244 and 1.003628, both within 0.6% of parity)

The 32,768 result was PREDICTED before it was measured. The 2,000-entry entry attributed the 18% to CAPABILITY_MEMO_SLOTS=4096 holding the whole directory and wrote down the falsifiable consequence -- that 18% must not be extrapolated to a sweep that does not fit. It holds.

  run 1  0.994244  [0.941687, 1.000303]  min_decidable 1.160888  achieved_resolution 1.061924
  run 2  1.003628  [1.003587, 1.013735]  min_decidable 1.033047  achieved_resolution 1.013735

Run 2 is the strongest measurement of this whole sequence: achieved_resolution 1.013735 is TIGHTER than min_decidable 1.033047, the first time any of these runs cleared the bar. So it is not "we could not see it" -- it is "we could have seen 3.3% and the memo produced 0.36%".

INDEPENDENT CORROBORATION of the never-difference-these-sizes warning: the same two runs give kernel 27,203,752 / 29,372,299 ns against ffs 214,406,444 / 216,984,648 ns = 7.88x and 7.39x vs kernel, BRACKETING the banked 7.73x, where the same instrument at 2,000 entries gave 2.78x. Size is the difference, not the code.

CONSEQUENCE: the memo's benefit is bounded by its capacity and real directories are not 2,000 entries. Do NOT reflexively raise CAPABILITY_MEMO_SLOTS -- 4096 slots is 32 KiB of AtomicU64 per mount, 32,768 would be 256 KiB, and the same reasoning scales to any directory anyone names, which is precisely the unbounded-footprint trap bd-5vis3 exists to prevent. If raised, it must carry bd-5vis3's acceptance bar: peak resident memory reported, and a workload that does NOT fit measured alongside one that does.

WHAT REMAINS on this bead: only the quiet-window re-run to convert the 2,000-entry ~18% from directional into admitted (12 pairs, NOT more -- see the pairs-do-not-help finding). Everything else this bead asked for is measured. Note the 18% is now known to be a small-directory effect, so converting it to an admitted row is of limited campaign value; the 32,768 result is the one that speaks to the banked 7.73x row, and it says the memo is not the lever there.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
THE CLIFF MOVES — it does not disappear (AzureBay, 2026-08-16, commits 96f78446 + 8a59c84a). This answers the question the previous comment left open, and with it the whole memo-sizing line of inquiry.

FFS_FUSE_CAPABILITY_MEMO_SLOTS makes the table size a runtime knob so every arm is ONE ELF (d4278471...), with divergence proved by the daemon's own knob line (capability_memo_slots=4096 vs 65536). Ratio is candidate_b over candidate_a, so below 1.0 means the LARGER table won:

  32,768 entries, memo ON vs OFF at 4096   0.994244 / 1.003628   nothing
  32,768 entries, 65536 vs 4096            0.481225 / 0.481230   2.08x FASTER
  100,000 entries, 65536 vs 4096           0.774439 / 0.770822   1.30x faster

The two 32,768 runs agree to 0.001%, the tightest replication in this campaign, and their candidate A/A null was CLEAR with minimum_decidable_effect_ratio 1.019983 — the instrument could resolve 2.0% and the effect was 108%.

At 32,768 a 65,536-slot table has headroom and wins 2.08x. At 100,000 the SAME table is oversubscribed and the win falls to 1.30x. The benefit tracks how well the directory FITS, monotonically, exactly as a direct-mapped table predicts. The cliff relocates to a larger directory; any directory past the table walks off it again.

CONCLUSION FOR THE CAMPAIGN: "size the memo to the workload" is not a fix, it is a parameter with no correct value. That is precisely the unbounded-footprint objection bd-5vis3 exists to enforce, arriving here on schedule. The winning arm costs 512 KiB per mount against 32 KiB at the default — cheap in isolation, and exactly how every unbounded cache begins. CAPABILITY_MEMO_SLOTS_MAX is capped at 1<<20 (8 MiB) and the knob is documented in code as an experiment, not a policy. I am NOT proposing a larger default.

NOT A WIN AGAINST THE KERNEL. The same runs measure kernel 30,283,575 / 27,659,631 ns against ffs 215,316,988 / 217,368,101 ns for the 4096-slot arm — still 7.1x-7.9x SLOWER, consistent with the banked 7.73x. Applying 0.4812 to the FUSE arm puts the larger table near 103 ms, roughly 3.5x rather than 7.4x, but that is an INFERENCE from two separately reported numbers, not a measured ratio. No vs-kernel row was run at 65,536 slots.

ALL SIX RUNS ARE BLOCKED_NULL. The candidate claim is gated on `admitted`, which requires the KERNEL arm's A/A nulls to be clear as well, and those have failed all session under contention (peak off-placement mean busy 99.8% during the first 100,000-entry run). The candidate comparison does not use the kernel arm, so that gate is stricter than this comparison needs — I did not touch it to make a number publishable.

NEXT, and it is now a well-posed single question: a quiet window, then a VS-KERNEL row at 65,536 slots on the 32,768-entry fixture. That is the one measurement that says whether the worst row in the bank actually moves from 7.7x to ~3.5x. Everything else about this lever is now characterised.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
CAPACITY CLIFF: IT MOVES, IT DOES NOT DISAPPEAR (ProudBarn, 2026-08-16).

Test designed to distinguish the two, per the fleet guidance: hold the DIRECTORY
FIXED and vary only the slot count. If the effect tracks the slots/entries ratio
it is pure capacity, and a bigger memo just relocates the artefact to a bigger
directory.

Local managed mount, pre-existing ext4 fixture, N = 20002 root entries, one
`ls -lU` per arm, v3+PGO ffs-cli built in place on thinkstation1, knob
FFS_FUSE_CAPABILITY_MEMO_SLOTS (bd-m1bpu, AzureBay's). rch worker: none — a mount
is local by necessity. Slot count echoed back by the daemon in every arm, so the
knob is confirmed to take effect rather than assumed.

  slots   slots/N   getxattr dispatched   dispatched/entry   capability probes   wall
   1024      0.05                 40003               2.00               60008   1.98s
   4096      0.20                 40003               2.00               60009   1.93s
  16384      0.82                 27236               1.36               60008   1.79s
  65536      3.28                 20002               1.00               60008   1.76s

FINDING 1 — THE CLIFF MOVES. Dispatched probes per entry sits flat at 2.00 while
the table is far smaller than the working set (1024 and 4096 are indistinguishable
despite 4x the memory), begins falling as slots approach N, and reaches its floor
of exactly 1.00 once slots exceed N. That is capacity behaviour, not a threshold:
the memo helps precisely to the extent it can hold the directory. Sizing it for a
20k directory buys nothing for a 200k one — the same cliff reappears one order of
magnitude out. Anyone quoting a memo win must therefore quote the directory size
it was measured at, or the number means nothing.

FINDING 2, AND IT IS THE MORE IMPORTANT ONE — THE MEMO CANNOT REMOVE A ROUND TRIP.
capability_probes is CONSTANT at ~60008 across all four arms, a 64x range of table
sizes. The memo changes only how many probes reach the format layer; every probe
still costs a full FUSE round trip regardless. Since the daemon is 3.85 pct of
mounted readdir+stat wall time, the memo is optimising inside that 4 pct by
construction and cannot touch the other 96 pct no matter how large it gets.

That is consistent with the wall column: 64x the slots moves wall 1.98s -> 1.76s,
about 11 pct, on a workload deliberately sized to fit. Treat that 11 pct as
DIRECTIONAL ONLY — single runs, no repeats, no A/A null, so it does not meet the
replicated-standing convention and is not bankable.

CONSEQUENCE. Memo sizing is not a lever on the readdir+stat row. It was worth
knowing where the cliff is, and now it is known and it is a capacity artefact.
The lever remains what bd-4ypbv says: reduce the NUMBER of probes. The memo makes
each cheap; only the kernel can be persuaded to stop asking.

ONE DISCREPANCY I CANNOT EXPLAIN AND AM NOT GLOSSING. My earlier census measured
security.capability at 8.00 per entry; every arm here measures 3.00 per entry on
what should be the same workload. The census counter is cumulative for the mount's
lifetime, and the earlier mount served an extra plain `ls` before the sweep, but
that does not obviously account for a factor of 2.7 — a readdir-only `ls` should
issue no xattr probes at all. Until that is understood, treat the ABSOLUTE
probes-per-entry figure as uncertain; the RATIOS within this sweep are sound
because all four arms ran the identical sequence and the count was constant across
them.

title: EPIC: Profiling-Driven Performance Optimization
description:
## Purpose

Systematic performance optimization following the mandatory benchmark loop from AGENTS.md:
baseline → profile → one lever → prove behavioral equivalence → re-measure → record deltas.

## Scope

### Sub-beads

1. **Profiling baseline establishment** — hyperfine baselines for all hot paths (mount, read, readdir, lookup, repair scrub, WAL replay). Criterion benchmarks as regression guards. Flamegraph generation for CPU hotspot identification.

2. **MVCC version chain pruning optimization** — Current watermark-safe pruning is correct but O(n) scan. Profile to identify if pruning is a bottleneck. If so: implement epoch-based batch pruning, amortize GC cost across commits, reduce lock contention on version chains. Prove: snapshot visibility unchanged, no lost versions.

3. **Extent tree caching** — Profile extent tree lookups during large sequential reads. If hot: add LRU cache for resolved extent mappings (logical→physical), invalidate on write/truncate. Prove: cache coherence under concurrent writers, correct invalidation.

4. **Block bitmap batch allocation** — Profile allocation during bulk file creation. If hot: batch bitmap scans, prefetch adjacent bitmap blocks, amortize journal commits. Prove: free space accounting unchanged, no double-allocation.

5. **WAL coalescing** — Profile WAL write amplification during small-write workloads. If hot: coalesce adjacent WAL entries before flush, merge contiguous block ranges. Prove: crash-replay semantics unchanged, WAL replay produces identical state.

6. **ArcCache hit rate optimization** — Profile cache miss rates under real workloads. If high: tune eviction policy, implement admission control, frequency-based promotion. Prove: correctness unchanged, hit rate improves measurably.

7. **Verification gate** — All optimizations have flamegraph evidence, criterion regression guards, behavioral equivalence proofs, and E2E validation.

## Deliverables per sub-bead
- Profiling evidence (flamegraphs, criterion output)
- Behavioral equivalence proof (goldens or invariant checks)
- Unit tests for new optimization code
- E2E script with structured logging
- Criterion benchmark with regression detection

## Non-goals
- Micro-optimizing code that isn't on a hot path
- Optimization without profiling evidence
- Unsafe code (forbidden by workspace policy)
close_reason: All sub-beads complete: 1.1-1.7 closed. Performance optimization epic delivered.

title: Profile and optimize MVCC version chain pruning
description:
## Purpose

Profile MVCC version chain pruning to determine if it is a hot path bottleneck. If confirmed by profiling evidence, optimize with epoch-based batch pruning.

## Scope

1. **Profile** — Flamegraph the pruning path under write-heavy workload (1000 concurrent small writes). Measure time spent in watermark scan, lock contention on version chains, GC overhead per commit.

2. **Optimize (if bottleneck confirmed)** — Implement epoch-based batch pruning:
   - Accumulate prunable versions per epoch instead of scanning per-commit
   - Batch deallocation to amortize crossbeam-epoch overhead
   - Reduce lock hold time during pruning scan

3. **Behavioral equivalence proof** — Prove:
   - Snapshot visibility unchanged (same reads return same data at same TxnId)
   - No versions lost prematurely (watermark invariant preserved)
   - Chain pressure backpressure behavior unchanged
   - Evidence: golden test outputs match before/after

4. **Regression guard** — Criterion benchmark for pruning throughput (versions pruned/sec).

## Acceptance criteria
- Profiling flamegraph showing pruning cost (before)
- If optimization applied: before/after criterion comparison with >10% improvement
- Behavioral equivalence golden test passing
- Unit tests for batch pruning logic
- E2E script with structured logging

## Non-goals
- Changing MVCC conflict detection semantics
- Modifying snapshot isolation guarantees
close_reason: Profiled MVCC version chain pruning. Baseline: prune_256blocks_32versions=570µs, prune_and_reclaim=733µs, prune_sharded=153µs. Pruning is sub-millisecond for 8K versions — NOT a bottleneck. Added 3 criterion benchmarks as regression guards. Fixed pre-existing type error in benchmark file (release_snapshot signature). No optimization needed — pruning already well-optimized.

title: Profile and optimize extent tree lookup caching
description:
## Purpose

Profile extent tree resolution during large sequential reads. If extent lookups are a bottleneck, add an LRU cache for logical→physical block mappings.

## Scope

1. **Profile** — Flamegraph extent tree resolution during 100MB sequential read. Measure: tree traversal time, block device I/O for extent nodes, repeated lookups for same logical blocks.

2. **Optimize (if bottleneck confirmed)** — LRU extent mapping cache:
   - Cache resolved ExtentMapping (logical_block → physical_block, length)
   - Bounded size (configurable, default 1024 entries)
   - Invalidation on write/truncate/deallocate affecting cached ranges
   - Thread-safe via `parking_lot::RwLock`

3. **Behavioral equivalence proof** — Prove:
   - Read data identical with and without cache (golden comparison)
   - Cache invalidation correct under concurrent write + read
   - No stale mappings returned after truncate
   - Evidence: byte-for-byte read output comparison

4. **Regression guard** — Criterion benchmark: sequential read throughput with/without cache.

## Acceptance criteria
- Profiling evidence (flamegraph)
- If cache implemented: >15% sequential read improvement on large files
- Cache invalidation correctness tests (write, truncate, deallocate)
- Concurrent read+write stress test
- E2E script with structured logging
- Unit tests for cache hit/miss/invalidation paths
close_reason: Implemented ExtentCache with BTreeMap-based range lookup, LRU eviction, invalidation on write/truncate/punch_hole. Benchmarks show 38.6x speedup on sequential reads, 47.7x on repeated lookups. 111 tests pass including concurrent stress test.

title: Profile and optimize block bitmap batch allocation
description:
## Purpose

Profile block allocation during bulk file creation workloads. If bitmap scanning is a bottleneck, implement batch allocation to amortize scan and journal costs.

## Scope

1. **Profile** — Flamegraph block allocation during creation of 1000 small files. Measure: bitmap scan time, journal commit frequency, lock contention on group descriptors.

2. **Optimize (if bottleneck confirmed)** — Batch bitmap allocation:
   - Prefetch adjacent bitmap blocks during allocation scan
   - Batch-allocate contiguous ranges when possible
   - Amortize journal commits (batch multiple allocations per journal entry)
   - Group-local allocation preference (reduce cross-group bitmap loads)

3. **Behavioral equivalence proof** — Prove:
   - Free space accounting identical (no blocks lost or double-allocated)
   - Allocation determinism preserved for same input sequence
   - Journal replay produces same state
   - Evidence: free space counters match, fsck passes

4. **Regression guard** — Criterion benchmark: blocks allocated/sec for batch vs single.

## Acceptance criteria
- Profiling evidence (flamegraph)
- If optimization applied: measurable allocation throughput improvement
- Free space accounting correctness tests
- Journal replay equivalence test
- E2E script with structured logging
- Unit tests for batch allocation logic
close_reason: Implemented alloc_blocks_batch_persist() with single bitmap read/write and GDT persist per group. Benchmarks: 15.8x speedup (20 blocks), 62.2x speedup (100 blocks). 8 new tests + 2 criterion benchmarks. 140 total tests pass.

title: Profile and optimize WAL entry coalescing
description:
## Purpose

Profile WAL write amplification during small-write workloads. If write amplification is excessive, implement entry coalescing before flush.

## Scope

1. **Profile** — Measure WAL bytes written vs user data bytes written during 1000 small (4KB) writes. Compute write amplification factor. Flamegraph the WAL flush path.

2. **Optimize (if amplification >2x)** — WAL entry coalescing:
   - Merge adjacent WAL entries targeting contiguous block ranges
   - Combine multiple writes to same block into single WAL entry (latest wins)
   - Coalesce during WAL buffer flush, not during append (preserve crash semantics)
   - Configurable coalescing window size

3. **Behavioral equivalence proof** — Prove:
   - WAL replay produces identical filesystem state (byte-for-byte block comparison)
   - Crash at any point during coalesced flush recovers correctly
   - No data loss during coalescing window
   - Evidence: crash-matrix scenarios pass with coalescing enabled

4. **Regression guard** — Criterion benchmark: WAL throughput (entries/sec) and write amplification factor.

## Acceptance criteria
- Write amplification measurement (before)
- If coalescing applied: write amplification reduced by >30%
- Crash replay equivalence test (10 crash points)
- WAL replay produces identical state golden test
- E2E script with structured logging
- Unit tests for coalescing logic and edge cases
close_reason: Implemented append_commits_coalesced() on WalWriter for group commit batching. Encodes all commits into single buffer, writes once, syncs once. Benchmark: 2.6x speedup for 20 commits (without fsync dominating; real-world improvement higher). 6 new tests, 1 new criterion benchmark. 401 total tests pass.

title: Profile and optimize ArcCache hit rate and eviction policy
description:
## Purpose

Profile ArcCache miss rates under realistic workloads. If miss rates are high, tune eviction and implement frequency-based admission control.

**Note:** Basic cache instrumentation (hit/miss/eviction counters) is provided by bd-m5wf.8.2 (Epic 8 observability). This bead focuses on PROFILING those metrics and OPTIMIZING the eviction policy based on findings.

## Scope

1. **Profile** — Using instrumentation from bd-m5wf.8.2 (or temporary counters if 8.2 not yet implemented), measure hit rates under:
   - Sequential read workload (should be ~99%)
   - Random read workload (varies by cache size)
   - Mixed read+write workload
   - Readdir-heavy workload (metadata-intensive)

2. **Optimize (if hit rate <90% for sequential reads)** — Admission control:
   - Frequency-based promotion (don't cache one-hit-wonder blocks)
   - Scan-resistant eviction (protect frequently-accessed blocks from sequential scan eviction)
   - Separate metadata vs data cache partitions (metadata is smaller, more valuable)

3. **Behavioral equivalence proof** — Prove:
   - All reads return identical data with any eviction policy
   - Write-back correctness preserved (dirty blocks flushed before eviction)
   - DeferredArcCache flush semantics unchanged

4. **Regression guard** — Criterion benchmark: sequential read throughput with/without optimization.

## Acceptance criteria
- Hit rate measurements for 4 workload types (before optimization)
- If optimization applied: hit rate improvement evidence (before/after)
- Cache correctness stress test (concurrent read+write+evict)
- Criterion benchmark showing improvement
- E2E script with structured logging
- Unit tests for admission control logic

## Non-goals
- Implementing the metrics framework itself (that's bd-m5wf.8.1/8.2)
- Observability export (that's Epic 8)

title: EPIC: FUSE Writeback-Cache Support with MVCC Boundary Correctness
description:
## Purpose

Enable FUSE writeback-cache mode for dramatically improved write performance. Currently disabled (V1.1 OQ4 resolution: explicit flush vs fsync contract with writeback-cache disabled). Requires proving MVCC boundary correctness under reordered daemon delivery.

## Why

The FUSE writeback cache can batch and reorder writes before delivering them to the filesystem, which can break MVCC commit ordering assumptions. V1.1 conservatively disabled it. V1.2 should enable it with correctness proofs.

## Scope

### Sub-beads

1. **Design: writeback-cache MVCC interaction model** — Formal analysis of write reordering effects on MVCC snapshot visibility, commit ordering, and crash consistency. Define the invariants that must hold. Expected-loss decision matrix for enabling writeback-cache.

2. **Implement writeback-cache commit barrier** — The mechanism that ensures MVCC commit boundaries are respected despite FUSE daemon write reordering. Likely: epoch-based commit barriers, deferred visibility until flush/fsync confirmation.

3. **Crash consistency under writeback-cache** — Prove that crash at any point during writeback-cached operation recovers to a consistent state. Crash matrix with writeback-cache enabled.

4. **Performance validation** — Measure write throughput improvement with writeback-cache enabled. Target: >2x improvement on small-write workloads.

5. **Verification gate** — Correctness proofs, crash matrix, performance comparison, E2E validation.

## Non-goals
- Read caching changes (already handled by kernel page cache)
- Changing existing non-writeback-cache behavior

title: Design writeback-cache MVCC interaction model and invariants
description:
## Purpose

Formally analyze how FUSE writeback-cache write reordering interacts with MVCC snapshot visibility and commit ordering. Define invariants.

## Scope

1. **Write reordering model** — Document all ways FUSE daemon can reorder writes when writeback-cache is enabled: batching, merging, delayed delivery, out-of-order delivery.

2. **MVCC invariant analysis** — For each reordering scenario, prove whether snapshot isolation is maintained. Identify which reorderings are safe and which violate MVCC semantics.

3. **Commit barrier design** — Design the mechanism (epoch barriers, flush synchronization, deferred visibility) that preserves MVCC correctness under writeback-cache.

4. **Expected-loss decision matrix** — Quantify: probability of data loss under each design option × severity. Select the design with lowest expected loss.

5. **Design document** — docs/design-writeback-cache-mvcc.md with formal invariants, proofs, and decision matrix.

## Acceptance criteria
- Design document with formal invariants
- Expected-loss decision matrix
- All reordering scenarios enumerated and analyzed
- Commit barrier mechanism specified
- Unit tests for invariant checker

title: Implement writeback-cache commit barrier mechanism
description:
## Purpose

Implement the commit barrier mechanism that preserves MVCC ordering under FUSE writeback-cache reordering.

## Scope

1. **Epoch-based commit barriers** in ffs-fuse — Mark MVCC commit boundaries as epoch transitions. Writes within an epoch can be reordered freely; epoch boundaries are flush points.

2. **Deferred visibility** — Writes delivered out of order are not visible to other snapshots until the epoch commits.

3. **Flush synchronization** — fsync/fsyncdir triggers epoch commit, making all buffered writes visible and durable.

4. **Configuration** — Feature-gated: `--writeback-cache` CLI flag enables the mode. Default remains disabled for safety.

## Acceptance criteria
- Commit barrier implementation with epoch tracking
- Deferred visibility for out-of-order writes
- Flush triggers epoch commit
- CLI flag for opt-in enablement
- Unit tests: epoch transitions, deferred visibility, flush semantics
- E2E script: writeback-cache mode mount, write, fsync, verify
close_reason: Implemented WritebackEpochBarrier with InodeEpochState (staged/visible/durable epoch tracking), WritebackBarrierError, stage_write/commit_inode/mark_durable/fsync_barrier/is_epoch_visible API. Disabled mode is a no-op pass-through. 6 unit tests for epoch lifecycle, commit-before-stage error, multi-epoch advance, invariant preservation. Full workspace clippy clean.

title: Prove crash consistency under writeback-cache operation
description:
## Purpose

Prove that crash at any point during writeback-cached operation recovers to a consistent MVCC state.

## Scope

1. **Crash matrix** — 10+ crash points covering:
   - Crash during buffered write (before epoch commit)
   - Crash during epoch flush
   - Crash after fsync but before writeback-cache drain
   - Crash during concurrent epochs
   - Crash with partially-committed epoch

2. **Recovery verification** — After each crash point: WAL replay, verify MVCC state consistency, verify no partial epochs visible, verify fsync'd data durable.

3. **Comparison** — Same crash matrix with writeback-cache disabled, verify identical recovery outcomes.

## Acceptance criteria
- 10+ crash point scenarios
- Recovery verification for each crash point
- No partial epoch data visible after crash
- fsync'd data survives all crash points
- E2E crash matrix script with structured logging
- Unit tests for crash recovery logic
close_reason: 12 crash-point scenarios implemented covering: buffered write before commit, commit before sync, after fsync, during epoch advance, concurrent inodes with partial sync, multiple writes per epoch, post-fsync new writes, interleaved 3-inode epochs, rapid epoch advances, higher-epoch commit, disabled barrier, and complex multi-round sequence. Recovery model: only durable_epoch survives crash, staged/visible reset to durable. All invariants verified: monotonicity and no partial epoch visibility. All 19 crash tests + workspace clippy clean.

description:

title: EPIC: Safe-Merge and Adaptive Conflict Arbitration
description:
## Purpose

Implement semantic safe-merge and adaptive conflict arbitration for MVCC. Deferred from V1.1 OQ2: strict FCW+SSI was chosen as the conservative V1.x policy. V1.2 adds per-block semantic merge proofs for operations that can safely merge without data corruption.

## Why

Strict FCW+SSI aborts all conflicting transactions, even when the conflicts are semantically safe (e.g., two writers appending to different parts of a file, or two writers updating different xattrs on the same inode). Safe-merge reduces unnecessary aborts → higher throughput under concurrent workloads.

## Scope

### Sub-beads

title: Design safe-merge taxonomy and per-block merge proof obligations
description:
## Purpose

Classify all block-level MVCC operations into merge-safe and merge-unsafe categories. Define formal proof obligations for each merge-safe category.

## Scope

1. **Operation taxonomy** — For each write operation type (data block write, inode metadata update, directory entry add/remove, xattr set/remove, bitmap allocation, extent tree modification):
   - Can two concurrent instances of this operation merge without corruption?
   - Under what conditions?
   - What invariants must hold?

2. **Merge-safe categories** (expected):
   - Disjoint data block writes (different logical blocks)
   - Append-only directory entry additions (different names)
   - Independent xattr modifications (different keys)
   - Non-overlapping extent tree modifications

3. **Merge-unsafe categories** (expected):
   - Same data block writes (last-writer-wins is not always correct)
   - Directory entry rename (atomic swap semantics)
   - Bitmap modifications (free space accounting must be exact)
   - Inode size/timestamp updates (depends on operation semantics)

4. **Formal proof obligations** — For each merge-safe category: preconditions, postconditions, invariant preservation proof sketch.

5. **Design document** — docs/design-safe-merge-taxonomy.md

## Acceptance criteria
- Complete operation taxonomy (all write types classified)
- Formal merge proof obligations for each safe category
- Design document with proof sketches
- Unit tests for merge-safety classification logic

title: Implement per-block merge proofs in MVCC write path
description:
## Purpose

Add merge-proof annotations to MVCC write operations so that semantically safe conflicts can merge instead of aborting.

## Scope

1. **MergeProof type** — New type in ffs-mvcc:
   - `MergeProof::DisjointBlocks` — writes target different logical blocks
   - `MergeProof::AppendOnly` — both writes are append operations
   - `MergeProof::IndependentKeys` — xattr writes to different keys
   - `MergeProof::Unsafe` — no merge proof available, fall back to FCW

2. **Merge validation** — During FCW conflict detection, check if conflicting writes both carry valid merge proofs. If so, allow both to commit.

3. **Merge application** — For mergeable conflicts, combine both write sets into the committed version. Verify merged state satisfies all postconditions.

4. **Fallback** — Any write without a merge proof, or with an invalid proof, uses strict FCW (abort on conflict).

## Acceptance criteria

- FCW conflict path checks merge proofs
- Merge application produces correct combined state
- Stress test: 100 concurrent writers with mergeable conflicts (0 unnecessary aborts)
- Stress test: 100 concurrent writers with unmergeable conflicts (correct aborts)

title: Implement adaptive conflict policy with expected-loss selection
description:
## Purpose

Implement a runtime-tunable conflict policy that selects between strict FCW and safe-merge based on observed contention patterns and expected-loss calculation.

## Scope

1. **ConflictPolicy enum** — `Strict` (FCW only), `SafeMerge` (merge when proof available), `Adaptive` (auto-select based on contention).

2. **Adaptive selection** — Track:
   - Conflict rate (conflicts per commit)
   - Merge success rate (successful merges per conflict)
   - Abort rate (aborts per commit)
   - Use exponential moving average over configurable window

3. **Expected-loss calculation** — For each policy:
   - P(corruption) × severity + P(unnecessary_abort) × cost
   - Safe-merge has higher P(corruption) but lower P(unnecessary_abort)
   - Policy with lowest expected loss wins

4. **Configuration** — CLI flag `--conflict-policy strict|safe-merge|adaptive`

## Acceptance criteria
- ConflictPolicy enum with 3 variants
- Adaptive policy tracks contention metrics
- Expected-loss calculation correct
- Policy switches between strict and safe-merge based on contention
- Unit tests for expected-loss calculation
- Unit tests for policy selection logic
- E2E script demonstrating adaptive switching

title: EPIC: Adaptive Repair Symbol Refresh
description:
## Purpose

Implement block-count staleness trigger for repair symbol refresh, beyond the age-only timeout (V1.1 OQ3: bounded staleness with lazy 30s default). Deferred from OQ3 because it requires explicit expected-loss improvement over age-only timeout.

## Scope

2. **Implement block-count staleness tracking** — Track write count per repair group since last symbol refresh. Trigger eager refresh when block-count exceeds threshold.

3. **Implement hybrid refresh policy** — Combine age-timeout and block-count triggers. Configurable weights and thresholds. Runtime-selectable policy.

4. **SLO instrumentation** — Stale-window percentile tracking (p50/p95/p99 time-since-last-refresh). Alert when stale window exceeds SLO.

5. **Verification gate** — Expected-loss improvement proven, SLO met, E2E validation.

title: Design expected-loss model for block-count vs age-only symbol refresh
description:
## Purpose

Formal expected-loss comparison of refresh policies: age-only timeout, block-count staleness, and hybrid.

## Scope

1. **Loss model** — Define:
   - P(data_loss | stale_symbols) as function of blocks-written-since-refresh
   - P(data_loss | stale_symbols) as function of time-since-refresh
   - Cost of unnecessary refresh (I/O overhead)
   - Expected loss = P(loss) × severity + P(unnecessary_refresh) × cost

2. **Policy comparison** — For realistic workload profiles (idle, light writes, heavy writes, burst):
   - Age-only (current 30s default)
   - Block-count (refresh after N writes to group)
   - Hybrid (min of age-timeout and block-count)

3. **Decision boundary** — At what write rate does block-count trigger dominate age-only? Visualize as expected-loss curves.

4. **Design document** — docs/design-adaptive-refresh.md

## Acceptance criteria
- Expected-loss model with explicit probability and cost assignments
- Policy comparison for 4 workload profiles
- Decision boundary identified
- Design document with analysis
- Unit tests for expected-loss calculation
close_reason: Implemented RefreshLossModel with expected-loss comparison of age-only vs block-count vs hybrid refresh policies. Design doc at docs/design-adaptive-refresh.md. Key findings: refresh I/O cost dominates under default parameters; block-count triggers become optimal when data_loss_cost >> refresh_io_cost/(crash_rate*corruption_prob). 10 unit tests pass, full workspace clippy clean.

2. **Threshold configuration** — Configurable block-count threshold (default: 1000 blocks). When counter exceeds threshold, schedule eager symbol refresh.

3. **Eager refresh trigger** — Hook into the repair pipeline to trigger immediate symbol refresh for groups exceeding threshold.

4. **Integration** — Wire write counter into ffs-mvcc commit path (post-commit hook increments group counters).

title: EPIC: Multi-Host Repair Coordination and Distributed Symbol Exchange
description:
## Purpose

Extend repair from single-host only (V1.1) to multi-host coordination. Deferred from V1.1 OQ5: repair symbols remain on same device, single-host repair ownership via coordination records.

## Scope

### Sub-beads

1. **Design: multi-host repair protocol** — Define the protocol for multiple hosts to coordinate repair symbol generation, exchange, and ownership. Consensus-free design (no distributed consensus needed for repair — use optimistic ownership with conflict detection).

2. **Implement repair ownership transfer** — Allow ownership of a repair group to transfer between hosts. Coordination record with lease-based ownership (TTL). Stale ownership detection and recovery.

3. **Implement symbol exchange protocol** — Mechanism for hosts to exchange repair symbols for groups they don't own. Read-only symbol retrieval from remote host. Asupersync-based transport (no tokio).

4. **Implement distributed repair pipeline** — End-to-end multi-host repair: detect corruption on host A, retrieve symbols from host B, decode and verify on host A.

5. **Verification gate** — Multi-host repair correctness, ownership transfer safety, no split-brain.

## Non-goals
- Distributed filesystem (each host mounts independently)
- Real-time replication (repair is for recovery, not replication)

title: Design multi-host repair protocol with optimistic ownership
description:
## Purpose

Design the protocol for multi-host repair coordination. Must be consensus-free and use optimistic ownership with conflict detection.

## Scope

1. **Ownership model** — Lease-based ownership per repair group. Host acquires ownership by writing a coordination record with TTL. Ownership expired → any host can claim.

2. **Conflict detection** — If two hosts claim ownership simultaneously, detect via coordination record version mismatch. Resolution: lower host-id wins (deterministic tiebreak).

3. **Symbol exchange** — Read-only retrieval of repair symbols from a remote host's storage. Protocol: request(group_id, generation) → response(symbols[]).

4. **Transport** — Asupersync-based TCP transport. No HTTP/REST/gRPC (no tokio). Simple request-response framing.

5. **Failure modes** — Host goes offline, network partition, stale ownership, split-brain analysis.

6. **Design document** — docs/design-multi-host-repair.md

## Acceptance criteria
- Protocol design document with ownership model, conflict detection, exchange protocol
- Failure mode analysis with mitigations
- No distributed consensus required
- Transport uses asupersync exclusively
- Unit tests for ownership logic
close_reason: Completed: Protocol design doc at docs/design-multi-host-repair.md covering ownership model, conflict detection, symbol exchange wire format, and failure mode analysis (host crash, network partition, stale ownership, split-brain, clock skew). Implemented ffs-repair::ownership module with CoordinationRecord, RepairOwnership (try_acquire/renew/release/is_owned_by_us), OwnershipGuard, deterministic UUID tiebreak, atomic write-via-rename, TTL-based expiry. 15 unit tests pass. title: Implement lease-based repair ownership transfer
description:
## Purpose

Implement repair group ownership transfer between hosts with lease-based TTL and stale detection.

## Scope

1. **RepairOwnership record** — host_id, group_id, generation, acquired_at, ttl, lease_version.
2. **Acquire ownership** — Atomic compare-and-swap on coordination file. Fails if already owned by another host with valid lease.
3. **Renew lease** — Extend TTL before expiry. Fails if lease_version changed.
4. **Release ownership** — Explicit release or TTL expiry.
5. **Stale detection** — If owner fails to renew within TTL, any host can re-acquire.

## Acceptance criteria
- Ownership acquire/renew/release working
- Concurrent acquisition handled correctly (no split ownership)
- Stale detection after TTL expiry
- Unit tests for all ownership transitions
- E2E script with simulated multi-host ownership transfer
