title: perf: mounted small-file create/delete storm comparator gap
description: Coverage gap measured 2026-07-10: mounted ext4/btrfs performance suite currently has 0 same-boundary comparator rows for small-file create/delete storms. No safe fixture mutation was attempted in this lane because prior mounted write attempts corrupted filesystems. Required follow-up: private fixture, kernel ext4 and FrankenFS arms in one binary/one remote invocation, interleaved create+fsyncdir+delete batches, byte/count parity, e2fsck-clean validation, release-perf profile and cv_pct<5 before any keep/reject ledger row.
notes: PROFILE-FIRST (2026-07-11, binary-in-hand, create-bench 10k x4 fresh-copy, cold): CONFIRMS the documented write-path frontier — NO solo lever. Top self-time: add_entry_reject_existing_tracked 5.46% (MINE, ffs-dir — SWAR/array-ref reslice ALREADY DONE); crc32c HW parallel3+append+gf2 ~7% (HW crc32c + landed INCREMENTAL dir-block csum 56cb5f94 = FLOOR); __memmove 7.19% resolves to __clone3 (thread creation 7.13%) under ShardedMvccStore::install_committed_version [PEER ffs-mvcc] + add_entry; ShardedMvccStore::commit 1.39% + install_committed_version 0.96% [PEER]; ffs_alloc::try_alloc_inode 0.86% [PEER]; parse_from_bytes 1.31% (existence-check, note_dir_name_index metadata-parse already landed 1.24x). Matches the ledger's FINAL FRONTIER SUMMARY + datalayout-move closeout (copy-elim REJECTED e2e-neutral on BOTH adapters, commit-dominated). NEW peer-flag (tentative, ffs-mvcc/cod lane): install_committed_version appears to spawn threads per commit/install (clone3 ~7%) -> a persistent-pool opportunity IN THE PEER MVCC store, not solo. VERDICT: SURFACE, write-path solo headroom = NONE; the create-storm gap is MVCC-commit/install + alloc (peer) dominated.

Decide only when the A/B median effect exceeds that function's A/A null spread, and record the A/A null median. Every WIN or REJECT must also record binary SHA-256, profile-verified non-zero self-time, worker ID, per-arm CV, and null-control median. title: ffs-ondisk: ext4 group descriptor encode/decode lacks proptest round-trip coverage
description:
Finding (via /testing-metamorphic skill): `Ext4GroupDesc::write_to_bytes`
and `Ext4GroupDesc::parse_from_bytes` (crates/ffs-ondisk/src/ext4.rs:1425, 1605)
are paired encode/decode functions on the hot ext4 metadata path:
they're called by every group-descriptor read in ffs-core, ffs-alloc,
ffs-ext4, ffs-cli, and ffs-harness. They have **fixed-input** roundtrip
unit tests (`group_desc_write_to_bytes_roundtrip_32` / `_64`) but **no
proptest coverage** that exercises the encode/decode bijection across
the full input space.

Concrete metamorphic invariants that are not currently asserted:

  MR1 (full bijection at desc_size=64): for ALL field values,
      parse(write(gd, 64), 64) == gd
  MR2 (truncating bijection at desc_size=32): for ALL field values,
      parse(write(gd, 32), 32) == truncate_lo_halves(gd)
      where the high 32 / 16 bits of every multi-byte field are
      forced to zero. This pins the contract that 32-byte descriptors
      MUST drop the hi halves on write AND zero them on parse — a
      regression here would silently corrupt 64-bit-mode block bitmap
      pointers if the parser/writer pair drifts.
  MR3 (encode determinism): write(gd) is a pure function — initialising
      the destination buffer to different bytes must not perturb the
      written `[..ds]` region.
  MR4 (encode/decode/encode idempotence): the second encode must be
      byte-equal to the first — pins that parse never silently
      normalises a field.
  MR5 (size-violation errors): write to undersized buffer must err;
      parse from undersized input must err.
  MR6 (32-byte parser ignores tail): on a 64-byte buffer, parse(.., 32)
      must equal parse(write(gd, 32), 32) regardless of bytes >= 0x20.

Repro: any future refactor of the field offsets, the lo/hi split, or
the desc_size branching could pass the existing fixed-input tests and
silently corrupt mounted images.

Acceptance: a proptest suite at the bottom of ext4.rs::tests block
covers MR1-MR6 with PROPTEST_CASES sufficient to exercise the full
field-value space (>=64 cases), uses `#[expect(clippy::cast_possible_truncation)]`
where the lo-half projection is intentional, and passes under workspace
pedantic+nursery clippy.
notes: Completed via commit shipping 7 proptest MRs (MR1-MR6 plus an encoder-purity relation). MR3 caught documented writer padding windows (0x14..0x18 / 0x34..0x38 / 0x3C..0x40 at desc_size=64) — relation refined to compare parsed structs rather than raw bytes.

title: crc32c_append associativity proptest MR
description: ffs_types::crc32c_append is the btrfs-side foundational CRC32C primitive (used by btrfs superblock checksum, tree block checksums, send stream commands). Multi-region checksumming requires: crc32c_append(seed, a||b) == crc32c_append(crc32c_append(seed, a), b). Sister ext4_chksum has bd-8pbjm covering this property; crc32c_append currently has only proptest_crc32c_seed_zero_equiv. A regression that broke associativity (e.g., swapping for a non-CRC fold) would silently corrupt every multi-region btrfs checksum. Add proptest_crc32c_append_associative_across_appends + three-way variant.

title: [parity] ext4 htree: casefold insert + multi-level (>86k entry) rebuild support (bd-rzq1y follow-on)
description: Follow-on to bd-rzq1y (htree leaf split landed in db2968f8 via rebuild-on-overflow). Two narrow edge cases currently return a clean UnsupportedFeature error (NOT corruption) instead of succeeding: (1) CASEFOLD htree dirs (EXT4_CASEFOLD_FL): inserts error because dx_hash on the raw name targets the wrong leaf — needs a casefold-aware target-leaf locator (ext4_casefold_key) in both htree_target_leaf_block and the rebuild's entry hashing. (2) MULTI-LEVEL htree (dx_root indirect_levels>0, ~86k+ entries in one dir): ext4_rebuild_htree_dir guards and errors because it assumes logical blocks 1..n are all leaves, but with indirect levels some are dx interior nodes that parse_dir_block would mis-read; needs a real dx-index walk to enumerate the actual leaf blocks before gathering entries. Both are rare; the common single-level non-casefold path is fully correct + e2fsck-clean (proven by many_creates_in_htree_dir_trigger_rebuild_and_keep_all_findable_bd_rzq1y). Also still open: htree REMOVE-path leaf collapse / dx maintenance (currently remove is safe — no dx_root mutation — but doesn't shrink the index).
notes: REBUILD DONE (ef6926c3, IronMarten): casefold htree leaf-full rebuild now works for ASCII dirs — build_htree_layout casefold mode (fold-hash, store original case) via build_htree_directory_{stamped_,}with_large_dir_casefold; ext4_rebuild_htree_dir detects casefold, refuses non-ASCII entries, else rebuilds fold-consistent; insert leaf-full branch routes here instead of erroring. So ASCII casefold htree is now COMPLETE end-to-end: READ (W7 lookup) + INSERT (W8 non-full + this rebuild). Multi-level >86k rebuild already done (da7683c7). REMAINING = non-ASCII casefold ONLY → split out to bd-vsuni (byte-exact UTF-8 NFD tables). Consider closing bd-owt2r once bd-vsuni tracks the non-ASCII piece.
close_reason: ASCII casefold htree now COMPLETE end-to-end: READ/lookup (W7 15672195), INSERT non-full (W8 0326ffea), INSERT leaf-full REBUILD (ef6926c3). Multi-level >86k rebuild already done (da7683c7). All three named deliverables (casefold insert + multi-level rebuild) functional for ASCII names, the dominant real-world case, proven by htree_find_entry_casefold/target_leaf/rebuild_is_fold_navigable unit tests + create_in_casefold_htree_dir E2E. The ONLY residual is non-ASCII casefold (needs byte-exact kernel UTF-8 NFD tables), which is a distinct Unicode-table epic now tracked as bd-vsuni; non-ASCII casefold writes refuse cleanly (no corruption) and reads fall back to the linear casefold scan (correct). title: fuzz: no dedicated fuzz target for Ext4Extent split-bit encoding (actual_len + is_unwritten)
description:
Finding (via /testing-fuzzing skill, NEW target): fuzz/fuzz_targets has 51 targets and Ext4Extent::actual_len / is_unwritten are referenced in 2 (fuzz_ext4_dir_extent.rs, fuzz_extent_tree.rs) but ONLY as helpers to validate other parsers. There is NO dedicated libfuzzer target that pumps random u16 raw_len through Ext4Extent and asserts the split-bit encoding contract.

The newly-shipped bd-j0zo3 proptest (32 cases per relation) pins the [actual_len][unwritten_bit] u16 encoding. A libfuzzer target lifts the algebraic laws to >1M iterations/session with corpus learning across the EXT_INIT_MAX_LEN boundary, the all-ones case, and the smooth-vs-overflow edge.

Acceptance: new fuzz/fuzz_targets/fuzz_ext4_extent_actual_len.rs that, for arbitrary u16 raw_len, asserts:
  * MR1 — Determinism: actual_len(ext) called twice gives same result
  * MR2 — Bound: actual_len <= EXT_INIT_MAX_LEN
  * MR3 — Boundary at EXT_INIT_MAX_LEN: written, actual_len == 0x8000
  * MR4 — Written range (raw_len <= MAX): actual_len == raw_len, is_unwritten == false
  * MR5 — Unwritten range (raw_len > MAX): actual_len == raw_len - MAX, is_unwritten == true
  * MR6 — Never panics
Plus a [[bin]] entry in fuzz/Cargo.toml.
close_reason: done

title: Operationalize 64-core swarm performance and resource-control roadmap
description:
Idea-wizard/alien-graveyard workstream for making FrankenFS compelling for massive agent swarms on 64+ CPU cores and 256GB+ RAM hosts.

Phase synthesis:
- Phase 1 terrain: README says tracked parity is complete, but performance readiness is still experimental; default mount does not wire optional backpressure/per-core scheduling hooks; bd-rchk5, bd-rchk5.8, bd-q029i, bd-rchk0.5.*, and proof-bundle beads own adjacent evidence lanes.
- Phase 2 top ideas: tail-latency decomposition ledger, NUMA/shard-aware workload harness, RCU/QSBR metadata-read proof surface, parallel WAL/group-commit scaling gate, and 256GB cache admission/memory-budget controller.
- Phase 3 next ideas: morsel-driven scrub/repair scheduler, canary/soak resource controller, exokernel/FUSE-boundary reduction study, operator proof cards, multi-agent workload corpus expansion, regression-bead payloads, host fingerprinting, expected-loss tuning rules, and rollback-safe feature exposure.
- Phase 4 overlap: reuse bd-rchk5 performance evidence, bd-rchk0.4 artifact schema, bd-rchk0.5 proof bundle, and bd-rchk0.5.7 workload corpus instead of inventing isolated report formats.
- Phase 5/6 operationalization: this epic owns granular implementation beads with explicit artifact schemas, unit tests, E2E/dry-run lanes, no overclaiming, and release-gate consumers.

Alien-graveyard candidates selected for this repo:
- RCU/QSBR or epoch-based reclamation for hot metadata and MVCC read paths, constrained by zero unsafe code and deterministic tests.
- Parallel WAL/group commit with replay proof and fsync tail SLOs.
- Cache-admission and memory-budget control inspired by S3-FIFO/ARC under 256GB hosts, with fallback to current ARC behavior.
- Tail-latency decomposition: queueing, service, I/O, retries, synchronization, allocator, repair backlog, and FUSE wrapper overhead.

Acceptance: child beads produce executable validators and artifacts, not marketing prose. Every child must state invariants, loss or SLO rule, fallback mode, validation commands, and how public claims remain experimental until evidence is current.
close_reason: All child beads closed with executable swarm performance artifacts: tail-latency ledger, NUMA workload harness, RCU/QSBR proof surface, WAL group-commit gate, cache budget controller, scrub/repair scheduler plan, and operator decision report

title: ext4_write_compressed fallback to uncompressed write loses sparsity
description: In ext4_write_compressed, if the data is handed to write_ext4_uncompressed_cluster as a fallback, the input cluster_data is fully zero-padded to cluster_bytes. The uncompressed writer checks 'if start >= data.len() { /* create hole */ }' to skip trailing blocks, but since data.len() is always exactly cluster_bytes, this condition never evaluates to true. As a result, the uncompressed fallback unconditionally allocates and writes physical zero blocks for the entire tail of the cluster instead of maintaining holes/sparsity.
close_reason: Preserve sparse tail when e2compr falls back to uncompressed cluster writes; added regression coverage and passed fmt/check/clippy + focused tests.

title: FUSE E2E: fuse_spec_i5_delete_reclaims_free_counts fails at file 169
description:
The test creates 1000 files in a subdirectory then tries to delete them all. File 169 consistently returns ENOENT during fs::remove_file. File 169 is the first entry in the second directory block (the directory transitions from 1 block to 2 blocks at this point).

Root cause analysis:
- Core-level test (create 1000 + lookup + unlink) passes - the filesystem logic is correct
- The failure is FUSE-specific - kernel dentry cache or FUSE protocol interaction
- The MVCC store correctly holds all committed data
- Adding sync/flush between create and delete phases does not fix it
- The failure is 100% deterministic at file 169

Possible causes:
1. FUSE kernel negative dentry caching interfering with create/unlink sequence
2. Directory extent resolution issue specific to the FUSE lookup path under kernel cache pressure
3. Kernel dentry eviction + daemon lookup returning stale data

Next steps: Add FUSE-level tracing/logging to the lookup and unlink paths to capture the exact sequence of FUSE operations around file 169
close_reason: Fixed: checksum tail was not initialised in new directory blocks, causing parse_dir_block to fail with rec_len overflow

title: delete/truncate of e2compr file frees the 0xFFFFFFFF compressed-block sentinel as a real block
description: Regression from bd-c7t59 (W23). inode_uses_indirect_blocks (ffs-inode) excluded extents+inline but NOT e2compr (EXT4_COMPR_FL/EXT4_COMPRBLK_FL). e2compr files are indirect-mapped and store the EXT2_COMPRESSED_BLKADDR sentinel (0xFFFFFFFF) in i_block slots, not real block numbers. So delete_inode's W23 free_indirect_blocks walk (and truncate_indirect_blocks) called free_blocks_persist(BlockNumber(0xFFFFFFFF)) -> split_free_block_segments 'group out of range' Corruption error -> delete of a compressed file with compressed clusters spuriously fails (and in a pathological layout could corrupt a bogus group bitmap). Pre-W23 the same delete benignly leaked; W23 turned the leak into a delete-time failure. FIX: exclude EXT4_COMPR_FL|EXT4_COMPRBLK_FL from inode_uses_indirect_blocks so the indirect-free walk skips compressed files (their cluster-aware block freeing stays unimplemented = benign leak, never a sentinel free). PROOF: compressed_inode_not_treated_as_indirect_and_delete_skips_sentinels (guard returns false for both compr flags; delete of an inode with 0xFFFFFFFF in i_block[0] now succeeds). ffs-inode 133.
close_reason: done

title: perf: parallel read plateaus at ~8 threads (~2.8x vs kernel at 16t) — per-read shared-cacheline contention; needs lock-free hot-inode read or handle-scoped resolution
description: EVIDENCE (CrimsonFox 2026-06-22, HEAD c8219750). Like-for-like matched-thread A/B (btrfs big.bin uncompressed, 50k x4KiB): kernel 4t/8t/16t = 7523/14699/21725 MiB/s; frankenfs = 5080/8091/7751. frankenfs PLATEAUS at ~8 threads (8091->7751 from 8t->16t) while kernel scales; gap WIDENS 1.48x->1.82x->2.80x with thread count = per-read shared-cacheline contention signature. RAYON sweep shows negative scaling past 16t (64t collapses ~2200, partly oversubscription). The old 'parallel ~10x' headline was frankenfs-64t (collapsed) vs kernel-16t = apples-to-oranges; real gap is ~2.8x at matched 16t. RULED OUT: mvcc snapshot RwLock (removal wall-neutral c8219750), rayon single-job dispatch (inert). CANDIDATE LEVERS (deep, coordination family, .414/.382): (1) lock-free hot-inode read fast-path in front of ext4_inode_table_block_cache ShardedCache (single-file read = all threads hit one hot key on one shard Mutex -> convoy; an ArcSwap<last-hot-block> checked before the Mutex would let the hot single-file stream read lock-free); (2) open-file-handle-scoped resolved (parsed-inode + extent) snapshot taken once per open and reused lock-free across that handle's reads, so a hot 4KiB random-read stream touches zero shared cache locks after the first. Both reduce per-read shared-cacheline traffic = the thing that widens the gap with thread count. Bench predicate: frankenfs 16t should approach the kernel curve (not plateau at 8t). Higher blast radius (hot read dispatch) -> needs careful build+conformance; flagged for the coordination owner. docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md has the full table.
notes: LEVER UPDATE: checkpoint-throttle MEASURED WORSE at 16t plateau (base ~7700 vs throttle ~6200 MiB/s, 0.8x) -> Cx::checkpoint RwLock is NOT contended at moderate concurrency (fast-path cheaper than the TLS throttle bookkeeping; the 24% incl was the cheap vDSO clock read counted under it). RULES OUT checkpoint as the lever (joins mvcc snapshot RwLock = both per-read shared-lock candidates eliminated, both wall-neutral-or-worse). REMAINING scaling-ceiling suspects: (1) per-read ALLOCATION churn (~13%: staging-buffer alloc/zero/free in the read_contiguous path — same family as the shipped scrub bd-scrub-chunk-buffer-reuse fix; a read-path equivalent that reuses staging buffers could help); (2) memory-bandwidth/pread throughput at the syscall boundary (may be a hard floor). The lock-free hot-inode / handle-scoped candidates are now LOWER priority given both lock-removal experiments were neutral/worse. NEXT: attack the per-read staging-buffer allocation in the read path.
close_reason: STRUCTURAL, not a fixable contention lever. 5 removable-contention experiments this session all neutral/worse (mvcc snapshot RwLock neutral; Cx::checkpoint throttle 0.8x WORSE; small-read staging-copy/FFS_DIRECT_READ_MIN_BYTES lower = neutral parallel + 0.74x single-thread; rayon single-job inline inert; thread-local read scratch inert). The ~2.8x-at-16t ceiling is the inherent userspace pread+safe-copy memory-bandwidth tax of a forbid(unsafe) FS vs the kernel in-page-cache copy path = same ~2x copy ceiling across all warm reads, closable only via forbidden mmap/splice. frankenfs read is single-thread parity-or-faster (no per-read syscall) and ~2.8x at the kernel 16t sweet spot. Reopen only if a forbid-unsafe-free zero-copy path (io_uring/registered buffers) becomes viable. Full evidence in docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md.

title: btrfs partial-overwrite produces btrfs-check-invalid image — 'errors found in fs roots'
description: Phase-B probe (btrfs_complex_mutation_btrfs_check_probe, ffs-core tests): of 4 post-bd-x3fcu mutation sequences run through real btrfs check (btrfs-progs v6.16), three are CLEAN — A: 24 files x 16KB, B: one 2MB file, D: create+write+delete. But C: PARTIAL OVERWRITE (write 64KB at off 0, then overwrite 16KB at off 16384) yields 'found 212992 bytes used, error(s) found' + 'ERROR: errors found in fs roots' (phase [5/8]). So FrankenFS's overwrite-split path (btrfs_remove_overlapping_extent_data -> split extent, free middle, re-insert head/tail segments via btrfs_insert_regular_extent_segment) leaves the fs tree's EXTENT_DATA items in a state the kernel checker rejects. Likely an EXTENT_DATA key/extent_offset/num_bytes inconsistency after the split (gap/overlap in the file's extent map, or a re-inserted segment with wrong extent_offset). Single full writes, appends, multi-file, large files, and delete are all clean — the gap is specifically partial overwrite of an existing regular extent. NEXT: get the exact [5/8] fs-roots line (probe prints full output), then inspect the post-split EXTENT_DATA items vs btrfs's expectations (file offset coverage must be gapless + non-overlapping; extent_offset must point into the referenced disk extent). Validation harness: the probe test (ignored) + a focused overwrite btrfs-check test.
close_reason: FIXED in 4bf1fbb1. The overwrite-split re-insert path (btrfs_insert_regular_extent_segment) didn't capture data csums; with datasum-by-default (bd-x3fcu) the re-inserted head/tail of an overwritten file had no csum items -> btrfs check 'some csum missing' (I_ERR_SOME_CSUM_MISSING). Factored the main-path capture into shared helper btrfs_capture_data_extent_csums and called it from the segment path (gated on datasum). Validated by new btrfs_overwrite_passes_btrfs_check_bd_pb0ey (real btrfs-progs v6.16, write 64K + overwrite middle 16K -> clean); 244/244 ffs-core btrfs tests. Phase-B probe (btrfs_complex_mutation_btrfs_check_probe, ignored) confirmed many-files/large-file/create+delete were already clean — overwrite was the sole gap. FOLLOW-UP (low priority, near-unreachable): the inline->regular conversion site in btrfs_fallocate (~prev_allocation, lib.rs ~18689) also creates a regular data extent without csum capture; FrankenFS never writes inline extents so it only triggers on a mounted real image's inline extent + fallocate — file a P3 if a fallocate-inline btrfs-check scenario is added. The shared helper makes adding it a 6-line gated call.

title: btrfs SEEK_DATA/SEEK_HOLE misreport explicit hole extents (disk_bytenr==0) as data
description: btrfs_lseek_data and btrfs_lseek_hole iterate all EXTENT_DATA items and treat every present extent as DATA. But a btrfs explicit hole is an EXTENT_DATA with disk_bytenr==0 (type REG, reads as zeros) — common on kernel-created images WITHOUT the NO_HOLES feature. btrfs_read_file already treats disk_bytenr==0 as a hole (lib.rs ~8075), so the lseek paths are inconsistent with the read path: SEEK_DATA returns an offset inside a hole as data, and SEEK_HOLE skips past the hole (advancing covered_until), so cp --sparse / tar / qemu-img sparse detection get wrong results on such files. Prealloc (BTRFS_FILE_EXTENT_PREALLOC, disk_bytenr!=0) correctly stays DATA, matching the kernel (EXTENT_MAP_HOLE is the only hole). ext4 is unaffected (holes are implicit gaps; unwritten extents are data per iomap_seek_*). FIX: filter out disk_bytenr==0 (explicit hole) extents in both btrfs lseek paths so holes become gaps, mirroring the kernel's find_desired_extent. Test: inject a disk_bytenr==0 EXTENT_DATA between two data extents and assert SEEK_DATA/SEEK_HOLE land on the hole boundaries.
close_reason: Fixed in ffea0708: btrfs_lseek_data/hole now filter disk_bytenr==0 explicit hole extents (via new btrfs_extent_is_hole), so SEEK_DATA skips holes and SEEK_HOLE finds them — matching btrfs_read_file and the kernel. Prealloc stays data. Regression btrfs_lseek_treats_explicit_hole_extent_as_hole_bd_pb6bs. ffs-core 1045/0; clippy clean.

title: attribute the ext4 readdir+stat re-measurement delta: same-window A/B of baked vs seeded fixture, because the 18% moved in OUR favour on a 4-way-confounded comparison
description:
bd-plkzd's re-measurement (2026-08-08) moved the ext4 readdir+stat row from `4.967448x` to ≈`4.1x` — 18% in FrankenFS's favour — and NOBODY CAN CURRENTLY SAY HOW MUCH OF THAT IS THE FIXTURE FIX. Four things changed at once: the fixture (unindexed -> htree), the candidate ELF, the PGO profile, and the kernel version, plus the window. A movement in our own favour is exactly the kind that must not be banked on a confounded comparison.

WHAT IS ALREADY NARROWED, from the recorded absolute arm medians (bd-4sull item 3 earning its keep):
    banked 2026-07-30/31   kernel 22.84 ms   FrankenFS 113.44 ms   4.967448x
    run 1  2026-08-08      kernel 28.98 ms   FrankenFS 117.00 ms   4.052605x
    run 2  2026-08-08      kernel 27.99 ms   FrankenFS 115.62 ms   4.163402x
Our arm moved +3.1% against the old row; the KERNEL arm moved +26.9%. The kernel arm does not execute our binary, so the candidate ELF and PGO profile cannot explain any part of the kernel-arm move. That leaves fixture, kernel version, and window drift — and bd-4sull has measured window drift alone at up to +18.3% on the incumbent, so it cannot be dismissed either.

THE HYPOTHESIS WORTH TESTING, WHICH WOULD MEAN bd-plkzd's STATED DIRECTION WAS BACKWARDS. bd-plkzd asserted an unindexed directory "INFLATES the ext4 arm". For a full enumerate-then-stat-every-entry sweep the reverse is plausible: with an htree, `readdir` returns entries in HASH order, so the stat pass walks the inode table in effectively random order; a linear directory returns creation order, which is also inode-allocation order, so the stat pass is sequential. On that reading the OLD unindexed fixture made the KERNEL arm faster, inflating the published ratio and making FrankenFS look worse than it was. The observed pattern (kernel arm markedly slower on the corrected fixture, our arm nearly flat) is consistent with it. Consistent is not proven, and the alternative explanations above are live.

WHY IT CANNOT BE ANSWERED TODAY: bd-plkzd removed the `mke2fs -d` path outright, so there is no way to build the old fixture for comparison. That was the right call for correctness and it closed off the attribution at the same time.

WHAT WOULD CLOSE THIS
1. A fixture-construction flag on `ffs-mounted-kernel-bench` (e.g. `--fixture-construction baked|seeded`, default seeded) that restores the `mke2fs -d` path FOR MEASUREMENT ONLY. It must fail closed if used for a banked row: the baked fixture is known-unfair and no scorecard row may ever be produced with it again.
2. Both arms in ONE window on ONE ELF: same candidate, same kernel, same governor, back to back. That removes every confounder except the fixture, which is the entire point.
3. Report the KERNEL arm's absolute median for both, not just the ratio — the hypothesis is a claim about the incumbent's cost, so the incumbent's absolute is the measurement, and the ratio is secondary.
4. If the hypothesis holds, correct bd-plkzd's DIRECTION statement in the ledger and in both scorecards. It currently tells readers the defect made us look BETTER; the evidence so far points the other way, and a wrong direction in a closed bead propagates.

WHY THIS IS WORTH A WINDOW even though the row is already re-measured correctly: the same fixture defect exists on the btrfs readdir+stat row (`8.322812x`) and on both parallel-read rows (bd-c5210), and the btrfs parallel-read row is the campaign's ONLY honest_win. Knowing the sign and rough size of the fixture effect tells us whether re-measuring those rows is urgent or routine, and whether the win survives.

Not blocking bd-plkzd, which is closable on its own terms — its fixture is fixed, asserted fail-closed, and re-measured. This is the attribution debt the fix created.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
ITEM 1 LANDED (dff16cb8, verified green): --fixture-construction seeded|baked on ffs-mounted-kernel-bench.

WHAT IT DOES
  seeded (DEFAULT, unchanged behaviour) — entries created through a kernel mount, each filesystem builds its own native index. The only bankable form.
  baked — entries written into the host tree so mke2fs -d bakes them, i.e. the pre-bd-plkzd linear/unindexed construction, restored FOR ATTRIBUTION ONLY.

FAILS CLOSED, MECHANICALLY. A baked run is forced to a new BLOCKED_UNFAIR_FIXTURE verdict, checked FIRST in the verdict chain and unconditionally — no combination of clear nulls, clear placement or a favourable ratio can produce a bankable verdict from it. This is deliberately not a convention a reviewer has to notice. The report also records fixture_construction and fixture_construction_bankable on EVERY run including the default, so a banked row's provenance never depends on remembering which flag was in force.

ONLY THE MECHANISM DIFFERS. Both modes produce their entries through the SAME SeededFixture::create_entry — same names, same bytes, same count. That is what makes the planned A/B an attribution rather than another confounded comparison. The htree assertion is skipped under baked (a baked ext4 dir is unindexed BY CONSTRUCTION — asserting it would just fail the run and destroy the comparison); the fail-closed verdict, not that assertion, is what prevents banking.

Test: baked_fixture_construction_is_parsed_and_can_never_be_banked pins parse, is_bankable, an unknown-mode error, and — importantly — that the DEFAULT is the bankable one, so an inversion that silently makes every unflagged row unfair fails the suite. ffs-harness bin 55 passed / 0 failed.

STILL OPEN: items 2-4, which are the measurement itself. Both modes back to back in ONE window on ONE ELF, reporting the KERNEL arm's ABSOLUTE median for both (the hypothesis is a claim about the incumbent's cost, so the incumbent's absolute IS the measurement and the ratio is secondary). Then, if the hypothesis holds, correct bd-plkzd's DIRECTION statement in the ledger and both scorecards — it currently tells readers the defect made us look BETTER, and the evidence so far points the other way.

title: create/delete storm leaks ~1 inode per delete from the ext4 group-descriptor free-inode counters — e2fsck-dirty, and ENOSPC on an empty filesystem
description:
A create/delete storm leaks ~2000 inodes per cycle from the ext4 GROUP DESCRIPTOR free-inode counters while the inode BITMAPS stay correct. The image ends e2fsck-dirty, and on a small enough filesystem the drift exhausts the descriptors and allocation fails ENOSPC on a filesystem that is actually empty.

This is the INODE-side mirror of bd-ftev0 and bd-age6i: bitmap right, counter wrong.

FOUND running bd-4sull item 1 (a routine re-measurement of the banked create/delete-storm row), not by looking for it.

REPRODUCTION, and it is deterministic across independent arms:
    ffs-mounted-kernel-bench --filesystem both --workload create-delete-storm \
      --operations 2000 --image-size-mib 2048 --observation-repeats 1

    arm        e2fsck   inode-count errors   block-count errors
    kernel_a   rc=0     0                    0
    kernel_b   rc=0     0                    0
    fuse_a     rc=4     11                   0
    fuse_b     rc=4     11                   0

Both kernel arms clean; BOTH FrankenFS arms dirty, independently, with identical error counts. Only inode counters are affected — block counters are correct in every arm, which rules out a missing durability flush (that would corrupt both).

THE DAMAGE, from `e2fsck -fn` on ext4.fuse_a.img:
    Free inodes count wrong for group #5  (0, counted=8192)
    ... identically for groups #6 through #13 ...
    Free inodes count wrong for group #14 (1920, counted=8192)
    Free inodes count wrong (51056, counted=131056)

Ten whole groups report ZERO free inodes while every one of their 8192 inodes is free in the bitmap. Total drift 80000 inodes = exactly 40 x 2000, and the run performs ~40 create/delete cycles of 2000 files on that arm. The arithmetic is exact: one leak per file deleted.

USER-VISIBLE CONSEQUENCE, not just an fsck complaint. The same command at --image-size-mib 1024 fails outright mid-run:
    mounted_kernel_gate,error=storm create .../fuse_a/create-delete-storm/storm-00001520:
      No space left on device (os error 28)
The 1 GiB image has fewer inodes, so the drift exhausts the descriptors sooner and allocation starts failing with ENOSPC while the filesystem is empty. A long-running FrankenFS mount doing ordinary create/delete work will eventually refuse to create files.

WHAT IS ALREADY RULED OUT
- Not a missing flush: block counters are correct in the same images.
- Not the fast-commit recovery path (bd-age6i): this is the ordinary runtime unlink path, no recovery involved.
- Not a transient-versus-live alloc-state split of the kind bd-age6i had: `ext4_unlink_impl` takes the LIVE state via `require_alloc_state()?` and `.write()`.
- The in-memory credit exists: `ffs_alloc::free_inode_persist` does `groups[gidx].free_inodes.saturating_add(1)` (crates/ffs-alloc/src/lib.rs:3764), and `ffs_inode::delete_inode` calls it (crates/ffs-inode/src/lib.rs:1038).

SO THE ROOT CAUSE IS NOT YET IDENTIFIED and I am not guessing at it. The live counter is credited on free and the live counter is what the durability boundary flushes, yet the persisted descriptor is short by exactly one per deleted file. The candidates worth checking first:
  1. Whether the storm's deletes actually reach `ext4_unlink_impl`, or take another path that clears the bitmap without crediting.
  2. Whether allocation decrements a DIFFERENT GroupStats instance than the one free credits (the create path has several backends — SingleLockDirAlloc, the sharded path, rollback paths).
  3. Whether `ext4_write_group_descriptors_to`'s inode-bitmap override rule interacts badly: it passes an override only when `gs.free_inodes < geo.inodes_in_group(group)`, so a group that is FULLY free passes None — which is exactly the state groups #5-#13 should be in.

Candidate 3 is the one I would test first: it is the only place the code treats "all inodes free" as a special case, and groups #5-#13 are precisely the fully-free ones.

ACCEPTANCE
- a create/delete storm of >=2000 files over >=40 cycles leaves the image e2fsck-clean on the FrankenFS arms;
- the same shape at --image-size-mib 1024 completes without ENOSPC;
- a regression test drives enough create/delete cycles to move the counter and asserts group descriptor free_inodes matches the bitmap, so the drift cannot return silently;
- the fix names which of the three candidates above was responsible.

PROVENANCE: driver 6c041003, candidate 913c36a4, PGO b30de364, v3 attested, kernel 6.17.0-41. Images retained at /data/tmp/frankenfs-4sull-storm-q1/scratch/ext4/ until the next run clears that scratch root.
close_reason: P0 exposure closed by mitigation, verified both ways on the rebuilt binary: default mount --rw is now e2fsck CLEAN, while FFS_BHH0I_SHARDED=1 still reproduces the identical 3000-inode leak. The opt-in reproducing byte-for-byte proves the fix is exactly the default flip and nothing incidental. comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
NEGATIVE RESULT THAT NARROWS THIS SHARPLY: the defect is PATH-SPECIFIC, not scale-specific, and the direct in-process write path is CLEAN.

An in-process reproduction attempt drives 12 cycles x 64 files = 768 create/delete operations through `OpenFs::create` / `OpenFs::unlink`, flushes, and runs real `e2fsck`. It comes back CLEAN — no "Free inodes count wrong", no ENOSPC.

That is decisive about scale. The comparator's drift is exactly ONE PER FILE DELETED (80000 leaked over ~40 cycles of 2000). If the same leak existed on this path, 768 deletes would leave 768 phantom-used inodes and e2fsck would say so. It does not. So the direct path does not leak at all, and the ~40x2000 scale of the comparator run is not what makes the difference.

WHAT DIFFERS, and it is concrete. The FUSE handler (crates/ffs-fuse/src/lib.rs:3103) calls the SAME `FsOps::unlink`, but wraps it:

    with_request_scope(cx, RequestOp::Unlink, |cx, scope| {
        ops.unlink(cx, scope, parent, name)?;
        ops.commit_request_scope(scope)?;      <-- the mounted path does this
    })

whereas the in-process test goes through `OpenFs::unlink`, which uses `with_latest_scope`. Same `ext4_unlink_impl`, same `delete_inode`, same `free_inode_persist` — different SCOPE handling and an explicit per-request commit.

So the next place to look is `commit_request_scope` and how a per-request scope interacts with the live `Ext4AllocState`. The in-memory credit (`groups[gidx].free_inodes.saturating_add(1)`, ffs-alloc:3764) provably executes on both paths since both reach the same function; what differs is what happens to that state afterwards.

ALSO RULED OUT along the way, so nobody re-checks them:
- Not a missing durability flush — block counters are correct in the same images that have wrong inode counters.
- Not the descriptor write dropping the field — `persist_group_desc_force_with_bitmap_overrides` sets `free_inodes_count: stats.free_inodes` UNCONDITIONALLY, independent of whether a bitmap override is passed. My earlier suspicion that the fully-free-group `None` override was responsible is therefore WRONG and is withdrawn: the override only governs checksum re-stamping and the UNINIT flag, never the count.
- Not a failing delete — four-arm parity passes BEFORE and AFTER in the failing comparator run, so the files really are created and removed and the namespace is correct.
- Not the fast-commit recovery path (bd-age6i's shape) — no recovery is involved here.

A TEST IS LANDED, deliberately named so it cannot mislead:
`direct_path_create_delete_cycles_keep_free_inode_counters_exact_not_a_bd_pbyu0_repro`.
It PASSES, and its doc comment says in the first line that bd-pbyu0 is NOT fixed. It is bd-pbyu0's negative control: it pins the direct path as correct, so whatever fix lands cannot silently regress it, and if it ever starts failing the defect has spread.

STILL OPEN: the root cause and the fix. The bead's original candidate list is updated by the above — candidate 3 (the fully-free-group override) is eliminated, and the request-scope commit path replaces it as the primary suspect.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
SECOND NEGATIVE RESULT, AND IT WITHDRAWS MY OWN PREVIOUS NARROWING.

Last comment I claimed the defect was "PATH-specific, not scale-specific" and named the FUSE request-scope commit as the primary suspect. I built that test. It does NOT reproduce either — so that narrowing was wrong and is withdrawn.

WHAT WAS TESTED AND CAME BACK CLEAN
1. Direct path (`OpenFs::unlink`, `with_latest_scope`): 12 x 64 = 768 ops on 64 MiB. Clean.
2. Per-request scope path (`begin_request_scope` / `commit_request_scope` / `end_request_scope`, one scope per op, exactly as ffs-fuse's handlers do): 40 x 500 = 20,000 allocations on a 512 MiB image (~4 inode groups). Clean — no drift, no ENOSPC, e2fsck accepts.

So per-request scope commit is ELIMINATED, and so is scale: 20,000 allocations is a quarter of the comparator's 80,000 and well past the point a one-per-delete leak would be visible.

WHY MY SCALE ARGUMENT WAS ALSO SHAKY, stated because it matters for whoever picks this up. I originally reasoned "the leak is one-per-delete, so 768 deletes would show 768 phantom inodes". That assumed a per-delete leak. Re-reading the corrupt image, groups #5-#13 are at ZERO free with all 8192 free in the bitmap, which requires allocation to have consumed every inode in those groups WITHOUT REUSE. Non-reuse is what happens once a group's counter wrongly reads 0 — the allocator skips it and moves on. So the observed damage is partly a CASCADE of the defect, not a direct measure of its rate, and counting phantom inodes is not a reliable way to size it.

ELIMINATED SO FAR (five hypotheses, all with evidence rather than reading):
- Missing durability flush — block counters are correct in the same images that have wrong inode counters.
- The descriptor write dropping the field — `persist_group_desc_force_with_bitmap_overrides` sets `free_inodes_count: stats.free_inodes` unconditionally; the bitmap override governs only checksum re-stamping and the UNINIT flag.
- Failing deletes — four-arm parity passes BEFORE and AFTER in the failing comparator run.
- The direct in-process write path — negative control test, clean.
- The per-request scope commit path — negative control test at 20,000 allocations, clean.

WHAT IS LEFT, i.e. what only the mounted arm has:
1. A live FUSE mount with the kernel VFS driving the operations, rather than direct FsOps calls.
2. The daemon's unmount path — `flush_on_destroy` — where both tests use `flush_mvcc_to_device`. These are different functions and only one of them is exercised by a real unmount.
3. The image itself: the comparator CLONES `ext4.base.img` (built by `mke2fs -d` over a fixture tree) into each arm and mounts that, whereas both tests format a fresh image. A cloned base carries whatever descriptor and BG_INODE_UNINIT state mke2fs left, which a fresh in-test format may not reproduce identically.
4. Mount options and the daemon's own lifecycle (backpressure, request scheduling).

(2) and (3) are the cheapest to test next and I would take (3) first: `mke2fs -d` leaves most groups BG_INODE_UNINIT, and the damage starts precisely at group #5 rather than group #0 — which is consistent with something going wrong the first time allocation enters a lazily-initialised group, and inconsistent with a uniform per-delete leak.

BOTH TESTS ARE LANDED AS NEGATIVE CONTROLS and neither is named as a reproduction. They pin both in-process paths as correct at comparator-like volume, so any future fix cannot regress them, and if either ever starts failing the defect has spread into a path currently known-good.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
⭐ REPRODUCED, MINIMALLY, AND THE DISCRIMINATOR IS THE MOUNT.

`scripts/pbyu0_mounted_repro.sh` mounts FrankenFS on a single loop image, runs the storm through the kernel VFS with plain shell, unmounts, and runs e2fsck. No four-arm crossover, no comparator, ~40 seconds:

    6 cycles x 500 files, 512 MiB image
    Free inodes count wrong for group #1 (5192, counted=8192)
    Free inodes count wrong (29755, counted=32755)
    RESULT: DIRTY

Drift 3000 = exactly 6 x 500. One leaked inode per file deleted, confirming the rate that the comparator's cascade made hard to read.

THE CONTROLLED COMPARISON, which is now airtight:

    MOUNTED     6 cycles x 500 files,  512 MiB  ->  DIRTY, 3000 leaked
    IN-PROCESS 40 cycles x 500 files,  512 MiB  ->  CLEAN (20,000 ops, 3x the volume)

Same workload shape, same image size, same candidate binary, same scale or more. The only difference is that one goes through a real FUSE mount and the kernel VFS and ends with the daemon's unmount, and the other calls FsOps directly and ends with `flush_mvcc_to_device`. Everything I eliminated earlier stands; this adds the positive half.

SO THE DEFECT IS IN THE MOUNTED PATH SPECIFICALLY. The three remaining candidates from my last comment are now down to two, and they are testable independently:
  1. The daemon's unmount path — `flush_on_destroy` — versus `flush_mvcc_to_device` which both clean tests use. These are different functions; only the former runs on a real unmount. THIS IS THE PRIME SUSPECT and it is cheap to test: add a mid-run `sync` and re-check, or drive the same ops through a mount and kill the daemon before unmount to see whether the drift is already on disk or only appears at destroy.
  2. Something in the FUSE request path that the direct FsOps calls bypass — inode lifetime (`forget`), the nlookup accounting, or the daemon's own inode cache holding a stale GroupStats view.

(1) is testable in minutes with the script already written. Note the base image here is built with `mke2fs -d` exactly as the comparator does, so the "cloned/UNINIT base image" hypothesis I flagged last time is NOT what distinguishes the cases — the in-process tests format fresh and are clean, but this repro uses `-d` and is dirty, so the mkfs mode alone does not decide it. It remains a possible contributor, not the discriminator.

VALUE BEYOND THE DIAGNOSIS: the reproduction is now ~40 seconds and needs no root, no crossover, no quiet window, and no PGO build. Anyone fixing this can iterate directly instead of running a 2-minute four-arm comparator and reading e2fsck out of a scratch tree.

The script takes cycles/files/image-size as arguments so the threshold can be bisected. Two environment details it encodes, both of which cost me a run each: the mountpoint MUST be under /tmp (a user FUSE mount under /data/tmp is refused EPERM — which is why the comparator uses a /tmp MOUNT_ROOT), and FFS_AUTO_UNMOUNT=0 is required or auto_unmount forces allow_other and fusermount3 fails.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
⭐⭐ ROOT CAUSE IDENTIFIED: the bd-bhh0i SHARDED per-group create path, which is the SHIPPING DEFAULT for `mount --rw`.

CLEAN A/B, same script, same workload, same binary, one environment variable:

    FFS_BHH0I_SHARDED unset (shipping default, sharded ON)   -> DIRTY, 3000 inodes leaked
    FFS_BHH0I_SHARDED=0    (documented rollback, sharded OFF) -> CLEAN

The reproducing run's daemon log carries the confirmation in-band:
    "mount: bd-bhh0i sharded per-group create path ENABLED
     (set FFS_BHH0I_SHARDED=0 for rollback, previous=false)"
and the clean run has no such line.

THIS ALSO EXPLAINS EVERY EARLIER NEGATIVE RESULT, which is why I believe it rather than just noting the correlation:
- Both in-process tests run under `cargo test -p ffs-core`, and ffs-core's `bhh0i_sharded_alloc` feature is DEFAULT OFF. They exercised the single-lock path and were correct.
- The mounted daemon is `ffs-cli`, whose Cargo.toml has `default = ["bhh0i_sharded_alloc"]`, and `mount --rw` then turns the runtime flag ON unless told otherwise. So "mounted vs in-process" was never really the axis — it was "sharded vs single-lock", and the mount was just how the sharded path got selected.
- It explains the alloc/free asymmetry exactly: group #1's descriptor read 5192 = 8192 - 3000, i.e. every ALLOCATION decrement persisted and not one of the 3000 FREE increments. `ext4_flush_group_descriptors` sources its counts from `sharded.snapshot_group_stats()` when the sharded path is active, so a free that credits the single-lock `alloc.groups` array is simply not in the snapshot that gets written.

⚠ SEVERITY IS HIGHER THAN THE ORIGINAL FILING SUGGESTS, and this is the part to act on:
- The defect is ON BY DEFAULT in the shipped `ffs-cli mount --rw`. Any user doing ordinary create/delete work corrupts their filesystem's inode accounting, and on a small enough filesystem gets ENOSPC on an empty disk.
- ffs-core/Cargo.toml documents this same feature as "Default OFF - production keeps the single alloc `RwLock` (byte-identical)". ffs-cli/Cargo.toml line 39 says `default = ["bhh0i_sharded_alloc"]`. Those two statements contradict each other, and the CLI's is the one that ships. Whatever the fix, that contradiction should be resolved explicitly rather than left for the next person to trip over.
- The mounted-comparator rows measured since the cutover were all taken with the sharded path active. That does not invalidate the READ-ONLY rows (readdir+stat, warm stat, parallel read are `--rw`-free), but any MUTATING row measured on it — create/delete storm, parallel metadata writes, fsync, bulk durable write — was measured on a filesystem whose inode accounting was drifting during the run. Worth checking whether that perturbs those numbers before re-banking them.

IMMEDIATE MITIGATION available today, no code change: `FFS_BHH0I_SHARDED=0` restores correctness, at the cost of the parallel-create scaling the sharded path exists to provide.

WHERE THE BUG IS, narrowed but not yet pinpointed: the sharded free path. `ffs_core::ext4_sharded_free_inode` exists (crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs:19005) and delegates to `sharded.free_inode(...)`, but the ordinary unlink path (`ext4_unlink_impl`) calls `ffs_inode::delete_inode` with the SINGLE-LOCK `alloc.groups`. So creates debit the sharded records while deletes credit the single-lock array, and the flush reads only the sharded snapshot. That is consistent with all the evidence; confirming it is the next step, along with deciding whether the fix is to route deletes through the sharded records or to reconcile the two structures at the durability boundary.

REPRODUCTION: `scripts/pbyu0_mounted_repro.sh <ffs-cli> [cycles] [files] [mib]`, ~40s, no root, no comparator. It now forwards FFS_BHH0I_SHARDED so the A/B above is one command each way.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
FIXED BY MITIGATION, VERIFIED BOTH WAYS ON THE REBUILT BINARY. The P0 exposure is closed; the underlying defect is untouched and tracked as bd-y2t0r.

    default `mount --rw` (what a user gets)  ->  e2fsck CLEAN
    FFS_BHH0I_SHARDED=1 (explicit opt-in)    ->  e2fsck DIRTY, identical 3000 leak
                                                 "Free inodes count wrong for group #1
                                                  (5192, counted=8192)"

The opt-in reproducing byte-for-byte is the point: it proves the fix is exactly the default flip and nothing incidental, and it keeps the defect reachable in one command for whoever finishes the cutover.

WHAT CHANGED: `sharded_create_enabled_from_env` in ffs-cli treated `None` as ENABLED, so `mount --rw` used the sharded create path unless an operator opted out. `None` now means DISABLED. `FFS_BHH0I_SHARDED=1` still opts in, so the A/B and the parallel-create perf work remain available.

WHY MITIGATION AND NOT A REAL FIX, stated plainly: routing deletes through the sharded records is the actual repair, and it is not a small change — `ffs_inode::delete_inode` performs data-block frees, inode write-back and the inode free as one unit against `&mut [GroupStats]`, so it needs a backend seam (mirroring `SingleLockDirAlloc` on the create side) or a sharded-aware delete entry point. Doing that hastily on a P0 with a filesystem's inode accounting at stake is the wrong trade. Turning off an incomplete cutover is reversible, provable in 40 seconds, and costs only the parallel-create scaling — a performance property, against a correctness one. Filed as bd-y2t0r with the full design note.

REGRESSION GUARD: `sharded_create_mount_defaults_off_until_the_delete_side_lands_bd_pbyu0` asserts `None => false` and carries the reason plus the re-enable condition in its doc comment, so the flip cannot be quietly reverted. The two ffs-core negative controls stay as they are.

⚠ ONE THING I HAVE NOT VERIFIED AND WILL NOT ASSUME: the BLOCK side. The reproducing workload creates EMPTY files, so it frees no data blocks, which is exactly why e2fsck reported inode-count errors and ZERO block-count errors throughout. `delete_inode` also calls `free_blocks_persist` against the same single-lock `groups`, and the flush reads the same sharded snapshot, so deleting files WITH DATA should leak free-BLOCK counts by identical logic. Untested. Recorded on bd-y2t0r as an explicit acceptance item, and the repro script should be extended to write a block or two per file before anyone declares the sharded path fixed.

ALSO STILL TRUE AND WORTH SOMEONE'S DECISION: ffs-core/Cargo.toml documents `bhh0i_sharded_alloc` as "Default OFF - production keeps the single alloc RwLock", while ffs-cli/Cargo.toml has `default = ["bhh0i_sharded_alloc"]`. This fix changed the RUNTIME default, not the compile-time feature, so both statements remain simultaneously true and mutually misleading. Left alone deliberately — flipping the compile-time feature would also drop the sharded code from the binary and remove the ability to A/B it, which is not obviously right.

BEARING ON BANKED ROWS: every MUTATING comparator row taken since the bd-bhh0i cutover ran with inode accounting drifting mid-run — storm, parallel metadata writes, fsync, bulk durable write. The read-only rows (readdir+stat, warm stat, parallel read) are unaffected since they never mount `--rw`. Whether the drift perturbed the mutating numbers is unmeasured; they should be re-taken on the fixed default before being re-banked.

INDEPENDENTLY VALIDATED THROUGH THE FULL COMPARATOR, not just the 40-second repro.

The create/delete-storm row is the workload that EXPOSED bd-pbyu0: in FS11 the identical invocation aborted with "e2fsck did not report clean image ext4.fuse_a.img: exit status 4", and both FUSE arms carried 11 "Free inodes count wrong" errors each while both kernel arms were clean. Re-run on the fixed candidate (edbaeb4e, rebuilt with the default flip):

    arm        e2fsck
    kernel_a   rc=0, 0 inode-count errors
    fuse_a     rc=0, 0 inode-count errors
    fuse_b     rc=0, 0 inode-count errors

and the run proceeded past post-unmount validation to produce an admitted ratio, which it could not do before.

So the mitigation is confirmed by two independent instruments: the purpose-built repro script AND the four-arm comparator's own post-unmount e2fsck gate, on a workload that previously failed it deterministically.

ALSO WORTH NOTING: the external-load gate (bd-bt2dy) passed this run cleanly — samples=152, contended_fraction=0.0132, max_consecutive_over_limit=1 — during a period when the box's load average was 6-7, largely from the storm's own I/O. That is the corrected policy behaving as intended: it measures EXTERNAL CPU on off-placement cores, so a workload that loads the machine through its own arms does not trip its own gate. The pre-correction version would very likely have refused this run.

description:

title: ffs-fuse: FuseInodeLocks lock-ordering invariant (table → held) is undocumented and untested
description:
Finding (via /deadlock-finder-and-fixer skill, third visit, different
target): `FuseInodeLocks` (crates/ffs-fuse/src/lib.rs:986) holds two
nested locks — the table `Mutex<BTreeMap<InodeNumber, Arc<FuseInodeLock>>>`
that maps inodes to their per-inode locks, and the per-inode
`FuseInodeLock.held: Mutex<bool>` (paired with a Condvar). Static
audit confirms the canonical implicit lock order:

  table (rank 0) → per-inode held (rank 1)

with multi-inode acquires using **sorted-by-inode-number** ordering
to prevent AB-BA across inodes. Production callers comply:

  * `FuseInodeLocks::acquire` (l. 991): table.W → drop table → per-
    inode held.W (acquired in sorted inode order).
  * `FuseInodeLocks::try_acquire` (l. 1025): table.W → drop table
    → per-inode held.W (sorted), short-circuiting on contention.
  * `FuseInodeGuard::Drop` (l. 1127): table.W → held.W (nested)
    → set held=false → notify_one → check strong_count →
    optionally remove the table entry.

The order is consistent (table before held everywhere; sorted-inode
order across multi-inode batches; held released via Condvar wait
during contention). NO AB-BA in production. But:

  1. **No struct-level doc comment** names the invariant on
     `FuseInodeLocks`. A future contributor adding a method that
     took `held.lock()` BEFORE `table.lock()` would silently
     introduce a deadlock against `FuseInodeGuard::Drop`.

  2. **No regression test** exercises the lock ordering under
     contention. The existing tests (e.g.
     `fuse_inode_locks_release_evicts_entry`) run sequentially.

  3. **The sorted-inode-order multi-acquire invariant** is also
     implicit — `acquire([5, 7])` and `acquire([7, 5])` must both
     take inode 5 before inode 7. A future caller that bypassed
     `acquire`/`try_acquire` to lock inodes in a different order
     would deadlock against any concurrent batch.

This is the third in the lock-ordering doc series after bd-7zd94
(PersistentMvccStore) and bd-bky2f (ShardedMvccStore).

Acceptance: a doc comment on `FuseInodeLocks` names the canonical
order with rationale, per-field rank annotations, and a table of
production callers showing compliance. One unit test in the existing
tests module spawns concurrent acquire + drop + try_acquire workers
with a watchdog timeout that fails on hang.
notes: Shipped: struct-level doc on FuseInodeLocks documenting the canonical lock order table → per-inode held with sorted-by-inode-number multi-inode batch ordering, table of production-caller compliance, and the AB-BA scenario a hypothetical held-first caller would create. Added lock_ordering_under_concurrent_acquire_and_drop regression test with 3 concurrent workers (acquire pipeline / try_acquire short-circuit / reverse-order [7,3] pair to verify the sorted-inode invariant) guarded by a 15s watchdog that panics with bd-pfv55 tag on hang. Pairs with bd-7zd94 (PersistentMvccStore) and bd-bky2f (ShardedMvccStore) — third in the lock-ordering doc series. Verified via rch exec -- cargo test -p ffs-fuse --lib lock_ordering_under_concurrent_acquire_and_drop (passes in 0.05s).

title: ffs-block: PageLockTable wait/notify protocol lacks bounded regression guard
description:
Finding via deadlock-finder-and-fixer after source-aware tracker hygiene reported zero local claimable rows and RCH capacity remained blocked.

`PageLockTable` in `crates/ffs-block/src/lib.rs` uses a real wait/notify protocol: `PageLockTable::acquire` waits while a block is in `in_flight`, increments `PageLockShard.waiters` before the condvar wait, and `PageLockPermit::drop` removes the block then `notify_all`s when waiters are present. Current coverage proves same-block miss coalescing, but `arc_cache_same_block_concurrent_miss_coalesces_device_read` joins worker threads without a bounded timeout, and `page_lock_table_tracks_large_distinct_in_flight_set` only covers distinct permits. A lost-wake or missing-notify regression would hang the test process instead of failing with a controlled diagnostic, and no doc names the predicate-loop/waiter-count wake protocol.

Acceptance:
1. Add a doc comment on `PageLockShard`/`PageLockTable` naming the wait predicate, waiter-count discipline, and notify-after-remove requirement.
2. Add a deterministic regression that forces at least one same-block waiter to park, uses a main-thread timeout/watchdog before joining, asserts one underlying device read, and verifies `in_flight_len() == 0`.
3. Avoid blind fixed sleeps in the test; use barriers/channels or bounded polling with a named interval capped by the deadline.
4. title: meas(fuse): AtomicMetrics Debug and snapshot() can under-report a counter SILENTLY — hand-written Debug omits six counters, snapshot() falls through to Default
description:
Two ways a counter can exist, be incremented correctly, and still read as zero to anyone looking at it. Both found by reading during a build-free turn, both fixed in the same change as the bd-i353e/bd-4zokj counters.

1. AtomicMetrics has a HAND-WRITTEN std::fmt::Debug that lists fields explicitly. Unlike a derived Debug it does not go red when a counter is added -- it simply stops mentioning it. The mutation counters from 3145d182 were missing from it for exactly that reason: nothing failed, the dump just under-reported. Six counters were absent (mutation x2, other x2, handler_total x2).

2. AtomicMetrics::snapshot() ends with ..Default::default(). Adding a MetricsSnapshot field therefore compiles whether or not anyone wired the matching .load(). An unwired field reports a constant ZERO, which is the worst failure mode for an instrument because zero is a plausible reading -- and the create/delete attribution DIVIDES by these numbers, so a silent zero produces a confident wrong share rather than a crash.

FIX: the six missing fields added to the Debug impl and to the AtomicMetrics debug golden; a new test snapshot_loads_every_counter_and_none_default_to_zero exercises every counter through the public recording surface and asserts no field still prints ': 0'. The test works off DERIVED Debug on MetricsSnapshot rather than a hand-written field list, so it covers a new counter the moment the field exists -- deliberately, because a hand-listed assertion goes stale exactly when it matters, which is the failure this bead area has already hit twice (the bare '_ => {}' arm, then a hand-picked opcode list in the first version of the reconciliation test).

ACCEPTANCE: both goldens green and the new test green on a real build.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
I INTRODUCED THE snapshot() HALF OF THIS, AND HERE IS EXACTLY WHERE (ProudBarn, 2026-08-16).

Commit 7da2a8b8 (bd-k3g3g, "derive Default so a new counter is one line") added
`..Default::default()` to AtomicMetrics::snapshot(). Today it is inert - every field is still
listed explicitly, so no value changes. But it converts a COMPILE ERROR into a SILENT ZERO: the
moment someone adds a counter to MetricsSnapshot and wires it into AtomicMetrics but forgets
snapshot(), the snapshot reports 0 for it forever, with no error and no warning. That is the
exact failure class this campaign keeps paying for, and I created it while removing a different
tax. Reported here rather than left for someone to find.

THE PRINCIPLE I GOT WRONG, stated so the fix is not just a revert of one line. Struct-update
syntax is right for TEST FIXTURES and for callers that genuinely do not care about the other
fields - that was the real bd-k3g3g win, and ~26 such sites keep it. It is WRONG for the
SERIALISER: snapshot() is the one function whose whole job is to transcribe every counter, so
exhaustiveness there is not a tax, it is the safety property. The compiler refusing to build
until a new counter is wired is precisely the behaviour bd-k3g3g should have preserved.

FIX: delete the `..Default::default()` line from AtomicMetrics::snapshot() ONLY. Leave it on the
test-fixture and caller sites. One line, and it restores compile-time exhaustiveness where it
matters without giving back the 31-site tax.

WHY I HAVE NOT APPLIED IT MYSELF: crates/ffs-fuse/src/lib.rs currently carries ~300 lines of
uncommitted in-flight work (the bd-4zokj whole-request timer), and one of its hunks covers the
impl AtomicMetrics region that contains snapshot(). Editing that region would collide with, or
sweep, work I do not own - the failure mode that produced b56aad87 earlier in this campaign.
Whoever holds that file is already editing snapshot() to wire their new counters and will pass
directly over this line; it is a one-line deletion in the same edit. If it is still present when
the file is free, I will take it.

ON THE Debug HALF, which is NOT mine but is the same class: AtomicMetrics's Debug is hand-written
(lib.rs ~1206) and omits counters - mutation_dispatch_* were added in 3145d182 and never appeared
there. So ATOMIC_METRICS_DEBUG_GOLDEN passes while describing an incomplete struct, and the
golden cannot catch the omission because the golden IS the omission. Note the asymmetry that makes
this subtle: MountHandle DERIVES Debug, so its golden (mount_handle_debug_format) spells out every
field and DID go red when a counter was added - I fixed that in 7da2a8b8. Two goldens over the
same struct, one self-updating in its demands and one silently stale.

SUGGESTED SHAPE for the Debug half, so the fix does not just re-freeze the same hazard: assert
COVERAGE rather than content - a test that the Debug output contains every field name that
MetricsSnapshot declares. Then adding a counter fails the test until Debug lists it, instead of
passing because Debug never mentioned it. That is enforceable without a golden and does not go
stale.

NOT GATED: /data was at 54-59G against the 59G threshold all turn and the standing order barred
starting a build, so nothing here is compiled. The snapshot() diagnosis is from reading the
committed file (git show HEAD:crates/ffs-fuse/src/lib.rs), not from a run.

title: Canonical byte-layout snapshot for BtrfsInodeItem::to_bytes
description: Found via /testing-golden-artifacts audit. ffs_btrfs::BtrfsInodeItem::to_bytes (lib.rs:306) writes the 160-byte struct btrfs_inode_item per fs/btrfs/btrfs_tree.h. bd-nzs5f pinned the kernel offsets (parser side) and bd-0rsx6 pinned the round-trip MR, but the encoder's exact canonical output bytes for a known fixture are not pinned anywhere. A regression that drifted any field's offset would still pass round-trip if the parser were similarly broken. Pin a hardcoded  literal via assert_eq! for a fixed fixture using the same magic values as bd-nzs5f (generation 0x1111…, size 0x2222…, nbytes 0x3333…, nlink 0x44…, uid 0x55…, gid 0x66…, mode 0o100_644, rdev 0x77…, 4 timestamps with nsec values 100M/200M/300M/400M to stay under the 1B-nsec parser invariant). The expected literal pins both magic regions AND the implicit zero regions (transid@8, block_group@32, flags@64, sequence@72, reserved[4]@80) — so a regression that wrote non-zero into a skipped field would also be caught. Pattern matches bd-bq6l8 (BtrfsInodeRef), bd-2gb89 (BtrfsDirItem), bd-yjzhk + bd-fw55q (BtrfsExtentData Regular/Inline).

title: Enforce freshness policy for root conformance divergence reviews
description:
Discovery from a bounded testing-conformance-harnesses pass while source-aware ready work was 0 and RCH capacity remained blocked.

Concrete finding: `conformance/DISCREPANCIES.md` policy says active divergences must include review dates because divergences can become stale, and `crates/ffs-harness/tests/conformance.rs::root_conformance_discrepancies_follow_policy()` enforces required fields plus YYYY-MM-DD syntax. It does not define or enforce a freshness horizon, so accepted DISC rows can silently age past review without any conformance signal. Current evidence on 2026-05-18: DISC-001 and DISC-002 review dates are 2026-03-18, DISC-003 is 2026-03-27, DISC-004 is 2026-05-01, and DISC-005 is 2026-04-13; `conformance/DISCREPANCIES.md` itself is last updated 2026-04-15. Search found the existing closed `bd-zqjv2` syntax/metadata guard and no open local bead for review freshness.

Scope: make the root divergence freshness contract explicit and executable. This should stay non-permissioned and should not run xfstests or mutate fixture images.

Acceptance:
1. `conformance/DISCREPANCIES.md` defines an explicit active-divergence review freshness horizon, stale handling rule, and exemption format if any divergence is deliberately exempt.
2. The ffs-harness conformance guard fails when an active DISC-NNN review date is older than the allowed horizon, malformed beyond calendar validity, future-dated, or exempt without a reason/owner/follow-up bead.
3. Tests cover fresh, stale, future-dated, invalid calendar dates such as 2026-02-31, resolved DISC-R entries, and any allowed exemption path.
4. The report/error text names the stale DISC id, review date, horizon, and required next action so future agents can file or refresh a concrete follow-up instead of weakening the guard.
5. Validation includes focused RCH cargo tests for the conformance discrepancy guard, `cargo fmt --check` through RCH, `cargo clippy -p ffs-harness --all-targets -- -D warnings` through RCH, `jq empty .beads/issues.jsonl`, `git diff --check`, `br dep cycles --no-db --no-auto-import --json`, and source-aware hygiene. If RCH still has no admissible workers, keep this blocked on `bd-oowwx` and do not use local cargo as proof.

title: perf(journal): parallelize JBD2 replay apply-phase staged-block reads (I/O-overlap)
description: replay_jbd2_inner (ffs-journal lib.rs:824) applies committed transactions in a serial loop: for (target, staged) in final_writes { absolute=resolve_block(staged.journal_idx)?; data=dev.read_block(cx,absolute)?.to_vec(); verify_checksum (continue on mismatch); restore escaped magic; dev.write_block(cx,target,data)? }. On crash-recovery mount this serializes one device-read access latency per committed-dirty block (thousands for a busy fs crashed mid-workload), gating recovery/mount time. The staged-block READS are independent; resolve_block is an FnMut caller closure (must stay serial) and the verify/escape/write/count is order-sensitive. LEVER (serial-PLAN/parallel-READ/serial-CONSUME, my bd-g5v1s/bd-w52e5 family): (1) serial plan loop resolves every absolute BlockNumber via resolve_block (preserves first resolve-error in target order), (2) par_iter().map(|abs| dev.read_block(cx,abs)).collect::<Vec<Result>>() overlaps the read latencies up to pool size (blocking read parks worker), (3) serial consume zips planned+reads in target order: read? then verify (checksum continue), escaped magic, write_block, replayed_blocks++ — byte-identical skip/write-order/count/first-error. StagedWrite is Copy; BlockDevice:Send+Sync; needs rayon dep added to ffs-journal (in workspace). Bench target: journal_replay_apply_io_overlap (LatencyBlockDevice 250us/read, serial vs parallel staged-read then identical apply, N=16/64/256), assert_eq written blocks. cc filed, crash-recovery mount-time frontier.
close_reason: VERIFIED (scorecard, ffs-journal journal_replay_apply_io_overlap): parallel staged reads 8.74x/42.4x/51.9x (N=16/64/256) crash-recovery mount I/O-overlap. KEEP. Code shipped 6a24b56e.

title: the mounted comparator's ext4 readdir+stat fixture is NOT htree-indexed — mke2fs -d bakes a linear directory, so both banked readdir+stat rows are measured on an unfair fixture
description:
The mounted comparator builds the large-directory readdir+stat fixture by creating all entries on
the HOST filesystem and baking the tree into the image with mkfs. `build_fixture_tree`
(crates/ffs-harness/src/bin/ffs_mounted_kernel_bench.rs, Workload::ReaddirStat8) does:

    let parent = root.join("large-directory");
    fs::create_dir(&parent)?;
    for index in 0..config.operations { File::create(parent.join(...))?; }

and `create_base_image` then bakes `fixture_root` in with, verbatim:

    ext4 :  mke2fs -t ext4 -F -q -b 4096 -d <fixture_root> <image>
    btrfs:  mkfs.btrfs -f -q -r <fixture_root> <image>

MEASURED CONSEQUENCE, not assumed. Reproducing that exact ext4 construction at 32,768 entries:

    Filesystem features: ... dir_index ...          <- the filesystem SUPPORTS htree
    debugfs -R "htree_dump /large-directory":
        "htree_dump: Not a hash-indexed directory"  <- the DIRECTORY IS NOT INDEXED

`mke2fs -d` writes linear directory blocks and never builds the htree. So every lookup in the
bank's ext4 readdir+stat arm is an O(N) scan over a 32,768-entry directory, and the sweep is
O(N^2). btrfs has no analogue: DIR_ITEM/DIR_INDEX are inherent to the format, so `mkfs.btrfs -r`
produces a normally indexed directory. The two arms of the comparison are built by mechanisms
with DIFFERENT indexing outcomes.

WHAT IT IS WORTH. bd-3zx2x already measured this class once: when PlumRiver rebuilt his ext4
fixture through the mount instead of with `mke2fs -d`, his ext4 sweep moved 555 ms -> 281 ms on the
same binary and workload — roughly 2x. He VOIDED that run rather than report it. The comparator
has never had the same control applied.

ROWS AFFECTED. Directly: `Large-directory readdir+stat, 32,768 entries` on BOTH scorecards —
ext4 `4.967448x` (docs/MOUNTED_KERNEL_SCORECARD.md) and btrfs `8.322812x`
(docs/MOUNTED_BTRFS_SCORECARD.md), plus the `1.68x` ratio-of-ratios that bd-3zx2x exists to
attribute. Any other workload whose fixture is populated by `build_fixture_tree` and consumed
through `mke2fs -d` needs the same check — that audit is part of this bead, not assumed.

DIRECTION, stated because it is not the convenient one. An unindexed ext4 directory INFLATES the
ext4 arm, which inflates the ext4 ratio and therefore SHRINKS the btrfs/ext4 ratio-of-ratios. So
this defect does NOT manufacture the btrfs excess bd-3zx2x is chasing; if anything the banked
1.68x understates one. It is disqualifying for the ext4 row on its own terms, and it must not be
reported as the explanation for bd-3zx2x.

FIX. Build the readdir+stat fixture the way the filesystem would really be populated: mkfs an
EMPTY caller-owned `large-directory` and create the entries THROUGH the mount, for both formats,
so ext4 builds its htree as entries are added. (A fresh mkfs root is uid 0, so the directory must
be caller-owned in the seed tree or creation fails EACCES — seeding it EMPTY keeps the
"created through the mount" property intact.) Then assert the control in the harness rather than
leaving it to a reader: fail the run if `debugfs htree_dump` on the ext4 image does not report a
hash-indexed directory.

THEN RE-MEASURE both readdir+stat rows. Until that lands, both are measured on a fixture path that
does not survive inspection and neither should be quoted.

ACCEPTANCE
- the comparator's ext4 large-directory fixture reports a Hash Version under `debugfs htree_dump`;
- the harness FAILS CLOSED if it does not;
- both formats' entries are created through the mount by the same code path;
- both readdir+stat rows re-measured and the scorecards updated, with the old values marked
  superseded rather than silently replaced.

Found while running bd-3zx2x arm S. Reproduction script:
scratchpad/cmp_fixture_probe.sh (reproduces create_base_image's ext4 path verbatim and dumps the
htree state).
close_reason: All four acceptance items delivered 2026-08-08. The ext4 large-directory fixture is OBSERVED hash-indexed in a real run (debugfs: Hash Version 1, 73728 bytes, read off the run's own base image); the control fails closed; both formats seed through one code path; and BOTH readdir+stat rows are re-measured on the corrected fixture, each twice, all four admitted HONEST_LOSS with both A/A nulls clear and parity pass before and after. ext4 4.052605x / 4.163402x (was 4.967448x), btrfs 7.753405x / 7.649395x (was 8.322812x), candidate 913c36a4 / PGO b30de364 / v3 attested. Old values marked SUPERSEDED in both scorecards, not silently replaced. This bead's predicted direction is CONFIRMED: the corrected btrfs/ext4 ratio-of-ratios is 1.875x vs the banked 1.675x, so the defect was UNDERSTATING the btrfs excess bd-3zx2x chases, exactly as the description warned. The ext4 delta moved in our favour and is explicitly NOT claimed - fixture, ELF, PGO and kernel all changed - attribution filed as bd-pb85e. The residual audit of other fixtures was completed earlier and produced bd-c5210 (parallel-read has the same defect, code fixed, re-measurement open).

comments.text:
CODE FIX LANDED — 6dc07325. The bead stays OPEN: the re-measurement half is not done.
(AzureFrog, 2026-08-08.)

WHAT LANDED (crates/ffs-harness/src/bin/ffs_mounted_kernel_bench.rs)
- `create_fixture_tree` now leaves `large-directory` EMPTY and caller-owned. Caller ownership
  is load-bearing: a fresh mkfs root is uid 0 and `mke2fs -d` preserves the host tree's
  ownership, which is what lets the seeding step write into it without running as root.

  all four arms still clone from one byte-identical image. Seeding through the incumbent rather

  FrankenFS write defect cannot shape the fixture its own read arm is then measured on. It
  unmounts before propagating a seeding failure, so a failed seed cannot leak a loop device into
  every later arm.
- `ensure_ext4_large_directory_is_htree_indexed` FAILS THE RUN unless debugfs reports a
  hash-indexed directory. `dir_index` in the superblock feature set only says the filesystem MAY
  have htrees; asserting the directory itself is the point, because this defect stayed invisible
