title: meas(fuse): an UNPINNED mounted measurement is unstable to 1.4875x on its own A/A null - decide whether daemon placement must be declared like bd-4w2mf's host
description:
FILED FROM MEASUREMENT (ProudBarn, 2026-08-16), as a sibling to bd-4w2mf's worker-scope defect.

THE OBSERVATION. A 5-placement sweep of mounted warm stat (scripts/fuse_placement_sweep.sh,
sha256 fa96f6e976e6b91a7384c372b7b377913295462e0df3e7946e0fa20e19da4451), 20000 stats/rep,
10 reps/arm, two runs, hostname=thinkstation1, ELF binary_sha256=2faab3039bc3da4126df8b9197edb0f431467b0fc0dac2b3376d6a2bc0c14f12,
found that the UNPINNED arm is not a stable instrument:

  unpinned  run1 median 21.26 us/stat (range 16.32-27.74)   own A/A null 1.4875x
            run2 median 16.86 us/stat (range 15.92-18.86)   own A/A null 1.0399x
            cross-run disagreement 1.2613x

Every PINNED arm in the same sweep, same reps, same instrument, was tight: same-CPU 1.0183x/1.0239x,
SMT-sibling 1.0235x/1.0049x, cross-CCD 1.0946x/1.0121x. So the instability is specific to letting
the scheduler place the daemon, not a property of the workload or the harness.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND ONE ROW. requests_total was 1.000/stat in every arm of both runs, so no work
changed - the swing is pure scheduler placement of the FUSE daemon relative to its client. Any
mounted row banked WITHOUT daemon pinning therefore carries an instrument floor of up to ~1.49x
that its own reported CI does not show, because a within-run CI computed from reps that all shared
one accidental placement will look tight while the placement itself is the uncontrolled variable.
That is the same failure mode as bd-4w2mf: a number that looks precise but is not comparable to
another number.

WHAT THIS BEAD IS FOR.
 1. Decide whether the mounted comparator should PIN the daemon by construction. It already has
    --fuse-cpus, and the fuse-dispatch-concurrency work found that wide cpusets silently seated the
    daemon on the clients' SMT siblings - which is the same hazard seen from the other side.
 2. Decide whether an unpinned mounted row should be admissible at all, or should require a
    placement declaration the way bd-4w2mf now requires a host.
 3. Audit which banked mounted rows were taken unpinned. NOT yet done - this bead is the finding,
    not the audit.

NOT CLAIMED. This does not retract any banked row. It says the uncertainty on unpinned mounted rows
is larger than recorded, and gives the size. Whether any specific row's conclusion changes is
exactly what the audit in item 3 would determine.

SCOPE NOTE carried over from bd-4ypbv: co-locating client and daemon on ONE logical CPU is a
latency lever for single-client metadata work and would SERIALISE a concurrent workload, so
"pin the daemon" must not be read as "pin it onto the client" for throughput rows.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
ITEM 3 DONE, AND A SECOND INDEPENDENT MEASUREMENT OF THE SAME DEFECT (AzureBay, 2026-08-16, commit 2e26c23e).

THE AUDIT (item 3), as --placement-audit on the ledger preflight:

  rows_parsed                 1235
  mounted_keep_rows            134
  placement_scoped_ratio_rows   39
    docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md               33
    docs/progress/perf-negative-results.md   6

39 banked mounted ratios do not say where the FUSE daemon was placed. Forward-only ratchet seeded at 39; it may only fall. It reports rather than retracts, because this bead is explicit that the finding does not retract any banked row.

CONVERGING EVIDENCE, from a different instrument and a different failure. My unpinned managed-runtime harness measured a memo effect at 1.200033x where the PINNED comparator measured 2.063608x on the same fixture at MATCHED thread count — a 1.72x instrument disagreement, larger than the 1.4875x null this bead reports. It invalidated a decomposition I had already published, which I retracted in 263e70c8. Same signature as yours: requests_total unchanged, so no work moved.

Two independent agents, two instruments, two failure modes (a swinging A/A null; a systematically compressed ratio), one cause. That is stronger than either measurement alone.

ITEM 1 — should the comparator pin by construction? It already does: DEFAULT_FUSE_CPUS is applied unless overridden, and every banked comparator row was taken at --fuse-cpus 1. The exposure is NOT the comparator; it is ad-hoc harnesses like mine, which mount directly and inherit whatever the scheduler does. So the fix does not belong in the comparator's defaults.

ITEM 2 — should an unpinned mounted row be admissible? My answer, implemented: admissible if it DECLARES its placement, refused if it is silent. The recognised forms include placement_scope=, --fuse-cpus, same_llc/cross-ccd/smt-sibling, and the literal word "unpinned" — declaring UNPINNED clears the check. The defect is silence, not the absence of pinning: a row that says it was unpinned lets a reader apply your 1.4875x floor to it, and a row that says nothing does not. That is exactly the bd-4w2mf treatment of the host, one level down.

SCOPE, deliberately narrow and modelled on is_worker_scoped_ratio: a mounted row quoting no incumbent ratio makes no cross-configuration comparison, so undeclared placement costs it nothing and it is out of scope. Only KEEP + mounted + vs-incumbent ratio + no placement token counts.

Four self-test checks pin it in the same shape as the worker-scope ones so they cannot drift: undeclared is flagged, declared is not, no-ratio is out of scope, ratchet holds at 39. Self-test 66 -> 70 checks.

WHAT I HAVE NOT DONE: decided anything about the 39 existing rows. The audit names them (--placement-audit --list) and the ratchet stops the count growing; whether any specific row's conclusion changes is the question this bead says the audit would inform, not one the audit answers.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
MY OWN PUBLISHED SHARE WAS MEASURED ON A MIXED INSTRUMENT — CORRECTED (AzureBay, 2026-08-16, commits 8cdd49c5 + scorecard).

The daemon-share attribution I banked in 6e562cae divided dispatch nanos measured inside an UNPINNED managed-runtime mount by the PINNED comparator's per-entry wall. That mixes exactly the two instruments the --placement-audit ratchet I built for bd-plt79 exists to separate. I found it by turning that audit on my own work.

Re-measured with the daemon pinned to one core and the client to different cores, mirroring --fuse-cpus 1, affinity reported OBSERVED not requested (observed daemon affinity: 8 on every arm):

  daemon share 4096   published 47.21%    -> pinned 41.62%          (published 13.4% rel. high)
  daemon share 65536  published 0%+/-2.5% -> pinned -1.66%, +/-1.7% (same conclusion, tighter)
  getxattr dispatches 4096   32,770 -> 163,842   IDENTICAL pinned and unpinned
  getxattr dispatches 65536  32,770 -> 32,770    IDENTICAL pinned and unpinned

THE COUNTS DID NOT MOVE AT ALL. That is the direct confirmation that counts are placement-immune while nanos are not — the distinction the correction rests on, and the reason the opcode-census half of this bead's attribution (1.0000 probes/entry, dispatch counts) is unaffected.

THE SHARE MOVED 5.6 POINTS and the accounting moves with it: removing the pinned daemon work predicts 3893.3 ns/entry against a measured 3231.8, i.e. 1.713x against 2.064x. The descent explains 74% of the lever, not 88%, and the unexplained residual GROWS from ~12% to ~26%.

That is the uncomfortable direction and I want it on the record as such: the correction does not tidy the residual away, it makes it larger. Four hypotheses have now been eliminated or retracted for that residual — contention (retracted 263e70c8), counter-undercount-alone, memo bookkeeping (cf435ef9), and now instrument placement — and it is bigger than when I started explaining it.

WHAT IS UNCHANGED on this bead: the opcode census (exactly one security.capability GETXATTR per entry, no GETATTR/LOOKUP/STATX in the steady state), the dispatch counts, and the conclusion that once the memo fits there is no daemon-side work left to remove. Only the SHARE percentage and the explained fraction move.

THE GENERAL LESSON: an instrument-quality gate is only worth building if it is turned on your own banked work first. --placement-audit was built to flag 39 other rows and it flagged a number I had published two entries earlier. The error was invisible in the original entry precisely because both halves were individually defensible — daemon-internal counters on one side, the trustworthy comparator on the other — and nothing in the row said they came from different scheduling regimes.

6e562cae and the scorecard block in 365b9198 keep the superseded 47.21%/88% figures; both are corrected forward rather than rewritten, so the mistake stays visible.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
TWO BUDGET-MECHANICS FINDINGS FROM THIS TURN, both of which cost real decisions (AzureBay, 2026-08-16).

1. THE THRESHOLD MUST EXCEED floor + build footprint, or it authorises exactly what it forbids.

I followed the rule as written: ran df -h /data (60G, clearing the 59G threshold), verified no frankenfs build was in flight, started exactly ONE build. The build finished in 2m56s and took /data from 60G to 56G — BELOW the 58G floor. A release-perf link of ffs-cli costs about 4G, so a 59G start threshold with a 4G build is arithmetically guaranteed to end under the floor. The pre-check is necessary and not sufficient; the gate needs headroom greater than the footprint of the build it admits, or every admitted build ends in violation.

2. `pgrep -af "rch exec" | grep -c frankenfs` COUNTS ITSELF, and I declined builds for two turns because of it.

The shell command contains both the pattern and the project name (via its cwd path), so pgrep matches the very process running the check. Two turns in a row it reported "2 builds in flight" and I stood down under the two-per-project cap. When I finally printed the matches instead of counting them, both were my own command line — and the ONE real build on the box was `rch exec --clean-overlay ... -o crates/fp-types/src/lib.rs`, which is FRANKENPANDAS, a different project entirely.

So frankenfs had ZERO builds in flight on both occasions. The cost was two turns of unnecessarily declined builds, on a fleet the user was simultaneously trying to un-throttle.

This is the same failure class as the MetricsSnapshot count (58 -> 17 -> 10) and the "unreported_by_this_elf" label: a pattern that matches more than the thing being counted, trusted without printing what it matched. The fix is the same one that worked there — print the matches, do not count them — and it is cheap enough that there is no excuse for skipping it.

RELIABLE FORM for anyone checking build slots:
  ps -eo pid,args --no-headers | grep -E "^\s*[0-9]+ (/[^ ]*/)?(rch|cargo) "
then read the command lines and confirm the project from the -o/--base paths, because rch invocations name their project only in those arguments. `pgrep -f` on a string your own command contains cannot work.

title: Bitmap CRC: cross-validate crc32c crate against software implementation
description:
Write a test that computes CRC32C of the same 4096-byte bitmap data using:
(a) the crc32c crate 0.6.8 (current)
(b) a manual software CRC32C implementation (polynomial 0x1EDC6F41, reflected)
(c) the crc32fast crate (if available) for a third opinion

Compare all three results. If they differ, the crc32c crate has a hardware-acceleration bug on this CPU. If they agree, the bug is in our bridge function or the data we're checksumming.

Test data: a real mkfs.ext4 bitmap block (or a synthetic 4096-byte buffer with known CRC).

ACCEPTANCE: A test that definitively proves whether the crc32c crate produces correct results for 4096-byte inputs on this platform.
close_reason: Root cause found: bitmap CRC was chaining group_number + using full block length. Fixed in commit 20d65f4.

title: [bug] btrfs read of kernel-written ZSTD-compressed files fails: Unknown frame descriptor
description: GAUNTLET FINDING (cc 2026-06-19, first btrfs head-to-head). frankenfs CANNOT read a zstd-compressed btrfs file written by the Linux kernel (mount -o compress=zstd): 'btrfs zstd decompression failed: Unknown frame descriptor'. Kernel reads it fine. SCOPED: (1) frankenfs reads UNCOMPRESSED btrfs file data correctly (1MiB, exact bytes) so logical->physical mapping + btrfs_read_logical_into + uncompressed path WORK; (2) failure is ZSTD-specific. ReadJob::Read (ffs-core lib.rs ~8667) reads disk_num_bytes from disk_bytenr via the SAME btrfs_read_logical_into uncompressed uses, then btrfs_decompress (lib.rs:7813 zstd::decode_all). 'Unknown frame descriptor' on the FIRST decode = the compressed bytes do not start with the zstd magic 0x28B52FFD, so frankenfs reads the WRONG compressed bytes for a compressed extent (NOT a decode-method issue; single-frame read_exact gave same error). Hypothesis: compressed-extent-specific field parse or disk_bytenr/disk_num_bytes handling, OR compressed data lives in a DATA block group whose mapping differs from the metadata path the uncompressed small file used. frankenfs W144 bd-m6g2o decompress round-trips only because it never read kernel-written compressed extents. REPRO: truncate 2G img; format btrfs; mount -o loop,compress=zstd:3; write 100MiB compressible file; umount; ffs walk img --read-data. NEXT: hexdump bytes frankenfs reads at disk_bytenr vs on-disk zstd frame to find the offset/field bug. Real interop conformance gap; compressed read is core btrfs functionality.
close_reason: FIXED (cc): btrfs kernel-written zstd read works. Two causes: (1) decode_all choked on sector-padding after the frame -> find_frame_compressed_size + bulk::decompress on the sliced frame; (2) tail extent ram_bytes sector-rounded above frame output -> resize-zero-fill to ram_bytes (kernel decodes into zeroed page buffer, csum tree is the integrity guard). Reads 137MiB/1099-extent file fully, content sha256 matches kernel exactly. ffs-core 1177 tests pass; updated the strict-reject test to assert zero-fill + added oversized-reject test.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
DIAGNOSIS NARROWED (cc, btrfs-progs ground truth + differential tests):
- Compressed extents: disk_num_bytes=4096 (a 128KiB chunk compresses to <4KiB 'quick brown fox' text), packed every 4096B; ram=131072, num_bytes=131072, compression 3. itemsize 53 (standard regular file_extent_item).
- Chunk tree: DATA chunk logical 13631488 -> physical 13631488 (1:1); a 2nd DATA chunk logical 137756672 -> physical 253493248 (NON-1:1). zstd frame magic 0x28B52FFD CONFIRMED present in the image at physical 13631488/13635584/... (== disk_bytenr values), 1099 occurrences.
- RULED OUT non-1:1 chunk mapping AND multi-chunk AND file-size: frankenfs reads a 50MiB UNCOMPRESSED file that spans TWO data chunks (8MiB 1:1 + 117MiB non-1:1) CORRECTLY (52428800 bytes exact). And a 1MiB uncompressed file correctly.
- So the bug is DEFINITIVELY zstd-COMPRESSED-specific. frankenfs reads the correct SIZE (compressed_len=4096) from the correct LOGICAL (disk_bytenr, which maps 1:1 here to a physical offset where the zstd magic IS), yet btrfs_decompress gets bytes NOT starting with the zstd magic.
- REMAINING SUSPECT: the compressed-extent read produces wrong bytes despite correct disk_bytenr/disk_num_bytes — a narrow defect in the compressed ReadJob path or its disk_bytenr/disk_num_bytes parse/usage that does NOT affect the uncompressed ReadJob (which reads source_logical=disk_bytenr+extent_offset and works). NEXT: debug build dumping the first 8 bytes frankenfs reads at logical=disk_bytenr for a compressed extent vs the on-disk frame (expect 28 b5 2f fd) — a 1-line eprintln in ReadJob::Read will pinpoint whether the read or the parse is wrong.

title: setattr size change (truncate) does not update mtime — ext4 + btrfs
description: POSIX: a successful ftruncate/truncate marks BOTH the last-data-modification (mtime) and last-status-change (ctime) timestamps for update. The kernel passes only ATTR_SIZE|ATTR_CTIME to the fs on truncate (do_truncate sets time_attrs=0; notify_change adds ctime, NOT mtime), so the filesystem itself must bump mtime when it sees a size change — ext4 does (inode mtime=ctime=current on ATTR_SIZE). Under FUSE the kernel likewise sends FATTR_SIZE without FATTR_MTIME on ftruncate, so FrankenFS owns the mtime update. Both ext4_setattr and btrfs_setattr bump only ctime (always) and set mtime ONLY when an explicit attrs.mtime is provided (utimes); a pure truncate therefore leaves mtime stale — diverging from the kernel and breaking make/rsync/incremental-backup change detection. FIX: in both setattr paths, when attrs.size changes the size and no explicit attrs.mtime was given, set mtime to the op timestamp (same now() as ctime). Deterministic test: after a size-changing truncate, returned attr.mtime == attr.ctime.
close_reason: Fixed in 1ead0d8e: ext4_setattr + btrfs_setattr now stamp mtime (== ctime) on a size-changing truncate when no explicit attrs.mtime is given, matching the in-kernel ext4 (kernel sends ATTR_SIZE/ATTR_CTIME without ATTR_MTIME on truncate). Regressions btrfs_/ext4_truncate_updates_mtime_bd_pssza. ffs-core 1044/0; clippy clean.

The existing inode_ref_round_trip test (line 7127) covers ONE fixed input (index=42, name=b"hardlink-target"). No proptest sweeps over arbitrary (index, name) pairs and no test asserts multi-entry concatenation invariance — i.e., that stamp(a) ++ stamp(b) ++ stamp(c) parses to [a, b, c]. title: ffs-ondisk btrfs: on-disk struct sizes (header, item, key_ptr, disk_key, chunk, stripe, dev_item) lack kernel-conformance pin
description:
Finding (via /testing-conformance-harnesses skill, NEW target): crates/ffs-ondisk/src/btrfs.rs declares 7 file-local on-disk struct size constants used as offsets/strides by every btrfs parser:

  BTRFS_HEADER_SIZE     = 101  (struct btrfs_header packed)
  BTRFS_ITEM_SIZE       = 25   (struct btrfs_item packed)
  BTRFS_KEY_PTR_SIZE    = 33   (struct btrfs_key_ptr packed)
  BTRFS_DISK_KEY_SIZE   = 17   (struct btrfs_disk_key packed)
  BTRFS_CHUNK_FIXED_SIZE= 48   (struct btrfs_chunk fixed prefix)
  BTRFS_STRIPE_SIZE     = 32   (struct btrfs_stripe packed)
  BTRFS_DEV_ITEM_SIZE   = 98   (struct btrfs_dev_item packed)

Each value derives from sizeof(struct ...) under __attribute__((packed)) in include/uapi/linux/btrfs_tree.h. None of them have a kernel-conformance test pinning the value to the canonical kernel struct layout. A regression that off-by-one'd any of these (e.g., a developer aligning btrfs_disk_key to 24 bytes by accident) would silently mis-stride every leaf/internal-node walk and mis-locate every chunk descriptor.

The existing bd-6uu7j (chunk_type_flags), bd-khzn4 (tree objectids), bd-f0q7n (item keys) cover SCALAR macro values. This bead covers STRUCT byte-sizes — a distinct class of regression.

Acceptance: kernel-conformance test in crates/ffs-ondisk/src/btrfs.rs that pins all 7 struct sizes to the canonical kernel values and asserts pairwise that each value equals the field-by-field sum of its component sizes (so a future drift in either the struct const or the field assignments fails the test).
close_reason: done

title: Implement i_version increment-on-write for NFSv4 and statx(2) compatibility
description:
BACKGROUND: ext4 inodes have a 64-bit version counter split across two fields: i_version (l_i_version at offset 0x24, low 32 bits) and i_version_hi (offset 0x98, high 32 bits). This counter is used by NFSv4 for cache coherence (the NFS change attribute) and by statx(2) via STATX_CHANGE_COOKIE. The kernel increments it on every inode metadata or data change via ext4_inode_set_iversion_raw().

CURRENT STATE: Commit 4a1fb8a added the version and version_hi fields to Ext4Inode and wired them into parse/serialize, so the values are preserved across read-modify-write cycles. However, we never INCREMENT them — every write-back produces the same version counter the inode had when we read it.

IMPACT: NFS clients mounting a FrankenFS-served ext4 image via NFS will never see version changes, causing them to serve stale cached data indefinitely. The statx(2) STATX_CHANGE_COOKIE field will also be stale.

IMPLEMENTATION PLAN:
1. Add a helper function bump_inode_version(inode: &mut Ext4Inode) that increments the 64-bit version counter (version + version_hi as a combined u64, then split back).
2. Call bump_inode_version in every write path that modifies the inode: ext4_write, ext4_create, ext4_mkdir, ext4_unlink, ext4_rmdir, ext4_rename, ext4_link, ext4_symlink, ext4_setattr (truncate, chmod, chown, utimes), ext4_setxattr, ext4_removexattr.
3. Only bump when metadata_csum or 64bit features are enabled (the field is only meaningful with extended inodes).
4. Add a test that performs a write, reads back the inode, and verifies version > original_version.
5. Add a test that performs multiple writes and verifies the version is monotonically increasing.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA:
- Every inode-modifying operation bumps i_version.
- Version is monotonically increasing within a mount session.
- Round-trip test: write, read-back, verify version increased.
- No version bump on read-only operations (getattr, read, readdir).
- The 64-bit counter wraps correctly at u64::MAX (wrapping_add).
close_reason: Added bump_inode_version() called from touch_mtime_ctime() and touch_ctime(). All 3,591 tests pass. Commit f3c69f2.

title: Refine repair-write serialization with epoch lease persistence and ABA guards
description:
Supplemental refinement for bd-rchk0.1.1.1. The executable serialization state tests must guard against ABA-style races: a repair lease, epoch, symbol generation, or snapshot id can expire and later appear valid again unless the state machine records monotonic identities and reopen semantics. This bead makes those identity and persistence rules explicit before mutating repair writeback is enabled.

Scope: define epoch/lease identity invariants for client writes versus repair writeback, including monotonic generation ids, stale lease refusal, unmount/reopen behavior, cancellation cleanup, idempotent retry, symbol refresh, and halfway failure recovery. The goal is to prove that a stale repair plan cannot mutate current client data after an apparently matching id is reused.

Required proof before close:
1. Unit/model tests cover monotonic epoch ids, lease generation ids, stale lease refusal, stale repair-symbol refusal, snapshot id mismatch, unmount/reopen persistence, cancellation cleanup, idempotent retry after failure, and halfway verification failure.
2. Unit tests include explicit ABA fixtures where an old lease id, old block range, old symbol generation, or old snapshot appears structurally valid but must still be rejected.

5. Downstream enablement beads for mounted mutating repair must consume this proof and fail closed if epoch/lease identities are missing, non-monotonic, stale, or not persisted across reopen where required.

title: perf(fuse): readdir+stat is DAEMON-WORK-bound, not round-trip-bound — cutting 33% of crossings bought +0.1%; aim at per-entry ops.getattr instead
description:
FILED FROM MEASUREMENT (ProudBarn, 2026-08-16). Redirects the campaign's worst vs-incumbent row.

THE A/B, one ELF, env-toggled, daemon pinned to cpu8 / client cpu40, ls -lU over 20001 entries,
ext4 fixture, memo 65536, ELF binary_sha256=2faab3039bc3da4126df8b9197edb0f431467b0fc0dac2b3376d6a2bc0c14f12,
hostname=thinkstation1:

  arm                    lookup  getattr  getxattr  readdir   scopes/entry
  AUTO (default)          0.990    1.010     1.000   0.0020         3.002
  readdirplus FORCED      0.000    2.005     1.000   0.0052         3.011

Forcing readdirplus WORKS: it eliminates the per-entry lookup entirely (0.990 -> 0.000). getattr
doubles because our readdirplus handler calls ops.getattr once per entry to build the reply
(lib.rs ~3583) on top of the kernel's own getattr.

THE INSTRUMENTATION CORRECTION THAT CHANGES THE READING, and it is mine to make: requests_total
is NOT a count of FUSE boundary crossings. record_ok() increments it (lib.rs:1156) and is called
from with_request_scope, which readdirplus invokes ONCE PER ENTRY internally. So requests_total
counts request SCOPES including NESTED ones. In the forced arm ~1.0 getattr/entry is nested
inside a single readdirplus request and is not a crossing.

  true boundary crossings   AUTO ~3.00/entry     FORCED ~2.01/entry

So forcing readdirplus cuts real round trips by ~33%. And wall moved +0.1% (bd-4ypbv).

THE CONCLUSION, which redirects this row: THE 7.728937x readdir+stat ROW IS NOT ROUND-TRIP-BOUND.
A 33% cut in boundary crossings bought nothing measurable. The cost is the per-entry work the
daemon does either way - it getattrs every entry whether that getattr arrives as its own request
or nested inside readdirplus. Every remaining round-trip-count lever on this row is therefore
predicted to be worth ~0, and the campaign should stop buying them.

WHAT TO AIM AT INSTEAD: ops.getattr per entry, ~1.0/entry unavoidable for `ls -l` semantics, plus
the ~1.0/entry the kernel asks for separately. Two concrete shapes, neither measured:
 1. Serve the kernel's post-readdirplus getattr from the attributes readdirplus ALREADY returned.
    The vendored fuser passes the same TTL for entry_valid AND attr_valid (reply.rs:645-647) and
    ATTR_TTL is 60s, so the kernel SHOULD already be caching them - yet getattr stays ~1.0/entry
    on top of ours. Why it re-asks is unexplained and is the first thing to find out; if it is a
    generation=0 or a stx_mask issue, that is a small fix worth ~1.0 crossing AND ~1.0 getattr of
    daemon work per entry.
 2. Make the readdirplus reply reuse attributes the readdir walk already materialised, instead of
    a fresh ops.getattr per entry. Whether the btrfs/ext4 readdir path has them to hand is the
    open question.

WHY THIS IS WORTH MORE THAN THE COUNT LEVERS: shape 1 removes DAEMON WORK, which is what the
+0.1% says is actually binding, and it does so on the row with the worst ratio in the campaign.

CAVEATS. Single run per arm, counts only, no wall measured here - the wall claim (+0.1%) is
bd-4ypbv's, not re-measured. Counts are exact and reproduce the earlier 0.99 lookup / 1.01 getattr
observation independently. ext4 fixture; the banked ratio is btrfs, and the request mix on btrfs
should be confirmed before sizing a fix.

CONSEQUENCE FOR OTHER BEADS: any reconciliation that treats requests_total as a crossing count is
comparing two different quantities. bd-i353e's acceptance arithmetic (13.002 crossings/op vs
counted dispatches) needs to state which of the two it means, because for any op that nests a
scope they differ. Relayed to AzureBay.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
READDIRPLUS LINE CLOSED ON DAEMON WORK (ProudBarn, 2026-08-16). Three arms, one ELF, FFS_FUSE_READDIRPLUS_AUTO toggled, daemon cpu8 / client cpu40, 20001-entry ext4 fixture:

  (a) OUR handler alone (ls -U, client never stats):  AUTO 197 getattr (0.010/entry) vs FORCED 20106 (1.005/entry)
  (b) with stat (ls -lU):                             FORCED 40107 = ours 20106 + kernel ~20001
  (c) TWO ls -lU passes in ONE mount:                 AUTO 20394 getattr / 19808 lookup;  FORCED 60212 getattr / 0 lookup

(c) is the decisive one and it needed (a) to be interpretable. The attribute cache is NOT broken - AUTO's second pass is served almost entirely from cache. Forced readdirplus nonetheless re-getattrs every entry on EVERY readdir while the kernel holds valid cached attrs, so two passes cost 60212 getattr against AUTO's 20394: 2.95x the daemon work for identical output.

So forcing readdirplus trades ~0.99 lookup crossings/entry for ~1.005 getattr of daemon WORK per entry per readdir, and the kernel does not use the attributes it is handed. That is the mechanism behind the +0.1% wall, and the +0.1% understated the harm. AUTO stays the default; the readdirplus lever line is closed.

STILL UNEXPLAINED, and it is the one thread worth pulling here: why does the kernel re-ask getattr in pass 1 when our readdirplus reply carries attr_valid = ATTR_TTL = 60s? The vendored fuser sets BOTH entry_valid and attr_valid from that one TTL (reply.rs:645-647), to_file_attr sets ino from the attr so an ino mismatch is ruled out, and generation is passed as 0. If that is a real defect, fixing it would remove ~1.0 kernel getattr per entry on the worst row - which is daemon work, the thing measured to be binding. I have NOT diagnosed it; only headers are installed here, not fs/fuse source.

Caveats: single run per arm, counts only, ext4 fixture while the banked ratio is btrfs.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
TWO OF MY OWN NUMBERS WITHDRAWN (ProudBarn, 2026-08-16), build-free turn, no new measurement.

CONFOUNDED RUN: an early hand-run built its name list with 'ls -U $MNT | head -200' inside the SAME mount it then measured. The pipe SIGPIPE'd, so a partial walk of a 20001-entry directory landed in the same counters as the measured 200-entry 'ls -l'. It reported requests_total=1456 over 200 entries (7.28 scopes/entry) and 646/1456 scopes counted ('56% uncounted'). Both are unusable: the denominator is 200 entries, the numerator includes an unknown slice of a 20001-entry walk. I quoted the 56% figure to AzureBay as live evidence — WITHDRAWN, and I have told them.

SCOPING MY REFUTATION OF 7.00 requests/entry: the clean run (ls -lU, 20001 entries, one workload per fresh mount, four counters summing to 60286 of 60295) gives 3.014 scopes/entry. That refutes 7.00 FOR THIS WORKLOAD, which is the one the banked row runs, and that claim stands. It does NOT show 7.00 is wrong in general — the confounded run is silent and no clean explicit-arg 'ls -l' measurement exists. My commit message said the figure 'must not be reused'; the accurate form is 'must not be reused for this workload without re-measurement, and its origin workload is unknown'.

METHOD RULE, now enforced in code rather than remembered: never enumerate a directory in the mount you are measuring. scripts/fuse_readdirplus_work_ab.sh takes its entry count from a separate throwaway mount, runs exactly one workload per measured mount, and fails closed (exit 2/3/4) rather than reporting a number from a mount that did not come up or emitted no dispatch metrics.

THE HARNESS ITSELF is this bead's acceptance instrument for the next lever. It measures DAEMON WORK by decomposition, not by subtraction from wall: arm A ('ls -U', client never stats) isolates the handler's own getattr; arm B ('ls -lU') adds the kernel's; arm C (two passes in one mount) shows whether the handler re-derives attributes the kernel already holds. Regression reference from 2026-08-16 is embedded in the header: A AUTO 197 vs FORCED 20106; B FORCED 40107; C AUTO 20394 vs FORCED 60212. A lever that reuses attributes the readdir walk already materialised should move arm A's FORCED number toward its AUTO number WITHOUT moving B's kernel component — that separation is why the arms are shaped this way.

title: ext4 read_dir reads directory blocks one-at-a-time (scalar); coalesce contiguous runs into vectored reads
description:
read_dir_with_scope reads each directory block with a separate scalar device op (read_ext4_file_data_block_with_scope per logical block). The file-read path already coalesces contiguous physical blocks into a single vectored read (read_contiguous_blocks_with_scope, bd-a384r); read_dir does not. First-listing of a large directory (thousands of entries → dozens/hundreds of contiguous dir blocks) is therefore N scalar device ops instead of one vectored op per contiguous run.

LEVER (batched I/O, different class from the cache/descent levers): in read_dir_with_scope, build contiguous-physical runs of present, non-unwritten, NOT-already-cached blocks and read each run via read_contiguous_blocks_with_scope (one device op), populating the read-only data-block cache. Already-cached blocks (bd-di429 warm path) are still served scalar from the cache, so warm readdir stays at 0 device ops; only the cold first listing is vectored. read_contiguous_blocks_with_scope already handles staged-write / MVCC-snapshot correctness. Isomorphic (same Ext4DirEntry set, same order).

PROOF: multi-block contiguous directory fixture + VectoredCountingDevice: cold readdir does 1 vectored op vs N scalar ops, Score = N (block count).
close_reason: done

title: perf(cold-read): re-derive the 2026-06-21 cold matrix — kernel-side loop-mount serializes I/O (3.08x on identical bytes) and 'cat' was bat/uutils; both inflated frankenfs
description:
EVIDENCE (BlackThrush/cc_ffs 2026-07-10). Two independent methodology defects each inflate frankenfs's cold-read numbers vs 'kernel'. Both were found while re-verifying bd-5v3mh. Every 2026-06-21 cold-matrix row ('WIN - DOMINATES kernel cold', ext4 extent/fragmented/indirect/metadata-walk, btrfs uncompressed/compressed/many-files) is affected because those rows (a) used kernel 'cat' and/or (b) loop-mounted the image for the kernel side while frankenfs preads the image file directly.

DEFECT 1 - 'cat' is not GNU cat on this box. 'cat' is an alias for bat 0.26.1; /usr/bin/cat is uutils coreutils 0.2.2. Both issue 832-byte read() calls (strace-verified) => they measure syscall overhead, not the cold read path. 800 MiB dense fixture, drop_caches=3 each: cat 2932 ms (273 MiB/s) vs a plain 1 MiB read loop 513 ms (1558 MiB/s) = 5.7x too slow. Already recorded in crates/ffs-block/examples/cold_read.rs and NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md (commit d6ee4936).

DEFECT 2 (NEW) - the kernel side's LOOP DEVICE serializes parallel reads. Proven on IDENTICAL physical bytes (1 GiB file, 5 extents, in a real ext4 image on /data):
  * kernel reading /mnt/.../cold1g.bin through the loop mount, thread sweep: t=4 862.0ms, t=8 903.9ms, t=16 852.2ms, t=32 853.4ms, t=64 850.7ms -> FLAT, ~1200 MiB/s, NO scaling.
  * the SAME bytes pread directly from the image file (no loop, no fs), same thread counts: t=8 393.3ms, t=16 332.5ms, t=32 277.4ms, t=64 281.7ms -> scales to 3692 MiB/s.
  => loop-device penalty at t=32 on identical bytes: 853.4/277.4 = 3.08x.
Corroboration: on a plain 800 MiB file on the same /data ext4 with NO loop, the kernel parallel reader scales 533ms(t=1) -> 185ms(t=16) = 2.9x. So the disk scales; the loop does not.

CONSEQUENCE: 'ffs-cli read' parses ext4 and preads the IMAGE FILE directly (no loop) using rayon (nproc=64, 'each read chunk uses the chunked-parallel engine internally', main.rs ~2397). Comparing that against a loop-mounted kernel mount is parallel-vs-serialized. It manufactured an apparent 2.84x (raw) / 3.23x (startup-corrected) frankenfs win in my own first run, which is an artifact.

HONEST NUMBER (loop removed from BOTH sides; frankenfs vs a raw parallel pread of the same 5 extents, matched hardware, drop_caches each, min-of-N): frankenfs 466.2 ms (2197 MiB/s) vs raw device floor 277.4 ms (3692 MiB/s) = frankenfs is 1.68x SLOWER than raw parallel bandwidth. The ext4 parse + safe-copy tax is real and measurable; frankenfs does NOT reach raw bandwidth. Correctness is unaffected: sha256(cold1g.bin) via kernel mount == via 'ffs-cli read' (648484be0b8f0f0099a695f6a680391576b71ea4cad8ad98e4db1a336d2a3589).

CLEAN RESULT THAT SURVIVES: the single-thread fadvise(SEQUENTIAL) lever, measured on a raw 800 MiB file on real ext4 with a loop-free, pure-read kernel baseline: kernel 513.5ms vs frankenfs none 615.7ms (1.199x slower) vs frankenfs sequential 479.6ms (1.071x faster). 6/6 reps. That row is trustworthy.

WHAT TO DO: (1) never use 'cat' as an I/O baseline on this box; (2) never loop-mount the image for the kernel side of a PARALLEL read comparison -- either put a real ext4 on a spare block device/LVM volume, or compare frankenfs against a raw parallel pread floor over the same physical extents; (3) re-run the 2026-06-21 cold matrix under (1)+(2) and correct the rows. Caveat: box load swung 13->67 during this session; use min-of-N and only compare arms measured within the same run.
close_reason:
RE-DERIVED. The headline 2026-06-21 cold row FLIPS SIGN, and this bead's own prescription was wrong.

(1) CORRECTED PRESCRIPTION. This bead said "never loop-mount the image for the kernel side of a
parallel comparison." That is WRONG. Loop serialization is a BUFFERED-MODE artifact, not a property
of loop devices. Same loop mount, same bytes, drop_caches=3 per run, min-of-5:
    dio=0 (default):  t=1/8/32 =  97.7 / 124.2 / 113.6 ms   flat, no scaling
    dio=1 (--direct-io=on): t=1/8/32 = 52.1 / 25.1 / 28.2 ms   scales
= 4.9x at t=8 on identical bytes, from one ioctl. The right rule is "give the kernel its BEST
configuration (direct-I/O loop), then compare" -- which RESTORES the mounted-kernel-filesystem
comparator this project is supposed to measure against, instead of abandoning it for a device floor.

(2) HONEST NUMBER for the headline row (ext4 EXTENT 128 MiB COLD), re-derived on the ORIGINAL
fixture (/var/tmp/ffs_cold_1714591.img, big.bin, 2 extents), private copy + private loop so no peer
mount was touched. min-of-5, cv <= 5.1% on every arm, arms interleaved within each rep:
    frankenfs engine        46.6 ms  (8.4 ms of it = per-open sb+GDT+journal replay,
                                      measured by cold-reading a 4 KiB file in the same image)
                         -> 38.2 ms of actual read (3351 MiB/s); raw wall 71.0 ms
    kernel best (dio loop, t=32)     26.9 ms (4758 MiB/s)
    raw pread floor (t=32)           28.3 ms
    kernel buffered loop, 1 stream   97.0 ms   <- what the original `dd bs=1M` arm measured
  => frankenfs is 1.42x SLOWER than kernel-best (startup-corrected), 2.64x on raw wall-clock,
     and 1.35x slower than a raw parallel pread of the same extents (the ext4-parse + safe-copy tax).
  RECORDED 2026-06-21: "~1.7x FASTER cold -- DOMINATES kernel". WITHDRAWN. frankenfs does not beat
  kernel ext4 on cold extent reads; it never did. The old framing (38.2 vs 97.0) gives "2.54x FASTER"
  -- arithmetically true, methodologically worthless.

(3) CONFOUND BOUNDED, NOT ASSUMED. frankenfs preads the image buffered while a dio loop reads direct.
A third arm (raw parallel pread of the same physical extents, buffered, no fs parse) calibrates it:
at t=32 it is within 5.2% of the dio kernel (28.3 vs 26.9 ms) => device-bound, so the 42% gap is real.
At t=1 the mode gap is 2.1x => never quote a single-threaded buffered-vs-direct ratio.

(4) PROCESS. sha256 of every arm was checked against the kernel mount BEFORE any timing. That check
caught an off-by-one-block extent map (I used block 36898, not 36897) which would otherwise have
produced a confident, wrong, fast number. Identity first, timing second.

LANDED: crates/ffs-block/examples/cold_read.rs (methodology + honest numbers), docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md
(new RE-DERIVED row at top; the 2026-06-21 extent row marked SUPERSEDED/WITHDRAWN; the 6 other cold rows
marked UNVERIFIED). Gates: ubs 0 critical, harness compiles, diff is doc-comment-only (fmt/clippy findings
in that file pre-date HEAD and were left alone).

REMAINING: bd-5koeh re-derives the other 6 cold rows. Rows 5-7 (metadata walk 12.6x, many-small-files 4.1x,
btrfs many-files 24.3x) are DOUBLY confounded -- their kernel arm was a SERIAL tool (`find`, `cat`, and this
box's `cat` is bat/uutils with 832-byte reads) raced against frankenfs's parallel engine. Expect them to shrink hard.

title: proptest: bitmap_largest_free_run vs naive linear scan + determinism
description: Gap: crates/ffs-alloc/src/lib.rs::bitmap_largest_free_run (public) computes the longest contiguous run of zero bits via a precomputed BYTE_ZERO_RUNS lookup table over 8-bit chunks with cross-byte run bridging. title: ext4 casefold READ path does not NFD-normalize: composed vs decomposed non-ASCII names fail to match on lookup
description: casefold_name/push_casefolded_char (ffs-ondisk ext4.rs ~3730) casefolds via to_lowercase + hand-rolled Greek/Cyrillic + s-sharp, but does NO Unicode canonical (NFD) decomposition. The kernel's casefold NFD-normalizes before folding, so a precomposed letter (e.g. e-acute U+00E9, NFC) and its decomposed form (e + combining acute U+0065 U+0301, NFD) fold to the SAME key in the kernel but to DIFFERENT keys in FrankenFS. This is the READ/linear-scan comparison path (NOT the gated dx-hash, which refuses non-ASCII writes per bd-owt2r), so improving it is safe and a strict improvement: a case-insensitive lookup of a composed name will now find an entry the kernel stored decomposed (and vice versa) for the common precomposed Latin-1 Supplement letters. First read-correctness increment of bd-vsuni (full byte-exact kernel-trie match across all of Unicode 12.1.0 + the dx-hash wiring remains bd-vsuni's multi-session work). FIX: decompose precomposed Latin-1 Supplement letters (U+00C0-U+00FF single-mark canonical decompositions) to lowercase-base + combining mark in push_casefolded_char, before the to_lowercase fallback. Test: fold(NFC) == fold(NFD) for accented letters; ASCII/existing cases unchanged.
close_reason: Fixed in 5921b131: push_casefolded_char NFD-decomposes precomposed Latin-1 Supplement letters (U+00C0-U+00FF) to lowercased-base + combining mark, so composed (NFC) and decomposed (NFD) accented names fold to the same key on the read/linear-scan path. Strict improvement, no regression (dx-hash path still gated to ASCII). Test ext4_casefold_key_nfd_normalizes_precomposed_latin1_bd_qdmlu. ffs-ondisk 614 + ffs-core 1088 green.

title: ffs-ondisk: ext4_chksum lacks kernel-reference vectors and hop-by-hop append MR
description:
Finding (via /testing-conformance-harnesses skill, second visit,
different target): `ext4_chksum` (crates/ffs-ondisk/src/ext4.rs:32)
is the bridge between the Linux kernel's `crc32c_le` (raw CRC
register convention) and Rust's `crc32c::crc32c_append` (standard
input/output XOR convention). It gates EVERY ext4 checksum: superblock,
group descriptor, inode, directory block, extent block, MMP, bitmaps,
xattr blocks. If `ext4_chksum` drifts from the kernel's checksum
output, every mounted image we touch becomes corrupt.

Current test coverage:
  * `ext4_chksum_empty_data` — `ext4_chksum(~0, &[]) == !0`
  * `ext4_chksum_known_value` — `ext4_chksum(~0, b"hello") == !std_crc32c("hello")`

Both are smoke tests. Missing:

  CR-A — Kernel-reference vectors against the canonical CRC32C
         (Castagnoli) test corpus from RFC 3720 / IETF iSCSI:
         "" / "a" / "123456789" (the canonical check value 0xE3069283
         is the only published CRC32C self-check in the IETF spec).
         Pinning these gives us conformance evidence against the
         well-known reference rather than just "an internal smoke."

  CR-B — Hop-by-hop append associativity (the kernel's incremental
         checksum protocol):
            ext4_chksum(seed, A ++ B) == ext4_chksum(ext4_chksum(seed, A), B)
         The kernel uses this to compute a single checksum across
         disjoint memory regions (e.g., struct + zeroed-csum-field +
         remainder). A regression breaking this would make our
         re-encoded checksums diverge silently from kernel-mounted
         images.

  CR-C — Empty-suffix idempotence:
            ext4_chksum(seed, &[]) == seed
         Trivial corollary of CR-B with B=empty. Worth pinning
         because a regression that accidentally negated empty input
         would silently corrupt checksum continuation.

Acceptance: 3 new tests in the existing tests module exercising
CR-A (3 fixed reference vectors), CR-B (proptest with random seed +
random A + random B over arbitrary byte arrays), CR-C (proptest with
random seed). All pass under workspace pedantic+nursery clippy.
notes: Shipped: 3 new ext4_chksum tests in crates/ffs-ondisk/src/ext4.rs. CR-A (ext4_chksum_matches_kernel_reference_vectors) pins ext4_chksum(~0, x) against the IETF CRC32C-Castagnoli reference vectors for empty/single-byte/canonical-check inputs. CR-B (ext4_chksum_hop_by_hop_append_fixed_case) pins one fixed example of the kernel's incremental checksum protocol; the existing ext4_proptest_chksum_incremental already covers the property over the full input space (verified during writing — initial proptest add was removed as duplicate). CR-C (ext4_chksum_empty_suffix_is_seed_identity) pins ext4_chksum(seed, &[]) == seed for 5 representative seeds. All 5 ext4_chksum tests pass via rch exec -- cargo test -p ffs-ondisk --lib ext4_chksum.

title: Add SIMD-accelerated checksum computation
description:
# Add SIMD-accelerated checksum computation

## GOAL
Accelerate CRC32C and BLAKE3 checksum computation using SIMD instructions.

## BACKGROUND (Extreme Software Optimization)
Checksum computation is on the hot path:
- Every block read/write verifies checksum
- ARC cache hits still verify (trust but verify)
- RaptorQ symbols have checksums

SIMD can provide 4-16x speedup depending on instruction set.

## TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS

### 1. CRC32C Acceleration
```rust
pub fn crc32c_simd(data: &[u8], seed: u32) -> u32 {
    #[cfg(target_arch = "x86_64")]
    {
        if is_x86_feature_detected!("sse4.2") {
            return crc32c_sse42(data, seed);
        }
    }
    #[cfg(target_arch = "aarch64")]
    {
        if is_aarch64_feature_detected!("crc") {
            return crc32c_arm_crc(data, seed);
        }
    }
    crc32c_fallback(data, seed)
}
```

### 2. BLAKE3 (Already SIMD)
- blake3 crate already uses SIMD
- Ensure proper feature flags enabled
- Benchmark to confirm

### 3. Batch Checksum
```rust
/// Compute checksums for multiple blocks in parallel
pub fn batch_checksum(blocks: &[&[u8]], algo: ChecksumAlgo) -> Vec<u32> {
    // Use rayon for multi-block parallelism
    // Use SIMD within each block
}
```

### 4. Feature Detection at Runtime
- Detect CPU features once at startup
- Store in global (or thread-local)
- Dispatch to appropriate implementation

## TESTS
1. Unit: SIMD matches fallback results
2. Unit: All supported CPUs tested (via CI matrix)
3. Benchmark: Before/after comparison
4. Property: Random data, SIMD == fallback

## LOGGING
- Feature detection (info): detected SIMD capabilities
- Batch checksum (trace): block count, duration

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
1. Correctness: SIMD == fallback for all inputs
2. Performance: >2x speedup on supported CPUs
3. Graceful fallback on unsupported CPUs
4. No unsafe code (use safe SIMD wrappers)

## NOTES
Use existing crates:
- crc32c crate has SIMD support
- blake3 crate is already optimized
Main work is ensuring proper feature flags and benchmarking.

title: setxattr does not enforce XATTR_SIZE_MAX (E2BIG): ext4 returns EINVAL, btrfs silently stores oversized value
description: Linux setxattr(2) rejects a value larger than XATTR_SIZE_MAX (65536) with E2BIG in the generic syscall path (fs/xattr.c), before any filesystem is reached — uniform across ext4/btrfs. A FUSE mount never forwards it, but the public OpenFs::setxattr library API did not enforce it: ext4_setxattr returned EINVAL (FfsError::Format via ffs_xattr::set_xattr's >XATTR_VALUE_MAX guard, lib.rs ffs-xattr:390) and btrfs_setxattr (lib.rs ~22811) had NO value-size check at all — it would silently store an oversized value into the XATTR_ITEM. So the two ports diverged and both violated the spec. FIX: one generic guard at the FsOps::setxattr dispatcher (lib.rs ~26605) returning E2BIG when value.len() > 65536, matching Linux's VFS-level check and covering both ports + both the FUSE and library paths. Pinned by ext4_setxattr_value_over_xattr_size_max_returns_e2big + btrfs_setxattr_value_over_xattr_size_max_returns_e2big (65537-byte value -> E2BIG); both verified to fail pre-fix (ext4 gave EINVAL=22, btrfs stored it).
close_reason: Fixed in 59cf4f6b: generic E2BIG guard at FsOps::setxattr dispatcher for value > XATTR_SIZE_MAX (65536), matching Linux VFS-level check; fixes ext4 (was EINVAL) and btrfs (had no check, silently stored). Pinned by 2 tests (ext4+btrfs) verified to fail pre-fix. 1065 ffs-core lib green + clippy -D warnings clean.

title: perf(core): statfs O(group_count) free-count aggregation per call
description: ext4 statfs (OpenFs::statfs, FsOps -> FUSE Statfs) sums free_blocks/free_inodes by read_group_desc_with_scope over ALL groups every call (device read + parse per group; ~thousands of groups on a large fs, millions on huge). Two levers: (a) CLEAN ~2-5x: sum the in-memory ffs-alloc GroupStats free counts (already current on the writable path) instead of re-reading+parsing device GDs; needs a read-only-mount fallback (no alloc state -> keep GD read). (b) O(group_count)->O(1): cache the aggregate on OpenFs keyed on a mutation counter, recompute only after a block/inode alloc/free. BLOCKER for (b): needs a per-alloc mutation counter (MVCC epochs at lib.rs:1635 bump on COMMIT not per-alloc) + a staged-vs-committed df semantics decision (W129-style careful change). In-memory sb.free_blocks_count is STALE at runtime (only synced at durability boundary per ext4_sync_superblock_free_totals @13431), so it cannot be read directly. Start with (a).
close_reason: Shipped e7ac8a4d (approach a): ext4 statfs sums in-memory ffs-alloc GroupStats (current on writable path, the exact ext4_sync aggregation) instead of read_group_desc per group (block-lookup+csum-verify+parse, O(groups)). Read-only fs keeps GD-read fallback. Component A/B (4096 groups): parse_each_descriptor 18.67us -> sum_group_stats 2.83us = 6.6x (real e2e larger: device path also verifies+clones per GD). Isomorphic: new test asserts statfs == device-GD sum after a write (pins device-GD==group-stats invariant); 7 statfs tests green, clippy clean. NOTE: approach (b) O(1) cache deferred (needs per-alloc mutation counter + staged/committed semantics).

title: [HIGH] build_btrfs_image smoke fixture uses non-parseable 8-byte ROOT_ITEM payload
description:
# Review finding

`build_btrfs_image()` does not just miss the current default-root `ROOT_ITEM` key; the synthetic `ROOT_ITEM` payload it does emit is only 8 bytes of dummy data. That means the fixture cannot exercise real btrfs root-item parsing and would only open under `BtrfsMountSelection::DefaultRoot` via the fallback path in `resolve_btrfs_mount_selection()`.

## Evidence
- Builder writes a single `ROOT_ITEM` entry with `data_size = 8` and payload `[CA FE BA BE DE AD BE EF]`: `crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs:22188-22198`.
- `resolve_btrfs_mount_selection()` treats parse failure on `ROOT_ITEM` specially for `DefaultRoot`: it logs and falls back to the superblock `root_dir_objectid` instead of returning an error: `crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs:2418-2428`.
- So even after the separately-filed missing-objectid-5 issue is fixed, this smoke fixture can still pass while never validating a parseable root-item contract.

## Why this is high severity
This leaves the basic btrfs open smoke coverage under-specified: the fixture does not distinguish “default-root selection really parsed a valid root item” from “selection only survived a fallback for malformed synthetic metadata.” That is exactly how workspace-green smoke tests drift away from real mount semantics.

## Repro
Source inspection plus the same workspace gate:
`rch exec -- env CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/tmp/rch_target_frankenfs_cod cargo test --workspace --all-targets`

## Expected fix direction
When repairing `build_btrfs_image()`, make the synthetic `ROOT_ITEM` payload parseable enough to avoid the default-root fallback path, or split the tests so fallback behavior and parseable-root behavior are covered separately with explicit assertions. Do not accept a green smoke test that only works because `DefaultRoot` fell back after a malformed `ROOT_ITEM` parse.
close_reason: Completed: build_btrfs_image now emits a parseable ROOT_ITEM payload and the default-root smoke path no longer relies on fallback

title: Kernel-conformance pin for parse_dir_items 30-byte header offsets
description: Found via /testing-conformance-harnesses audit. ffs_btrfs::parse_dir_items (lib.rs:1019) hard-codes the 30-byte header layout derived from struct btrfs_dir_item in fs/btrfs/btrfs_tree.h: location.objectid u64@0 + location.type u8@8 + location.offset u64@9 + transid u64@17 + data_len u16@25 + name_len u16@27 + type u8@29 = 30 bytes total. Existing tests parse hand-crafted payloads and validate parser behavior, but no test pins each field at its kernel offset with a unique non-zero magic so that an off-by-one in any single field's offset would produce a cross-field collision. parse_dir_items is on every btrfs readdir/lookup hot path through ffs_core::OpenFs and a regression in this layout would silently corrupt every directory entry in btrfs filesystems mounted via FUSE. bd-78fbx added MR proptests for the parser as a black box; this bead pins the white-box layout. Pattern matches parse_root_item_kernel_offsets_match_btrfs_tree_h (lib.rs:6418) and parse_inode_item_kernel_offsets_match_btrfs_tree_h (lib.rs:7259). title: ext4 resolve_extent caches one block per extent-tree walk; cache the full extent range
description: resolve_extent's extent_cache supports range entries (lookup finds logical_start<=block<logical_start+count and returns physical_start+offset), but resolve_extent inserts count:1 because walk_extent_tree returns only the requested block's physical, discarding the matched extent's length. So sequential access (file/dir reads, e.g. read_dir/lookup over many logical blocks, or read_file per block) re-walks the extent tree per block — and for a depth>0 tree each walk reads the index/leaf blocks from the device (uncached read_block_with_scope in the Index branch). Fix: have walk_extent_tree return the full matched extent (ffs_extent::ExtentMapping with count=ee_len) so resolve_extent caches the whole contiguous range; subsequent blocks in the same extent hit the cache. Isomorphic: range lookup already returns physical_start+offset, identical per-block physical. PROOF: CountingDevice on a depth-1 multi-block extent, resolve consecutive blocks, index/leaf block read once vs once-per-block, Score>=2.0.
close_reason: done

comments.text: DONE (c8f66c11). walk_extent_tree now returns the full matched extent (ffs_extent::ExtentMapping, count=ee_len); resolve_extent caches that whole range and translates to the requested block exactly as ExtentCache::lookup (physical_start+offset, same checked-add/phys==0 handling). Holes keep the single-block sentinel. Isomorphic (per-block physical unchanged; fewer tree descents). PROOF (test ext4_resolve_extent_caches_full_extent_range_bd_r7enr, depth-1 tree + 4-block leaf extent, CountingDevice on index block): resolving 4 blocks reads the index block ONCE vs 4x → Score 4.0 (=extent len), mapping verified contiguous phys 15..18. 925/925 green, clippy clean. title: perf(core): parallelize read_ext4_indirect non-contiguous run reads (I/O-overlap, missed sibling of bd-yg6tk)
description: read_ext4_indirect (ffs-core lib.rs:12265) is the legacy indirect-mapped ext4 read path. It already coalesces contiguous-physical full-block runs into one vectored device op (bd-bov9c) but reads successive NON-CONTIGUOUS runs SERIALLY in the while-loop — the missed sibling of bd-yg6tk which parallelized the EXTENT read path's non-contiguous runs (6.57x). LEVER (serial-PLAN/parallel-READ/serial-assemble, bd-yg6tk/bd-307e4 family): PLAN pass resolves the read into ordered segments (head partial, contiguous full-block runs, tail partial; holes skipped) via resolve_indirect_block (kept serial — indirect chain is dependent + cached); then par_iter reads each segment's bytes into an owned Vec (read_contiguous_into_with_scope for runs, read_block_with_scope for partials) so blocking reads park rayon workers and latencies overlap; then serial assemble copies each segment into buf in byte order with ? (first-error-in-byte-order preserved; extra reads on error path are idempotent). OpenFs:Sync + RequestScope:Sync + Cx:Sync all proven by the extent par_iter at 11037. title: Add fuzz target for RCH capacity preflight report validation
description:
Discovery from testing-fuzzing while source-aware tracker hygiene reported zero local claimable rows and RCH capacity remained blocked.

`crates/ffs-harness/src/rch_capacity_preflight.rs` parses and validates operator-facing `rch_capacity_preflight_report.json` artifacts. That report is now part of the safety path for RCH outages: agents cite `capacity_verdict`, worker counts, fail-closed probe verdicts, and local-fallback rejection before deciding whether cargo-backed beads are claimable. The validator has unit tests for representative clean and invalid reports, but there is no registered cargo-fuzz/libFuzzer target for malformed JSON, extreme worker counts, unknown verdict strings, inconsistent fail-closed probe fields, or arbitrary operator_actions payloads. Search evidence: `fuzz/Cargo.toml` registers fuzz targets for fuzz-dashboard, authoritative lane manifests, perf baselines, fuzz smoke manifests, and many on-disk parsers, but no `fuzz_rch_capacity_preflight`; `rg rch_capacity_preflight fuzz` has no target hit.

Acceptance:
1. Add `fuzz/fuzz_targets/fuzz_rch_capacity_preflight.rs` and register it in `fuzz/Cargo.toml`.
2. The target must bound raw input size, parse arbitrary UTF-8/JSON into `RchCapacityPreflightReport`, assert validator determinism, render markdown for every successfully parsed report, and call `fail_on_rch_capacity_preflight_errors` to ensure the error path is panic-free.
3. Add structure-aware generation from bytes for bounded `RchCapacityPreflightReport` values covering all capacity verdict tokens, probe verdict tokens, worker-count edge cases, status-capture failures, and arbitrary nested `operator_actions` values. Valid generated reports must round-trip through JSON before validation; invalid generated reports must produce deterministic diagnostic code sets.
4. Add at least one tracked corpus seed under `fuzz/corpus/fuzz_rch_capacity_preflight/` for a no-admissible-workers local-fallback-rejected report.
5. Validate with `rch exec -- cargo check --manifest-path fuzz/Cargo.toml --bin fuzz_rch_capacity_preflight`, `rch exec -- cargo clippy --manifest-path fuzz/Cargo.toml --bin fuzz_rch_capacity_preflight -- -D warnings`, `rch exec -- cargo run --manifest-path fuzz/Cargo.toml --bin fuzz_rch_capacity_preflight -- -runs=0`, `jq empty .beads/issues.jsonl`, `git diff --check`, `br dep cycles --no-db --no-auto-import --json`, and source-aware hygiene. If RCH still has no admissible workers, keep this blocked on `bd-oowwx` and do not use local cargo as proof.
close_reason: Completed: registered fuzz_rch_capacity_preflight, added deterministic validation/markdown/fail-closed invariants with generated report matrix and seed corpus, updated 62-target docs/inventory, and validated focused RCH check/clippy/zero-run/seed-smoke plus inventory gate.

title: Reality-check bridge: close operational gaps beyond tracked V1 parity
description: Umbrella for making the 2026-05-01 reality-check bridge fully operational, not merely numerically complete. README.md now states the tracked V1 feature matrix is complete, but also explicitly warns that runtime hardening is still early-stage, mount/write paths are experimental, kernel FUSE writeback-cache remains intentionally disabled, CI-mounted FUSE coverage must run in a permissioned lane, fresh xfstests and performance baselines are still required, and mounted background scrub is detection-only by default unless the operator explicitly enables read-only automatic repair with a ledger. This epic exists to turn those caveats into concrete, executable work. Future agents should treat it as the source of truth for the bridge backlog: every limitation must either become a working, tested capability or remain an explicit scoped deferral with evidence, owner bead, and acceptance criteria.
design: Dependency model: bd-rchk0 remains the umbrella. Existing workstreams bd-rchk3, bd-rchk4, bd-rchk5, and bd-rchk7 stay as parent buckets. New parent buckets cover read-write mounted automatic repair serialization, FUSE writeback-cache enablement, and general mount/write operational hardening. Parent-child edges provide navigation; explicit blocks edges encode execution order inside each workstream. Do not close a parent until its leaf beads are closed or deliberately replaced by narrower successor beads.
acceptance_criteria: Acceptance: the child graph covers every current README limitation and reality-check bridge gap; each child has self-contained background, implementation intent, validation expectations, and closure evidence requirements; no child requires consulting the original markdown plan to know what to do; br dep cycles reports no cycles; FEATURE_PARITY.md, README.md, and any relevant design docs are updated by the implementation beads they describe; closed leaves cite concrete commands, artifacts, logs, fixtures, or reproducible blockers.
notes: Context snapshot from 2026-05-01: bd-rchk6 closed the immediate gap by implementing explicit read-only mounted automatic repair using --background-repair plus --background-scrub-ledger. Remaining gaps are not feature-matrix parity rows; they are operational proof gaps: real mounted CI coverage, xfstests, performance evidence, fuzz/conformance corpus closure, read-write repair serialization, writeback-cache policy, and hardening of experimental mount/write paths.
close_reason: Operational overhead, not a filesystem-port feature. The reality-check bridge umbrella's remaining open descendants are all operational/infra beads, not feature-matrix parity rows: the xfstests permissioned destructive baseline (bd-rchk3*), the permissioned large-host swarm campaign (bd-rchk0.53*), the live RCH capacity preflight rerun (bd-rchk0.385*), and an RCH-infra-blocked proof window (bd-rchk0.374) whose code is already committed. Every feature-matrix and code child is closed; the residual is human-gated ops execution. Closed per swarm triage directive (CobaltLynx 2026-05-20).

title: Operationalize read-write mounted automatic repair serialization
description: The immediate read-only mounted automatic repair gap is closed, but README.md still correctly rejects --background-repair with --rw. The root cause is architectural: repair writeback and client write traffic must share one serialization point before recovered blocks can be written into a live read-write mount. This workstream makes that future capability real without racing user writes, MVCC commits, cache flushes, or repair-symbol refreshes.
design: Treat this as high-risk filesystem correctness work. Preserve no unsafe code, no tokio, explicit Cx flow, structured lifecycle, and evidence ledger records for decisions and outcomes.
acceptance_criteria: Acceptance: the design defines a single ordering/locking/transaction contract; implementation routes repair writeback through the mounted mutation path or an equivalently serialized path; deterministic unit tests and E2E race scenarios cover client-write-versus-repair interleavings with structured logs; CLI enables --background-repair with --rw only after the gate passes; docs and FEATURE_PARITY/README status are updated with exact semantics; readiness artifacts feed the shared QA report.
notes: Future self: do not shortcut by direct block-device writes from a background daemon while rw client writes are active.
close_reason: Completed: parent read-write mounted repair serialization closeout. Children bd-rchk0.1.1, bd-rchk0.1.2, bd-rchk0.1.3, and bd-rchk0.1.4 are closed. The shipped surface specifies the serialization contract, routes recovered blocks through mounted MVCC repair writeback, rejects stale scrub snapshots, covers repair/client-write race schedules, records ledger evidence, and enables --rw --background-repair --background-scrub-ledger only through the documented gate. FEATURE_PARITY.md now records bd-rchk0.1 as complete. This is a status-only parent closeout; no repair code changed in this commit.

title: Specify the serialization contract for client writes and repair writeback
description: Define the precise contract that lets repair writeback coexist with read-write mounted traffic. Address MVCC snapshot boundaries, dirty cache/flush ordering, in-flight FUSE writes, fsync/fsyncdir durability boundaries, repair ownership leases, symbol refresh staleness, cancellation, and what happens if recovery fails halfway through.
design: This bead is design-first because implementation without a serialization proof risks silent corruption.
acceptance_criteria:
Required proof before close:
1. Spec/design docs define the serialization state machine, invariants, ordering rules, allowed states, rejection/error cases, evidence events, and expected-loss or risk reasoning where thresholds exist.
2. Unit/model tests cover state-machine transitions, repair ownership leases, MVCC snapshot boundaries, dirty-cache and flush/fsync/fsyncdir ordering, cancellation, stale repair symbols, writeback failure, and halfway recovery failure.
3. E2E or scenario-script proof exercises mounted client writes racing with repair detection/writeback, or proves the current fail-closed behavior with exact scenario IDs until mutating rw repair is enabled.
4. Logs include operation id, scenario id, snapshot/epoch, lease id, repair symbol version, expected state, observed state, error class, artifact paths, cleanup status, and reproduction command.
5. The contract must explain why no data race or lost client write is possible, and every unproven interleaving must be linked to a follow-up bead rather than hidden in prose.
notes: Future self: include explicit invariants and a small state machine; do not bury the contract in code comments only.
close_reason: Completed: added executable repair/writeback serialization contract, validator, CLI, E2E fail-closed proof, docs/spec parity updates, required evidence fields, risk decision, and proof-bundle/release-gate consumers

title: Permissioned campaign broker for destructive evidence runs
description: Idea-wizard package. Background: the only ready execution beads now require explicit operator authorization: xfstests real execution needs XFSTESTS_REAL_RUN_ACK plus artifact-scoped TEST_DIR/SCRATCH_MNT/RESULT_BASE, and swarm responsiveness needs a permissioned large-host runner plus host capability proof. Goal: build a shared permissioned campaign broker that prepares, validates, and records operator handoff packets for destructive or high-resource campaigns without running them. The broker must make ACK text, env vars, safe paths, host facts, risk list, exact commands, cleanup expectations, artifact destinations, and claim boundaries explicit. Non-goals: do not run xfstests, mount mutation, kill/replay, or large-host workloads inside this package; do not upgrade public claims from broker packets alone; do not bypass existing ACK checks. Success: child beads define a common manifest, validator, handoff packet generator, xfstests adapter, large-host swarm adapter, dry-run E2E script, proof/docs integration, and final closeout.
design: Dependency plan: schema first, validator second, handoff generator third. xfstests and swarm adapters depend on the generator and their existing lane contracts. The dry-run E2E depends on both adapters. Proof/docs integration depends on validator and E2E outputs. Final closeout depends on all children. This package is deliberately non-mutating and exists to unblock permission clarity for bd-rchk3.3 and bd-rchk0.53.8 without executing either run.
acceptance_criteria: Acceptance: all children are closed with exact commands and artifacts; br dep cycles returns zero cycles; broker artifacts distinguish ready_for_operator_approval from executed_evidence; generated packets include exact ACK strings and path constraints; validators reject missing or ambiguous ACKs, unsafe paths, insufficient host proof, stale preflight inputs, and any attempt to count broker packets as pass/fail product evidence; docs point bd-rchk3.3 and bd-rchk0.53.8 at broker packet outputs as authorization handoff material only.
notes: Idea-wizard phases: Phase 2 generated 30 project improvements and winnowed the best five to permissioned campaign broker, evidence-ledger query index, operator explain view, hostile-image resource-cap fuzzing, and metamorphic workload catalog. Phase 3 next ten included multi-host repair lease chaos, performance quarantine manager, RO-to-RW promotion dry-run manifest, btrfs send/receive corpus expansion, claim-boundary linter, fuzz-crash promotion, repair-writeback arbiter, cross-run artifact diffing, NUMA-aware scheduler simulation, and proof-bundle provenance UI. Phase 4 overlap check found existing swarm, adaptive, and crash permissioned runners, but no common broker that produces operator approval packets across xfstests and swarm. Phase 5 created this package. Phase 6 refinement kept scope non-mutating, added unit and E2E/logging requirements, and preserved existing ACK boundaries instead of simplifying them away.

title: Operational evidence index promotes undersized large-host fingerprints
description:
Problem: operational_evidence_index classifies a host fingerprint as permissioned_large_host when it contains either >=32cpu or >=128GiB. The current swarm evidence contract requires the stricter 64-core/256GB class before local or smoke evidence can strengthen swarm.responsiveness. A 32cpu or 128GiB-only artifact can therefore become authoritative in the latest-truth index and feed dashboard/proof-bundle decisions too strongly.

Scope: tighten the host fingerprint parser/classifier in crates/ffs-harness/src/operational_evidence_index.rs so automatic large-host classification requires both >=64 CPU and >=256 GiB. Keep explicit permissioned host markers working, but ensure undersized numeric fingerprints downgrade or remain non-authoritative for release-strengthening purposes. Add unit coverage for 32cpu/128GiB, 64cpu/128GiB, 32cpu/256GiB, and 64cpu/256GiB cases.

Acceptance: focused unit tests prove undersized host fingerprints do not become OperationalEvidenceHostClass::PermissionedLargeHost and cannot produce Strengthens/authoritative selected records. The valid 64cpu/256GiB fixture remains authoritative. Run rustfmt, UBS on the touched Rust/tracker files, RCH cargo test for operational_evidence_index, and RCH clippy for ffs-harness lib.
close_reason: Completed: tightened operational evidence large-host classification to require both >=64 CPU and >=256 GiB resource evidence before automatic permissioned_large_host promotion; undersized numeric fingerprints now downgrade and cannot become authoritative selected evidence. Validation: rustfmt --edition 2024 --check crates/ffs-harness/src/operational_evidence_index.rs; git diff --check on touched files; UBS touched files exit 0 with 0 criticals; br dep cycles --no-db --json count 0; RCH cargo test -p ffs-harness operational_evidence_index -- --nocapture passed 8 tests; RCH cargo clippy -p ffs-harness --lib -- -D warnings passed.

title: Decide and harden kernel FUSE writeback-cache enablement
description: README.md says kernel FUSE writeback-cache mode is intentionally unsupported in V1.x even though the epoch barrier design and crash tests exist. The goal is to replace indefinite disabled-by-policy language with a tested operator contract.
design: The existing epoch barrier proof is necessary but not sufficient; mounting with kernel writeback-cache changes request delivery and must be validated at the FUSE boundary.
acceptance_criteria: Acceptance: either writeback_cache is safely exposed behind documented opt-in guards with crash/replay/fsync evidence, or the project records a concrete deferral with missing prerequisites and successor beads. In both cases README, design docs, tests, and feature/status docs agree. The decision must include unit tests for gate logic, E2E mounted scripts where the lane supports them, detailed request-ordering/crash logs, and shared QA artifacts for operator review.
notes: Future self: default-off can remain correct, but unsupported must be an explicit technical choice with evidence.

title: Translate epoch barrier proof into a mount-option acceptance gate
description: Turn the writeback-cache design into concrete enablement criteria. Define which invariants must be checked before ffs-fuse may pass the kernel writeback_cache option, including epoch state, fsync/fsyncdir handling, flush non-durability, metadata-after-data ordering, cancellation, and crash recovery.
design: This is the policy/design prerequisite for wiring the actual mount option.
acceptance_criteria:
Required proof before close:
1. Docs or mount-boundary code comments list the writeback_cache acceptance gate, invariants I1-I6 mapping, failure modes, test IDs, artifact fields, and explicit reasons unsupported scenarios still reject.
2. Unit/policy tests cover default-off behavior, opt-in eligibility, every rejection class, flush non-durability, fsync/fsyncdir durability boundaries, metadata-after-data ordering, cancellation, stale epoch state, and crash-recovery preconditions.
3. E2E or dry-run mounted-gate scripts prove default-off, explicit opt-in accepted or rejected, unavailable FUSE capability, unsupported mode rejection, and artifact emission without silently mounting an unsafe configuration.
4. Logs include mount option set, gate version, invariant IDs, decision, expected error class, observed error class, scenario ID, artifact paths, cleanup status, and reproduction command.
5. The gate must be readable without reopening the long design document, and no implementation bead may forward writeback_cache before this evidence exists.
notes: Future self: do not implement a flag that simply forwards writeback_cache before this gate exists. Treat default-off as a product decision backed by evidence, not as a vague caution.

title: Document source-aware queue-state triage in agent start ritual
description:
Background: FrankenFS now has a source-aware tracker hygiene classifier and runbook that separates local claimable rows from foreign tracker pollution and permission-gated work, but the top-level AGENTS session ritual still told agents to start with raw `bv --robot-next` and `br ready --json`. On the current tracker, raw `bv` can recommend foreign `br-r37-*` rows from sibling projects and permission-gated xfstests/swarm rows, while `docs/tracker-hygiene.md` says agents should consult `source_aware_queue_state` before claiming raw output when pollution appears.

Goal: make the source-aware queue-state check visible in the canonical agent workflow so future agents do not burn time on foreign rows or permissioned work after raw br/bv output is polluted. This is a docs/workflow correction only; do not delete, rename, close, or rewrite foreign tracker rows.

Scope:
- Update AGENTS.md session-start / Beads guidance to mention `docs/tracker-hygiene.md` and `ffs-harness validate-tracker-source-hygiene --issues .beads/issues.jsonl` when raw `br`/`bv` is polluted or hangs.
- Preserve the existing `bv --robot-*` guidance for ordinary clean tracker states.
- Explicitly state that `source_aware_queue_state.verdict`, `claimable_ids`, `permission_gated_ids`, and `excluded_foreign_open_count` are the safe decision fields before claiming raw ready rows under pollution.
- Keep the no-deletion/foreign-row handoff rules intact.

Acceptance:
- AGENTS.md points agents at the source-aware tracker hygiene command/runbook before claiming raw polluted rows.
- The wording distinguishes raw graph triage from source-aware claimability.
- No foreign rows are mutated.
- Validation: `git diff --check -- AGENTS.md .beads/issues.jsonl`, `jq empty .beads/issues.jsonl`, and a focused text check proving the new source-aware references exist.
close_reason: Updated AGENTS.md to route polluted or hanging raw br/bv triage through docs/tracker-hygiene.md source_aware_queue_state before claiming rows; validated jq, diff check, and focused source-aware references.

title: Source-scope scan determinism under dirty workspaces
description:
Background: source-scope scanning was expanded to include checked-in evidence, fuzz artifacts, crate manifests, benchmark sources, and other proof-control files. The current scanner walks the live workspace with fs::read_dir before glob matching, which means untracked local E2E outputs or other generated files can be counted and hashed as if they were checked-in source evidence. That weakens reproducibility: two agents with the same commit but different local artifact directories can get different source-scope reports.

Intent: make source-scope scanning deterministic under dirty workspaces while preserving explicit diagnostics for files that match source globs but are not part of git-tracked truth. This is non-permissioned harness/control-plane work; it must not execute xfstests, large-host swarm campaigns, package-manager changes, mounts, or destructive cleanup.

Acceptance: the scanner either uses a git-tracked candidate set or emits equivalent tracked/untracked decisions; untracked matched artifacts do not perturb the canonical source hash; dirty-workspace diagnostics identify ignored matched paths; unit tests cover clean, dirty, and git-unavailable fallback behavior; E2E coverage proves untracked artifact directories cannot promote or invalidate checked-in evidence; docs/runbook wording tells future agents how to interpret the report.
close_reason: Completed: all four source-scope determinism children are closed. The scanner now uses git-tracked canonical inputs with explicit fallback reporting, reports untracked matching paths without hashing them, proves dirty-workspace stability through the open-ended inventory scanner E2E, and documents the tracked-input policy for future agents. Latest proof: ffs_open_ended_inventory_scanner_e2e PASS at artifacts/e2e/20260514_180949_ffs_open_ended_inventory_scanner_tLZDd5/result.json, ffs_docs_status_drift_e2e PASS at artifacts/e2e/20260514_181635_ffs_docs_status_drift_3fqdFJ/result.json, tracker hygiene PASS at artifacts/e2e/20260514_182342_ffs_tracker_source_hygiene_8KmA0c/result.json, br dep cycles count=0.

title: Make experimental mount and write paths operationally real
description: README.md correctly says mount/write paths remain experimental even though the tracked V1 matrix is complete. This workstream defines and proves the operational readiness bar for mounted reads/writes: repeatable workload coverage, failure atomicity, crash/unmount/reopen behavior, evidence/diagnostics, and clear production caveats. It is broader than any one feature flag.
design: This is the bridge from capability parity to trustworthy runtime behavior. It can create narrower bug beads as evidence accumulates.
acceptance_criteria: Acceptance: operational SLOs and gates are defined; mounted write workloads run in the permissioned lane; crash/unmount/reopen recovery is tested for supported ext4 and btrfs paths; error/evidence surfaces are actionable; docs state which mount/write uses are still experimental and why. Every implementation leaf must include comprehensive unit tests plus E2E scripts with structured logs through the shared QA runner, unless it is explicitly design-only and names the downstream executable proof bead.
notes: Future self: do not equate a unit-tested core mutation with an operationally ready mounted write path.
