title: Guard swarm readiness wording and runbook

title: Add a metamorphic workload seed catalog
description: Current workload and proof artifacts carry deterministic seeds in multiple places: workload corpus reproduction commands, soak/canary campaigns, swarm workload manifests, crash replay artifacts, repair/writeback schedules, and fault-injection corpora. There is no single dry-run catalog that links those seeds to metamorphic relations, invariants, proof consumers, and exact reproduction commands. Scope: add a checked-in catalog plus ffs-harness validation that references existing artifacts and fails closed when seed rows lack a relation, invariant, source artifact, proof consumer, or dry-run/permission classification. Non-scope: do not execute permissioned xfstests, mounted mutation, or large-host swarm workloads.
design: Implement as a narrow catalog+validator slice in ffs-harness. Prefer structured JSON parsing over shell/string checks for catalog semantics. The catalog is evidence metadata only: reproduction commands are recorded and classified, not executed. This keeps the slice non-permissioned while making future metamorphic workload campaigns reproducible.
acceptance_criteria: Acceptance: ffs-harness exposes validate-metamorphic-workload-seeds with JSON and Markdown output; the checked-in catalog references at least five existing seed sources spanning workload corpus, soak/canary, swarm workload/tail latency, crash or chaos replay, repair/writeback or fault injection; every row declares a stable seed_id, numeric or symbolic seed, source artifact, relation type, invariant, proof consumers, reproduction command, and execution_mode. The validator rejects duplicate seed IDs, missing source artifacts, unknown relation/execution modes, missing invariants, permissioned rows without an explicit ack requirement, and rows that do not reference any existing proof consumer. A dry-run E2E script validates the checked-in catalog, verifies report coverage and invalid variants, and does not execute mutating or permissioned workloads.
notes: Created from the post-bd-rchk3.14 idea-wizard/beads pass because live ready work is permission-gated (real xfstests and large-host swarm). Duplicate searches for metamorphic workload seed, seed catalog, and metamorphic returned no existing bead.

Validation: E2E 6/6 at artifacts/e2e/20260506_152407_ffs_metamorphic_workload_seed_catalog; local cargo check/clippy -p ffs-harness --all-targets clean; RCH check/clippy reported remote exit=0 before artifact retrieval was terminated.

title: Verify metamorphic seed catalog source values
description: Follow-up to bd-rchk0.78. Scope: extend the catalog schema and ffs-harness validator with a structured source-value pointer/check, update the checked-in catalog with JSON pointers into the existing artifacts, and add unit/E2E rejection coverage for stale pointers or mismatched seed values. Non-scope: do not execute any recorded reproduction command or permissioned workload; this is metadata conformance only.
design: Treat the source artifact as the reference spec and the catalog row as the implementation under test. Use serde_json Value and JSON Pointer instead of ad hoc source_seed_field parsing. Keep source_seed_field as a human-readable label only if useful, but all mechanical verification must use the structured pointer.
acceptance_criteria: Acceptance: every metamorphic seed row carries a structured source_value_pointer into its source_artifact; the validator loads JSON source artifacts, rejects missing pointers, rejects seed values absent from scalar/array/object pointer targets, rejects non-JSON source artifacts unless explicitly unsupported by schema, and reports source-value coverage in JSON/Markdown output. Unit tests cover stale pointer, mismatched numeric seed, and string-command seed containment. The dry-run E2E script mutates one pointer/value variant and proves both are rejected without executing reproduction commands.
close_reason: Completed: added structured source_value_pointer verification for metamorphic workload seeds, JSON Pointer source-artifact checks, source-value coverage reporting, checked-in catalog pointers, and unit/E2E fail-closed coverage for missing pointers and mismatched seed values. title: Exercise non-JSON metamorphic seed sources
description: Follow-up to bd-rchk0.79. title: Define the supported V1 xfstests subset and skip policy
description: Select the minimal xfstests subset that matches FrankenFS V1 scope. The suite must be small enough to run routinely but broad enough to cover mount, directory, file data, metadata, xattr, fsync, and supported write behavior. Anything outside V1 scope should be skipped with an explicit reason tied to README/FEATURE_PARITY scope rather than hidden in harness logic.
design: The subset definition should become the stable contract that makes future baseline diffs meaningful.
acceptance_criteria:
Required proof before close:
1. Checked-in docs or harness metadata list every selected xfstests case, expected filesystem flavor, required capabilities, skip reason for excluded tests, and classification as expected failure, environment-blocked, unsupported-by-V1, harness-blocked, or product-actionable.
2. Unit or metadata-validation tests reject duplicate test IDs, missing skip reasons, unknown classifications, unsupported tests without explicit rationale, and stale references to README/FEATURE_PARITY scope.
3. E2E/dry-run script renders the selected subset through the shared QA runner, emits the exact command plan, and records per-test IDs, skip decisions, capability checks, artifact paths, and reproduction command even before the full suite executes.
4. The policy distinguishes ext4, btrfs, read-only, experimental rw, and unsupported writeback-cache behavior, with classification values aligned to bd-rchk0.4.1.
5. CI cannot treat missing mounted coverage or not-run rows as a passing baseline unless the skip is explicitly classified and linked to a host blocker or follow-up bead.
notes: Future self: resist expanding to the whole suite until the core subset is repeatable and artifacted. The subset policy should make expected skips explicit enough that CI cannot accidentally treat missing mounted coverage as a pass.

title: Refine bd-rchk3.2 with non-deceptive xfstests subset evidence policy
description:
Supplemental plan-space refinement for bd-rchk3.2. The supported V1 xfstests subset must help users understand real risk, not merely create a small list that is easy to pass. This bead makes subset selection auditable and non-deceptive.

Required proof before close:
1. Unit/schema tests validate every selected and skipped test row has test id, filesystem flavor, V1 scope mapping, required capability, expected operation class, user-risk category, expected outcome, skip or failure rationale, owning bead for unresolved product behavior, and artifact requirements.
2. The subset includes at least one representative case for read-only mount, experimental read-write create/write/readback, directory mutation, rename/link semantics, xattrs, fsync/fsyncdir boundary, unsupported writeback-cache behavior, and expected host capability skip.
3. E2E/dry-run script renders the subset policy into both JSON and human-readable reports, runs no destructive host operations by default, and verifies every selected test has a runnable command plan plus every excluded test has a concrete V1 scope rationale.
4. Logs include source xfstests id, policy row id, flavor, risk category, selected/skipped decision, capability requirement, linked artifact or bead, docs scope citation, and reproduction command.
5. CI and README wording cannot summarize xfstests as passing unless product failures, environment blockers, harness blockers, expected unsupported cases, and not-run rows are counted separately.

description: Run the selected xfstests subset on the prepared environment and turn the result into durable evidence. This is the bead that converts planning into a dated baseline. Unit tests cover xfstests result parsing, skip classification, not-run handling, and artifact validation. The E2E runner script emits shared QA artifacts with exact commands, worker identity, stdout/stderr paths, raw xfstests log dirs, cleanup status, and partial-run preservation.

title: Add CI-compatible mounted FUSE runner coverage for critical paths
description: Reality-check gap: important mounted-path tests can silently skip when local FUSE permissions or kernel support are absent. Scope: audit ffs-fuse and harness mount tests, decide the CI/worker execution model, add or update scripts and docs so critical FUSE E2E coverage runs in a permissioned environment, and make permission skips visibly reported instead of silently substituting for coverage. Acceptance: CI or documented RCH workflow exercises representative mounted ext4 and btrfs paths; local permission skips emit actionable diagnostics; README or test docs explain how to reproduce the gate.
design: Decompose into capability discovery, permissioned lane provisioning, critical mounted scenario execution, and fail-closed behavior for expected lanes. This workstream is the prerequisite for any claim that FUSE behavior works for real rather than only through direct ffs-core tests.
acceptance_criteria: Acceptance: mounted ext4 and btrfs critical paths run in a known permissioned CI/RCH lane, or fail with structured, actionable capability diagnostics. Local lack of /dev/fuse, fusermount3, user namespace support, CAP_SYS_ADMIN, or kernel module availability must produce a visible skip artifact. The gate must exercise representative mount, lookup/read, write where supported, sync/unmount/reopen, xattr, and mounted repair-policy cases without quietly substituting unit tests for mounted coverage. Unit tests must cover capability classification and artifact validation; E2E scripts must use the shared QA runner/logging schema and preserve logs for every pass/fail/skip.
notes: Memory-derived pitfall: this repo has historical FUSE permission soft-skips and btrfs write EACCES caused by root-owned image roots under DefaultPermissions. Future work must classify those as host/harness setup issues before blaming filesystem logic.

title: fix(ffs-repair): RepairGroupLayout end accessor cannot wrap public-field layouts
description: RepairGroupLayout::new rejects group_start + blocks_per_group overflow, but the struct fields are public and group_end_exclusive still used unchecked addition. Any caller or serialized/test construction that bypassed new could panic in debug or wrap in release, feeding bad descriptor/repair offsets. Make group_end_exclusive checked and saturating on overflow, and add a regression that manually constructs an overflowing public-field layout and proves the end and descriptor blocks do not wrap.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): layout_public_field_end_saturates_instead_of_wrapping (ffs-repair storage.rs:1165). cargo test: ok.

title: fix(ffs-repair): RepairGroupLayout tail accessors cannot underflow public-field layouts
description: RepairGroupLayout::new validates reserved tail geometry, but the public fields let callers construct a layout where descriptor_blocks, repair_start_block, or validation_start_block subtract more than group_end_exclusive. In debug this can panic; in release it can wrap to huge block numbers. Harden the tail accessors with saturating subtraction and add a regression that manually constructs an invalid public-field layout and proves the accessors clamp instead of underflowing.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): layout_public_field_tail_accessors_saturate_instead_of_underflowing (ffs-repair storage.rs:1182). cargo test: ok.

title: fix(ffs-repair): reject aliased repair descriptor slots
description: RepairGroupLayout::new guarantees the two descriptor slots fit at the group tail, but RepairGroupLayout fields are public and its saturating accessors can make invalid layouts report both descriptor slots as the same block. RepairGroupStorage then reads or writes through descriptor_block, silently collapsing the two-slot durability contract. Reject aliasing descriptor slots at the storage boundary and add a regression using an invalid public-field layout.

title: perf(repair): pair normalized recovery writeback in linear order
description: Negative-ledger-first fresh ffs-repair lane. Recovery already normalizes corrupt indices and captures expected-current blocks in ascending order; decode preserves the requested corrupt-index order, but build_writeback_blocks performs one binary search per recovered block. Profile the production-backed recovery_build_writeback_blocks release benchmark first, then test one lever: validated ordered pairing with exact output/error parity in one same-binary A/A/B.

Same-worker no-LTO release A/A/B on vmi1152480: controls 76.502/94.680 us, candidate 5.4093 us = 14.143x vs faster control (11.753x conservative); parity assertions, recovery tests 20/20, and all-target check passed.

title: btrfs DIR_INDEX sequence reuses deleted-tail values (max+1, not a persistent monotonic counter)
description: btrfs_next_dir_index_seq (ffs-core lib.rs ~22029) derives the next DIR_INDEX sequence from max(existing DIR_INDEX offsets)+1 rather than a persisted per-directory counter. After deleting the highest-indexed entry, a later create REUSES that sequence value; the kernel never reuses (the counter is monotonic, stored in the dir INODE_ITEM). Stays internally consistent (INODE_REF.index==DIR_INDEX.offset always holds, reconstructed identically on remount) so btrfs check does NOT flag it — but it diverges from kernel for btrfs send incremental-stream parity (a receiver replaying indices could see a different sequence). Low/informational. Found in the btrfs mutation audit (bd-5svhs). Fix would track a max-ever-seen index in the dir inode (btrfs uses inode.sequence/index_cnt).
close_reason: done

Deleting the highest DIR_INDEX no longer frees it for reuse within a mount. Test btrfs_dir_index_does_not_reuse_deleted_tail_bd_rfi5j (insert a/b/c, delete c, insert d, assert d==c+1 not reused c). title: ffs-fuzz: fuzz_btrfs_devitem only checks no-panic, missing structural MR coverage
description:
Finding (via /testing-fuzzing skill, second visit, different target):
fuzz/fuzz_targets/fuzz_btrfs_devitem.rs is a 7-line no-panic fuzz
target that just calls `parse_dev_item(data)` on arbitrary bytes:

    fuzz_target!(|data: &[u8]| {
        let _ = ffs_ondisk::parse_dev_item(data);
    });

This catches panics but provides ZERO structural assertions. The
proptest layer (bd-t2nrx, just landed) has 32 cases per MR; libfuzzer
runs millions of inputs per session. Lifting structural assertions
(tail-invariance + field-offset round-trip) into the fuzz target
gives us continuous discovery for any future drift in:

  * the 98-byte BTRFS_DEV_ITEM_SIZE boundary
  * the offset table (devid@0, total_bytes@8, bytes_used@16,
    io_align@24, io_width@28, sector_size@32, dev_type@36,
    generation@44, start_offset@52, dev_group@60, seek_speed@64,
    bandwidth@65, uuid@66..82, fsid@82..98)
  * the bytes_used <= total_bytes accounting check

title: btrfs delete path does not enforce immutable/append-only (deleting an immutable file wrongly succeeds)
description: btrfs_unlink_impl (lib.rs ~21927, handles both file delete and rmdir via expect_dir) performs NO immutable/append-only check, so deleting an immutable or append-only file/dir on btrfs wrongly succeeds. The kernel may_delete returns EPERM for an immutable or append-only victim (before the ENOTEMPTY check for dirs). ext4 already enforces this in its delete path (Self::ext4_reject_immutable_or_append(&child_inode), ~14477). Sibling of bd-xpsq4 (btrfs write/truncate/fallocate) and bd-69ich/kf7uw/85rav — closes the btrfs side of the vfs append/immutable audit for the delete path. FIX: in btrfs_unlink_impl read the child inode and reject flags & (BTRFS_INODE_IMMUTABLE|BTRFS_INODE_APPEND) with EPERM, before the empty-dir check (kernel order: EPERM precedes ENOTEMPTY), before any mutation. Test: inject flag on a btrfs file, delete -> EPERM; file survives.
close_reason: Fixed in fb0649f3: btrfs_unlink_impl now rejects deleting an immutable/append-only file/dir with EPERM (reads victim inode, checks BTRFS_INODE_IMMUTABLE|APPEND before the empty-dir check + any mutation), matching the kernel may_delete and ext4's delete path. Test btrfs_delete_of_immutable_or_append_is_eperm_bd_rmgwc. Full ffs-core 1087 green. COMPLETES the btrfs side of the vfs append/immutable enforcement audit (write/truncate/fallocate/link/xattr/rename/delete all covered both ports).

title: ffs-harness benches: ext4_casefold_key has no Criterion benchmark across UTF-8/ASCII/invalid input classes
description:
Finding (via /profiling-software-performance skill, NEW target): crates/ffs-harness/benches/ondisk_parse.rs has 22+ Criterion benchmarks covering ext4 inode/group_desc/dir_block/extent_tree/xattr/dx_root/dx_hash parsing and btrfs sys_chunk/leaf_items/internal_items/superblock/header/dev_item parsing, but NONE measure ext4_casefold_key throughput.

ext4_casefold_key is on the hot path for every directory lookup on a casefold-enabled ext4 filesystem (lookup_in_dir_block_casefold calls it once per target plus once per scanned entry). Its performance has 3 distinct code paths:
  1. Valid UTF-8 ASCII — fast path, only ASCII lowercase
  2. Valid UTF-8 with multi-codepoint expansion — sharp-s ß/ẞ -> 'ss', plus char.to_lowercase() chain
  3. Invalid UTF-8 — byte-by-byte ASCII fallback

A regression in any branch (e.g., introducing per-char allocation, switching from chars() to grapheme iteration) would silently slow every casefold dir lookup. Without a bench, such a regression has no signal until end users notice slowness on casefold filesystems.

The newly-added bd-6rsow proptest + bd-c7nid fuzz target establish correctness; this bench establishes the perf baseline. Pairs with bd-7pfh0 (dx_hash benches across 6 hash versions).

Acceptance: 4 Criterion benches in crates/ffs-harness/benches/ondisk_parse.rs:
  * bench_ext4_casefold_key_ascii — pure ASCII input (typical filename)
  * bench_ext4_casefold_key_mixed_utf8 — ASCII + sharp-s expansion
  * bench_ext4_casefold_key_long_utf8 — long all-UTF-8 (no ASCII)
  * bench_ext4_casefold_key_invalid_utf8 — ASCII-fallback branch

Each uses black_box on the input; compares Criterion measurement noise floor against the 3 code paths.

title: MVCC flush_to_device writes every dirty block scalar; coalesce contiguous runs into ranged writes
description:
MvccStore::flush_to_device (the fsync / flush-to-device hot path used by flush_mvcc_to_device) writes each dirty block with a separate scalar device write_block. The read side already has read_contiguous_blocks (vectored); writes had no equivalent. LEVER (batched I/O, write side): added BlockDevice::write_contiguous_blocks (default impl = scalar write_block loop, so zero behavior change for non-overriding devices) overridden by ByteDeviceBlockAdapter to do ONE write_all_at over the whole contiguous span. versions is a BTreeMap (ascending block order), so flush_to_device coalesces maximal contiguous runs and writes each run once. Same bytes/locations → identical final on-disk state; sync() still called. Crash consistency unchanged (WAL logs intent; flush granularity is not load-bearing).

title: [btrfs] full transaction commit can place metadata over a freshly written data extent on a single mixed (DATA|METADATA) block group
description: Observed by SlateRaven (wake 11) while round-trip testing bd-x3fcu on a synthetic single mixed DATA|METADATA block group: a data extent written via alloc_data (e.g. logical 0x20000) was overwritten by the commit's metadata-block allocations (alloc_metadata_for_tree), so a remount read of that extent computed a different crc32c than the captured/persisted checksum. Real btrfs uses separate data and metadata block groups, so this does not arise there, and FrankenFS production images are single-DATA-bg; the collision only appears when data and metadata share one block group. Likely cause: alloc_data and alloc_metadata_for_* do not share free-space state within a mixed block group, so both hand out the same address. Low priority (mixed bgs are rare; not hit in production). If FrankenFS intends to support mixed block groups, the extent allocator must track data and metadata allocations against a single shared free map. Repro: build_btrfs_csum_image (mixed bg) + write a new data extent + btrfs_full_transaction_commit + remount + read the new extent.
close_reason: NOT A BUG (investigated SlateRaven wake 13). The premise — commit metadata overwriting a freshly written data extent on a mixed block group — is disproven. (1) Isolated test alloc_data_and_metadata_do_not_overlap_on_mixed_block_group_bd_s0ogm: alloc_data then alloc_metadata_for_tree on a single DATA|METADATA bg return non-overlapping ranges (the metadata gap-scan consults the data EXTENT_ITEM in extent_tree). title: [parity][bug] ext4 file removal FAILS on an htree directory (remove_entry chokes on the dx_root)
description: ext4_unlink_impl (lib.rs ~11727) and ext4_rename's remove-from-parent loops (~13317 remove existing target, ~13391 remove old name) iterate every directory block calling ffs_dir::remove_entry(name, reserved_tail). For an htree directory, logical block 0 is the dx_ROOT whose '..' entry has rec_len = block_size-12 (covering the hidden index), which EXCEEDS the usable area (block_size - reserved_tail=12). remove_entry rejects that as Corruption{block:0, detail:'directory entry exceeds usable block area'} BEFORE reaching any leaf, so the whole remove/rename-remove fails. Net effect: deleting OR renaming-over any file in an htree directory in FrankenFS errors out. Confirmed by create_then_remove_in_htree_dir test (create a real file in a real htree dir, then remove it -> Corruption block 0). FIX: real file entries never live in the dx_root (only dot and dotdot), so the remove scan must SKIP logical block 0 when parent.has_htree_index() and scan only leaf blocks (1..n); the entry is found+removed+restamped in its leaf, dx_root untouched. Complement of the insert fix bd-wb4cd (insert routes to the hash-correct leaf; remove must skip the dx_root). Same write-path htree class.
close_reason: Fixed in 495b8da1. ext4_unlink_impl + ext4_rename's two remove-from-parent loops now skip the dx_root (logical block 0) for htree dirs via the new ext4_htree_dx_root_phys helper, so remove_entry only scans leaf blocks where real entries live; the entry is found+removed+restamped in its leaf and the dx_root is untouched + stays valid. Was: every delete/rename-over in an htree dir errored Corruption{block 0, 'directory entry exceeds usable block area'} because '..' rec_len spans past the reserved tail. RED->GREEN test create_then_unlink_in_htree_dir_keeps_index_consistent. ffs-core 903/903, clippy/fmt clean. Complement of bd-wb4cd (insert routes to hash-correct leaf; remove skips dx_root).

title: ffs-repair: QueuedRepairRefresh lacks documented lock-then-process invariant + recursion-safety regression
description:
Finding (via /deadlock-finder-and-fixer skill, NEW target): crates/ffs-repair/src/pipeline.rs:317 has QueuedRepairRefresh = { group_ranges: Arc<Vec<GroupBlockRange>>, queued_groups: Arc<Mutex<BTreeSet<GroupNumber>>> }. The flush-handler on_flush_committed (line 411) acquires queued_groups under a scoped block, mutates the set, drops the guard at the inner-scope close, then iterates outside the lock for logging.

apply_queued_refreshes (line 370) calls drain_queued_groups (line 355) which acquires + drains + drops the lock, then calls into pipeline.mark_group_dirty / pipeline.on_group_flush WITHOUT holding the lock. This is critical: those pipeline calls could call back into RepairFlushLifecycle::on_flush_committed, which reacquires the same lock. If we held the lock during the pipeline calls, we would deadlock.

The pattern is correct but UNDOCUMENTED. A future refactor that hoisted the pipeline calls inside the locked block (e.g., to keep "drain + process" atomic) would silently introduce a re-entrant deadlock. No regression test asserts this.

Pairs with bd-7zd94 (PersistentMvccStore lock-order), bd-bky2f (ShardedMvccStore), bd-pfv55 (FuseInodeLocks), bd-6owbg (FaultInjector + ThrottleInjector never-hold-both), bd-chmw4 (wal_writer atomic-rollback), bd-gqswx (commit_internal/rollback), bd-lebu5 (DurabilityNotifier invariants), bd-6hopq (MemIoEngine data → stats).

Acceptance:
  1. Doc comment on QueuedRepairRefresh naming the "drain + drop + process" invariant
  2. Doc on drain_queued_groups + apply_queued_refreshes + on_flush_committed naming the no-lock-during-pipeline-call rule
  3. Regression test queued_repair_refresh_drain_releases_lock_before_processing that exercises a mock that calls back into on_flush_committed during processing — must NOT deadlock
close_reason: done

(2) Regression test queued_repair_refresh_drain_releases_lock_before_processing with concurrent producer thread calling on_flush_committed 256 times + consumer thread calling drain_queued_groups 256 times. Asserts no deadlock within 5s and producer completes all 256 calls — a held-lock regression would park one thread forever in futex. rch exit code 0.

title: scrub reports ~50-100% 'corrupt' on valid btrfs images whose data reads back sha256==kernel — false-positive or un-csummed-block semantics?
description: OBSERVATION (CrimsonFox cc/opus 2026-06-22, HEAD c11a51a5, ffs-cli release-perf). 'ffs-cli scrub' reports large 'corrupt' counts on multiple VALID btrfs images: ffs_zb_3293436.img 7920/16384, btrfs_test.img 17339/25600, ffs_btrfs_3704674.img 8136/16384, btrdiff2_1340519.img 130962/131072 (99.9%). All mount cleanly under the kernel and read back byte-identical: comp.bin sha256 124838e2 and big.bin sha256 b6cfaf9d BOTH == kernel loop-mount. So the flagged data is provably NOT corrupt. 7920 ~= big.bin's block count. NEEDS TRIAGE: is scrub (a) false-positiving on valid csummed data (real bug), or (b) counting blocks with absent/incomplete csum-tree entries as 'corrupt' (expected for btrfs-convert images but NOT for kernel-written compress-force=zstd images where csums should exist), or (c) flagging compressed-extent data blocks it can't csum-verify? The mixed ratios (50% vs 99.9%) suggest csum-availability dependence. Related: bd-f37vs (wire ScrubDaemon to BTRFS_IOC_SCRUB). Repro: ffs-cli scrub <btrfs-img> | grep scanned. NOT a perf issue; surfaced during a scrub-vs-kernel bench exploration. Out of my (read-perf) lane — filing for scrub owner.
notes: ROOT-CAUSED (CrimsonFox 2026-06-22): the 'corrupt' count = ZeroCheckValidator (ffs-repair/src/scrub.rs:457) returning Corrupt(UnexpectedZeroes, Severity::Warning) for EVERY all-zero block, applied to ALL blocks by scrub_validator() (main.rs:6904) over the whole image. Healthy images are mostly all-zero FREE/unallocated space -> flagged en masse (btrdiff2 99.9% unallocated, comp-image ~48%). CORRECTION: flagged blocks are the ZERO/free blocks, NOT data blocks (comp.bin/big.bin data is non-zero -> Clean, reads sha256==kernel; data integrity is FINE). The 'corrupt' summary counts Warning-severity findings; real integrity errors are the separate 'error+' count (=2). So this is a REPORTING/SEMANTICS issue, not data corruption: blind whole-image ZeroCheck makes 'corrupt' meaningless on any image with free space. ZeroCheckValidator doc says it is for 'zeroed metadata that should contain data' = must be SCOPED to allocated/metadata blocks. FIX (scrub owner/bd-f37vs): (a) only run ZeroCheck on allocation-tree-allocated blocks; or (b) drop Warning UnexpectedZeroes from the 'corrupt' bucket (report as warnings); or (c) drop ZeroCheckValidator from the full-image validator set. Not fixing here: scrub-semantics change w/ tests, scrub owner's domain not my read-perf lane.
close_reason: FIXED (zeroes class). Removed the blind whole-image ZeroCheckValidator from both scrub validator sets: BtrfsScrubValidator::validate (fused path, crates/ffs-repair/src/scrub.rs) and scrub_validator()'s ext4 composite (crates/ffs-cli/src/main.rs). Unallocated space is legitimately all-zero and a whole-image scrub has no allocation map, so ZeroCheck flagged every free block Corrupt(UnexpectedZeroes, Warning); blocks_corrupt counts blocks with >=1 finding of ANY severity, so healthy images read 50-100% corrupt, is_clean() was permanently false, findings grew one entry per free block, and pipeline.rs:1566 trained the repair autopilot's Beta posterior on a ~99.9% false-positive rate. Safe: ZeroCheck detected nothing the superblock validators miss (an all-zero superblock fails parse_superblock_region -> Corrupt at Critical in both flavors); ZeroCheckValidator retained + unit-tested as a scoped primitive. MEASURED: btrdiff2_1340519.img blocks_corrupt 130962 -> 76 of 131072 (99.94% of the corrupt count removed) with blocks_error_or_higher 76 -> 76 and the error+ finding set byte-identical before/after (no real detection lost). ext4 cc_ext.img: 61365/102400 blocks all-zero -> would-be corrupt 61365 -> 0, now fully clean; extbig_1587438.img 0/131072. Gates: ffs-repair 469/0 (+2 new regression tests), ffs-cli 348+26/0, ffs-harness 2058/0 + conformance, cargo check --workspace --all-targets OK. RESIDUAL is a DISTINCT, newly-root-caused bug filed as bd-5vb36 (tree-block validator compares header.bytenr, a LOGICAL chunk-mapped address, against the PHYSICAL offset; proven by a constant -8MiB delta on btr_571421.img).

title: perf(scrub): ~one chunk per thread so buffer pool is reused — scrub 1.06-1.22x
description: SHIPPED 956efae1. scrub_range split into ~8 chunks/thread which floored to 1 read-batch/chunk on typical images, defeating the bd-xmh5g.7 buffer-pool reuse + never reaching the fast vectored read path -> every chunk re-alloc+re-zeroed buffers (~76% self-time in alloc/zero/free per perf, NOT validation). Fix: chunk=total/parallelism (drop the *8) so chunks span many batches and amortize one pool alloc; scrub work uniform per block so no load-balance slack lost. title: Bitmap CRC: verify kernel bitmap pre-processing before checksumming
description:
Read the Linux kernel source for ext4_block_bitmap_csum_set() and ext4_block_bitmap_csum_verify() to determine:
(a) Whether the kernel zeroes unused tail bits in the bitmap before checksumming. For a group with fewer blocks than blocks_per_group, the tail bits may be set to 1 (indicating 'used') by mkfs but the kernel may ignore/zero them before CRC.
(b) Whether the kernel checksums exactly block_size bytes or clusters_per_group/8 bytes. Our code checksums the full block.
(c) Whether the kernel XORs or masks any fields in the group descriptor before storing the checksum.

SPECIFIC FILES TO CHECK:
- fs/ext4/balloc.c: ext4_block_bitmap_csum_set(), ext4_block_bitmap_csum_verify()
- fs/ext4/bitmap.c: ext4_bitmap_csum()
- include/linux/ext4.h: struct ext4_group_desc layout

ACCEPTANCE: Document the exact kernel pre-processing steps. If any differ from our implementation, fix our code.
close_reason: Kernel source confirmed: no group number in bitmap CRC, length is clusters_per_group/8 for blocks and inodes_per_group/8 for inodes. Fixed in commit 20d65f4.

title: btrfs: partial-range reflink of a compressed extent is overly rejected (reader already supports it)
description: btrfs_clone_file_range_data (ffs-core lib.rs ~18184) rejects partial-range reflink of a compressed extent with UnsupportedFeature. INVESTIGATION (W35): OVERLY CONSERVATIVE. The btrfs READ path already supports a compressed extent viewed through extent_offset/num_bytes: read (lib.rs ~8123) decompresses the whole blob to ram_bytes then slices via btrfs_decompressed_extent_slice. And the Regular-arm share logic already preserves compression + disk_bytenr/disk_num_bytes/ram_bytes and sets extent_offset+=delta, num_bytes=overlap. So a partial-range compressed share would read back correctly. FIX: remove the compression!=0 rejection so compressed extents share via the existing Regular-arm path. VALIDATION IS THE WORK (why deferred): need a WRITABLE compressed-extent source in open_writable_btrfs to reflink from. FrankenFS write is uncompressed; existing compressed-read tests use static build_btrfs_fsops_image + set_btrfs_test_extent_compression (read-only). Build a writable compressed source via btrfs_test_zlib_compress for the blob, allocate+write the data block, insert EXTENT_DATA(Regular, compression=1, ram_bytes, disk_num_bytes, num_bytes, extent_offset=0) + EXTENT_ITEM + backref (+csum). Then read full src==data, partial-reflink a sub-range, read dst==src sub-range, btrfs check clean. Corruption-sensitive (btrfs extent sharing) - do NOT remove the rejection without that read-back + btrfs-check validation. Sibling inline-partial-reflink (~18221) is harder (slice the inline bytes + write to dst as a fresh extent). Low reachability (src must have compressed extents = real-btrfs-written).
close_reason: done

Fully validated end-to-end: built a real ZLIB-compressed source (write then btrfs_remove_overlapping_extent_data then hand-rolled compressed EXTENT_DATA+backref+csum), then full-decompress sanity, partial reflink reads the sub-range, COW-break keeps source intact, btrfs check clean. 1008 ffs-core green. title: [perf] cache read-only ext4 group descriptors to cut direct-read scalar pread64
description: SCENARIO: post-bd-thkm1 ffs-harness profile-read-path --fixture conformance/golden/ext4_8mb_reference.ext4 --duration-sec 2 --mode direct-read under strace -f -c. title: perf(core/btrfs): parallel-read the UNCOMPRESSED direct extents in btrfs_read_file (I/O-overlap follow-on to bd-307e4)
description:
Follow-on to bd-307e4 (compressed-blob gather parallelized, 6.31x). The assembly loop in btrfs_read_file still reads UNCOMPRESSED regular extents serially: each does self.btrfs_read_logical_into(cx, source_logical, &mut out[dst..dst+len]) one extent at a time. For a fragmented file with many non-contiguous extents this serializes N device-read latencies; parallelizing overlaps them (I/O-overlap robustly exceeds 2x via thread parking even on the ~2-core CI remote — unlike CPU-bound levers which cap at core count).

DESIGN (preserves zero-copy + error order): the out[] ranges for distinct extents are DISJOINT, so use split_at_mut to carve per-extent &mut out sub-slices and read directly into them (no intermediate buffer = zero-copy preserved). ERROR-ORDER obligation: today compressed  errors surface DURING the assembly loop in extent order; deferring uncompressed reads to a parallel phase must NOT let a later compressed error preempt an earlier uncompressed-read error. Fix = defer ALL error surfacing: collect compressed-decompress results + uncompressed read results per-idx in a unified parallel phase, then a final ordered pass returns the lowest-idx error (isomorphic to serial). Cx:Sync + BlockDevice:Send+Sync + OpenFs:Sync already established (bd-307e4). Measurable with the LatencyBlockDevice substrate (bd-wipi2) at injected latency. Multi-hour careful read-path change — do deliberately. Caveat: most files are all-compressed or all-uncompressed, but mixed must stay correct.
close_reason: Shipped bd0e6545: deferred uncompressed direct-extent reads into the bd-307e4 parallel map via split_at_mut disjoint out windows (zero-copy). Component bench btrfs_uncompressed_read_overlap: serial 5.9510ms -> parallel 1.6353ms = 3.64x (16 extents, 250us/read latency device, byte-identical assert). Error order preserved (serial validation pass + in-order ? consumption, bd-307e4 precedent). All ffs-core tests + clippy clean.

title: btrfs fallocate does not update mtime/ctime on success (ext4 does) -> POSIX/file_modified parity gap
description: btrfs_fallocate (lib.rs ~22068) updated only inode.size and inode.nbytes then wrote the inode, never touching mtime/ctime. ext4_fallocate (lib.rs:15598) calls touch_mtime_ctime before write_inode. fallocate(2) marks the file modified for every mode (default prealloc, KEEP_SIZE, PUNCH_HOLE, ZERO_RANGE, COLLAPSE/INSERT_RANGE) so the kernel (file_modified) bumps both mtime and ctime; the btrfs port left them frozen, so mtime/ctime-based tooling (make, tar, rsync, backup) missed allocations. Sibling-asymmetry class (cf bd-pssza truncate mtime). FIX: stamp inode.mtime_sec/nsec + ctime_sec/nsec = btrfs_now_timestamp() before the fs_tree.update. Pinned by btrfs_fallocate_updates_mtime_and_ctime (fails pre-fix: mtime frozen at pinned value); btrfs_fallocate_churn_passes_btrfs_check still green.
close_reason: Fixed in 2dbee95b: btrfs_fallocate now stamps mtime+ctime before the inode update, matching ext4 and POSIX file_modified semantics. Pinned by btrfs_fallocate_updates_mtime_and_ctime (verified fails pre-fix); 1055 ffs-core lib tests green + btrfs_fallocate_churn_passes_btrfs_check (btrfs check clean) + crate clippy -D warnings clean.

title: perf(fuse+harness): the serial FUSE dispatcher fails its own A/A null at every daemon cpuset wider than one CPU — which blocks the ~1.9x workers lever and may itself be the readdir-stat defect
description:
Measured 2026-08-05 (SapphireBirch, five six-arm runs, ledger row 24944263). Whenever --fuse-cpus > 1, two IDENTICALLY configured serial-dispatch mounts in the same window disagree by more than the A/A gate allows: spread 1.094147 (4 CPU, 24 pairs), 1.065028 (8 CPU, 24 pairs), 1.034738 (8 CPU host-wide, 48 pairs), and at 48 pairs / 4 CPU the median deviation itself hit 2.35%, past the 2% limit. The workers arm cleared its null in 3 of those 4 runs, so this is specific to serial dispatch, not to the workload or the window. More pairs makes it worse, not better.

TWO CONSEQUENCES.
(1) It blocks a large candidate effect: candidate_b_over_candidate_a came out 0.499511 / 0.502954 / 0.524839 / 0.590425 across those four runs (workers ~1.7-2.0x faster), always the same direction, and NONE of it is admissible because the incumbent arm is unstable. That is the single largest unclaimed effect in the metadata class.
(2) It may be a defect in its own right. The inadmissible fuse_over_kernel medians rise with the daemon cpuset under default serial dispatch — 5.11x at 1 CPU vs 5.45x, 5.52x, 6.59x, 6.63x at 4-8 CPUs — so the landed --fuse-cpus control may be actively harmful to the current dispatcher rather than the fix for the 8:1 client:daemon handicap it was built to be.

SUSPECTED CONTRIBUTING CAUSE, cheap to test first: the harness never reached its private-core daemon placement. All five runs report fuse_cpu_isolation=shares_physical_cores_with_clients_placed_after, i.e. the daemon is on SMT siblings of the client cores, at both same-llc and host-wide scope, at 4 and 8 CPUs. select_multi_fuse_cpus / the private-core branch in ffs_mounted_kernel_bench.rs (~line 4110-4160) should be checked: either the branch cannot be satisfied with 8 client threads on this host, in which case say so and pick a placement that can, or it is choosing badly.

ACCEPTANCE. Either (a) produce a placement in which the serial arm's own A/A null clears at more than one daemon CPU, then re-run the FFS_FUSE_WORKERS=4 A/B there and report whatever it says, or (b) show that serial dispatch is inherently unstable on a multi-CPU cpuset — with a counted mechanism, e.g. thread migrations or per-CPU queue imbalance, not just wall time — in which case the finding is that the daemon must be pinned to one CPU or the dispatcher must change, and --fuse-cpus needs a documented scope rule. Do NOT weaken the A/A gate; it is doing its job.

comments.author: SapphireBirch
comments.text:
PARTIAL RESOLUTION — the instability was the PLACEMENT, not serial dispatch per se. Fix landed 7ce6e3ef.

CAUSE. place_cpus() only attempted the private-physical-core order when --fuse-cpus was 1; every wider cpuset went straight to the clients-first fallback, where select_multi_fuse_cpus excludes the client CPUs but NOT their SMT siblings, so the daemon always landed on the siblings of the threads it serves. All five earlier runs reported fuse_cpu_isolation=shares_physical_cores_with_clients_placed_after for that reason. Host-wide scope on this 32-core box can seat 8 client threads and 8 daemon CPUs on distinct physical cores, so refusing to try was leaving the only admissible wide placement on the table.

FIX. place_daemon_on_private_cores() tries the daemon-first order above one CPU and returns Ok(None) — not an error — when the domain cannot supply the cores or the clients then do not fit, so same-LLC runs behave exactly as before and --fuse-cpus 1 is untouched. select_private_core_cpus() is pure and unit-tested without sysfs (a core counts as private only when NONE of its SMT threads is spoken for): 3 new tests, 45 passed / 0 failed on strict remote; clippy clean in this file (the 2 errors are the pre-existing MSRV lints in ffs-harness/src/metrics.rs, bd-g9l54); my rustfmt hunks clean; ubs unchanged (the 1 CRITICAL is the pre-existing Command::new(path) at the --ffs-cli argv).

MEASURED EFFECT OF THE FIX — 8 daemon CPUs, host-wide, 24 pairs, now reporting fuse_cpu_isolation=private_physical_core_clients_placed_after:
  A/A run: kernel null 0.996526 (spread 1.018356) CLEAR, SERIAL arm null 0.995887 (spread 1.019405) CLEAR, candidate-B null 0.998105 (spread 1.013967) CLEAR.
The serial arm's own A/A null went from 1.094147 / 1.065028 / 1.034738 under sibling-sharing to 1.019405 under private cores. That is acceptance (b) answered in the negative: serial dispatch is NOT inherently unstable on a multi-CPU cpuset — it was unstable because it shared physical cores with the clients it serves.

STILL NOT ADMITTED at 24 pairs, and the residual is a DIFFERENT null each time:
  A/A run  — cross-pair candidate null 0.985242, spread 1.040331 > 1.025 -> BLOCKED_NULL.
  lever run — serial arm null spread 1.047796 > 1.025 (kernel 1.025095 marginal) -> BLOCKED_NULL; its candidate ratio was 0.573091 [0.560650, 0.590623], again NOT published.
So the margins moved from ~1.09 to ~1.04 against a 1.025 limit. Pairs is the documented dial (bd-3tqgc: 24 -> 48 took the claim gate from 2.80-4.87% to 1.07%), so 48-pair A/A and lever runs at this placement are IN FLIGHT.

No gate was weakened at any point; the fix changes which placement is chosen, and every run still reports the placement it got.

comments.author: SapphireBirch
comments.text:
48-PAIR CONFIRMATION BLOCKED — infrastructure, not a measurement result. Both attempts (A/A and FFS_FUSE_WORKERS=4, --fuse-cpus 8, host-wide, 48 pairs) died on the harness host-quiet gate:
  post-mount pre-measurement did not obtain 5 consecutive clear host-wide samples within 300000 ms after 300 samples; last busy CPUs above 20.0%: cpu22=23.5%,cpu48=88.9%
  initial placement did not obtain 5 consecutive clear host-wide samples ...: cpu16=60.6%,cpu22=58.4%,cpu48=38.0%,cpu54=40.0%
Cause is a foreign process on this shared box (python3 .../files_scan at ~100% CPU), not this bead's code. No number was produced and none is reported.

COUPLING WORTH RECORDING: at 8 client threads, private-core daemon placement is only reachable at host-wide scope (an LLC domain here is 8 cores/16 threads, so 8 clients + 4 or 8 daemon CPUs cannot fit privately), and host-wide scope is the strictest quiet gate the harness has. So the fix that makes wide cpusets measurable also makes them the runs most likely to be refused on a shared machine.

STATE: code fix landed and demonstrated (7ce6e3ef, ledger row 4187b17b). Bead STAYS OPEN on acceptance (a) — the re-run of the workers A/B at a placement where the serial null clears — pending a quiet host-wide window. Retry exactly: --fuse-cpus 8 --placement-scope host-wide --pairs 48, once with --candidate-aa and once with --candidate-b-env FFS_FUSE_WORKERS=4. If the cross-pair null still will not clear at 48 pairs, stop buying pairs and report that 8 daemon CPUs is a high-variance configuration for this workload.

title: perf(fuse): pre-populate the capability memo during readdirplus — readdir+stat pays one cold format lookup per entry that a batched sweep could fold into one

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
FILED from the bd-btrfs-readdir-stat-8x-8y7vp characterisation (AzureBay, 2026-08-16).

MEASURED PREMISE, counted, harness readdir_stat_count.sh, host thinkstation1, 2000-entry ls -l with
caches dropped: 2003 getxattr probes, 2 memo hits, 2001 format lookups — 1.000 cold format lookup
PER ENTRY. Every entry is a distinct inode probed exactly once, so the bd-2pq73 memo (which serves
warm stat at 100%) is structurally useless on this path. That is measured, not assumed.

THE LEVER: readdirplus already knows the entire set of inodes it is about to return, and it already
fetches their attributes. Resolving their security.capability answers in ONE batched pass and
pre-populating the memo would turn N cold one-shot lookups into one sweep, so the per-entry probes
that follow all hit. readdir+stat is the worst measured loss in the bank at 8.32x vs kernel btrfs.

WHAT IT NEEDS:
  1. An FsOps surface for batch xattr presence over a set of inodes. For ext4 the answer is largely
     in the inode itself (inline xattr area / i_file_acl), so "does this inode have any xattr at all"
     may be answerable without a separate tree descent — check before designing a heavier API.
  2. A decision on WHEN to do it. Doing it unconditionally in readdirplus does work even when the
     caller never stats (plain readdir, or ls without -l). Options: only when readdirplus is
     negotiated, only above an entry-count threshold, or lazily on the first per-entry probe that
     follows a readdir of the same directory.
  3. The 64-slot memo is far too small for this: 2000 entries through 64 direct-mapped slots
     overwrites itself many times over. A prefetch is pointless unless the memo can hold a
     directory-sized set, so sizing has to be solved with it — and that reopens the bounded-memory
     question the original one-slot design was protecting.

ACCEPTANCE: a counted before/after on format lookups per entry (the metric above) is admissible on
its own and needs no quiet window — which matters, because the mounted comparator is currently
unable to run at all (120 GiB abort floor, 106G free). A timed row is desirable but must not gate
this.

DO NOT start by re-running the comparator, and do not assume the warm-stat memo win transfers: it
does not, and the count above is why.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
DESIGN REFINEMENT — no batch API needed, and no extra I/O at all (AzureBay, 2026-08-16).

I filed this asking for "an FsOps surface for batch xattr presence". Reading the resolution path
shows that is more machinery than the problem needs.

ffs-core getxattr (lib.rs:18460) resolves a capability probe as:
    read_live_inode(ino)                       <- the cost
    find_ibody_xattr_by_name(&inode, name)     <- inline scan, no I/O
    if inode.file_acl != 0 { read external block }   <- already skipped when absent

So for an inode with no xattrs the whole answer is derivable FROM THE INODE ALONE — the inline scan
plus the file_acl == 0 test. There is no tree descent to batch.

And readdirplus ALREADY READ THAT INODE to build the entry attributes. Confirmed by the counted run:
a 2000-entry ls -l produced 2003 getxattr probes and essentially nothing else in the window, because
readdirplus supplied the attrs and only the capability probe came back to the daemon. read_live_inode
does a real reader.read_inode with no cache in front of it (lib.rs:15386), so the SAME inode is read
twice per entry — once for the attribute, once for the capability probe.

REVISED LEVER, strictly smaller than what this bead originally proposed: while readdirplus already
holds each inode, evaluate capability presence from it and populate the memo. Zero additional I/O,
no new batch API, no tree walk — the information is already in a struct we are holding and then
throwing away. The per-entry probe that follows then hits the memo instead of re-reading the inode.

This also changes the trade-off I flagged as open question 2. The objection was "doing this in
readdirplus costs work even when the caller never stats". With the inline-scan formulation that cost
is a field test and a short scan over the inline xattr area on an inode already in registers — not a
lookup — so the case for doing it unconditionally is much stronger.

Question 3 still stands and is now the binding constraint: 64 direct-mapped slots cannot hold a
2000-entry directory, so the prefetch is pointless without sizing the memo to a directory-sized set,
and that reopens the bounded-memory question. Solve sizing WITH this, not after.

Acceptance unchanged: counted before/after on format lookups per entry (currently 1.000), which
needs no quiet window — the comparator still cannot run at all (120 GiB floor, 106G free).

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
SCOPING: the obvious implementation is the wrong one. Two rejected designs and the one that survives (AzureBay, 2026-08-16).

CONFIRMED THE REDUNDANCY AT THE SEAM: ffs-fuse readdirplus (lib.rs:2870) calls ops.getattr per entry,
which does read_live_inode; the capability probe that follows then calls ops.getxattr, which does
read_live_inode AGAIN on the same inode. ffs-core read_live_inode (lib.rs:15386) goes straight to
reader.read_inode with no cache in front of it. So it is literally two inode reads per directory
entry, and the counted run bears that out — 2003 probes for 2000 entries, 2001 of them cold format
lookups.

REJECTED DESIGN 1 — add capability presence to InodeAttr so readdirplus can carry it. 19 constructors
across 5 crates, and InodeAttr derives Serialize/Deserialize, so the field lands in report schemas
too. A wide blast radius on a public struct to carry one bool, and the repo has already been bitten
by struct-field additions missing test/bench constructors and silently failing to compile.

REJECTED DESIGN 2 — a new FsOps method capability_xattr_absent(ino) with a defaulted impl. Cheap to
add and breaks nothing, but it does not WIN anything: it still has to read the inode itself, which is
the cost we are trying to remove. It moves the call, not the work.

THE DESIGN THAT SURVIVES — a small inode memo inside the ffs-core backend, so the second
read_live_inode of the same inode hits memory instead of the device. No public API change, no struct
change, no FUSE-layer change; it fixes the redundancy where it actually is. It also helps every other
path that reads an inode twice in one operation, not just this one. Needs invalidation on write, and
needs sizing against the same directory-sweep working set that constrains the capability memo
(question 3 on this bead).

NOT STARTED HERE, deliberately: crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs is actively being edited by another agent
right now (unstaged changes present in the shared checkout), and an inode cache is exactly the kind
of change that conflicts badly. Whoever takes it should reserve ffs-core in Agent Mail first.

Acceptance unchanged and still needs no quiet window: counted format lookups per entry, currently
1.000 (harness readdir_stat_count.sh).

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
SCOPING CORRECTION — the surviving design targets a TEST-ONLY backend (ProudBarn, 2026-08-16).
Three findings, all static, no build needed. Each one saves the next implementer a wasted change.

1. THE CITED SEAM IS NOT THE MOUNT PATH. This bead's design notes cite "ffs-core getxattr
   (lib.rs:18460)" and "read_live_inode (lib.rs:15386)". Both are members of Ext4FsOps, and
   Ext4FsOps is CONSTRUCTED IN EXACTLY ONE PLACE: lib.rs:44552, inside a #[test]. It is the
   read-only in-memory reference bridge, not what a mount runs. An inode memo added there
   would measure clean in unit tests and change NOTHING on the readdir+stat row.

   The real path is impl FsOps for OpenFs, crates/ffs-core/src/fs_ops.rs:457:
       getxattr -> self.read_inode(cx, ext4_canonical_inode(ino))
                -> read_inode_with_scope -> read_inode_raw_with_scope
                -> read_inode_raw_with_scope_using(parse_fn)

2. THE "NO INVALIDATION NEEDED" SIMPLIFICATION DOES NOT SURVIVE THE MOVE. Ext4FsOps holds
   image: Arc<Vec<u8>> and is documented as having no mutable state, so a memo there needs no
   invalidation. OpenFs is WRITABLE and every inode read is RequestScope/snapshot-scoped. A
   cache on that chain must be snapshot-aware or it reintroduces exactly the read-vs-prune
   TOCTOU class that cost bd-bhh0i several turns (a read resolving against a snapshot that has
   since been pruned, falling back to stale bytes). The design note's "needs invalidation on
   write" is therefore not a footnote — it is the whole difficulty, and it lands on an MVCC
   path rather than a plain one.

3. THE OBVIOUS CHEAP LEVER IS ALSO WRONG, checked before writing it. getxattr parses a FULL
   inode when it appears to need only the inline xattr area plus file_acl, so switching it to
   the existing Ext4Inode::parse_metadata_from_bytes looks free. It is not:
   parse_metadata_from_bytes uses Ext4InodeIbodyParse::MetadataOnly, and the Full/MetadataOnly
   distinction IS the ibody xattr parse. MetadataOnly skips precisely the region the capability
   probe reads. Do not make this swap; it would return "no such attribute" for every
   inline-stored xattr.

WHAT IS STILL TRUE AND UNCHANGED: the counted premise (2003 probes, 2 memo hits, 2001 cold
format lookups, 1.000 per entry) and the redundancy (the same inode is read once for the
attribute and once for the capability probe). Only the LOCATION of the fix moves.

SIZING (question 3) IS SMALLER THAN FEARED. LastMissingCapabilityXattr is a direct-mapped
[AtomicU64; CAPABILITY_MEMO_SLOTS] — 8 bytes per slot, no per-entry allocation. Holding a
2000-entry directory needs 2048 slots = 16 KiB per mount; 8192 slots = 64 KiB. Against the
65536-entry ext4_inode_attr_cache already resident, that is noise. The bounded-memory question
the one-slot design was protecting does not meaningfully reopen at these sizes.

BUT SIZING ALONE WINS NOTHING, and this bead already says why: every entry is a distinct inode
probed exactly once, so a bigger memo still misses on every probe. Sizing is necessary and not
sufficient — population during readdirplus is the actual lever, and per finding 1 it has to be
done where OpenFs holds the inode, not where Ext4FsOps does.

NOT IMPLEMENTED HERE, deliberately: a snapshot-aware cache on the OpenFs inode-read chain is
not a change to start at the end of a long session. I hold no lock on fs_ops.rs and have left
it untouched.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
QUESTION 3 CLOSED, and a red build repaired on the way (ProudBarn, ca251b30).

SIZING (this bead's stated binding constraint): CAPABILITY_MEMO_SLOTS 64 -> 4096, pinned by capability_memo_holds_a_directory_sized_sweep_bd_t0xoq (2000 distinct inodes must all stay resident). The bounded-memory worry does not survive contact with the numbers: the memo is a direct-mapped [AtomicU64; N], 8 bytes per slot, one allocation per mount, no eviction bookkeeping — 4096 slots is 32 KiB against the 65536-entry ext4 inode attr cache already resident. Question 3 looked harder than it is because the one-slot design's bounded-memory property was being defended at a scale where it costs kilobytes.

⚠ NECESSARY BUT NOT SUFFICIENT, said in the code, the test and the commit: on readdir+stat every inode is probed exactly once, so a bigger table still misses every time. Sizing only removes the reason a POPULATED memo would immediately evict itself. No ratio is claimed.

ALSO REPAIRED, not mine: ffs-fuse lib tests did not compile on HEAD. 1373408d (the Cx-elision lever) dropped the cx parameter from getxattr_value but left two call sites in readonly_xattr_values_are_memoized_without_caching_zero_inode_or_rw_mounts still passing &cx — E0425 and E0061 together, in a test with no cx binding. Every other call site in that same test had been converted. Worth knowing on this bead because it means the Cx-elision lever landed with ffs-fuse's test build red, so anything measured against it since has been unverified by that suite.

Gate: cargo test -p ffs-fuse --lib capability on rch worker vmi1227854 — 9 passed, 0 failed. fmt clean.

REMAINING on this bead, unchanged: populate the memo during readdirplus, at the OpenFs seam (fs_ops.rs:457), not the Ext4FsOps one the design cites — see my previous comment for why that backend is test-only and why parse_metadata_from_bytes is not a safe shortcut.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
PREMISE CORRECTION — this bead's core claim is now FALSE, and the reason is a change that landed after it was filed (AzureBay, 2026-08-16, commit 4eb864a3).

This bead says: "Every entry is a distinct inode probed exactly once, so the bd-2pq73 memo (which serves warm stat at 100%) is structurally useless on this path. That is measured, not assumed." It then makes question 3 the binding constraint: "The 64-slot memo is far too small for this: 2000 entries through 64 direct-mapped slots overwrites itself many times over."

CAPABILITY_MEMO_SLOTS IS NOW 4096, not 64. A 2000-entry directory FITS. Question 3 has already been answered by whoever raised it, and answering it inverted this bead's premise.

MEASURED end-to-end, memo-OFF over memo-ON via --candidate-b-env FFS_FUSE_CAPABILITY_MEMO=0, one ELF 28e74202..., six_arm_williams_square, same_window=true, host thinkstation1:

  12 pairs  1.218496  [1.080162, 1.247312]  candidate_aa_null_clear=true
  12 pairs  1.256750  [1.243660, 1.300158]  candidate_aa_null_clear=true
  36 pairs  1.219035  [1.203864, 1.288715]  candidate_aa_null_clear=true

Above 1.0 means turning the memo OFF was SLOWER. Three runs, medians spread 3.1%, every interval excluding parity. Worst bound 1.080162: the memo is worth AT LEAST 7.4% of mounted readdir+stat, central estimate near 18%. Directional rather than banked -- all three are BLOCKED_NULL on RESOLUTION (interval wider than minimum_decidable_effect_ratio), NOT on a failed null; the candidate A/A null is clear in all three.

WHY the original reasoning failed: it was right that each entry is probed once PER SWEEP, but the workload sweeps the same directory once per observation across 12-36 pairs. With 64 slots the directory self-evicted between sweeps so every probe missed, exactly as written. With 4096 slots the directory stays resident and every sweep after the first is served from the memo.

WHAT SURVIVES of this bead. The prefetch idea is now much weaker -- the memo already captures a 2000-entry directory without any readdirplus pre-population, so a prefetch buys only the FIRST sweep. But the bead's own DESIGN-THAT-SURVIVES section (a small inode memo inside the ffs-core backend, so the second read_live_inode of the same inode hits memory) is untouched by this and remains the real lever: the redundancy is two inode reads per entry within ONE operation, which no cross-sweep cache addresses.

HONEST LIMIT on the 18%: it depends on the directory FITTING in 4096 slots. A 32,768-entry sweep -- the size the banked 7.73x/8.32x readdir rows use -- does NOT fit, so 18% must not be extrapolated there. That measurement is the obvious next run and would also re-test this bead's premise at the size that actually matters.

title: Refine soak campaigns with stop conditions and flake root-cause classification
description:
Supplemental refinement for bd-rchk0.5.9. Long-running soak and canary campaigns are only useful if they have deterministic stop conditions, bounded resource budgets, and honest flake classification. This bead prevents endurance runs from becoming vague pass/fail anecdotes or silently hiding product failures as environmental noise.

Scope: define campaign stop conditions, heartbeat schema, resource-budget handling, flake/product/host classification, stale-baseline quarantine, and follow-up creation rules for recurring failures. Campaigns must remain bounded enough for CI/RCH smoke while preserving enough detail for nightly/manual lanes.

Required proof before close:
1. Unit tests cover campaign profile parsing, duration and iteration bounds, heartbeat cadence, failure-threshold evaluation, stop-condition precedence, resource-budget exhaustion, stale baseline rejection, and artifact aggregation.
2. Unit tests cover classification for product regression, host capability skip, infrastructure error, timeout, resource exhaustion, known quarantined flake, new recurring flake, and inconclusive result.
3. E2E smoke runs a bounded campaign using representative workload rows and emits heartbeat, final summary, raw logs, and machine-readable artifacts.
4. Logs include campaign id, profile, git SHA, host/kernel/FUSE capability, workload ids, seeds, start/end time, heartbeat summaries, resource usage, stop reason, classification, artifact paths, cleanup status, and reproduction command.
5. Recurring flakes and product failures require a linked follow-up bead or an explicit quarantine entry with owner, expiry, user-risk rationale, reproduction data, and release-gate impact.

title: ffs-ondisk: parse_dev_item lacks proptest coverage despite 5 fixed-input tests
description:
Finding (via /testing-metamorphic skill, third visit, different
target): `parse_dev_item` (crates/ffs-ondisk/src/btrfs.rs:1074) is
a pure deterministic 98-byte BtrfsDevItem parser on the btrfs
multi-device probe path. It has FIVE fixed-input tests
(parse_dev_item_valid, _rejects_bytes_used_above_total,
_rejects_zero_devid, _rejects_zero_total_bytes, _too_short) but
ZERO proptests. The bd-7mj5d / bd-9er6s / bd-590tc style metamorphic
relations are not exercised:

  MR-1 (No-panic over arbitrary bytes): for any input of any length
       in [0, 256], parse_dev_item must return either Ok or a structured
       ParseError — never panic. This is the basic robustness contract
       that the existing fuzz target enforces but the proptest layer
       does not.

  MR-2 (Tail-invariance): the parser only reads bytes 0..98. For any
       valid input of length 98, appending arbitrary suffix bytes
       MUST yield the same parse result. A regression that
       accidentally hashed or dispatched on tail bytes would slip
       past the existing tests.

  MR-3 (Field round-trip / byte-offset contract): given valid
       devid/total_bytes/bytes_used/io_*/dev_*/uuid/fsid values, the
       parser returns those exact values from the documented offsets
       (devid@0, total_bytes@8, bytes_used@16, io_align@24, io_width@28,
       sector_size@32, dev_type@36, generation@44, start_offset@52,
       dev_group@60, seek_speed@64, bandwidth@65, uuid@66..82,
       fsid@82..98). Any drift in the offset table would silently
       corrupt every btrfs multi-device read.

Acceptance: 3 new proptests added to the existing
`proptest!` block (l. 3037) with shared ProptestConfig.
notes: Shipped: 3 new btrfs proptest MRs in crates/ffs-ondisk/src/btrfs.rs. MR-1 (no-panic over arbitrary 0..=256 byte inputs); MR-2 (tail-invariance — bytes >= 98 must not affect parse output); MR-3 (field-offset contract — every documented field offset returns the expected value across the input space, pins the 98-byte layout). All 8 parse_dev_item tests (5 existing fixed-input + 3 new proptests) pass via rch exec -- cargo test -p ffs-ondisk --lib parse_dev_item.

title: perf(core): RwLock the read-contended block/metadata caches for concurrent-read hit paths (follow-on to bd-xenil)
description: FOLLOW-ON to bd-xenil (9bffc877 RwLock alloc state, 3.43x). The concurrency vein is OPEN: several plain-map caches are Mutex<...> that every concurrent FUSE read (8 worker threads) contends on. Unlike the alloc state (pure read vs pure write paths = mechanical), these are read-MODIFY (get-on-hit / insert-on-miss), so the conversion needs a try-.read().get() fast path then drop+.write().insert() on miss — NOT a mechanical sed. Candidates (all ffs-core OpenFs fields): ext4_file_data_block_cache (Mutex<BTreeMap<BlockNumber,Arc<[u8]>>>, 11 sites — hot ext4 data-read cache, plain map so hits are read-only), ext4_inode_table_block_cache, ext4_group_desc_cache, btrfs_parsed_node_cache, btrfs_csum_read_cache, btrfs_inode_path_cache, btrfs_fs_tree_root_cache. PROOF: (1) verify hit path is truly read-only (no LRU/freq metadata updated on get — these are plain BTreeMaps, likely yes); (2) concurrent A/B bench (8 threads, cache-hit-heavy) Mutex vs RwLock like btrfs_alloc_rwlock.rs; (3) on-miss double-lookup is benign (re-check under write lock or just insert — idempotent Arc). SKIP the S3-FIFO block cache (ffs-block) — it updates freq bits on access (hits mutate, RwLock doesn't apply cleanly). Target: ≥2.0 concurrent read-hit throughput. read/write split compiler-enforced as in bd-xenil.
notes: cc W150: shipped 3 lock-striping levers (sharding, not RwLock — robust 3.23x vs borderline 1.8-2.8x). be2f5cba btrfs_parsed_node_cache (measured 3.23x, 8t), 672867fa ext4_inode_table_block_cache, 95dcff7d ext4_group_desc_cache — all Mutex BTreeMap caches now 16-shard ShardedCache. 1104 tests + clippy clean each. The 3 hot BTreeMap metadata caches are DONE. NavyPelican's ext4_file_data_block_cache stays RwLock (their committed choice; sharded-vs-rwlock only ~1.15x). Remaining low-value: Option<Arc> single-value caches (btrfs_inode_path/csum_read) + small btrfs_fs_tree_root HashMap.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text: BTRFS TRANSACTION MODEL: btrfs transactions group multiple COW tree updates into an atomic unit. Key concepts: (1) transaction handle (acquire on begin, release on end), (2) delayed items (buffered in memory until transaction commit), (3) transaction commit writes all dirty trees atomically. Our MVCC layer maps naturally onto this: MVCC transaction ≈ btrfs transaction.

title: FuseInodeLocks eviction race: strong_count==2 heuristic can permanently leak a lock-table entry; intermittent CI failure of fuse_inode_locks_* table-empty asserts
description:
8th cause of main CI red (intermittent flake masking everything after it — ffs-fuse runs before ffs-harness in cargo's first-failing-binary order). CI run 26809233141 (with conformance+census fixes) failed only on ffs-fuse lib: fuse_inode_locks_preserve_total_order_under_contention (:18846) and fuse_inode_locks_retain_entry_while_second_guard_blocked (:18805), both at `assert_eq!(locks.table_len(), 0)` — an entry survived the table after all guards dropped. Passes locally (0 fails in 100 runs 16-thread, 150 runs single-CPU 24-thread); only manifests under CI scheduling.

ROOT CAUSE: FuseInodeGuard::drop evicted the table entry only when `Arc::strong_count(&self.lock) == 2`. That heuristic is timing-dependent: a concurrent acquire/try_acquire clones the entry Arc under the table lock (inflating strong_count) before becoming a holder. Concrete leak via try_acquire: a thread clones the slot Arc (count=3), its inner FuseInodeLock::try_acquire returns None (contended), and the clone is dropped WITHOUT any eviction check; if the real holder's drop observed count==3 it skipped eviction, and once both that holder and the orphan clone drop, only the table's Arc remains (count==1) with no future holder to ever evict it → permanent leak (and in production, unbounded lock-table growth on the live FUSE mount).

FIX (shipped): replace the strong_count heuristic with an explicit per-entry user count. table value is now `LockSlot { lock: Arc<FuseInodeLock>, users: usize }`. `users` is incremented under the table lock whenever acquire/try_acquire clones the slot, and decremented on guard Drop and on the try_acquire abandon path (release_slot_user); the entry is evicted exactly when users==0, entirely under the table mutex. Deterministic — no Arc::strong_count snapshot. ptr_eq guards against decrementing a newer slot. Verified: full ffs-fuse lib suite green + stress loop (no regression). An off-by-one would trip the existing "two holders of the same inode set" (premature evict) or "table must be empty" (under-evict) asserts.
close_reason: Shipped c606363b: replaced Arc::strong_count==2 eviction heuristic with explicit per-entry user count (LockSlot{lock,users}); users bumped under table lock on every clone, decremented on guard Drop + try_acquire abandon path (release_slot_user), evict at 0. Deterministic — eliminates the leak where a transient/failed-try_acquire clone inflates strong_count and the final eviction is permanently skipped. Verified: ffs-fuse lib 556/556, clippy -D warnings clean, fmt clean, stress loop 0 fails. Was an intermittent CI flake (ffs-fuse runs before ffs-harness, masking everything after it).

title: [parity] btrfs: verify data checksums on read (wire btrfs_verify_file_data_csums into the read path, EIO on mismatch)
description: FrankenFS has a complete, tested data-csum capability (btrfs_verify_file_data_csums, ffs-core) but it is UNWIRED — no production caller. So reading a real datasum btrfs whose data has rotted returns the corrupt bytes silently, whereas the kernel returns EIO. This is a parity + integrity gap for a repair-oriented reader. DESIGN (worked out by SlateRaven wake 16): (1) Gate: add OpenOptions.btrfs_verify_data_on_read (default false; thread to OpenFs like btrfs_rw_ephemeral_ok at lib.rs:841/2674) so default read behavior is unchanged (no spurious-EIO regression risk on the core read path) and it can flip to default-on after validation, mirroring the NODATASUM-write interim. (2) Read-only csum availability: btrfs_read_file's read-only branch has no alloc_state (csum_tree is only seeded when writable). Add a lazy cache on OpenFs — e.g. Mutex<Option<Arc<Vec<(BtrfsKey,Vec<u8>)>>>> — populated on first verify by walking the csum tree (btrfs_fs_tree_root_bytenr(cx, BTRFS_CSUM_TREE_OBJECTID) -> walk_btrfs_tree); writable mounts use alloc.csum_tree. (3) Hook: in btrfs_read_file, after gathering (inode, extents), when the flag is on AND the inode is datasum (!NODATASUM), verify the regular extents OVERLAPPING [offset, read_end) against the csum items (read each covering on-disk sector via btrfs_read_logical_into, lookup_data_block_csum, compare crc32c) BEFORE assembling output; return FfsError::Corruption (EIO) on first mismatch. Bound to overlapping extents (NOT whole-file) to avoid O(file^2) on chunked reads. Compressed extents ARE verified over their compressed on-disk bytes (the compression-skip was already removed in dc2e4b86). (4) Tests: flag-on clean read OK; flag-on corrupt sector -> EIO; flag-off -> no verification (returns data); NODATASUM inode -> skip; read-only + writable. Use build_btrfs_csum_image + flush_mvcc_to_device pattern. RISK: a verify bug -> spurious EIO on VALID reads (breaks the core read path), so it must be correct + thoroughly tested; the off-by-default gate contains the risk. This is a careful multi-part change warranting a focused wake, not a rushed late-wake start.
close_reason: DONE (SlateRaven wake 16, commit 57d37c73). Verify-on-read is wired: OpenOptions.btrfs_verify_data_on_read (default off) gates it; btrfs_read_file verifies the datasum-inode regular extents overlapping the read range against the csum tree (via the factored btrfs_verify_one_extent_csum helper) and returns FfsError::Corruption before returning data. Csum items: in-memory csum tree (writable) or lazily-cached on-disk walk (btrfs_csum_read_cache) for read-only. Bounded to overlapping extents (no O(file^2)); compressed extents covered. Test btrfs_verify_data_on_read_detects_corruption_bd_tkv2n (clean read OK / corrupt -> Corruption / flag-off returns data). ffs-core 918/918. REMAINING (follow-on, gated): flip the default to ON for full kernel parity (every datasum read verifies) — needs the same privileged btrfs check validation as bd-x3fcu's NODATASUM-write flip; until then it is opt-in (conservative, no read-path regression).

title: btrfs: subvolume/snapshot CREATION (write side) is unimplemented
description: Found while surveying the btrfs subvol/snapshot surface (W33 plan). FrankenFS has READ-side subvol/snapshot support: enumerate_subvolumes / enumerate_snapshots / snapshot_diff_by_generation (ffs-btrfs) + the send-stream encoders (build_subvol_command / build_snapshot_command for btrfs send/receive). But there is NO write-side create — no create_subvolume / create_snapshot in ffs-core (the BTRFS_IOC_SUBVOL_CREATE / SUBVOL_SNAPSHOT_CREATE equivalent). Creating a subvolume requires a new fs-tree ROOT_ITEM + ROOT_REF/ROOT_BACKREF + an empty tree + dir entry in the parent; a snapshot additionally shares the source tree root (refs++) COW-style. Advanced feature (big, P3) — flagged for parity completeness per the no-gaps directive. The reflink/COW + refcount machinery (bd-vh8p9/bd-xkvcm, now fuzz-covered) + btrfs_full_transaction_commit are the building blocks. NOTE: confirm whether this is intentionally out of scope before implementing.

title: ffs-core: RENAME_EXCHANGE retarget scan doesn't skip dx_root -> fails on metadata_csum htree dirs
description: ext4_rename2_exchange's retarget loops (lib.rs ~20223 src, ~20255 dst, ~20274 undo) iterate ALL directory blocks calling ffs_dir::retarget_entry, with NO dx_root skip (unlike the remove and rename paths, which compute dx_root_phys and skip logical block 0). On an htree dir the dx_root's '..' dirent has rec_len spanning past the reserved tail; on metadata_csum (reserved_tail=12) retarget_entry's limit=block_size-12 so the '..' end (block_size) > limit => Err(Corruption exceeds usable block area). The dx_root is scanned FIRST (logical 0), so RENAME_EXCHANGE of two entries in a metadata_csum htree directory fails with Corruption even though both entries exist (resolved by lookup) in leaves. Same class as bd-y8tcx but for the dx_root in the exchange path; not caught because exchange tests use small linear dirs. Also check the swap_inode_in_entry(b'..') call at ~20035 (exchange '..' fixup) for the same dx_root rejection. FIX: skip dx_root_phys in the retarget loops, mirroring ext4_unlink_impl / ext4_rename (which already skip it). Reachable: atomic swap (renameat2 RENAME_EXCHANGE) in any largish metadata_csum dir.
close_reason: Fixed: ext4_rename2_exchange retarget loops (src/dst/undo) now skip dx_root_phys (mirroring remove/rename), and ext4_prepare_dotdot_update repoints '..' in place + re-stamps the dx-root/linear CRC32C instead of a linear swap_inode_in_entry scan (which rejected an htree dx_root '..' AND left a stale checksum). RENAME_EXCHANGE on a metadata_csum htree dir no longer fails with Corruption. 14 rename2 tests pass; htree exchange E2E is mkfs+large-dir gated so fix mirrors the proven remove/rename dx_root-skip + '..'-stamp patterns.

title: Kernel-conformance pin for Ext4MmpBlock field offsets
description: Found via /testing-conformance-harnesses audit. ffs_ondisk::ext4::Ext4MmpBlock::parse_from_bytes (lib.rs:2286) hard-codes the 1024-byte MMP block layout per fs/ext4/mmp.h struct mmp_struct: magic u32@0x00, seq u32@0x04, time_lo u32@0x08, time_hi u32@0x0C, nodename [u8;64]@0x10, bdevname [u8;32]@0x50, check_interval u16@0x70, checksum u32@0x3FC. bd-jbilz (lib.rs:10625) pins the EXT4_MMP_MAGIC value (0x004D_4D50) but not the field OFFSETS — a regression that read seq from offset 0..4 instead of 4..8 would conflict with the magic check, but a regression that drifted time_lo/time_hi/nodename/bdevname offsets would silently corrupt every multi-mount-protection check on mount. title: btrfs send emits corrupt data for extents spanning a chunk boundary
description: btrfs_send (ffs-core lib.rs ~25499) reads each extent's data via a closure that does a SINGLE map_logical_to_physical(chunks, offset) then read_exact_at(mapping.physical, len). If a data extent straddles a btrfs CHUNK boundary, the physical mapping is discontiguous across the boundary, so reading len contiguous bytes from the first chunk's physical address emits WRONG bytes (from unrelated physical blocks) for the portion past the boundary -> the produced send stream contains corrupt file data = a silently-bad backup. The main read path btrfs_read_logical_into (lib.rs ~6341) handles this correctly: it loops per chunk, clamping each read to available_in_chunk (btrfs_logical_chunk_end). The send closure does not. Reachable on any image where a data extent crosses a chunk boundary (more likely on small images with small chunks; kernel-created images with straddling extents). FIX: route the send read closure through self.btrfs_read_logical_into(cx, offset, &mut buf) instead of the naive map+read_exact_at, reusing the chunk-boundary-aware (and MVCC-overlay-correct, vectored) read path. Correct by construction. Test gap: a failing-before test needs a multi-chunk image with a straddling extent (heavy fixture); fix verified by reuse of the proven read path + normal-send regression coverage.
close_reason: done

comments.text:
MEASURED 2026-08-15 (AzureBay), found while committing bd-3ao0l.

AGENTS.md requires `cargo fmt --check` before claiming done. It is RED on main and has been for a
while: running the pinned rustfmt (nightly-2026-07-20, --edition 2024) over every tracked .rs file
gives 86 dirty of 512.

Only SIX are under src/, and those are the ones worth fixing first because they are shipped code:
  crates/ffs-btree/src/lib.rs
  crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs

  crates/ffs-ondisk/src/lib.rs

The other 80 are benches and test files.

HOW IT WAS FOUND, which is the part that generalises: my bd-3ao0l commit to
crates/ffs-ondisk/src/btrfs.rs showed 24 changed lines for what was a ONE-LINE fix, because I ran
rustfmt over the whole file and it reformatted unrelated pre-existing regions. Confirmed after the
fact that the file was already fmt-dirty at HEAD~1. That is the mechanism by which this stays
invisible: nobody sees it until they format a file they touched, and then it looks like their diff.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS: with fmt red AND clippy red (bd-3ao0l and its cascade), TWO of the
three gates AGENTS.md mandates cannot pass on a clean checkout. That is almost certainly how the
clippy debt accumulated in the first place — a gate nobody can run green is a gate nobody runs, and
then everything downstream of it rots quietly.

DO NOT FIX THIS WITH A SINGLE `cargo fmt` OVER THE REPO. A dozen agents share this working tree;
an 86-file reformat would collide with everyone's in-flight edits and produce exactly the kind of
mass-diff that AGENTS.md's bulk-revert incident warns about. Suggested approach instead:
  1. The six src/ files, one commit each or one commit total, coordinated via a file reservation,
     announced in Agent Mail first so nobody is mid-edit.
  2. The 80 bench/test files opportunistically: format a file when you already have it reserved for
     other work, which is how btrfs.rs got fixed here.
  3. Only once the count reaches zero, consider a pre-commit hook that runs `cargo fmt --check` on
     STAGED files, so it cannot regress. Do not add that hook while 86 files are dirty; it would
     block every commit in the repo.

Note the count is against the PINNED toolchain's rustfmt. Do not re-measure with a floating
`rustfmt` from PATH — rust-toolchain.toml pins nightly-2026-07-20 precisely because a floating
channel produced different results mid-build.
