comments.text: REVERTED (reject — perf wash, not a robust Score>=2.0 win). The lever (search_leaf_raw: raw one-pass leaf scan replacing parse_leaf_entries Vec materialization for depth-1 point lookups) is isomorphic — I verified search_leaf_raw matches parse_leaf_entries+search_leaf exactly (same zero-length+sort/overlap validation order and messages, same Found/Hole/offset, byte layout matches), confirmed by the cross-check test + 146 ffs-btree/141 ffs-extent tests. But the same-binary A/B (extent_single_block_leaf_search_ab) is a LAYOUT-DOMINATED WASH across 7 runs: raw faster in 3 (only the original worker run had non-overlapping CIs at 1.22x), SLOWER in 4 (3 with non-overlapping CIs). Direction flips run-to-run with non-overlapping CIs in BOTH directions = sub-noise / not a real algorithmic difference (same class as bd-xmh5g.17/.20). The commit recorded Score=2.7 from a SINGLE optimistic A/B run (old 1.164us vs raw 950ns); the fuller 7-run picture leans slightly slower. Per the bead keep gate (Score>=2.0) and the wash->simpler-code-wins principle, reverted e957918c to restore the simpler parse_leaf_entries+search_leaf path (removes 196 lines of duplicated parse/validation). #![forbid(unsafe_code)] intact.

title: test(ffs-btrfs): proptest alloc_data/free_extent restores block-group used_bytes for any size
description: Cross-review of free_extent confirmed it decrements the owning block group used_bytes immediately and the existing tests show alloc then free restores used_bytes to 0 — but only for fixed sizes (4096, 8192). A size-dependent asymmetry (e.g. alloc rounding num_bytes one way and free accounting another) would not be caught. Add proptest_alloc_free_restores_block_group_used_bytes: for size in 1..=0x8000, alloc_data then free_extent the returned extent and assert used_bytes returns to its pre-alloc value (and that alloc consumed space). Pure, no mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): proptest_alloc_free_restores_block_group_used_bytes (ffs-btrfs:15337). cargo test: ok.

title: test(ffs-ondisk): differential proptest for map_logical_to_physical binary-search path
description: map_logical_to_physical uses a binary-search fast path when chunks.len() > CHUNK_MAP_BINARY_SEARCH_THRESHOLD (16), else a linear scan. Every existing test (unit + the single_chunk proptest) uses <= 2 chunks, so the partition_point fast path (bd-6u6xb) is NEVER exercised — a pp/pp-1 off-by-one or <=/< boundary error there would only surface on real filesystems with >16 chunks. Add btrfs_proptest_map_logical_to_physical_binary_path_matches_linear: build 17..=24 disjoint sorted Single chunks (forcing the binary path) and assert the result equals an independent linear-scan reference for arbitrary logical addresses (hits, gaps, and out-of-range). Pure, no mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc/BlackThrush): btrfs_proptest_map_logical_to_physical_binary_path_matches_linear (btrfs.rs:4655) matches spec — 17..=24 disjoint sorted Single chunks force the partition_point binary path (>16 threshold), differential vs independent linear-scan reference over hits/gaps/out-of-range. cargo test -p ffs-ondisk: 2 passed.

title: test(ffs-ondisk): differential proptest for map_logical_to_stripes binary-search path
description: map_logical_to_stripes (the multi-device stripe dual of map_logical_to_physical) has the same binary-search fast path when chunks.len() > CHUNK_MAP_BINARY_SEARCH_THRESHOLD (16). Its tests use small or permuted chunk lists (<16), so the partition_point selection (bd-6tygu/bd-6u6xb) is never exercised; a selection off-by-one would only surface with >16 chunks. Add btrfs_proptest_map_logical_to_stripes_binary_path_matches_linear: build 17..=24 disjoint ascending chunks (forcing the binary path) and assert the result equals a linear scan calling the shared chunk_stripes resolver, isolating the selection logic across hits/gaps/out-of-range. Sibling of bd-xmh5g.251. Pure, no mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc/BlackThrush): btrfs_proptest_map_logical_to_stripes_binary_path_matches_linear (btrfs.rs:4709) matches spec — stripe dual, 17..=24 chunks force binary path, differential vs linear scan via shared chunk_stripes resolver. cargo test -p ffs-ondisk: 2 passed.

title: test(ffs-btrfs): lookup_data_block_csum skips an interleaved non-csum item during walk-back
description: lookup_data_block_csum binary-searches to the suffix of items with key.offset<=disk_bytenr then walks back in reverse, skipping non-EXTENT_CSUM items (continue at 416-418) to find the covering csum item. The existing split-items test covers multi-item hits, before/after/unaligned misses, and a pure-non-csum list, but never an EXTENT_CSUM item shadowed in the walk-back by a higher-offset non-csum item — the exact case the skip handles. A regression returning the non-csum item would extract a bogus csum from its value. Add lookup_data_block_csum_skips_interleaved_non_csum_item: a 2-sector csum item at base plus an INODE_ITEM at base+sectorsize, look up sector 1 and assert the real crc is returned (skip honored). Pure, no mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): lookup_data_block_csum_skips_interleaved_non_csum_item (ffs-btrfs:8847). cargo test: ok.

title: test(ffs-btrfs): roundtrip+tamper proptest for verify_extent_csum across sector counts
description: verify_extent_csum checks each data sector's crc32c against the stored csums and reports the first mismatching sector. Its unit tests use fixed 2-sector examples (accept, one corruption at index 1, bad-args). There is no property test, so correct verification and first-mismatch reporting across varying sector counts and corruption positions is unpinned. Add proptest_verify_extent_csum_roundtrip_and_tamper: build 1..=8 sectors of deterministic data, assert the correct csums verify, then corrupt one sector and assert the mismatch is reported at exactly that sector index. Pure, no mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): proptest_verify_extent_csum_roundtrip_and_tamper (ffs-btrfs:8713). cargo test: ok.

title: test(ffs-btrfs): proptest build_extent_csum_items then lookup recovers every sector csum
description: build_extent_csum_items packs per-sector crc32c into EXTENT_CSUM items (optionally split across multiple items), and lookup_data_block_csum recovers a sector's csum. The existing test covers one fixed config (5 sectors, split 2, base 0x80000). Add proptest_build_csum_items_then_lookup_each_sector: for 1..=12 sectors, split 1..=4, varying sector-aligned base and random data, build the items and assert lookup returns the correct crc32c for every sector and a miss just past the run. Pins the csum-tree build/lookup roundtrip across item-boundary layouts. Pure, no mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): proptest_build_csum_items_then_lookup_each_sector (ffs-btrfs:8761). cargo test: ok.

title: test(ffs-ondisk): pin timestamp_full nsec extraction and epochs 2/3
description: timestamp_full reconstructs an ext4 timestamp as (base as i32 sign-extended) + (epoch<<32) seconds and (extra>>2) nanoseconds. timestamp_sign_extension covers only epoch 0 and 1 with nsec=0, so the nanosecond extraction (high 30 bits of *_extra) and epoch bits 2/3 are untested. A regression swapping the nsec/epoch bit split or widening the epoch mask would corrupt decoded timestamps. Add timestamp_full_decodes_nsec_and_high_epochs: parse inodes with nonzero nsec, epoch 2, epoch 3, and a combined negative-base+epoch3+nsec case, asserting atime_full's exact (seconds, nanoseconds). Pure, no mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): ext4_proptest_extra_nsec_and_epoch_are_disjoint (ffs-ondisk:20771). cargo test: ok.

title: test(ffs-ondisk): pin is_fast_symlink size boundary, extents, and non-symlink conditions
description: is_fast_symlink is true only when is_symlink && !uses_extents && size <= EXT4_FAST_SYMLINK_MAX (60). The existing fast-symlink tests use one short (9-byte) non-extent symlink, so the size boundary (60 fast vs 61 slow), the uses_extents exclusion, and the non-symlink case are untested. A regression in any condition (off-by-one boundary, missing extents check) would mis-route symlink target reads (inline vs block). Add is_fast_symlink_respects_size_boundary_and_conditions building inodes via the public struct: assert size 60 fast / 61 slow, a small extents-flagged symlink is not fast, a regular file is not fast, and fast_symlink_target follows. Pure, no mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): is_fast_symlink_respects_size_boundary_and_conditions (ffs-ondisk:13406). cargo test: ok.

title: test(ffs-ondisk): pin dir_logical_block_count ceil boundaries and u32-overflow rejection
description: dir_logical_block_count computes file_size.div_ceil(block_size) and rejects a count exceeding u32 with IntegerConversion, preventing a silently-truncated directory block count for a corrupt oversized directory size. It is only exercised via the dir-read integration path with small valid sizes, so the ceil boundaries (0, exact multiple, one over) and the overflow rejection are untested. Add dir_logical_block_count_boundaries_and_overflow asserting 0/1/exact/+1 and that u64::MAX with block_size 1 is rejected. Pure, no mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): dir_logical_block_count_boundaries_and_overflow (ffs-ondisk:13455). cargo test: ok.

title: test(ffs-core): pin inode_to_attr HUGE_FILE st_blocks scaling
description: inode_to_attr computes InodeAttr.blocks (st_blocks, 512-byte sectors). For a normal inode i_blocks is already in 512-byte units and passes through; for a HUGE_FILE inode i_blocks is in filesystem blocks and must be scaled by block_size/512. The existing inode_to_attr tests only cover rdev/kind/perm with non-huge inodes, so the HUGE_FILE scaling is untested. A regression (missing or wrong multiply) would report wrong st_blocks to stat/du/df for large files. Add inode_to_attr_huge_file_scales_blocks_to_512_sectors: assert blocks pass through without the flag and are scaled by block_size/512 (8 fs-blocks -> 64 sectors at 4K) with it. Pure, no mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): inode_to_attr_huge_file_scales_blocks_to_512_sectors (ffs-core:36544). cargo test: ok.

title: [perf][no-gaps] O(1) ARC queue metadata
description: Profile-backed target from rch Criterion on 2026-06-03 (vmi1149989): block_cache_arc_mixed_seq70_hot30 mean 20.893 ms [18.898,22.960], database_like 18.073 ms [17.295,18.594], zipf 13.466 ms [12.571,14.251]. Code path uses VecDeque queues plus linear remove_from_list on hit promotion and eviction selection. Single lever: replace ARC metadata queues with a safe O(1) ordered set while preserving front/back eviction order, ghost lists, metrics, hit/miss semantics, and dirty-block non-eviction. Keep only with same-binary A/B, golden sha256, focused ffs-block tests/check/clippy/fmt, and Score >= 2.0.
close_reason: Rejected: O(1) safe linked ARC queue did not clear Score>=2.0. Same-worker rch vmi1149989 baseline vs after: mixed_seq70_hot30 20.893 ms -> 22.271 ms regression on the primary slowest row; zipf 13.466 ms -> 14.078 ms slight regression; database_like 18.073 ms -> 15.996 ms improvement. Production src restored to HEAD; no code kept. Trigger: move to a deeper algorithmic/cache-policy or workload-structure lever rather than repeating queue micro-structure.

title: test(ffs-ondisk): pin permission_bits preserves setuid/setgid/sticky
description: permission_bits returns mode & 0o7777, which includes the setuid (0o4000), setgid (0o2000), and sticky (0o1000) bits in addition to the 0o777 permissions. Every existing test uses plain perms (0o755/0o644/0o700), so the special-bit preservation is untested. A regression narrowing the mask to 0o777 would silently strip the setuid bit off setuid binaries - a real security regression - while still passing all current tests. Add permission_bits_preserves_setuid_setgid_sticky: assert 0o4755/0o2755/0o1777/0o7777 survive and that the S_IFMT file-type bits are excluded. Pure, no mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): permission_bits_preserves_setuid_setgid_sticky (ffs-ondisk:17397). cargo test: ok.

title: test(ffs-core): pin inode_file_type Symlink/Fifo/Socket and unknown fallback arms
description: inode_file_type maps inode mode to the VFS FileType via an 8-arm if/else (regular/dir/symlink/blkdev/chrdev/fifo/socket, else RegularFile fallback). The attr.kind tests cover only Directory/BlockDevice/CharDevice/RegularFile; Symlink, Fifo, Socket, and the unknown-type fallback are untested (the Fifo/Socket asserts elsewhere are for dir_entry_file_type, a different function). A regression in those arms would mis-report file types to readdir/getattr. Add inode_file_type_maps_symlink_fifo_socket_and_unknown: assert S_IFLNK->Symlink, S_IFIFO->Fifo, S_IFSOCK->Socket, and an undefined S_IFMT (0o030000) -> RegularFile. Pure, no mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): inode_file_type_maps_symlink_fifo_socket_and_unknown (ffs-core:36580). cargo test: ok.

title: test(ffs-core): pin ext4_flags_to_xflags exact per-flag projection
description: ext4_flags_to_xflags projects ext4 i_flags onto the fsx_xflags namespace (lsattr/FS_IOC_FSGETXATTR): IMMUTABLE/APPEND/SYNC/NOATIME/NODUMP/PROJINHERIT each map to their FS_XFLAG_* bit, and HASATTR is set iff any bit is set. The integration test only presence-checks IMMUTABLE/APPEND/SYNC (& != 0), so NOATIME/NODUMP/PROJINHERIT exact projection, the empty (no HASATTR) case, and the no-extra-bits guarantee are untested. A regression mis-projecting a flag or leaking an extra xflag would show wrong attributes to lsattr. Add ext4_flags_to_xflags_projects_each_flag_exactly with exact equality per flag, the all-flags combination, empty->0, and an unmapped flag (EXTENTS)->0. Pure, no mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): ext4_flags_to_xflags_projects_each_flag_exactly (ffs-core:36625). cargo test: ok.

title: test(ffs-core): pin xflags_to_ext4_flags EINVAL/EOPNOTSUPP/preserve/clear
description: xflags_to_ext4_flags is the chattr write-path projection of fsx_xflags onto ext4 i_flags. It rejects the output-only HASATTR bit with EINVAL, rejects unsupported xflags (e.g. NODEFRAG) with EOPNOTSUPP, preserves non-user-settable current flags (EXTENTS etc.) and clears user-settable flags absent from the new xflags. Integration tests cover EOPNOTSUPP/clearing/round-trip but the EINVAL-on-HASATTR guard and the critical current-flags preservation (clobbering EXTENTS_FL would make the extent tree uninterpretable) are not directly pinned. Add xflags_to_ext4_flags_validates_preserves_and_clears: assert HASATTR->EINVAL, NODEFRAG->EOPNOTSUPP, EXTENTS preserved when setting IMMUTABLE, and APPEND cleared while EXTENTS kept. Pure, no mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): xflags_to_ext4_flags_validates_preserves_and_clears (ffs-core:36684). cargo test: ok.

title: test(ffs-core): pin btrfs write enforcement of immutable/append-only (EPERM)
description: btrfs_write rejects writes to an immutable inode (EPERM) and rejects non-EOF writes to an append-only inode (EPERM), matching ext4_write and the kernel (bd-xpsq4). ext4 has immutable_and_append_attributes_enforced_on_writes coverage and btrfs has link/setxattr/rename enforcement tests, but the btrfs WRITE path enforcement is the untested missed sibling — a regression would allow content mutation of an immutable btrfs file (security). Add btrfs_write_to_immutable_or_append_only_is_eperm: set BTRFS_INODE_IMMUTABLE and assert a write is EPERM; set BTRFS_INODE_APPEND and assert a non-EOF write is EPERM while an EOF append succeeds. Mirrors the existing btrfs_setxattr enforcement test setup. No mocks.
close_reason: duplicate of pre-existing btrfs_immutable_and_append_enforced_on_content_ops_bd_xpsq4; removed redundant test

title: test(ffs-core): pin btrfs_dir_type_to_file_type all type codes incl unknown fallback
description: btrfs_dir_type_to_file_type maps a btrfs DIR_INDEX file_type byte to a VFS FileType (readdir). btrfs_readdir_mixed_types covers only REG_FILE/DIR/SYMLINK, so the BLKDEV/CHRDEV/FIFO/SOCK arms and the unknown-code RegularFile fallback are untested (the btrfs CharDevice whiteout test uses btrfs_mode_to_file_type, a different function). A regression would mis-report device/fifo/socket types in btrfs readdir. Add btrfs_dir_type_to_file_type_maps_all_codes: assert each BTRFS_FT_* code maps to its FileType and that 0 and 0xFF fall back to RegularFile. Pure, no mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): btrfs_dir_type_to_file_type_maps_all_codes (ffs-core). cargo test: ok.

title: test(ffs-core): pin ext4_read_buffer_len EOF-clamping boundaries
description: ext4_read_buffer_len clamps a read to EOF: returns 0 when offset>=file_size or requested==0, else min(file_size-offset, requested). It has no direct test - only integration read tests (read_file_data_past_eof, oversized_eof_request) exercise it, covering past-EOF but not the exact spanning-EOF clamp, exactly-to-EOF, zero-request, or empty-file boundaries. An over-read bug here would expose stale bytes past EOF. Add ext4_read_buffer_len_clamps_to_eof asserting within-file=full, exactly-to-EOF=full, spanning=remaining, at/past-EOF=0, zero-request=0, empty-file=0. Pure, no mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): ext4_read_buffer_len_clamps_to_eof (ffs-core:43444). cargo test: ok.

title: test(ffs-core): pin ext4_max_file_size block-size scaling and EFBIG boundary
description: ext4_max_file_size(block_size) = (1<<32) * block_size (the extent tree addresses 2^32 logical blocks), and ext4_reject_oversized_file returns EFBIG above it. The integration EFBIG tests use a single block size and a value clearly past the max, so the block-size scaling (4TiB/8TiB/16TiB for 1K/2K/4K) and the exact boundary (end==max allowed, max+1 EFBIG) are not directly pinned. A scaling regression (wrong shift or dropped block_size multiply) would mis-set the limit. Add ext4_max_file_size_scales_with_block_size_and_rejects_above asserting the max for 1K/2K/4K and that end==max is Ok while max+1 is EFBIG. Pure, no mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): ext4_max_file_size_scales_with_block_size_and_rejects_above (ffs-core). cargo test: ok.

title: test(ffs-core): pin btrfs_align_up/down boundaries and align_up overflow
description: btrfs_align_up rounds a value up to an alignment (passing already-aligned values through) and rejects rounding past u64::MAX with InvalidGeometry; btrfs_align_down rounds down. Neither has a direct test - they are only exercised via fallocate/extent alignment integration, and the align_up overflow branch (aligned offset overflow) appears only at the source. A mis-alignment or missing overflow guard would corrupt extent/block placement. Add btrfs_align_up_and_down_boundaries: align_up already-aligned/round-up/zero/overflow and align_down already-aligned/round-down/zero. Pure, no mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): btrfs_align_up_and_down_boundaries (ffs-core). cargo test: ok.

title: test(ffs-core): pin btrfs_checked_physical_offset/span overflow guards
description: btrfs_checked_physical_offset(base,pos) returns base+pos and rejects a u64 overflow with Corruption; btrfs_checked_physical_span(base,len) is a no-op for len 0 and otherwise checks base+(len-1). Neither has a direct test and the overflow detail string (btrfs physical address overflow) appears only at the source, so the overflow guards are untested (siblings of the ffs-extent validate_physical_span tests). A regression would let a btrfs physical address wrap u64 and map to a bogus device offset. Add btrfs_checked_physical_offset_and_span_reject_overflow: normal add, u64::MAX overflow rejection, span zero-len ok, span normal ok, span overflow rejection. Pure, no mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): btrfs_checked_physical_offset_and_span_reject_overflow (ffs-core). cargo test: ok.

title: [perf][no-gaps] make S3-FIFO the default block cache policy
description: Profile-backed algorithmic target from same-worker rch Criterion on 2026-06-03 (vmi1149989). Current default ARC rows: zipf 13.466 ms [12.571,14.251], mixed_seq70_hot30 20.893 ms [18.898,22.960], database_like 18.073 ms [17.295,18.594]. Existing feature-gated S3-FIFO rows on the same worker: zipf 10.168 ms [9.4517,10.721], mixed_seq70_hot30 17.405 ms [15.952,18.284], database_like 12.029 ms [11.463,12.916]. Alien primitive: alien_cs_graveyard §15.1 S3-FIFO, three FIFO queues plus ghost admission, no per-access ARC list manipulation. Single lever: enable ffs-block's existing s3fifo implementation by default. Preserve BlockDevice API, dirty non-eviction, write-back flush durability, output behavior, ordering/tie-breaking for block payloads, FP/RNG N/A. Proof: crate-scoped rch check/test/clippy under default features, default-feature Criterion after rows, golden sha256 manifests unchanged. Keep only if Score>=2.0.
close_reason: Completed: default ffs-block cache policy switched from ARC to S3-FIFO. Same-worker rch Criterion means on vmi1149989: ARC default baseline zipf 13.466 ms, mixed_seq70_hot30 20.893 ms, database_like 18.073 ms; S3-FIFO default after zipf 8.8841 ms, mixed_seq70_hot30 16.580 ms, database_like 10.883 ms. Score 4.5 = impact 3 x confidence 3 / effort 2. Isomorphism: BlockDevice payload ordering/tie-breaking unchanged; FP/RNG N/A; deterministic benchmark seed unchanged; golden sha256 manifests unchanged. rch check/test/clippy passed.

title: test(ffs-core): pin ext4/btrfs nlink-delta overflow and underflow guards
description: ext4_checked_links_count_delta (u16) and btrfs_checked_nlink_delta (u32) adjust an inode link count by a signed delta and reject overflow (too many hardlinks) and underflow (a link-removal below zero) with Corruption. Both are heavily used by link/remove/mkdir/rmdir but have no direct test, and the over/underflow branches are only reachable at extreme nlink values integration tests never produce. An unguarded underflow would wrap nlink to a huge value and leak the inode; an unguarded overflow would wrap to a small value and free a still-linked inode. Add nlink_delta_guards_reject_overflow_and_underflow covering normal +/-/0, overflow at u16::MAX/u32::MAX, and underflow from 0 and below, for both fs. No mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): nlink_delta_guards_reject_overflow_and_underflow (ffs-core:57018). cargo test: ok.

title: test(ffs-core): pin ext4_checked_inode_blocks_delta accounting bounds
description: ext4_checked_inode_blocks_delta adjusts i_blocks (512-byte sectors) by a signed i128 delta and rejects overflow, underflow, and a delta that does not fit u64 with Corruption. It is used by 24 call sites across write/truncate/fallocate but has no direct test, and the bounds are only reachable at extreme values integration tests never produce. An unguarded underflow (releasing more sectors than the inode holds) would wrap i_blocks to a huge value, corrupting du/df reporting and quota accounting. Add ext4_checked_inode_blocks_delta_bounds: normal +/-/0, overflow at u64::MAX, underflow from 0 and below, and a delta exceeding u64. Pure, no mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): ext4_checked_inode_blocks_delta_bounds (ffs-core). cargo test: ok.

title: test(ffs-core): pin btrfs nbytes-delta apply/accumulate over/underflow guards
description: btrfs_apply_nbytes_delta applies a signed i128 delta to an inode's nbytes (u64), rejecting positive-overflow, underflow, a delta whose magnitude exceeds u64, and the i128::MIN negate edge with InvalidGeometry; btrfs_accumulate_nbytes_delta sums deltas rejecting i128 overflow. Neither has a direct test and the bounds are only reachable at extreme values integration tests never produce. An unguarded underflow (releasing more bytes than the inode holds) would wrap nbytes to a huge value, corrupting du/df. The btrfs sibling of the ext4 i_blocks guard. Add btrfs_nbytes_delta_guards_reject_overflow_and_underflow covering apply normal/overflow/underflow/exceeds-u64/i128::MIN and accumulate normal/overflow. Pure, no mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): btrfs_nbytes_delta_guards_reject_overflow_and_underflow (ffs-core:57072). cargo test: ok.

title: test(ffs-core): pin btrfs_checked_chunk_available and logical_advance guards
description: btrfs_checked_chunk_available(chunk_end, logical) returns the bytes from logical to chunk_end, rejecting a logical bytenr past the chunk end (would map to the wrong chunk) and a logical bytenr exactly at chunk_end (no bytes) with Corruption; btrfs_checked_logical_advance(logical, amount) returns logical+amount rejecting u64 overflow. Neither has a direct test. A chunk-availability bug would resolve a logical address against the wrong chunk's stripes. Completes the standalone btrfs_checked_* address-guard family (after the physical offset/span tests). Add btrfs_checked_chunk_available_and_logical_advance_guards: chunk available/past-end/at-end and advance normal/overflow. Pure, no mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): btrfs_checked_chunk_available_and_logical_advance_guards (ffs-core). cargo test: ok.

title: test(ffs-repair): pin config_supports_global_repair GF(256) and divisibility conditions
description: config_supports_global_repair gates repair_global on a valid LRC config: data_blocks>0, local_group_size>0, data_blocks divisible by local_group_size, global_parity_count<=255, and (no global parity OR data_blocks<=255) for the GF(256) global encoding. It mirrors LrcConfig::new's asserts but is the defensive re-check for configs built via the public fields. It has no direct test. A regression dropping the data_blocks<=255-with-global-parity check would let global repair encode more than 255 symbols, which GF(256) cannot represent, producing broken recovery. Add config_supports_global_repair_enforces_gf256_and_divisibility: valid config true; zero data/group, non-divisible, >255 global parity, and >255 data with global parity all false; >255 data WITHOUT global parity true. Pure, no mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): config_supports_global_repair_enforces_gf256_and_divisibility (ffs-repair:947). cargo test: ok.

title: test(ffs-repair): pin validate_repair_symbol_lengths wrong-length rejection
description: validate_repair_symbol_lengths refuses to decode a group when any repair symbol payload length differs from the device block_size (RepairFailed), preventing a malformed symbol from corrupting the erasure decode. It has no direct test and no malformed-symbol rejection test exists; integration decode tests only pass correctly-sized symbols. A regression would feed a wrong-length symbol into the GF decode, producing garbage recovery or a panic. Add validate_repair_symbol_lengths_rejects_wrong_length: all-matching and empty return Ok, a symbol shorter than block_size returns RepairFailed. Pure, no mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): validate_repair_symbol_lengths_rejects_wrong_length (ffs-repair:1838). cargo test: ok.

title: fix(ffs-core): btrfs_inode_to_attr panics on a corrupt out-of-range inode timestamp
description: btrfs_inode_to_attr builds the atime/mtime/ctime/crtime SystemTimes with UNIX_EPOCH + Duration::new(secs, nsec). The seconds (u64) and nsec (u32) are parsed unvalidated from the on-disk btrfs inode item (read_u64 at offset 112; the parser accepts atime_sec=u64::MAX). SystemTime's Add operator panics when the result is unrepresentable, and Duration::new panics if a >=1e9 nsec carry would overflow the seconds, so a getattr/readdir/lookup on an inode with an out-of-range timestamp panics (DoS on a malformed image). ext4_inode.to_system_time already fails soft via checked_add. Fix: add btrfs_inode_timestamp(secs, nsec) that clamps nsec to a valid sub-second range and uses UNIX_EPOCH.checked_add, saturating at UNIX_EPOCH on overflow; route all four timestamp fields through it. Add a regression that an inode with atime_sec=u64::MAX yields an attr without panicking.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): btrfs_inode_timestamp saturates at UNIX_EPOCH (no panic) + test btrfs_inode_to_attr_saturates_out_of_range_timestamp_without_panic (ffs-core:75694). cargo test: ok.

title: test(ffs-core): pin btrfs sparse-hole read returns zeros
description: btrfs_read_file pre-zeroes holes: a file region with no backing extent (disk_bytenr==0 or unmapped) must read as zeros. The ext4 sparse read is tested (write_sparse_hole_reads_as_zeros) but the btrfs equivalent is not - all existing btrfs write tests write at offset 0 (contiguous). A regression would surface a hole as uninitialized/wrong data. Add btrfs_write_sparse_hole_reads_as_zeros: create a file, write at offset 8192 leaving [0,8192) a hole, then read the hole (full 8192 bytes, all zero) and the written tail (DATA). No new mocks (open_writable_btrfs).

title: test(ffs-core): pin btrfs setattr-extend sparse region reads zeros
description: Extending a btrfs file via setattr (truncate up to a larger size) creates a sparse region beyond the original data that must read as zeros, not stale or uninitialized bytes. The ext4 equivalent is tested (write_setattr_extend_sparse_reads_zeros); the btrfs sibling is not. This is a distinct path from bd-xmh5g.324 (which extends via a write past a gap): here the extension comes from a size-only setattr. A regression would leak stale data or surface garbage in the extension. Add btrfs_setattr_extend_sparse_reads_zeros: write HEAD, setattr size=8192, assert getattr size, head intact, and the extension reads as zeros. No new mocks (open_writable_btrfs).
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): btrfs_setattr_extend_sparse_reads_zeros (lib.rs:75750) pins the size-only-setattr extension path exactly as specified — open_writable_btrfs, write "HEAD" at 0, setattr size=8192, then getattr.size==8192, read[0,4)=="HEAD" (head intact), read[4,104) all-zero (sparse extension reads zeros, no stale data). Distinct from bd-xmh5g.324 (write-past-gap extension). Guards the btrfs sparse read zero-fill (relevant to the read-into-dst out.fill(0) path). cargo test -p ffs-core green.

title: test(ffs-core): pin btrfs truncate-then-reextend does not leak stale data
description: Truncating a btrfs file down then re-extending it (writing past a gap) must zero-fill the gap, not resurface the bytes that were truncated away - a data-confidentiality invariant. The ext4 version is tested (write_truncate_then_sparse_extend_zero_fills_gap_ext4); the btrfs sibling is not. Unlike bd-xmh5g.324/.325 (gaps that never held data), here the gap previously contained file data, so a regression that fails to drop the truncated extent would leak stale contents. Add btrfs_truncate_then_sparse_extend_zero_fills_gap: write 'hello world!', truncate to 5, write 'Z' at offset 10, then assert the [5,10) gap reads zeros (not ' worl'). No new mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): btrfs_truncate_then_sparse_extend_zero_fills_gap pins the data-confidentiality invariant — write 'hello world!', truncate to 5 (drops ' world!'), write 'Z' at offset 10, then the [5,10) gap reads ZEROS (not the stale ' worl' bytes that were truncated away). Distinct from .324/.325 (gaps that never held data); here the gap PREVIOUSLY held file data, so it catches a failure to drop the truncated extent. cargo test -p ffs-core green.

title: test(ffs-core): pin btrfs hardlink shares inode data
description: A btrfs hardlink is a second name for the same inode (objectid), so a write through one name is visible through the other and both resolve to the same inode number. The ext4 equivalent is tested (write_link_shares_data); the btrfs link tests only cover link-count churn and btrfs-check structure, not lookup-resolves-to-same-inode plus data sharing. A regression putting the wrong objectid in the new directory entry would make the link resolve to a different inode (silent data divergence). Add btrfs_hardlink_shares_inode_data: create+write, link, update via the original, then lookup the link (assert same ino) and read via it (sees the update). No new mocks.

Catches a regression putting the wrong objectid in the new dir entry (silent data divergence). cargo test -p ffs-core green.

title: test(ffs-core): pin btrfs rename overwrites existing target with source data
description: A POSIX rename onto an existing target replaces it: the target name resolves to the SOURCE inode and holds the source data, the source name is gone, and the old target inode is detached. btrfs_write_rename only covers renaming to a fresh (nonexistent) name; the overwrite-existing-target path is untested for btrfs (ext4 has rename2_classic_flag_zero_overwrites_target). A regression would leave the target with its old data, point it at the wrong inode, or fail to remove the source. Add btrfs_rename_overwrites_existing_target: create src(SOURCE) and dst(TARGET) as distinct inodes, rename src onto dst, then assert src is gone, dst resolves to the source inode, and reads back SOURCE. No new mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): btrfs_rename_overwrites_existing_target (lib.rs:75657) pins rename-overwrite — renaming src onto an existing target replaces the target's data with the source's (target dir entry now points to src inode/data). cargo test -p ffs-core green.

title: test(ffs-core): pin btrfs removing one hardlink keeps data via the other
description: Removing one of two hard-link names for a btrfs file must decrement the link count without freeing the inode; the surviving name keeps the inode and its data. btrfs_hardlink_churn only checks btrfs-check structure after a name removal, not that the data is still readable through the remaining name. A regression that freed the inode on the first name removal would lose data for the surviving link. Add btrfs_removing_one_hardlink_keeps_data_for_other: create+write, link a second name, remove the first name, then assert the first lookup fails, the second resolves to the same inode, and reads back the original data. No new mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): btrfs_removing_one_hardlink_keeps_data_for_other (lib.rs:75567) pins that unlinking one of two hardlinks keeps the inode + data reachable via the surviving name (nlink decremented, data intact, not reclaimed while a link remains). cargo test -p ffs-core green.

title: test(ffs-core): pin btrfs delete reclaims data blocks
description: Removing a btrfs file's last name must return its data blocks to the free pool (statfs blocks_free recovers). Existing btrfs statfs tests cover fallocate accounting but not reclamation on delete. A regression that failed to free the inode's extents on the final name removal would leak blocks and march the filesystem toward spurious ENOSPC. Add btrfs_delete_reclaims_data_blocks: record blocks_free, create+write a 128 KiB file (free drops), remove the file, and assert blocks_free recovers above the post-write level. Directional asserts avoid exact-count fragility. No new mocks.

title: test(ffs-core): pin ext4 delete reclaims data blocks
description: Removing an ext4 file's last name must return its data blocks to the free pool: the block bitmap is cleared and the group descriptor free count incremented, so statfs blocks_free recovers. Existing ext4 statfs tests cover the group-descriptor aggregation but not reclamation on delete. This is the ext4 sibling of bd-xmh5g.330 (btrfs); a regression failing to free the inode's blocks on the final name removal leaks blocks toward spurious ENOSPC. Add ext4_delete_reclaims_data_blocks: record blocks_free, create+write a 128 KiB file (free drops), remove it, and assert blocks_free recovers. Directional asserts. No new mocks (open_writable_ext4).

This is the ext4 sibling of bd-xmh5g.329 (btrfs). A regression that freed the inode on the first name removal would lose data for the surviving link. Add ext4_removing_one_hardlink_keeps_data_for_other: create+write, link a second name, remove the first, then assert the first lookup fails, the second resolves to the same inode, and reads back the original data. No new mocks (open_writable_ext4).

title: test(ffs-core): pin btrfs reflink write-independence at the data level
description: After reflinking src into dst (shared extent, refcount 2), writing to dst must copy-on-write the touched block, leaving src's data byte-for-byte unchanged; dst must reflect the overwrite only where written. btrfs_overwrite_shared_extent_passes_btrfs_check_bd_xkvcm verifies the refcount STRUCTURE passes btrfs check after such an overwrite but never reads src/dst back to confirm data independence. A regression mutating the shared extent in place would corrupt src silently while still passing the structural check. Add btrfs_write_to_reflink_does_not_disturb_source_data: fill src (3 blocks of 0xA5), clone into dst, overwrite dst's middle block with 0x5A, then assert src reads all 0xA5 and dst reads 0xA5/0x5A/0xA5. No new mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): btrfs_write_to_reflink_does_not_disturb_source_data (lib.rs:66257) pins reflink COW write-independence at the DATA level — fill src (3 blocks 0xA5), clone into dst (shared extent), overwrite dst middle block with 0x5A, then src reads all-0xA5 (unchanged) and dst reads 0xA5/0x5A/0xA5 (COW only the touched block). Catches an in-place mutation of the shared extent that would silently corrupt src while still passing the structural btrfs-check (bd_xkvcm). cargo test -p ffs-core green.

title: test(ffs-core): pin btrfs truncating reflink source preserves clone data
description: After reflinking src into dst (shared extent, refcount 2), truncating src to zero must drop only src's reference (refcount 2 -> 1) and keep the shared extent alive for dst; dst must still read its full original data. The existing shared-extent truncate tests verify btrfs-check structure but never read the clone back to confirm its data survived. This is the refcount-aware-FREE complement of bd-xmh5g.333 (which covered COW-on-write). A regression doing a non-refcount-aware free would release the still-referenced extent and corrupt dst. Add btrfs_truncate_reflink_source_preserves_clone_data: fill src (2 blocks 0xC3), clone into dst, truncate src to 0, then assert src size 0 and dst still reads all 0xC3. No new mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): btrfs_truncate_reflink_source_preserves_clone_data (lib.rs:66310) — truncating a reflink SOURCE leaves the CLONE data intact (COW shared extents; source shrink must not drop the clone view). cargo test green.

title: test(ffs-core): pin btrfs xattr survives a data overwrite
description: A btrfs xattr is a separate XATTR_ITEM in the inode's tree, independent of its EXTENT_DATA. Overwriting the file's data (which COWs the data/inode items) must carry the xattr items forward unchanged. Existing btrfs xattr tests cover the set/remove round-trip and btrfs-check structure but never write data after setting an xattr to confirm it survives. In a COW filesystem the data write must copy ALL the inode's items; a regression that rebuilt only the data/inode items would silently drop the xattr. Add btrfs_xattr_survives_data_overwrite: write data, setxattr user.tag=KEEPME, overwrite the data, then assert getxattr still returns KEEPME and the data reads back the new content. No new mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): btrfs_xattr_survives_data_overwrite (lib.rs:64957) — overwriting a btrfs file data leaves its xattrs intact. cargo test green.

title: test(ffs-core): pin ext4 xattr survives a data overwrite
description: An ext4 xattr lives in the inode body (inline) or an external xattr block, separate from the file's data blocks. Overwriting the file's data rewrites the inode (size/mtime) and the extent tree, and must preserve the inode-body xattr region and the external-block reference. Existing ext4 xattr tests cover set/get/remove round-trips, modes, and external-block allocation but never write data after setting an xattr to confirm it survives. This is the ext4 sibling of bd-xmh5g.335 (btrfs) and exercises a different code path (inode-body preservation across the inode rewrite). A regression would drop the xattr on a data write. Add ext4_xattr_survives_data_overwrite: write data, setxattr user.tag=KEEPME, overwrite the data, then assert getxattr still returns KEEPME and the data reads back the new content. No new mocks (open_writable_ext4).
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): ext4_xattr_survives_data_overwrite (lib.rs:53657) — overwriting an ext4 file data leaves its xattrs intact. cargo test green.

title: test(ffs-core): pin btrfs rmdir of non-empty directory returns ENOTEMPTY
description: Removing a non-empty btrfs directory must fail with ENOTEMPTY, leaving the directory and its children intact; otherwise the children would be orphaned. The btrfs emptiness guard exists in the directory-removal path but no btrfs test exercises it - the existing ENOTEMPTY tests are all ext4 (write_rmdir_non_empty_returns_enotempty). A regression weakening the btrfs emptiness check would silently orphan child entries. Add btrfs_rmdir_non_empty_returns_enotempty: mkdir a dir, create a child in it, attempt rmdir (assert ENOTEMPTY), then assert the dir and child still resolve. No new mocks.
close_reason: VERIFIED (cc): btrfs_rmdir_non_empty_returns_enotempty (lib.rs:75612) — rmdir on a non-empty btrfs directory returns ENOTEMPTY. cargo test green.

title: test(ffs-core): pin btrfs removal-path type guards (EISDIR/ENOTDIR)
description: The btrfs removal path enforces POSIX type guards: removing a directory through the file-removal call must fail with EISDIR, and rmdir on a regular file must fail with ENOTDIR. These guards exist in the btrfs may_delete path but no btrfs test exercises them - the existing EISDIR/ENOTDIR removal tests are all ext4. A regression confusing the type checks would let a directory be removed through the wrong path (orphaning/corrupting the subtree) or reject valid operations. Add btrfs_unlink_dir_and_rmdir_file_reject_by_type: mkdir d and create f.txt, assert file-removal of d is EISDIR and rmdir of f.txt is ENOTDIR, and both still resolve. No new mocks.

title: test(ffs-core): pin btrfs mknod fifo and socket round-trip through getattr

A regression mis-encoding the S_IFSOCK/S_IFIFO mode bits would surface the wrong file type. Add btrfs_mknod_fifo_and_socket_round_trip_through_getattr: mknod a fifo and a socket, assert each returned kind and the getattr kind match. No new mocks.

title: test(ffs-core): pin btrfs mknod rejects unsupported file type with EINVAL
description: btrfs mknod only accepts special-file types (char, block, fifo, socket); a regular-file or directory mode passed to mknod must be rejected with EINVAL and create no entry. The guard exists (the S_IFMT match falls through to EINVAL) but no btrfs test exercises it - the btrfs mknod tests cover the valid types and the fifo-with-nonzero-rdev rejection only. ext4 has ext4_mknod_unsupported_file_type_returns_einval. title: test(ffs-core): cover the path-separator rejection in validate_single_path_component
description: validate_single_path_component is the shared guard every name-taking operation (create/mkdir/mknod/link/rename/symlink) runs before touching the tree. It rejects empty, '.', '..', NUL-bearing, and over-255-byte names AND any name containing the path separator '/'. The existing test validate_single_path_component_rejects_special_names covers every branch EXCEPT the '/' rejection - which is the most security-relevant one (a component containing '/' would span directories, i.e. path traversal). A regression dropping the contains('/') check would let a slash-bearing name through to the directory layer. Extend the existing test with assertions for an embedded slash, a leading slash, and a trailing slash. No new mocks.

title: test(ffs-core): pin btrfs plain rename of directory into own descendant returns EINVAL

A regression weakening it would let a directory become a child of its own subtree, corrupting the tree. Add btrfs_rename_directory_into_own_descendant_returns_einval: mkdir a and a/b, rename a into b (assert EINVAL), then assert a and a/b are unchanged. No new mocks.

title: test(ffs-error): pin to_errno mapping for all direct FfsError variants
description: FfsError::to_errno is the authoritative boundary that turns every internal error into the syscall errno returned to userspace. Its unit test only asserts a handful of variants (ModeViolation, UnsupportedFeature/IncompatibleFeature/UnsupportedBlockSize, InvalidGeometry, Format) plus the Io/ErrorKind sub-mapping; the 14 direct variants Corruption, RepairFailed, Parse, MvccConflict, Cancelled, NoSpace, NotFound, PermissionDenied, ReadOnly, NotDirectory, IsDirectory, NotEmpty, NameTooLong, Exists have no direct mapping assertion (several - MvccConflict=EAGAIN, Cancelled=EINTR, Corruption/RepairFailed=EIO, Parse=EINVAL - are likely not exercised by any op test). A regression swapping or mis-mapping any of these would surface the wrong errno to applications. Add to_errno_maps_all_direct_variants asserting each. No mocks.

title: fix(ffs-dir): retarget skips interior htree dx_node blocks
description: Fallback quality work after br ready returned only stale already-landed rows. remove_entry already recognizes an interior htree dx_node fake dirent (inode 0, rec_len spanning the whole block) and reports not-present instead of corrupt when metadata_csum reserves a tail. The rename retarget path shares the same directory-block scan surface but still treats that block as corrupt because rec_len exceeds the usable area. Existing tests cover the no-edge case (ssi_disjoint_key_spans_do_not_create_edges) and the both-edges case (ssi_span_guard...), but not the single-edge case. A regression that treated one edge as a dangerous structure would abort serializable transactions spuriously (false conflicts, livelock). Add ssi_single_rw_edge_is_not_a_dangerous_structure: a record forming only an incoming edge, and one forming only an outgoing edge, each yield no dangerous structure. No mocks.

title: test(ffs-mvcc): pin SSI skips records already visible in the transaction snapshot
description: detect_ssi_dangerous_structure only considers committed records whose commit_seq is strictly after the transaction's snapshot high; a record visible in the snapshot (commit_seq <= snapshot.high) is skipped before any edge check and not counted. The existing SSI tests always use records committed after the snapshot, so the skip branch is untested. A regression dropping the skip would derive rw-edges from records the transaction already observed, aborting serializable transactions spuriously. Add ssi_skips_records_visible_in_snapshot: a record at commit_seq == snapshot.high whose key spans would otherwise form both edges yields zero checks and no dangerous structure. No mocks.

title: test(ffs-mvcc): pin SSI empty-write-set transaction is never a dangerous structure
description: detect_ssi_dangerous_structure returns (0, None) immediately when the transaction has no writes - a read-only transaction can never be the pivot of a write-skew, so under SSI it never aborts (a core SSI guarantee). The existing read-only coverage is end-to-end via commit_ssi; the direct early-return branch (write_set empty -> no records examined) is not unit-tested. This completes the detect branch coverage alongside bd-xmh5g.370 (single edge) and .371 (snapshot-visible skip). A regression dropping the early return could abort a read-only txn whose reads were invalidated. Add ssi_empty_write_set_is_never_a_dangerous_structure: a writeless pivot against a record that would otherwise form an incoming edge yields zero checks and no dangerous structure. No mocks.

title: fix(ffs-mvcc): correct swapped SSI edge-direction assertions in single-edge test
description: ssi_single_rw_edge_is_not_a_dangerous_structure (bd-xmh5g.370) mislabeled its two records and swapped the ssi_incoming_edge/ssi_outgoing_edge is_some/is_none assertions. The actual semantics: ssi_incoming_edge = record.read_set intersect pivot.write_set; ssi_outgoing_edge = pivot.read_set intersect record.write_set. The record that writes a block the pivot read forms an OUTGOING edge (not incoming), and vice versa. The detect_ssi_dangerous_structure assertions (each single edge yields None) were always correct; only the explicit edge-direction asserts were inverted and would have failed under cargo test. Corrected the labels and the four edge assertions to match the real direction. Found by re-reading the edge definitions against the test.

No swap remains; the four edge asserts + detect-yields-None are all correct. Confirms bd-xmh5g.370's test is correct (not failing). git show HEAD: verified.

title: perf(extent): lock-free hot-hit path for ExtentCache lookup within a shard
description: After ns-sharding (bd-e8us8), ExtentCache::lookup still takes the EXCLUSIVE per-shard write lock on every call (hit included) to bump hits/misses and touch_entry (which mutates the eviction_index BTreeSet). So N FUSE readers of the SAME inode (e.g. parallel read of one large file) all route to one shard and serialize on that shard's write lock - the sharding only parallelizes DIFFERENT inodes. LEVER: make the hit path lock-free under a SHARED read lock - per-entry last_access and the hits/misses counters become atomics, the hit path takes .read()+atomic-touch, and only miss/stale/eviction take .write(). Tradeoff: dropping the eviction_index means the victim is found by an O(N) min_by_key scan (the historical pre-index behavior, byte-identical single-threaded => golden eviction-trace digest preserved); net win depends on read-hit:insert ratio, so it MUST be measured. Bench target: extent_cache_same_ns_8t (8 threads, same namespace) write_lock_hit vs read_lock_atomic_hit. Sibling of bd-9rdyf (4.62x) / bd-tag2s (3.23x) but for the same-inode case the sharding can't reach. This bead ships the A/B measurement guard first (profile-first); the production change lands once the bench confirms the win and the O(N)-eviction regression is bounded.
close_reason: Measured rejected: final rch hz2 extent_cache_same_ns_8t write_lock_hit 14.201ms vs read_lock_striped_atomic_hit 18.341ms = 0.774x; striped only 1.11x over single atomic and still slower than write-lock. Production striped-counter code reverted; synthetic A/B guard and negative ledger retained.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: MEASURED REGRESSION 0.81x (cc, rch hz1, 8 threads): extent_cache_same_ns_8t write_lock_hit 17.5ms vs read_lock_atomic_hit 21.7ms — the read-lock 'lock-free' hit path is SLOWER. Mechanism: every lookup does self.hits.fetch_add(1) on ONE shared atomic counter, so all 8 threads ping-pong that single cache line — contention RELOCATED from the RwLock to the atomic counter, net worse. Corroborated by extent_cache_real_same_ns: production scales 1t 1.23ms -> 8t 21.9ms (17.8x degradation). RECOMMEND REVERT unless redesigned: the hit/miss counter must be sloppy/per-shard/removed from the hot path (not a single shared atomic) for the read-lock path to actually win. assert_eq fold guard passed (behaviorally correct, just slower). Owner's file (ffs-extent) — flagging.

title: perf(mvcc): read_block returns the visible Cow via into_owned, not to_vec
description: MvccBlockDevice::read_block (ffs-mvcc lib.rs:4108) finished a version-store hit with Cow::to_vec(). read_visible returns Cow::Owned for any COMPRESSED version (resolve_data_with decompresses into a fresh Vec), so to_vec() did a SECOND full-block allocation + copy of an already-owned buffer on every compressed read hit. Switched to Cow::into_owned(): the owned Vec is MOVED out (O(1)); an uncompressed Cow::Borrowed still clones exactly as before, so the returned block is byte-identical. Clean-by-construction (into_owned <= to_vec for every Cow variant), conformance-neutral, on the innermost MVCC read hot path (every FUSE block read that hits the version store). Bench target: mvcc_read_block_cow_owned (to_vec_clone vs into_owned_move across 4K/16K/64K) isolates the eliminated copy; the saved work scales with compressed-extent size. Found by clean-lever sweep.
close_reason: Superseded/obsolete: MvccBlockDevice::read_block (ffs-mvcc lib.rs:4128) no longer does Cow::to_vec() — it returns read_visible_block_buf(block, snap) which yields an Arc-shared BlockBuf for uncompressed versions (bd-xmh5g.394 Arc-backed read) and materializes only compressed bytes. The into_owned-vs-to_vec code path this bead describes was replaced by the superior Arc-backed path; nothing to implement. Verified by cc.

title: [perf][no-gaps] ffs-btrfs floor-key containing extent lookup
description: Code-first performance bead for the no-gaps campaign. Current code materializes every extent-tree item from objectid 0 through logical and keeps the last EXTENT_ITEM that covers logical, so a fragmented extent tree pays O(E) allocation and scan per query. Lever: use InMemoryCowBtrfsTree::floor_key as a predecessor probe, walking backward across interleaved non-EXTENT_ITEM keys until the greatest data EXTENT_ITEM at or before logical is found, then check its exclusive end. Benchmark target: ffs-btrfs extent_fetch resolve_containing_extent_floor_ab range_from_zero_scan vs floor_key_predecessor over 4096 extents plus interleaved keyed refs. Guard: existing mid-extent/logical-ino regression plus an added interleaved-non-extent floor fallback case. Batch benchmark/conformance verdict remains pending per cod-a local-check-only instruction; record outcome in the negative-evidence ledger.

title: perf(inode): move owned read buffers via into_inner instead of copying via to_vec
description: Three read-modify-write paths in ffs-inode read a block (dev.read_block returns an OWNED BlockBuf) then did buf.as_slice().to_vec() to get a mutable Vec, copying the whole 4KiB block. buf is consumed (used only for the to_vec), so buf.into_inner() MOVES the underlying Vec out with no copy. Sites: write_inode read-patch-writeback (lib.rs:127), indirect-block free (539), POSIX-ACL read (761). Byte-identical (into_inner returns the same bytes), conformance-neutral, clean-by-construction (move <= copy). Same lever class as bd-xmh5g.387 read_block Cow::into_owned; quantified by the same move-vs-copy-of-owned-read-buffer rationale (mvcc_read_block_cow_owned bench). Found by clean-lever sibling sweep.
close_reason: Measured in VERIFY/GAUNTLET: RCH Criterion blockbuf_into_inner on vmi1227854 showed 4K small win but 16K/64K regressions (0.878x/0.880x old/new), so production ffs-inode into_inner lever was reverted to as_slice().to_vec(); ledger and scorecard updated; focused ffs-inode gates passed.

title: perf(core): btrfs partial-block write moves the read buffer via into_inner
description: btrfs_write_logical partial-block read-modify-write (ffs-core lib.rs:7674) read a block (read_block returns an OWNED, sole-referenced BlockBuf) then did .as_slice().to_vec() to get a mutable Vec, copying the whole block. into_inner() moves the Vec out (Arc::try_unwrap, O(1)) instead. Every UNALIGNED btrfs write (sub-block or non-block-aligned offset/length) hits this RMW path - common on realistic write workloads. Byte-identical (into_inner returns the same bytes; falls back to a copy only if the Arc were shared, which it is not after a single read_block), conformance-neutral, clean-by-construction. Same lever as bd-xmh5g.387 (read_block Cow::into_owned) and bd-xmh5g.389 (3 ffs-inode into_inner sites). Found by clean-lever sweep.
close_reason: MEASURED KEEP (cc, rch hz1): blockbuf_into_inner_vs_to_vec sole-owned into_inner WINS all sizes (4K 1.11x/16K 1.04x/64K 1.09x). btrfs partial-block RMW reads a sole-owned buffer then mutates -> O(1) move beats to_vec copy. .389 16K/64K regression did NOT reproduce; family reconciles by ownership not size.

title: perf(mvcc): Arc-backed uncompressed reads to eliminate the read_block clone on the common path
description: DEEP SWING. read_block on an UNCOMPRESSED version is the common read path: read_visible returns Cow::Borrowed(&store_data) under the read lock, and into_owned() (bd-xmh5g.387) must CLONE the whole block into the BlockBuf's Vec because BlockBuf owns a Vec. The .387 win only helped the COMPRESSED case (Cow::Owned -> move); the uncompressed case still copies the block on every read. LEVER: store VersionData::Full as Arc<[u8]> instead of Vec<u8>, have read_visible_shared return the Arc (Arc::clone = refcount bump, no copy), and give BlockBuf an Arc-backed constructor so read_block shares the stored block instead of cloning it. Makes the common uncompressed read ALLOCATION-FREE. Requires: (1) version-store Full -> Arc<[u8]> (ffs-mvcc, mine); (2) BlockBuf::from_shared(Arc<[u8]>) or equivalent (ffs-block - needs coordination); (3) measurement to confirm Arc-refcount + cache-line traffic < the eliminated clone (worth it for large/hot blocks; verify small-block break-even). Bench target: read_block_uncompressed_clone_vs_share (this bead ships it) - Cow::Borrowed.into_owned (clone) vs Arc::clone (share) across 4K/16K/64K. The clone arm scales with block size; the share arm is flat - that delta times uncompressed-read frequency is the headroom. Conformance-neutral (same bytes, just shared). Found after the move-owned-buffer vein (bd-xmh5g.387/.389/.390/.393) was mined dry.

title: perf(ondisk): metadata-only ext4 inode parse skips eager xattr_ibody allocation
description: Ext4Inode::parse_from_bytes (ffs-ondisk ext4.rs:2852) UNCONDITIONALLY allocates xattr_ibody = bytes[128+extra_isize..].to_vec() (~150B inline-xattr region) on EVERY inode parse when extra_isize>0 (nearly all modern ext4). But the METADATA hot path - getattr/lookup/readdir/access -> read_live_inode -> read_inode -> parse_from_bytes -> to_file_attr - NEVER reads xattr_ibody. For an ls/find over a large directory that is one wasted heap allocation per inode (thousands/sec). LEVER: a metadata-only parse variant (parse_from_bytes_metadata) that leaves xattr_ibody empty, used by getattr/lookup/readdir/access; the full parse_from_bytes (with xattr_ibody) stays for the ops that need it. CORRECTNESS CONSTRAINT (do NOT just blank it): xattr_ibody IS consumed by parse_ibody_xattrs/listxattr/getxattr (ext4.rs:5202/5650/5690/5728) and ext4 inline-data reads - blanking it unconditionally breaks those. So a VARIANT/lazy split is required, not a one-line Vec::new(). OWNERSHIP: ffs-ondisk is swarm-owned (active); this bead is for that crate's owner or to carry when it frees up - cc filed it from a metadata-path sweep and shipped the bench target. Bench target: ext4_metadata_parse_xattr_ibody (eager_to_vec vs lazy_empty across an N-file ls workload) quantifies the per-inode allocation removed. Clean-by-construction once the variant exists (byte-identical FileAttr; xattr ops unaffected).
close_reason: MEASURED 4.50x WIN (cc, rch hz1): ext4_metadata_parse_xattr_ibody eager-to_vec 115648ns -> lazy-empty 25721ns. Skips per-inode xattr_ibody alloc on getattr/lookup/readdir hot path; full parse retained for xattr/inline-data. Byte-identical FileAttr (guard). Keep.

title: perf(core): readdir-driven parallel inode-table prefetch for ls -l (I/O-overlap)
description: REALISTIC WORKLOAD: ls -l / find / stat-heavy. readdir(dir) yields N entries (name, ino); the shell then getattr()s each ino -> read_inode -> reads that ino's inode-table block. Adjacent directory entries' inodes are scattered across inode-table blocks, so on a COLD cache the N getattrs each pay a SERIAL inode-table-block I/O. LEVER (I/O-overlap, the robust 6-9x class on this infra - parking reads overlap across the rayon pool, see W152/W154): during readdir, PREFETCH the inode-table blocks for all returned entries in PARALLEL (into_par_iter over the distinct inode-table block numbers, warming the sharded ext4_inode_table_block_cache), so the subsequent getattrs hit the cache with no I/O. Pairs naturally with FUSE READDIRPLUS (attrs in the readdir reply). Conformance-neutral (prefetch is a transparent cache warm; getattr results unchanged; bounded to the entries actually returned). Bench target: ls_dir_inode_prefetch on a LatencyBlockDevice (sleep+delegate per read, the W152 measurement device) - serial_getattr_reads (N serial inode-block reads) vs parallel_prefetch (into_par_iter), across a 256-entry dir. The delta is the per-directory cold-listing latency the lever removes. Distinct from the swarm's read/parse levers (.394/.396/.397/.398) - this is metadata I/O-overlap. cc filed from the realistic-workload frontier; ships the bench target.

title: [perf][no-gaps] word-at-a-time bitmap_find_contiguous_linear free-run scan
description: ffs-alloc bitmap_find_contiguous_linear currently advances 8 bits/iteration over used (0xFF) and free (0x00) byte regions. title: perf(mvcc/fuse): write-back commit batching to amortize per-write commit overhead
description: DEEP SWING, realistic write-heavy workloads (cp, builds, databases). The FUSE write path commits PER WRITE REQUEST: ext4/btrfs write -> with_request_scope(RequestOp::Write) -> commit_request_scope at the end of every ~128KiB FUSE write. So writing a 1GiB file = ~8000 commits, each paying SSI validation + WAL append + snapshot bump (and a WAL sync if durable-per-commit). LEVER: WRITE-BACK - accumulate a file handle's staged writes in a long-lived per-fh MVCC txn and commit ONCE on fsync/flush/release (or when the dirty buffer crosses a threshold), instead of per write request. Amortizes the commit overhead across all the writes between fsyncs. DURABILITY (POSIX-correct, the page-cache / FUSE_WRITEBACK_CACHE model): write() need not be durable until fsync; a crash before fsync legitimately loses the un-committed writes, while the committed state (from prior fsyncs) stays crash-consistent via the WAL/journal. READ-YOUR-WRITES is preserved because the long-lived txn's staged_writes are visible to reads on that fh (read_visible already checks staged writes). Careful design needed: fsync/flush/release must commit; conflicting concurrent writers; bounded dirty buffer; the SSI/serializability contract. Bench target: mvcc_commit_batching (per_write_commit: N x begin/stage/commit vs batched_commit: one begin / stage N / one commit) quantifies the per-commit overhead amortized. Distinct from the swarm's read levers - this is the write-path commit model. cc filed from the realistic write-workload frontier; ships the bench target.

title: perf(journal): stream commit checksum CRC without block clone
description: Code-first perf lever for JBD2 replay checksum verification. Surface: verify_jbd2_block_checksum on commit blocks in ffs-journal. Current code clones the full commit block into a temporary Vec only to zero the 4-byte checksum field at offset 16 before crc32c, paying an allocation and full-block copy for every commit-block verification during journal replay. Lever: compute the same CRC as three crc32c_append segments over prefix, a constant zeroed 4-byte checksum field, and suffix, eliminating the temporary Vec while preserving the exact Linux JBD2 zero-field checksum model and stored-checksum comparison. Bench target: extend journal_replay_apply_io_overlap with journal_commit_checksum_zero_field_clone_vs_segmented over 1KiB/4KiB/16KiB commit blocks, asserting old clone and segmented CRC equality. Conformance guard: descriptor/revoke tail checksums unchanged, commit block length rejection unchanged, checksum seed/stored field behavior unchanged, and existing JBD2 checksum tests remain the arbiter. Local code-first gate only: CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/data/projects/.rch-targets/frankenfs-cod-b cargo check -p ffs-journal; no tests/rch/bench in this commit.
close_reason: Measured in VERIFY/GAUNTLET before this closeout: segmented JBD2 commit checksum lost on the realistic 4 KiB row (0.803x old/new, 24.5% slower) despite non-realistic 1 KiB/16 KiB wins. title: [perf] ext4 indirect read = 31x kernel gap ROOT-CAUSE: single-block (4KiB) preads, no run coalescing
description: MEASURED root-cause (cc 2026-06-21, strace+head-to-head) of the BIGGEST documented vs-kernel loss (cod-b: ext4 indirect read 147.9ms vs kernel cat 4.7ms = 31.78x). Fixture: mke2fs -O ^extent,^64bit, 50MiB double-indirect file (14 physical extents per filefrag). FrankenFS read --discard: 109.9ms (455 MB/s), **2149 preads, median 4096 bytes (SINGLE BLOCK), 58MiB total (only 1.16x amplification)**. So NOT amplification and NOT chunk size (FFS_INDIRECT_READ_CHUNK_BLOCKS sweep 128->2048 INERT: 2153->2066 preads, ~84ms flat). The indirect read path reads data blocks ONE 4KiB BLOCK AT A TIME with no contiguous-run coalescing — kernel reads the same 14 extents coalesced (<10ms). Pread offsets are NON-sequential with repeated indirect-block offsets (e.g. 114688 x10), suggesting per-pointer indirect-block re-reads too. LEVER (potential 31x->near-parity, the largest in the codebase): in the ext4 indirect resolve/read path, scan the memoized indirect pointer block and COALESCE contiguous data-block pointers into large runs, then issue one pread per run (turn ~12800 single-block preads into ~14 run reads). This is the W160-deferred 'scan memoized depth-0 ptr block in the run-extension inner loop' work. ffs-core (codex-BlackThrush actively on .411 ext4 indirect direct-output — COORDINATE before editing; their .411 was a different 2.39x internal lever, the gap remains 31x). ffs-core/src/lib.rs read_ext4_indirect / resolve_indirect_block.
notes: FURTHER (cc 2026-06-21, backtrace instrumentation, REVERTED uncommitted): the 2024x re-read of offset 114688 (phys block 28) is NOT via read_block_with_scope — a temp backtrace counter at read_block_with_scope's entry for block.0==28 NEVER fired, yet strace (BOTH debug and release) shows offset 114688 pread 2024x. So the re-read is via the byte-device data-read path read_contiguous_into_with_scope (read_ext4_indirect_segments_into Run jobs → FileByteDevice), NOT indirect-metadata. Either the PLAN emits ~2024 Run segments at phys0=28, or read_contiguous re-reads its start block per call. NEEDS: instrument read_contiguous_into_with_scope (count phys0==28 calls) + dump the segs Vec for this read to see if 2024 Run segs share phys0=28 (resolution aliasing) vs read_contiguous internal re-read. My per-PLAN-memo fix was correctly inert (this isn't the memo). Deep byte-device path — cod-a.
close_reason: ROOT-CAUSED + FIXED (cc, fe00c75e). The '31x ext4-indirect read' gap was MISDIAGNOSED — backtrace proved the 2024x re-read of the journal inode's double-indirect block happens in collect_ext4_journal_segments during maybe_replay_ext4_journal at OPEN (mount-time journal replay), NOT the file read. The sequential journal-inode walk used the non-memo resolve_indirect_block (re-reading the dind block per logical block). FIX: switched to resolve_indirect_block_memo (single-slot, exact fit for sequential walk, bd-vdlyu). MEASURED: preads 2149->127 (17x fewer syscalls), sha256 byte-identical to kernel, 20 indirect tests + conformance 100/0/2 green. Warm tmpfs wall ~50ms (modest — warm preads cheap; not claimed as wall win); big expected cold/real-disk win (each re-read was a seek). title: [perf] btrfs compressed read decompression does NOT scale with threads (1≈all cores) — serial bottleneck, parallelize
description: MEASURED (cc 2026-06-21) root-cause of the btrfs compressed read loss (5.56x vs kernel cat). Fixture: btrfs-convert + mount -o compress-force=zstd, 50MiB compressible file (~18x, 2.7MiB on-disk). FrankenFS read --discard 39.9ms vs kernel cat <10ms. strace: 669 preads / only 2.7MiB on-disk → READ negligible, gap is DECOMPRESSION. **RAYON_NUM_THREADS sweep: 1=39.2ms, default(64)=39.9ms, 4=34.3ms, 16=34.3ms** → decompression does NOT scale with cores (1 thread ≈ all cores; caps ~1.14x at 4 threads). 39ms ≈ single-thread libzstd of 50MiB (~1.3GB/s). The kernel parallelizes decompression across compressed extents (btrfs worker threads, >5GB/s) → its <10ms. So FrankenFS btrfs decompression is effectively SERIAL/parallelism-capped despite bd-307e4's into_par_iter — likely too-few parallel units (few extents) or a serial dependency in the read/decompress loop. LEVER: make compressed-extent decompression scale with cores (finer parallel units / remove serial dependency) — potential ~4-16x on large compressed reads. ffs-core btrfs_read_file_into / btrfs_decompress (cod-a's decompression-scheduling area .411 — COORDINATE; this is the parallelism ceiling, distinct from their tiny-frame scheduling probe). NOTE distinct from bd-xmh5g.412 (ext4-indirect = read-granularity); this is decompression-parallelism.
notes: CORRECTED root-cause (cc 2026-06-21 flamegraph): NOT a decompression-parallelism issue. perf self-time: __memmove_avx **15.14%** (dominant), rayon steal 4.4% + epoch 2.2% + wait_until_cold 1.3% (~8% coordination, workers PARK), and ZSTD_decompressSequences only **3.42%**. So decompression is cheap; the gap is the MEMMOVE: btrfs_decompress_zstd_frame (ffs-core lib.rs:7969) decompresses each extent into a fresh Vec::with_capacity(uncompressed_size), then the caller copies that Vec into the output window. The file has 648 extents (plenty to parallelize), so thread count barely helps because the per-extent Vec-alloc+memmove + rayon coordination dominate, not decompress. CORRECTED LEVER (analogous to the read_exact_at/read_into-dst pattern): decompress DIRECTLY into the caller's output-window slice via zstd::bulk::Decompressor::decompress_to_buffer(frame, &mut window) — eliminates the per-extent Vec allocation AND the 15% memmove. The bd-307e4/W162 job structure already has the output window (BtrfsOutputSpec); change btrfs_decompress_zstd_frame to take &mut [u8] dst instead of returning Vec. ffs-core (cod-a's area). Supersedes the earlier 'parallelize decompression' framing.
close_reason: SHIPPED the decompress-into-window lever (76308cac, btrfs_decompress_zstd_into): whole-extent zstd decompresses straight into the output window via decompress_to_buffer — flamegraph __memmove_avx 15.14%->0.14%, per-extent Vec alloc eliminated, sha256 byte-identical, conformance 100/0/2, 358 btrfs tests green. CPU/alloc win KEPT. BUT single-read wall NEUTRAL (~40ms, still ~5.5x vs kernel) — the compressed read is rayon-COORDINATION-bound at 64 threads (sweep 1=39.9/4=35.4/8=35.5/64=41.1ms). The remaining WALL lever (thread-cap, ~1.16x) is filed separately as a follow-up for cod-a. The decompress-into-window part of this bead is DONE.

title: [perf] btrfs compressed read is rayon-coordination-bound at 64 threads — cap decompress par_iter to ~4-8 (1.16x wall)
description: MEASURED (cc 2026-06-21, after 76308cac memmove fix): btrfs compressed read wall is rayon-coordination-bound. RAYON_NUM_THREADS sweep on the read: 1=39.9ms, 4=35.4ms, 8=35.5ms, 64=41.1ms — 4-8 threads is **1.16x faster** than the default 64. The decompress par_iter (ffs-core btrfs_read_file_into ~line 8928, jobs.into_par_iter) over hundreds of small compressed extents incurs more rayon steal/epoch/parking overhead at 64 threads than the (now memmove-free, ~3% CPU) decompression work justifies. LEVER: give the compressed-extent decompress par_iter a TARGETED thread cap (~4-8) — e.g. a scoped rayon pool or .with_min_len chunking — WITHOUT lowering the global pool (the parallel uncompressed/multi-extent reads DO scale and need all cores). Distinct from the memmove fix (76308cac, done) which is CPU-positive but wall-neutral because of this coordination ceiling. ffs-core (cod-a's area). Flamegraph: steal 4.4%+epoch 2.2%+wait_until_cold 1.3% at 64 threads.
notes: RESOLVED-BY-SWARM (cc 2026-06-21 measured at HEAD): the btrfs-compressed read gap has CLOSED — it now BEATS kernel dd-materialize. Interleaved A/B: frankenfs 14.5-16.5ms vs kernel dd 23.4-24.5ms = ~1.5x FASTER (was 2.2x slower), byte-identical. The over-subscription characterization stands as the diagnosis, but the practical gap is gone after the swarm landed peer 512e1110 (elide btrfs read zero-fill) + my .413 (decompress-into-window) + cod-a btrfs-plan work. The thread-cap micro-lever (both avenues ruled out) is moot — frankenfs already wins. Consider closing .414 as superseded-by-win.

title: [perf] apply serialize-when-undersubscribed guard to read-path segment par_iters (over-subscription on small reads)
description: Follow-up to the readdir-prefetch fix (1411c3f1, which serializes when blocks.len() < current_num_threads()). The SAME over-subscription pattern exists in other read-path into_par_iter sites that lack a small-N guard: ffs-core/lib.rs ~L9017, L9455, L11566, L12326 (e2compr cluster), L12856 (read_ext4_indirect_segments_into). For LARGE reads these have many segments (fine), but a SMALL read (few segments) fans a handful of jobs across the 64-wide pool = futex over-subscription churn — matters cumulatively for MANY-SMALL-FILE read workloads (e.g. walk --read-data over thousands of small files, grep -r, build systems). FIX (proven byte-identical pattern): serialize the segment reads when count < rayon::current_num_threads(). NOT shipped yet: needs a many-small-files-WITH-data fixture to MEASURE the win (the existing 30k-file dir is 0-byte; large-file fixtures don't trigger it) — do not blind-ship 5 guards unmeasured. Construct mke2fs -d with ~10k small (4-64KiB) files, walk --read-data with/without guards. cc found the pattern; deferred for measurement.
notes: MEASURED + REJECTED (cc 2026-06-21): the serialize-when-undersubscribed guard is WRONG for read_file_data's segment par_iter — it OVER-CORRECTS. Constructed fixture (1000x512KiB extent files = ~4 chunks each), walk --read-data: thread sweep showed over-subscription (8thr=98.7ms < 64thr=131.5ms, 1.33x). BUT applying the serialize guard (serial when jobs < threads) made it 228ms — WORSE than the 64-thread baseline (131.5)! Reason: unlike the readdir prefetch (cheap cache-hit reads where parallelism barely helps), read_file_data's per-file segment reads have real work/latency — the par_iter parallelism HELPS (98.7ms at 8 threads); serializing kills it. The issue is thread-COUNT (over-subscription at 64), NOT parallelism. A thread-cap would help (8 < 64) but conflicts with single-LARGE-file reads which need all 64 (extent read dominates at 64). So NO clean fix in read_file_data: serialize=regression, global-cap=conflicts-with-large-reads (same dead-end as btrfs .414). The real fix would be parallelize-ACROSS-files in walk --read-data (architecture change, cod-a). Guard NOT shipped (reverted). LESSON: serialize-when-undersubscribed only works when the parallel benefit is marginal (cheap reads); for real-work reads it over-corrects — verify per-site, do not blanket-apply the prefetch pattern.

title: [perf] walk --read-data reads files SERIALLY — many-small-files read 3.85x slower than kernel cat (parallelize across files)
description: MEASURED gap (cc 2026-06-21, mounted 1000x512KiB-file ext4): frankenfs walk --read-data reads 500MiB in ~231ms (2.2 GB/s) vs kernel 'cat f*.bin' ~60ms (8.3 GB/s) = 3.85x SLOWER. Isolated: metadata walk only = 1.1ms (negligible), so the loss is the READ — walk_one_dir (ffs-cli main.rs ~2287) reads files SERIALLY (for entry { read_into }), ~0.18ms/file overhead (extent-resolve + scope + par_iter setup + read) x 1000 files. The per-file segment par_iter parallelism doesn't help here (8thr≈64thr≈232ms at load 7) — the cost is the SERIAL-across-files per-file overhead. FIX: parallelize ACROSS files within a dir for --read-data — entries.par_iter().map_init(|| per-thread buffer, |buf, entry| read file into buf) — frankenfs's 64 cores reading files concurrently vs kernel's serial cat should FLIP this to a WIN. Correctness: per-thread buffers (map_init, not the shared read_buf), byte-tally aggregation (sum), error handling (first error), keep subdir collection. ffs-cli walk command (mine). NOTE: distinct from .418 (per-file segment serialize, which REGRESSED); this is across-FILE parallelism. The current --parallel mode only parallelizes across DIRS (thread::scope), useless for one big dir.
