title: [perf] ExtentCache::insert is 17% of deep-tree walk --read-data (one-pass reads never re-hit the cache)
description: PROFILED (cc 2026-06-21, perf record tree --read-data @64 threads, 2042 dirs/30k files): top self-time = ExtentCache::insert 17.19% (ffs-extent) + its parking_lot RwLock (lock_shared_slow 1.02% / unlock_exclusive_slow 0.83%). Each file read resolves extents and INSERTS into the shared ExtentCache (exclusive lock). For a one-pass walk --read-data (each file read exactly once), these inserts are PURE OVERHEAD — the cache is populated but never re-hit, and the exclusive-lock inserts serialize/contend at high thread counts (explains the 16-thread scaling ceiling: 16=460ms, 64=593ms). LEVER candidates (ffs-extent/ffs-core, cod-a domain): (a) a read hint / bypass that skips ExtentCache population for sequential one-pass reads; (b) shard the ExtentCache lock (per-inode or striped) to cut the insert contention; (c) bounded/sampled insertion. NOT a CLI-level fix. Tree walk --read-data already WINS at 16 threads (1.46x vs kernel find|cat) — this is about scaling further. cc found+profiled; ffs-extent owner to action.
notes: SHARD-BUMP FIX ATTEMPT — MEASURED INERT, REVERTED (cc 2026-06-21). Hypothesis: since each shard is sized to the full capacity (per the with_capacity code + comment, lib.rs:1419) and namespace is per-inode (extent_cache_namespace packs inode#+generation, lib.rs:14294), bumping EXTENT_CACHE_SHARDS 16->64 should spread the 30k tree inodes to ~469/shard < 1024 capacity => no eviction => the 4.8x. MEASURED: tree --read-data stayed 440-460ms at 64 shards (vs 450ms at 16; vs 93.8ms at cap-65536) across re-measures at load 13 and 21 — INERT. So sharding does NOT resolve the eviction thrash even though the model predicts it should; only raising per-shard capacity does (cap-65536 = 93.8ms, but that regresses >cap workloads via O(capacity) scans). The discrepancy (per-inode ns + full-cap-per-shard should spread, but doesn't help) suggests either the live entry count per shard is far higher than inode count (multiple entries/inode) or the eviction triggers differently than the per-shard model implies — needs the owner's deeper read of the eviction path. ffs-extent==HEAD (reverted). NO safe localized fix found from the CLI/measurement side; the principled fix (O(1) exact-LRU preserving the pinned victim, or one-pass-read bypass) remains the ffs-extent owner's call. ffs-extent tests stay green (153).
close_reason: FIXED+SHIPPED (cc): the ExtentCache eviction thrash was a SHARD DISTRIBUTION BUG — shard(ns)=ns%SHARDS keyed the low bits but extent_cache_namespace packs the inode into the high bits (rotate_left 32), so same-generation inodes all collapsed onto ONE shard (striping inert, lone shard thrashed its LRU = the profiled 17%). FIX: hash-mix the namespace (shard_index Fibonacci) so inodes spread + bump shards 16->64. MEASURED ext4 tree --read-data 450->98ms = 4.6x (6.7x vs kernel find|cat). No capacity change so no >cap scan regression (unlike the rejected capacity bump). Byte-identical, conformance 100/0/2, 153 ffs-extent tests green. NOTE: btrfs many-files read still has the separate .421 walk_node_body issue (dominant there).

title: [perf] btrfs many-files read is super-linear — BtrfsParallelTreeWalker::walk_node_body 53% self-time, per-file full-tree walk
description: MEASURED+PROFILED (cc 2026-06-21, btrfs-convert tree image 2042 dirs/30k files, RO loop mount, WARM/tmpfs so CPU-bound not I/O): btrfs walk --read-data is PATHOLOGICAL — serial TIMED OUT at 90s, --parallel ran 9 MINUTES at 13 cores, vs ext4 same fixture 908ms serial / 450ms parallel = >100x SLOWER. perf record (warm, -F199): top self-time 53.35% ffs_btrfs BtrfsParallelTreeWalker::walk_node_body (RECURSIVE, 31% nested self-call) + hashbrown HashMap::insert 3.72% (per-walk visited set) + collect_leaf_items 3.58% + btrfs_read_parsed_node 2.35%. ROOT CAUSE (hypothesis from profile): each per-FILE btrfs read drives a BtrfsParallelTreeWalker descent over the btrfs tree (fs/extent tree) instead of a targeted B-tree lookup — so reading N files = O(N x tree-nodes), super-linear. The per-walk HashMap visited-set compounds it. This is INSIDE the per-file read (ffs-btrfs / ffs-core btrfs read path), so the bd-xmh5g.419 walk-level across-file parallelism does NOT help btrfs (per-file cost dominates). FIX (ffs-btrfs owner): per-file extent resolution should be a targeted tree SEEK (descend to the inode items by key) not a full parallel tree traversal; or share one fs-tree walk across files. CAVEAT: fixture is btrfs-convert (native btrfs unavailable, the btrfs format tool is dcg-blocked) — convert tree structure may amplify, but walk_node_body-per-file is a code-path issue a native image would also hit. cc found+profiled; ffs-btrfs owner to action. P1 (>100x, worst read gap found this session).
notes: ADDITIONAL EVIDENCE (cc 2026-06-21): NOT scale-specific to the 30k tree — even a 1000-file SINGLE-DIR btrfs --read-data (smallfiles→btrfs, 1000×512KiB) TIMES OUT >60s. walk_node_body's per-file full-tree walk is catastrophic at any scale beyond a handful of files (O(N_files × tree_nodes)). CONSEQUENCE: bd-xmh5g.422 (cache_shard shard-0 collapse) is UNMEASURABLE until .421 lands — every btrfs read workload that would exercise the node-cache contention times out first. .422 fix is written+verified-safe (ext4-neutral, conformance green), ready to apply+measure once .421 makes btrfs walks complete.

title: [perf] ffs-core ShardedCache cache_shard() & 0xFFF collapses aligned-bytenr keys (btrfs node cache) onto shard 0
description: FOUND (cc 2026-06-21, same bug class as the .420 ffs-extent shard fix). ffs-core ShardedCache (lib.rs:1174) lock-stripes 16 shards via shard(key)=key.cache_shard() % FFS_CACHE_SHARDS, and cache_shard() for u64/BlockNumber/GroupNumber returns (key & 0xFFF) — the LOW 12 bits. Used by ext4_group_desc_cache, ext4_inode_table_block_cache, ext4_file_data_block_cache (BlockNumber keys — sequential, low-bit entropy, spread FINE) AND btrfs_parsed_node_cache (lib.rs:1008, key = node LOGICAL address = nodesize-aligned, >=4KiB → low 12 bits ALWAYS 0). So EVERY btrfs parsed node hashes to shard 0 → the 16-way striping is INERT for btrfs nodes → all parallel node-cache access serializes on one Mutex<BTreeMap>. FIX (written + tested by cc, then reverted — see below): add mix_cache_key(v)=usize::try_from(v.wrapping_mul(0x9e3779b97f4a7c15)>>32).unwrap_or(0) and use it in all three cache_shard impls (GroupNumber.0 is u32 → u64::from). VERIFIED SAFE: ext4 extent 23.9ms + tree --read-data 87ms (no regression — BlockNumber keys still spread), conformance 100/0/2, byte-identical, no pinned cache_shard test. NOT SHIPPED: the btrfs benefit is UNMEASURABLE in isolation right now — the only node-cache-contended workload is the parallel btrfs tree walk, which TIMES OUT (>90s even with the fix) due to the SEPARATE .421 walk_node_body super-linearity. So I reverted (ffs-core==HEAD) per the measured-win discipline. RECOMMEND: ffs-extent/ffs-btrfs owner apply this alongside fixing .421 — once the walk completes, this removes the node-cache shard-0 serialization (a confounder). The fix is correct + safe; it just needs .421 fixed to demonstrate a ratio.
close_reason: Kept ffs-core ShardedCache mixed shard selector for 16KiB-aligned btrfs parsed-node keys: RCH hz2 Criterion old low-bit mean 30.874 ms vs mixed mean 4.8474 ms (6.37x old/new); RCH check/test/conformance/build green.

title: btrfs_read_plan_index Mutex locked per-read — 4.4pct lock_slow contention in parallel reads (post-.421 residual)
description: PROFILED (cc 2026-06-21, perf -F999 on btrfs tree --read-data AFTER .421 landed, now 47.9ms = 14.4x vs kernel). Post-.421 residual hot spots: parking_lot RawMutex lock_slow 4.42pct + memset 7.1pct (buffer zeroing) + btrfs_read_file_into 2.54pct. The lock_slow is btrfs_read_plan_index.lock at ffs-core/lib.rs:8415/8420/8429 — the BtrfsReadPlanIndex (cod-a .421 prewarm) lives in a Mutex of Option of Arc, locked PER read (line 8429 does lock then as_ref then cloned) to clone the Arc. On a RO mount the index is IMMUTABLE after prewarm, so per-read mutex-locking is pure contention across the parallel file readers. FIX (cod-a, refines .421): clone the Arc ONCE before the parallel read loop and pass it to workers, OR make the field lock-free for reads (arc_swap ArcSwap, or OnceLock of Arc, or RwLock read). Est ~4pct wall on btrfs many-files read. NOTE: btrfs read already DOMINATES kernel 14.4x post-.421+.422; incremental headroom on a won path. cc profiled+filed; cod-a owns ffs-core btrfs read path. memset 7.1pct is the .419 per-read buffer zeroing, inherent to forbid(unsafe), separate.
notes: SCALING EVIDENCE (cc 2026-06-21): the .423 per-read mutex contention COMPOUNDS with file count. Measured btrfs many-files READ-DATA cold at 30k vs 60k files: frankenfs grew 53ms->121ms = 2.28x for 2x files (slightly SUPER-linear), while the kernel grew 1.96x (~linear), so the domination ratio shrank 24.3x->20.9x. By contrast the ext4 metadata WALK (no per-read index mutex on the hot path) AMPLIFIES with scale (11.9x->17x, frankenfs sub-linear). The btrfs read's super-linearity is consistent with the per-read btrfs_read_plan_index.lock() (30k->60k = 2x more per-file lock acquisitions -> more contention across the parallel readers). CONCLUSION: the ArcSwapOption (or caller-cache) fix from this bead matters MORE at scale — the larger the many-files workload, the bigger the .423 win. Recipe + dep note in prior comments.

title: [perf][no-gaps] fsck reads whole image into RAM but only needs SB+GDT prefix
description: ffs-cli build_fsck_output does let image = std::fs::read(path) — loads the ENTIRE filesystem image into a Vec (8MB alloc+copy+read) on every fsck. For btrfs the buffer is NEVER used (only image_len, from byte_dev). For ext4 it feeds Ext4ImageReader + validate_ext4_group_descriptors, which ONLY call read_group_desc (the group-descriptor table, a small prefix right after the superblock) — never read_inode/data. The Scrubber re-reads all blocks anyway (batched, bd-a384r). Lever: read only the [0, gdt_end) prefix for ext4 (compute from parsed sb: group_desc_offset(last)+group_desc_size, clamped to file len to preserve malformed-descriptor error parity) and skip the read entirely for btrfs. Rank-2 hotspot (8MB __memmove/__memset). Proof: fsck -f --json golden sha256 byte-identical on ext4_8mb_reference + a malformed-GDT case; strace bytes-read / peak-RSS reduction; Score>=2.0 on I/O-bytes or wall. #![forbid(unsafe_code)], clippy/fmt clean.

description: strace of fsck -f (2026-06-02 TealMarten, post bd-a384r+bd-xmh5g.6) shows fsck I/O is optimal (32 batched preadv, whole-image read gone). comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: HEADS-UP for the fast-path design (TealMarten reviewed the synced-then-reverted WIP): the lock-free CAS-publish fast path had a latent WEAK-MEMORY LOST-WAKEUP. The publisher does {CAS completed; load waiters} and the slow-path waiter does {fetch_add waiters; re-check completed; park}. With AcqRel/Acquire (not SeqCst) on this cross-flag handshake, two RMWs on DIFFERENT atomics have no single total order, so on aarch64 the 'both-miss' is allowed: publisher reads waiters==0 (skips notify) while the waiter reads stale completed (then parks) -> lost wakeup -> deadlock. It is masked on x86 because LOCKed RMWs are full barriers, so unit tests on the x86 rch workers will NOT catch it. FIX when re-landing: make the four handshake ops SeqCst (publisher CAS + publisher waiters.load; waiter waiters.fetch_add + waiter completed re-check). That yields the single total order ruling out both-miss (Dekker-style), and is provably correct without ARM hardware. Also: a proper Score>=2.0 proof needs a SAME-BINARY A/B (old lock-always publish vs new fast path), not a cross-run compare vs the 124ms baseline. Keep the slow path (lock-mediated) as-is; only the lock-free fast path needs SeqCst.

title: ext4 fallocate PUNCH_HOLE rejects unaligned offset/length (parity gap vs kernel)
description: Found by the randomized mutation fuzz ext4_write_fallocate_random_matches_reference_model (a5d400b4). FrankenFS ext4 PUNCH_HOLE returns EOPNOTSUPP for a non-block-aligned offset or length (ffs-core lib.rs:14643 and :15791: 'ext4 punch_hole currently requires block-aligned offset/length'). The Linux kernel supports unaligned PUNCH_HOLE: it zeroes the partial portions of the head/tail edge blocks that fall inside the range and deallocates only the fully-covered aligned interior blocks (size unchanged, KEEP_SIZE semantics). NOTE: ZERO_RANGE already handles unaligned ranges (partial-block zeroing) — see tests write_fallocate_zero_range_unaligned_within_one_block_preserves_neighbors / _across_block_boundary. FIX PATH: reuse that partial-edge-zeroing for punch's edge blocks, then punch_hole the aligned interior [align_up(off), align_down(off+len)). VALIDATE: extend the fuzz to also generate unaligned punch (remove the align_down for kind 2) + a curated e2fsck/neighbor-preservation test. Low severity (clear EOPNOTSUPP, no corruption) but a real behavior-parity gap an app hitting fallocate(PUNCH_HOLE) with unaligned args would see.
close_reason: done

title: btrfs write/truncate/fallocate do not enforce immutable/append-only attributes (immutable files are writable; data-integrity gap)
description: btrfs_write, btrfs_setattr (size/truncate), and btrfs_fallocate perform NO immutable or append-only flag checks (the only btrfs BTRFS_INODE_IMMUTABLE/APPEND refs are in link/xattr/rename from bd-69ich/kf7uw/85rav). So on btrfs: writing to an IMMUTABLE file silently succeeds (corrupts a protected file); truncating/fallocate-ing an immutable file succeeds; a non-EOF write to an append-only file succeeds; shrinking an append-only file succeeds. ext4 enforces all of this (immutable_and_append_attributes_enforced_on_writes_bd_hbld5, ext4-ONLY) via: ext4_write (ext4_reject_immutable + append rejects offset!=i_size), ext4_setattr (immutable + append rejects new_size<size), ext4_fallocate (immutable + append rejects punch/collapse/zero/insert). FIX: mirror those exact checks in btrfs_write/btrfs_setattr/btrfs_fallocate (EPERM, before mutation), reading link_target/inode flags. Data-integrity parity (P2 — immutable means immutable). Extends the vfs append/immutable audit (bd-69ich link, bd-kf7uw xattr, bd-85rav rename) to the btrfs CONTENT-mutation paths. Test: inject flag on a btrfs file, attempt write/truncate/fallocate -> EPERM (append: EOF-append still allowed).
close_reason: Fixed in 41b5316b: btrfs_write/btrfs_setattr/btrfs_fallocate now enforce immutable (all content mutations EPERM) and append-only (non-EOF write EPERM, shrink EPERM, data-altering fallocate modes EPERM; EOF append + plain prealloc still allowed), mirroring ext4's bd-hbld5 rules. Test btrfs_immutable_and_append_enforced_on_content_ops_bd_xpsq4. Full ffs-core 1086 green. Closes the btrfs side of the vfs append/immutable enforcement audit (content-mutation paths) alongside bd-69ich/kf7uw/85rav (metadata paths).

title: scrub(btrfs): backup superblocks (64MiB/256GiB mirrors) are now skipped, not validated — validate them as superblocks
description:
CONTEXT (BlackThrush/cc_ffs 2026-07-09). While closing bd-scrub-btrfs-false-corrupt-afw8y I found that btrfs backup superblocks (mirrors at 64 MiB and 256 GiB; primary at 64 KiB) were being MIS-validated: a superblock carries its fsid at 0x20..0x30, exactly where a tree block does, so BtrfsTreeBlockValidator's cheap fsid pre-check misclassified the mirror as a tree block and applied a tree-block checksum over the full block (16 KiB) instead of the 4096-byte superblock region -> a spurious ChecksumMismatch/Critical on block 4096 of EVERY real btrfs image (verified: magic _BHRfS_M, self-consistent sb.bytenr=67108864).

FIXED (commit on main): BtrfsTreeBlockValidator now Skips all three mirror block numbers (BTRFS_SUPER_MIRROR_OFFSETS). Every valid btrfs+ext4 test image now scrubs 0 findings.

REMAINING GAP (this bead): the mirrors are SKIPPED, not validated. BtrfsSuperblockValidator still targets only the primary (BTRFS_SUPER_INFO_OFFSET). So a genuinely corrupt BACKUP superblock is not reported. This is not a regression (before the fix the mirror was reported as corrupt 100% of the time, valid or not -- an always-firing alarm with zero information), but it IS missing coverage.

PROPOSED: teach BtrfsSuperblockValidator the mirror offsets, with the intra-block offset (offset % block_size) per mirror. Policy question: a mirror that btrfs never wrote (device big enough for the offset to exist, but sb absent) is all-zero and must NOT be reported as corrupt -> validate the mirror only when the btrfs magic (_BHRfS_M at sb+0x40) is present; report parse/csum failures only for magic-bearing mirrors. Primary stays strict (a zeroed primary IS corruption; pinned by test btrfs_scrub_still_detects_zeroed_superblock).

Also worth verifying the mirror's sb.bytenr equals its own byte offset (self-consistency) -- that check IS valid for superblocks (unlike tree-block bytenr, see bd-5vb36) because a superblock's bytenr is its physical offset, not a chunk-mapped logical address.
close_reason:
FIXED. BtrfsSuperblockValidator::new(block_size, total_bytes) now holds a target for the primary AND every mirror the filesystem spans (64KiB/64MiB/256GiB), validating each as a superblock: parse + checksum + bytenr == its own physical offset. The bytenr check is well-founded here (a superblock copy stores its own PHYSICAL offset; verified 15/15 valid images: primary=65536, 64MiB mirror=67108864) and is NOT the bd-5vb36 mistake (a tree block's bytenr is a chunk-mapped LOGICAL address).

EXPECTED-MIRROR RULE (measure-first): a mirror is validated only where offset+4096 <= sb.total_bytes -- the FILESYSTEM size, not the image file size. Surveying all 16 btrfs images caught btr2_572550.img: a 2 GiB file whose 64MiB region is all-zero because it contains no filesystem at all (total_bytes=0, no primary sb). A naive 'block exists => mirror must be valid' rule would have created a NEW false positive.

FUSED-GATE FIX: BtrfsScrubValidator gates mirror blocks on BLOCK NUMBER, not fsid. A wrongly-zeroed mirror has no fsid to match, so the fsid-only fast path would have short-circuited it to Clean and never validated it.

PROVEN ON REAL IMAGES (copies of btrunc_838059.img): (A) untouched -> 0 findings; (B) 1-bit flip at 64MiB+0x100 -> checksum_mismatch/critical @ blk 4096; (C) mirror wholly zeroed -> bad_magic + checksum_mismatch; (D) mirror rewritten with the primary's bytenr and a RECOMPUTED VALID checksum -> structural_invariant/critical, caught only by the new bytenr check.

KERNEL IDENTITY: btrunc_838059.img loop-mounted read-only under the kernel btrfs driver; sha256(/plain.bin)=172c15dc2e12b50e523d8e657cbe7fbb11c1053252bbf1e1431077d57d8128fd, byte-identical to 'ffs-cli read' of the same path, and that image scrubs 0 findings with the mirror validated. 10/10 valid images (8 btrfs + 2 ext4) scrub 0 corrupt / 0 findings.

Gates: ffs-repair 477/0 (+5 tests), ffs-cli 348+26/0, ffs-harness 2058/0, cargo check --workspace --all-targets OK, fmt+clippy clean on changed files, ubs 0 critical.

title: Cap btrfs decompression target size before allocation
description: Btrfs regular compressed extent reads cap disk_num_bytes and ram_bytes before decompression, but inline compressed extents pass ram_bytes directly into btrfs_decompress, whose zlib/LZO paths reserve output capacity before decoding. A malformed inline extent with huge ram_bytes can trigger oversized allocation before validation. Add a shared 128MiB decompression target cap at the decompressor boundary, reuse the constant at existing regular-extent guards, and add regression coverage that oversized targets are rejected before allocation.
close_reason: Capped btrfs decompression targets at the decompressor boundary before output allocation, reused the 128MiB limit for regular compressed extent guards, and added an oversized-target regression; fmt/check/clippy/focused test/UBS passed.

title: ffs-ondisk: DX_HASH_LEGACY through SIPHASH constants + EXT4_HTREE_EOF_32BIT lack kernel-conformance pin
description:
Finding (via /testing-conformance-harnesses skill, NEW target): crates/ffs-ondisk/src/ext4.rs:4838-4845 declares 7 DX hash version constants and EXT4_HTREE_EOF_32BIT used by every htree directory lookup. These are file-private (no pub), not exposed for downstream consumers, and have NO conformance pin to canonical kernel values from fs/ext4/ext4.h:

  DX_HASH_LEGACY               = 0     (#define DX_HASH_LEGACY 0)
  DX_HASH_HALF_MD4             = 1     (#define DX_HASH_HALF_MD4 1)
  DX_HASH_TEA                  = 2     (#define DX_HASH_TEA 2)
  DX_HASH_LEGACY_UNSIGNED      = 3     (DX_HASH_LEGACY | DX_HASH_UNSIGNED_BIT)
  DX_HASH_HALF_MD4_UNSIGNED    = 4
  DX_HASH_TEA_UNSIGNED         = 5
  DX_HASH_SIPHASH              = 6     (kernel SipHash-2-4 variant)
  EXT4_HTREE_EOF_32BIT         = 0x7FFFFFFF  (= (1<<31) - 1, htree EOF sentinel)

A regression that swapped DX_HASH_TEA (2) and DX_HASH_HALF_MD4 (1) would silently mis-classify every htree directory and route lookups through the wrong hash function — invisible until end users notice broken lookups.

Critical: the unsigned variants are derived by OR'ing the signed variant with bit 2 (DX_HASH_UNSIGNED_BIT in some kernel headers). The structural invariant (unsigned == signed | 2) prevents drift between the two variants.

Acceptance: ext4_dx_hash_version_constants_match_kernel_header conformance test in crates/ffs-ondisk/src/ext4.rs that pins all 7 hash version values + EXT4_HTREE_EOF_32BIT, plus the structural invariant that unsigned variants are signed OR'd with 2. Pairs with bd-bevt2 (40 feature flags), bd-jbilz (magic + state flags), bd-glkri (BG flags), bd-tyeic (27 inode flags).
close_reason: done

comments.author: ubuntu

Structural invariants: unsigned variants are signed + 3 (kernel layout); strict-monotonic ascending across all 7 hash versions; EXT4_HTREE_EOF_32BIT round-trips via the kernel formula (1<<31) - 1. rch exit code 0.

title: A0: btrfs RW safety interlock - stop silent data loss (P0)
description: P0 / ACTIVE DATA LOSS. btrfs metadata mutations write only to an in-memory InMemoryCowBtrfsTree (ffs-core/src/lib.rs:560), never serialized to disk; btrfs_sync_with_logging (ffs-core/src/lib.rs:13493) logs outcome=applied while persisting nothing. FIX (ships before any other A-item): the btrfs metadata-mutating operations - create, mkdir, mknod, unlink, rmdir, rename, link, symlink, write, truncate/setattr-size, setattr, fallocate, setxattr, removexattr, plus btrfs_sync/fsync/fsyncdir - fail closed with EROFS by default. ENFORCE THE INTERLOCK AT THE ffs-core FsOps/btrfs-mutation boundary, not the ffs-fuse layer, so BOTH FUSE callers AND direct library-API (OpenFs) callers are fail-closed - the harness and library consumers must not bypass it. No code path may log outcome=applied for a btrfs metadata change not on disk; on refusal emit a structured warn-level log line carrying operation_id + error_class (never silent). PRESERVE the in-memory-RW capability behind an explicit opt-in flag --btrfs-rw-ephemeral-ok (and the equivalent library OpenOptions field), documented as non-durable, so no functionality is lost for callers who knowingly want ephemeral RW.
acceptance_criteria: Unit tests: every btrfs metadata mutator + btrfs_sync/fsync/fsyncdir returns EROFS when --btrfs-rw-ephemeral-ok is absent. E2E script scripts/e2e/ffs_btrfs_rw_interlock_e2e.sh with detailed per-step logging proves (a) mutate->unmount->remount loses nothing because the mutation was refused, (b) the ephemeral flag still permits in-memory RW. Structured refusal log line asserted. cargo check/clippy/fmt/test green.
notes: STOPGAP SCOPE: the EROFS interlock and the --btrfs-rw-ephemeral-ok flag are temporary. When A5 proves durable btrfs RW, btrfs --rw becomes durable by default and BOTH the interlock and the stopgap flag must be retired (no permanent tech debt - AGENTS.md). A5's acceptance owns that retirement.

title: Investigate and fix ext4 bitmap CRC32C mismatch against real mkfs.ext4 images
description:
PROBLEM: The kernel_reference integration test ext4_bitmap_free_space_matches_kernel fails because our computed block bitmap checksum (via verify_block_bitmap_checksum -> block_bitmap_checksum_value -> ext4_bitmap_checksum) does not match the checksum stored by mkfs.ext4 1.47.2 on real images.

EVIDENCE: On a fresh 8MB ext4 image (mkfs.ext4 -L test -b 4096 -q -O ^has_journal), seed=0xba6605a8, our code computes 0xcd45611c but the stored checksum is 0xb8339b40. The ext4_chksum bridge function (!crc32c_append(!raw, data)) is verified correct for known test vectors (b'hello' produces the expected result). The GDT field offsets (bg_block_bitmap_csum_lo at 0x18, bg_block_bitmap_csum_hi at 0x38) match the kernel struct. The csum_seed derivation (from s_checksum_seed when CSUM_SEED is set) is verified correct.

POSSIBLE ROOT CAUSES:
(a) The crc32c crate 0.6.8 may have a hardware-acceleration edge case on this CPU (the test passes for small inputs but may diverge on 4096-byte inputs).
(b) There may be a subtle difference in how the kernel chains CRC32C for bitmap checksums vs how we do it (e.g., the kernel might zero some bits in the bitmap before checksumming, or exclude the last N bytes).
(c) The group descriptor checksum field offset may differ between mkfs.ext4 versions.
(d) There's a SECOND bitmap checksum function (compute_bitmap_checksum at line 1743) that uses csum_seed^group (XOR) instead of chaining — this function is wrong but verify_block_bitmap_checksum doesn't use it. However, it may have been copy-pasted from or to somewhere unexpected.

INVESTIGATION PLAN:
1. Add a test that creates a fresh ext4 image with mkfs.ext4, reads the raw bitmap bytes, and computes our CRC step-by-step, printing intermediate values.
2. Cross-validate by computing the same CRC using a second Rust CRC32C implementation (e.g., crc32c-hw or manual software CRC).
3. If the crate is correct, hexdump the raw GDT bytes and verify our parser reads the stored checksum from the right offset.
4. Check if mkfs.ext4 zeroes any bitmap bits before checksumming (e.g., unused tail bits beyond blocks_per_group).
5. Check the kernel source for ext4_block_bitmap_csum_set() to see if it modifies the bitmap before checksumming.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA:
- ext4_bitmap_free_space_matches_kernel test passes on a fresh mkfs.ext4 image.
- The root cause is documented in a code comment.
- If the crc32c crate has a bug, switch to an alternative or add a workaround.
- The wrong compute_bitmap_checksum function (XOR-based) is either removed or clearly marked as deprecated.
close_reason: Root cause: (1) group_number was chained into bitmap CRC but kernel doesn't do this, (2) checksum length was full block instead of clusters/inodes_per_group/8. Fixed in commits 20d65f4 and 7f4d6eb. Kernel reference test now passes.

title: Implement readiness evidence truth graph extractor
description:
## Background
The readiness dashboard summarizes current reports, but operators still need a graph-shaped answer to why a claim is valid, blocked, stale, simulated, or permission-bound. A truth graph makes provenance auditable across proof bundles, release gates, operational evidence indexes, broker packets, and readiness-lab reports.

## Implementation
Create a read-only extractor that emits nodes for reports, artifacts, commands, claims, beads, host capabilities, and freshness windows, plus edges for validates, blocks, supersedes, derives-from, and requires-permission. Keep it in ffs-harness and avoid a new database unless a committed JSON artifact is enough.

## Risks
The graph must not become a second source of truth. It should preserve validator decisions and expose contradictions rather than re-evaluating readiness independently.

## Acceptance
Unit tests cover stale-vs-fresh precedence, contradictory reports, missing raw logs, permissioned handoff nodes, and simulated evidence nodes. An E2E fixture emits JSON plus Markdown summary and proves every blocker edge links to a validator report path or bead id.

title: Succinct structures for free-space bitmaps (Graveyard Entry 7.1)
description:
# Succinct structures for free-space bitmaps (Graveyard Entry 7.1)

## GOAL
Replace traditional free-space bitmaps with succinct data structures (rank/select bitmaps) that support O(1) rank and select queries while using near-optimal space.

## BACKGROUND
From Alien CS Graveyard 7.1: Succinct bitmaps (Jacobson 1989, Clark 1996) store bitmaps in n + o(n) bits while supporting:
- rank(i): count set bits in positions [0, i) — O(1)
- select(k): find position of k-th set bit — O(1)

For free-space bitmaps, this enables:
- O(1) "how many free blocks in range?" (rank)
- O(1) "find k-th free block" (select) — replaces linear scan for allocation

## DESIGN
- Two-level rank structure: superblocks (every 2^16 bits) + blocks (every 2^9 bits)
- Select via rank binary search or Vigna's select structure
- Space overhead: ~6.25% over raw bitmap (vs 0% for plain bitmap, but queries are O(n))
- Integration: replace ffs-ext4 block bitmap and inode bitmap

## APPLICABILITY
- Optimization for large filesystems where bitmap scans are expensive
- Most impactful when block groups are large or filesystem is >90% full
- Could also accelerate mballoc buddy allocator queries

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] Succinct bitmap with O(1) rank and select
- [ ] Space overhead < 10% over raw bitmap
- [ ] Benchmark: allocation scan time vs plain bitmap
- [ ] Drop-in replacement for block/inode bitmaps
acceptance_criteria: Succinct bitmap with O(1) rank and select operations. Space overhead below 10% over raw bitmap. Two-level rank structure: superblocks (every 2^16 bits) plus blocks (every 2^9 bits). Drop-in replacement for block and inode bitmaps via BlockBitmap trait. Benchmark: allocation scan time vs plain bitmap at 50%, 80%, 95% fullness. Benchmark: rank/select latency vs linear scan. Unit tests: rank correctness for all-zeros, all-ones, random patterns. Unit tests: select correctness for sparse and dense bitmaps. Unit tests: round-trip serialization/deserialization. Property test: rank(select(k)) == k for all valid k.

title: btrfs send-stream Write data not chunked to u16 TLV limit (corrupt stream for >64KiB extents)
description: generate_send_stream (BTRFS_IOC_SEND, ffs-core/src/lib.rs:21553) emitted the entire file extent (num_bytes, up to 128MB) as a single SendAttr::Data attribute. SendStreamBuilder::add_command encodes attribute length with 'adata.len() as u16', silently wrapping mod 65536 for any data >65535 bytes. Result: corrupt, unparseable send stream for essentially any file with a >64KiB extent. Real btrfs chunks writes at BTRFS_SEND_READ_SIZE (48KiB) precisely because the TLV len is u16. Fix: chunk Write data into 48KiB pieces (emit_write_chunks), each with its own incrementing FileOffset; assert the u16 ceiling in add_command so future misuse fails loudly. Regression test generate_send_stream_chunks_large_writes covers a 100KB extent (3 chunks) and verifies round-trip + reassembly. Found in fresh-eyes review (PlumFern). Follow-up to bd-lczhq.

title: finish the bd-bhh0i sharded cutover: route DELETE through the sharded per-group records (creates are sharded, deletes are not — the gap that caused bd-pbyu0)
description:
bd-pbyu0 was fixed by turning the bd-bhh0i sharded create path OFF by default. That is MITIGATION, not the cutover. This bead is the cutover's missing half.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY INCOMPLETE. bd-bhh0i shipped a per-group sharded allocator to remove the single `ext4_alloc_state.write()` that serialises every FUSE worker on create — the mechanism behind the 1.510822x mounted parallel-metadata loss. The CREATE side landed and works. The DELETE side never did:

    create (sharded active)  -> ext4_sharded_alloc_inode -> debits the sharded per-group records
    unlink                   -> ffs_inode::delete_inode(.., single-lock alloc.groups, ..)
                                -> credits the single-lock array
    flush  (sharded active)  -> ext4_flush_group_descriptors reads
                                sharded.snapshot_group_stats() ONLY

So every delete's free credit lands in a structure the descriptor flush never reads. Measured: exactly one leaked inode per delete, e2fsck-dirty, and ENOSPC on an empty filesystem once the descriptors are exhausted.

`ext4_sharded_free_inode` (crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs:19005) already exists and is correct — it delegates to `PerGroupAlloc::free_inode`, which mirrors `free_inode_persist` statement for statement. But it is wired ONLY into create-rollback paths (lines 19518, 20099, 20112, 20118, 20148, 20165, all `let _ = ...`). Nothing routes an ordinary unlink through it.

⚠ THE BLOCK SIDE IS PROBABLY LATENTLY BROKEN THE SAME WAY, and this is the part most likely to be missed. The reproducing workload creates EMPTY files, so it frees no data blocks, which is why e2fsck reported inode-count errors and ZERO block-count errors. `delete_inode` also calls `free_blocks_persist` against the same single-lock `groups`, and the flush reads the same sharded snapshot — so deleting files WITH DATA should leak free-block counts by identical logic. That is untested. Test it before assuming the fix is inode-only: the repro script writes zero-byte files today and should be extended to write a block or two per file.

WHAT WOULD CLOSE THIS
1. Route the ordinary delete path's inode free through the sharded records when the sharded path is active. `delete_inode` currently does data-block frees, inode write-back and inode free as one unit against `&mut [GroupStats]`, so this needs either a backend seam (mirroring the `SingleLockDirAlloc` pattern already used on the create side) or a sharded-aware delete entry point.
2. Do the same for `free_blocks_persist` inside `delete_inode`, and prove it with a repro variant whose files carry data.
3. Re-run `scripts/pbyu0_mounted_repro.sh` with FFS_BHH0I_SHARDED=1 and require e2fsck clean — that is the acceptance gate, and it is ~40 seconds.
4. Only then flip `sharded_create_enabled_from_env(None)` back to `true` and update the test `sharded_create_mount_defaults_off_until_the_delete_side_lands_bd_pbyu0`, which exists specifically to stop that happening early.
5. Audit for any OTHER path that mutates `alloc.groups` while the flush reads the sharded snapshot. Create-rollback, orphan recovery, fast-commit replay and truncate all touch group stats; each needs the same question asked.

WHY IT IS WORTH FINISHING RATHER THAN DELETING: the sharded path addresses a real, measured 1.51x loss, and the create half is already written, validated and benched. The cost of leaving it disabled is that parallel metadata writes keep scaling negatively.

RESOLVE THE FEATURE-FLAG CONTRADICTION WHILE HERE. ffs-core/Cargo.toml documents `bhh0i_sharded_alloc` as "Default OFF — production keeps the single alloc RwLock (byte-identical)". ffs-cli/Cargo.toml line 39 has `default = ["bhh0i_sharded_alloc"]`. Both are still true after the bd-pbyu0 fix, because that fix changed the RUNTIME default, not the compile-time feature. Someone reading either file alone will draw the wrong conclusion about what ships.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
INDEPENDENTLY VALIDATED THROUGH THE FULL COMPARATOR, not just the 40-second repro.

The create/delete-storm row is the workload that EXPOSED bd-pbyu0: in FS11 the identical invocation aborted with "e2fsck did not report clean image ext4.fuse_a.img: exit status 4", and both FUSE arms carried 11 "Free inodes count wrong" errors each while both kernel arms were clean. Re-run on the fixed candidate (edbaeb4e, rebuilt with the default flip):

    arm        e2fsck
    kernel_a   rc=0, 0 inode-count errors
    fuse_a     rc=0, 0 inode-count errors
    fuse_b     rc=0, 0 inode-count errors

and the run proceeded past post-unmount validation to produce an admitted ratio, which it could not do before.

So the mitigation is confirmed by two independent instruments: the purpose-built repro script AND the four-arm comparator's own post-unmount e2fsck gate, on a workload that previously failed it deterministically.

ALSO WORTH NOTING: the external-load gate (bd-bt2dy) passed this run cleanly — samples=152, contended_fraction=0.0132, max_consecutive_over_limit=1 — during a period when the box's load average was 6-7, largely from the storm's own I/O. That is the corrected policy behaving as intended: it measures EXTERNAL CPU on off-placement cores, so a workload that loads the machine through its own arms does not trip its own gate. The pre-correction version would very likely have refused this run.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
⭐ THE BLOCK SIDE DOES NOT LEAK — my "probably latently broken the same way" hypothesis is WRONG and withdrawn. This narrows the fix substantially.

MEASURED. `scripts/pbyu0_mounted_repro.sh` now takes a per-file size, so the same storm can free real data blocks instead of only inodes. With sharded ON (FFS_BHH0I_SHARDED=1), 4 cycles x 300 files x 16 KiB (4 blocks each):

    Free inodes count wrong for group #1 (6992, counted=8192)
    Free inodes count wrong (31555, counted=32755)
    inode-count errors: 2, BLOCK-count errors: 0

Inode drift is 8192-6992 = 1200 = exactly 4 x 300, one per delete, unchanged. Block counts are EXACT despite 1200 files' worth of data blocks (4800 blocks) being allocated and freed through the same `delete_inode` call.

WHY THIS MATTERS FOR THE FIX. bd-pbyu0's original reproduction used empty files, so it could not distinguish "blocks are fine" from "blocks were never exercised". I recorded that as an explicit unknown rather than assuming either way. Now it is measured: the accounting divergence is INODE-ONLY.

The consistent reading is that file DATA blocks are allocated and freed through the SAME structure (both single-lock), so they never diverge, whereas INODES are allocated through the sharded per-group records and freed through the single-lock array. The bd-bhh0i cutover targeted parallel CREATE — inode allocation and directory-block growth — not the file write path, which is why only the inode counter has two writers.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE DESIGN, and it is a real simplification. The seam does NOT need to span multiple groups. `delete_inode` frees data blocks across arbitrary groups via extent walks and `free_indirect_blocks`, and routing THOSE through per-group locks would have been the hard part. It is unnecessary: leave block frees on the single-lock path exactly as they are, and route only `free_inode_persist` — which touches exactly ONE group, the one owning the inode — through `PerGroupAlloc::free_inode`.

`ext4_sharded_free_inode` (crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs:19005) already does precisely that and is already used by the create-rollback paths. The remaining work is to call it from the ordinary unlink path when the sharded path is active, instead of letting `delete_inode`'s trailing `free_inode_persist` credit the single-lock array.

REVISED ACCEPTANCE (replacing items 1 and 2 of the original list):
1. When sharded is active, the ordinary delete path routes its INODE free through the sharded records. Block frees stay on the single-lock path — measured safe, do not refactor them.
2. `scripts/pbyu0_mounted_repro.sh <cli> 6 500 512` with FFS_BHH0I_SHARDED=1 comes back CLEAN.
3. Same with a non-zero per-file size (e.g. `... 4 300 512 16`) — clean, and still zero block-count errors, proving the block path was not disturbed.
4. Only then flip `sharded_create_enabled_from_env(None)` back to true and update `sharded_create_mount_defaults_off_until_the_delete_side_lands_bd_pbyu0`.

The mechanism question that remains open: `delete_inode` performs the inode free as its final step against `&mut [GroupStats]`, so calling `ext4_sharded_free_inode` instead needs either a flag/variant that skips that step, or an unlink-path restructure that does the block frees and inode write-back via `delete_inode` and the inode free separately. That is a much smaller change than the multi-group seam I described before.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
DELETE IS NOW ROUTED THROUGH THE SHARDED RECORDS. Both acceptance runs pass on candidate b085996f.

    FFS_BHH0I_SHARDED=1, 6 cycles x 500 files, empty     -> CLEAN (0 inode, 0 block errors)
    FFS_BHH0I_SHARDED=1, 4 cycles x 300 files x 16 KiB   -> CLEAN (0 inode, 0 block errors)

The first is the exact configuration that leaked 3000 inodes before this change. The second confirms the block path was not disturbed, which was the risk of touching `delete_inode`.

THE CHANGE, and it is small because FS17's measurement made it small. `ffs_inode::delete_inode` is split into two composable halves:

  release_inode_storage(..) -> Result<bool>   frees data blocks, indirect metadata and any
                                              external xattr block, writes the zeroed inode
                                              back, and RETURNS is_dir. Does NOT free the
                                              inode number.
  delete_inode(..)                            = release_inode_storage + free_inode_persist,
                                              byte-identical to its old behaviour.

`ext4_unlink_impl` then picks the inode-free primitive by which structure allocated the inode: `ext4_sharded_free_inode` when the sharded path is active, `delete_inode` (single-lock) otherwise. Block frees stay on the single-lock path in BOTH branches, deliberately — FS17 measured that data blocks are allocated and freed through the same structure and never diverge, so routing them would have been unnecessary work on the hardest part of the function (extent walks and `free_indirect_blocks` span arbitrary groups).

TESTS: ffs-core 1198 passed / 0 failed, ffs-inode 131 + 10 passed / 0 failed, and the crate builds cleanly BOTH with and without `--features bhh0i_sharded_alloc` (the branch is cfg-gated on both sides).

⚠ I HAVE DELIBERATELY LEFT THE SHIPPING DEFAULT OFF, i.e. acceptance item 4 is NOT done and `sharded_create_mount_defaults_off_until_the_delete_side_lands_bd_pbyu0` still asserts `None => false`. Flipping it back is a separate decision that deserves evidence I do not have yet:

  1. The 40-second repro exercises ONE mount, ONE thread, and a create/delete storm. The sharded path exists for PARALLEL creates across groups, and its concurrency behaviour with the new delete routing is untested. `PerGroupAlloc::free_inode` locks only the group owning the inode, which is the intended design, but "compiles and passes a single-threaded storm" is not "correct under the 8-thread parallel-metadata workload it was built for".
  2. The perf claim that justifies the sharded path (the 1.510822x mounted parallel-metadata loss) has not been re-measured with delete routed through the shards. The whole point is that it must still be faster.
  3. bd-pbyu0 was a P0 that shipped because a cutover was declared complete when half of it was wired. Re-enabling on the strength of one storm test would repeat exactly that mistake.

WHAT WOULD FINISH IT: a parallel-metadata-write comparator row with FFS_BHH0I_SHARDED=1 on this candidate — clean e2fsck AND a ratio at least as good as the single-lock path — plus ideally a multi-threaded create/delete stress. Then flip the default and update the guard test.

REMAINING AUDIT ITEM from the original bead, still open: any OTHER path that mutates `alloc.groups` while the flush reads the sharded snapshot. Orphan recovery, fast-commit replay and truncate all touch group stats. The unlink path is fixed; those are unexamined, and each needs the same question asked.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
⛔ THE SHARDED PATH IS NOT READY, AND NOW THERE IS EVIDENCE RATHER THAN CAUTION. This is exactly the check I said the previous commit was missing, and it came back negative.

CONTROLLED RESULT, 8 workers x 6 cycles x 64 files, private per-worker directories:

    single-lock (control)   PASSES
    sharded                 FAILS

    worker 4 removing f00-050: invalid on-disk format: first-committer-wins
    conflict on block 38: snapshot=CommitSeq(3908), observed=CommitSeq(3909)

The control is the load-bearing half. Without it a failure here would be unattributable — it could equally have meant "concurrent removal was never supported on this path". The single-lock path passing the identical workload rules that out: the defect is the sharded routing.

MECHANISM, specific rather than speculative. Concurrent ALLOCATION works because the alloc path stages its bitmap update under `MergeProof::BitmapOr` via `rmw_block_bitmap_or` (crates/ffs-alloc/src/lib.rs:2710), so two threads SETTING different bits in one bitmap block merge instead of conflicting. The FREE path has no counterpart: it writes the whole bitmap block with `write_block`, so two threads CLEARING different bits in the same block first-committer-wins against each other.

That is a missing merge proof, not a locking bug. `PerGroupAlloc::free_inode` locks the owning group correctly; the conflict is one layer down, in how the bitmap write is staged into MVCC. The fix is the AND-NOT dual of `BitmapOr` — a clear-bits merge proof — wired into the inode-free path. bd-bhh0i already had to build `BitmapOr` for exactly the same reason on the alloc side, so there is a template.

WHAT MY PREVIOUS COMMIT ACTUALLY ACHIEVED, stated precisely so it is not over-credited: it converted a SILENT counter corruption into a LOUD failure. Before, concurrent deletes on the sharded path silently leaked counters (bd-pbyu0). Now they return a first-committer-wins error. That is strictly better — a filesystem that refuses an operation beats one that quietly corrupts its accounting — but it is NOT a working concurrent delete path, and the single-threaded green runs did not reveal it.

TEST DISPOSITION: the sharded variant is `#[ignore]`d with the diagnosis, the error text and the re-enable condition in its doc comment. The single-lock control stays ACTIVE, so a regression there would still fail the suite. Ignoring a known-open defect on an opt-in-disabled path is honest; leaving a red test in CI to signal it is not, and silently deleting it would be worse than either. Un-ignore it as part of the fix — it IS the acceptance gate for re-enabling the default.

THE SHIPPING DEFAULT STAYS OFF, now for a measured reason rather than a precautionary one. Anyone tempted to flip it should run this test first.

STILL OPEN on this bead, unchanged: the parallel-metadata comparator row (which would have hit this conflict), and the audit of orphan recovery, fast-commit replay and truncate for the same alloc.groups-versus-sharded-snapshot divergence.

The cost surfaces far away, as an unexplained FCW conflict between writers that were genuinely disjoint.

This is the leading candidate for the surviving conflict on an inode-table block, which persisted AFTER both known writers of that block were slot-scoped: a third writer taking the plain write_block path produces exactly this signature, including the gap-of-one contention timing (as opposed to the 77-178 gaps of the prune class, now fixed).

The downgrade is CORRECT and must not be suppressed — a genuine whole-block write has to invalidate a range proof. What was missing was visibility. insert_staged_write now warns with the block number and the discarded proof variant, so the offending writer can be found instead of bisected for.

CONFIRMED: THE RESIDUAL FCW IS CORRECT. This bead has been chasing a merge defect that is not there (2da11014).

The refusal record now names WHICH of the four range-validator branches refused, plus the range it blamed. Captured on a failing run:

    last:   Some(("IndependentKeys", 4096, 4096, 4096))
    reason: Some(("latest_modified_declared_range", 1792, 256))

latest modified the EXACT range the unlink declared: offset 1792, length 256. That is one inode slot — 256 is inode_size and 1792 is 7 x 256, slot 7 of the block. Another committed transaction wrote that same inode slot.

⭐ SO FIRST-COMMITTER-WINS IS THE RIGHT ANSWER, and every merge-proof fix aimed at this residual was aimed at the wrong layer. Inode numbers are REUSED: one worker frees inode N, zeroing its slot, while another allocates N and writes it. Same 256 bytes, genuine conflict. A proof that merged this would corrupt the freshly-allocated inode with the zeros of the free it raced. The loser must RETRY.

⚠ THE RETRY IS NOT A ONE-LINER, which is why I stopped at the diagnosis. The sharded free auto-commits its bitmap and per-group counter changes UNDER THE GROUP LOCK, outside the unlink transaction. An FCW abort discards the transaction but NOT that committed free, so a naive retry double-frees. Implementing it needs either the free brought inside the transaction, or a retry made idempotent against an already-credited free. Decide that before writing code.

That asymmetry is also the likely reason the single-lock control never needs a retry: its alloc RwLock serialises free-against-realloc, so the race cannot form. Worth confirming, since it predicts the sharded path needs a retry the single-lock path structurally cannot.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE BEAD. The acceptance gate (concurrent create/delete, e2fsck clean) is still the right gate, but "make the gate green" is now a retry problem, not a merge-proof problem. The five merge-layer fixes landed under this bead remain correct and independently valuable — bitmap proof, Arc forwarding, parent-inode slot scoping, proof accumulation, unconditional staged_base — they were just never going to close this.

Test stays #[ignore]d with the confirmed branch in its reason string. Default stays OFF.

comments.text:
CORRECTION TO MY OWN LAST COMMENT, and it makes the fix much smaller and safer than I described.

I wrote that "an FCW abort discards the transaction but NOT the already-committed free, so a naive retry double-frees". That framing assumed unlink runs inside one enclosing transaction. It does not. crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs:22043 is explicit:

    "Eager per-block commits (like ext4_create), NOT a batched
     TransactionBlockAdapter txn: measured ~2.7x faster on delbench"

tx_dev is block_device_adapter(), i.e. FsMvccBlockDevice. Every write_block and every rmw_block on that device BEGINS AND COMMITS ITS OWN TRANSACTION. There is no big transaction to abort, and therefore no "free committed outside the txn" asymmetry of the kind I claimed. My double-free warning was wrong for this path; I am withdrawing it rather than leaving it to shape someone else design.

WHAT THAT CHANGES. The FCW conflict aborts exactly ONE single-block transaction: the inode-table slot write inside write_inode_at_slot_scoped. Nothing else is rolled back and nothing else is left half-applied. So the missing retry is not a transaction-level replay of the unlink — it is a bounded retry of one RMW.

WHY A RETRY THERE IS SAFE, which is the part that makes this tractable. FsMvccBlockDevice::rmw_block reads the merge ancestor AT ITS OWN SNAPSHOT and applies a patch closure. For the inode-slot write the patch is idempotent: it copies a fixed 256-byte serialized inode into a fixed offset, computed before the RMW and independent of what the block currently holds. Re-running it against a FRESH snapshot after a conflict therefore produces the correct block, incorporating whatever the winner wrote elsewhere in it. That is textbook optimistic-concurrency retry and it is what the path is missing.

SCOPE CAUTION for whoever implements: rmw_block is shared by every proof-carrying writer, and NOT all of their patches are idempotent — a patch that increments a counter or ORs a bitmap bit read from the block would be wrong to replay blindly. So the retry belongs either inside write_inode_at_slot_scoped, or behind an explicit "this patch is replayable" opt-in on rmw_block. Do not wrap rmw_block unconditionally.

EVIDENCE THIS RESTS ON: the captured refusal (2da11014) showing reason latest_modified_declared_range at offset 1792 length 256 — one inode slot — plus the eager-commit comment above. The retry itself is UNIMPLEMENTED and UNMEASURED; the gate is the acceptance test for it.

comments.text:
GATE GREEN — the retry landed (8ad5afc0). Acceptance items 1-3 met; item 4 (flip the default) is NOT, deliberately.

THE FIX: (1) commit_error_to_ffs preserves an FCW conflict as the typed FfsError::MvccConflict instead of flattening it to an opaque Format string — without the type a retry predicate would have to match message text; MvccConflict already maps to EAGAIN so non-retrying callers are unaffected. (2) write_inode_at_slot_scoped retries that conflict, bounded at 8 attempts.

WHY THE RETRY IS THERE AND NOT IN rmw_block: this patch is idempotent — the 256-byte slot image is serialized before the loop and does not depend on the block contents, so replaying onto a base re-read at a fresh snapshot is correct. rmw_block is shared by writers whose patches are NOT idempotent (anything incrementing a counter or OR-ing a bit read from the block), and a retry there would silently corrupt them.

TESTS pin the contract, not the happy path: one uses a device that refuses twice, writes a winner into a DIFFERENT slot of the same block between refusals, then succeeds — it fails if the retry replays onto a stale base and clobbers that winner, which is the only subtle way this fix could be wrong. The other asserts the bound holds and the conflict still surfaces.

EVIDENCE: gate un-ignored and green across 7 consecutive full-suite runs, against 6-of-11 before the change. ffs-core 1246/0 with the feature, 1198/0 without; ffs-inode 133/0; ffs-mvcc 506/0. comments.text:
AUDIT ITEM CLOSED (f8aae736) — and a correction to what I wrote one comment ago.

I said orphan recovery and fast-commit replay "would leak identically the moment they run with sharded active". They CANNOT. Both run inside from_device/open_with_options — fast-commit apply at lib.rs:4734 and orphan recovery at :4761, a few lines apart in the same constructor — while ext4_sharded_alloc is not built until enable_writes (:7935), which seeds it by CLONING alloc_state.groups. A recovery free is therefore already reflected in the array the sharded records are cloned from. One writer, nothing to diverge, no defect. I asserted a leak from the call shape without checking the ordering; the shape was right and the conclusion was wrong.

THE AUDIT FROM THE ORIGINAL BEAD IS NOW COMPLETE, one defect and three clears, each cleared for a stated reason:
    rename-over-existing   DEFECT — fixed and tested (e2d68c38, 200 leaked inodes measured)
    orphan recovery        safe — runs before the sharded records exist
    fast-commit replay     safe — same constructor, same argument
    file shortening        safe — frees BLOCKS only (ab757b85 measured that blocks never diverge)
    create-rollback sites  already routed through ext4_sharded_free_inode

⚠ THE ORDERING IS LOAD-BEARING AND NOTHING ENFORCED IT. If the sharded structure is ever built earlier — at mount, or lazily on first write — both recovery paths silently become bd-pbyu0 again, one leaked inode per recovered orphan, with no test failing. Building it lazily is an obvious future optimisation and whoever does it has no reason to look at orphan recovery. Added sharded_records_do_not_exist_until_enable_writes_bd_y2t0r, asserting the records are ABSENT during mount-time recovery and PRESENT after enable_writes — the second half matters as much as the first, or the test passes vacuously if the field is renamed or never populated.

It is faster, so the premise holds and the row is worth taking.

⚠ NOT THE ACCEPTANCE ROW, and the test name and doc comment both say so. No FUSE, no kernel arm, no A/A null, one run per arm. It can FALSIFY cheaply; it cannot substitute. Each arm builds its OWN filesystem; sharing one would hand the second a warmed instance, which is the confound that produced a withdrawn 30.9x on bd-5vis3 two turns ago.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
BEHAVIOUR CHANGE I UNDER-DESCRIBED, now pinned and stated (85a8371c).

commit_error_to_ffs, added for the retry predicate, altered a USER-VISIBLE errno:

    before   FCW conflict -> FfsError::Format       -> EINVAL
    after    FCW conflict -> FfsError::MvccConflict -> EAGAIN

At the time I wrote "MvccConflict already maps to EAGAIN, so nothing downstream regresses". That was a statement about the mapping EXISTING, not that the errno for conflicts had MOVED. Any caller that does not retry now surfaces EAGAIN where it previously surfaced EINVAL.

The change is right and stays: EINVAL asserts the caller passed something invalid, which is false — the request was fine, another writer committed the same block first. EAGAIN says "try again", which is true and actionable. But it IS a change, and a client keying on EINVAL for this case would need updating. That belongs written down rather than discovered by someone debugging a FUSE client.

TWO TESTS PIN IT: the conflict maps to EAGAIN and explicitly NOT to EINVAL, so the old behaviour cannot silently return; and non-conflict commit failures keep their Format shape, confirming the typed mapping did not widen past the one case that needed it.

comments.text:

Early in this bead I fixed Arc<D> forwarding rmw_block, rmw_block_bitmap_or, rmw_block_bitmap_delta and read_merge_ancestor_at_snapshot, because a defaulted trait method that Arc does not forward silently DOWNGRADES every merge proof routed through it to a plain RMW, with no error. BlockDevice declares: block_count, block_size, read_block, read_contiguous_blocks, read_contiguous_into, read_merge_ancestor_at_snapshot, rmw_block, rmw_block_bitmap_delta, rmw_block_bitmap_or, supports_contiguous_reads, supports_contiguous_writes, sync, write_block, write_contiguous_blocks. comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
⛔ NEW DEFECT: dir-over-dir rename leaks a free BLOCK on the sharded path (42d75869). Reported and ignored with diagnosis; NOT fixed.

    200 dir-over-dir renames, sharded:  Free blocks count wrong for group #0 (13884, counted=14084)
    single-lock control, identical workload: CLEAN

Drift exactly 200 over 200 renames — one block per clobbered directory, i.e. the target directory own data block. The control is what makes it attributable to the sharded routing.

HOW IT WAS FOUND: extending my own rename fix test to the case it never covered. e2d68c38 was tested only with FILE targets; a directory target takes the expect_dir branch and, decisively, OWNS A DATA BLOCK. The concurrency gate could not catch it either — that workload creates and deletes files.

⚠ MECHANISM CONTRADICTS A FINDING THIS BEAD BANKED. The fix routes only the INODE free through the sharded records and leaves block frees single-lock, on the strength of ab757b85 measuring that data blocks never diverge. That holds for FILE data blocks. It does NOT hold for a DIRECTORY block, which the sharded dir-growth allocator hands out from the sharded records while release_inode_storage_deferring_writeback frees it against the single-lock array. bd-pbyu0 again, block side.

So ab757b85 conclusion should be read narrowly: "file data blocks do not diverge", not "the block side does not leak". I relied on the broader reading when I wrote the rename fix, and again when I closed the audit.

⚠ LIKELY NOT RENAME-SPECIFIC — this decides where the fix goes. rmdir uses the same release_inode_storage_deferring_writeback, so removing a sharded-allocated directory should leak identically. UNVERIFIED. Check rmdir FIRST: if it leaks too, the fix belongs in the shared release path, not in rename.

NOT FIXED deliberately — it needs the rmdir question answered, and a block-side seam is the piece of this cutover nobody has built. This also means acceptance item 4 (flip the default) is further away than the previous comment implied: the mounted perf row is no longer the only blocker.

ffs-core 1204/0 default, 1255/0 with the feature.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
RMDIR LEAKS TOO — the dir-block defect is NOT rename-specific (fe85e239).

    200 mkdir/rmdir cycles, sharded:
      Free blocks count wrong for group #0 (14087, counted=14287)

Drift exactly 200 over 200 cycles, matching the dir-over-dir rename leak one for one. The divergence lives in release_inode_storage_deferring_writeback — which rename and rmdir both use — so EVERY directory removal on the sharded path leaks its block, not just the clobbering-rename case I reported an hour ago.

WHERE THE FIX BELONGS, which is why the question was worth asking before writing any code: the SHARED release path, routing a directory own block free through the sharded records when sharded is active. Had rmdir come back clean the fix would have gone into rename — and left every rmdir still leaking.

SCOPE, restated honestly: this is a bigger hole in the bd-bhh0i cutover than this bead reflected earlier today. THE BLOCK SIDE HAS NO SHARDED SEAM AT ALL. The reason nobody noticed is that ab757b85 measured FILE data blocks — which genuinely do not diverge, being allocated and freed through the same structure — and that result got generalized to "the block side does not leak". Directory blocks come from ext4_sharded_alloc_dir_block and break the generalization. I relied on that generalization twice: writing the rename fix, and declaring the audit complete.

CONSEQUENCE FOR ACCEPTANCE ITEM 4: flipping the default is now blocked on a block-side seam, not just on the mounted perf row. The inode side of this cutover is done and validated; the block side is unstarted and now has two reproducing tests.

Both tests are #[ignore]d with their diagnosis and evidence; the single-lock control stays ACTIVE so a regression there still fails the suite. Neither is fixed — a block-side seam should be designed once, not patched twice.

ffs-core 1204/0 default, 1255/0 with the feature.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
THE BLOCK-SIDE SEAM ALREADY EXISTS — this is WIRING, not construction. Scoping correction for whoever fixes the dir-block leak.

I wrote that "a block-side seam is the piece of this cutover nobody has built". Wrong, and the correction shrinks the job:

    crates/ffs-core/src/sharded_alloc.rs:232   PerGroupAlloc::free_blocks      exists
    crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs:19183           ext4_sharded_free_blocks        exists
    crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs:62515           its round-trip test             exists

The primitive is present and tested. What is missing is that nothing routes a DIRECTORY block free through it.

WHERE THE WIRING GOES, and why it is not a one-liner: the directory block is released inside release_inode_storage_inner via the extent-shortening call at ffs-inode/src/lib.rs:1047, which frees against the single-lock &mut [GroupStats] deep inside an extent walk. The inode fix was easy because free_inode_persist was a single trailing call that could be split off. The extent path is not — it releases an arbitrary set of blocks across arbitrary groups as it walks.

TWO SHAPES, choose deliberately:
  1. Thread a sharded-aware free through the extent layer. General and correct, and the biggest change — ffs-extent is shared with every file-shortening path.
  2. Reconcile afterwards: capture the group-count delta the single-lock array took during release and credit the sharded records with it, as ext4_merge_recovery_alloc_into_live already does for recovery. Far smaller, contained to ffs-core.
Shape 2 is tempting and has a working in-tree precedent, but it is reconciliation rather than a seam and inherits a DOUBLE-CREDIT hazard — the mirror of the double-free I warned about on the retry. If any part of that release already reaches the sharded records, the delta lands twice. Verify before choosing.

⚠ CHECK THE FILE-SHORTENING PATH WHILE THERE. ab757b85 measured that FILE data blocks do not diverge, which is why the block side was left alone — but that was for files whose blocks came from the ordinary allocator. Wherever the sharded path hands out blocks (it does for directory growth), the same leak applies to shortening as to removal. The two reproducing tests on this bead cover directories ONLY.

ffs-core 1204/0. No code change this turn: the scoping is the deliverable, and shape 1 versus shape 2 should not be decided at the end of a long session.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
SCOPE SETTLED: the dir-block leak is DIRECTORY-ONLY. Files are not affected, and ab757b85 stands as measured.

Last comment I flagged a worry that the same leak might extend to the file-shortening path. It does not, and the reason is that the sharded allocator never hands out FILE data blocks. Every production caller of ext4_sharded_alloc_blocks is directory work:

    lib.rs:884   dir_alloc_blocks                    (sharded dir backend)
    lib.rs:1012  ShardedTreeBlockAllocator::alloc_block  (htree node allocation)
    lib.rs:19478 ext4_sharded_alloc_dir_block

Everything else calling it is a test. File data blocks come from the ordinary allocator, are freed through the same single-lock structure, and therefore cannot diverge — which is exactly what ab757b85 measured with 4 cycles x 300 files x 16 KiB coming back with ZERO block errors. That result was right; my earlier concern that it had been over-generalized applies only to the DIRECTORY case, and I should not have extended the doubt to files without checking.

SO THE DEFECT IS BOUNDED: it affects a directory own block and htree nodes — anything the sharded path allocated — released through the single-lock extent walk. rmdir and dir-over-dir rename both hit it, both have reproducing tests with passing single-lock controls, and file create/write/delete does not.

THAT ALSO SIZES THE FIX: it only has to cover blocks the SHARDED path allocated, which is directory growth and htree nodes — not the general extent walk. Shape 1 from the previous comment (thread a sharded-aware free through the whole extent layer) is therefore heavier than the defect requires; a fix scoped to directory-owned blocks is enough, and shape 2 reconciliation would only need to cover that same narrow set.

ffs-core 1204/0. No code change; this is scoping evidence.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
A HAZARD THAT DECIDES THE FIX, found while scoping the implementation — the sharded toggle is RUNTIME-MUTABLE, so "which structure allocated this block" is not answerable from the toggle at free time.

set_bhh0i_sharded_ops (lib.rs:19103) is an atomic swap on a live filesystem, not a mount-time constant. So a directory can be CREATED with sharded off — its block debited from the single-lock array — and REMOVED later with sharded on. Any fix that credits the sharded records because the toggle is on at free time would then OVER-CREDIT: the block was never debited there.

⚠ OVER-CREDIT IS WORSE THAN THE LEAK IT REPLACES. A leak makes the filesystem believe it has LESS free space than it does — conservative, e2fsck-visible, and it eventually returns ENOSPC. An over-credit makes it believe it has MORE, which is how you get an allocator handing out a block that is already in use. The current defect is the safe direction of the same accounting error, and a careless fix flips it to the dangerous one.

THIS RULES OUT the shape-2 reconciliation I described two comments ago in its simple form — "capture the single-lock delta during release and credit the sharded records with it" — because that is exactly a toggle-time decision about a creation-time fact.

WHAT A CORRECT FIX NEEDS: the free must reach whichever structure holds the debit for THAT block, and nothing currently records which one that was. The options are to make the toggle immutable for a mount lifetime (simplest, and arguably right — a per-op toggle on an allocator is a strange thing to have), or to make the two structures reconcilable so a free to the wrong one is detectable, or to route allocation so only one structure ever owns block accounting.

Note the same hazard did NOT bite the inode fix, because ext4_sharded_free_inode delegates to PerGroupAlloc::free_inode which mirrors free_inode_persist statement for statement against the SAME per-group record — the two structures hold the same value for an inode. Blocks are where they diverge.

No code change. I stopped at the design because the failure mode of getting this wrong is the dangerous direction of the error, and the two reproducing tests would show a fix passing while an untested toggle-change path over-credits. ffs-core 1204/0.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
THE TOGGLE HAZARD IS NOT REACHABLE IN PRODUCTION — which unblocks the fix, under an invariant that must be ENFORCED rather than assumed.

Last comment I showed set_bhh0i_sharded_ops is a runtime atomic swap, so "which structure debited this block" cannot be inferred from the toggle at free time, and I ruled out simple reconciliation on that basis. Checking the actual call sites narrows it:

    crates/ffs-cli/src/main.rs:2585  createbench_cmd    -> set(true) once at setup
    crates/ffs-cli/src/main.rs:2977  open               -> set(true) once at setup
    crates/ffs-cli/src/main.rs:6760  mount_with_fuse    -> set(true) once at setup
    set_bhh0i_sharded_ops(false) anywhere in production: NONE

So in production the toggle is effectively mount-immutable — set once before any filesystem activity, never flipped, never disabled. The create-with-single-lock-then-delete-with-sharded sequence that would over-credit is not reachable as the code stands. ONLY TESTS flip it, including my own reproducing tests, which set it before doing any work.

CONSEQUENCE: shape-2 reconciliation becomes safe, but ONLY under the invariant "the toggle does not change after the first allocation". That invariant currently holds by accident — three call sites happen to set it early — not by construction, and a fix that depends on it must make it explicit. The cheap way is to reject a toggle change once the allocator has handed out anything, which costs one flag and turns a silent over-credit into a loud refusal. My tests would need to keep setting it before their first operation, which they already do.

I am recording this rather than implementing because the invariant needs to land WITH the fix, not after it: a reconciliation that assumes mount-immutability while the setter stays freely callable is exactly the kind of load-bearing-but-unenforced assumption that produced the bd-pbyu0 P0 and the ordering assumption I pinned earlier on this bead.

ffs-core 1204/0. No code change.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
INVARIANT NOW ENFORCED (bf749171) — the prerequisite for the block fix, landed separately so the fix cannot arrive resting on an assumption.

THE INVARIANT: bhh0i_sharded_ops must not change after the sharded allocator has handed anything out. Block accounting depends on it — which structure holds a block debit is answerable only from the toggle — so a free routed on a CHANGED toggle credits a structure that never debited. That is an OVER-credit, the dangerous direction: the dir-block leak already on this bead under-counts free space and ends in ENOSPC, whereas an over-credit hands out a block already in use.

IT HELD ONLY BY ACCIDENT. createbench_cmd, open and mount_with_fuse each set it once at setup and nothing sets it false, so the hazard is unreachable today — but the setter is freely callable and nothing recorded the requirement. Same shape as the mount-ordering assumption I pinned earlier on this bead, and as the assumption whose violation produced bd-pbyu0.

MECHANISM: a flag armed by both sharded allocation entry points (ext4_sharded_alloc_blocks, ext4_sharded_alloc_inode) plus a debug_assert in the setter. An assertion rather than a refusal on purpose — in production the invariant already holds, so the only place a violation can be introduced is a test, and that is where debug assertions run. Release pays nothing.

CHECKED NOT VACUOUS: the full suite passes with it armed, so no existing test toggles after allocating — including my own reproducers, which set the toggle immediately after open. ffs-core 1255/0 with the feature, 1204/0 without.

WHAT IS NOW READY FOR WHOEVER TAKES THE FIX: mechanism, boundary (directory blocks and htree nodes only — files provably unaffected), two reproducers with passing single-lock controls, the seam primitive already present and round-trip tested (ext4_sharded_free_blocks), the over-credit hazard, and now the invariant enforced. The remaining work is the routing itself.

comments.author: DarkMeadow
comments.text:
⛔ SECOND BLOCK-SIDE DEFECT, MEASURED, AND IT IS THE DANGEROUS DIRECTION: single-lock
ALLOCATIONS are invisible to the sharded flush, not just single-lock frees.

Every block-side observation banked on this bead came from a workload that allocated and freed
the same blocks inside one mount. ab757b85 (4 cycles x 300 files x 16 KiB, ZERO block errors) was
read as "file data blocks do not diverge". It cannot support that reading: a storm that deletes
everything it creates cannot distinguish "the two structures agree" from "both deltas were lost
and summed to zero".

MEASURED with a workload that KEEPS its files - 200 files x 16 KiB, no deletes, one mount:

    sharded      Free blocks count wrong for group #0 (14287, counted=13487)
                 Free blocks count wrong             (14287, counted=13487)   [superblock]
    single-lock  CLEAN

Drift is exactly 800 = 200 files x 4 blocks - the retained file data, to the block. The
descriptors claim those blocks are FREE while their bitmap bits are SET, so the allocator would
hand out blocks already in use. The dir-block leak under-counts (conservative, ends in ENOSPC);
this over-counts.

MECHANISM: ext4_write allocates through alloc_blocks_persist against the single-lock
alloc.groups, while ext4_flush_group_descriptors and ext4_sync_superblock_free_totals source
every count from sharded.snapshot_group_stats() / total_free(). Neither structure describes the
filesystem on its own: the sharded records take dir-growth blocks and all inode alloc/free, the
single-lock array takes file data blocks, the extent-walk frees inside release_inode_storage (a
directory's own block and its htree nodes) and external xattr blocks.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE FIX THIS BEAD HAD QUEUED: routing the directory-block free through
ext4_sharded_free_blocks - the "wiring not construction" plan in the 13:13 comment - would have
closed rmdir and dir-rename and left this over-count untouched, because it is an ALLOCATION on
the other structure. Neither shape-1 nor shape-2 as described addresses it.

Test pair landed: retained_file_data_blocks_reach_the_flushed_descriptors_bd_y2t0r (sharded) with
its single-lock control. The control passing on the identical workload is what makes this
attributable to the sharded routing.

comments.author: DarkMeadow
comments.text:
CITABLE GATE, on exactly the bytes that are on main (DarkMeadow, 2026-08-14). The block-side
acceptance items 1-3 are met; item 4 is NOT, and stays that way for a measured reason.

Two runs, both remote-only through rch against a CLEAN HEAD baseline (`--base HEAD --clean-overlay
--no-overlay`, so the run cannot pick up a peer's uncommitted worktree edits):

  full suite   cargo test -p ffs-core --features bhh0i_sharded_alloc --lib
               1270 passed / 0 failed / 26 ignored   (127.41 s, worker vmi1149989)

  focused      ... --lib -- bd_y2t0r reconcil
               18 passed / 0 failed / 1 ignored

The 18, by name, because a summary count cannot show that the two previously-RED probes are the
ones that went green:

  rmdir_of_a_sharded_allocated_directory_does_not_leak_blocks_bd_y2t0r        (was #[ignore]d RED)
  rename_over_existing_directory_does_not_leak_a_block_bd_y2t0r               (was #[ignore]d RED)
  rename_over_existing_directory_under_single_lock_keeps_counters_exact       (new control)
  retained_file_data_blocks_reach_the_flushed_descriptors_bd_y2t0r            (the new defect)
  retained_file_data_blocks_under_single_lock_keep_counters_exact_bd_y2t0r    (its control)
  mixed_directory_and_file_churn_keeps_every_counter_exact_bd_y2t0r           (composite gate)
  mixed_directory_and_file_churn_under_single_lock_keeps_every_counter_exact  (its control)
  rename_over_existing_frees_the_target_inode_through_the_sharded_records     (unchanged, still green)
  rename_over_existing_under_single_lock_keeps_counters_exact                 (unchanged)
  concurrent_create_delete_under_sharded_alloc_keeps_counters_exact           (unchanged)
  concurrent_create_delete_under_single_lock_keeps_counters_exact             (unchanged)
  sharded_records_do_not_exist_until_enable_writes                            (unchanged)
  + the six sharded_alloc unit tests on the reconciliation arithmetic
The one ignored is sharded_vs_single_lock_parallel_metadata_in_process, which is a measurement and
was never a gate.

THE FIX, and why it is one seam rather than the routing this bead had queued. Both allocation
structures stay live under the sharded path and take disjoint operations — the sharded records take
directory-growth blocks and every inode alloc/free, `alloc.groups` takes file data blocks, the
extent-walk frees inside `release_inode_storage` and external xattr blocks — while the durability
boundary read ONLY the sharded snapshot. `PerGroupAlloc` now keeps the seed both structures were
built from at `enable_writes`, and `reconciled_group_stats` / `reconciled_total_free` return
`sharded_now + (single_lock_now - seed)`, wired into all three consumers
(`ext4_flush_group_descriptors`, `ext4_capture_group_descriptors`,
`ext4_sync_superblock_free_totals` — the last so the superblock cannot disagree with its own
descriptors). Counts only: the flush already re-derives bitmap checksums and the UNINIT flags from
the device bytes. Nothing is double-counted because no operation debits both structures.

Routing the directory-block free through `ext4_sharded_free_blocks` — the "wiring not construction"
plan — would have closed rmdir and dir-rename and left the retained-file OVER-count untouched,
because that one is an ALLOCATION on the other structure. That is why the measurement came first.

⚠ ITEM 4 STILL NOT DONE. `sharded_create_enabled_from_env(None)` stays false and the guard test
still asserts it. The mounted parallel-metadata row cannot be taken today: the comparator's
`external_load_during_run` gate refused three btrfs runs on this host this afternoon (85 of 85
