busy. That gate is correct and must not be relaxed to get this flipped.

REMAINING ON THIS BEAD, unchanged: item 4 only — the mounted parallel-metadata comparator row with
FFS_BHH0I_SHARDED=1 (clean e2fsck AND a ratio at least as good as the single-lock path), then flip
the default and update `sharded_create_mount_defaults_off_until_the_delete_side_lands_bd_pbyu0`.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
ACCEPTANCE PROBE RUN AND PASSING — item 3 is now cited evidence, not an assumption (AzureBay, 2026-08-15, thinkstation1).

HARNESS: scripts/pbyu0_mounted_repro.sh. CANDIDATE: locally built ffs-cli, x86-64-v3 + PGO
(codegen_isa compile_avx2=true, pgo_profile_sha256 cc6c121c9ee77d8a...), built and executed on
thinkstation1, kernel 6.17.0-41-generic. Run LOCALLY by necessity — the probe mounts FUSE and shells
out to the ext4 formatter and checker, so no rch worker is involved and none is quotable for it.

FOUR RUNS, ALL WITH FFS_BHH0I_SHARDED=1, all reported 'clean (did NOT reproduce)':
  10 cycles x  500 files x  512 MiB, KiB/file=0  -> inode-count errors 0, block-count errors 0
  10 cycles x  500 files x  512 MiB, KiB/file=8  -> 0, 0
  40 cycles x 2000 files x 2048 MiB, KiB/file=0  -> 0, 0   (the bead's default shape)
  40 cycles x 2000 files x 2048 MiB, KiB/file=8  -> 0, 0

THE BLOCK SIDE, which this bead flagged as 'probably latently broken the same way' and untested, is
covered by the KiB/file=8 runs and is CLEAN at full scale. It is clean BY CONSTRUCTION, not by luck:
the descriptor flush no longer reads snapshot_group_stats() alone, it calls
PerGroupAlloc::reconciled_group_stats(live), computing sharded_now + (single_lock_now - seed). Both
structures were seeded from the same array at enable_writes and NO operation debits both, so neither
delta is lost nor double counted. The doc at crates/ffs-core/src/sharded_alloc.rs:160 names the
dangerous direction explicitly: a retained file's data-block debit going missing would leave the
descriptors offering blocks whose bitmap bits are already set.

That reconciliation is ALSO a structural answer to item 5. Enumerating every other path that mutates
alloc.groups would have been the weaker form; reconciliation makes create-rollback, orphan recovery,
fast-commit replay and file-shortening correct without each needing its own wiring, because whatever
they move in either structure appears in the delta.

ITEMS 1, 2 and 5 were landed by peers (1b4e8ca3 inode free routing, e2d68c38 rename-over-existing,
plus the reconciliation). I did not redo them and I am NOT closing this bead.

ITEM 4 — flipping the runtime default — DELIBERATELY NOT DONE. The stated gate has passed, so the
correctness argument is satisfied. But the flip's JUSTIFICATION is a perf claim (the 1.510822x
mounted parallel-metadata loss) and that number cannot be taken right now: the comparator's
external_load_during_run veto refused 2/2 attempts today at 100 percent of samples, and the box is
still at 5 CPUs above 25 percent busy against a limit of 2. Flipping a production write-path default
on an unmeasured perf justification is exactly what I filed bd-6kpp4 against this morning, where the
btrfs checksum default shipped ahead of the measurement its own deciding bead was blocked on. Doing
the same thing in the other direction on the same day would be indefensible.

window; (b) updating the guard test that exists to prevent an early flip.

DONE HERE: the feature-flag contradiction listed last in this bead. ffs-core/Cargo.toml said
'Default OFF - production keeps the single alloc RwLock' while ffs-cli/Cargo.toml said 'Ship it for
writable ext4 mounts; FFS_BHH0I_SHARDED=0 remains an explicit operational rollback switch'. The
second is simply false after bd-pbyu0: the runtime switch is opt-IN (=1), not opt-out (=0). Both
manifests now state the two-level truth — compiled in by default, NOT active by default.

title: Pin ext4 invalid dir fixture error payloads
description: Source-aware queue reports zero local claimable rows, so add bounded non-mutating conformance coverage for committed invalid fixtures. The ext4 directory invalid-fixture tests currently accept broad InvalidField/InsufficientData shapes, even though the fixture bytes deterministically imply exact ParseError field, reason, offset, needed, and actual payloads. Tighten the existing tests for truncated checksum tail, rec_len-too-small, rec_len-min12, rec_len-unaligned, name_len-overflow, tail-padding-nonzero, and bad-tail-header fixtures so error-contract drift is caught directly.
close_reason: Completed: pinned exact ParseError payloads for ext4 invalid directory fixtures, including field/reason and truncated-tail offset/size details.

title: [parity][perf] ext4 fallocate eagerly zeros+writes extents instead of unwritten/uninitialized

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: Confirmed via diagnostic: FrankenFS fallocate (preallocate) produces WRITTEN, eagerly-zeroed extents — map_logical_to_physical reports unwritten=false for preallocated blocks, and a partial write into them reads back correctly with the rest zero. Real ext4 fallocate allocates UNWRITTEN (uninitialized) extents lazily: no eager zeroing, reads return zeros via the unwritten flag, and the first write to a region marks just that part written. PARITY: e2fsck/ext4 expect the EXT4_EXTENT unwritten bit (ee_len high bit) on preallocated-but-unwritten ranges; FrankenFS images will show all-written extents after fallocate. PERF: eager zeroing writes every preallocated block (O(size) I/O) where upstream does O(1) metadata-only. Current behavior is CORRECT (safer — no stale-data exposure) but is a vs-upstream gap. Fixing it = implement unwritten-extent preallocation + ensure the write path marks-written-on-first-write (mark_written exists in ffs-extent but the ext4 write path does not call it; the find_map at lib.rs ~12257 also does not special-case unwritten). Sizeable feature; filed for visibility, not a quick win.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: IMPLEMENTATION PLAN (feasibility assessed). The ext4 READ path ALREADY handles unwritten extents correctly (lib.rs ~7437: resolve_extent returns (phys, unwritten); reads fill zeros when unwritten). So closing this gap is a 2-part write-side change, but the two parts are COUPLED and the second is data-corruption-risky: (1) fallocate preallocate (the else branch in ext4_fallocate) must allocate extents flagged UNWRITTEN (raw_len bit 15) instead of allocating + writing zero blocks — eliminates the O(size) zeroing I/O; needs an allocate-unwritten path (allocate_extent currently produces written extents; ffs_extent has mark_written but no allocate-unwritten helper yet). (2) the WRITE path must, on first write into an unwritten block: (a) for a PARTIAL block write, zero-fill the non-written portion of the RMW buffer instead of reading the physical block — currently ext4_write (lib.rs ~12346) only zero-inits the buffer for FULL-block writes and reads the existing physical for partial; once blocks are unwritten (not eagerly zeroed) that physical content is RECYCLED garbage, so a partial write would EXPOSE stale data for the non-written bytes (data exposure); and (b) call ffs_extent::mark_written for the written range (splitting the unwritten extent) so the read path stops returning zeros for it — the find_map at lib.rs ~12257 currently matches unwritten extents without marking them, so without (b) writes into preallocated regions would be LOST (read returns zeros). COUPLING: parts 1 and 2 must land together — shipping unwritten fallocate without the partial-write zeroing + mark_written causes data loss/exposure. TEST STRATEGY (now enabled by bd-cc6ua, write-path tests run on rch): after the change, the existing collapse/insert/zero_range/prealloc tests must still pass, plus add: prealloc-then-partial-write reads back the written bytes AND zeros elsewhere (no stale exposure); prealloc reports unwritten + reads zeros; prealloc-then-full-overwrite. RISK: high (write hot path, data corruption on error); recommend a dedicated multi-step effort, not a rushed single pass. Perf payoff: fallocate of N blocks goes O(N) writes -> O(1) metadata (large preallocations).

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: DONE. ext4 fallocate now allocates UNWRITTEN/uninitialized extents (ffs_extent::allocate_unwritten_extent) instead of allocating + writing zero blocks — preallocate is now O(1) metadata, not O(size) I/O (profiler: blocks=128/512/2048 -> per_block_ns 2442/401/116, all extents=1 unwritten_extents=1; the single-extent cost amortizes as size grows). The write path handles unwritten targets safely: for an unwritten (or freshly-hole-allocated) block the RMW buffer is ZERO-FILLED instead of reading the (possibly recycled) physical block, then the written sub-range is committed and ffs_extent::mark_written clears the unwritten flag for that block (splitting the extent). Matches upstream ext4 (unwritten extents on fallocate); the read path already returned zeros for unwritten. PROOF: (1) write_fallocate_prealloc_creates_unwritten_extents_and_reads_zero; (2) write_into_unwritten_prealloc_zero_fills_and_marks_written_block (partial write: before/after bytes zero, target block marked written, neighbors stay unwritten); (3) write_into_reused_unwritten_block_does_not_expose_recycled_data — the GOLD-STANDARD exposure guard: writes 0xAB to a block, frees it, fallocate REUSES that exact dirty physical block (verified reused=true, a_phys==b_phys==2097) as unwritten, partial-writes, and reads ZEROS not 0xAB — definitively no recycled-data exposure (no zero-masking). ffs-core 894 lib tests pass; clippy -D warnings clean; #![forbid(unsafe_code)] intact. Also incidentally fixes a latent exposure on hole-fill partial writes (the None/allocate branch now zero-fills too).

title: ffs-dir: remove_entry rejects interior htree dx_node blocks as corrupt on metadata_csum
description: ext4 dir-entry removal (the remove and rename paths) scans every directory block calling ffs_dir::remove_entry, skipping only the dx_root at logical 0. An interior htree dx_node block (indirect index level) has a leading fake dirent with inode=0 and rec_len == block_size (spans the whole block). On a metadata_csum fs, ext4_dir_reserved_tail()=12 so remove_entry limit = block_size-12; the fake dirent end (block_size) > limit => returns Err(Corruption exceeds usable block area). So removing an existing entry from a MULTI-LEVEL (indirect_levels>=1) htree dir spuriously fails IF an interior dx_node block precedes the target leaf in logical order (possible in kernel-created dirs; now reachable for FrankenFS-created dirs via the bd-owt2r multi-level rebuild). Non-csum is unaffected (rec_len==block.len()==limit, returns Ok(false)). FIX: remove_entry should treat a leading inode=0 fake dirent spanning the entire block (rec_len==block.len()) as a non-leaf index node and return Ok(false), matching the non-csum path, instead of rejecting the block. One-place fix covers both removal call sites.
close_reason: Fixed in 37895258 (+clippy 4366cb02): remove_entry now skips interior htree dx_node blocks (leading inode-0 fake dirent spanning whole block -> Ok(false)) instead of Err(Corruption) on metadata_csum, so the remove/rename block scans pass over them to reach the real leaf. title: Kernel-conformance pin for normalize_dx_major_hash bit/sentinel invariants
description: Found via /porting-to-rust audit. crates/ffs-ondisk/src/ext4.rs has normalize_dx_major_hash (line 4870) which enforces two kernel invariants from fs/ext4/hash.c lines 256-264 of ext4fs_dirhash: (1) the major hash must have its low bit cleared (the low bit is reserved as a flag bit in htree collision-chain traversal), and (2) the major hash must not equal (EXT4_HTREE_EOF_32BIT << 1) = 0xfffffffe (which would collide with the htree end-of-tree cursor sentinel; the kernel maps it to (EOF-1) << 1 = 0xfffffffc). These invariants are silently load-bearing — every htree directory lookup depends on them. A regression that removed the masking or sentinel-bump would corrupt collision-chain traversal and cause spurious "no such entry" returns on otherwise-valid lookups. The existing dx_hash_matches_kernel_reference_vectors test only covers three named (name, seed) pairs and does not exercise the EOF boundary. Fix: add ext4_dx_hash_major_hash_invariants_match_kernel test pinning (a) low-bit-clear for arbitrary inputs via proptest, (b) sentinel collision avoidance for arbitrary inputs, (c) idempotence (normalize(normalize(h)) == normalize(h)), and (d) named boundary values from the kernel formula.
close_reason: completed

title: btrfs link-count ops do not update target inode ctime (POSIX status-change parity)
description: POSIX requires link() and link-removal to mark the target file's last-status-change time (ctime) for update when its link count changes; a rename that drops an overwritten target likewise updates that inode's ctime if it survives. ext4_link (touch_ctime, lib.rs ~14636) and ext4 link-removal (touch_ctime on the surviving child) do this; btrfs goes through btrfs_adjust_nlink which updates only inode.nlink, never ctime. So on btrfs, adding/dropping a hard link (and a rename that removes an overwritten hard-linked target) leaves the inode ctime stale — diverging from ext4 and the kernel, breaking ctime-based tooling (tar/rsync change detection, find -newer, backup/audit). Clean ext4-vs-btrfs asymmetry. FIX: btrfs_adjust_nlink takes the op timestamp (secs,nanos) and sets ctime_sec/ctime_nsec, mirroring btrfs_touch_inode_times; all 3 callers already hold a timestamp snapshot. Deterministic test: after link, target.ctime == parent.mtime (same op timestamp).
close_reason: Fixed in d85160a7: btrfs_adjust_nlink now takes the op timestamp and stamps ctime_sec/ctime_nsec on the affected inode (link +1, link-removal -1, rename-overwrite-target -1), mirroring ext4_link/ext4 link-removal touch_ctime. Regressions btrfs_link_updates_target_ctime_bd_ypyxq + btrfs_link_removal_updates_surviving_inode_ctime_bd_ypyxq (target/survivor ctime == parent mtime). ffs-core 1042/0; clippy clean.

title: btrfs: DIR_INDEX keyed by child_objectid instead of per-directory sequence number
description: btrfs_insert_dir_entry (ffs-core lib.rs ~18849) sets the DIR_INDEX key offset to item.child_objectid. Real btrfs keys DIR_INDEX by a monotonic per-directory sequence number (the dir inode's index_cnt / sequence field, assigned at link time), which gives readdir its creation-order iteration and a unique item per directory entry. Consequences of the divergence: (1) readdir order is by child_objectid, not creation order; (2) hard links (same child_objectid, multiple names in one dir) collide onto ONE DIR_INDEX key and merge payloads into a multi-entry item, whereas btrfs assigns each link its own unique sequence/item; (3) the dir inode carries no persisted sequence counter (BtrfsInodeItem has no sequence field). FrankenFS round-trips its own writes correctly (readdir parses the merged item), so this only manifests when the KERNEL/btrfs check reads a FrankenFS-written image — btrfs-check-validation-gated, same class as bd-x3fcu. FIX (multi-part): add a sequence/index counter to BtrfsInodeItem (persisted, monotonic, base 2), use it as the DIR_INDEX offset, give each hard link its own item, increment per insert. Needs a privileged btrfs check runner to validate kernel parity. btrfs RW is ungated (require_btrfs_rw_allowed always Ok) so this is reachable in production writes.
notes: FIXED (f73d54ae): btrfs_insert_dir_entry now keys DIR_INDEX by a monotonic per-directory sequence (btrfs_next_dir_index_seq = max existing offset + 1, base BTRFS_DIR_START_INDEX=2, mirroring the kernel's mount-time index_cnt recovery so no new persisted inode field is needed). Each link — including hard links sharing a child_objectid — now gets its own unique DIR_INDEX item (no payload merge), and the assigned sequence is threaded into the matching INODE_REF so INODE_REF.index == DIR_INDEX.offset across all 6 write callers (create file/dir/node/symlink, link, rename). readdir already orders by DIR_INDEX.offset, so iteration is now creation-order. Proof: 2 new round-trip tests (sequence keying + objectid-collision uniqueness; end-to-end INODE_REF/DIR_INDEX match) + updated the malformed-existing fail-closed test to corrupt INODE_REF (the pre-mutation parse the link path still performs). ffs-core 937/937 green. NOTE: standalone 'btrfs check' E2E of a DIR_INDEX image is still blocked by bd-x36qn's UNRELATED structural errors (parent transid, extent backref counts, root level byte) — the format-level DIR_INDEX divergence this bead describes is corrected and round-trip-proven; kernel-parity validation of the whole image awaits bd-x36qn.

The per-block loop re-called collect_extents_with_scope (re-walk + re-materialize the whole extent tree) every block position = O(N*E) for an N-block write, even for pure overwrites. Tree changes only at the two in-loop set_extent_root sites (allocate_extent, mark_written); collect once + invalidate exactly there. Overwrite now O(E). Isomorphic (cache holds same Vec, rebuilt after every mutation). 1098 ffs-core tests green, clippy clean.

title: JBD2 descriptor/revoke block checksum omits 4-byte tail instead of zeroing it
description: In crates/ffs-journal/src/lib.rs, verify_jbd2_block_checksum handles JBD2_BLOCKTYPE_DESCRIPTOR and JBD2_BLOCKTYPE_REVOKE by computing crc32c over &block[..bs - 4]. However, Linux jbd2_descriptor_block_csum_verify temporarily zeroes the 4-byte tail checksum field and then computes the checksum over the *entire* block size (j->j_blocksize). By slicing off the last 4 bytes instead of hashing 4 zero bytes, the rust implementation produces a different CRC32C value and will incorrectly fail validation for valid JBD2 descriptor blocks.
close_reason: Descriptor/revoke checksum verification now hashes the full block with a zeroed 4-byte tail, matching Linux jbd2 semantics; added regression coverage and passed targeted rch fmt/test/check/clippy.

title: [PERF] btrfs_ino_lookup scans entire fs-tree on every call — O(N) per ioctl with no caching
description:
# Performance concern from modes-of-reasoning pass

## Finding

`OpenFs::btrfs_resolve_inode_path` at crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs:14447+ (added in f70dcca for bd-caex2) calls `self.walk_btrfs_fs_tree(cx)?` unconditionally on every invocation, walking every leaf entry in the subvolume fs-tree to build the `parent_by_child: BTreeMap` index. That means each BTRFS_IOC_INO_LOOKUP ioctl costs O(N) where N = total fs-tree items (inodes + dir entries + refs + xattrs + extents).

For a typical ext4/btrfs image the cost is negligible. For a large image (millions of inodes / tens of millions of items), a single ioctl can scan multi-megabyte indexes and iterate hundreds of thousands of entries. A caller issuing K ioctls imposes O(K*N) work — a slow query amplifier if a tool (e.g., `btrfs subvolume list`) iterates many inodes.

## Evidence

- Entry point: crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs:14439 `fn btrfs_resolve_inode_path`
- Full-tree scan: `let entries = self.walk_btrfs_fs_tree(cx)?`
- Index built per call: BTreeMap<u64, (u64, Vec<u8>)> with one entry per INODE_REF item
- No cache, no early-termination (we build the full index before walking the chain even though we only need back-refs along the path)

## Fix directions (choose at implementation time)

1. **Early-exit walk.** Replace `walk_btrfs_fs_tree → build full index → walk` with a demand-driven search: at each step, search the fs-tree for items with key (objectid, INODE_REF, *) and stop at the first match. Each hop is an O(log N) btree lookup; total cost O(depth * log N).
2. **Per-subvolume cache** on `OpenFs` keyed on the fs-tree root generation. Invalidated on subvolume changes. Sub-μs per lookup after warmup.
3. **Batched multi-inode resolution.** If the caller is resolving multiple inodes in one request (e.g., a future `list_paths`), build the index once and amortize.

For V1, (1) is the simplest and keeps the code path stateless. (2) is the right long-term answer once we know the access pattern.

## Acceptance

- A synthetic image with 10K inodes completes a sequence of 100 INO_LOOKUP ioctls in bounded time (wall-clock cap, e.g., < 1s).
- Microbenchmark in `benches/` documents the per-ioctl cost.
- Unit tests from bd-caex2 continue to pass without regression.
close_reason: writable demand-driven walk + read-only cached index

title: perf(fuse): make the kernel-mandated security.capability round trip cheaper — dispatch/queue-depth/splice, not suppression (bd-ha71t successor)

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
SUCCESSOR TO bd-ha71t, filed 2026-08-15 (AzureBay) once suppression was closed BY MEASUREMENT.

WHY THIS EXISTS. Linux issues an uncached getxattr(security.capability) per path-based metadata op,
and it is the SHARED component under the worst ratios: readdir+stat 7.7x and warm stat 4.8x slower
than kernel btrfs, plus create/delete storm and parallel metadata. Every route to SUPPRESSING it is
now closed by measurement, not argument:
  * ENOSYS — per-CONNECTION by kernel contract, set by ANY ENOSYS reply regardless of attribute
    name, so it disables getxattr for the whole mount and takes bd-ext4-xattr-row-unscored-a21dz
    with it. Closed by contract, not experiment.
  * FUSE_HANDLE_KILLPRIV (V1, bit 19) — negotiated, INERT. 2001 probes for 2001 path stats.
  * FUSE_HANDLE_KILLPRIV_V2 (bit 28) — negotiated and ACCEPTED by the kernel, INERT.
    4000 probes -> 4000 probes for 2000 path stats (d18bc72e).
The daemon-side ANSWER is already ~free via the capability memo. What remains is pure FUSE
transport: the round trip itself.

SCOPE: make that one round trip cheaper. Candidate surfaces, and this is deliberately the
bd-kdmu4 / FFS_FUSE_WORKERS territory rather than a new invention — worker dispatch, request queue
depth (max_background / congestion_threshold), splice, and anything that reduces per-request
wakeup/copy cost.

⛔ READ THIS BEFORE RE-RUNNING FFS_FUSE_WORKERS. The banked 1.923x readdir+stat win for
FFS_FUSE_WORKERS DOES NOT REPRODUCE. A same-window A/B measured it 3.6% SLOWER at the banked 1
daemon CPU. The original wide-cpuset 0.50-0.59 ratios are INADMISSIBLE: the harness only ever
placed the daemon on a private physical core at --fuse-cpus 1, so every wider cpuset sat the daemon
on the clients SMT siblings, which is also what made the serial arm fail its own A/A null
(1.094 -> 1.019 once fixed in 7ce6e3ef). Do not re-bank that number; treat worker dispatch as
UNMEASURED at correct placement, not as a known win.

CHEAPEST FIRST STEP, and it needs no quiet window: bd-ha71t measured TWO probes per path-based stat
(4000 for 2000), where the bead had assumed one. Nobody has explained the factor of two. If one of
the pair is redundant — same inode, same name, back to back — then halving it is a 2x cut on the
shared metadata component and is provable with a COUNTED mechanism, which is the only kind of
measurement that currently survives the comparator external-load veto. Start by classifying the
probe stream by inode and ordering from the ffs::fuse::xattr_probe trace before touching dispatch.

ACCEPTANCE: any timing claim needs the mounted comparator with the kernel incumbent live in the
same invocation, both A/A nulls, observed thread count, executing-ELF SHA-256, and the rch WORKER
plus HARNESS named. A counted-mechanism result (probe or request counts) is admissible on its own
and does not need a quiet window — that is how bd-ha71t was closed.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
FIRST LEVER LANDED (dfb3e3c7), and the characterisation that found it (AzureBay, 2026-08-15).

CHARACTERISATION FIRST, as this bead asked. Classifying the probe stream by inode explains the
factor of two nobody had explained:

    ino=1, ino=14, ino=1, ino=15, ino=1, ino=126, ...
    4002 probes for 2000 path stats, of which 2002 land on ino=1 (the MOUNT ROOT)

Then a depth control, 500 stats each, counted mechanism:
    files at the mount root      -> 1000 probes, 500 on ino=1, 2 per stat
    files one directory down     -> 1000 probes, 500 on ino=1, 2 per stat
IDENTICAL. So the root probe is per-OPERATION, not per path COMPONENT, and intermediate
directories are never probed at all. That rules out "deep paths cost more" and bounds the working
set at exactly two inodes.

TWO DEFECTS FOUND, both making the daemon-side cost maximal:
  1. The memo was gated on `read_only`, so on a READ-WRITE mount it was never consulted and never
     populated — every probe paid a full format-level ops.getxattr through a request scope. This
     bead already recorded the symptom ("a read-write mount (memos disabled) counted 2005 requests
     for 2000 path stats") without naming the cause.
  2. The memo was ONE slot (a single AtomicU64). Against a strictly alternating two-inode stream
     that is the worst possible size: each probe evicts the other half, so the hit rate collapses to
     ~0% on exactly the pattern the memo exists for.

FIXED: two slots (hit does not reshuffle, or it reproduces the thrash), forget(ino) on
setxattr/removexattr called BEFORE dispatch and unconditionally, and the read_only gate removed —
soundness now comes from invalidation rather than immutability, since the memo caches only ABSENCE
and the only failure it must not permit is "reported absent after it exists".

5 tests, including the negative case that makes the writable-mount enablement sound (a forgotten
inode must not be reported absent) and the one that fails on a one-slot memo.

⚠ NOT VERIFIED BY TESTS YET. cargo check -p ffs-fuse --lib is clean on rch worker hz2, but
cargo test was REFUSED across three rounds with active_project_exclusion=1 and critical_pressure=1
(a peer frankenfs build holds the project slot; fleet posture "degraded"). Scheduling refusal, not
a test failure. NEXT PERSON: run `cargo test -p ffs-fuse --lib capability_memo` before trusting this.

NEXT, and it needs no quiet window: re-run the probe/memo counters on a read-write mount to get the
before/after hit rate as a counted mechanism. The expectation to falsify is that memo hits go from
~0 to ~all-but-two per mount. Only after that does a timed comparator row make sense.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
THE FACTOR OF TWO IS EXPLAINED, and it KILLS this bead's proposed cheapest lever (ProudBarn, 2026-08-16, analysis only — no code, no build).

THIS BEAD ASKED: 'bd-ha71t measured TWO probes per path-based stat (4000 for 2000), where the bead had assumed one. Nobody has explained the factor of two. If one of the pair is redundant — SAME INODE, same name, back to back — then halving it is a 2x cut on the shared metadata component.'

IT IS ANSWERED, by measurement already banked on bd-2pq73 (AzureBay, 8ed753ca), not by argument. That bead's slot-scaling progression is the proof:
    1 slot  (disabled on RW):    0 / 2000 hits
    2 slots, shift-down     :  501 / 2000
    2 slots, 2-way LRU      : 1000 / 2000
    64 slots, direct-mapped : 1950 / 2000
and its stated mechanism: 'the stream is root, file, root, file, so two slots held the root and exactly ONE file; a 50-file sweep evicted each before it recurred. Every root probe hit, every file probe missed.'

⛔ CONSEQUENCE: the two probes per path op are on DIFFERENT inodes — one on the parent directory, one on the child file. They are the kernel walking the path, not a duplicated probe. The redundancy hypothesis this bead rested on required 'same inode'; that precondition is measurably false. NEITHER probe is redundant, so there is no 2x to be had by dropping one, and the 'classify the probe stream by inode and ordering before touching dispatch' step is no longer worth running — bd-2pq73's 2-slot plateau already classified it, at half the cost, as a side effect of a different experiment.

WHAT THIS LEAVES. The daemon-side answer is now ~free (2000 format lookups -> 50, a 40x cut, bd-2pq73). What remains is exactly what this bead's title says and nothing cheaper: the TRANSPORT. Two full FUSE round trips per path-based metadata op, both legitimate, both kernel-mandated. That is dispatch / queue-depth (max_background, congestion_threshold) / splice territory — the bd-kdmu4 surface — and per this bead's own warning FFS_FUSE_WORKERS must be treated as UNMEASURED at correct daemon placement, not as a known 1.923x win.

TWO INSTRUMENTATION TRAPS that each produced a confident wrong answer first:

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
TRANSPORT SHARE MEASURED ON THE MOUNTED PATH — no comparator, no 120 GiB floor
(ProudBarn, 2026-08-16).

The comparator is blocked, but the transport question does not need it: comparing
FrankenFS's own daemon-side dispatch time against client wall time on a real FUSE
mount decomposes the cost without any kernel arm. That is what the bd-zpc3q
dispatch counters were added for.

SETUP. Local mount (FUSE must be local; rch cannot mount), v3+PGO ffs-cli built in
place on thinkstation1, candidate ELF
c33f3565c9f1d3661b04433941643a58127cb1d8eb7b41aa2eec37e1b86a2664, image
/data/tmp/ffs-pgo-train.img (ext4, 20003 root entries, pre-existing PGO training
fixture — nothing created, nothing deleted). Mounted read-only,
--runtime-mode managed --no-background-scrub, FFS_MOUNT_BENCH_EVIDENCE=1.
Workload: two `ls -lU` sweeps of the root directory. rch WORKER: none — a mount is
local by necessity and no worker is quotable for this row.

    mount_dispatch_metrics,filesystem=ext4,
      getattr_dispatch_count=40499   getattr_dispatch_nanos=20847403
      getxattr_dispatch_count=160014 getxattr_dispatch_nanos=61156783
      lookup_dispatch_count=2        lookup_dispatch_nanos=23104
      readdir_dispatch_count=186     readdir_dispatch_nanos=16241051

    daemon dispatch total   98.3 ms
    client wall total     2550   ms   (1.20 s + 1.35 s)
    DAEMON SHARE OF WALL     3.85 %
    per entry: daemon 2.46 us, wall 63.7 us
    per op: getattr 515 ns, getxattr 382 ns, readdir 87.3 us

TWO FINDINGS.

1. THE DAEMON IS ~4% OF MOUNTED readdir+stat WALL TIME. Even allowing that
   dispatch_nanos covers only the `with_request_scope` interval and excludes FUSE
   request/reply I/O and queueing — so 3.85% is a LOWER bound on daemon share —
   the format layer would have to be understated by more than an order of
   magnitude to be the dominant cost. It is not. This corroborates the in-process
   figure (356 ns/stat with the memo on) from the other direction: format work is
   small, and the mounted cost is somewhere else.

2. getxattr RUNS 4.00 TIMES PER ENTRY, not twice. 160014 probes for 40006 entry
   visits, against 1.01 getattr per entry. bd-ha71t measured 2 probes per path
   stat; `ls -l` asks for more than one attribute name per entry (capability plus
   ACL/security names), so the real multiplier on this workload is 4.
   ⭐ THAT MAKES ROUND-TRIP COUNT THE LEVER, NOT PER-OP DAEMON COST. Each probe is
   382 ns of daemon work inside roughly 15 us of wall. Making the daemon answer
   faster — which is what the capability memo did — cannot touch the 96%. Removing
   probes can.

CONSEQUENCE. The metadata path's remaining cost is round trips, and the count is
5 per entry (1 getattr + 4 getxattr). The productive directions are the ones that
reduce or amortise round trips: a negative xattr cache the kernel will honour, a
readdirplus that also answers the xattr questions, or FUSE-level batching. Making
format-layer lookups cheaper is finished as a lever on this row — bd-5vis3 already
drove node lookups to 0.07 per stat and the row did not move, which is the same
conclusion reached twice by different routes.

CAVEATS, so this is not over-read.
  * NOT A RATIO. There is no kernel arm here; this decomposes FrankenFS's own
    cost. It says where OUR time goes, not how far we are from kernel ext4/btrfs.
  * Wall time includes `ls` itself, so the 96% is transport PLUS client, not
    transport alone.
  * ONE RUN, not replicated, and no A/A null. Under the replicated-standing
    convention this is not bankable as a ratio — it is a mechanism attribution,
    which is admissible on counted evidence (the counts are exact).
  * ext4, not btrfs. Warm stat is 4.812194x on ext4 and 4.977803x on btrfs, a
    3.4% spread, which is the existing evidence that the floor is shared; the
    readdir+stat 7.7x row is btrfs and its btrfs-specific excess is a separate
    question (bd-3zx2x).
  * The 87.3 us per readdir is 186 calls doing 20003 entries across two sweeps —
    a large batched op, not a per-entry cost, and it is only 16.5% of daemon time.

WARM STAT IS 99.4 PCT CAPABILITY PROBE — measured (ProudBarn). Full detail on bd-btrfs-warm-stat-5x-9pxn1.

500 stats of ONE file inside a single stat process: 1.016 requests/stat, 1.010 capability/stat. 500 distinct files: 3.012 requests/stat, 1.008 capability/stat.

The kernel NEVER caches the negative — 505 probes for 500 repeat stats of the same inode within milliseconds. But lookup and getattr ARE cached (ATTR_TTL 60s works), so on a warm stat the capability probe is 1.010 of 1.016 requests: essentially the entire FUSE cost.

This is the sharpest form of this bead's premise. The daemon-side answer has been ~free since bd-2pq73; the transport cost is one round trip per stat and it exists solely to answer 'no'. bd-ha71t already closed ENOSYS (per-connection by contract) and FUSE_HANDLE_KILLPRIV V1/V2 (both measured inert), so unless 6.17 exposes an SB-level 'no security.* here' declaration, ~1 round trip per warm stat is a FUSE PROTOCOL FLOOR rather than a FrankenFS defect — and this bead should say so rather than stay open as if a lever were pending.

title: btrfs read ops re-resolve the fs-tree root bytenr from disk every call; memoize on read-only mounts
description: Even after bd-b61hz made the ROOT_ITEM resolve an O(log R) targeted descent, every read-only btrfs op (getattr/lookup/readdir/read/...) still re-resolves the subvolume's fs-tree root bytenr from disk on each call via btrfs_fs_tree_root_bytenr. On a read-only mount the root tree is IMMUTABLE (no writes), so the resolved bytenr is constant for the mount lifetime. Memoizing it per subvol_id drops the resolve from O(log R) device reads to O(1) amortized, removing the root-tree descent from the hot read path entirely (lookup/readdir resolve it 2x+ per op). Gated on btrfs_alloc_state.is_none() (writable mounts resolve fresh since a commit moves the root). Isomorphic (read-only root tree is constant). PROOF: reuse build_btrfs_multileaf_root_image + device-read count A/B, cached vs uncached resolve over K calls, Score>=2.0.

title: Byte-layout pin for WAL header encode/decode (16-byte field offsets)
description: Found via /testing-conformance-harnesses audit. ffs_mvcc::wal::encode_header / decode_header serialize a 16-byte WAL header with a fixed field layout: magic@0..4 (u32 LE), version@4..6 (u16 LE), checksum_type@6..8 (u16 LE), reserved@8..16 (zeros). Existing OQ7 tests pin individual constants (WAL_MAGIC, WAL_VERSION, CHECKSUM_TYPE_CRC32C, HEADER_SIZE) but no test pins the BYTE-LEVEL OFFSETS of each field within the encoded header. A regression that swapped field offsets (e.g., put magic at 4..8) would round-trip via encode/decode if both sides drifted symmetrically but break wire compatibility with any external tool reading the WAL. Fix: add wal_header_encode_byte_layout test that stamps a non-default WalHeader with distinct magic/version/checksum_type values and asserts each field bytes appear at its expected canonical offset.

title: [parity][corruption] ext4 fs-verity files are writable — content mutation breaks the merkle tree
description: EXT4_VERITY_FL (inode flag bit 20, 0x00100000) is not defined in ffs_types (the flag list jumps from EXT4_EXTENTS_FL bit19=0x80000 to EXT4_EA_INODE_FL bit21=0x200000, skipping bit20), so FrankenFS does not recognize fs-verity inodes. ext4_write/ext4_fallocate/the ext4_setattr truncate path have no verity check (and the new immutable guards do NOT cover verity — fs-verity sets EXT4_VERITY_FL on disk, NOT EXT4_IMMUTABLE_FL). A verity file is sealed read-only and protected by a Merkle tree stored past i_size; any write/truncate/punch to its data invalidates that tree, so the kernel's fs-verity verification fails on subsequent reads = the file becomes unreadable (silent corruption). Reachable on any fs-verity image with a verity-enabled file (Android APKs, signed system files). Same accepted-but-unhandled special-file class as bd-4sfty (encrypt) and bd-4y9ca (inline_data). FIX: define EXT4_VERITY_FL=0x00100000 and reject content mutation (write/fallocate/truncate) of verity inodes with EPERM — verity files are immutable-content by design; reads remain allowed (FrankenFS returns the correct data, just unverified). PROOF: set EXT4_VERITY_FL on a file inode (persist_ext4_inode_for_testing) and assert write/fallocate/truncate return errors.
close_reason: Fixed in 047b295f. Defined EXT4_VERITY_FL=0x00100000 (was missing — flag list skipped bit 20) and added ext4_reject_verity, guarding ext4_write/ext4_fallocate/ext4_setattr-truncate with EPERM. A verity file's content mutation would break its Merkle tree (unreadable); reads stay allowed. Not covered by the immutable guard (fs-verity sets VERITY_FL, not IMMUTABLE_FL). Test verity_file_content_mutation_rejected_bd_yz6c6. ffs-core 911/911, clippy/fmt clean. Completes the unsupported-special-file content guard set (inline_data, encrypt, immutable/append, verity).

title: perf(fuse): stop the kernel SENDING the per-stat security.capability probe — it is ~99% of the warm-stat 4.80x gap
description:
THE ONLY REMAINING LEVER ON WARM STAT, and the attribution that says so is now banked.

MEASURED (bd-btrfs-warm-stat-5x-9pxn1, 2026-08-16, three identical runs): 2,000 warm
stats of ONE already-resolved path produce EXACTLY 2,000 FUSE round trips, and every
one is a security.capability GETXATTR. No GETATTR, no LOOKUP, no STATX — the 60-second
ATTR_TTL works and the kernel never asks for attributes.

Of those 2,000 probes exactly 2 reach the format layer; the capability memo answers
1,998. Total daemon dispatch time is 0.27%-0.35% of wall, and against the banked
comparator absolutes (11,168 ns/stat for us vs 2,345 ns for the kernel, gap 8,823 ns)
the daemon's filesystem work is 66-88 ns/stat = 0.75%-0.99% OF THE GAP.

So ~99% of warm stat's 4.80x is one kernel-issued round trip for an xattr that does not
exist on any of these files. No filesystem-side change can move this row.

WHAT IS ALREADY EXCLUDED, by measurement not argument:
  - FUSE_HANDLE_KILLPRIV_V2 (bd-ha71t): 4000 probes -> 4000 probes, a genuine null with
    a positive control proving the kernel accepted the capability. DO NOT RETRY on 6.17.
  - the capability memo (bd-2pq73, bd-m1bpu): already answers 1,998 of 2,000 without a
    dispatch, and is separately measured worth under 10.7% end-to-end. It makes the
    ANSWER free; it cannot stop the SEND.
  - btrfs inode resolution, the floor-leaf memo, the parsed-node cache: all inside the
    <1% the filesystem contributes.

WHAT HAS NOT BEEN TRIED, in rough order of cost:
  1. Does the probe rate change when security.capability actually EXISTS on the file?
     If the kernel caches a present value but re-asks for an absent one, that is a
     different and possibly addressable shape. Counted experiment, no quiet window.
  2. Does mounting with default_permissions change it? Cheap to test, one mount flag.
  3. Is the rate kernel-version dependent? Host is 6.17.0-41-generic. Worth knowing
     before anyone builds on the current behaviour.
  4. Is there a FUSE ABI route to declare "this inode has no security.* xattrs" so the
     kernel can cache the negative? bd-ha71t's retry predicate already asks for exactly
     this; if none exists, that is worth establishing definitively so the door is closed
     with evidence rather than assumption.

ACCEPTANCE: a COUNT is sufficient and preferred — probes per stat, before and after,
with a positive control proving whatever was changed actually took effect. No quiet
window needed, which matters because every timed run on this host is currently
CONTENDED. A timed row is desirable but must not gate this.

METHOD: --runtime-mode managed emits the dispatch counters that the comparator's
standard runtime discards (bd-viil0), so this attribution can be repeated without any
code change. scripts-local warm_stat_attr.sh / warm_stat_trace.sh; RUST_LOG must name
BOTH ffs_fuse and ffs::fuse, and NO_COLOR=1 is load-bearing.

comments.text:
HYPOTHESIS 1 CLOSED — the kernel does not cache security.capability in EITHER direction (AzureBay, 2026-08-16, commit cf453184).

One image, two files, one mount, 1,000 stats each, counted from the daemon trace:

  positive_control_setcap=yes
  absent   getxattr_round_trips=1000   per_stat=1.0000
  present  getxattr_round_trips=1000   per_stat=1.0000

1000 probes vs 1000 probes. Exactly equal, not merely close, on a counted mechanism with no timing involved.

THE POSITIVE CONTROL IS REPORTED rather than assumed: setcap cap_net_raw+ep returned success on the `present` file before the image was synced and unmounted, so the two files genuinely differ. Without that, this would be indistinguishable from a run that silently compared two identical files -- the same failure mode the comparator's configurations_differ gate exists to catch, which this hand-rolled harness does not have.

So there is no negative-caching behaviour to exploit and no presence-dependent path. DO NOT re-test presence versus absence.

WHAT SURVIVES ON THIS BEAD, now the only remaining shapes:
  2. default_permissions — one mount flag, still untried, cheapest thing left.
  3. kernel-version dependence — host is 6.17.0-41-generic; worth establishing before anyone builds on current behaviour.
  4. a FUSE ABI route to declare an inode free of security.* so the kernel can cache the negative. bd-ha71t's retry predicate already asked for exactly this, and this result makes it the only shape that could still work. If no such route exists, that is worth establishing definitively so the door closes with evidence.

Note the asymmetry that makes (4) the important one: the memo already makes the ANSWER free (1,998 of 2,000 probes answered without a dispatch) and the daemon is 0.75%-0.99% of the gap. Nothing daemon-side is left. The entire remaining cost is the kernel choosing to SEND, and only the kernel can be persuaded not to.

Harness scripts-local probe_present_vs_absent.sh. Candidate d4278471..., isa=x86-64-v3, host thinkstation1, run locally because a FUSE mount runs only on the executing machine -- no rch worker took part. Counted, so the host's contention cannot confound it and no quiet window was needed.

  path_file  probes=1000   per_op=1.0000
  path_dir   probes=1000   per_op=1.0000
  path_root  probes=1000   per_op=1.0000
  fstat      probes=1      per_op=0.0010

NOT PER PATH COMPONENT: stat("<mnt>") on the mount ROOT — shortest possible walk, zero intermediate components — pays the same 1.0000 as a two-component path. There is no depth to amortise, so the entire "resolve the parent once / batch the walk" family of ideas is dead for this row.

This also corrects a loose reading of bd-ha71t's "TWO probes per path-based stat (4000/2000)". That count came from COLD path resolution. Warm, on an already-resolved path, it is exactly ONE.

NOT THE ATTRIBUTE FETCH: fstat on an already-open fd pays ZERO — the single probe in that arm is from the one open() that created the fd. A thousand attribute fetches through FUSE cost nothing, because ATTR_TTL (60s) lets the kernel serve them from its own cache and it never asks the daemon. That is worth restating because it means the FUSE attribute path is ALREADY free; only the probe is not.

WHAT THIS LEAVES ON THIS BEAD, and it is now a short list:
  2. default_permissions — still untried, and NOT currently testable: ffs-fuse exposes no such mount option, so it needs a code change, and crates/ffs-fuse/src/lib.rs was under ProudBarn's exclusive reservation when this was measured.
  3. kernel-version dependence — host 6.17.0-41-generic.
  4. a FUSE ABI route to declare an inode free of security.* so the kernel can cache the negative. Hypothesis 1 (present-vs-absent) is already closed: the kernel caches NEITHER, 1000 probes vs 1000 probes with a positive control.

It also BOUNDS the round-trip thread's effect on this row: warm stat is exactly one round trip per operation, so halving round-trip cost halves the warm-stat gap and no more. That is a useful ceiling for pane 1.3 to know before optimising.

USER-FACING CHARACTERISATION, worth stating plainly because it is actionable today: a workload that holds file descriptors pays none of this; one that stats by path pays all of it. ls -l, find, and every stat()-per-entry tool are the worst case by construction.

DO NOT re-test path depth or fd-vs-path. Both are measured, exact, reproducible, and in one within-window mount.

Harness scripts-local probe_binding.sh. Candidate d4278471..., isa=x86-64-v3, host thinkstation1, kernel 6.17.0-41-generic, run locally because a FUSE mount runs only on the executing machine. All COUNTS, so contention cannot confound them.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
FIFTH NULL, AND THE ROUND-TRIP COST QUANTIFIED (AzureBay, 2026-08-16, commits f2cc4de1 + 3835a574).

NULL ON CALLER PRIVILEGE. If the kernel short-circuited the capability check for a caller that already has capabilities, the probe would be a property of the CALLER rather than the path. It is not:

  positive_control_root_can_stat=yes
  uid=1000     probes=1000   per_stat=1.0000
  uid=0(root)  probes=1000   per_stat=1.0000

CORRECTION TO MY OWN EARLIER CLAIM: the cross-filesystem entry recorded this arm as "skipped: sudo python3 unavailable". THAT WAS WRONG. sudo -n python3 works fine. The real reason root could not stat the mount is that a FUSE mount WITHOUT allow_other denies every user except the mounting one, root included -- the arm needed --allow-other, not a different interpreter. The arm had run under 2>/dev/null, which discarded the real error, and its failure branch printed a GUESS as though it were an observation. Corrected in place in the ledger rather than edited away.

THE SCORE ON THIS BEAD IS NOW FIVE NULLS, every one counted with a positive control:
  present vs absent            1.0000 vs 1.0000
  path depth                   root 1.0000 == nested 1.0000
  filesystem                   ext4 1.0000 == btrfs 1.0000
  caller privilege             uid0 1.0000 == uid1000 1.0000
  FUSE_HANDLE_KILLPRIV_V2      4000 probes -> 4000 probes (bd-ha71t)

Five nulls on one mechanism is itself a finding: this looks like unconditional kernel behaviour on the path-resolution path, not a policy any userspace-reachable parameter turns off. The remaining routes -- default_permissions (no such mount option exists in ffs-fuse today, and the crate is under another agent's reservation), kernel-version dependence, and a FUSE ABI route to cache a negative security.* -- should be attempted in that light. The prior is now strongly against any of them, and the honest next step may be to establish the door is CLOSED with evidence rather than keep pushing it.

THE COST OF ONE ROUND TRIP, which is what makes this bead worth or not worth more slices:

  stat  (1 round trip)   median 15236.8 ns/op
  fstat (0 round trips)  median  1362.8 ns/op
  A/B  stat/fstat  median 11.180674x  CI [8.753012, 12.312406]
  A/A  null        median  1.055089x  CI [0.976038, 1.094971]
  ONE ROUND TRIP = 13874.0 ns/op

The A/B interval clears the null interval with no overlap; the effect's lower bound is 8x the null's upper bound. Replicates an earlier pass (13307.1 ns, 10.44x) to 4.3%.

WORST BOUND: one round trip is AT LEAST 88.6% of a path-based stat. Warm stat is one round trip per op, so a fractional improvement in round-trip cost buys the same fractional improvement in this row and no more. That is the ceiling for pane 1.3's lane on THIS row, and it is worth having before optimising rather than after.

LABELLED INFERENCE, not a claim: comparator kernel 2345 ns/op, our arm 11168 ns/op, our fd path 1362.8 ns/op. Eliminating the probe would put a path-based stat near the fd path -- BELOW the kernel's own -- which would invert the 4.80x row rather than narrow it. That is arithmetic across two configurations (the absolutes here are inflated by a Python loop on an unpinned managed mount on a contended host) and needs its own measured row. Recorded because it changes how valuable this bead is.

comments.text:
TWO SHAPES CLOSED NEGATIVE (ProudBarn, 2026-08-16). Measured, not reasoned. Detail on bd-4ypbv.

This bead asks to stop the kernel SENDING the probe. Two candidate ways of doing that are now
ruled out:

 1. CALLER PRIVILEGE. Root pays the probe too: 1.087 capability probes/stat as uid 0 vs
    1.243/stat as uid 1000, 2000 distinct-file stats each, --allow-other mount, same file list,
    same single-process shape. Neither collapses toward zero, so the probe is not an
    unprivileged-caller check that a privileged workload could skip.

 2. CLIENT ORIGIN. The probe is KERNEL-originated. strace of stat -c %s across the mount shows
    the client issues ZERO getxattr/lgetxattr/fgetxattr syscalls -- only statx -- while the
    daemon logs security_capability probes for the same operation. So there is no client-side
    behaviour to change, and the earlier "the kernel never caches the negative" result is
    genuinely about the kernel rather than about coreutils.

With ENOSYS closed by contract and FUSE_HANDLE_KILLPRIV V1/V2 measured inert (bd-ha71t), and
forced readdirplus rejected at +0.1% (bd-4ypbv), the remaining surface for THIS bead is narrow
and entirely kernel-side: an SB-level declaration that no file carries security.* (an
SB_NOSEC-style shortcut), or a FUSE ABI capability that suppresses the probe per-connection
without disabling getxattr wholesale. If neither exists on 6.17 then the COUNT is a protocol
floor and this bead should be re-scoped to say so rather than left open as if a lever were
pending.

WHAT I AM NOT CLAIMING: I have not read the 6.17 source to establish which kernel path issues
the probe on a stat. The behaviour is measured precisely; the mechanism inside the kernel is
not, and identifying it is the obvious next step for anyone continuing this bead.

WHERE THE MONEY MOVED. Even if the count cannot be cut, the per-round-trip COST is not fixed:
12.02 to 21.26 us on this box purely by daemon placement, with requests_total held at exactly
1.000/stat across every arm. Co-location is >= 1.2210x vs SMT-sibling and >= 1.4979x vs
cross-CCD, two runs, both nulls passing. So the warm-stat row has a live lever even under the

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
CLOSING NEGATIVE (ProudBarn, 2026-08-16). The last remaining ABI shape is excluded by the ABI
itself, read from the kernel headers installed on this box.

/usr/src/linux-headers-6.17.0-41/include/uapi/linux/fuse.h, every capability-related flag:
  FUSE_HANDLE_KILLPRIV     (1<<19)  "fs handles killing suid/sgid/cap on write/chown/trunc"
  FUSE_HANDLE_KILLPRIV_V2  (1<<28)  "fs kills suid/sgid/cap on write/chown/trunc"
  FUSE_WRITE_KILL_SUIDGID  (1<<2)   write-side
  FUSE_OPEN_KILL_SUIDGID   (1<<0)   open-side
  FUSE_SETXATTR_ACL_KILL_SGID       setxattr-side
  FUSE_SECURITY_CTX        (1<<32)  SENDS security context TO the daemon on
                                    create/mkdir/symlink/mknod - opposite direction, creation only
Every one of them is about MODIFICATION semantics: what happens to suid/sgid/cap bits when a file
is written, chowned, truncated or opened. NONE of them concerns the READ-side probe that a stat
triggers, and there is no negotiable INIT flag on 6.17 whose effect is "do not ask this connection
about security.capability".

So the shape I left open last turn - "a FUSE ABI capability that suppresses the probe
per-connection WITHOUT disabling getxattr wholesale" - does not exist on this kernel. It is not
that we have not found the right flag; the flag space has been enumerated and the semantics of
every candidate are write-side.

THE FULL CLOSED SET for cutting the COUNT, each with how it was closed:
  ENOSYS                       closed by contract (disables getxattr wholesale)
  FUSE_HANDLE_KILLPRIV V1/V2   measured INERT (bd-ha71t)
  forced readdirplus           measured, rejected at +0.1% (bd-4ypbv)
  daemon-side memoisation      measured, changes dispatch counts but NEVER the boundary count
                               (bd-2pq73 cut format-level work 40x with requests_total unchanged)
  caller privilege             measured negative - root pays too, 1.087 probes/stat vs 1.243
  client-side change           measured impossible - strace shows the client issues ZERO getxattr
                               syscalls; the probe is kernel-originated
  FUSE INIT flag               closed here by enumerating the 6.17 ABI

WHAT IS LEFT IS NOT REACHABLE FROM THIS REPO. The only shape still standing is an SB-level
declaration that no file on the superblock carries security.* - the kernel's own SB_NOSEC-style
shortcut. That is internal kernel state, not a FUSE mount option and not in the uapi header, so
it would require a kernel change, not a FrankenFS change. Recording it as out of scope rather
than as an open lever.

CONCLUSION: ~1 FUSE round trip per warm stat is a PROTOCOL FLOOR on Linux 6.17, not a FrankenFS
defect. Closing this bead negative rather than leaving it open as if a lever were pending.

WHERE THE VALUE WENT INSTEAD, so this close is not a dead end: the count is a floor but the COST
per round trip is not. Measured 12.02-21.26 us on this box purely by daemon placement with
requests_total held at exactly 1.000/stat - co-location is >= 1.2210x vs SMT-sibling and
>= 1.4979x vs cross-CCD, two runs, both A/A nulls passing (bd-4ypbv, banked). That is the live
lever on the warm-stat row.

NOT ESTABLISHED, stated so nobody reads more into this than it says: I have not identified WHICH
kernel path issues the probe on a stat, because only headers are installed here, not fs/fuse
source. The behaviour is measured precisely and the ABI surface is enumerated exhaustively; the
in-kernel call site is not. That does not change the conclusion - no uapi-reachable flag controls
it either way - but it is the piece a kernel-side follow-up would start from.

comments.text:
bd-z0rb8 ROUTE CLOSED BY READING, NOT BY MEASURING: `default_permissions` is already on, and has been for every probe measurement ever banked (AzureBay, 2026-08-16).

I had this listed as remaining work in the form "default_permissions needs an ffs-fuse mount option" — i.e. as an untried lever awaiting a code change and a build. That was wrong, and the correction cost one file read.

  crates/ffs-fuse/src/lib.rs:4346  fn build_mount_options(options: &MountOptions) -> Vec<MountOption> {
  crates/ffs-fuse/src/lib.rs:4350      MountOption::DefaultPermissions,

It sits in the unconditional base `vec![]`, above every `if options.… { opts.push(…) }`. There is no flag that turns it off and no caller that can decline it. Every mount this project has ever measured — including the warm-stat runs that established one uncached `getxattr(security.capability)` round trip per path-based metadata op, and including the 4.98x btrfs and 4.81x ext4 warm-stat rows — already ran with `default_permissions` enabled.

WHAT THAT SETTLES. The probe fires WITH `default_permissions` on. So enabling it cannot be the fix, because it is not off. This is not evidence that the option is irrelevant to the probe in general; it is evidence that this particular route is unavailable to us, because we are already at the end of it. The correct disposition is CLOSED-ALREADY-IN-EFFECT, not REJECTED-ON-MEASUREMENT — the distinction matters, since a future reader could otherwise conclude the option was tried and found not to help.

WHY IT WENT UNNOTICED. The route was carried on the bead as a to-do phrased as a code change ("needs a mount option"), which is a claim about the code that nobody had checked against the code. Six lines of reading refutes it. The general form is worth stating because this bead area has now produced three of them in two turns: a to-do that asserts something about the incumbent is a to-do that can be closed by reading the incumbent, and it should be, BEFORE it is scheduled behind a build slot on a machine at 59G.

WHAT REMAINS ON bd-z0rb8, now genuinely two routes rather than three:
  1. kernel-version dependence of the probe (needs a second kernel; not available on this box)
  2. a FUSE ABI negative-cache route — whether the protocol lets the daemon tell the kernel "this inode has no security.capability, stop asking"

Route 2 is the only one that is both in our control and unexamined. It is a protocol question answerable against the vendored fuser ABI, which is also readable without a build.

NOT CLAIMED: no ratio, no measurement, nothing withdrawn. The banked warm-stat numbers are untouched — this changes only what is left to try, and removes a build-gated task from the queue that never needed a build.

No kernel .c sources are on this box (only linux-headers-6.17.0-41), so the probe's call site cannot be traced here; I am not going to guess at which kernel path emits it.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
bd-z0rb8: ALL THREE DAEMON-SIDE ROUTES ARE NOW CLOSED. The kernel cannot be talked out of the per-path `security.capability` probe on this kernel, and the FUSE protocol has no mechanism to try (AzureBay, 2026-08-16, by reading — no build, no measurement).

ROUTE 1 — `default_permissions`: CLOSED, ALREADY IN EFFECT.
  crates/ffs-fuse/src/lib.rs:4350, in the unconditional base vec! of
  build_mount_options(), above every `if options.… { opts.push(…) }`. No flag
  disables it and no caller can decline it. Every probe measurement ever banked
  already ran with it on, so enabling it cannot be the fix — it is not off.

ROUTE 2 — a FUSE ABI negative-cache for xattrs: CLOSED, NO SUCH MECHANISM.
  The full capability set in vendor/fuser/src/ll/fuse_abi.rs (lines 200-260) is
  32 flags. Exactly one of them caches a metadata reply — FUSE_CACHE_SYMLINKS
  (1 << 23), "cache READLINK responses". There is no xattr counterpart, no
  negative-xattr flag, and no way in the protocol for the daemon to tell the
  kernel "this inode has no security.capability, stop asking". The nearest
  candidate, FUSE_HANDLE_KILLPRIV_V2 (1 << 28), was already negotiated
  experimentally and is MEASURED INERT against this probe: 4000 probes for 2000
  path stats with the kernel reporting the capability ENABLED, identical to the
  4000 without it (recorded at crates/ffs-fuse/src/lib.rs:3007). That the kernel
  confirmed it enabled is what makes the null trustworthy rather than a wiring
  failure.

ROUTE 3 — kernel-version dependence: NOT CLOSED, NOT AVAILABLE.
  Needs a second kernel. This box has one (6.17.0-41-generic) and carries only
  linux-headers, no .c sources, so the probe's call site cannot even be traced
  here. I am not guessing at which kernel path emits it.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE WARM-STAT ROW, stated plainly because it redirects the lever rather than ending it: the probe is one uncached round trip per path-based metadata op, and there is no daemon-side way to stop the kernel sending it. So the remaining work is NOT "eliminate the round trip" — that door is shut on this kernel — but "make the round trip cheaper", which is where the capability memo already sits. The memo removed the format-layer work; what is left is the crossing itself, and bd-4zokj's whole-handler timer is the instrument that can finally say how much of that crossing is ours versus the kernel's.

A NOTE ON THE VENDORED ABI, not a defect for us but a live footgun for whoever
touches it next: three macOS/OSXFUSE-only flags share the same const namespace as
the Linux ones and one of them COLLIDES — FUSE_EXCHANGE_DATA and
FUSE_HANDLE_KILLPRIV_V2 are both `1 << 28`, and FUSE_ALLOCATE (1 << 27) is listed
after FUSE_INIT_RESERVED (1 << 31), out of order. On Linux 1 << 28 is
KILLPRIV_V2, so the inert result above stands and nothing measured is affected.
But `add_capabilities(FUSE_EXCHANGE_DATA)` on Linux would silently negotiate
KILLPRIV_V2 instead, and nothing in the type system would object.

DISPOSITION: the two routes in our control are closed on evidence, not on
judgement. bd-z0rb8 should not stay open waiting on route 3, which needs hardware
this box does not have — it should be closed as NO-ROUTE-ON-THIS-KERNEL with
route 3 recorded as the condition that would reopen it.

NOT CLAIMED: no ratio, nothing withdrawn. The banked warm-stat rows (btrfs 4.98x,
ext4 4.81x) are untouched.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
CORRECTION TO MY OWN CLOSURE, SAME TURN: route 3 is NOT "kernel-version dependence". The probe's origin was already captured and it is Linux AUDIT, conditional on THIS HOST's audit rules (AzureBay, 2026-08-16).

I closed the two daemon-side routes above and described the remaining one as "kernel-version dependence — needs a second kernel this box does not have". That framing is wrong, and the evidence that makes it wrong was already in the ledger before I wrote it: docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md:6874 (PlumRiver, 2026-08-06) captured the call site directly with bpftrace on `fuse_getxattr`, 300 of 300 stats:

  fuse_getxattr / __vfs_getxattr / get_vfs_caps_from_disk /
  audit_copy_inode / __audit_inode / filename_lookup / vfs_statx /
  vfs_fstatat / __do_sys_newfstatat / do_syscall_64

It is Linux audit collecting file capabilities into the audit record during path resolution. Not a permission check, not an LSM label fetch, and nothing FUSE asks for. And it is conditional on configuration we can name: `auditctl -l` on this host carries path-based rules over the agent working tree (`-w /data/projects -p wa`, plus an `-F dir=/data/projects/` destruct rule). A path-based rule forces per-lookup inode collection for any syscall that could match, because the kernel cannot evaluate `-F dir=` until it has resolved and collected the inode — which is why the probe fires even for mounts under /tmp.

WHAT MY TWO CLOSURES STILL GET RIGHT. Routes 1 and 2 stand exactly as written: `default_permissions` is unconditionally on, and the FUSE ABI has no xattr-cache flag, so there is no daemon-side way to stop the probe. Audit does not negotiate with the filesystem. Nothing in the daemon can decline to be audited.

WHAT CHANGES. The reopen condition is not a different kernel — it is a host whose audit rules do not force per-lookup inode collection. That is a question about the measurement environment, and it is answerable by `auditctl -l` rather than by acquiring hardware. It also means the honest scope of the warm-stat row is narrower than "FUSE is 4.8x slower at warm stat": it is 4.8x slower AT WARM STAT ON A HOST WITH PATH-BASED AUDIT RULES OVER THE WORKING TREE.

WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE, and I want to be precise rather than convenient here. The banked ratios are NOT invalidated and nothing is withdrawn. Kernel ext4 and kernel btrfs were measured on the same host under the same audit rules and paid the same audit probe — the comparison is fair. What differs is the COST of paying it: for an in-kernel filesystem the capability fetch is a cached inode xattr read (native ext4 path stat measured at 2.83 us total); for FUSE it becomes a full userspace round trip. The asymmetry is real and it is ours.

WHY I GOT IT WRONG, since the failure is repeatable. I reconstructed the route list from the bead's own to-do text instead of from the ledger, and the bead text predated the bpftrace capture. That is the second time this turn that a to-do asserting something about the world survived after the world had been checked — the first was "default_permissions needs a mount option" when it had been unconditional all along. A route list is a claim about evidence and should be re-derived from the evidence before it is acted on, not carried forward from when it was written.

DISPOSITION UNCHANGED, REASON CORRECTED: bd-z0rb8 stays closed. The reopen condition is a host without path-based audit rules over the working tree, verified by `auditctl -l` — not a second kernel.

title: e2compr: implement single-indirect block pointer read-modify-write
description:
Implement write support for indirect block pointers (i_block[12] -> pointer block -> data). This is the first level of indirect addressing and covers logical blocks 12 through 12+ptrs_per_block-1 (for 4K blocks: 12 through 1035).

STEPS:
1. When logical_block >= 12 and < 12 + ptrs_per_block:
   a. Read i_block[12]. If 0, allocate a new block, zero-fill it, write i_block[12].
   b. Read the indirect block.
   c. Write the target pointer at the correct 4-byte offset within it.
   d. Write the indirect block back to disk.
2. For freeing: when all pointers in the indirect block become 0, free the indirect block itself and set i_block[12] = 0.
3. Update set_indirect_block_ptr to dispatch to this path when lb >= 12 && lb < 12 + ptrs_per_block.

ACCEPTANCE: Compressed write works for files up to 4MB (1024 clusters * 4 blocks * 4K = 16MB with shift=2).
close_reason: Added write_block_ptr() with single-indirect allocation + read-modify-write. All callers updated. Max file size for e2compr writes extended from 48KB to ~4MB. 490 tests pass. Commit 18cd3d7.

title: Kernel-conformance pin for ext4 checksum offset constants
description: GD_CHECKSUM_OFFSET (0x1E), INODE_CHECKSUM_LO_OFFSET (0x7C), and INODE_CHECKSUM_HI_OFFSET (0x82) are private module constants determining where the per-structure CRC32C is read/written. They are NOT pinned to the kernel struct offsets. A regression that drifted any by even one byte would silently break checksum verification (read garbage as csum) and stamping (write csum into wrong field), but the existing stamp/verify roundtrip MRs would pass because the same bad offset is used on both sides. Add ext4_checksum_offset_constants_match_kernel_header pinning each value with explicit kernel header reference: GD_CHECKSUM_OFFSET = offsetof(struct ext4_group_desc, bg_checksum) = 0x1E. INODE_CHECKSUM_LO_OFFSET = offsetof(struct ext4_inode, i_checksum_lo) = 0x7C. INODE_CHECKSUM_HI_OFFSET = offsetof(struct ext4_inode, i_checksum_hi) = 0x82.

title: Expand inode checksum metamorphic relations beyond field-content invariance
description:
The current inode-checksum metamorphic harness in crates/ffs-core/tests/metamorphic.rs (added in 785bb74) covers exactly one relation: the checksum is computed after zeroing the on-disk checksum bytes, so any prior garbage in those bytes does not affect the new checksum.

That is a useful but narrow property. The checksum function has several other behavioral contracts that protect against collision attacks and silent corruption, none of which are currently exercised:

- MR-INO: writing identical inode bytes to two different inode numbers must produce different on-disk checksums (so a per-inode forgery cannot be replayed at a different inode slot).
- MR-SEED: identical inode bytes + identical inode number with a different filesystem checksum seed must produce different checksums (so cross-filesystem tampering is detectable).
- MR-GEN: changing only the generation field flips the checksum (verifies generation participates in the digest, the standard kernel anti-replay mechanism for NFS handles).
- MR-DETECT: flipping any single bit outside the checksum field bytes must invalidate verify_inode_checksum (proves the digest covers the full inode body, not just a prefix).

Each of these maps directly onto a class of real-world ext4 vulnerabilities. Add them as proptest cases alongside the existing inode_checksum_field_content_invariance test.
close_reason: Added MR-INO, MR-SEED, MR-GEN, MR-DETECT proptests covering inode-number sensitivity, seed sensitivity, generation sensitivity, and single-bit-flip detection. All 5 metamorphic.rs cases pass (cargo test -p ffs-core --test metamorphic), clippy clean. sha=99e8455

title: [parity][bug] ext4 rename INTO an htree directory fails (preflight capacity check chokes on the dx_root)
description: ext4_rename calls ext4_preflight_dir_entry_insert (lib.rs:11574) before mutating, to validate that the new name can be placed. That preflight dry-runs ffs_dir::add_entry(placeholder ino=1, name) over EVERY directory block of the target parent. For an htree target dir, logical block 0 is the dx_root whose '..' rec_len spans the hidden index past the reserved-tail boundary, so add_entry rejects it as Corruption{block:0,'directory entry exceeds usable block area'} and the whole rename fails. Net: you cannot rename/move any file INTO an htree directory. Same root cause + class as bd-s9ckh (remove loops) — a 4th linear-scan site that mishandles the dx_root; caught by the new link_and_rename_into_htree_dir_place_entries_in_index test (the LINK path already worked since fs.link goes straight to ext4_add_dir_entry's htree branch; only rename's preflight choked). FIX: skip logical block 0 (dx_root) in the preflight scan when parent.has_htree_index() (reuse ext4_htree_dx_root_phys) — the real insert routes htree entries to the hash-correct leaf / rebuilds on overflow, so an htree insert always has room and the preflight need only validate the name against a leaf / the empty-block fallback.
close_reason: Fixed in 4e45c862. ext4_preflight_dir_entry_insert now skips logical block 0 (dx_root) for htree dirs via ext4_htree_dx_root_phys, so the rename capacity-check no longer chokes on the dx_root's index-spanning '..'. 4th dx_root linear-scan site fixed (after bd-wb4cd insert routing + bd-s9ckh remove loops). title: perf(read): close the structural ~2x copy-tax with a zero-copy read path (io_uring registered buffers / mmap ByteDevice) — the only lever left after 5 contention levers proved neutral
description: EVIDENCE (CrimsonFox 2026-06-22, session-long). The dominant remaining read gap vs kernel is STRUCTURAL: warm random read ~2-3x, parallel ~2.8x at matched 16t, sparse ~2.1x — all the same ~2x userspace pread+safe-copy memory-bandwidth tax of a forbid(unsafe) FS vs the kernel in-page-cache copy path. PROVEN not contention: this session tested+reverted FIVE removable-contention/alloc levers, ALL neutral or worse — mvcc snapshot RwLock (neutral), Cx::checkpoint throttle (0.8x WORSE), small-read staging-copy/FFS_DIRECT_READ_MIN_BYTES lower (neutral parallel/0.74x single), rayon single-job inline (inert), scrub buffer pre-size (neutral), plus the prior thread-local read scratch (inert, bd-cc-rscratch). frankenfs read is already single-thread parity-or-FASTER than kernel (no per-read syscall) + binary-searched extents + decompress cache (this session's shipped wins) — the residual is purely the per-byte copy. THE LEVER (exotic, the only thing that closes it): eliminate the userspace copy on reads. Options: (1) mmap-backed ByteDevice (memmap2) so reads are page-cache-resident slices, served zero-copy where the read API can hand out borrowed bytes (needs read_into to accept a borrow path / scatter); cold-regress risk (page-fault per first touch) -> hybrid with the current pread path (bd-jgbam filed this earlier). (2) io_uring with REGISTERED buffers (fixed buffers + registered files) so the kernel DMAs into pre-registered memory with no per-read copy/syscall — needs a safe io_uring wrapper crate (tokio-uring/io-uring) since ffs-core is forbid(unsafe); biggest potential win (removes both the copy AND the per-read syscall that caps parallel scaling). (3) splice/sendfile for the discard/streaming path (already idealized in cat baseline). RISK: all touch the core read/device abstraction (high blast radius) and (2) adds a runtime dependency; needs a focused effort + careful conformance (byte-identity, error semantics, the preserve-on-error contract). Bench predicate: parallel read should scale past 8 threads toward the kernel curve (the structural ceiling lifts). This is the documented endpoint of the read-perf campaign: everything cheap-and-safe is shipped; the last ~2x needs zero-copy. See docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md (multiple 2026-06-22 entries).
close_reason: Continuation closeout: fresh hz2 Criterion confirmed safe direct-read/preadv paths are already harvested; mmap/io_uring cutover requires explicit audited-unsafe backend/API policy change before production code is valid.

title: Refine oracle evidence with cross-oracle disagreement arbitration
description:
Supplemental refinement for the invariant and mounted differential oracle refinements. FrankenFS will have multiple truth sources: an executable invariant model, kernel differential runs, repair confidence artifacts, crash replay survivors, and explicit unsupported-scope records. The plan needs an arbitration contract for cases where those sources disagree, otherwise teams can cherry-pick the friendliest oracle.

Scope: define disagreement categories, owner routing, follow-up bead requirements, release-gate impact, and logs for cross-oracle conflicts. Arbitration should not decide filesystem truth by majority vote; it should preserve evidence, classify likely source of error, and fail closed for user-facing claims until the conflict is resolved or explicitly scoped out.

Required proof before close:

title: [bug] ext4 ZERO_RANGE corrupts neighbor bytes on unaligned ranges

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: FOUND+FIXED. ext4 fallocate ZERO_RANGE (FALLOC_FL_ZERO_RANGE, 0x10) permits byte-granular (unaligned) ranges, unlike punch_hole/collapse/insert which require block alignment. The impl computed logical_start=floor(offset/bs), logical_end=ceil(end/bs) and wrote a FULL zero block for every covered block -- so for an unaligned range it zeroed the ENTIRE head/tail boundary blocks, destroying bytes OUTSIDE [offset,end) = silent data corruption. Linux ext4_zero_range zeroes only the in-range bytes of edge blocks. The only existing test used a fully block-aligned range (offset=4096,len=4096) so the bug was untested; also the test helper open_writable_ext4 skips on rch (no committed fixture), so the whole surface had zero rch coverage. FIX: intersect each mapped block span with [offset,end); full-coverage blocks get a full zero write (unchanged), partial head/tail blocks get a read-modify-write that zeroes only the sub-range, preserving neighbors; holes/unwritten extents already read zero and are skipped. Added 2 regression tests (within-one-block unaligned + across-block-boundary spanning a full interior block plus both partial edges) using open_writable_ext4_mkfs(64) so they actually RUN on rch (4096 block size). Confirmed RED before fix (clobbered bytes-before), GREEN after; 54 fallocate tests pass, clippy clean, #![forbid(unsafe_code)] intact.

title: ext4 extent-tree metadata blocks not counted in i_blocks (e2fsck: i_blocks short for depth>=1 trees)
description: ffs-extent allocate_extent/allocate_unwritten_extent insert into the extent B+tree via ffs_btree::insert, which allocates real on-disk index/leaf metadata blocks when the tree grows past its inline 4-extent root (depth>=1). Those metadata blocks are charged to the block bitmaps/free totals but their count was NEVER returned to the caller, so ext4_write + ext4_fallocate (zero_range + default prealloc) added only DATA blocks (mapping.count) to inode.i_blocks. Once a file's extent tree reaches depth>=1, e2fsck reports 'Inode N, i_blocks is X, should be Y' (Y-X = the metadata blocks) and leaves the fs with errors. CONFIRMED via real e2fsck: write 6 single-block extents at logical 0,2,4,6,8,10 (holes defeat coalescing) -> tree grows to level 1 -> 'i_blocks is 12, should be 16'. The indirect (legacy) write path already counts its metadata correctly (write_block_ptr returns meta blocks) — the extent path was the asymmetric omission. Direct ext4 analog of bd-5svhs. FIX: ffs-extent returns ExtentAllocation{mapping,meta_blocks} via a MetaCountingAllocator wrapper + new allocate_*_with_meta fns; ext4_write/fallocate add meta_blocks to i_blocks. Found via Phase B ext4-accounting audit. FOLLOW-UP: directory extent-tree growth (direct ffs_btree::insert callers at lib.rs 13181/13682/13963/24654.. ) has the same latent gap (rarer).
close_reason: done

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: FIXED in ed3bc048: ext4_write/ext4_fallocate now charge extent-tree metadata blocks to i_blocks via an OPERATION-LEVEL meta snapshot — count extent-tree index+leaf blocks before any tree mutation, apply the signed delta at the end. KEY DESIGN LESSON (two wrong approaches first): (1) per-allocation u64 meta count saturates to 0 on a net-shrink call (coalescing collapses the tree) so i_blocks never decreases; (2) per-extent-site before/after over-counts because the shrink happens in mark_written/coalesce OUTSIDE the allocate site. The op-level wrap (snapshot at fn start, apply before the single inode writeback) is robust to growth AND coalescing-shrink regardless of which internal path mutated the tree. ext4_count_extent_tree_meta_blocks returns 0 for depth-0 (no device reads in the common case). VALIDATED: new e2fsck test ext4_extent_tree_growth_counts_metadata_in_iblocks_bd_zpe9s (16 discontiguous extents -> depth>=1), proven to fail pre-fix; the grow-then-shrink interleave e2fsck test stays clean; randomized write/fallocate fuzz green; 1012 ffs-core tests. NOTE: directory extent-tree growth (direct ffs_btree::insert callers) has the same latent gap (rarer) -> follow-up bd-rdt4f.
